en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Udāna in the Khuddaka Nikāya.
Introduction to the Work:
I pay homage to the Lord of Great Compassion, who has reached the further shore of the ocean of all that is to be known, and who teaches through methods that are skillful, profound, and diverse.
I pay homage to that supreme Dhamma, honored by the Fully Enlightened One, which leads those endowed with true knowledge and conduct out from the world.
To him who is perfected in virtues such as morality and is established in the paths and fruits, I pay homage.
I pay homage to that Noble Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit.
By the power of whatever merit has arisen from this homage to the Triple Gem,
may I be everywhere free from obstacles.
Those Udānas which were taught by the Great Seer, who seeks the welfare of others, according to their various causes through his pure *apadāna*—
let all of them be compiled together by those who arrange them in a single collection.
The *Udāna* is a collection compiled by the Dhamma-recorders,
which illustrates the Victor’s spiritual urgency and joy through verses arising from gladness.
Because it must be plunged into by means of profound knowledge,
although the commentary on the meaning is difficult for me to compose,
I shall nevertheless undertake it together with the commentary, so that the Teacher’s Dispensation may endure.
The exposition of the lions among former teachers remains established.
Therefore, relying upon that, having plunged into all five Nikāyas,
and depending on the method of the ancient commentaries—
Thoroughly purified and unadulterated, with precise determination of meaning,
this is the doctrine of the Mahāvihāravāsins, not deviating from tradition.
Having carefully avoided meanings that have been repeatedly introduced [by others], [I have composed this].
"I shall compose a commentary on the meaning of this Udāna according to my ability.
May the virtuous ones accept it with approval as I analyze its meaning, desiring thus the long endurance of the True Dhamma."
In this context, in what sense is it called *udāna*? In the sense of exultation (*udānana*). What is this that is called *udāna*?

It is an utterance brought forth by the force of joy. For just as that which cannot be contained by a measuring vessel—such as oil—and flows over is called a "spillage" (*avaseka*), and just as water that cannot be contained by a pond and overflows...

Whatever flows out is called a "flood" (ogha). In the same way, when the expansion of thought (vitakkavipphāra) produced by the surge of joy cannot be contained within the heart, it becomes excessive;

failing to settle within, it issues forth through the door of speech as a specific utterance independent of a recipient, and this is called an "inspired utterance" (udāna). This also occurs by way of spiritual urgency (dhammasaṃvega).
This characteristic is indeed found.
It occurs in some instances by way of verse composition and in others by way of prose sentences.
As for the definition of an *udāna* stated in the commentaries—that it is "connected with verses consisting of joy and knowledge"—that is said by way of general prevalence.
It has been stated. For, generally speaking, an *udāna* is spoken in the form of verse and is originated by joy and gladness (*pītisomanassa*).
However, other [types of utterances] are also found, such as: “There is, bhikkhus, that sphere where there is neither earth nor water,” and so forth;
and “Beings who desire happiness, he who harms them with a stick”; and “If you fear suffering, if you... [are afraid of it].”
And it is found in such passages as "suffering is disagreeable.
Thus, this [Dhamma] is threefold: spoken by an omniscient Buddha, spoken by a Paccekabuddha, and spoken by a disciple.
Among these, that spoken by a Paccekabuddha is as follows: "Having laid aside the rod toward all beings, not harming..."
This is indeed found in the *Khaggavisāṇa-sutta* with the words, "Of those [others]... and so forth. There are also words spoken by disciples, such as:
"All passion has been abandoned by me; all hatred has been uprooted;
all delusion has been dispelled by me; I have become cooled and am extinguished."
In the *Theragāthā*, beginning with:
“I was restrained in body, and likewise in speech and mind;
having uprooted craving, I have become cooled and attained nibbāna.”—
These are also found in the *Therīgāthā*. However, these utterances of those elders and elderesses are not merely *udānas*;
they are also "lion's roars. Furthermore, there are those spoken by deities such as Sakka, beginning with: "Oh, what a gift! A supreme gift, well-established under Kassapa!
and those spoken by humans such as the Brahmin Ārāmadaṇḍa, beginning with: "Homage..."
The *udānas* such as "Of that Blessed One," which have been included in the three councils (*saṅgīti*), do indeed exist, but they are not intended here.

Rather, those which were spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One himself directly, which constitute the word of the Victor (*jinavacana*), and with reference to which the Blessed One—while dividing the Dhamma of the scriptures into ninefold and reciting it—said "the *udāna*": [these are what is meant].
Those very [verses] spoken by the compilers of the Dhamma were chanted as the "Udāna," and it is precisely these that are taken here for the purpose of commentary.
Furthermore, those verses beginning with "Through many births in saṃsāra" (AN 1.148), which were uttered by the Blessed One at the foot of the Bodhi tree as spontaneous utterances (*udāna*),
and which have never been abandoned by the many hundreds of thousands of Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas— these, however, in later times...
Because it was taught by the Blessed One to the Dhamma-treasurer (the Venerable Ānanda), the compilers of the Dhamma did not include it in the Udāna-pāḷi, but chanted it in the Dhammapada.
Furthermore, the utterance of the exclamation, "Koṇḍañña has indeed understood!
Koṇḍañña has indeed understood!", which produced a resonance capable of proclaiming itself to the gods and humans throughout the ten-thousandfold world system, [was likewise included].
That which was spoken by the Blessed One— namely, at the conclusion of the teaching of the *Dhammacakkappavattana-sutta*—
was due to the Elder’s being the very first among the disciples to realize a portion of the Dhamma he himself had attained, specifically the Noble Path as it was taught;
it arose from reflecting on the fruitfulness of his own exertion, and during his first awakening, it arose from reflecting on the correct practice of all the bhikkhus.
It should be understood that such statements as “At one time, indeed, the bhikkhus pleased me” are merely utterances produced by joy and gladness;
they do not clarify either the forward progression or the cessation [of the Dhamma], like the statement beginning with “When, indeed, phenomena become manifest.
Therefore, they were not included in the Udāna collection by the compilers of the Dhamma.
Furthermore, this Udāna is included within the Sutta Piṭaka among the three Piṭakas—namely, the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Sutta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka;
it is included within the Khuddaka Nikāya among the five Nikāyas—namely, the Dīgha Nikāya, the Majjhima Nikāya, the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the Aṅguttara Nikāya, and the Khuddaka Nikāya;
and it belongs to the categories of Sutta, Geyya, and Veyyākaraṇa.
Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla—among these nine factors of the teaching (sāsanaṅga), the Udāna is included.
As it is said: “I received eighty-two thousand [teachings] from the Buddha, two thousand from the Bhikkhus;
thus eighty-four thousand are the Dhammas that have been transmitted to me.”
Thus, from among the eighty-four thousand sections of the Dhamma acknowledged by the Dhamma-treasurer, this is a compilation of certain sections of the Dhamma:

eight chapters by way of chapter—namely, the Bodhi-vagga, Mucalinda-vagga, Nanda-vagga, Meghiya-vagga, Soṇa-vagga, Jaccandha-vagga, Cūḷa-vagga, and Pāṭaligāmiya-vagga; eighty suttas by way of sutta; and [certain] verses by way of verse.
It is a compendium of ninety-five *udāna* verses. By way of recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*), it consists of eight and a half recitation sections.

By way of thematic connections (*anusandhi*), there is one connection based on the sequence of questions in the *Bodhisutta*; two connections based on the sequence of questions and the natural flow of the narrative in the *Suppavāsā-sutta*;
in the remaining suttas, there is only one connection each based on the natural flow of the narrative; and herein, there is also the connection by way of underlying intention (*ajjhāsayānusandhi*).
There is none. Thus, the compendium of all eighty-one connections consists of twenty-one thousand one hundred words;
twenty-three thousand four hundred and twenty-three lines of verse;
and sixty-seven thousand three hundred and eighty-two syllables. Therefore, this is said:
“In brief, there are exactly eighty discourses (suttantas) and eight chapters;
ninety-five verses have been proclaimed in the Udāna.
As for its extent, it measures eight and a half recitation sections.”
There are eighty-one connections (*anusandhi*) for the *Udāna*.
"The wise one should point out that there are twenty-one thousand and one verses counted in this *Udāna*."
As for the number of verses:
"There are eight thousand and four hundred verses;
these are the stanzas of the Udāna, and twenty-three [sections] are indicated."
“Sixty-seven hundred and three eighty-two syllables have been proclaimed for the Udāna.
Of its eight chapters, the Bodhi-vagga is the first; among the suttas, the Bodhi-sutta is the first; and of that [sutta] as well, it is thus:
The introduction beginning with "Thus have I heard" (me sutaṃ) was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council (paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti).
This First Great Council was indeed recorded in the textual tradition of the Vinaya Piṭaka.

Furthermore, the method of exposition that should be discussed here for the sake of proficiency regarding the introduction has already been stated in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya.
This should be understood in the manner already stated.
1. *Bodhivagga* 1.
Commentary on the First *Bodhi Sutta*.
1. As for the introduction here, beginning with “Thus have I heard,” in that context: *evaṃ* is a particle;
*me* and so forth are nouns; and in the phrase *uruvelayaṃ viharati*, *vi-* is a prefix and *harati* is a verb.
In this very manner, the analysis of the words is to be understood everywhere.

As for its meaning (*attha*), the word *evaṃ* (thus) has many distinct senses, such as comparison, instruction, praise, censure, acceptance, manner, indication, determination, inquiry, "this," purpose, measure, and so forth. For instance, it occurs in the sense of comparison in such passages as:
"By a mortal thus born, much wholesome [deed] must be done. Likewise, it occurs in the sense of instruction in: "Thus you should approach..."
In such cases as "you should withdraw in this manner," it is used as an instruction (*upadesa*). In such cases as "So it is, Blessed One;

so it is, Well-Gone One," it is used for encouragement (*sampahaṃsana*). In such cases as "In this very way, O outcaste woman, she praises that shaven-headed ascetic, whoever he may be," it is used for censure (*garahaṇa*).
In such cases as "‘Yes, venerable sir,’ those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One," [it is used for assent].
In the sense of receiving a statement: in such instances as, “Venerable sir, it is in this way that I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One.
In the sense of manner: “Come, young man, approach the ascetic Ānanda;
having approached, inquire in my name after the ascetic Ānanda’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical lightness, strength, and well-being.”
“‘The young brahmin Subha, son of Todeyya, asks after the venerable Ānanda’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical lightness, strength,
and well-being,’ and say this as well: ‘It would be well, indeed, if the venerable Ānanda would visit the residence of the young brahmin Subha,
son of Todeyya, out of compassion’”— in such instances [the term *nidassana* is used].
“What do you think, Kālāmas? Are these things wholesome or unwholesome? “Unwholesome, venerable sir. “Blameworthy or blameless?
“Blameworthy, venerable sir. “Censured by the wise or praised by the wise? “Censured by the wise, venerable sir.
“When fully taken up and practiced, do they lead to harm and suffering, or not?”
In such passages as, “What do you think of this? and “Venerable sir, they lead to harm and suffering when fully undertaken and observed;

such is our view on this,” it has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). In such passages as, “Thus these [people] are well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, wearing garlands and ornaments,” it has the sense of inquiry (*pucchā*).
In such passages as, “The various fields of craft have reached such a state; such is their kind, such is their form,” [it has the sense of a demonstrative].

Regarding the meaning of the word *idaṃ* (this): the word *gata* is a synonym for *pakāra* (manner), as are the words *tathā* and *vidhākāra*. For indeed, worldly people say that the word *gata*, when joined with *vidha*, means "manner.
In such instances as “*evaṃ lahuparivattaṃ evamāyupariyanto*,” it refers to measure (*parimāṇa*).
But is it not the case that in the passage, “*evaṃ vitakkitaṃ no tumhehi, evamāyupariyanto*,” the word *evaṃ* [expresses] the manner of the question and the manner of the measure?
It is not correct to say that the word *evaṃ* (thus) has only the sense of "manner" (*ākāra*) because it has been so stated; for there exists a distinction [between its uses].
Here, when the word *evaṃ* expresses merely the manner, it is intended in the sense of "manner. However, in such instances as “*Evaṃ byā kho...*” (Thus indeed...), it expresses a specific manner.

And these words *evaṃ*, which express specific manners, are denoters of either the manner of questioning or the manner of measurement. Having established this, [we understand] such passages as “*Evaṃ jātena maccenā...*” (By a mortal born thus...).
Examples by way of similes are appropriate here. For therein it is said:
“Just as one would make many garlands from a heap of flowers, so should much wholesome merit be performed by a mortal who has been born.”

In this context, the mass of flowers (*puppharāsi*) is used as a metaphor for the human birth—due to its excellence in such factors as reliance upon true persons, hearing the true Dhamma, and wise attention—as well as the accumulation of causes consisting in meritorious deeds such as giving;

and because it possesses specific qualities such as beauty and fragrance, many meritorious deeds, which resemble a string of garlands (*mālāguṇa*), must be performed by one who is subject to death (*maccu*) due to their nature of being mortal. Thus, they are called a "mass of flowers" (*puppharāsi*) because of this identity [of purpose].
The string of garlands is the simile; the manner of that comparison was stated without restriction by means of the word *yathā*.
Then it was stated by means of the word *evaṃ* in the sense of restricting it. Since that manner of comparison, when so restricted, is in meaning simply a simile, it is said: "It occurs as a simile.

Likewise, it is said in reference to the conduct befitting a recluse (*samaṇasāruppa*), which is being pointed out by such expressions as: "In this way, by this manner, one should advance," and so forth.
Regarding the manner of instruction found therein concerning the perfection of deportment, it is said that in substance it is indeed instruction itself—as in the passage:
“In this way you should advance, in this way you should retreat,” and so forth.
In the phrase, “So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata,” the meaning spoken by the Blessed One is [confirmed] without error.
That which is done by those who know—namely, the gladdening and the making of one elated by means of proclaiming the qualities existing therein—is "gladdening" (*sampahaṃsana*);
this should be applied there according to the method already stated as "the manner of gladdening.
"But in this way, however, for her..."—here it should be applied according to the method already stated as "the manner of censuring. And that manner of censuring...
It is understood that here the word "thus" (*evaṃ*) is used to indicate [the meaning] due to the proximity of the sounds of reproach beginning with "outcaste" (*vasalī*).

And just as it is here, so too the forms of similes and the like should be understood as being stated by way of simile and so forth due to the proximity of words such as "heap of flowers," which are themselves expressed as similes.
In the phrase "even so for us" (*evaṃ no*), it is also for the purpose of producing a definitive conclusion regarding those aforementioned phenomena as being bringers of harm and suffering.
Because, when the question "What do you think about this? was asked by way of seeking consent, the reply "It is so for us in this matter" was given;
thus, the determination of that mode [of operation] is revealed by the word *evaṃ*.
Furthermore, since that mode—consisting in the leading to harm and suffering of those phenomena—is being restricted, it has an exclusive (restrictive) sense; hence it is said: "In this way..."
In phrases such as *no ettha hoti* (“there is nothing here”), it has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).

Regarding the phrase *evaṃ ca vadehi* (“speak thus”), the manner of speaking—namely, “speak to the ascetic Ānanda in the same way that I speak”—is what is now to be stated; since this is indicated by the word *evaṃ*, it is said to have the sense of indication (*nidassana*).

Furthermore, although these instances of the word *evaṃ* express specific modes of being, they possess the sense of comparison and so forth because they function to convey specific meanings such as simile (*upamā*) and the like; thus, they have the sense of simile and so on.

It has been said. However, because the monks—having been directed toward the careful hearing and attention to the Dhamma—spoke by way of acknowledging their established state therein, the word *evaṃ* (thus) there has the sense of accepting what was said.

Therefore, "Evaṃ, bhante" means "Very well, Bhante," "Excellent, Bhante," or "Well done, Bhante. And here, this [word *evaṃ*] should be understood in the senses of indicating a manner, or as a restriction.

In this context, by the word *evaṃ* (thus) in the sense of "manner," he illuminates this meaning: the speech of that Blessed One— in all its aspects— is endowed with various methods, produced from manifold inclinations,
perfect in both meaning and phrasing, possessing diverse wonders, profound in its penetration of the Dhamma, the meaning, the teaching, and realization,
and reaching the range of hearing for all beings according to each one’s own language.

Who is capable of fully understanding it? Nevertheless, having generated a desire to hear it with all one's might, one should understand: "Thus have I heard; by me too has it been heard in this manner.

And herein, there are the methods known as *nandiyāvaṭṭa*, *tipukkhalo*, *sīhavikkīḷita*, *disālocana*, and *aṅkusa*, which consist of unity, diversity, non-agency, and the nature of phenomena (*evamdhammatā*).

And "various methods" (*nānānayā*) refers to the various methods distinguished by way of the gratification and so forth, as well as the objects and so forth; or alternatively, "methods" (*nayā*) refers to the courses of the text (*pāḷigatiyo*), and these are manifold by way of the original formulation and its subsequent addition,

by way of the categories such as "partaking of defilement" and so forth, "mundane" and so forth, and their mixture, by way of the wholesome and so forth, by way of the aggregates and so forth, by way of the groupings and so forth, by way of the "liberated at times" and so forth,
by way of the "setting aside" and so forth, by way of the roots of the wholesome and so forth, and by way of the *Tikapaṭṭhāna* and so forth.
"And of various kinds" (*nānappakārā*) means various methods (*nānānayā*); "skillful in those various methods" (*nānānayanipuṇaṃ*) means subtle, gentle, and refined by means of them.

"Inclination" (*ajjhāsaya*) is the same as "disposition" (*āsaya*); and that is manifold, being divided into categories such as eternalism and so forth, or into categories such as having little dust in one's eyes (*apparajakkha*) and so forth.

Alternatively, the many inclinations beginning with one's own inclination (*attajjhāsayādika*) constitute "manifold inclinations" (*anekajjhāsayo*). That [manifoldness] is the source, the cause of arising.
"Of this" refers to that which arises from manifold underlying tendencies (*ajjhāsaya*).

It is [expounded] by means of six "meaning-terms" (*atthapada*)—namely, by way of proclaiming, manifesting, explaining, analyzing, making clear, and describing—and by means of six "phrase-terms" (*byañjanapada*)—namely, by way of the description of syllables, phrases, phonemes, modes, etymologies, and explanations;
[all] through the perfection of the meaning such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth, and the perfection of the phrasing used to clarify them.
And because it is endowed with these [qualities], it is "perfect in meaning and phrasing" (*atthabyañjanasampanna*).

It is "possessing manifold wonders" (*vividhapāṭihāriya*) because it has various and many kinds of miracles—classified as the miracle of psychic power (*iddhi*), the miracle of mind-reading (*ādesanā*), and the miracle of instruction (*anusāsani*)—and because each of these possesses a variety of objects and so forth. Among those, it is called "the removal of the opposite" (*paṭipakkhaharaṇa*) because it removes the defilements such as lust (*rāga*).

Regarding "a miracle" (*pāṭihāriya*): since the Blessed One has no opposing factors such as lust (*rāga*) that must be removed, and since even for ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) the supernormal power (*iddhividha*) proceeds when the mind is free from defilements (*vigatūpakkilesa*), endowed with the eight qualities, and its opposites have been destroyed, it is therefore not possible to call this a "miracle" here by using the conventional terminology applied to that [other case]. However, if [one considers] the Greatly Compassionate One...
The defilements present in those to be trained by the Blessed One are the adversaries; it is called a "miracle" (pāṭihāriya) because of the removal of these.
This being so, this [definition] is appropriate. Alternatively, the adversaries of both the Blessed One and his Teaching are the sectarians (titthiya);
it is a miracle because of the removal of them. For they are [adversaries] insofar as they are unable to manifest their own views due to the removal of their views.
By means of psychic power (*iddhi*), direct instruction (*ādesanā*), and instruction (*anusāsanī*), they are carried away and removed.
Alternatively, this word *paṭi* conveys the meaning of "after," as in such examples as, "When he had entered, another brahmin arrived.

Therefore, because it is to be carried away—that is, to be set in motion—after the mind has been concentrated, freed from defilements, and its task accomplished, it is called a "wonder" (*paṭihāriya*).
Or, "patihāriya" refers to the subsequent removal [of defilements] once one's own defilements have been removed by the paths of the fourth jhāna.

The miracles of supernormal power (*iddhi*), mind-reading (*ādesanā*), and instruction (*anusāsani*) should be performed again for the benefit of beings by one who is free from defilements and has completed his task;
and because they serve to remove the defilements of other beings once one's own defilements have been removed, they are called "patihāriya."

[They] come into being. *Pāṭihāriya* is that which is marvelous (*paṭihāriya*); or, it is called a "marvel" because each individual [act] within the collection consisting of psychic power (*iddhi*), instruction (*ādesanā*), and guidance (*anusāsanī*) occurs in relation to what is marvelous.
Alternatively, the fourth jhāna and the Path are "marvelous" because they remove opposing factors (*paṭipakkha*).
The meaning of *pāṭihāriya* should be understood as "that which is born therein," being its sign, or "that which has come from that."
However, because the teaching of the meaning of the texts— comprised of what is called the "designation" and the "realization" of that [meaning]— or alternatively,
the penetration of the designation and realization of both cause and effect and their mutual relationship— is profound; and because, like the great ocean to sea-monsters and the like,
it provides no foothold and is difficult to fathom for those who have not accumulated the equipment of merit, it is therefore endowed with these four kinds of profundity.
The Blessed One’s word is profound in its teaching and penetration of the meaning of the Dhamma.

Though the sound of the Blessed One’s single utterance of the Dhamma occurs at one single moment, it becomes accessible for beings of various languages to grasp simultaneously, each according to their own tongue. For the power of the Buddhas is inconceivable.
It should be understood that "the power of the Buddha" means it comes within the range of hearing for all beings according to each of their respective languages.

By way of illustration, in order to exempt himself [from responsibility], saying, "I am not self-become; this was not realized by me," he indicates the entire discourse to be spoken now with the words, "Thus have I heard; it was heard thus by me.
By way of emphasis, as in: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus who are learned, namely..."
“Ānanda is the foremost among those who possess a [good] gait, those who possess mindfulness, those who possess steadfastness, and those who are attendants— namely, Ānanda. Thus,

in accordance with the state of being praised by the Blessed One, and likewise by the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) as one “skilled in the meaning, skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in the phrasing, skilled in the terminology,
and skilled in what precedes and follows,” he displayed his own power of retention.
By thus declaring it, he generates in sentient beings a desire to hear: "Thus have I heard; and that is neither deficient nor redundant in meaning or in phrasing;

it is to be understood exactly so and not otherwise. "Not otherwise" means not otherwise than the manner in which it was heard in the presence of the Blessed One, but not otherwise than the manner in which it was taught by the Blessed One. For the power of the Blessed One is inconceivable.

The meaning of what was said—that this teaching cannot be fully understood in every aspect—is precisely this. For the power of retention consists solely in not contradicting the manner in which [the teaching] was heard.
The particle *me* is seen in three senses. Thus, in such passages as "What is sung to the accompaniment of verses is not for me to eat," the sense is "by me.
In such passages as "It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach the Dhamma to me in brief," the sense is "for me" (*mayhaṃ*).
The meaning is "mine. In such passages as, "Bhikkhus, be my heirs to the Dhamma," the meaning is "mine.
Here, however, it is appropriate in two senses: "heard by me" and "my hearing.
And here, that which is not another is called "self" (atta); thus, in what is termed one's own internal continuum (niyakajjhattasaṅkhāte sasantāne), it is to be spoken of in this way.
Although this word *me*— which is threefold because it functions as a case ending— is seen in only one sense,

it should be understood that the statement "the word *me* is seen in three senses" refers to the fact that a distinction in meaning is indeed perceived, characterized by specific roles such as the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the recipient (*sampadāna*).
As for the word *suta*, this term *suta*— whether with or without a prefix— denotes going, being well-known, being moistened, accumulation, application, and what is cognizable by the ear.
The term *suta* is divided into many meanings according to the sense-door it follows, such as "cognized" (*viññāta*) and so forth.

Although a prefix (*upasagga*) qualifies the action, because its function is merely to indicate [that qualification], the word *suta* itself expresses each respective meaning even when that prefix is present.
Therefore, in the extraction of the meanings of the unprefixed word *suta*, the inclusion of the prefixed form is not contradictory.
In such passages as “intent upon the army,” the meaning is “going. In such passages as “of one who has heard the Dhamma and sees it,” the meaning is “of one whose Dhamma is well-known.
In such passages as “the lustful toward the lustful,” the meaning is “defiled by defilement, [toward one] defiled.
In such passages as “by you, abundant merit has been accumulated,” the meaning is “heaped up. In such passages as “those wise ones intent upon meditation,” [the meaning is “devoted to”].
The meaning is "devoted to meditation. In such passages as "seen, heard, sensed," the meaning is "cognizable by the ear-faculty.
In such passages as "one who retains what is heard, one who accumulates what is heard," the meaning is "one who retains what is cognized by following the ear-door.
Here, however, the meaning is either "ascertained by means of the ear-door" or simply "ascertainment. For when the word *me* has the sense of *mayā* ("by me"), [it connects with] "thus..."

It is appropriate [to say]: "By me it was heard; it was ascertained by means of the ear-door. When the sense of "by me" (*mama*) is present, it is appropriate [to say]: "In this way, by me it was heard;
it was ascertained by means of the ear-door. Thus, among these three terms, because of the word *evaṃ* (thus) employed in proximity to the word *sutaṃ* (heard), which indicates the act of hearing—

"It must be so" (*bhavitabbaṃ*); therefore, "thus" (*evaṃ*) indicates the function of the mind-door consciousness that arises immediately after the ear-door consciousnesses, such as the receiving consciousness (*sampaṭicchana*).
"He" (*so*) indicates the person possessing the aforementioned consciousness. For all sentences possess the sense of the particle *eva*, because their fruit is restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
"Heard" (*sutaṃ*) indicates a grasping that is neither deficient, nor excessive, nor erroneous, by way of negating the state of not having heard.
For just as that which is heard deserves to be called "heard," so too that which is rightly heard is a grasping that is neither deficient nor excessive,
and is a grasping that is non-perverted. Alternatively, according to the position that a word expresses its meaning by way of excluding the meanings of other words,
since it is stated that for the term "heard" (*suta*), there is no such thing as "not heard" (*asuta*), this is the meaning expressed.

Therefore, "thus" (*suta*)—by way of negating the state of not having heard—is an indication of grasping [the teaching] without deficiency, without excess, and without error. This is what is meant: "Thus have I heard;

this was not seen by me, nor realized through self-originated knowledge (*sayambhū-ñāṇa*), nor apprehended otherwise; rather, it was indeed heard, and that too correctly. Or, it serves the purpose of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).
Thus, regarding the word *sadda*, this is the application of its meaning; for the word *suta* when dependent on that [word *sadda*], a restrictive sense is possible.

Therefore, it should be understood that for the word *suta* dependent on that, there is a negation of the state of not hearing, as well as an indication of grasping [the sound] without deficiency, excess, or error.
In this way, the application of the meaning of the word *suta* should be seen as having been made by way of both the cause of hearing and the specific nature of the hearing.
The word *tathā* (thus) signifies the manner in which that stream of consciousness proceeding through the ear-door functions by grasping various meanings and phrases;
it indicates the state of its occurrence upon a manifold object. The word *evaṃ* (so) has the sense of "in this way.

The word *me* (by me) is a declaration of the self. The word *sutaṃ* (heard) is a declaration of the Dhamma, because the aforementioned stream of consciousness has the Dhamma of the scriptures as its object.
This is the summary here: "By me, who am the agent for the course of consciousness proceeding toward various kinds of objects, nothing else was done;
rather, this was done, and this Dhamma was heard.
Likewise, since the word *evaṃ* (thus) has the sense of indicating—that is, making manifest that which is to be indicated—by taking it as an indicator of what is to be pointed out...
Because it is that which is to be demonstrated. Therefore, it should be understood that by the word "thus" (*evaṃ*), the entire sutta is referred back.
"Me" (*me*) is the designation of the person. "Sutta" (*suta*) is the designation of the person's function.

For the act of hearing (*savana-kiriyā*) obtained through the word "heard" (*suta*) is bound up with a continuity of auditory consciousness, and therein lies the conventional designation of a "person" (*puggala-vohāra*); yet this is not [the case] where the conventional designation of a person is absent.
The act of hearing is obtained regarding a continuous stream of teachings (*dhammappabandha*). This is its summary meaning:
"That discourse which I shall point out, that was heard by me in this way.
Likewise, "in this way" refers to the grasping of various meanings and phrases within a continuum of consciousness (*cittasantāna*) due to the occurrence of diverse objects.
There is [the word] *hoti*; since the purpose of the word *evaṃ* is precisely the description of its various modes (*ākāra*), it is a designation of mode (*ākāra-paññatti*).

For this [word] *evaṃ* is a designation of mode because it is to be designated as the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena by way of their respective modes of occurrence. *Me* is a designation of the agent (*kattuniddeso*).

*Sutaṃ* is a designation of the object (*visayaniddeso*), for a phenomenon that is to be heard is so called by way of the act of hearing performed by the person who is the agent of that act of hearing.

This is the locus of occurrence. Up to this point, the final determination of the grasping of an object by the agent—who possesses that [stream]—has been demonstrated by means of the mental continuum proceeding in various modes.
Alternatively, "thus" (*evaṃ*) is a designation for the function of the person (*puggala*), as it indicates the mode of the phenomena (*dhamma*) that have been heard and grasped.

Or rather, by the word *evaṃ* (thus), which has the nature of manifesting a determination, the function of a person (*puggala-kicca*) is indicated, because the act of grasping that form and so forth involves the operation of phenomena (*dhamma*) that serve as the basis for the conventional designation of a "person.

The term *sutaṃ* (heard) is a description of the function of consciousness (*viññāṇa-kicca*), for even for a proponent of a person (*puggalavādin*), the act of hearing does not exist independently of consciousness.
The term *me* (by me) is a description of the person endowed with both functions.
For the occurrence of the word "heard" (suta) refers exclusively to a specific type of being, and the function of consciousness must be applied to that very same object.

Herein, this is the summary: it is "heard" by me—that is, by a person endowed with the consciousness whose function is hearing—by way of the conventional designation "hearing" obtained through the function of consciousness.
"Thus," "so," and "it is mine"— these are designations of what does not exist by way of the ultimate meaning of actual reality.
For all meanings attainable through words must be approached solely by means of designations,

and because all designations are included within the six types of designations beginning with "existent," that which has an unreal object— like a magical illusion or a mirage— [is a designation of the non-existent].
Even the "unsurpassed goal" (anuttama-attha) is not something to be grasped through mere hearsay.

That which has the intrinsic nature of the ultimate (paramattha-sabhāva)—consisting of the deformation of matter, the experiencing of sounds, and so forth—exists by way of the ultimate as the true reality (saccikaṭṭha-paramattha).
However, that aspect of meaning which is expressed as "thus" (evaṃ) and "mine" (me) is of a non-ultimate nature; it is not found by way of the ultimate as the true reality.
This is called a designation for what does not exist. Therefore, what is there here that exists in the ultimate sense (paramattha) such that it could receive a designation as "this" or "mine"?
"Hearing" is a designation for what exists; for that which is apprehended here by the ear exists in the ultimate sense.
"Thus" (*tathā*) refers to the act of referring back (*paccāmasana*) to the aspects and so forth that were determined when phenomena entered the range of hearing.

"I" (*me*) is a designation by way of grasping (*upādāpaññatti*), because it is spoken in reference to the aggregates included within one's own continuum as distinguished by specific functions and so forth.

"Heard" (*suta*) is a designation by way of comparison (*upanidhāpaññatti*), because it is spoken in comparison with what has been seen and so forth. [It applies] to that which is devoid of the intrinsic nature of what has been seen and the rest.

Even though the conventional usage of "heard" (suta) occurs with respect to the sense-base of sound, it must be spoken of in relation to the seen, the sensed, and the cognized— just as the terms "second" and "third" depend upon "first" and so on—
because it is understood as "heard" only by depending on those [other] categories. For this meaning is expressed as "heard" in the sense that "it is not unheard."

And here, by the expression "thus" (*evam*), he illuminates non-delusion. For it was precisely those specific modes of what he had heard that were penetrated by himself which were restated here by the Venerable Ānanda; thus his non-delusion is illuminated.

Indeed, one who is deluded is not capable of penetrating various modes, nor are the various modes [of the dependent origination] easy to penetrate when considered according to their conditional aspects.
"It is explained by the word *suttanta*": by the term *sutanta*, he demonstrates the non-forgetfulness of what has been heard (*suta*), because the mode of having heard is shown exactly as it is.
For one whose hearing has been forgotten does not, at a later time, claim, "I have heard this.
Thus, through non-delusion, wisdom (*paññā*) is established; or rather, through the absence of delusion, there is the very wisdom that arose at the time of hearing.
The accomplishment of wisdom occurs at a time subsequent to that; likewise, the accomplishment of mindfulness occurs through non-forgetfulness.
In this context, it is the capacity to grasp the phrasing by means of mindfulness preceded by wisdom. For the mode of the phrasings to be penetrated is not exceedingly profound;
since what must be done there is simply the retention of what has been heard, the function of mindfulness is predominant, while wisdom becomes secondary therein.
Having taken "preceded by wisdom" as the basis: it is the capacity for penetrating the meaning by means of wisdom preceded by mindfulness.
For since the mode of the meaning to be penetrated is profound, the activity of wisdom is predominant, while mindfulness is merely subordinate therein;

thus, having taken "preceded by mindfulness" [in that sense], there is the possession of the treasury of the Dhamma, which is endowed with both meaning and phrasing through the application of the capacity of both.
The status of being the "Dharma-treasurer" (dhammabhaṇḍāgārika) is established by his capacity to preserve [the Dharma].
Another method of interpretation: by the word "thus" (evam), he illuminates wise attention (yonisomanasikāra);

and by that, there is the establishment of the non-erroneous nature of the various modes of penetration to be explained below—which indicate the manner, the illustration, and the determination of the meanings of what is being spoken—because they have the Dharma as their object.

For one who attends to things in an improper manner (ayoniso manasikaroto), penetration in its various forms is not possible. By the word "sūtra" (sutanti), he illustrates non-distraction (avikkhepa):

hearing a sūtra that has reached the stage of formal treatment (pakaraṇa) and is about to be explained—by way of such questions as "Where was the *Paṭhamabodhi-sutta* spoken?"—is not possible without concentration, because there is no hearing for one whose mind is distracted.
For indeed, a person with a distracted mind, even when being told of every kind of excellence, says, "I have not heard it; speak again.

And herein, through wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), one accomplishes right self-application and the merit previously performed, because these are absent in one who has not rightly applied themselves or who has not performed merit in the past. Through non-distraction, there is the hearing of the true Dhamma.
And one accomplishes reliance upon true persons (*sappurisūpanissaya*), because that [listening] is absent for the unlearned who lack reliance upon true persons.
For one whose mind is distracted is not able to listen, and there is no listening for one who does not rely upon true persons.
Another method: "In the mental continuum of which [person], through its various modes of activity, there is the grasping of various meanings and phrases..."

"...there is the description of its various aspects. And because such a fortunate aspect— which consists in the complete fulfillment of the welfare of others through the thorough mastery of the entire excellence of the Dispensation by way of discerning the distinctions in meaning and phrasing of the Blessed One’s word—

does not arise for one who has not previously performed merit and whose mind is not rightly set on the wishless (*appaṇihita*), therefore, by means of this word "thus" (*evaṃ*), [the text indicates] that fortunate [aspect].

By the word "ākāra" (manner), he demonstrates his own perfection of the latter two wheels; by the word "suta" (heard), he demonstrates the perfection of the former two wheels through the application of hearing.
For there can be no hearing for one dwelling in an unsuitable place and lacking reliance upon a virtuous person.
Thus, through the accomplishment of the latter two wheels, the purity of his disposition (*āsaya*) is established. And previously, with a mind rightly directed...
One who has performed merit possesses a purified intention because of the distancing of the defilements that are the causes of its impurity. Thus it is said:
"A mind rightly directed makes one better than before," and "You have performed merit, Ānanda;
apply yourself to striving, and you will soon be free from taints. Through the accomplishment of the first two wheels, there is purity of application. By dwelling in a suitable locality...
For indeed, through reliance upon true persons and by following the example of the virtuous, one’s application becomes purified.

By that purity of disposition (*āsaya*), there is the accomplishment of proficiency in realization (*adhigama*); and because the defilements of craving and views have already been cleansed, there is the accomplishment of proficiency in the scriptures (*āgama*) through the purity of application (*payoga*). For when the application of body and speech is perfectly pure, there is an absence of remorse.

One whose mind is undistracted is confident in the scriptures. Thus, for one whose application and disposition are pure and who is endowed with both scriptural learning (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*), their speech—just as the breaking of dawn precedes the rising of the sun, and just as wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) precedes wholesome action—is worthy of being the precursor to the word of the Blessed One.
Establishing the "source" (*nidāna*) in its proper place, he said: "Thus have I heard," and so forth.

Another method: by the word *evaṃ* (thus), which indicates the penetration of various aspects according to the very manner previously stated, he demonstrates the possession of his own analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) and of ingenuity (*paṭibhāna*).

By the word *sutaṃ* (heard), which—due to its proximity to the word *evaṃ* or because it refers to what is about to be spoken—indicates the penetration of the various kinds of things to be heard, he demonstrates the possession of his analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*) and of linguistic expression (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).
It illuminates. And by speaking these words that illuminate wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) in the manner just described, he demonstrates:
"These phenomena have been examined by me with the mind and thoroughly penetrated through right view. For the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyattidhamma*) [is illuminated] by such means as:
"Herein virtue is taught; herein concentration; herein wisdom; herein there are so many connections," and so forth.

Having well-defined, by way of the method beginning with "This is form, this much is form," etc., the various material and immaterial phenomena as they have been described in various places— by means of a view characterized as the acceptance of reflecting on the Dhamma (*dhammanijjhānakkhanti*),
which consists of mental investigation accompanied by hearsay and modes of reflection— and having thus penetrated them, it brings about welfare and happiness for both oneself and others.
"It is heard" (*sutaṃ*): this is a statement illustrating the application of hearing; by speaking thus, one demonstrates: "Many teachings have been heard, retained, and mastered by me through speech.
For the hearing, retention, and mastery of the Dhamma of the scriptures are dependent upon the application of the ear.
By both of these, while demonstrating the perfection of both the meaning and the phrasing through the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma, one shows due regard for hearing.
He generates [respect]. For one who does not listen with reverence to the Dhamma, which is complete in both meaning and phrasing, becomes excluded from great benefit;
therefore, having generated reverence, the Dhamma should be heard attentively.
By this entire statement, "Thus have I heard," the Venerable Ānanda [establishes] that which was proclaimed by the Tathāgata...
By not withholding the Dhamma from himself, he transcends the plane of the unworthy person; by professing discipleship, he enters the plane of the worthy person.
Likewise, he draws his mind away from what is not the true Dhamma and establishes it in the true Dhamma.
By declaring, "This has been heard by me only as such, yet it is the word of that Blessed One," he liberates himself and [glorifies] the Teacher.
He refers back [to the source], applies the word of the Conqueror (jinavacana), and establishes the guide of the Dhamma.
Furthermore, by not claiming for himself the state of having produced [the teaching] with the words "Thus have I heard," but rather disclosing his prior hearing, he shows:
"This was received by me directly from that Blessed One, who is confident in the four grounds of self-confidence and who possesses the ten powers."

“Regarding the Perfectly Enlightened One— the one who stands in the place of the bull, the roarer of the lion’s roar, the supreme among all beings, the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Sovereign of Dhamma, the Island of Dhamma, the Refuge of Dhamma, the Excellent Wheel-Turner of the True Dhamma—
no doubt or uncertainty should be entertained here concerning the meaning, the Dhamma, the phrases, or the syllables,” [he said] to all gods and humans.
In this Dhamma, it destroys lack of faith and generates perfection of faith. Therefore, this is said:
"It destroys lack of faith and increases faith in the Teaching;
Thus saying, 'Thus have I heard,' is the disciple of Gotama."
The Exposition of the Delimitation of Numbering by "One" (Eka). For this word *eka* is seen used in the senses of "other," "best," "without companion," and "number," among others.
Thus, in such passages as, "Some assert thus: 'The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is vain,'" it is seen in the sense of "others.
In "the state of oneness of mind" (*cetaso ekodibhāva*), it is used in the sense of "best. In "alone, withdrawn," it is used in the sense of "without companion."
In such passages as, “Bhikkhus, there is indeed one moment and one occasion for living the holy life,” it should be understood here as well as a numerical term.
Therefore it is said: “‘One’ is a designation for the delimitation of number.
“Occasion” (*samaya*) is a designation for that which is delimited. “At one occasion” (*ekaṃ samayaṃ*) is an indication of non-specification. In this context, the word *samaya*—
“It is seen in the sense of conjunction, moment, time, collection, cause, view, acquisition, abandoning, and penetration.
For instance, in such passages as: “Perhaps tomorrow we might go, taking into account the time and the occasion,” and so forth.

The meaning is "conjunction" (*samavāya*); for the intended sense is "having obtained the appropriate time and the completeness of conditions. Therefore, it should be understood as the "conjunction of conditions" (*paccaya-samavāya*).
In such passages as, "Monks, there is indeed only one moment and one occasion for living the holy life," the meaning is "opportunity" (*okāsa*).
For the appearance of a Tathāgata and so forth is the opportunity for the holy life of the Path, because it is the cause for obtaining its requisite conditions.
The meaning is that the "moment" (*khaṇa*) and the "occasion" (*samaya*)—which are both called "moment" and "occasion"—are indeed one and the same.

In such expressions as "the occasion of heat" (*uṇhasamaya*) or "the occasion of fever" (*pariḷāhasamaya*), it refers to time. In such expressions as "the great assembly in the forest" (*mahāsamayo pavanasmim*), it refers to a multitude;
for "great assembly" (*mahāsamaya*) means a great gathering of monks and deities. [As it is said: "Furthermore, Bhaddāli, you have not penetrated even the occasion."
“The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī; the Blessed One will know me as the bhikkhu named Bhaddāli who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.
This is the reason [given] in such passages as, “This occasion, Bhaddāli, was not understood by you.
For here, the word *samaya* (occasion) is intended to mean the cause for a training rule (*sikkhāpada*). “Then, indeed...”

In such passages as, "At one time the wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Samaṇa Muṇḍikā, was staying at Mallikā’s Park in the Tindukācīra grove of Ekasālaka, where they propound their own tenets," it refers to *diṭṭhi* (view).
For there, the sectarian teachers sitting [there] propound (*pavadanti*) their respective tenets (*samaya*), which consist of their views;
thus that wanderers’ park is called "Samayappavādaka" (the Propounder of Tenets).
“In the benefit pertaining to this present life, and in the benefit pertaining to the future life—the wise person who has the realization of these benefits is called ‘learned.
In such passages as these, it refers to acquisition. For “realization of the benefit” (atthābhisamaya) means the attainment of the benefit. “Through the realization of conceit... [and so forth].

In such passages as "he made an end of suffering," it refers to abandoning (*pahāna*). In the sense of "the settling of a legal issue, its resolution, its subsiding, and its disappearance," *abhisamaya* means abandoning.

In such passages as "the meaning of suffering is oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of burning, the meaning of change, and the meaning of realization (*abhisamaya*)," it refers to penetration (*paṭivedha*).
For it is called *abhisamaya* because it is to be realized; thus, "the meaning of realization" means the very fact of realization itself.
Oppression and the rest are spoken of as being unified by way of their state of being to be fully understood (*abhisametabba*);
or, the meaning that constitutes the object of full understanding (*abhisamaya*) or penetration is the "meaning of full understanding," and thus they are spoken of as such in an absolute sense.

Therein, oppression (*pīḷana*) is the harming of one who possesses that [truth], the making of the Truth of Suffering non-expansive. Torment (*santāpa*) is by way of the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*), and so forth.
It is the heating and the burning.
And here, it is a *samavāya* (conjunction) because it comes together (*sameti*) and meets (*samaveti*) through the presence of cooperative causes; it is a *samaya* (occasion).

It is a *khaṇa-samaya* (moment-occasion) because the holy life of the Path comes together (*sameti*) and converges (*samāgacchati*) here with the persons who are its support. Or else, it is so called because one comes together (*sameti*) by means of this [path] or in this [place].

A *satta* (being) or a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*) comes together with [factors] such as arising and so forth, or with [factors] such as co-nascence and so forth; thus, it is "time" (*kāla*) or "occasion" (*samaya*).

For although time does not exist in reality apart from the mere occurrence of phenomena, it is nevertheless designated by way of a mere conceptual construction as the locus or the instrument of the occurrence of phenomena.
Alternatively, a "collection" (*samūha*) is called *samaya* because it is the coming together (*samaṃ*), or the simultaneous (*saha*) movement (*ayana*) and persistence of its constituent parts.
"Just as a collection" (*yathā samudāyo*): for a collection (*samūha*) is simply the state of existing together with its constituent parts (*avayava*).

When there is a coming together of the remaining conditions, the fruit "goes forth" (*eti*)—that is, it arises and proceeds—from this; thus, the cause (*hetu*) is a "coming together" (*samaya*), just as a "collection" (*samudaya*).

It "comes together" (*sameti*) because of its state of being a fetter (*saṃyojana*), [meaning] it is a connection (*sambandha*) that "goes forth" (*eti*) and proceeds within its own domain; or, because of its state of firm grasping, those things which are "conjoined" (*saṃyutta*) "go forth" (*ayanti*) and proceed.
"View" (*diṭṭhi*) is "conviction" (*samaya*) because beings adhere to it according to their own inclinations; for by the fetter of view, beings are bound exceedingly tight.

"Conviction" (*samaya*) is also acquisition, in the sense of coming together, meeting, and convergence. "Conviction" (*samaya*) is also abandonment, in the sense of calming, thorough calming, and disappearance.
Furthermore, because it is a superior conviction due to its nature as abandonment through complete eradication, it is "clear conviction" (*abhisamaya*), just as [the term] *Abhidhamma* [is used].
*Abhisamaya* means that which is to be correctly approached (*abhi*) and fully realized (*sameta*) by means of knowledge; it is the unerring intrinsic nature of phenomena.

Or, *abhisamaya* means that which goes (*eti*) or proceeds (*gacchati*) correctly toward (*abhimukha*) [reality] and awakens (*bujjhati*); it is the awakening to the phenomena’s nature as it truly is (*yathābhūta*).
In this way, the application of the term *samaya* should be understood according to each specific meaning.
Regarding the extraction of the meaning of the word *samaya*, the reason for taking the word *abhisamaya* [as a synonym] should be understood according to the method already stated.
However, in this context, its meaning is "time," because other meanings such as "convergence" (*samavāya*) and so forth are impossible.

For, just as the place, the teacher, and the assembly are required as the basis for the teaching, time alone must be intended here as the basis. Since "time" (*kāla*) is intended here by the term *samaya*, therefore...
It indicates "at one time" (ekaṃ samayaṃ) with respect to those temporal divisions consisting of years, seasons, half-months, days and nights, forenoon, midday,
afternoon, the first watch, the middle watch, the last watch, moments, and so forth.
But why is time indicated here in an indefinite manner, rather than by specifying it as a season, a year, or the like?

If it is asked, "Has it been pointed out?"—although among these periods such as the year and so forth, whatever discourse was spoken in whichever year, season, month, fortnight, portion of the night, or portion of the day, all of that was well-known and well-determined by the Elder through his wisdom.
However, because [he thought], "Thus have I heard: in such-and-such a year, in such-and-such a season..."
When it is stated thus— “in such a month, in such a fortnight, in such a part of the night, or in such a part of the day”— it is not possible to easily memorize,
recite, or cause others to recite it, and much would have to be said; therefore,
condensing that meaning into a single phrase, he said, “at one time.”

Furthermore, there are these various occasions of the Blessed One among gods and humans— extremely renowned and distinguished by many different times— such as the occasion of his descent into the womb,

the occasion of his birth, the occasion of his spiritual urgency, the occasion of his great renunciation, the occasion of his practice of austerities, the occasion of his victory over Māra, the occasion of his full enlightenment, the occasion of his dwelling in happiness in this very life,
the occasion of his teaching, and the occasion of his final Nibbāna; among these...
Among the "occasions" (*samaya*), he illuminates one occasion, namely that which is designated as the "occasion of teaching.

Or else, among the occasions for the functions of wisdom and compassion, it is the occasion of the function of compassion; among the occasions for practicing for one's own welfare and for the welfare of others, it is the occasion of practicing for the welfare of others;

among the occasions for the two duties of those who have assembled, it is the occasion of the discourse on the Dhamma; and among the occasions for the practice of teaching, it is the occasion of teaching. Among these—
He said "at one time" with reference to a particular occasion among the many times [the Buddha taught].
But why is it not stated here as it is in the Abhidhamma— "at whatever time a wholesome consciousness pertaining to the sense-sphere has arisen"—
or as in other Sutta passages— "at whatever time, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures..."?
In the passage, “having secluded himself from unwholesome states,” the designation is made using the locative case;

and in the Vinaya, in the phrase, “At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One,” the designation is made using the instrumental case. Why, instead of doing it that way, is the designation here made using the accusative case in the sense of absolute connection (accantasamyoga) as “at one time”?
In that case [it is] so, and here it is otherwise, because of the possibility of different meanings. Therein:
For in the Abhidhamma and in other Suttantas besides this, two meanings are possible:
the locative sense known as the "substratum" (ādhāra-visaya), and the sense of "characterization by one action through another action" (bhāvena-bhāva-lakkhaṇa).

Indeed, "occasion" (samaya) is the locus of time and the locus of a collection for the phenomena such as contact mentioned therein; likewise, "time" (kāla) is so called because it is merely the occurrence of phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāva-dhamma).
Although it does not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), it is designated as a support for those things occurring at that moment— because they are absent both before and after it—
just as in such expressions as "born in the forenoon" or "born in the afternoon. Likewise, even though a "collection" (*samūho*) does not exist in the ultimate sense apart from its constituent parts,
it is nevertheless designated as the support for those parts by way of a form established through mere conceptual construction (*kappanāmattasiddhena rūpena*).
As in the expressions, “a branch on a tree,” or “barley arisen from a heap of barley,” and so forth. For the meaning there is this:

at the very time that a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen within a collection of phenomena (*dhammapuñja*), at that same time contact and the other mental factors are also present within that collection of phenomena.
Likewise, by virtue of the occasion (*samaya*)—which is defined as the causal concurrence of moments—...
In this context, the existence of the phenomena such as contact (phassa) that have been mentioned is indicated.

For just as in the expression, "He went while the cows were being milked; he returned when they had been milked," the act of going is indicated by the act of milking the cows, so too here, when it is said "at whatever time" (*yasmiṃ samaye*), since the meaning of the word lacks a state of non-existence, the sense of "being present" (*sati*) is understood.
Thus, by the phrase "at this time," the activity of the existence of the moment, the activity of the arising of consciousness,
and the activity of the becoming of contact and so forth are characterized. Likewise, at whatever time, in whatever ninth moment,
and when whatever cause— such as wise attention— or the concurrence of conditions exists, such that a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen, at that time, in that moment...
Since contact and the other [mental factors] also exist when there is a cause and a convergence of conditions, the locative case is employed here to indicate that meaning.

Furthermore, in the Vinaya, both the sense of cause—as in "he lives by means of food" (*annena vasati*) or "he lives by means of study" (*ajjhenena vasati*)—and the sense of instrument—as in "he cuts with an axe" (*pharasunā chindati*) or "he digs with a spade" (*kudālena khaṇati*)—are possible. For at the time of the promulgation of the training rules...
It was difficult to understand even for the Dhamma-Senāpati and others; therefore, having heard of the transgression at that time— which served as both the occasion and the cause—
he convened the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, interrogated the individual involved in the matter, and having rebuked him,
he laid down the training rules without exceeding the specific time designated by the occasion of the incident.
Expecting the cause for the promulgation of the training rules (sikkhāpada) as in the case of the third *pārājika* and others, he dwelt here and there;
therefore, for the purpose of indicating that meaning, the description is made in the Vinaya using the instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*).
But here and in other similar cases, the sense of absolute conjunction (*accantasaṃyoga*) is possible. For at whatever time [he was] together with...
This *udāna* arose by way of its originative cause; at that very time, the Blessed One dwelt in the contemplation of the Dhamma preceded by noble abiding.
Therefore, as in the case of expressions such as "he studies for a month," the description here is made in the accusative case for the purpose of indicating the object. Thus it is said:
“Having regard for each respective meaning, [the term *samaya*] is stated here as the locative, the instrumental, and—excluding the specific occasion—as the accusative.
However, the ancients explain it thus: “at which time,” or “by that time,” or “at one time.”

Or rather, this exposition is distinguished merely by its verbal expression; in every case, the meaning is simply the locative case. Therefore, even when "at one time" (*ekam samayam*) is stated, it should be understood to mean "at one time" (*ekasmiṃ samaye*).

"Bhagavā" means venerable. For in the world, those who are venerable are called "Bhagavā. And he is venerable to all beings because he is preeminent in all virtues; therefore, he is to be known as "Bhagavā. It has also been said by the ancients:
“‘Bhagavā’ is the best of words; ‘Bhagavā’ is the supreme of words.
He is venerable and worthy of reverence; therefore he is called ‘Bhagavā.
In this context, the word expressing “best” is said to be “seṭṭha” because it is associated with the quality of being best. Alternatively, it is said: “He is called [Bhagavā]...”
The word (*vacana*) and its meaning (*attha*). "Bhagavā" is the word for what is best: the meaning is that the meaning which is to be expressed by this word "Bhagavā" is the best.
Regarding "Bhagavā is the supreme word," the meaning should be understood here in the same manner as stated previously.
"Worthy of reverence" (*gāravayutta*): it means connected with a state of weightiness, either because of being endowed with weighty qualities or because of being deserving of special respect.

“Endowed with reverence. Thus, it should be understood that the word *bhagavā* is a designation for one who possesses profound reverence for the Supreme Being distinguished by such qualities. Furthermore:
“He possesses (bhagī), he frequents (bhajī), he shares in (bhāgī), he is the distributor (vibhattavā);
he has broken (bhagga), he is venerable (garu), he is fortunate (bhāgyavā).”
“He whose self is well-developed through many methods is called the Blessed One who has reached the end of existence”—
according to the method found in the *Niddesa*.

“The meaning of the term *bhagavā* should be understood by means of this verse: ‘He is fortunate (*bhāgyavā*), he has destroyed the defilements (*bhaggavā*), he is endowed with the [eight] fortunes (*bhagehi yutto*), he has analyzed the fortunes (*vibhattavā*), he has partaken of them (*bhattavā*), and he has gone beyond existence (*vantagamano*);

therefore, he is the Blessed One (*bhagavā*)’. Furthermore, this meaning has been explained in its entirety in the *Visuddhimagga*; therefore, it should be elucidated according to the method stated therein.
Furthermore, he is called the Blessed One (*bhagavā*) because he has sought (*vane*), or because he has vomited out (*vamī*), fortune (*bhaga*).

For the Tathāgata has sought, cultivated, and frequently practiced the perfections such as generosity and virtue, as well as the superhuman states such as the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and liberations (*vimokkha*); therefore, he is the Blessed One.

Alternatively, he is the Blessed One because he sought (*vane*) and aspired for those very same qualities to arise within the mental continuums of beings who were to be trained (*veneyya-sattā*). Or else, [he is so called] because of the fortune known as...
"The Blessed One vomited up sovereignty and fame and cast them away without regard, like a globule of spittle. For the Tathāgata,
regarding the glory of a wheel-turning monarch already in his hand— sovereignty over the four continents comparable to lordship over the world of the gods,
and the fame resplendent with the seven treasures which is the basis for the success of a wheel-turner— did not consider them even as much as a blade of grass, being entirely without regard.

Having abandoned [worldly life] and gone forth, he awakened to perfect enlightenment; therefore, he is called the Blessed One (*bhagavā*) because he possesses these fortunes (*bhaga*) beginning with glory (*siri*).
Alternatively, "fortunes" (*bhaga*) refers to the constellations (*bhāni*); those things which proceed or function in accordance with them are also called fortunes.

This is because the excellence of the receptacle world—consisting of Sineru, Yugandhara, Uttarakuru, Himavanta, and so forth—is beautiful due to its dependence on them, and because it remains stable throughout the duration of an eon.
He vomits those defilements; because he has transcended the dwelling-place of beings that resides therein, and because he has abandoned the desire and lust bound to them, he "abandons" them.
Thus, by such methods as "he vomits the defilements (bhage vamī), therefore he is the Blessed One (Bhagavā)," the meaning of the word *Bhagavā* is to be understood.
Up to this point, by the phrase "Thus have I heard," he speaks the Dhamma exactly as it was heard, by way of having heard it.

He makes the Dhamma-body of the Blessed One manifest, thereby comforting those people who are distressed by not seeing the Teacher, saying: "This teaching is not one whose Teacher has passed away; this is your Teacher. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Ānanda, whatever Dhamma and Vinaya have been taught and laid down by me, that shall be your Teacher after my passing."
By the phrase "at one time the Blessed One," he demonstrates that at that time the Blessed One was no longer present, thereby establishing the parinibbāna of the physical body (rūpakāya).

By this, [the author] intends: "Even the Blessed One—the teacher of such a Dhamma, the possessor of the ten powers, whose body was like a mass of thunderbolts—has attained parinibbāna; who then could harbor hope for life?"
He inspires a sense of urgency in people intoxicated by the pride of life and generates enthusiasm for the True Dhamma.
By saying "Thus," he indicates the excellence of the teaching, as this serves as the introduction to the entire discourse that is about to be spoken.
By saying "heard by me," he indicates the excellence of the disciple and the excellence of the hearing, [the latter] because he has attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
Because the Dharma-treasurer, who was designated by the Blessed One as foremost among five categories, elucidated the nature of what has been heard, saying, "And that indeed was heard by me alone;
it is not based on hearsay, nor is it handed down through tradition," this [phrase] elucidates the meaning of "Thus have I heard.
"At one time" indicates the perfection of time, by way of the period during which the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā.
Because it illustrates the state of being adorned by the arising of a Buddha. For the perfection of time has the arising of a Buddha as its supreme excellence.
By the word *Bhagavā*, he indicates the perfection of the teacher, because it demonstrates the weightiness of the Supreme Being distinguished by his special qualities.

*Uruvelāyaṃ* means "at the great bank" (*mahāvelāyaṃ*), or "in a great heap of sand" (*mahante vālukārāsimhi*). Alternatively, *uru* is said to mean "sand," and *velā* means "boundary. Thus, the meaning here should be understood as follows: it was brought [to that place] because of the transgression of the boundary (*velātikkamana-hetu*), hence it is called *uruvelā*.
It is said that in the past, before a Buddha had arisen, ten thousand ascetics were dwelling in that region.
They thought: "Bodily and verbal actions are evident to others, but mental action is not.
Therefore, whoever entertains wrong thoughts should, having reproached himself, bring sand in a leaf-bag and scatter it in this place; this shall be his [punishment]."
Having made a formal agreement regarding the "penance" (*daṇḍakamma*), from that time onward, whoever would entertain such a thought would bring sand in a leaf-bag and scatter it there.
In this way, a great heap of sand gradually formed there;
subsequently, later generations surrounded it and established it as a shrine site (*cetiya-ṭṭhāna*). It was with reference to this that it was said:
"—'At Uruvelā, at Mahāvelā': the meaning should be understood as 'at a great heap of sand.
"Dwells" (*viharati*) is a general indication of being endowed with any one of the modes of dwelling—whether postures, divine, brahma, or noble.
Here, however, it indicates association with the posture known as sitting among the various postures distinguished as standing, sitting, walking, and lying down.
And it should be understood as an exposition of being possessed of the noble abidings (*ariyavihāra*).

In this context, because one carries and maintains the personal existence (*attabhāva*) without it falling away by interrupting the obstruction of one posture with another posture, the meaning of the term "dwells" (*viharati*) here should be understood in the sense of dwelling in postures (*iriyāpathavihāra*). Furthermore, because the Blessed One...
It carries, brings, conveys, and produces manifold benefit for beings by means of the divine abodes and so forth;
therefore, the meaning should be understood as "it carries manifold [benefit] even by way of those.
*Najjā* means that which flows or streams, thus it is a river (*nadī*); the meaning of *tassā najjā* is "of that river," or "of the flowing stream. *Nerañjarāyā*—[refers to] the Nerañjarā.
Because its water (*jala*) is free from impurity (*nela*), it should have been called "Nelañjalā," but by changing the letter *la* to *ra*, it is called "Nerañjarā";
the meaning is "of the river whose waters are free from defects such as mud, moss, and aquatic plants.
Some say that it should have been called "Nīlajalā" (Blue-Watered), but it is called "Nerañjarā. Alternatively, this should be understood as simply the name of this river. Of that...
In order to indicate the bank of the river where the Blessed One stayed, it is said, "at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
In that context, regarding the statement, "Bodhi is said to be the knowledge of the four paths," path-knowledge is called *bodhi*.
In the statement, "The one of excellent and vast intelligence attains *bodhi*," it refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). The Blessed One attained both of these forms of *bodhi* here.

The tree that was the *patta* (the leaf) received the name "Bodhi-tree. Alternatively, the Blessed One is called "Bodhi" because he awakened (*bujjhi*) to the seven factors of awakening (*bojjhaṅga*);
because it is supported by him who has awakened, that tree also received the name "Bodhi-tree. [The word] "of that Bodhi-tree" refers to its vicinity (*mūle*).
For this word *mūla* appears in such passages as: "He should pull up the roots, even down to the size of a fibrous root of *usīra* grass," and so forth.

It is seen in the sense of "root" in such passages as, "Greed is a root of unwholesomeness. It is seen in the sense of a "specific cause" in such passages as, "To whatever extent the shadow extends at midday, or to whatever extent leaves fall in a windless place, to that extent is the base of the tree.

It is seen in the sense of "proximity" in such passages as, "To whatever extent the shadow extends at midday, or to whatever extent leaves fall in a windless place, to that extent is the base of the tree.
Here too, it is intended in the sense of proximity; therefore, the meaning here should be understood as "in the vicinity of the base of the Bodhi tree."
"Paṭhamābhisambuddho" means having become fully enlightened for the first time; the sense is "absolutely at the very beginning.

Up to this point, by the Dhamma-treasurer establishing the introduction to the Udāna teaching, the occasion (kāla), the place (desa), and the teacher (desaka) have been clearly elucidated together with their specific details.
Here it may be asked: "Why was the introductory statement uttered when the compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya was being performed? Is it not true that [it was spoken] by the Blessed One..."
"Should a compilation of the spoken words alone be made? It is replied: for the purpose of ensuring that the teaching remains long-lasting, is not forgotten, and is worthy of trust.

For a teaching established by being bound together through factors such as time, place, teacher, and subject matter remains long-lasting, is not forgotten, and is trustworthy—just as a legal decision is reliable when it is bound together by the indications of the time, place, agent, cause, and motive. Therefore...
And when the Venerable Mahākassapa asked questions regarding the location and other details, beginning with, "Friend Ānanda, where was the first Udāna spoken?",
the Dharma-treasurer (Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika) provided the answer by stating the introductory formula of the Udāna, beginning with, "Thus have I heard."

Furthermore, the introductory statement (nidāna) is for the purpose of manifesting the perfections of the Teacher. For the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, his status as a Perfectly Enlightened One (sambuddha) is established by the absence of prior composition, inference, scripture, or reasoning.

Indeed, there is no need for a Perfectly Enlightened One to rely on prior composition and the like, because his range of knowledge is unimpeded in all respects and he is the sole authority regarding all knowable phenomena.
Likewise, this is due to the absence of the "teacher’s fist" (ācariyamuṭṭhi), stinginess regarding the Dhamma, or favoritism toward disciples in the dispensation.

The accomplishment of the state of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). For indeed, in one whose taints are completely exhausted, there can be no "teacher’s fist" or similar secrecy regarding anything;

thus, his assistance to others proceeds from one who is perfectly pure. Thus, by means of those [qualities] which manifest the perfection of knowledge and the perfection of abandonment—which indicate the absolute absence of ignorance and craving, the very defects of a teacher that corrupt the attainment of right view and virtue—...
Through the states of purity of a Perfectly Enlightened One (*sambuddha*), the first two grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajjadvaya*) are established;

and from that, through the establishment of the absence of delusion regarding obstructive and emancipating phenomena (*antarāyika-nyānika-dhamma*), the latter two grounds of self-confidence are established.

Thus, by means of the introductory statement (*nidāna-vacana*), the Blessed One’s possession of the four grounds of self-confidence and his practice for his own welfare and the welfare of others are made manifest to the assembled audiences in their respective places.

Because it illustrates the teaching of the Dhamma through spontaneous eloquence arising at the appropriate moment in accordance with the inclinations [of the audience]. Here, however, it should be connected as follows: by means of the manifestation of the experience of the bliss of liberation and the exposition of the attention directed toward dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).
Therefore it was said: "The introductory statement (nidāna) is for the purpose of manifesting the excellence of the Teacher.
Likewise, the introductory statement is for the purpose of manifesting the excellence of the Dispensation (sāsana). For one whose every action is encompassed by wisdom and compassion...
Indeed, for the Blessed One, there is no practice that is purposeless or intended solely for his own benefit.

Therefore, all the bodily, verbal, and mental actions of the Perfectly Enlightened One—which proceed solely for the sake of others—are called the "Teaching" (*sāsana*) in the sense of instructing beings, as appropriate, through the immediate, future, and ultimate goals, according to how they actually occurred;
it is not a mere literary composition. This, then, is the conduct of the Teacher.
