In various places, [the teaching] is elucidated as appropriate through the mention of the *nidāna* (introductory setting) along with factors such as time, place, teacher, assembly, and location;
however, here it should be connected with "the experience of the bliss of perfect enlightenment and liberation, and mental attention to dependent origination.
Therefore it was said: "The *nidāna* statement is for the purpose of elucidating the excellence of the Dispensation (*sāsana*)."
Furthermore, the introductory statement (*nidānavacana*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the authoritative nature of the Teaching by way of demonstrating the authoritative nature of the Teacher.
And this demonstration of its authoritative nature is to be understood according to the method explained below.

For, by the term "Bhagavā," there is an illumination of the Tathāgata’s abandonment of all stains, misconduct, and faults such as lust, hatred, and delusion, as well as an illumination of his status as the supreme among all beings.
Furthermore, by demonstrating the possession of extraordinary qualities such as unique knowledge and compassion, this meaning is elucidated in every respect;
thus, this is merely a brief indication of the purpose of the introductory statement (*nidānavacana*) here.
This [purpose] extends from the words "Thus have I heard" up to the phrase "uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*)."
This should be understood as the introduction (*nidāna*) to this *udāna*. For it is the speech uttered by the compilers at the time of the recitation,
beginning from the start, for the purpose of explaining the bodily and mental practice of the Blessed One in the manner in which he uttered this *udāna*.
But surely, the statement beginning with "When this exists, that comes to be" ought to be the word of the Blessed One himself;
for indeed, no one other than the Teacher is capable of teaching dependent origination. This is true.
However, it was at the foot of the Bodhi tree that the Blessed One [realized] dependent origination through the contemplation of the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
Having mentally reflected upon this, and likewise for the sake of awakening those kinsmen who were to be awakened,

the Great Elders who compiled the Dhamma took as the occasion for the origin (aṭṭhuppatti) this Udāna spoken by the Blessed One, following the manner in which the words of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) were taught in such discourses as the *Paṭiccasamuppādasīhanāda Sutta*.
Regarding the phrase "they recited the Nidāna": it must be understood that these words refer specifically to the speech of those who performed the recitation (*saṅgītikāra*).
This same principle applies to the subsequent Suttantas as well.

Furthermore, in this context, there are four ways in which a Sutta is introduced: by one's own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*), by another's inclination (*parajjhāsaya*), by way of a question (*pucchāvasika*), and by way of an occasion for a discourse (*aṭṭhuppattika*).

They should be understood as follows: Just as even the discourses (suttas), though divided into many hundreds and thousands of types, do not exceed sixteenfoldness according to the method of the *Paṭṭhāna* beginning with those "partaking of defilement" (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*), so too all of them do not exceed a fourfold state according to the manner of their delivery (*suttanikkhepa*), such as those arising from one's own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*).

Now, in this context, [one should understand] that of those arising from one's own inclination and those arising from an occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*), [the inclusion of] those arising from the inclination of others and those arising from a question is implied.
A combination through association is possible because of the occurrence of connections by intention (*ajjhāsaya*) and connections by inquiry (*anusandhi*);

however, since there is no mutual association between personal intention (*attajjhāsaya*) and the arising of a topic (*aṭṭhuppatti*), the entire method of the *Paṭṭhāna* is not possible [in that respect].

Alternatively, it is stated that there are four ways of arranging the suttas (*suttanikkhepa*) by way of the fundamental arrangement (*mūlanikkhepa*), because all other possible arrangements are included therein.
Herein, this is the word-meaning: *nikkhepa* is laying down; the laying down of a discourse is *suttanikkhepa*, meaning the teaching of a discourse.
Alternatively, that which is laid down is a *nikkhepa*; the discourse itself as the thing laid down is *suttanikkhepa*. *Attajjhāsaya* means one’s own inclination;
it is called *attajjhāsaya* because that [inclination] exists in him as its cause. Or, it is that which has his own inclination.
Or it is according to one's own inclination (*attajjhāsayo*). The same method applies to the inclination of others (*parajjhāsayo*).

"Control by question" (*pucchāvaso*) means that which has such control; thus, it is "dependent on a question" (*pucchāvasiko*). The arising of the meaning that serves as the basis for the teaching of the discourse is "arising of meaning" (*atthuppatti*);

"arising of meaning" itself is *aṭṭhuppatti*; that which possesses this is "dependent on an occasion" (*aṭṭhuppattiko*). Alternatively, it is called so because the discourse (*sutta*) is deposited by means of it.

The "presentation" (nikkhepa) consists precisely of one's own inclination and so forth. In this interpretation of the meaning, however, "one's own inclination" (*attajjhāsaya*) means the inclination of oneself;
"the inclination of others" (*parajjhāsaya*) means the inclination of others. That which is asked is an "inquiry" (*pucchā*), namely the matter to be asked about.
The speech of those who receive the teaching, proceeding by way of inquiry, is "based on inquiry" (*pucchāvasa*); that very thing, with regard to the word "presentation," [is what is meant].
"Pucchāvasika" (dependent on a question) is stated using the masculine gender. Likewise, "Aṭṭhuppattika" (arising from a specific occasion) should be understood here in the same sense.

Furthermore, in this context, it is appropriate that discourses arising from one's own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*) are established as independent suttas, because they proceed solely for the purpose of establishing the framework of the Dhamma through one's own inclination, without depending on causes such as the ripening of the faculties of others; whereas those dependent on the inclinations of others or on questions remain [categorized differently].

But how is it that there is no restriction regarding the *aṭṭhuppatti* (the arising of the subject matter) when it occurs upon the arising of questions concerning the inclinations of others—which serve as the cause for the unfolding of the teaching—or when it occurs through compliance with the inclinations of others, preceded by questions based on the *aṭṭhuppatti*?
This need not be questioned. For [the Buddha speaks] only of those instances entirely free from the determination of others’ intentions, inquiries, and so forth.

Because the arising of the cause for the delivery of a Sutta teaching is included under the category of "occasion-arising" (*aṭṭhuppatti*), those [teachings] dependent on the inquiries of others' inclinations are mentioned separately.
For instance, in the *Brahmajāla*, *Dhammadāyāda*, and other suttas, the occasion is said to be the motive for the teaching, such as praise or blame, or the acquisition of material goods;
whereas a teaching given by making one's own inclination the motive, without an inquiry from others, is called "dependent on another's inclination."
The meaning of "taught by way of questioning" (*pucchāvasika*) as being "that which is taught by way of a question" is well known.
In that regard, the first three Bodhi-suttas— the Mucalinda Sutta, the Āyu-saṅkhāra-ossajjana Sutta, and the Paccavekkhaṇa Sutta—
as well as the Papañca-saññā Sutta, are the compositions (*nikkhepa*) of these Udānas according to the Master’s own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*).
The *Huhuṅka-sutta*, the *Brāhmaṇajātaka-sutta*, and the *Bāhiya-sutta*— the delivery of these Udānas is occasioned by a question.
The *Rāja-sutta*, the *Sakkāra-sutta*, the *Ucchādana-sutta*, the *Piṇḍapātika-sutta*,
the *Sippa-sutta*, the *Gopāla-sutta*, the *Sundarika-sutta*, the *Mātu-sutta*, the *Saṅghabhedaka-sutta*, the *Udapāna-sutta*, and the *Tathāgatuppāda-sutta*.
The *Moneyyasutta*, the *Pāṭaligāmiyasutta*, and the two *Dabbasuttas*—these Udānas are presented as arising from specific occasions (*aṭṭhuppattika*).

The *Pālileyyasutta*, the *Piyasutta*, the *Nāgasamālasutta*, and the *Visākhāsutta*—these Udānas are presented according to the Teacher’s own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*) and the inclination of others (*parajjhāsaya*). As for the remaining fifty-one discourses, they are presented according to the inclination of others.

This is the laying down [of the Udānas]. Thus, the specific manner of the laying down of these Udānas should be understood by way of their being based on the Master’s own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*) and so forth.

And herein, those Udānas which were spoken by the Blessed One in the presence of the monks were, by them, mastered verbally as the suttas were spoken, examined mentally, and reported to the Dharma-treasurer (Ānanda). However, those [Udānas] which were spoken by the Blessed One...
It should be understood that those discourses spoken in the absence of the monks were later repeated by the Blessed One to the Dharma-treasurer (Ānanda).
Thus, the Venerable Ānanda, having collected all of them together, retained them in his memory and taught them to the monks;
subsequently, at the time of the First Great Council, he included them in the compilation under the very title "Udāna."
Regarding the phrase "Tena kho pana samayena" and so forth: *tena samayena* is an instrumental case used in the sense of a locative;
*kho pana* is a particle; the meaning is "at that time. At what time?
At the time when the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having just attained full enlightenment. At that time.
"Seven days" (*sattāhaṃ*) means seven days (*satta ahāni*), that is, a period of seven days; this is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).

Because the Blessed One dwelt during those seven days in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) with uninterrupted continuity, it is therefore stated as the accusative case by way of continuous connection.
"In one sitting" (*ekapallaṅkena*): on the full moon day of Visākha, even before the sun had set...
From the time he sat upon the supreme Aparājita throne, the Vajrāsana, until the sun [set], he did not rise even once,
but remained in a single cross-legged posture just as he had assumed it.
"Experiencing the bliss of liberation" means he sat experiencing the bliss of liberation, which is the bliss of the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*).

The meaning is "it occurs. In that context, "liberation" (*vimutti*) refers to five kinds of liberation: liberation by way of substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-vimutti*), suppression-liberation (*vikkhambhana-vimutti*), eradication-liberation (*samuccheda-vimutti*), tranquillization-liberation (*paṭippassaddhi-vimutti*), and escape-liberation (*nissaraṇa-vimutti*).

Among these, [the liberation] which—by means of those various factors of virtue such as the relinquishing of the objects of giving, and by means of the factors of insight such as the discernment of name-and-form, up to the point of each respective factor—...
Abandoning is liberation because of being liberated from each respective opposite through its occurrence by way of non-retrogression.

For example: by means of giving, from stinginess, greed, and so forth; by means of virtue, from killing living beings and so forth; by means of the discernment of name-and-form, from the view of a self-existent body (sakkāyadiṭṭhi);
and by means of the investigation of conditions, from the views of no-cause and irregular cause. Subsequently to that very [investigation],...
By the overcoming of doubt, one is freed from the state of being a sceptic; by the comprehension of groups (*kalāpasammasana*), one is freed from the grasping "I" and "mine";

by the determination of what is and is not the path, one is freed from the perception of a path where there is no path; by the vision of arising, one is freed from the annihilationist view; by the vision of passing away, one is freed from the eternalist view;

by the vision of danger, one is freed from the perception of safety where there is danger; by the vision of disadvantage, one is freed from the perception of gratification; and by the contemplation of disenchantment...
Liberation by way of substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgavimutti*) is as follows: through the perception of delight, there is liberation from the desire for deliverance;

through the knowledge of the desire for deliverance, there is liberation from the lack of desire for deliverance; through the knowledge of equanimity, there is liberation from the lack of equanimity; and through conformity (*anuloma*), there is liberation from the state of opposition to the stability of phenomena and to Nibbāna.

Through the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*), there is liberation from the state of being the sign of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*). Furthermore, that which occurs by means of concentration—distinguished as access and absorption—up to its...

The occurrence by way of non-decline, which is the liberation characterized by the non-arising of the hindrances such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and other opposing states such as applied thought (*vitakka*),

is called "liberation by suppression" (*vikkhambhana-vimutti*). That which, through the cultivation of the four noble paths, occurs accordingly within the continuum of the Noble One who possesses those respective paths—
as described in the passage beginning, "for the abandoning of speculative views" (*diṭṭhigatānaṃ pahānāya*)— is [liberation by eradication].

The liberation through the complete non-occurrence of the group of defilements belonging to the side of origination—which were previously stated according to the method—by way of their total eradication, is called "liberation by eradication" (*samuccheda-vimutti*).

Furthermore, that state of the defilements being subsided at the moment of the fruit is called "liberation by subsidence" (*paṭippassaddhi-vimutti*). Because it has escaped from all conditioned things...

However, Nibbāna, which is liberated from all conditioned phenomena, is called liberation as escape (*nissaraṇavimutti*). Here, however, the liberation as fruition (*phalavimutti*) having Nibbāna as its object is intended by the Blessed One. Therefore it was said:
“Experiencing the bliss of liberation” means he sits experiencing the bliss of liberation, that is, the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).

"Liberation" (*vimutti*) refers to the state of the mind being liberated by way of the subsiding of the secondary defilements (*upakkilesa*), or it should be understood as the mind itself thus liberated.
"Liberation-bliss" (*vimuttisukha*) is the pleasure that has arisen from or is associated with that liberation.
Furthermore, because of the statement, "Venerable sir, this equanimity (*upekkhā*) which has been called 'bliss' by the Blessed One when [the mind] is at peace," equanimity is also included here.
It should be understood as pleasure (*sukha*) itself. And so it is stated in the *Sammohavinodanī*: "But equanimity (*upekkhā*), because of its peacefulness, is spoken of as pleasure.
For the Blessed One enters the attainment of Arahantship belonging to the fourth jhāna, and not the other [types].
Alternatively, it is just as in such passages as "The subsiding of those [formations] is pleasant," where the subsiding of the suffering of formations is called "pleasant."

Thus, because it is the state of the subsiding of all defilements and suffering, it should be understood that here "happiness" refers specifically to the liberation-by-tranquillization (paṭippassaddhi-vimutti) obtained at the fruit of arahantship.

This happiness of liberation is twofold, distinguished by its occurrence either during the course of the path or at a later time, according to the arising of the fruition-consciousness. For immediately after each noble path, there arises [the corresponding] fruition...
Two or three resultant consciousnesses, having Nibbāna as their object, arise because they are the immediate results of supramundane wholesome states (*lokuttara-kusala*).
For in that impulsion series (*javana-vāra*) where the Noble Path arises, when there are two moments of conformity (*anuloma*),
then the third is the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*), the fourth is the path-consciousness (*maggacitta*), and after that, there are three resultant consciousnesses.

When, however, there are three conformities (anuloma), then the fourth is the change-of-lineage (gotrabhu), the fifth is the path-consciousness (magga-citta), and after that there are two fruition-consciousnesses (phala-citta).
Thus, the fourth and fifth occur by way of absorption (appanā); beyond that, they do not, because of the proximity to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
Some, however, say that "even the sixth consciousness enters absorption"; this [view] is [refuted] in the Commentaries (aṭṭhakathā).
[This] is rejected. Thus should the fruit be understood in the context of the path-process.

As for the fruit that occurs at another time, it is included by this very [explanation] as that which proceeds by way of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), and that which arises in one emerging from cessation (*nirodha*).
This attainment of fruition, however, should be regarded in its actual meaning as a absorption (*appanā*) consisting of the result of supramundane wholesome states, having Nibbāna as its object.
Who attains these, and who does not? All worldlings (*puthujjana*) do not attain them because they have not yet reached them.

Likewise, lower noble ones (*ariya*) do not attain the higher [attainments], nor do higher noble ones attain the lower ones, because those states have become stilled through their transition into the status of another type of person (*puggalantara*).
Each of those noble ones attains only their own respective fruit. However, some say that stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*)...
They say, "They do not attain the fruition-attainments; they attain only the two higher ones because of their state of being fulfillers of concentration.
That is not a valid reason, because even an ordinary person can attain the mundane concentration he himself has acquired. Or rather, what is the point of investigating the reason here?
For this is stated in the *Paṭisambhidā*: "What are the ten equanimities regarding formations?"

In the answers to these questions—"They arise by way of insight; which ten change-of-lineage states arise by way of insight?"—the attainment of the fruit of fruition for those noble ones is mentioned, namely, for the sake of attaining the fruit of stream-entry and for the sake of attaining the fruit of once-returning.
Therefore, all noble ones [attain] according to their respective [fruit].
One must conclude that they enter these fruits [of the path].
But why do they enter them? For the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*).
Just as kings experience the pleasure of sovereignty and deities experience divine bliss, so too the Noble Ones, thinking, "We shall experience supramundane bliss," set a limit for their duration.
Having done so, they enter the attainment of fruition at the desired moment.
How is its entry, how its maintenance, and how its emergence? First, its entry occurs in two ways:
by not attending to any object other than Nibbāna, and by attending to Nibbāna. As it is said:

“There are, friends, two conditions for the attainment of the signless deliverance of mind: non-attention to all signs and attention to the signless element. This, moreover, is the procedure for attaining it:

a noble disciple who maintains the attainment of fruition, having gone into seclusion and retired to a solitary place, should practice insight into formations by way of their arising and passing away. For him, as he thus proceeds with successive insight...
Immediately after the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) which has formations as its object, the mind enters into cessation by way of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti).
Due to the inclination toward the attainment of fruition, even for one still in training (sekkha), only the fruit arises, not the path. However, some say:

"A stream-enterer (sotāpanna), having developed insight with the thought 'I shall attain my own attainment of fruition,' becomes a once-returner (sakadāgāmī); and a once-returner likewise becomes a non-returner (anāgāmī)."
They should be told: "If that were so, it would follow that a non-returner would become an arahant, an arahant a paccekabuddha, and a paccekabuddha a fully enlightened Buddha (sambuddha).
Therefore, since insight accomplishes its purpose according to one's inclination and intention, even for a trainee (sekha) only the fruit arises, not the path.
And as for his fruit, if by him [the path] belonging to the first jhāna..."
When the path is attained, it arises with the first jhāna alone; if it is associated with any one of the second jhānas and so forth, it arises with that particular jhāna.
But why is it that, in this case, change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhu-ñāṇa) does not have Nibbāna as its object, as path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) does when it precedes it?
Because the knowledges of fruition lack the quality of leading out (niyyānika). For it is only the states of the Noble Path that lead out; indeed, this has been said:
"Which states lead out? The four Noble Paths, which are not included [in the mundane].

Therefore, by means of the knowledge that serves as the proximate condition for the state of leading out—which occurs through the emergence from both sides—one must emerge from the sign (nimitta) with absolute certainty.
It is logical that "it must be developed" refers to its having Nibbāna as its object; however, because the Noble Path has already been developed,
the preliminary knowledge (purecārika-ñāṇa) of the fruition-knowledges— which do not eradicate the defilements existing as its resultants,
which are non-emancipating, and whose nature is not to emerge— never at any time has Nibbāna as its object in either case, [just as] with the conformity knowledges (anuloma-ñāṇa).

By way of incomparable mode: for within the course of the Noble Path, the conformities of knowledge (*anuloma-ñāṇa*) arise—conducive to the knowledge of the path and reaching the highest perfection of mundane knowledge—by means of the exceedingly powerful shattering of the gross aggregates of greed and so forth that have never before been pierced.
However, in the course of the attainment of fruition (*phala-samāpatti*), those various defilements [are abandoned] by each respective path.

Because they have been completely cut off there, these [formations] arise merely as preliminary preparations for the state of possessing the bliss of the Noble Ones’ attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), and thus there is no possibility of emerging from them anywhere;

for it is at their conclusion that knowledge, having emerged from the sign of formations (*saṅkhāranimitta*), may have Nibbāna as its object. And having established this for one in training (*sekkha*)...
Furthermore, for one who comprehends formations by way of their arising and passing away,

etc., for the purpose of entering the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), it is established that only the fruit arises according to the sequence of insight-knowledge, and not the path. In this way, first of all,
the entering of the attainment of fruition should be understood.
“There are, friends, three conditions for the maintenance of the signless deliverance of mind: non-attention to all signs, attention to the signless element, and prior volitional formation.
Because of this statement, its maintenance occurs in three ways. In this context, “prior volitional formation” refers to the delimitation of time prior to the attainment;
for it is delimited by the thought: “I shall emerge at such-and-such a time.”
As long as that time does not arrive, there is no emergence from it.

However, according to the statement: “There are two conditions, friends, for emerging from the signless deliverance of mind: attention to all signs and non-attention to the signless element,” its emergence occurs in two ways.
In this context, “all signs” refers to the signs of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Granted that one does not attend to all these [factors] together at once, this has nevertheless been stated by way of a comprehensive inclusion.
Therefore, emergence from the attainment of fruition occurs through attending to that which is the object of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga);
thus should its emergence be understood. And so, this entering upon and emerging from the attainment here consists in the fruit of Arahantship.
“With distress stilled, beautiful with the deathless as its object, having cast off the bait of the world, peaceful—this is the supreme fruit of recluseship.

Thus it was said that he experienced the bliss of liberation, which is exceedingly sweet. Therefore it is said: “Experiencing the bliss of liberation” means he sat experiencing the bliss of liberation, the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
Now, *atha* is a particle used in the sense of introduction (*adhikāra*). *Ko* is for the purpose of completing the metrical line (*padapūraṇe*).

Among these, by means of this word *atha* in the sense of introduction, he shows an introduction other than the experience of the bliss of liberation. But what is this? It is the mental attention (*manasikāra*) directed toward dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
Alternatively, *atha* is a particle used in the sense of "afterwards" (*pacchā*); thus, it illuminates the very meaning that is about to be stated: "At the end of those seven days."

"Of that seven-day period" means of the seven days of the cross-legged posture (*pallaṅka*). "With the passing" means with the elapse. "From that concentration" means from the concentration of the fruit of Arhatship.
Now, some have explained those [periods] in detail, saying that standing here, seven seven-day periods must be shown in succession.
We, however, shall explain them later by way of showing their non-contradiction with this *Udāna* text through the reading of the *Khandhaka*.

We shall explain [this]. "Of the night" (*rattiyā*) is the genitive case (*sāmivacana*) expressing a relationship of parts. "The first" (*paṭhamaṃ*) is the accusative case (*upayogavacana*) used in the sense of continuous connection (*accantasamyoga*).
For the Blessed One was engaged with that very same mental attention throughout the entire first watch of that night.

"Dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) refers to the phenomena that serve as conditions (*paccayadhamma*). For ignorance and the other factors are the phenomena that constitute dependent origination.
If it is asked, "How is this to be known? it is by the word of the Blessed One. For the Blessed One has stated that ignorance and the rest are the causes, saying:
"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for aging-and-death, namely birth...
[and so on] ...for volitional formations, namely ignorance. Thus, just as there are twelve conditions, there are twelve factors of dependent origination.

Herein, this is the etymological analysis (*vacanattha*): it is *paṭiccasamuppāda* because, having depended upon one another—that is, having turned toward one another—it brings about an arising in combination without rejecting the collection of causes.
Alternatively, *paṭicca* means having gone toward a condition that is to be understood as such, worthy of being a condition;
thus, an arising that occurs through a connection not devoid of that [condition] is *paṭiccasamuppāda*. This is what is meant by "dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

And here, "dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) should be understood as a cause (*hetu*)—to be known by the expression "arising together"—which is capable of producing a fruit; it is not to be understood as mere dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppattimatta*).

Alternatively, it is "dependent" (*paṭicco*) because the wise are worthy (*arahanti*) to depend upon it, and it is "origination" (*samuppādo*) because it arises rightly by itself; thus, being both dependent and origination, it is "dependent origination."
The meaning here should be understood in this way.

"In forward order" (*anuloma*): the mode of conditionality beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*), stated by way of the formula "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," etc., is called "forward order" because it performs the function that each respective factor is to perform.
Alternatively, it is so called because it is stated starting from the beginning and carried through to the end.
"Conformable" means conformable to the process [of dependent origination]; that is "conformity. "He attended to it thoroughly" means he gave it careful attention.

Whatever condition-dhamma is a condition for whatever conditionally arisen dhamma, and in whatever way—by way of being a cause-condition and so forth—he reflected upon all of that without error, without omission, and without remainder by way of reviewing.
The meaning is "he brought to mind. To show briefly how the Blessed One brought to mind the forward order of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppādānuloma*), it was said:
"Thus, when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.
In this context, "thus" (*iti*) means "in this way," that is, by this manner. "When this exists, that comes to be" refers to when ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth exist...
"When this condition exists, this result—beginning with volitional formations—comes to be.
"With the arising of this, this arises" means that with the arising of this condition, beginning with ignorance, this result, beginning with volitional formations, arises.
"When this is absent, this does not come to be; with the cessation of this, this ceases" means that in the absence of ignorance and the rest, volitional formations and the rest [do not arise].

By means of the statements in the second and third suttas regarding the cessation of volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) and so forth upon the cessation of ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth, a restriction is shown in this characteristic of conditionality:
"only when this exists, not when it does not exist; only through the arising of this, not through its non-arising;
only through its non-cessation, not through its cessation. Therefore, this characteristic includes within itself that restriction here.
It should be understood that this was stated regarding dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
"Cessation" (*nirodha*) refers to the non-arising and non-occurrence in the future of ignorance and the other factors through the attainment of their fading away (*virāga*). For it has been said:

"With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations," and so forth. And the "cessation of cessation" is spoken of by way of the cessation of arising, as in: "With the cessation of this, that ceases."
This shows that non-cessation is what is called arising, and that here it is also termed "existence.

For the very characteristic expressed as "when this exists, that comes to be" is qualified by the former [phrase] when another person states it by way of a synonym as "with the arising of this, that arises.
Therefore, it is not with reference to mere persistence that it is said, "when this..."
It is stated, "when this exists," yet it is understood that there is also the state of not being ceased by means of the path.
And because, when providing the exposition for the characteristic taught in both ways—as "When this does not exist, this does not come to be;
with the cessation of this, this ceases"—[the Buddha] said, "But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease," and so forth, [cessation is established].

Thus it has been said; therefore, since even non-existence (*natthibhāva*) is cessation (*nirodha*), it is shown that existence (*atthibhāva*), which is the opposite of non-existence, is non-cessation (*anirodha*).
By means of this existence termed "non-cessation," he distinguishes [it] from arising (*uppāda*).
Consequently, the meaning intended here is not merely the state of existence as arising, but rather existence as characterized by non-cessation.
"This meaning has been clarified. Thus, it should be understood that this statement of the two characteristics is purposeful by way of their mutual relationship as qualifier and qualified.
But what is this "non-cessation" (anirodha) which is called both "existence" (atthibhāva) and "arising" (uppāda)? It is the state of not having been abandoned.
And there is the non-arising of fruits due to the non-abandonment of those things that ought to have produced fruit but did not;

for there is the state of those unwholesome phenomena which ought to be abandoned not having been eradicated by the Noble Path, and the state of the fetters regarding those wholesome and indeterminate phenomena which ought not to be abandoned not having been fully exhausted in those whose taints are not yet destroyed. This is due to the state of underlying tendencies (anusaya) not having been eradicated.
For dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is the occurrence of the aggregates accompanied by fetters (*saṃyojana*). And thus it has been said:
"Monks, that ignorance by which the fool is shrouded, and that craving with which he is associated—by these this body has come to be.
That very ignorance of the fool is not abandoned, and that craving is not exhausted. Why is that?"
"What is the cause? It is because, monks, the fool did not practice the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering;
therefore, with the breakup of the body, the fool becomes subject to a [new] body. Being subject to a body, he is not liberated from birth, aging, and death," and so forth.

However, for those whose fetters are exhausted, due to the absence of ignorance, volitional formations do not arise; and due to the absence of craving and clinging, grasping and becoming cannot occur. Thus, the cutting off of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) will be discerned. For this very reason, it was said:

“Phagguna, through the remainderless fading away and cessation of the six bases of contact, there is the cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling,” and so forth.
For it is not the case that the six sense-bases (*saḷāyatana*) and the rest do not function from the attainment of the supreme path until final *parinibbāna*.
Rather, their non-existence—the state expressible by the word “cessation” and the exhaustion of the fetters—is what is called “cessation. Furthermore, even that which was done long ago...
Kamma is called "fit for fruit" precisely because its fruit has not yet been produced and its nutriment has not yet been abandoned;

it is not that which has already produced fruit, nor is it that whose nutriment has already been abandoned. The state of being fit for fruit—consisting of ignorance, volitional formations, and so forth, which are the conditions for the arising of the fruit—should be understood as "non-cessation" in the manner already described. For it is by this very state of non-cessation that [the kamma]...
Without the fruit, it does not come to be; that cause, even though past, is expressed by the phrase "when this exists.

For that very reason, the arising of conditions—which has not yet entered the state of non-occurrence for one whose holy life (*brahmacariya*) is unfulfilled—is said to be the arising of this [fruit] precisely for the sake of non-retrogression, without taking into account a difference in time.
Alternatively, when the remaining conditions are assembled...
The state of being oriented toward the arising of a fruit—whether for that which does not yet exist, or even more so for that which already exists—is what is called its "arising" (uppāda).

For indeed, because the fruit arises from it, the cause, when it has reached that specific state, is said to have "risen" (uppatita) in the sense of having stood up (uṭṭhita) to produce the fruit. Thus, arising should be understood as being in that specific state; it is not merely existing while not in that state.
In this context, by the phrase "when there is" (*sati*), he shows the non-agency of dependent origination by stating that it functions as a condition merely by way of its existence.

By the phrase "with arising" (*uppādā*), he shows the impermanence of dependent origination by indicating that it is subject to the nature of arising, does not exist at all times, and is oriented toward the production of its fruit.
Furthermore, the statement "when there is, not when there is not; with arising, not with cessation" [is said].

This demonstrates the state of being the source (*nidāna*), origin (*samudaya*), birth (*jāti*), and arising (*pabhava*) of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) by means of locative and ablative case endings having the sense of cause (*hetuattha*).

Here, the fact that the locative endings have the sense of cause should be understood as referring to the occurrence [of the result] in that which, when present, characterizes the presence of a result invariably concomitant with it;
just as in the expression, "when wealth is not bestowed upon those who are poor, poverty [persists]."
And [it is said]: "It went to abundance," and "When the crops have ripened, a good harvest arises.
Even in the case of an ablative expression, it has the sense of a cause, because it occurs in the sense of the origin of a fruit and in its primary sense; as in:

"From the *kalala* comes the *abbuda*, from the *abbuda* is born the *pesī*," and "The Ganges originates from the Himavat, the lake is born from the peak. This applies to states such as ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth.
Furthermore, because of the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with that [ignorance], the state of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) and so forth is characterized;
and since volitional formations and the rest arise and are manifested by ignorance and the other factors, these [latter] are their source (*pabhava*) and their nature (*pakati*).

Therefore, in order to illuminate this meaning, the locative case with the elision of the particle (*nissakka*) is employed in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), as in: "When this exists, through the arising of this..."
And because here, following the brief statement of dependent origination as "When this exists, that comes to be;

with the arising of this, that arises," there follows the detailed exposition beginning with "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," it is understood that the aforementioned existence and arising constitute the state of being conditions for those various phenomena that have arisen dependently. For indeed, [the state of being a condition] is not merely the fact of not having ceased...
Apart from the state of existence and arising— which are characterized as having an irreversible nature or as being in the state of origination—
and which are expressed by statements containing the restrictive conditions "only when present, not when absent" and "only when arising,
not when ceasing," there is no other such thing as a causal relation; therefore, the aforementioned state of existence and arising constitute the causal relation.

This should be understood. Furthermore, those twenty-four conditions beginning with "cause" (hetu) that appear in the *Paṭṭhāna* should also be understood as specific varieties of this very state of being a condition.
Thus, in order to show how he attended to dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) in detail according to its direct order (*anuloma*), it was said:
"That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," and so forth.

In this context, *yadidaṃ* is a particle; its meaning is "that which. Regarding the phrase *avijjāpaccayā* and so forth: ignorance (*avijjā*) is so called because it finds (*vindati*) that which is not to be found (*avindiya*), such as bodily misconduct;
it is ignorance because it does not find that which is to be found (*vindiya*), such as bodily good conduct; it is ignorance because it renders the non-perverted nature of phenomena unknown;
and it is ignorance because it causes sentient beings to rush (*javāpeti*) through existence and the other states within the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) which is devoid of end.

It is called *avijjā* (ignorance) because it flows toward things that do not exist and does not flow toward things that do exist; it is called *avijjā* because it is the opposite of *vijjā* (knowledge).

It should be understood as fourfold, beginning with "lack of knowledge regarding suffering. A *paccaya* (condition) is so called because it goes toward (*eti*) its fruit—that is, it arises and occurs—dependent upon (*paṭicca*) and not without [the cause];
or else, *paccaya* has the sense of being helpful. Thus, it is both ignorance and a condition, hence *avijjā-paccaya*.
Ignorance is the condition; therefore, "with ignorance as condition. They form, thus they are "formations" (*saṅkhārā*);

these are mundane wholesome and unwholesome volitions, which should be understood as threefold according to the formations of merit, demerit, and the imperturbable. It cognizes, thus it is "consciousness" (*viññāṇa*); that is thirty-two-fold according to mundane resultant consciousness.
It bends toward, thus it is "name" (*nāma*); this refers to the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling. It is affected, thus it is "form" (*rūpa*); this refers to derived form.
And the derived matter of the eye and so forth. It is called an *āyatana* because it stretches out (*āyatati*) and leads to the suffering of saṃsāra.

It is called contact (*phassa*) because it touches (*phusati*). It is called feeling (*vedanā*) because it feels (*vedayati*). This pair is sixfold by way of the doors; when taken by way of result (*vipāka*), it is thirty-sixfold.
It is called craving (*taṇhā*) because it causes agitation (*paritassati*); it is briefly threefold by way of craving for sense-pleasures and so forth, and in detail—
And it is of one hundred and eight kinds. It is called *upādāna* because it is grasped; it is fourfold by way of the clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*) and so forth.
It is called *bhava* because it comes into being (*bhavati*) and it causes to come into being (*bhāvayati*); it is twofold according to the distinction between karma and rebirth.
*Jāti* is birth. *Jarā* is aging. *Maraṇa* is that by which beings die. *Soka* is sorrowing. *Parideva* is lamentation. *Dukkha* is that which afflicts.

It is called *dukkha* because it cuts (*khaṇati*) in two ways by way of arising and by way of persisting. *Domanassa* is the state of being dejected (*dumana*). *Upāyāsa* is intense distress (*āyāsa*).
"Sambhavanti" means they are produced (*nibbattanti*). And not only with the words beginning with "sorrow" (*soka*), but rather the word "sambhavanti" should be construed with every preceding term.
For thus [it is said]: "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) arise."
The determination of conditions and conditionally arisen phenomena has thus been shown.

This same method applies everywhere. In this context, ignorance (avijjā) is characterized by unknowing; its function is delusion; it is manifested as concealment; and its proximate cause is the taints (āsava).
Volitional formations (saṅkhārā) are characterized by the act of forming; their function is accumulation; they are manifested as the process of directing; and their proximate cause is ignorance.
Consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing; its function is to precede [the other mental factors]; it is manifested as rebirth-linking;

its proximate cause is volitional formations, or alternatively, the physical basis and the object. Name has the characteristic of bending toward [an object]; its function is association; it is manifested as inseparability;
its proximate cause is consciousness. Matter has the characteristic of being affected (resistance); its function is dispersal; it is manifested as the state that cannot be avoided.

Consciousness has its proximate cause in the mind-base. The six sense bases have the characteristic of being a sphere; their function is seeing and so forth; they are manifested as the state of being the physical basis and the door;
and they have name-and-form as their proximate cause. Contact has the characteristic of touching; its function is impingement; it is manifested as conjunction;

and it has the six sense bases as its proximate cause. Feeling has the characteristic of experiencing; its function is the enjoyment of the flavor of the object; it is manifested as pleasure and pain.

Craving has contact as its proximate cause; it is characterized by the state of being a cause, has the function of relishing, is manifested as the state of insatiability, and has feeling as its proximate cause.
Grasping is characterized by seizing; it has the function of non-relinquishing, is manifested as intensified craving and views, and has craving as its proximate cause.
Becoming is characterized by karma and the fruit of karma; it has the function of bringing about existence, and is manifested as wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states.
It has clinging as its proximate cause. Birth is characterized by the initial manifestation in this or that state of existence; its function is to bring forth;
it is manifested as having arisen here from a past existence, or it is manifested as the diversity of suffering. Aging is characterized by the maturation of the aggregates;
its function is to lead toward death; it is manifested as the destruction of youth. Death is characterized by the passing away; its function is dissociation.
It has the manifestation of being separated from one's destination. Sorrow has the characteristic of inward brooding; its function is the brooding of the mind; it manifests as constant grieving.
Lamentation has the characteristic of wailing; its function is the proclaiming of virtues and faults; it manifests as agitation. Pain has the characteristic of bodily affliction;
its function is producing mental distress in those lacking wisdom; it manifests as physical ailment. [Suffering] has the characteristic of mental affliction.
Grief has the characteristic of mental distress, the function of afflicting the mind, and is manifested as a mental ailment.

Despair has the characteristic of burning the heart, the function of groaning, and is manifested as dejection. Thus, these factors beginning with ignorance should be understood by way of their characteristics and so forth.
This is the summary here; however, for one desiring a detailed exposition complete in all its aspects, [it should be sought] from the *Sammohavinodanī*.

It should be understood from the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*. "Of this" (*etassa*) refers to what has been stated above. "Of the whole" (*kevalassa*) means unmixed or complete. [The term *dukkhakkhandha* is explained as follows: It is called a "mass" (*khandha*) because it is a heap (*rāsi*), a collection (*puñja*), a multitude (*nikāya*), a flow (*pabandha*), and a continuity (*santati*). It is called "suffering" (*dukkha*) because it is painful (*dukkha*), hard to bear (*duruddhara*), difficult to endure (*dussaha*), and disagreeable (*appiyarūpa*). It is the origin of the aggregate of suffering, not of a sentient being (*satta*), nor of a soul (*jīva*), nor of beauty, pleasure, and so forth.
"There is an origin" means that there is an arising or a coming-to-be.
"Having understood this matter" refers to this fact: that there is an origin of the mass of suffering beginning with volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) by way of ignorance (*avijjā*) and the rest.
It is said to "occur" because this matter was understood in every aspect. "At that time" means at the time when that matter had been understood.

"He uttered this *udāna*" means he uttered this—beginning with "When indeed they become manifest"—which illuminates the power of the knowledge of both the cause and the phenomenon arisen from the cause, and which is originated by wisdom associated with joy, once that matter had been understood.
"He uttered an *udāna*" means he let out a voice of joy.
Its meaning is as follows: *yadā* means "at which time. *Hava* is a particle used in the sense of "one who is skilled" (*byatta*).
Some, however, explain the meaning as "in *hava*, that is, in battle (*āhave yuddhe*)," based on the statement: "Fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom."
Their intention is that this refers to the time of battling with the Māra of the defilements (*kilesamāra*). "Manifesting" means arising.

"Dhammas" refers to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*) which accomplish the penetration of the modes of conditions in their forward order (*anulomapaccayākāra*). Alternatively, "manifesting" means they reveal themselves;
through the process of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), they become distinct and evident. "Dhammas" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths; "ardor" (*ātāpa*) is what is being spoken of.
Viriya (energy) is so called in the sense of burning away the defilements (*kilesa*). "Ardent" (*ātāpī*) means one who possesses the energy of the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*).

"Meditating" (*jhāyato*) means for one who is meditating by means of contemplation upon the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) and contemplation upon the characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*). "Of the brahmin" (*brāhmaṇassa*) means of one who has banished evil, whose taints (*āsava*) are exhausted.

"Then all his doubts fade away" (*atha-ssa kaṅkhā vapayanti sabbā*) means that for such a person in whom the Dhamma has thus become manifest, whatever these doubts may be—"O Bhante, who indeed... [and so forth].
“‘It touches,’ [the Blessed One said]. ‘That is not a proper question,’ the Blessed One replied,” and so forth;

and by the method beginning with, “What now, Bhante, is aging-and-death, and to whom does this aging-and-death belong? ‘That is not a proper question,’ the Blessed One replied,” and so forth, doubt regarding the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*) has been stated.
And because that very mode of conditions has not been penetrated, [one wonders]: “Did I exist in the past?”... [and so on].
The sixteen doubts have come forth in the passage beginning with, "I [regard] the past time," and so on.
All of these vanish, depart, and cease. Why? Because one understands phenomena together with their causes;

that is, because one understands, knows, and penetrates this entire mass of suffering—consisting of volitional formations and the like—as being accompanied by its cause, such as ignorance and so forth.
But when do the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) or the factors of the Four Noble Truths become manifest, arise, or are revealed?

It is in the knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of the path (magga-ñāṇa). Therein, mindfulness and the other factors associated with insight-knowledge, as well as insight-knowledge itself, abandon the perception of beauty and so forth within their respective objects through the method of abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna), by way of the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) and the rest.

They arise individually; however, at the moment of the Path, having taken Nibbāna as their object, they abandon the opposites by way of total eradication and arise all at once as the means for achieving unconfused penetration into the four Noble Truths.
Thus, in this context, the manifestation of the factors conducive to enlightenment should be understood in the sense of their arising.

However, the manifestation (*pātubhāva*) of the Noble Truths should be understood in the sense of their being made manifest (*pakāsanaṭṭhena*): at the moment of insight, by way of making them the object of insight for mundane truths;
by way of being intent upon them for supramundane truths; at the moment of the Path, by way of the clear realization of the object, which is the Truth of Cessation;
and for all of them, by way of the clear realization of their function.
Thus, although all phenomena were manifest to his own knowledge in every respect, because he had applied himself to insight through the gateway of dependent origination,
and because the mode of conditions is subtle, profound, and very difficult to see, the Blessed One— having reflected upon that and having experienced a powerful joy of mind arising therefrom—
uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) here, which serves to illustrate the power of his own realization by way of revealing the eradication of opposing factors.
The textual passage, "This *udāna* too was spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard," is found only in certain manuscripts.

In this context, the word "too" (*api*) has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍana*), as in such examples as "this jewel of the Buddha is sublime" or "this one is also one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.

By means of it, he includes what follows. As for the word "spoken" (*vutta*): this term "spoken" functions as a designation for the state of being shaved, plucked, sown, planted, leveled, lived, maintained, liberated, and uttered.

It is seen in such contexts as "causing to proceed," "recitation," and "speaking. Indeed, it occurs in the sense of "shaving" in passages such as, "The young brahmin student Kāpaṭika, with his head shorn. It also occurs in the sense of "sown" in the verse:
"Cattle are born from him; what is sown in his field flourishes;
he who does not betray his friends eats the fruit of what has been sown."
In such cases as these, it refers to sowing. In passages such as “nor has it been ploughed back,” it refers to the leveling of the ground for sowing by means of the eight-fold staff and so forth.
In passages such as “with hair fallen out, living on what is given by others, dwelling with a mind become like that of a deer,” it refers to the maintenance of life.

In passages such as “the withered leaf, fallen from its bond, is incapable of greenness,” it refers to the state of being released from bondage. In passages such as “sung, spoken, or striven,” [it refers to that which has been uttered].

In the sense of being set forth as the True Word (*pāvacana*); in such passages as "The *Pārāyaṇa* has been spoken," it refers to study (*ajjhena*); in such passages as "This was indeed said by the Blessed One:
'Bhikkhus, be my heirs in the Dhamma, not my heirs in material things,'" it refers to speaking (*kathana*).
Here too, it should be understood as referring specifically to speaking; thus the meaning is that this *udāna* was also spoken. *Iti* means "thus. Regarding the two words *me sutaṃ*:
The meaning has already been stated in every respect in the commentary on the introduction (*nidāna*).

For the meaning that was previously stated by way of the introduction as "Thus have I heard" is here stated again by way of the conclusion as "So have I heard. Indeed, the restatement of a meaning already stated is called a conclusion (*nigamana*).
As for the word *iti*, its extraction of meaning is due to its being synonymous with the word *evaṃ* (thus).
Just as in the phrase "Thus have I heard," the application of the meaning has already been explained by us in the commentary on the *Itivuttaka*;
therefore, it should be understood according to the method stated therein.
[From] the *Paramatthadīpanī*, the Commentary on the Minor Collection (*Khuddakanikāya*).
The commentary on the first *Bodhi-sutta* of the *Udāna-vaṇṇanā* is finished.
2. Commentary on the second *Bodhi-sutta*.

Regarding the second [sutta], "in reverse order" (*paṭiloma*) refers to the sequence beginning with "from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations" (*avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodho*), which deals precisely with ignorance and the following factors.
The mode of condition (*paccayākāra*), while ceasing through non-arising and cessation, is called "reverse" because it does not perform its own function.

Or, it is "reverse" because it is contrary to the process of occurrence (*pavatti*). However, since it has not been stated starting from the end, the middle, or even the beginning and proceeding toward the start, no other sense of "reversal" is applicable here. And as for the term "reverse," it means "uneven" (*visamaṃ*).
This is a neuter locative designation, as in such passages as "the moon and sun revolve.

"When this does not exist, that does not come to be" means that when this condition—ignorance and so forth—is absent because it has been abandoned by the Path, this result—volitional formations and so forth—does not exist and does not proceed.
"With the cessation of this, that ceases" refers to this condition, ignorance and so forth.
Because it has been brought to a state of non-arising by means of the path through cessation, this fruit—consisting of formations and so forth—ceases;

the meaning is that it no longer proceeds. Here too, just as in the passage, "When this exists, this comes to be; with the arising of this, this arises," there is an implicit restriction to the effect that "only when this exists, and not when it does not exist; only with the arising of this, and not with its cessation."

Thus it should be understood that in this context, the characteristic of internal inclusion and determination—namely, "only when this is absent, not when it is present," and "only from the cessation of this, not from its arising"—has been shown.
Whatever else remains to be said here should be understood according to the method explained in the commentary on the *Paṭhamabodhi Sutta*.
Having thus briefly shown how the Blessed One attended to dependent origination in reverse order:
Now, in order to show this in detail, it is said: “With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations,” and so forth.
Therein, “with the cessation of ignorance” means with the cessation of ignorance without remainder by means of the Noble Path;

the meaning is that ignorance is completely eradicated by the final path through the abandoning of its underlying tendencies (*anusaya*). Even though the ignorance abandoned by the lower paths is indeed [abandoned] by way of complete eradication—
It is abandoned; nevertheless, it is not abandoned without remainder. For ignorance leading to the states of misery (apāya) is abandoned by the first path.

Likewise, ignorance that serves as the condition for rebirth everywhere in this world and in all the planes of the ignoble (anariya-bhūmi) is abandoned respectively by the second and third paths, and not otherwise. Indeed, [only] by the path of Arahantship...
"It is abandoned without remainder. "Cessation of formations" means the cessation through non-arising of formations.

To show that when formations have thus ceased, consciousness ceases because of the cessation of formations, and that name-and-form and the rest likewise cease because of the cessation of consciousness and so forth, he said: "With the cessation of formations, there is the cessation of consciousness," and so on; "In this way, for him..."
"...there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. Regarding this, what is to be said has already been stated according to the method explained above.

Furthermore, although the cessation of the entire mass of suffering without remainder is expressed even by the statement, "With the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness," nevertheless, just as...

In the forward order (*anuloma*), it is said, "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]... [and so on]... there is an origination," for the purpose of showing this meaning: that by the presence of whichever condition-dharma, whichever conditionally arisen dharma does not cease but rather proceeds.
Likewise, by way of its opposite, when each respective condition-dharma is absent, each respective conditionally arisen dharma [does not arise].
It is stated here, "With the cessation of ignorance there is the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations there is the cessation of consciousness...
[and so on] ...there is the cessation of the mass of suffering," for the purpose of showing that it ceases and does not proceed.

It is not, however, for the purpose of showing the cessation of the mass of suffering as comprised within the three times, as is the case in the forward order (anuloma). For it is only of the future [mass of suffering] that there is cessation through the cultivation of the Noble Path.
Furthermore, this distinction should be understood: that the cessation of the mass of suffering—which is liable to arise when it is absent—is desired through the cultivation of the Noble Path.

"Having understood this matter" means having understood in every aspect this matter which was stated as: "Through the cessation of ignorance, etc., there is the cessation of the mass of suffering beginning with volitional formations. "He uttered this exclamation" refers to this [context].

When the goal was known, he uttered an inspired utterance (udāna) that illustrates the power of his realization of the destruction of the conditions—ignorance and the rest—declared thus: "With the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations.
Herein, this is the summary meaning: because [he realized] the destruction of the conditions, ignorance and the rest, which is termed their non-arising and cessation...

He knew, he understood, he penetrated; therefore, for this brahmin who is ardent and meditating in the manner described, the factors conducive to enlightenment or the factors of the Four Truths of the type mentioned arise, appear, or become manifest.
Then, those doubts of the various kinds previously mentioned that might have arisen due to a lack of correct knowledge regarding the cessation of conditions—those [are now dispelled].
"All [these] vanish and cease. The remainder is exactly as explained below.
The commentary on the Second Bodhi Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Third Bodhi Sutta.
3. In the third [section], "in forward and reverse order" means both in forward order and in reverse order;

that is to say, by way of the forward order as previously stated and by way of the reverse order. But was it not already stated in two previous suttas that the application of attention to dependent origination occurs by way of both forward and reverse order?
Why, then, is the application of attention by way of both these orders mentioned again here?
Why is it so called? Because attention is applied there for a third time by way of both of those.

But how is attention applied by way of both? Is it not impossible to apply attention to dependent origination in forward and reverse order simultaneously, neither first nor last? This should not be viewed in that way; rather, [it is] "by way of both."

“...attended to it all at once,” but rather, he did so by turns. For the Blessed One, having first attended to dependent origination in forward order, uttered a first inspired utterance (udāna) corresponding to that.

Having again attended to it in reverse order, he uttered a second inspired utterance corresponding to that as well. But on the third turn, at one time [he attended to] the forward order and at another time—

He brought it to mind in direct and reverse order by way of reflecting in reverse. Therefore it was said: "In direct and reverse order" means both in direct and in reverse order, namely, by way of the aforementioned direct order and by way of the reverse order.
By this, the state of being proficient and strong, as well as mastery, of the mental application (manasikāra) is made manifest. And herein, "direct order..."

The distinction between these [mental applications] should be understood by way of the prior mental orientations (pubbābhoga) that occur thus: “I will attend [to it], I will attend to it in reverse order, I will attend to it in direct and reverse order.
In that context, “but of ignorance indeed” means “but of ignorance alone. “By the fading away and cessation” means by the path, which is designated as fading away (virāga).
"Unremaindered cessation" means the abandonment through the highest path (aggamagga) such that there is no further arising of anything whatsoever.
"Cessation of formations" (*saṅkhāranirodha*) is the remainderless cessation through non-arising of all formations.
For by the three lower paths, some formations cease while others do not, because ignorance has been ceased with a remainder; however, by the highest path, there is its remainderless cessation.
“No formations do not cease.

Having understood this matter: having understood in every aspect this matter which was stated as the arising and cessation of the mass of suffering beginning with formations through ignorance and so forth, and the arising and cessation of ignorance and so forth.

"He uttered this inspired utterance (udāna)" means: he uttered the aforementioned inspired utterance which illuminates the power of that Noble Path by which the meaning—consisting of the origin and cessation of the mass of suffering—was known through its function and through the act of taking it as an object. This is the meaning.
Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: When, indeed, phenomena become manifest to the ardent, meditating brahmin, then that brahmin,
by means of those arisen factors conducive to enlightenment— or rather, by means of that noble path through which the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths have become manifest—
stands dispelling Māra’s army with the words, “Sensual pleasures are your first army,” and so forth.
He stands dispelling, dispersing, and destroying the army of Māra described according to the method [previously stated].
How so? Just as the risen sun stands illuminating the sky with its own radiance while dispersing the darkness, even so does that Brahmin whose taints are exhausted stand by means of those qualities.
Or, by means of that noble path, he stands shaking off Māra’s army while penetrating the Truths.

Thus, these three udānas were spoken by the Blessed One during the three watches of the night: the first to proclaim the power of understanding the mode of conditions, the second the power of attaining the destruction of conditions, and the third the power of the noble path.
On which night? On the seventh night from his full enlightenment.

For on the night of the Visākha full moon, having recollected his past lives during the first watch, purified the divine eye during the middle watch, and applied his knowledge to dependent origination during the last watch, the Blessed One contemplated the conditioned phenomena of the three planes through various methods; then, as dawn was breaking—
Thinking, “The dawn will break,” he attained supreme enlightenment; and at the very moment he reached omniscience, the dawn rose.

Then, remaining on that same seat at the foot of the Bodhi tree for seven days, when the night of the first day of the fortnight had arrived, he reflected upon dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) during the three watches of the night according to the method already described, and uttered these inspired utterances (*udāna*) in their proper sequence.
Furthermore, because it is stated in all three sections of the *Khandhaka* that "he attended to dependent origination in forward and reverse order," the *Khandhaka-aṭṭhakathā* explains:
"Having thus attended to it during all three watches of the night— the first [udāna] by way of reflecting on the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*),
the second by way of reflecting on Nibbāna, and the third by way of reflecting on the Path— thus these..."
It has been said, “The Blessed One uttered inspired utterances (udāna),” and this too is not contradictory.
For during the six weeks following the seven days spent in the Jewel House, the Blessed One dwelt for the most part reviewing the Dhamma from time to time, experiencing the bliss of liberation;
however, during the seven days in the Jewel House, he dwelt solely through his mastery of the Abhidhamma.
The commentary on the Third Bodhi Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Huṃhuṅka Sutta:
Regarding "at the Goatherds’ Banyan Tree" in the fourth [sutta], it is said that goatherds used to go there and sit in its shade; therefore, it was named after them.

Thus, the name “Ajapāla-nigrodha” (The Goatherd’s Banyan) arose. However, some say that the name “Ajapāla-nigrodha” originated because elderly brahmins who were unable to recite the Vedas there built dwellings surrounded by walls and all resided within them; therefore, it became known by that name.
In this regard, the etymology is as follows: they do not recite (*na japanti*), thus they are *ajapā*—those who do not study the mantras.
"Meaning" (*attha*): because they take up their dwelling here, it is called "Ajapāla.

Or, others say that because at the time of midday, when goats have entered within, he protects (*pāleti*) and guards them with his own shadow, therefore the name "Ajapāla" has become conventional for him.
In every respect, this is the name of that tree; [the word *ajapāle*] is used in the locative case in the sense of proximity to it. For this locative ending is used here in the sense of proximity.
“At the Goatherd’s Banyan Tree.
“Experiencing the bliss of liberation” means that he sat there investigating the Dhamma and experiencing the bliss of liberation.
This tree is located in the eastern direction from the Bodhi tree. And as for the phrase “for seven days,” this—
The period following the seven days spent sitting cross-legged. For the Blessed One spent another three weeks near the Bodhi tree immediately after those seven days sitting cross-legged.
Herein is the sequential account:
it is said that when the Blessed One had attained supreme enlightenment, he remained for seven days in a single cross-legged posture.

As he sat there, the thought occurred to some deities: "The Blessed One does not emerge from his attainment; could there perhaps be other qualities that constitute Buddhahood? Then, on the eighth day, the Blessed One emerged from his meditative absorption.
Knowing the doubt of the deities, and for the purpose of dispelling their uncertainty, he rose into the air and displayed the Twin Miracle, thereby [dispelling] theirs.
Having dispelled all doubt, he stood slightly to the northeast of his seat upon the throne;

for seven days he spent gazing with unblinking eyes at the Bodhi tree and the throne— the site where he attained the power of the perfections accumulated over four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand kalpas— and that place is known as the Animisa Cetiya.

Thus it was named. Then, walking back and forth on a jeweled walkway that extended eastward and westward between the place where the couch stood and [the Bodhi tree], he spent seven days; that became known as the Ratanacaṅkama Cetiya (Jeweled Walkway Shrine).
Thereafter, in the western direction, the deities constructed a jeweled house, and there, sitting cross-legged, he...
Spendning seven days investigating the Abhidhammapitaka—specifically the *Samantapāṭhāna* with its infinite methods—he passed that time;

that place became known as the Ratanaghara Cetiya. Thus, having spent four weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree, on the fifth week he approached the Ajapāla banyan tree from the Bodhi tree and sat cross-legged at its foot.
"He emerged from that concentration" means he emerged from the concentration of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) according to the time-limitation [he had set].
And having emerged, while the Blessed One was seated right there, a certain brahmin went to him and asked a question.
Therefore it is said: "Then a certain one," and so forth. In this context, "a certain one" refers to someone not well-known by name or clan.
One was Apākaṭa. He was called Huṃhuṅkajātika because, it is said, he was a Diṭṭhamangalika who was arrogant and stubborn;
seeing everything as impure by way of pride and anger, he wandered about making the sound "huṃ huṃ" out of disgust, and for that reason he is called "Huṃhuṅkajātika.
There is also a reading, "Huhukkajātiko. He was a brahmin by birth.
"Where the Blessed One was" (*yena bhagavā*) means in whichever direction the Blessed One was seated; for this instrumental case is used in the sense of a locative.
Or, it means by whichever direction the Blessed One was to be approached, he approached by that very direction. Alternatively, the instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause:
"by which reason" (*yena*), meaning for the reason that the Blessed One is to be approached by gods and humans.
For that reason, the meaning is "he approached. And for what reason should the Blessed One be approached?
Because he is like a physician of great power who approaches those with diseased bodies—afflicted by various kinds of diseases and suffering—in order to treat their illnesses;

likewise, because they are afflicted by the disease of the various defilements, gods and humans with afflicted minds approach him through such means as listening to the Dhamma and asking questions, in order to treat the disease of the defilements.
“The Blessed One is to be approached. Thus this brahmin also, desiring to cut through his own doubt, approached him.
“Having approached” (*upasaṅkamitvā*) is an indication of the conclusion of the act of approaching.

Alternatively, it means that having gone to a place even closer to the vicinity of the Blessed One than the place he had originally approached. “He exchanged greetings” (*sammodi*): equally and properly.
The Blessed One was pleased by him, and he too was filled with joy by the Blessed One through the performance of greetings such as, "I hope you are bearing up, I hope you are getting along.
*Sammodanīyaṃ* means worthy of greeting, suitable for generating mutual joy. *Kathaṃ* means conversation or discourse.
*Sāraṇīyaṃ* means fit to be remembered; it is that which should be practiced by virtuous people at the appropriate time.
Or it should be reflected upon. *Vītisāretvā* means having finished. *Ekamantaṃ* is a neuter singular demonstrative.
It means in one place, having avoided the six faults of sitting such as being too close to the front and so forth; the meaning is "in a certain spot.
*Etadavoca* means he spoke these words that are now to be stated, beginning with "In what way, indeed... and so on.
In that context, *kittāvatā* means "by what measure. *Nu* is a particle used in the sense of doubt. *Kho* is for the purpose of completing the metrical line.
*Bho* is an address derived from the birth-status of brahmins; for it has been said: "He is called a 'bho-vādi' (one who addresses others as 'bho') if he is one who possesses something.
*Gotama* is an address to the Blessed One by his clan name. But how did this brahmin [know his lineage]?
"Does he know the clan of the Blessed One by having met him personally? "He has not met him personally;

for even while traveling with the group of five monks who were attending upon him during the six years of his ascetic practice, and later, when he had abandoned that discipline and was wandering for alms alone and without a companion in Senānigama at Uruvelā, he had already been seen by that brahmin."

And he had conversed with him before. Therefore, recollecting the clan-name of the Blessed One as it was previously used by the group-of-five monks when addressing him, he addresses the Blessed One by his clan-name, saying, “O Gotama.
Or rather, from the time the Blessed One went forth on the Great Renunciation and was ordained on the bank of the Anoma River, from that point onward, [he was known as] “the ascetic Gotama.”
He is as well-known and renowned as the moon and the sun; there is no need to search for a reason to know his lineage.
"Brāhmaṇakaraṇā" means those things which make one a brahmin (*brāhmaṇaṃ karonti*); the meaning is "those that produce the state of a brahmin.
And here, by the phrase "in what way" (*kittāvatā*), he asks about the measure of those qualities (*dhammā*) by which one becomes a brahmin.
"And which ones?"—with this, he asks about their specific nature.

"Having understood this matter": having understood the matter that had reached its culmination regarding the question asked by him, at that time he uttered this inspired uttering (udāna), but he did not teach the Dhamma to that brahmin. Why? Because of the teaching of the Dhamma...
Because he was not a fit vessel. For when that brahmin heard this verse, there was no realization of the Truth (saccābhisamaya).
And just as it was with him, so it was with Upaka the Ājīvaka regarding the proclamation of the Buddha’s qualities.
Indeed, prior to the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, even when others heard what was spoken by the Blessed One, there was the granting of refuge to Tapussa and Bhallika.
It has arisen as something pertaining only to the realm of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), not to the realm of the trainee (*sekkha*), nor to the realm of penetration (*nibbedha*).

For this is the nature of things (*dhammatā*). In that context, "he who is a brahmin" refers to one who is a brahmin by virtue of having banished evil qualities; it does not refer to one who, while still possessed of evil qualities such as making oaths, uttering "hum-hum," or being a mere ritualist, claims the status of a brahmin solely on account of birth. That brahmin, because he has banished evil qualities...
By the abandonment of the utterance "huṃ-huṃ," he is *nihuṃhuṅka*; by the absence of the impurities such as passion (*rāga*), he is *nikkasāva*;
by his mind being devoted to the practice of meditation, or by his mind being restrained through the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃyama*), he is *yatatta*;

he has reached the end of the Vedas—that is, Nibbāna, the conclusion of conditioned phenomena—by means of the knowledges comprised within the four paths, or because he has gone to the end of the Vedas, he is *vedantaga*. [This is] of the holy life of the path (*magga-brahmacariya*).
Because he has lived [the holy life], he is one who has lived the holy life (*vusitabrahmacariya*);
he may rightly and according to the Dhamma speak the Brahma-declaration, saying, "I am a brahmin.

This means that in his entire dwelling within the world, there is not even in regard to a single object any excess of lust, excess of hatred, excess of delusion, excess of conceit, or excess of wrong view; these excesses have been abandoned without remainder.
The commentary on the fourth sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Brāhmaṇa Sutta:
