"In Sāvatthī" means in the city of that name. For it was the dwelling place of the seer named Savattha.
It is called Sāvatthī because it is "well-measured" (māpita), just as Kākandī and Mākandī [are named after their founders]. Thus say the grammarians first.
But the teachers of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathācariyā) say: "Whatever is a requisite for human enjoyment or use, all that exists here;
thus it is Sāvatthī. And when asked, in the context of a market, "What goods are there here?", they would also reply, "Everything is there."
"Based on the word, it is called Sāvatthī:
'All requisites at all times are gathered in Sāvatthī;
therefore, based on everything, it is proclaimed as Sāvatthī.'"
"In that Sāvatthī": this locative case is used here in the sense of proximity (*samīpa*).

"In Jetavana": he conquers his own adversaries, thus he is *Jeta*; or, it is called *Jeta* because it was produced when the king had conquered his enemies; or, out of a desire for auspiciousness, he gave it that very name, thus it is *Jeta*.
It "causes one to delight" (*vanayati*), thus it is a *vana*; [it is so called] because through its own excellence, it inspires devotion in beings toward itself.
"Produces" means "causes to arise. Regarding the term *vanuke*: it is a forest (*vana*).

Its meaning is that it is as if begging living beings, saying, "Come, enjoy me," through the warbling conversations of intoxicated cuckoos and other birds delighted by the fragrance of various flowers, and through the hands of tree branches and sprouts shaken by a gentle breeze.
*Jetassa vanaṃ* is *jetavanaṃ*. For it was planted and nurtured by Prince Jeta.
It was protected [by him]. He himself became its owner; therefore it is called "Jeta’s Grove" (Jetavana), and [the phrase] "in that Jeta Grove" refers to this.
Regarding the phrase "Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery": that great merchant was named Sudatta according to the name given by his parents;
however, because he was successful in all his desires, because he was free from the stain of stinginess, and because he possessed qualities such as compassion, he was constantly...
He gives alms to the destitute; therefore, he is called Anāthapiṇḍika. Living beings—especially those who have gone forth—find delight here, thus it is an *ārāma*.

The meaning is that they come from here and there and dwell without longing, finding pleasure and joy due to the beauty of its flowers, fruits, and so forth, and due to the fivefold perfection of the requisites for a dwelling, such as being neither too far nor too near. By the aforementioned manner...
Or, because one brings [the mind] back into oneself and delights therein even when it has gone here and there toward external objects, it is called an *ārāma*.
For that [garden] was purchased by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika from Prince Jeta for eighteen crores of gold by covering it with a layer of gold coins;
and having built dwellings for eighteen crores of gold, [he dedicated it]. For eighteen...

Having completed the construction of the monastery with ten million pieces of gold, and having thus dedicated it to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha through the relinquishment of fifty-four million pieces of gold, it is therefore called "the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika. In that monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika;
and here, the mention of "in Jetavana" is a description of its former owner, while "in the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika" [indicates its current dedication].

This is the description of the latter benefactor. Both [sections] serve to illustrate the specific nature of the two acts of relinquishment, so that those desiring merit may follow their example in the future.

In that regard, Jetta’s relinquishment consisted of eighteen crores of gold obtained from the sale of the land, as well as trees worth many crores, acquired through the construction of gate-towers and palaces; [the other] was forty-five...

There were ten million [pieces of gold] belonging to Anāthapiṇḍika. Thus, by praising their generosity, the Dharma-treasurer shows that "those who desire merit perform meritorious deeds," thereby encouraging others who desire merit to follow in their footsteps.
In this regard, it might be argued: if the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, then it should not be said that he was "in the Jeta Grove."
If [the Buddha] was dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, it should not be said that he was "in Sāvatthī," for it is impossible to dwell in both places at one and the same time.
However, this should not be viewed in that way; did we not say that "this locative expression is used in the sense of proximity"?
Therefore, while dwelling there in Jeta’s Grove, which is in the vicinity of Sāvatthī, he is said to be "in Sāvatthī."

"...dwells in Jeta’s Grove. The mention of Sāvatthī is for the purpose of indicating the village of his alms-round; the remaining words are for the purpose of indicating a dwelling place suitable for one who has gone forth.
In the phrase "the Venerable Sāriputta," etc., "Venerable" (āyasmā) is a term of endearment. The word "and" (ca) has the sense of conjunction.
He is Sāriputta because he is the son of a brahmin woman named Rūpasārī. "Mahāmoggallāna" is a term of honor; he is "great" (mahā) due to his distinguished qualities.
"Moggallāna" refers to Mahāmoggallāna. "Revata" refers to Khadiravanikārava, not Kaṅkhārevata.

For on one day the Blessed One was like a golden sacrificial pillar encircled by a red woolen cloth, like a golden mountain surrounded by coral banners, like Dhataraṭṭha, the king of swans, surrounded by ninety thousand swans, and [resplendent] with the seven jewels...
Surrounded by a fourfold army like a wheel-turning monarch,
or like the moon rising in the midst of the sky surrounded by a great assembly of monks, he sat teaching the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly.
At that time, these chief disciples and great disciples approached in order to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One.
“Addressed the bhikkhus” means that, having seen those bhikkhus who were sitting surrounding him approaching, he spoke to them.
For the Blessed One, seeing those venerable ones—who were endowed with the qualities of virtue, concentration, wisdom, and so forth; possessed of supreme tranquility;
and disciplined in the highest perfection of deportment—approaching with a serene mind, spoke thus for the purpose of proclaiming their specific excellence of qualities.
He addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, these brahmins are coming; bhikkhus, these brahmins are coming.
This repetition is used in the sense of endearment, though it is also appropriate to say it is used in the sense of praise.
When it was said thus—when the Blessed One had addressed those venerable ones as “brahmins”—one among them, whose name and clan were not well-known, [spoke] in that assembly.
A certain bhikkhu was sitting there. "Born of brahmin stock" means he was born into a brahmin family;
for he had gone forth from a distinguished and wealthy brahmin mahāsāla clan. It is said that this thought occurred to him:

"These worldly people say that one becomes a brahmin through being of pure birth on both sides and through the accomplishment of brahmin training, and not otherwise; yet the Blessed One calls these venerable ones 'brahmins'."
"Come now, let me ask the Blessed One about the characteristics of a brahmin.

It was for this very purpose that the Blessed One then addressed those elders as "brahmins. For the etymology of "brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*) as "one who breathes the *brahman*" refers to brahmins by birth.
However, the Noble Ones (*ariya*) are brahmins because they have cast out evil. For it has been said: "One who has cast out evil is a brahmin; through even conduct..."
“He is called a *samaṇa*. And he will say: “Having banished evil states.

“Having understood this meaning” means having known this ultimate sense of the word *brāhmaṇa*, which has reached its pinnacle. “This inspired utterance” means he uttered this *udāna* which illuminates the state of being an ultimate *brāhmaṇa*.
In that context, “having banished” (*bāhitvā*) means having placed outside, having removed from one’s own continuum, and having abandoned by way of eradication.
The meaning is as follows: "Evil states" (*pāpakā dhammā*) means base states; by way of misconduct, they are the three types of misconduct;
by way of mental arising, they are the twelve unwholesome states of consciousness; by way of courses of action, they are the ten unwholesome courses of action;

and by way of their various modes of occurrence, they comprise all unwholesome states divided into numerous categories—this is the meaning. "Those who always walk with mindfulness" (*ye caranti sadā satā*) refers to those who have attained the fullness of mindfulness.
At all times, by way of constant abiding, they move about through the four postures having become mindful and possessed of mindfulness regarding all six objects, beginning with visible forms.
It should be understood that by the mention of mindfulness alone, clear comprehension is also included here.
They are "those whose fetters are destroyed" because the ten kinds of fetters have been utterly eradicated by means of all four noble paths.

"Buddhas" means they are awakened through the awakening to the Four Noble Truths. Furthermore, they are of three kinds: disciple-buddhas (*sāvakabuddha*), solitary-buddhas (*paccekabuddha*), and perfectly self-awakened ones (*sammāsambuddha*);

among these, it is the disciple-buddhas who are intended here. "They indeed are brahmins in the world" means that they are born by noble birth into the Dhamma designated as "brahmin" in the sense of being supreme; or, they are the legitimate sons of the Blessed One, who has become a brahmin.
In this world of beings, those who are called "brāhmaṇas" in the ultimate sense are not so by mere birth or lineage, nor by the mere wearing of matted hair and such;
this is the meaning. Thus, in these two suttas, the qualities that make one a brāhmaṇa are described as culminating in arahantship.
However, due to the differing inclinations of beings and through the skillful display of teaching, one should understand the diversity of the teaching through its various modes of expression.
The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Mahākassapa Sutta:
Regarding the sixth [sutta], "at Rājagaha" means in the city of that name. For it was so called because it was occupied by Mahā-Mandhātu, Mahā-Govinda, and others.

"It is called ‘Rājagaha. Others explain it here by another method, saying: "Because it was difficult for rival kings to overcome, it was a 'home' (gaha) [for them], thus it is Rājagaha. But what do they mean? This is merely the name of that city.
Furthermore, this city exists during the time of a Buddha and during the time of a Wheel-turning Monarch; at other times, it is empty and possessed by *yakkhas*, serving as their dwelling place.
"Having offered, he remains. Regarding "in the Kalandaka-nivāpa at Veḷuvana": *Veḷuvana* is the name of that monastery.

It is said to have been surrounded by a wall eighteen cubits high, adorned with a great fragrant chamber (*gandhakuṭī*) suitable for the dwelling of the Blessed Buddha, as well as other palaces, huts, caves, pavilions, walkways, gatehouses, and so forth.
It was surrounded on the outside by bamboo groves that were blue-hued and delightful; therefore, it is called "Veḷuvana" (Bamboo Grove).
Furthermore, they provided fodder for squirrels there, and thus it is called "Kalandakanivāpa" (Squirrels' Feeding Place).
It is said that formerly a certain king, having entered that park for recreation, fell asleep during the day while intoxicated with liquor.
His attendants, thinking "the king is asleep," wandered here and there, tempted by flowers, fruits, and other such things.
Then, drawn by the scent of the liquor, a black snake emerged from a hollow in a certain tree and came toward the king.
Seeing this, a tree deity, thinking "I shall give back the king's life," approached in the guise of a *kalandaka* bird and [stood] at the base of his ear.

He made a sound. The king woke up, and the black snake had retreated. Seeing this, [the king] thought, "My life was given back to me by this black one," and he established a food offering for the black ones there and caused the proclamation of safety to be announced.
Therefore, from that time on, it became known as "Kalandakanivāpa" (The Food Offering for the Black Ones). For "Kalandaka" refers to black ones.
[He was] named [Mahākassapa], in that Veḷuvana, the Kalandakanivāpa.
"Mahākassapa" means he is a great Kassapa because he is endowed with the great aggregates of virtue and so forth;
furthermore, this Great Elder is called "Mahākassapa" in relation to the Elder Kumārakassapa. "[In] the Pippali Cave."
It is said that near the entrance of that cave there was a *pippali* tree; therefore, it became known as the "Pippali Cave.
In that Pippali Cave. "Afflicted" (*ābādhika*) means one who has an affliction (*ābādha*), that is to say, one who is diseased (*byādhika*).
"Suffering" (*dukkhita*) means one to whom bodily suffering has arisen, that is to say, one who has reached a state of pain.
"Severely ill" means afflicted with a grave illness; however, he endured that illness with mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Then the Blessed One, having learned of this situation, went there and recited the Bojjhaṅga-paritta (the Protection of the Factors of Enlightenment).
By that very act, the Elder's affliction was pacified. For it is said in the Bojjhaṅga-saṃyutta:
Now at that time, the Venerable Mahākassapa was staying in the Pippali Cave, afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Mahākassapa.
Having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Once seated, the Blessed One... [as before] ...said this:

“I hope it is bearable for you, Kassapa; I hope you are getting by; I hope that painful feelings are subsiding and not increasing, and that their subsiding is apparent, not their increase? “It is not bearable for me, Bhante; I am not getting by.
My painful feelings, Bhante, are severe; they are increasing and not subsiding, and their increase is apparent.”
...nor is there any withdrawal discerned.

‘Kassapa, these seven factors of enlightenment have been rightly expounded by me; when developed and cultivated, they lead to direct knowledge, to full awakening, and to Nibbāna. What are the seven? The factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, Kassapa, has been rightly expounded by me...’”

When developed and cultivated, they lead to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna... Kassapa, the enlightenment factor of equanimity has been rightly expounded by me; when developed and cultivated, it leads to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.
These, Kassapa, are the seven factors of enlightenment rightly expounded by me, which, when developed and cultivated, [lead to the same].

“...they lead to direct knowledge, to full awakening, and to Nibbāna. “Truly, Blessed One, they are factors of awakening; truly, Sugata, they are factors of awakening. This is what the Blessed One said.

The Venerable Mahākassapa was satisfied and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words. And the Venerable Mahākassapa rose from that affliction; thus was that affliction of the Venerable Mahākassapa abandoned.
Therefore it was said: “Then, after some time, the Venerable Mahākassapa recovered from that illness. He thought thus:
Previously, on the days he was ill, he had remained in the monastery itself after consuming the alms-food brought by his co-residents.
Now that he had recovered from that illness, this thought occurred to him: “What if I were to go to Rājagaha for alms?”

The thought occurred to them, "We should enter. "About five hundred deities" refers to five hundred *accharā* celestial nymphs with peacock-feather feet who were attendants of Sakka, the king of the gods.
They "became diligent" means that they prepared five hundred portions of alms-food, thinking, "We shall give alms-food to the Elder," and taking it in golden vessels, they stood by the way.
Saying, “Venerable sir, please accept this almsfood; show us your favor,” they became intent upon the offering of alms.
Therefore it is said: “For the sake of obtaining almsfood for the Venerable Mahākassapa.
It is said that Sakka, the king of the gods, having understood the Elder’s state of mind, dispatched those celestial nymphs, saying, “Go!”
“Give almsfood to the noble Elder Mahākassapa and thereby establish a firm footing for yourselves.
For it occurred to him: “When all of you have gone, perhaps the Elder might accept almsfood from the hand of even one of you;
that will be for her long-term welfare and happiness. But the Elder declined.

To those who said, "Venerable sir, please accept my almsfood; please accept my almsfood," he replied, "Go away, you who have performed merit and possess great wealth; I shall provide support for the poor.
When they said again, "Venerable sir, do not ruin us; please show us favor," he rejected them once more and turned away.
To those who were begging while not desiring [to give], he said, "You do not know your own measure;
go away! and snapped his fingers. Hearing the sound of the elder’s finger-snap, they were terrified; unable to remain, they fled and went back to the world of the gods.
Therefore it is said: "Having rejected about five hundred deities."
"At the time of the morning" means at one time in the forenoon, at a certain hour.
"Having dressed" means having firmly put on the lower robe by way of changing from the monastery robe. "Taking bowl and robe" means having donned the upper robe and taken the bowl in his hand.
"He entered for alms" means he entered for the purpose of almsfood. "A street of the poor" means [the street] of destitute people.

The dwelling place of the poor. The street of the wretched refers to the residence of destitute people who have fallen into the loss of their wealth. The street of the weavers refers to the residence of those who weave cloth.

"The Blessed One saw": how did he see it? While seated in Veḷuvana, the Blessed One, reflecting—thinking, "My son Kassapa has recovered from his illness; what indeed is he doing?"—saw it with his divine eye.

"Having understood this matter": having known this matter—that which was described as the venerable Mahākassapa’s practice of favoring the poor, after he had refused the divine alms-food consisting of many soups and many condiments offered by five hundred nymphs.
"This inspired utterance": this [utterance] concerning one whose taints are destroyed, by way of demonstrating supreme fewness of wishes.
He uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) which illuminates his state of being and his experience.
In that context, "not supporting another" (*anaññaposī*): one who supports another is "supporting-another" (*aññaposī*); one who does not support another is "not-supporting-another" (*anaññaposī*).
This means he is without a second, being alone due to the absence of anyone else to be supported by him. By this, the Elder’s ease of maintenance (*subharatā*) is shown. The Elder...

Indeed, by maintaining himself with robes that merely suffice for the body and almsfood that merely suffice for the belly, he dwells as one of supreme fewness of wishes, nourishing only himself and not nourishing anyone else among his relatives, friends, or others, because he is unattached to anything.
Alternatively, he is "not nourished by another" (*anaññaposī*) because there is no need for him to be supported by anyone else. For he [does not depend] on even a single provider of requisites.
One who is dependent on the four requisites does not truly deserve the name "not supported by others," because his livelihood is reliant on a single source.
However, the Elder, following the method described in the verse beginning, "Just as the bee [gathers from the flower]," wanders for alms by the strength of his own legs;
being ever-new to each family, he sustains himself with mixed alms-food. For it was in this regard that the Blessed One spoke to him of the practice comparable to the moon.
*Thomesi*. "Known" (*aññāta*) means renowned (*abhiññāta*), being spread abroad by virtue of his qualities as they truly are;
or else, it is known through his state of not seeking support from others, by way of fewness of wishes and contentment.

Alternatively, "unknown" (*aññāta*) means that he is not made known as a self for the sake of desiring gain, honor, and fame, because of having abandoned craving in every respect. For one who has not removed craving, being of evil desire, acts out of hypocrisy with the intention of gaining esteem.
He makes himself known. "Tamed" means tamed by the supreme taming of the faculties through the sixfold equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*).

"Established in the essence" means established in the essence of liberation (*vimuttisāra*), or established in the essence of virtue and so forth, such as the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training (*asekkha*).

"One whose taints are destroyed and whose faults have been vomited out" means because of the complete abandonment of the four taints (*āsava*), beginning with the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*).
One whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). Precisely because of that, due to having completely vomited out passion and the other defilements, he is one who has "vomited out faults" (*vantadosa*).
"Him I call a brahmin"—I say that one possessing the aforementioned qualities, the ultimate brahmin, is a "brahmin.
Here too, the diversity of the teaching should be understood according to the same method explained below.
The commentary on the sixth sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Ajakalāpaka Sutta:
In the seventh [sutta], "at Pāvā" refers to the city of the Malla kings by that name; "at the Ajakalāpaka Shrine" refers to [the shrine] by Ajakalāpaka.
It was a place held in high esteem by people, having been taken possession of by a *yakkha* named Ajakalāpaka.
It is said that this *yakkha* accepts an offering only when goats are tied up in bundles together with a portion of goat meat, and not otherwise;
therefore, it became known as "Ajakalāpaka. Some, however, say that it is so called because it causes sentient beings to bleat like goats.
"Ajakalāpaka" means "goat-hair bundle. It is said that when beings bring an offering and present it while making the sound "aja," he is pleased;
therefore, it is called "Ajakalāpaka. Furthermore, that yakṣa was endowed with supernatural power, harsh and cruel, and resided there;
for that reason, people held that place in high esteem from time to time.
They offer a sacrifice at the proper time. Therefore it is said: "At the Ajakalāpaka Shrine.
"In the abode of the yakkha Ajakalāpaka" means in that yakkha’s celestial palace (*vimāna*).
At that time, it is said, the Teacher, desiring to subdue that yakkha, went alone, without a companion, taking his bowl and robe in the evening.
Having gone to the gate of the dwelling of the yakkha Ajakalāpaka, he requested the doorkeeper to allow him entry into the residence.
The doorkeeper replied, "Venerable sir, the yakkha Ajakalāpaka is harsh; he shows no respect for one who is a recluse or a brahmin.
Therefore, you yourselves must know [how to proceed]; yet it is not proper for me not to inform him. At that very moment—
With the speed of the wind, he went to the presence of Ajakalāpaka, who had gone to the assembly of the *yakkhas*.
The Teacher entered the inner palace and sat upon a seat prepared in the sitting pavilion of Ajakalāpaka.
The *yakkha*’s female attendants approached the Teacher, paid homage, and stood to one side. The Teacher delivered to them a discourse on the Dhamma appropriate for the occasion.
He spoke. Therefore it was said: “He was dwelling at Pāvā, at the Ajakalāpaka Shrine, in the abode of the yakkha Ajakalāpaka.

At that time, Sātāgira and Hemavata, while traveling through the air above the abode of Ajakalāpaka on their way to a gathering of yakkhas, reflected on why their progress was failing and, while investigating the cause, [beheld] the Teacher at Ajakalāpaka’s...
Seeing him seated in his dwelling, they went there, paid homage to the Blessed One, and requested permission, saying, "Venerable sir, we are going to the assembly of the *yakkhas*.

Having circumambulated him, they departed. Upon reaching the gathering of the *yakkhas*, they saw Ajakalāpaka and expressed their joy, saying, "It is a gain for you, friend Ajakalāpaka, that in this world with its devas, in your dwelling..."
“The Blessed One, the Supreme Person, is seated; go to him, attend upon the Blessed One, and listen to the Dhamma.

Having heard their words, he thought, “These are telling that shaven-headed ascetic about my presence in his dwelling,” and being overcome with anger, he resolved, “Today I shall have a battle with that ascetic!”
Having reflected thus, he rose from the assembly of *yakkhas*, lifted his right foot, and stepped upon a mountain peak sixty *yojanas* in extent;
it split and broke into two. Whatever else remains to be said here should be understood according to the method already set forth in the commentary on the *Āḷavaka-sutta*.
Indeed, the encounter with Ajakalāpaka was just like the encounter with Āḷavaka, except for the posing of questions and their answering;
[the only difference being] his threefold exiting and entering from existence.

For even as he was approaching, thinking, "By these very means I shall drive that ascetic away," Ajakalāpaka raised nine storms, such as whirlwinds and the like, and with those [he assailed] the Blessed One.
Being unable to cause even a slight movement, he conjured up hosts of spirits with various weapons in their hands and forms of extreme terror;
approaching the Blessed One together with them, he moved right up to his very edge and caused all manner of disturbances throughout the entire night,
yet he could not move the Blessed One even a hair’s breadth from his seated position.

He was unable to do anything; however, he blazed up with anger, thinking, "This ascetic has entered my dwelling and sat down without asking my permission. Then the Blessed One, knowing the movement of his mind, [thought]:
"Just as if one were to break bile into the nose of a fierce dog, it would become even more fierce than before."
"Even so, this spirit defiles my mind while I am sitting here; what if I were now to go outside?
Thinking thus, he himself emerged from his dwelling and sat in the open air. Therefore it was said:
"At that time, the Blessed One was sitting in the open air during the pitch-black darkness of night."
In that context, "in the darkness of the night's gloom" means in the darkness that makes the night blind;
the meaning is in a thick darkness devoid of the arising of eye-consciousness. It is said that at that time, the darkness was endowed with four factors.
A "god" (deva) here refers to a cloud, which causes each individual drop of water to fall. Then the *yakkha*, thinking, "I shall terrify him with this sound..."
Thinking, "I shall cause this ascetic to flee," he approached the Blessed One and terrified him with the words beginning with "confused.
Therefore it is said: "Then Ajakalāpaka... and so forth. In that context, *bhaya* means mental terror;
*chambhitatta* means the state of the body being paralyzed, such as the stiffening of the thighs; *lomahaṃsa* means the bristling of the body hairs. By all three [terms],...
By these words, he demonstrates the very arising of fear. As for the phrase "he approached": why did he approach with such an intention?
Was it not because he had previously committed a failure that ought to have been avoided by himself? It is true that he did commit one; however, he [thought]:
"While I was standing on firm ground in a secure place within the palace, nothing could be done against me; but now, while I am standing outside, thus..."

Thinking, "I shall be able to frighten him away," he approached. For this yakkha considered his own abode to be a "secure place," and thought, "Because he is standing there, this ascetic does not fear.
He uttered "Akku-lo, Pakku-lo" three times; thus, he made the "Akku-lo, Pakku-lo" sound on three occasions.
Desiring to terrify them, he made such a sound. For this is an imitative sound.

At that time, that *yakkha*, with great effort—as if lifting up Mount Sineru or overturning the great earth—produced a roar like a mass of a hundred thunderclaps gathered in one place, [resembling] the trumpeting of the elephants of the quarters and the lion-roars of maned lions.
It was like the lion’s roar, the *hiṃkāra* sound of the *yakkhas*, the loud laughter of the *bhūtas*, the clapping noise of the *asuras*,
and the thundering crash of the thunderbolt of Indra, the king of the gods; by its own depth, vastness, and terror,
it seemed to mock and overwhelm all other sounds, like the great whirlwind that arises at the end of an aeon.
He let out his own yakkha-roar three times— a great, terrifying sound with indistinct syllables that seemed to split the hearts of ordinary people—
thinking, "By this, I will frighten this ascetic and make him flee.
With every sound he uttered, the mountains shed their bark and the lords of the forest trees likewise.
The leaves, fruits, and flowers on all the trees, creepers, and thickets withered;
even the Himalayan king of mountains, though three thousand *yojanas* in extent, trembled, shook, and quaked.
Starting from the earth-deities, for the most part even among the deities there arose fear, trepidation, and horripilation, let alone among human beings. And of others...
It was a time of great terror, like the shaking of the great earth by footless beings, two-footed beings, and four-footed beings;
a great clamor arose throughout the entire surface of Jambudīpa. Yet the Blessed One, not wondering "What is this sound?", sat motionless and resolved: "May no one be hindered by this."
However, because that sound reached the range of hearing of beings in the form "akkula pakkula," they recorded it in the compendium as "he made an akkulo-pakkulo" by way of imitation;
and considering that the yakkha had the habit of making such "akkula-pakkula" noises during that utterance,
they entered it into the collection as "he made an akkulapakkulika."
However, some say that the term *akkulo bakkulo* was stated as a synonym for the two words *ākulabyākula*, just as one says *ekaṃ ekakaṃ*.
This is because the meaning of *ākula* is "born once," in the sense of being produced by way of its first arising;
and by adding the letter *k* to that [word] and making it short, [the form *akkulo* is derived].
But Bakkula was born twice; here, "birth" (*jāti*) is used as a synonym for "clan" (*kula*), as in such expressions as *kolaṃkola*.

Since the application of terms follows their intended meaning, by the first term [“twice-born”] womb-born lions, tigers, and so forth are meant, and by the second term [“twice-born”] egg-born venomous snakes, black cobras, and so forth are meant;
therefore, like a lion and the like, or like a venomous snake and the like—
Others say that the *yakkha* shows this meaning—“I am the taker of your life”—by means of these two lines.
Still others, however, citing the reading “*akkhulo bhakkhulo*,” explain: “He who moves (*ulati*) to throw (*akkhetuṃ*), to exhaust (*khepetuṃ*), or to destroy (*vināsetuṃ*) is an *akkhula*;
he who moves (*ulatī*) to devour (*bhakkhituṃ*) or eat (*khādituṃ*) is a *bhakkhula*. But who is this? [It refers to] among *yakkhas*, *rakkhasas*, *pisācas*, lions, tigers, and so forth.”
"Any one who brings harm to human beings"—this is what they say is its meaning. Here too, the application of the underlying intention should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

"This, ascetic, is your *pisāca*": having conjured a terrifying form and stood before the Blessed One, saying, "O ascetic, a flesh-eating *pisāca* has appeared before you," the *yakkha* speaks thus with reference to himself.

"Having understood this matter": having understood in every way that disorder being manifested by that *yakkha* through body and speech, and having understood the state of being untainted by worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*), which is the cause of his own invincibility.
"At that time": at the very moment of producing that disorder. "This inspired utterance (*udāna*"): [refers to] that disorder.
Disregarding him, he uttered this *udāna* which illuminates the power of the Dhamma that serves as the cause for such disregard.

Therein, "when among his own states" (*yadā sakesu dhammesu*) means at the time when, among the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*)—which are reckoned as his own personal existence—he has "gone beyond" (*pāragū*).

He has gone beyond by way of the fulfillment of the clear realization through full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*); and for that very reason, [he has also gone beyond] their cause, the origin (*samudaya*).

He has reached the further shore by way of the fulfillment of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) through abandoning, witnessing, and developing, regarding cessation characterized by the non-arising of that [suffering] and the path leading to cessation.
He is called a "brahmin" because he has thus entirely banished evil;
and even in the complete awakening to one's own personal existence, there is the clear realization of the Four Noble Truths. And this has been said: "In this very fathom-long body..."
“I proclaim the world and the origin of the world with respect to this conscious body possessed of perception,” and so forth.

Alternatively, “in regard to one’s own states” means in regard to one’s own phenomena (*dhammas*). One’s own phenomena refer to the phenomena such as virtue (*sīla*) belonging to a person who desires their welfare.
For the purifying phenomena (*vodānadhammas*), such as virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation, bring about the attainment of absolute benefit and happiness for a person.
"One's own qualities" refers to those qualities that do not bring harm, unlike the defiled qualities which are unwholesome.
"One who has gone to the further shore" means one who has reached the limit, the ultimate boundary, through the fulfillment of those qualities such as virtue (*sīla*).
In this regard, virtue is first of all twofold: mundane and supramundane. Of these, the mundane is the virtue belonging to the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga-sīla*). That—
In brief, it is fourfold by way of the restraint of the Pātimokkha and so forth; in detail, however, it has many divisions.
Supramundane virtue is twofold by way of the paths and fruits; in terms of its meaning, it consists of right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
And just as with virtue, concentration and wisdom are each twofold by way of being mundane and supramundane. Among these, mundane concentration...
The eight attainments together with their preliminary stages (*upacāra*) are mundane; supramundane concentration is that which is included within the path (*magga*).
Wisdom (*paññā*)—whether consisting of hearing, reflection, or cultivation—is defiled when mundane, but supramundane when associated with the path and the fruit (*phala*).

What is called "liberation" (*vimutti*) refers both to the liberation of the fruit and to Nibbāna; therefore, it is exclusively supramundane. Knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuttiñāṇadassana*)...
It is purely mundane, consisting of nineteen kinds due to its nature as reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*). Thus, because he has reached the further shore—
the limit— by means of the complete production and fulfillment of these qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) within his own continuum through the attainment of the fruit of Arhatship,
he is "one who has gone beyond" (*pāragū*) in regard to his own qualities.

Alternatively, by the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), one is a master (*pāragū*) in virtue (*sīla*). For he is described as "one who fulfills [the precepts] regarding virtues.

And here, by the mention of the stream-enterer alone, the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*) is also included. By the attainment of the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*), one is a master in concentration (*samādhi*).
For he is described as "one who fulfills [the practice] regarding concentration. By the attainment of the fruit of arhatship (*arahatta-phala*), [one is a master] in the others...

He is one who has gone to the further shore in three respects. For the Arahant, because he has attained the unshakable liberation of mind (cetovimutti), which is the foremost for the full development of wisdom, and because he has reached the culmination of the knowledge of reviewing, he is called "one who has gone to the further shore" in regard to both the liberation through wisdom (paññāvimutti) and the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana).
Thus, in every way, by means of the four paths regarding the four noble truths, [he has fulfilled] the sixteenfold [tasks] such as full understanding (pariññā).
Through the accomplishment of what is to be done, at each respective time as previously described, he has gone beyond his own respective states;
thus, "he is a brahmin. At that time, by virtue of having banished evil qualities, he is a brahmin in the ultimate sense.
Then, "he transcends this Piśāca and Pakkula"—that is, subsequent to that aforementioned state of having gone beyond, O Ajakalāpaka, he transcends this...

It surpasses, exceeds, and overcomes even the Pisāca demon—who had been manifested by her for the purpose of providing a meal of flesh and raised up for the sake of instilling fear—along with the Akula and Pakkuli spirits; the meaning is that he does not fear them.
This verse, too, was spoken by referring specifically to Arahantship. Then Ajakalāpaka, by means of such [power] as he himself had performed...
Seeing that state of equanimity of the Blessed One, who was unshakable despite the terrifying and horrific form [of the demon], he thought with a mind full of faith,

"Oh, how wonderful is this person! Manifesting the presence within himself of a faith belonging to ordinary worldlings, he declared his status as a lay follower (upāsaka) in the presence of the Teacher.
The commentary on the seventh sutta is concluded.
8. Commentary on the Saṅgāmajī Sutta:
In the eighth [sutta], "Saṅgāmajī" is his name. For this venerable one was from a certain very wealthy family in Sāvatthī.
The merchant’s son, having reached maturity, was joined by his parents with a suitable wife;

after being entrusted with the family estate, he became bound by the ties of domestic life. One day, at the time of the morning meal, he gave alms to the lay followers residing in Sāvatthī and undertook the precepts of virtue.
Then, in the evening, wearing clean lower garments and a clean upper robe, with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in hand—
Seeing them walking toward Jetavana for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma, he asked, "Where are you going?

When they replied, "To Jetavana, into the presence of the Teacher, for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma," he said, "In that case, I shall go as well," and went to Jetavana together with them. At that time, the Blessed One was delivering the Lion's Roar in the Golden Cave.
Roaring like a maned lion, he sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the pavilion of the True Dhamma and taught the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly.
Then those lay followers paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side;
the clansman Saṅgāmajī also sat down at the edge of that assembly to listen to the Dhamma. Having delivered a gradual discourse, the Blessed One—
He proclaimed the Four Noble Truths; at the conclusion of the teaching on the truths, there was a penetration of the Dhamma by many thousands of living beings.

When the assembly had risen, the noble youth Saṅgāmaji, having attained the fruit of stream-entry, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and requested the going-forth, saying, “May the Blessed One let me go forth. “But have you been permitted? [the Blessed One asked].

“Have you been permitted by your mother and father to go forth? “I have not been permitted, Bhante. “Saṅgāmaji, the Tathāgatas do not grant the going forth to a son who has not been permitted by his mother and father. “Bhante, I shall act in such a way that my mother and father will permit me to go forth.
Having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him, he departed.
Having approached his mother and father, he said, "Mother and father, please grant me permission to go forth.
Thereafter, it should be understood according to the method set forth in the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta.
Then, having given his promise, "I will show myself after going forth," and being permitted by his parents, he [approached] the Blessed One.
Having approached, he requested the going-forth. He received the going-forth and the full ordination in the presence of the Blessed One.
Not long after his ordination, striving and exerting himself for the sake of the higher path, he spent the rains retreat in a certain forest dwelling.
Having become one possessed of the six direct knowledges, at the end of the rains retreat, he went to see the Blessed One and his parents.
He went to Sāvatthī for the purpose of being released from his probation. Therefore it was said: "At that time, the Venerable Saṅgāmaji had arrived at Sāvatthī.
After that venerable one had walked for alms in the village of Dhura and returned from his alms round after the meal, he went to the Jeta Grove.

Having entered and approached the Blessed One, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, declared his higher knowledge (*aññā*), and once again paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him.
Having departed, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
Then his parents and kinsmen and friends, having heard of his arrival, said, "It is said that Saṅgāmaji has come here."
Joyful and delighted, they went to the monastery in great haste;

searching for him there, they saw him sitting, approached him, and after exchanging greetings, they entreated him, saying, "Lest the kings should seize this wealth of yours because you have no son, or lest unwelcome heirs should take it—this is not fit for the life of renunciation;
come, dear one, return to the world. Hearing this, the Elder said, "These [people] of mine, through sensual pleasures..."
“They do not understand their state of needlessness; like a dung-carrier clinging to a lump of dung, they desire only sensual pleasures.
They cannot be persuaded by a discourse on the Dhamma. Speaking thus, he sat as if he were not hearing them.
Seeing that they had made various requests but that he would not accept their word, they entered the house and, together with their son, approached his wife.
They sent her off with her retinue, saying, "We have come back after failing to win his heart despite entreating him in various ways;
go, dear lady, and persuade your husband by requesting that he show you their son.
It was while she was pregnant that this venerable one had gone forth. She consented, saying, "Very well," and taking the child, [she departed].
He went to Jetavana with a great retinue. With reference to him, it was said: “The Venerable Saṅgāmaji heard,” and so forth.
In that context, *purāṇadutiyikā* means a former companion during the time he was a householder; it signifies his wife.
*Ayya* is used as a term appropriate for those who have gone forth, where one would otherwise say “noble son” (*ayyaputta*). *Kira* is used in the sense of hearsay.
The word *nipāto* (particle) should be understood as being connected with *tassa anuppatto kira* (it has indeed come upon him).
"O ascetic, you have gone forth while saying, 'Support me, who have but a young son'; yet you abandoned me even when I was only seven months pregnant. Now I am one with a young son;

it is improper for you to practice the duty of an ascetic while abandoning such a person as me. Therefore, O ascetic, [support] me, who have my son as my companion, with food, clothing, and so forth."
“‘Support me! But the Venerable Saṅgāmaji, having withdrawn his faculties, neither looked at her nor spoke to her.
Therefore it was said: ‘When this was said, the Venerable Saṅgāmaji remained silent.
Having spoken thus three times and seeing that he remained silent, she thought: ‘Men indeed may be indifferent toward their wives;’”
People are full of longing for their children; a father’s affection for his child persists even down to the marrow of his bones.
Thinking, "Perhaps she will come under my influence through love for her son," she placed the boy in the elder’s lap, stepped aside, and after saying, "Monk, here is your son;
support him," she walked a short distance away. It is said that this was due to the power of the monk’s spiritual majesty.
She was unable to stand before him. The Elder neither looked at the child nor spoke to him.
Then that woman, standing nearby, turned her face away and watched;
perceiving the Elder’s disposition, she turned back, thinking, “This ascetic has no interest even in his own son,” and taking the child, she departed. Thus it is said: “Then...”
“...he was the former wife of the venerable Saṅgāmajī,” and so forth.
In that context, “even by his own son” means: this ascetic has no need even for his own legitimate son, let alone others; such is the intended meaning. Regarding the word “divine” (*dibba*):
here it is called “divine” because it resembles what belongs to the gods (*deva*). For [the vision] produced by the well-performed karma of deities is free from bile, phlegm, blood, and so forth.

The divine eye of clarity (*pasādacakkhu*) is unobstructed and capable of receiving objects even at a distance. This supernormal eye (*abhiññācakkhu*), produced by the concentration of the fourth jhāna, is similar to that;

thus it is "divine" (*dibba*) because it is like the divine, or it is "divine" because it is obtained by relying on the divine abodes (*dibbavihāra*), or it is "divine" because of its great radiance and great range. By that "divine" [eye]. "Purified" (*visuddha*) means...
"By means of that which is perfectly pure through the removal of defilements such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). "Transcending the human" means beyond the sphere of ordinary humans.
"This kind of disfigurement" refers to this very disfigurement—the aforementioned unsuitable conduct for those who have gone forth, namely the deformed act consisting of placing a son on one's lap.

"Etamatthan" means having understood in every aspect this matter (attha), which consists of the venerable Saṅgāmajī’s state of being entirely without expectation regarding his children, wife, and so forth.
"Imaṃ udānan" means he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which illuminates his state of equanimity (tādibhāva) toward the desirable, the undesirable, and so on.
In that context, "āyantin" means coming; the intention is "his former wife. "Nābhinandati" means [he does not rejoice] at seeing her.
"He does not rejoice" means he is not glad that "she has come. "She departs" refers to her going away while she has not even been greeted by him;
"he does not grieve" means he does not fall into mental distress. To show the reason why the Elder neither rejoices nor grieves in this way, it is said:
"He who has conquered the battle is freed from attachment. In this context, "attachments" (saṅga) refers to the attachment of lust (rāga).

The "entanglements of hatred, delusion, conceit, and views" refers to the fivefold entanglements; the monk who has conquered the battle is one who is liberated through liberation by total eradication and liberation by subsiding.
"Him I call a brahmin": him who has attained the state of suchness and whose taints are exhausted, I call a brahmin because he has entirely banished all evil.
The commentary on the eighth sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Jaṭila Sutta:
In the ninth [sutta], "at Gayā," *Gayā* refers here to both a village and a ford (*tittha*). For it is not far from the village of Gayā...
While residing there, the Blessed One is called "dwelling at Gayā," as is the bathing-place (tittha) of Gayā.
For near the village of Gayā there is a lotus pond and also a river; both of these are addressed by the worldly populace as the "bathing-place for the washing away of evil.
At Gayāsīsa, there is a certain mountain with a peak resembling the head of an elephant.
At Gayāsīsa—where there is a back rock resembling an elephant’s frontal globe, providing space for a thousand bhikkhus—the Blessed One was dwelling.
Therefore it is said: “He was dwelling at Gayā on Gayāsīsa.
*Jaṭila* refers to ascetics; for they are called *jaṭila* here because they wear matted hair (*jaṭā*). During the intermediate eight-day period of the falling of snow.
During the eight-day period at the end of the month of Māgha and the beginning of the month of Phagguṇa—
within the winter season— at a time when snow falls, some emerge from the water at Gayā; that is,
having first submerged their entire bodies in that water which is esteemed as a bathing-place (tittha), they then emerge, rise up, and surface.
"They sink" means they submerge into the water up to their heads. "Making both surfacing and sinking" means they perform repeated acts of surfacing and submerging.
For in that regard, some hold the view that "purification from evil occurs by a single surfacing alone";
they go away after performing only the surfacing. However, since there is no surfacing without submerging, because of this inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), there is also submerging.

They do indeed perform it. Even those who hold the view that "purification from evil occurs by means of a single immersion" likewise, having immersed themselves once, emerge according to the aforementioned method because it is inseparable [from the act], and then depart.
But those who hold the view that "purification from evil occurs by immersing oneself in that very bathing place," having immersed themselves there, during their inhalation...
Having suppressed [their breath], they reach the end of their life right there, like those fallen from a precipice in the desert.
Others hold the view that "purity from evil comes through bathing after repeatedly performing acts of emerging and submerging";
they perform acts of emerging and submerging from time to time. It was said with reference to all of them: "They emerge and they submerge."
"And performing the act of diving in and out. Here, although emerging is preceded by diving, it is said that while only a few perform the diving alone, many perform both the emerging and the diving;
thus, "emerging" is mentioned first in order to show their predominance. Likewise, the phrase "many matted-hair ascetics" is stated because of the predominance of matted-hair ascetics.
At that time, there were also brahmins there who wore shaven heads with tufts of hair and sought purification through water; they acted in such a manner.

"They sprinkle" means that some, having taken water from the Gayā river with their hands, sprinkle it upon their own heads and bodies, while others take water in jars and, standing on the bank, act in the same way. "They offer oblations into the fire" means that some, on the bank of the Gayā...
Having prepared the sacrificial altar and brought forward the necessary implements such as incense and offerings, they offer the fire-sacrifice and attend upon the fire.

"By this [there is] purification" means that by this—namely, by bathing at Gayā and so forth, and by attending upon the fire—there comes to be purification from the defilement of evil, the removal of evil, or even purification from the cycle of existence (saṃsāra); having held such a view, is the meaning.
In this context, it should be understood that emerging from the water and so forth are mentioned merely as illustrations.
For among those [practitioners], some dwell in the water; some offer handfuls of water; some, standing in that water, circumambulate the moon and sun;
some mutter the Sāvittī and other mantras many thousands of times; and some perform the recitation of spells (*vijjājapa*) such as "Inda, come! and so on.
They call out; some perform great acts of attendance, and while doing so, some descend, some ascend, and some, having ascended, perform the simple rinsing of the mouth.
Some, standing within the water, play cymbals (*tantī*) or play the lute (*vīṇā*);
they display various kinds of such activities. Or rather, because they perform such transformative actions as these...
Even while performing [the ritual], they first perform the acts of diving in and emerging from that water;
therefore, including all of that within the act of emerging, it is said, "they emerge," and so forth.

Thus, while such a tumultuous commotion was occurring there, the Blessed One, standing on the mountain above, heard their clamor and, looking down with the thought, "What is this?", observed that display of activity.
It was said with reference to him: “The Blessed One saw... ‘[Thinking] by this [means] there is purity’”; that has the same meaning as what was stated.

“Having understood this matter” means: having understood in every aspect that matter—namely, their adherence to impure paths such as plunging into water as the way to purity, and his own unerring realization regarding the path to purity consisting of truth and so forth. “This inspired utterance” (udāna).

He uttered this *udāna*, which illuminates that purification by water is not the path to purity, and which illuminates, according to reality, that truth and the other qualities are indeed the path to purity.
In this regard, the phrase "one is not pure by water" (*na udakena sucī hoti*): here, "by water" means by such acts as immersion in water.

For immersion in water and the like are referred to here as "water" (*udaka*) through the elision of the final member of the compound, just as the realm of form (*rūpabhava*) is called "form" (*rūpa*). Alternatively, "by water" (*udakena*)...
There is no such thing as the purification of a being by means of water that serves as an instrument for acts such as immersion; the meaning is that it does not exist.
Alternatively, "suci" means that a being is not truly pure—that is, cleansed from the stain of evil—by means of that aforementioned water. Why?
Because many people bathe here. For if the purification of evil were achieved through such practices as descending into water as previously described...
It might be said: "Many people bathe here in this water;
therefore, even those who have committed evil deeds such as matricide, as well as others such as cow-slayers and buffalo-slayers, down to fish and turtles—might all of them be purified of their evil.
But this is not so. Why? Because bathing is not an antidote to the causes of evil. For whatever destroys something is its antidote.
Just as light is to darkness, and knowledge is to ignorance, so bathing is not [the remedy] for evil. Therefore, one must reach the conclusion here:
“One does not become pure by water.
To show that by which one does become pure, he said, “In whom there is truth,” and so forth. Therein, “in whom” means in that person.
Regarding the person (*puggala*): "Truth" (*sacca*) refers both to verbal truth and to the truth of abstinence.
Alternatively, "truth" refers both to the truth of knowledge (*ñāṇasacca*) and to the ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*). "Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the Noble Path and the Dhamma of the Fruit;
that person in whom all of this is found is pure and is a brahmin—that noble person, specifically one whose taints are destroyed.
“...and the pure brahmin for ultimate purity. But why, in this context, is truth (*sacca*) taken separately from the Dhamma?
Because of its great utility. For it is said: “Truth indeed is the deathless word; truth is the sweetest of all flavors;
in truth, in the goal, and in the Dhamma, the virtuous say they are established; established in truth are the recluses and brahmins.”

The qualities of truth have been elucidated in numerous passages of the Sutta, beginning with the words "And... and so forth. Furthermore, the opposite of truth has been elucidated by such passages as:
"For a person who has transgressed against one single principle, the speaker of falsehood, the liar, goes to hell.
The commentary on the ninth sutta is concluded.
10. The Commentary on the Bāhiya Sutta.
In the tenth [sutta], "Bāhiya" is his name. "Dārucīriya" means one who wears a garment made of wood-shavings. He dwelt at the port city named Suppāraka.
But who was this Bāhiya, how did he come to be a wearer of wood-shavings, and why did he reside at the port city of Suppāraka?

In this regard, the sequential account is as follows: It is said that at the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Padumuttara, some two hundred thousand aeons ago, a certain son of good family in the city of Haṃsavatī, while listening to the Dhamma teaching of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers, saw the Teacher designate a certain bhikkhu as the foremost among those of quick higher knowledge.
Seeing this, he thought: "Great indeed is this bhikkhu, since he has been so designated by the Teacher."

"He is established as foremost in this; oh, may I too in the future, having gone forth in the dispensation of such a Perfectly Enlightened One, be established by the Teacher in such a position as foremost among monks, just as this bhikkhu is!
Having thus aspired to that state, performed the corresponding meritorious deeds, and practiced virtue throughout his life, he became destined for the heavenly realms.

Wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he went forth in the dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa. Having fulfilled his moral conduct and practiced the duties of a recluse, he passed away and was reborn in the world of the gods.

After dwelling in the world of the gods for the interval between two Buddhas, he took rebirth in a noble family in the kingdom of Bāhiya during this current arising of a Buddha; because he was born in the kingdom of Bāhiya, [he is known as Bāhiya].
They knew him as Bāhiya. When he reached maturity and was living the life of a householder, he filled a ship with many goods for the purpose of trade,
entered the ocean, and traveling back and forth, returned to his own city seven times together with his retinue.
On the eighth occasion, however, having loaded his goods with the intention of "going to Suvaṇṇabhūmi," Bāhiya boarded a ship.
After the ship had plunged into the great ocean, it was wrecked in the midst of the sea before reaching its intended destination. The great multitude of people became food for fish and turtles.
But Bāhiya, seizing a plank from the ship, was being carried along very slowly by the force of the waves as he swam.
Having spoken thus, he fell into the ocean and lay upon the shore as if made of gold.
Having dispelled his exhaustion and regained a measure of breath, he rose up;
out of shame, he entered into a thicket, and seeing no other covering, he cut reed stalks, wrapped them with bark fibers, and fashioned them into lower and upper garments which he then put on.
However, some say that he "wore it after boring holes in wooden planks, threading them with bark-cord, and making them into lower and upper garments.
Thus, because he wore robes made of wood in every respect, he was known by the ancient designation "Dārucīriya" (Wood-Robed) and also as "Bāhiya.
Seeing him walking for alms in the port-city of Suppāraka, carrying a single bowl according to the aforementioned manner, people—
They thought, "If there are those called Arahants in the world, they must be like this;
would this noble one accept the robe being offered, or would he not accept it out of fewness of desires?
Thus, while testing him, they brought robes from various directions. He thought: "If I do not come by way of this method, they will not [believe] thus regarding me."
“They might have confidence; what if I were to refuse these and live according to this very same practice? In this way, gain and honor will arise for me.
Having thought thus, he stood in hypocrisy and did not accept the robes. The people, thinking, “Oh, how truly modest this venerable one is!
became even more deeply inspired in their minds and performed great acts of hospitality and respect toward him.
Having finished his meal, he went to a certain shrine located not far away. The great multitude followed him there, maintained that shrine, and offered it to him.
He thought, "These people, having gained confidence in me merely because I wear robes, are showing such honor and respect; therefore, it is fitting for me to live a life of strict austerity."
With few possessions and having few desires, he lived his life. Yet, being esteemed by others as an "Arahant," he considered himself an "Arahant.
His honor and respect increased further and further, and he became a recipient of excellent requisites.
Therefore it was said: "Now at that time, Bāhiya of the Bark Robe was residing at Suppāraka..."
"...honored and revered on the seashore," and so forth.
Therein, "honored" (*sakkata*) means honored by way of attentive and respectful service.

"Revered" (*garukata*) means revered by way of holding [him] in high esteem, with the intention that he is endowed with distinguished qualities, like a stone parasol (*pāsāṇacchatta*). "Venerated" (*mānita*) means [venerated] by the mind...
"Respected" means honored by way of being held in high esteem. "Worshipped" means worshipped by way of offerings such as flowers, perfumes, and so forth.
"Honored" means honored by those with minds full of serene confidence through acts such as providing a path, offering a seat, and bringing forth [gifts]. "A recipient of robes...
requisites" means a recipient by way of obtaining the four requisites—robes and so forth—which are of the most excellent kind and are presented one after another in succession.
Another method: "Honored" (sakkata) means having received honor. "Venerated" (garukata) means having received veneration.
"Revered" (mānita) means highly esteemed and cherished in the mind. "Worshiped" (pūjita) means worshiped with the offering of the four requisites. "Respected" (apacita) means having attained respect.
For one to whom they give the four requisites—having honored them—with well-prepared and most excellent things, he is "honored."

He toward whom they present offerings while establishing a sense of reverence is "one who is held in high esteem" (*garukato*). He whom they love in their minds and hold in great honor is "one who is honored" (*mānito*).

He toward whom they perform all these acts by way of worship is "one who is worshipped" (*pūjito*). He toward whom they perform the highest expression of deference through such acts as prostration, rising from one's seat, and joining the palms in salutation is "one who is venerated" (*apacito*). But for Bāhiya, they performed all of this. Therefore—
It is said: “Bāhiya Dārucīriya was living at Suppāraka, honored [by the people],” and so forth.
And here, although he did not actually accept the robe, he is nevertheless described as a “gainer of robes” by virtue of the act of offering: “Come, venerable sir, please accept this cloth.
“Having gone into seclusion” means having gone to a private place. “Being in retirement” means being alone, free from many people. “An arahant”...
As he was being addressed, a reflection arose in his mind in the manner now being described, and a wrong intention occurred to his heart.
How so? "Whatever Arahants there are in the world, or those who have entered the path to Arahantship, I am one among them.
The meaning of this is: "Those in this world of beings who, because they have slain the enemies that are the defilements (kilesa), [are worthy of] honor, respect, and so forth..."
“They are Arahants by virtue of their state as Arahants; they are those who have entered the path of Arahantship by slaying the enemies that are the defilements, and among them I am one.
“Ancient blood-relatives” means deities who were blood-relatives—like kinsmen—in a previous existence, having together practiced the duty of a recluse.
Some, however, say: “‘Ancient blood-relatives’ refers to a deity who was a blood-relative, specifically one’s mother, in a former time and another existence.”
Although they say this, it has been rejected in the *Aṭṭhakathā* and the former account alone has been adopted.
It is said that formerly, when the teaching of the Blessed One Kassapa was declining, seven bhikkhus, having seen the misconduct of the novices and others,
were moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and thought, "We shall establish our own foundation before the teaching disappears."
Having paid homage to the Golden Cetiya, they entered the forest. Seeing a mountain, she said, "Those who still have attachment to life may turn back;
those who are free from attachment may ascend this mountain. Having spoken thus, she constructed a ladder, and all of them ascended that mountain.
Once they had climbed up, she pulled down the ladder and they practiced the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*). Among them, the senior elder of the Saṅgha, after the lapse of only a single night—
He attained arahantship. Having brought almsfood from Uttarakuru, he said to those bhikkhus, "Friends, eat this almsfood.
They replied, "Venerable sir, you have accomplished this through your own spiritual power;
if we too were to produce such a distinction as you have, we would bring it ourselves and eat. [And so they ate.]
They did not wish to accept. Then, on the second day, the second elder attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
He likewise took almsfood and went there, inviting the others; they too rejected him in the same manner.
Among them, the one who had attained arhatship passed into parinirvāṇa, while the non-returner was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa realm. As for the other five persons, however, they continued striving.
Even though they strove, they were unable to produce any distinction. Being unable to do so, they withered away right there and were reborn in the world of the gods.

After wandering among the gods for the duration of one interval between Buddhas, at the arising of this present Buddha, they passed away from the world of the gods and were reborn here and there in various noble families. Among them, one became King Pakkusāti, and another...
Kumārakassapa, Dabba Mallaputta, Sabhiya the wanderer, and Bāhiya Dārucīriya.
Among them, it was with reference to the one who was a non-returner reborn in the Brahma-world that this was said: "an ancient blood-relative deity.
For even a son of a god, like a daughter of a god, is called a "deity" (devatā) by treating him as simply a "god" (deva).
As in such passages as, "Then a certain deity," and so forth; however, here "deity" is intended to mean Brahmā.

For that Brahmā, immediately upon being reborn there, having observed his own attainment of the state of Brahmā, reflected on the place from which he had come and saw seven people who, having climbed a mountain, were practicing the religious life (samaṇadhamma).
There, one of them perceived his own state of final Nibbāna (parinibbāna) and his own rebirth there after having attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
He thought, "Where indeed are the other five people? and upon reflecting, he knew that they had been reborn in the sense-sphere deva world (kāmāvacara-devaloka).
Thereafter, from time to time, he would simply observe their activities, wondering, "What are they doing now? In this regard...
Then, at that time, while reflecting, "Where could he be?", he saw Bāhiya living near the port of Suppāraka, wearing a bark garment and making his living through deception;
[he recognized him as] the one who had previously climbed the mountain with him after they had fastened a ladder together,
practicing the duty of a recluse, and who— through an excessively austere way of life— had been indifferent to life even when offered by an Arahant.
"Without having consumed his alms-food, he now wanders about, desiring honor though he is unworthy, falsely claiming to have attained Arahatship while yearning for gain, offerings, and fame;
moreover, he does not know that the One Possessed of the Ten Powers has appeared.
Come, let me stir him with a sense of urgency and make him aware of the arising of a Buddha. Having said this, he descended from the Brahma-world at that very moment during the night.
He appeared before Dārucīriya at the port city of Suppāraka. Seeing a magnificent radiance in his own dwelling place, Bāhiya thought, "What could this be?
He went outside and, looking about, saw the Great Brahmā standing in the sky.
Raising his hands in reverential salutation, he asked, "Who are you? Then that Brahmā replied to him, "I am your old friend."
At that time, having attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), he was reborn in the Brahma-world;

you, however, being unable to attain any such distinction, died then as an ordinary worldling (puthujjana) and, wandering through the cycle of existence, have now come here wearing the garb of a heretic.

Knowing that you are indeed not an arahant, yet wander about having adopted the conviction, "I am an arahant," [the Buddha] approached you. Indeed, you— [The text continues: ...neither... (as per the original fragment).
“Bāhiya, you are an arahant; relinquish this evil course of view. Let it not lead to your harm and suffering for a long time.
A Fully Enlightened One has arisen in the world. That Blessed One is indeed an arahant;
go and attend upon him,” he said. Thus it was said: “Then a deity who had been a former blood-relative of Bāhiya Dārucīriya... and so forth.

In this context, "compassionate" (*anukampika*) means one whose nature is to assist, characterized by compassion (*karuṇā*). "Desiring welfare" (*atthakāma*) means desiring benefit, characterized by loving-kindness (*mettā*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that by the first phrase, the deity’s desire to remove Bāhiya’s suffering is shown, while by the latter, the provision of benefit is shown.
By the word "with mind" (*cetasā*), it is his own mind; and here, by the term "mind," it should be understood that the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) is intended.
"Cetoparivitakka" means the movement of his mind. "Aññāya" means having known it. "Tenupasaṅkami" means:

just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, even so, having vanished from the Brahma-world, he approached by way of appearing before Bāhiya. "Etadavoca" means... [he said this].

Brahmā spoke these words now being uttered—“Indeed, Bāhiya, you are not an Arahant,” and so forth—seizing upon Bāhiya’s erroneous reflection as it arose in the form of “Whoever in the world are Arahants...
and so on, just as one would seize a thief caught with stolen goods.
By the statement, “Indeed, Bāhiya, you are not an Arahant,” he thereby rejects Bāhiya’s status as one beyond training (asekha) at that time.

Nor has he entered the path of arahantship; by this, he indicates his status as one still in training (*sekha*), and by both [statements], he demonstrates his very state of being a non-noble (*anariya*).

"That practice of yours does not exist, by which you might be an arahant or have entered the path of arahantship"—by this, however, he also rejects his status as a virtuous worldling (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*).
In that context, "practice" (*paṭipadā*) refers to the purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*) and the other stages.
There are six purifications. It is called *paṭipadā* (the way) because one proceeds by means of it toward the Noble Path. *Assa* means "you would be.
On what basis has this overestimation of having attained *arahantship* arisen for him? "It is due to his fewness of wishes, contentment, austerity, and long-standing practice;
it arises through the abandonment of defilements by means of their specific counteractive factors (*tadaṅgappahāna*), leading to the overestimation of having attained *arahantship*."
Some say, "It has arisen. Others, however, say, "Bāhiya was an attainer of the four jhānas from the very first;
therefore, because his defilements did not manifest due to their suppression, the overweening conceit of having attained Arahantship arose in him.
Both of these views are merely their own opinions, for the Commentary states: "He was one who, desiring gain, honor, and fame, intended to win prestige."
Because he had arrived. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood according to the method already stated.
Then Bāhiya, standing in the sky, looked at the Great Brahmā as he spoke and thought:
"Alas, what a grave deed this is! I thought of myself as an Arahant, yet he says, 'In you there is not even the path leading to Arahantship.'"
He asked, "Is there indeed anyone in the world who is an arahant? Then he questioned him further. Thus it was said:
"Now then, O deity, who in the world are arahants, or who have entered the path to arahantship?
In this context, *atha* is a particle used at the beginning of a question. *Ke carahi* means "who now. *Loke* refers to the world as a spatial realm (*okāsaloka*). This is what is meant here.

The intention is this: "In what place upon the entire surface of Jambudīpa—which serves as a vessel for the world—do the Arahants or those who have entered the path to Arahantship currently dwell, so that we might approach them, abide by their instruction, and be liberated from the suffering of saṃsāra?
By "in the north," it is meant the northeastern direction relative to the port of Suppāraka.

An *arahant* is so called because of being "far removed" (*āraka*). For he stands far, very far away from all defilements, because the defilements together with their latent tendencies have been destroyed by the Path.
Or, he is an *arahant* because of having "slain the enemies" (*ari-hata*); for the enemies that are the defilements have been slain and utterly eradicated by the Blessed One through the Noble Path.
Or, he is an *arahant* because of having "slain the spokes" (*ara-hata*); and that which has the hub consisting of ignorance, existence, and craving—

The wheel of saṃsāra— which has been set in motion upon the chariot of the three realms of existence since beginningless time, with volitional formations such as merit as its hub, aging and death as its rim,
and pierced by the axle made of the origin of the taints— was, at the seat of enlightenment, mounted upon the earth of virtue with the feet of energy; and there,
taking up the axe of knowledge that brings about the destruction of karma with the hand of faith, he struck and shattered all its spokes.

"Viddhaṃsita" means destroyed. Or, he is an "Arahant" because he is worthy (arahati). For the Blessed One is worthy of the most excellent offerings and special honors, such as robes and other requisites, due to being the foremost recipient of gifts in the world including the devas.

Alternatively, he is an Arahant because of the absence of secrecy (raha-bhāva). For the Tathāgata, having completely eradicated defilements such as lust and because evil defilements are impossible for him, he is called an Arahant also because there is no secrecy regarding the performance of evil.
He is the "Perfectly Enlightened One" (Sammāsambuddha) because he has awakened perfectly and by himself to all phenomena.

For the Blessed One has fully awakened to phenomena that are to be directly known as things to be directly known; to phenomena that are to be fully understood as things to be fully understood; to phenomena that are to be abandoned as things to be abandoned;
to phenomena that are to be realized as things to be realized; and to phenomena that are to be developed as things to be developed. For this has been said:
“‘What is to be directly known has been directly known; what is to be developed has been developed;
what is to be abandoned has been abandoned by me—therefore, O brahmins, I am a Buddha.
Furthermore, [this is understood] by way of wholesome states having blameless and pleasant results, and unwholesome states having blameworthy and painful results, and so forth.”

This meaning should be understood by way of the "all-at-once" (sabbattika) dyads and so forth. Thus, he is called the "Perfectly Enlightened One" (Sammāsambuddha) because he has fully awakened to all phenomena in every aspect through his own unerring knowledge;

this is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Visuddhimagga*. "For the sake of arahantship" means for the attainment of the supreme fruit (*aggaphala*). The Dhamma...

"Teaches" means he instructs and explains the Dhamma of the practice of virtue and so forth, or indeed the Dhamma of serenity and insight, endowed with the specific qualities such as being "good in the beginning," in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained.
"Aroused by a sense of urgency" means: "Alas! Fie upon this state of being a worldling, since I, though not yet an arahant, [claim to be one]..."
"I thought, 'I did not know that a Perfectly Enlightened One had arisen in the world and was teaching the Dhamma.

Indeed, this life is difficult to understand, and death is difficult to understand. Thus he attained a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*); the meaning is that his mind was moved by the words of the deity in the manner described.
"At that very moment" means at that same instant. "He departed from Suppāraka" means [thinking], "The Buddha..."
Urged by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) arising from the joy inspired by the Buddha upon hearing even his name, he set out from the port of Suppāraka toward Sāvatthī.
"Staying one night everywhere" means that he traveled along the entire road, halting for only a single night at each place. For Sāvatthī is two hundred yojanas from the port of Suppāraka.
And he covered this entire distance in a single night’s stay. When he departed from Suppāraka, he arrived at Sāvatthī on that very same day.
But how did he travel in such a manner? It was by the power of the deities; some also say, "by the power of the Buddha. Everywhere...
However, because it is stated, “by staying for one night,” and because the journey was two hundred yojanas long,
the meaning illustrated is that wherever he stayed during the night along the way— in villages, market towns, or royal capitals— he did not let a second dawn rise there,
but rather reached Sāvatthī by staying only one night at every place. This is not how it should be understood.
Because the intended meaning is that he stayed for only one night on the entire two-thousand-league journey.
Having stayed for just one night along that whole path, he arrived at Sāvatthī on the following day during the morning.
The Blessed One, knowing of Bāhiya’s arrival, [thought]: "His faculties have not yet reached maturity; in the meantime..."
Thinking, "However, they will reach full maturity," he waited for the ripening of their faculties and,
surrounded by a great community of monks, entered Sāvatthī for alms at that moment. Having entered Jetavana and finished his morning meal,
he saw many monks walking back and forth in the open air to dispel physical fatigue, and he asked, "Where is the Blessed One now?"
He asked. The monks, saying, "The Blessed One has entered Sāvatthī for alms," asked him, "But from where have you come?
