"I have come from the port of Suppāraka," he replied. "You have come from afar; sit down now, wash your feet, anoint them, and rest for a while. When you have arrived, you shall see the Teacher. "Venerable sir, I—"

“I do not know if there is any danger to my life; having come by this single night’s journey along a road of two hundred yojanas, without stopping or sitting anywhere for long, I shall rest only after seeing the Teacher,” he said.
Then, hurrying on his way, he entered Sāvatthī and saw the Blessed One shining with the incomparable splendor of a Buddha. Thus it was said:
“Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were walking up and down in the open air.
Then Bāhiya Dārucīriya approached those bhikkhus,” and so forth.
In this context, *kahaṃ* means “where. *Nu* expresses doubt; *kho* is a particle used for filling out the meter. Thus, the meaning is: “In which place indeed?”
"Desirous of seeing" means we wish to see. For we [regard] that Blessed One as the blind man does sight, the deaf man does hearing, the mute man does the faculty of eloquent speech,
the one deprived of hands and feet does his hands and feet, the poor man does the attainment of wealth,
the one traveling through a wilderness does a land of safety, and the one overcome by disease does [health].
"Health! Like one whose ship has been wrecked in the great ocean, I desire to see and approach a great raft"—this is what he shows.
"In a state of haste" means having the appearance of hurrying.
"Pleasant to behold" means because it is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor characteristics, the fathom-wide aura, and the halo of light.
It brings confidence from every side to people intent on beholding the physical body (*rūpakāya*) because of the perfection of the beauty of his own form, according to the *Samantapāsādikā*.
It is "inspiring" because of the perfection of the Dhamma-body (*dhammakāya*), which is endowed with an immeasurable multitude of qualities such as the ten powers,
the four grounds of self-confidence, the six unique knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, for those who are like-minded.

"Inspiring confidence" means worthy of being inspired with confidence, or suitable for inspiring confidence. "With tranquil faculties" means having the five faculties—beginning with the eye—tranquilized by the departure from their state of restlessness.
"With a tranquil mind" means having a mind tranquilized by the attainment of a state free from the activity of the sixth faculty, the mind-faculty.
"Having reached the highest self-mastery and composure" refers to what is known as supramundane wisdom, liberation, and the liberation of the mind.
Having attained and reached the highest self-restraint and tranquility, he stands firm.
"Tamed" means tamed in body through the state of perfectly pure bodily conduct, due to the absence of misconduct regarding hands and feet and the absence of frivolity and so forth.

"Guarded" means guarded in speech through the state of perfectly pure verbal conduct, due to the absence of useless talk and the absence of frivolity and so forth. "With senses restrained" means [restrained] through the state of perfectly pure mental conduct...

The faculty of effort (*yatindriya*) is so called by way of the faculty of mind (*manindriya*) because it is not distracted by noble supernormal powers (*ariyiddhi*) and because of the presence of equanimity through non-deliberation.
It is a "Nāga" for these reasons: because it does not go astray through desire and the like; because defilements such as lust, once abandoned, do not return;
because no harmful action whatsoever is ever committed; and because there is no further going toward renewed existence (*punabbhava*). In this context...

By the phrase "and serene" (*pāsādika*), he illustrates the Blessed One’s state of being a standard by means of his physical body (*rūpakāya*); by "inspiring confidence" (*pasādanīya*), he illustrates it by means of his Dhamma-body (*dhammakāya*);
and by the remaining terms beginning with "with tranquil faculties" (*santindriya*), he illustrates his state of being a standard for the rest.
Thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One’s status as a standard for all beings without exception within the fourfold world-system has been made manifest.
Seeing the Blessed One in such a state walking along the street, he thought, "At long last, I have seen the Perfectly Enlightened One!
Overjoyed and delighted, his body was suffused throughout with five-colored rapture; his eyes were wide open and motionless from the overflow of joy.
From the moment he saw him, his body bent forward, plunging into the midst of the radiance emanating from the Blessed One’s body.
Thereupon, diving down and approaching the Blessed One, he paid homage with the fivefold prostration;
then, massaging and kissing the Blessed One’s feet, he said, “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma. Thus it was said:
“Having bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, he addressed the Blessed One thus: ‘Venerable sir, may the Blessed One teach me...’”
“Teach the Dhamma, O Sugata; teach the Dhamma that may be for my welfare and happiness for a long time.

In this context, “Sugata” means one who has gone to a beautiful state (*sobhanagamanattā*), one who has gone to a lovely place (*sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ gatattā*), one who has gone rightly (*sammā gatattā*), or one who has spoken rightly (*sammā gadattā*).
For even going is called “gone,” and that going of the Blessed One is beautiful, utterly pure, and blameless.
But what is that? It is the Noble Path. For by means of that going, he has gone to the secure direction without being obstructed, and he causes others to go as well;

thus, because his going is beautiful (*sobhana-gamana*), he is the Well-Gone One (*Sugata*). Furthermore, he has gone to that beautiful place—the deathless *nibbāna*—because he has gone to a beautiful state, he is the Well-Gone One.
And because he has gone rightly, he is the Well-Gone One; for the defilements abandoned by each respective path do not [return].
Because of not returning. For this has been said:

"By the path of stream-entry, those defilements which have been abandoned, he does not bring back, does not return to, does not go back to those defilements; thus he is 'Well-Gone' (sugata). [Likewise] by the path of once-returning... [and so on] ...by the path of Arahantship... he does not go back; thus he is 'Well-Gone'.
Alternatively, it means "because of having gone rightly," that is, because of having proceeded correctly through right practice in all three stages, or because of being well-practiced.
The purpose [is as follows]. For, from the time he was at the feet of Dīpaṅkara until he reached the Great Seat of Enlightenment (mahābodhimaṇḍa),
having reached the pinnacle of the conduct for the benefit of himself, the world, and enlightenment— through the practice of right conduct that fulfills the thirty perfections—
he fostered only the welfare and happiness of the entire world, avoiding eternalism, annihilationism, sensual pleasure, and self-mortification.
Because he has gone by the Middle Way— consisting of the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment which does not approach these two extremes—

and because he has subsequently attained mastery over the Dhamma regarding the Noble Truths, and because he has entered upon the right practice that is beyond the scope [of ordinary concern] toward all beings,
he is the "Well-Gone" (Sugata) due to having gone rightly (*sammā-gatatā*). Furthermore, he speaks rightly (*sammā gadati*) in a manner that is entirely appropriate to the occasion.
The Sugata speaks words that shine. For this has been said:

“He speaks at the proper time, he speaks what is true, he speaks what is beneficial, he speaks on the Dhamma, he speaks on the Vinaya; he is one who utters words that are well-founded, timely, definitive, and connected with the goal.
Furthermore, it has been said:
“That speech which is untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, and that which is unpleasant and disagreeable to others—that kind of speech the Tathāgata does not utter,” and so forth.
He is also the Sugata because he speaks rightly (*sammā gadattā*).
“That which will be for my benefit and happiness for a long time”—this refers to the teaching of the Dhamma which, for a long duration, [leads] to my...
It may be for the sake of the meditations, liberations, and so forth, and for the happiness to be attained therein.

"Now is not the time, Bāhiya" means that it is not yet the time for your teaching of the Dhamma. But is there ever a time when the Blessed One’s practice for the welfare of beings is not timely, since the Blessed One is known as one who speaks at the right time?
It is said in reply: here, "time" refers to the time for the ripening of the faculties of those to be trained.
This is what is intended. However, because at that time it would have been difficult for Bāhiya to discern whether his own faculties were mature or immature, the Blessed One did not say that;
instead, citing the reason that he was standing in the middle of the street, he said, "We have entered among the houses.
"Dujānaṃ" means difficult to discern. "Jīvitantarāyānaṃ" [means] of obstacles to life...
Desiring to state whether there is the occurrence or non-occurrence of conditions that cause obstacles, he said "obstacles to life" out of haste.
For life, which depends on many conditions for its maintenance, and its obstacles are of many kinds. Thus it has been said:
"One should exert oneself this very day; who knows if death will come tomorrow?"
“For we have made no compact with that Death who leads a great army.
But why does he first consider this obstacle to his life? Some say it is “because of his skill in discerning signs or because of his expertise regarding what has not yet been seen.
Others say it is “because he heard of the obstacle to his life in the presence of a deity,” for he was in his final existence.
But being urged by the perfection of his supporting conditions (*upanissaya*), he spoke thus: "For there is no passing away for those who have not yet attained Arhatship.
Yet for what reason did the Blessed One refuse him twice even while desiring to teach him the Dhamma?
It is said that this thought occurred to him: "From the moment I saw him, his entire body has been continuously filled with rapture."
"It is clear that the surge of intoxication is exceedingly powerful; even after hearing the Dhamma, he will not yet be able to penetrate it.

Let him wait until his equanimity is established; furthermore, because he has traveled a road of two hundred yojanas, the exhaustion in his body is also intense—let that too subside for now. Therefore, he declined twice. However, some say...
They say that the Blessed One acted in this way for the purpose of generating reverence for the hearing of the Dhamma. But when requested for a third time,
seeing that his state of equanimity had become neutral, that his distress had subsided, and that there was no longer any obstacle to his life, he thought,
"Now is the time for the teaching of the Dhamma," and began the discourse with the words, "Therefore, wait," and so forth.

In this context, *tasmā* means "because": because you have become diligent and entreat me most earnestly, or because you say that the obstacles to life are difficult to discern, and because your faculties have reached maturity—therefore. *Tiha* is a mere particle. *Te* means "by you";
*evaṃ* expresses the manner in which what is now to be said shall proceed.

“Should be trained in” means that training should be undertaken by way of all three trainings, beginning with the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*). To show how one should be trained, he said: “In the seen, there will be only the seen,” and so forth.
Therein, “in the seen, only the seen” refers to the mere seeing of the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) by eye-consciousness (*cakkhu-viññāṇa*).

For just as eye-consciousness sees in a form only the mere form, and not its intrinsic nature such as impermanence and so on, so it is with the rest. By means of consciousness belonging to the eye-door...
The meaning is: "One should train thus: 'It shall be for me merely what is seen.

Alternatively, "the seen" (*diṭṭha*) means the cognition of form by visual consciousness; "merely" (*matta*) means a measure. "Merely what is seen" (*diṭṭhamatta*) means that the mind shall consist of visual consciousness alone.
This is what is meant: just as when [an object] has come into the range of perception...

"Visual consciousness does not lust for a visible form, does not hate it, and is not deluded by it; thus, through the absence of lust and the other defilements, my impulsion will consist of visual consciousness alone.
I shall establish the impulsion at the very measure of visual consciousness.
Alternatively, "the seen" refers to the visible form seen by visual consciousness, while "the mere seen" refers to that which has arisen right there [in the object].
The triad of consciousnesses known as reception, investigation, and determining:
"Just as it does not become lustful, hateful, or deluded, so too, when a visible form has come into range, I shall arouse impulsion by that same measure of reception and so forth;
I will not allow it to arise by way of lust and the rest, exceeding that measure"—thus it is here.

The meaning should be understood [in this way]. The same method applies to the "heard" and the "sensed. "Sensed" should be understood as the sense-bases of odors, tastes, and tangibles together with the consciousnesses that take them as objects.
Regarding "in the cognized, the mere state of being cognized": here, "cognized" refers to an object cognized by the mind-door adverting consciousness (*manodvārāvajjana*).
In that which is cognized, "the mere state of being cognized" refers to the extent of the adverting consciousness itself; just as the adverting consciousness does not lust, nor does it hate.
"It does not become deluded"—the meaning here is that, by not allowing [the mind] to arise through passion and so forth, one should stabilize the mind by the measure of mere adverting.
"In this way, Bāhiya, you should train yourself" means: in this manner, Bāhiya, you should train yourself by following the three trainings according to this method of practice.

Thus the Blessed One, because Bāhiya delighted in what was concise, analyzed for him—along with the six groups of consciousness—the object of insight as divided by the sixfold classification of objects, using the four categories beginning with "seen. How so?
For here, the visible base (*rūpāyatana*) is called "the seen" in the sense of being something to be seen; eye-consciousness...
However, together with the consciousnesses associated with those [bases], in the sense of seeing, both of these—occurring according to conditions—are merely phenomena (dhammamatta).
Herein, there is no agent or instigator whatsoever; therefore, since they exist by way of non-existence after having been, they are impermanent in the sense of being subject to destruction;

they are suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away; and they are non-self in the sense of being devoid of mastery. So how could there be [a self] therein for a wise person?
Is it the occasion for lust and so forth? This is the intended meaning here, as it is also in the case of hearing and the other [bases].

Now, in order to show the full understanding through abandonment (*pahāna-pariññā*)—which occurs together with the Path and its Fruit—for one who is established in the full understandings of the known (*ñāta*) and the scrutinized (*tīraṇa*), the passage beginning “When, Bāhiya,” and so on, was commenced.
Therein, *yataḥ* means “when” or “because. *Te* means “your. *Tataḥ*...
Then, or from that. "By that" means by that [state] such as views and so forth, or by passion and so forth bound up with views and so forth.

This is what is meant: Bāhiya, at whatever time or by whatever cause, for you who are practicing according to the method I have taught regarding views and so forth, there will be the mere presence of views and so forth through the realization of their unerring nature—at that time, or by that cause—
"You shall not exist together with lust and so forth bound to what is seen and so on; you shall not be lustful, or hateful, or deluded;
because lust and so forth have been abandoned by you, you shall not be bound together with that which is seen and so on.
Therefore, Bāhiya, "you are not there"—that is, since you are not lustful through that lust, nor [hateful] through that hatred...
When you are neither corrupted by hatred nor deluded by ignorance, then you will not exist in relation to that [object], such as what is seen and so forth;
nor will you be attached to or established upon that which is seen, heard, sensed, or cognized through craving, conceit, and views, thinking, "This is mine, this I am, this is my self.
By this much, having brought the full understanding of abandonment (*pahāna-pariññā*) to its culmination, the stage of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is demonstrated.
"Therefore, Bāhiya, neither here, nor beyond, nor between the two"— when you, Bāhiya,
are no longer bound by that lust and so forth to those objects seen and the rest, then you are neither in this world, nor in the world beyond, nor in both places.
"This itself is the end of suffering" means that this very [state] is the end of the suffering of the defilements and the suffering of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
For this very point is that there is no state of an intermediate existence (*antarābhava*); this indeed is the meaning here.

As for those who, taking the phrase "between both," assert the existence of what is called an intermediate existence, their view is incorrect. For the existence of an intermediate existence is indeed rejected in the Abhidhamma.
The word "between" (*antarena*), however, indicates an alternative formulation; therefore, this is the [correct] sense here.
The meaning is: “Neither here nor in the hereafter; there is no other alternative. Alternatively, the word *antarena* indicates the absence of another alternative. Its meaning is:
“Neither here nor in the hereafter, but there is no other place between the two. And as for those who say, “an *antarā-parinibbāyī*...”

Having grasped the meaning of these scriptural passages, such as "one who is bound to be reborn" (*sambhavesī*), in an improper manner, they claim that "the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) certainly exists. However,
even they [must admit] that one is called an "attainer of Nibbāna in the interval" (*antarāparinibbāyī*) because, in various places such as the Aviha heaven,

one attains Parinibbāna through the realization of the highest path and the total extinction of all defilements in the interim— without having exceeded the midpoint of the lifespan there— and not because of the existence of an intermediate state.
This is the meaning of the first sutta-phrase. Regarding the latter phrase: those who have already come to be and will not come to be again are the "exhausted of taints" (*khīṇāsava*);

they are called "those who have come to be" (*bhūta*) in the first phrase. Because they are the opposite of that, those who "seek birth" (*sambhavesin*) are the trainees (*sekha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*), owing to their failure to abandon the fetter of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*).
Alternatively, among the four modes of birth (*yoni*), those beings born from eggs and from a womb [are included] as long as they remain within the egg-shell or the fetal membrane.

As long as they do not break [the eggshell or the womb], they are called "seeking existence" (*sambhavesī*); once they have emerged from the eggshell or the membrane of the womb, they are called "beings" (*bhūta*).

For moisture-born and spontaneously born beings, they are called "seeking existence" during the first moment of consciousness, and from the second moment of consciousness onward, they are called "beings.
Or, for as long as they remain in the posture in which they are born and have not yet reached another, they are so designated.

The meaning is: "up to that point they are 'seeking birth' (sambhavesin), and beyond that they are 'born' (bhūta). Therefore, [the existence of an intermediate state] must be rejected as non-existent.

For when the meaning is straightforward and follows the canonical text (pāḷi), what is the purpose of postulating an intermediate state (antarābhava) whose functional capacity has not been determined?
As for those who say: "The manifestation of phenomena occurring as a continuum in other locations occurs without interruption..."

"It has been seen that, just as in the case of non-conscious continua such as rice and so forth, there must likewise be an appearance in different locations without interruption even in conscious continua.
And this principle is consistent with the existence of an intermediate state (antarābhava), and not otherwise"—thus they state the reasoning.
For, by that [reasoning], when one possessing psychic power (iddhimā) who has attained mastery over the mind resolves upon a body that follows the mind...
A logical justification must be stated for their arrival here from the Brahma-world in an instant, or for their departure from here to the Brahma-world.

Even if one maintains that the occurrence of phenomena takes place only in an uninterrupted location, and even if it be granted that the domain of the psychic power (*iddhi*) of those possessing such power is inconceivable—that applies equally here as well, because of the statement: "The ripening of kamma (*kammavipāka*) is inconceivable. Therefore, regarding them...
It is precisely because they possess intelligence. For phenomena that have an intrinsic nature are by their very nature inconceivable;

they manifest in some places at a distinct location due to the influence of conditions, while in other places they manifest at an undistinct location. Thus, through conditions such as the face and the voice, the reflection and the echo—which are conditionally produced—arise in another place, such as the region of a mirror or a mountain.
It is seen; therefore, everything should not be applied everywhere—this is the summary here.

For the detailed exposition, however, the investigation of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), beginning with the proof of its status as an illustration by means of a reflected image, should be taken from the commentary on the *Kathāvatthu-pakaraṇa*.

Others, however, say: "‘Here’ refers to the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*); ‘there’ refers to the formless-sphere existence (*arūpabhava*); and ‘in between both’ refers to the fine-material-sphere existence (*rūpabhava*)."
Others say: “‘Here’ refers to the internal bases; ‘there’ refers to the external bases; ‘in between the two’ refers to consciousness and mental factors.
Or they say: “‘Here’ refers to conditions; ‘there’ refers to conditioned phenomena; ‘in between the two’ refers to conceptual designations (paṇṇatti).
None of this is found in the Commentaries. Thus, first, regarding “in the seen, only the seen”:
By the passage beginning with “it will be,” the phenomena of the three planes are to be classified fourfold according to views and so forth.

Therein, by way of avoiding the grasping after the beautiful, the pleasant, the permanent, and the self, the contemplations of the foul, suffering, impermanence, and non-self are shown; thus, insight (vipassanā) has been explained in brief together with the preceding purifications.
By the statement, “Therefore, Bāhiya, you [are] not that,” the intended meaning is the complete eradication of lust and the other defilements.
The path [is indicated by the words] “Then you, Bāhiya, will not be there. By the words “Neither here...
and so forth, it should be understood that the element of final Nibbāna without residue is described. Therefore it was said: “Then, Bāhiya’s mind was liberated from the taints.
By this teaching in brief, “at that very moment” means at that same instant, not at another time. “Without clinging” means...

"Having taken up. "By the taints (*āsava*)" means by those things called "taints"—namely, sensual lust and so forth—which, because they flow down to the peak of existence (*bhavagga*) and up to the stage of lineage (*gotrabhū*), and because they have been fermented for a long time and resemble fermented liquor (*madira*) and the like, have received that name.

"Was liberated" means he was liberated and released through both liberation by eradication (*samuccheda-vimutti*) and liberation by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi-vimutti*). For while he was hearing the Dhamma from the Teacher, his moral virtues (*sīla*)...
Having purified his mind and established insight based on the concentration of mind he had attained, he quickly exhausted all taints through swift higher knowledge;
together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), he reached Arahantship.
Having cut the stream of saṃsāra, having brought an end to the cycle of existence, and bearing his final body, he [performed] the nineteen kinds of reviewing.
Being urged by the natural course of events as they unfolded, he requested the Blessed One for the going-forth (*pabbajjā*). When asked, "Is your bowl and robe complete?
he replied, "They are not complete. Then the Teacher said to him, "In that case, go and seek out a bowl and robe," and departed.
Thus it was said: "Then the Blessed One... [as above] ...departed."

It is said that while practicing the ascetic life for twenty thousand years under the dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa Dasabala, he held the view that "when a bhikkhu has received requisites himself, it is permissible for him to use them only after making a distribution according to what was given";

consequently, he did not provide even a single bhikkhu with any assistance by means of a bowl or a robe. Therefore, for him, there was no ordination by the "Come, bhikkhu" formula (*ehibhikkhu-upasampadā*).

There was no proximate cause [for his attainment]. However, some say: "It is said that when the world was empty of Buddhas, he became a bandit and, having equipped himself with a bow and quiver, was committing robberies in the forest.

Seeing a Paccekabuddha there, out of greed for his bowl and robes, he pierced him with an arrow and seized the bowl and robes. Because of that, the supernaturally produced bowl and robes did not arise for him."
The Teacher, knowing this, did not grant him the going-forth by means of the "Come, monk" formula.
While he was wandering in search of a bowl and robes, a cow rushed toward him with great speed, struck him, and brought about his death.
It was with reference to this that it was said: "Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, a cow with a young calf [struck Bāhiya Dārucīriya]..."
"...attacked him and deprived him of life.
In that context, "not long after he had departed" means not long after the Blessed One had gone away.
"A cow with a young calf" refers to a certain female *yakkha* in the form of a cow with a young calf. "Attacked" means having overcome and crushed him. "Deprived him of life" means...
Because he had harbored resentment toward him in a previous existence, upon merely seeing him, he gave rise to a mind of enmity,
struck him with his horn, and deprived him of life. The Teacher,
having wandered for alms and finished his meal, was departing from the city together with a large company of bhikkhus.
Seeing Bāhiya’s body fallen in a charnel ground, he commanded the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, standing at a certain house door, have a bier brought; having carried this body out from the city, cremate it and erect a stupa.
The bhikkhus did so. Having done this, they went to the monastery and approached the Teacher.
Having reported what he had accomplished for himself, they asked about his future destiny.
Then the Blessed One explained to them that he had attained final nibbāna. The monks asked, "Venerable sir, you say that Bāhiya Dārucīriya attained arahantship;
when did he attain arahantship? When it was replied, "At the moment he heard my Dhamma," [the monks were amazed].
“When was the Dhamma spoken by you? “Just today, while walking for alms, while standing in the middle of the street.
“Venerable sir, that Dhamma spoken by you while standing in the middle of the street was but a small amount;
how could it produce such distinction in so short a time? “Bhikkhus, why do you think my Dhamma is ‘little’?”

"Do not measure [the value of speech] by whether it is much or little," he said, showing that even many thousands of verses that are unconnected with the goal are not better than even a single line of verse that is grounded in the goal:
"Even if there are a thousand verses, if they are connected with words of no meaning..."
“A single verse-line is better, hearing which one attains peace.
Having spoken this verse in the *Dhammapada*, [the Blessed One] said:

“Monks, this is the foremost: not only because of his attainment of final Nibbāna, but also because he is worthy of honor as the foremost among my disciple monks who possess swift direct knowledge (*khippābhiññā*). Thus he declared: “This is the foremost, monks...”
“Among my disciples, monks, who possess quick direct knowledge, this is Bāhiya Dārucīriya.
Thus the Blessed One placed that venerable one in this foremost position. It was with reference to him that it was said: “Then, monks, after walking for alms in Sāvatthī... [the Blessed One said:
‘Bāhiya Dārucīriya has attained final Nibbāna, monks.’”
Therein, "after the meal" means after the duty of eating. "Having returned from alms-round" means having turned back from the search for alms-food;
by both phrases, it is said that he has finished his meal. "Having carried out" means having led outside the city.
"Burn it" means cremate it. "And build a stupa for him" means taking the bodily relics of this Bāhiya.
"And build a *cetiya*. He states the reason for this: "A fellow practitioner of the holy life (*sabrahmacārī*), monks, has passed away.

Its meaning is as follows: he practiced that same *brahma*—the Dhamma consisting of the higher training in virtue and so forth, which you yourselves practice in a visible way in its supreme sense—which was common to you;
thus he was a "fellow practitioner of the holy life" precisely because he reached the time of death.
"He has passed away; therefore, carry him out on a bier, cremate him, and erect a stupa for him.

Regarding "What is his destination?"—among the five destinations (*gati*), which destination, rebirth, or state of existence has he attained? "Destination" (*gati*) means accomplishment. The meaning is:

what is the conclusion—is he a noble one (*ariya*) or an ordinary person (*puthujjana*)? "The future life" (*abhisamparāya*) refers to the arising of existence after passing away, or the cessation of existence.

Or rather: although the fact that he had attained final nibbāna was already implied by the Buddha’s command to build a stupa, those monks who did not understand from that alone asked, "What was his destination?
Or perhaps they asked the Blessed One in this way because they wished to have the matter made even more clearly evident.
"Paṇḍita" means one who has gone (ito) by means of the "paṇḍa," which is the wisdom of the supreme path; thus he is a "paṇḍita. "Paccapādī" means he practiced.
"Dhammassa" refers to the supramundane Dhamma. "Anudhammaṃ" refers to the practice of the Dhamma, such as the purification of virtue (sīlavisuddhi) and so forth.
Alternatively, "dhammassa" refers to the Dhamma of Nibbāna, and "anudhammaṃ" refers to the Dhamma of the Noble Path and its Fruits. And... [text truncated]
"I am one who deals with the Dhamma" means that for the sake of teaching the Dhamma, he did not harass me, because he practiced according to the instructions.

For whoever, having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher or having taken up a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), does not practice according to the instructions, he is said to harass the Teacher.
It was with reference to this that it was said: "Perceiving it as harmful, I did not speak what was well-mastered."
“O Brahmā, [I teach] the sublime Dhamma among men. Alternatively, it means: “Neither am I a legal dispute regarding the Dhamma, nor is this a legal dispute regarding the Dhamma.
This is what is meant: because of my correct practice, this Sāsana-Dhamma of mine—which is the cause for escaping from the suffering of saṃsāra—does not cause harm.
For one who practices wrongly, while destroying the Dispensation, [harms] the Teacher’s Dhamma-body.
"Deals a blow" means this. But he, having brought right practice to its ultimate consummation, attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue.
Therefore it was said: "Bhikkhus, Bāhiya of the Bark Robe has attained final Nibbāna.
"Having understood this matter" refers to the fact that the Elder Bāhiya had attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue.
Having understood in every way that the destination of those whose taints are exhausted and who have thus attained final Nibbāna is difficult for ordinary people to discern, he uttered this *udāna*—

this inspired utterance illuminating the power of non-abiding final Nibbāna. In that context, "where" means in that Nibbāna where water finds no footing, and where earth, fire, and air find no footing.
It does not find a footing. Why? Because of the unconditioned nature (*asaṅkhata-sabhāva*) of Nibbāna. For not even a trace of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*) can exist there.
"White" refers to the constellations, lunar mansions, and stars, which have received the name "white" because of their white color.
"They do not shine" means they do not radiate light. "The sun does not illuminate" refers to that [sun] capable of pervading the three continents with light at a single moment.

Even the sun does not shine there by way of its radiance. "The moon does not gleam there" means that although the moon possesses a brilliant nature, it does not shine forth by manifesting its own light because the moon itself is absent from that Nibbāna.
One might suspect: "If the sun, moon, and so forth do not exist there, then that place would be perpetually dark, like the world beyond. To address this doubt:
With this in mind, he said: "Therein darkness is not found. For if there were an absence of form, that which is called "darkness" would not exist.

And when one knows by oneself—that noble disciple who is a "Brahmin" because he is a sage (*muni*) through his silence (*mona*) due to having realized the Four Noble Truths, and who is named a "sage" because he is endowed with the knowledge of the Path known as *mona* and with bodily silence and so forth—he is a "Brahmin" by virtue of being a sage.

When, at the moment of the supreme path (*aggamagga*), by means of that very knowledge of penetration known as "mona," he himself—having abandoned hearsay and the like, and having made it his own direct experience—realized and penetrated *nibbāna*. There is also the reading "avedī," which has the meaning "he knew.
Then, "from forms and formless things, from pleasure and pain, he is liberated"—the word "then" (*atha*) refers to that *nibbāna*.

"Subsequently, by way of knowing. "Materiality" (*rūpa*) refers to material phenomena; by this, both five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*) and one-aggregate existence (*ekavokārabhava*) are included.

"Immateriality" (*arūpa*) refers to immaterial phenomena; by this, the immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*)—which is not mixed with materiality—is included. That is also called "four-aggregate existence" (*catuvokārabhava*).
"Pleasure and pain" (*sukhadukkha*) refers to the pleasure and pain that arise in all places, as well as from the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). Alternatively, "materiality" refers to...
"From the rebirth-linking of the form-world. "The formless" means from the rebirth-linking of the formless world.
"Pleasure and pain" refers to the rebirth-linking of the sense-sphere; for sense-sphere existence consists of a mixture of pleasure and pain.

Thus, by these two verses, the Blessed One demonstrates: "Such is the destiny of Nibbāna for my son Bāhiya," showing that he is absolutely liberated even from this entire cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
The commentary on the Tenth Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Bodhi Vagga is also finished.
2. The Mucalinda Vagga.
1. Commentary on the Mucalinda Sutta 11.
Regarding the first sutta of the Mucalinda Chapter, in the phrase "at the foot of the Mucalinda tree" (*mucalindamūle*): here, *mucalinda* refers to the *nīpa* tree.
It is also called *nicula*. [The Buddha was] near it. Some, however, say that *mucala* is the name of that tree.

They say, however, that he is called Mucalinda because he was the leader of the forest deities (*vanajetthaka*). "A great unseasonable cloud" refers to a great rain-cloud that arose even before the rainy season had arrived;
for it appeared in the last month of summer, filling the entire interior of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
"A seven-day downpour" means that when it arose, there was continuous rain for seven days. "Cold winds and cloudy weather."
And because that seven-day period was spoiled by cold winds mixed with spray from the water blowing from all sides, it was called "bad weather.
The Naga King named Mucalinda had his abode beneath a lotus pond near that very Mucalinda tree; there he was born as a Naga King of great power.
“From his own abode” means from his own nāga-abode. “Having surrounded him seven times with his coils” means having encircled the Blessed One’s body seven times with the coils of his own body.

“Spreading a great hood over the top of [the Buddha’s] head” means extending his own great hood over the region of the Blessed One’s head. There is also a reading, “having formed a hood,” which has the same meaning.
It is said that this Nāga king thought: “The Blessed One is sitting at the foot of a tree near my abode, and this seven-day storm is occurring;
it would be fitting for him to obtain a dwelling. Although he was capable of creating a palace made of the seven precious gems, he thought:
“If I were to do so, the essence of the body [of the Buddha] would not be honored. [He reflected thus regarding the Ten-Powered One.]
Thinking, "I shall perform service for the body," he assumed a massive physical form, encircled the Teacher seven times with his coils, and held him aloft with his hood spread above him.
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Khandhaka-ṭīkā* that "the space within the enclosure was the size of the storehouse chamber in the Lohapāsāda.
However, in the *Majjhima-ṭīkā*, it is said to have been "the size of the lower Lohapāsāda."
It is said that the intention of the Nāga King was: "The Teacher shall dwell in whatever posture he desires.
However, the Blessed One spent the seven days remaining exactly as he was seated. That place became like a gabled chamber with well-shuttered windows and well-lubricated door-panels.
The phrase "lest it be cold for the Blessed One," and so forth, is an explanation of the reason for acting in such a manner.
For he stood there having acted thus, thinking: "May cold not afflict the Blessed One; may heat not afflict him; may contact with gadflies and the like not afflict him.
In that regard, although there was indeed no heat during the seven-day storm, should a cloud nevertheless disappear from time to time, [he remained there].
"It might become hot; may it not afflict him"—it is appropriate for him to think thus. However, some say here:
"The mention of heat is a statement of the cause for making the enclosure of the dwelling spacious.
For if it were small, the heat produced from the body of the Naga would afflict the Blessed One; but by making it spacious..."
“Having acted thus, he stood [there], thinking, ‘May the heat not afflict such a one as this.
*Viddha* means risen up; the meaning is that it has become distant due to the departure of the clouds. *Vigatavalāhaka* means free from clouds.
*Deva* means the sky. *Viditvā* means having understood: “Now the sky is free from clouds; there is no affliction of cold or other discomfort for the Blessed One.”
"Having known": having removed. "Having cast off his own form": having set aside his own appearance as a nāga. "Having withdrawn": having made it disappear.
"The form of a young brahmin boy": the physical form of a youth. "This matter":

having understood in every way this matter—that for one who experiences the bliss of seclusion (*vivekasukha*), there is only happiness wherever he may be. "This inspired utterance (*udāna*)": he uttered this *udāna* which illuminates the power of the bliss of seclusion.
In this context, "seclusion is bliss" means that seclusion from the substrates of existence (*upadhiviveka*), which is synonymous with Nibbāna, is blissful.
"Of one who is content" means of one who is satisfied by the peace of the knowledge of the four paths.

"Of one who has heard the Dhamma" means of one for whom the Dhamma has been proclaimed or whose Dhamma is well-known. "Beholding" means beholding that seclusion, or whatever else is to be seen, all of it with the eye of wisdom attained through the power of one's own energy.
"Of one who passes by": *abyāpajja* means the state of being unprovoked; by this, the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (*mettā*) is shown.
"Restraint toward living beings" means restraint toward sentient beings, the state of non-harming; the meaning is "happiness. By this, the preliminary stage of compassion (*karuṇā*) is shown.
"The fading away of passion in the world is happiness": even the absence of passion in the world is happiness. Of what kind? It is "the transcendence of sensual desires," which is...
"Transcending sensual desires" is what is said; the meaning is that even this state of being free from lust is happiness. By this, the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*) is described.
"The subduing of the conceit 'I am'" describes, however, Arhatship (*arahatta*). For Arhatship is called the subsiding and subduing of the conceit "I am";
beyond this, there is no such thing as happiness. Therefore he said: "This indeed is supreme..."
"Happiness. Thus he took up the peak of the teaching by means of Arahantship.
The commentary on the first sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Rājasutta.
12. In the second [case], regarding "a number" (*sambahulā*): according to the method of the Vinaya, three persons are called "a number," and beyond that it is a Saṅgha.
However, according to the method of the Suttanta, only three [persons] constitute "three," and more than that is "a number.
Therefore, here too, they should be understood as "a number" according to the method of the Suttanta. "In the assembly hall" (*upaṭṭhānasālā*) means in the pavilion of the Dhamma assembly.
For it is called an "assembly hall" (*upaṭṭhānasālā*) because it is the place where monks attend upon the Tathāgata when he has come to teach the Dhamma.
Alternatively, that hall or pavilion where monks settle legal disputes, discourse on the Dhamma, engage in discussion, and naturally assemble together is also called an "assembly hall."
It is said. For even there, the Buddha’s seat is always prepared. This is indeed the proper conduct for monks during the lifetime of the Buddhas.
“Of those who have sat down” means of those who have gathered and sat down by way of sitting.
“Of those who have assembled” means of those who have assembled by way of coming together from here and there. Alternatively, having placed the Buddha’s seat in front [of them]...
Of those who are seated respectfully, by way of sitting with reverence as if in the very presence of the Teacher;

and of those who have gathered together, by way of falling well and properly into mutual accord because of their shared inclinations. The word "ayaṃ" (this) points to that which is now being described.
"Antarākathā" (intermediate talk) refers to the intervals between the attention to meditation subjects, the recitation of summaries, the asking of questions, and so forth.

"One talk" (aññā ekā kathā) means another conversation; or, it is called "intermediate talk" (antarākathā) because it occurs between the instruction received from the Sugata at midday and the hearing of the Dhamma to be received in the evening;
or, it is "intermediate talk" because it is another conversation occurring in the interval of the ascetic’s customary conduct. "Arose" (udapādi) means it originated.
"Of these two kings": this is the genitive case used for selection (*niddhāraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "one who possesses greater wealth" (*mahaddhanataro*) and so forth:
he who has great wealth (*mahaddhana*) consisting of a heap of the seven jewels deposited and placed within the earth is called "one who possesses great wealth";
one who is more than that is "one who possesses greater wealth. The particle *vā* has the sense of an alternative. This applies to the remaining terms as well.
The same method applies here. However, this is the distinction: he whose great wealth (*mahābhoga*) consists of permanent provisions is "one of great wealth.
He whose great treasury (*mahākosa*), which serves as a source of daily income, exists is "one of great treasure. Others, however, say:
"Wealth (*dhana*) is the property belonging to one's possession, consisting of various items such as gems, pearls, and fine timber, which serves as a source of daily income; that very [property]..."
They say that a treasury is deposited within the heartwood and so forth.

[The gems are: vajira, mahānīla, indanīla, marakata, veḷuriya, padumarāga, phussarāga, kakketana, pulāka, vimala, lohitaṅka, phalika, pavāḷa, jotirasa, gomuttaka, gomedaka, sogandhika, muttā, saṅkha, añjanamūla, rājapaṭṭa, and amataṃsaka.
"Priyaka" and "brāhmaṇī"—these are the twenty-four types known as *maṇi*. The seven metals and the *kahāpaṇa* coin are known as *sāra* (hardwood).
Beds, coverings, cloaks, ivory, stone, and so forth are known as *pheggu* (sapwood). Sandalwood, agallochum, saffron, tagara, camphor, and so forth are known as *gumba* (shrubs).

In this context, by the first [category] and the word "etcetera," there are the various kinds of grains such as *sāli* and *vīhi*, and pulses such as *mugga* and *māsa*, categorized as food for the morning and food for the evening.
Beginning with processed grain, everything that serves as an object of enjoyment and utility for sentient beings is included therein.
He whose conquered realm (*vijita*) is vast is *Mahāvijita*. He whose mounts—elephants, horses, and so forth—are great is *Mahāvāhana*.
He whose military force (*senābala*) and physical strength (*thāmabala*) are great is *Mahabbala*. [The term] *icchitanibbatti* signifies the manifestation of what is desired.

One who possesses great psychic power (*iddhi*) produced by meritorious deeds is "of great psychic power" (*mahiddhika*). One who possesses great majesty (*anubhāva*)—consisting of splendor (*teja*), or characterized by energy, mantras, and abundant power—is "of great majesty" (*mahānubhāva*).
And here, by the first [term] there is the perfection of wealth; by the second, the perfection of material possessions and requisites; and by the third, the perfection of opulence.
By the fourth [quality], the excellence of the territory; by the fifth, the excellence of the vehicle; by the sixth, the excellence of the retinue together with the excellence of the self;
by the seventh, the excellence of meritorious deeds; and by the eighth, the excellence of majesty—these are declared of those kings.
By this, that which is the excellence of wealth, the excellence of ministers, the excellence of the army, and the excellence of the kingdom [is established].
The seven natural endowments desired by kings are: the perfection of wealth, the perfection of friends, and the perfection of difficult terrain.
It should be understood that all of these have been explained as appropriate.

He is called a *rājā* because he delights the assembly (*parisa*) through the four means of attraction (*saṅgahavatthu*), such as giving. He is called a *māgadha* because he is the lord of the Magadhas.
He is called Seniya because he was endowed with a great army (*senā*) or because his clan was the Seniya clan. *Bimbi* refers to gold;
therefore, he is called Bimbisāra because of his golden-colored complexion. However, some say that this is merely the king’s personal name.
He is called Pasenadi because he conquers (*jināti*) enemies and hostile armies. He is called Kosala because he is the lord of the kingdom of Kosala. And furthermore:
In this context, *carahi* is merely a particle. *Vippakatā* means unfinished; the meaning is that this conversation among those bhikkhus was not yet concluded.

*Sāyanhasamayaṃ* means at one time in the evening. *Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito* means having emerged from seclusion—that is, from the withdrawal of the mind from various objects such as forms, or from the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) known as seclusion, according to its proper temporal limit.

He had emerged. For the Blessed One, having entered Sāvatthī in the morning surrounded by the community of monks, and having made alms-food easily available for the monks, finished his meal, and departed from Sāvatthī together with the monks, entered the monastery, stood at the entrance of the fragrant chamber, and performed the customary duties;
then, for the monks standing there, he spoke according to the circumstances that arose.
Having given his instructions to them, when they had departed for their daytime dwellings in the forest, at the roots of trees, and so forth, the Sugata entered the Fragrant Chamber (*gandhakuṭī*).
There he spent part of the day in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). When the time limit arrived, he emerged from that attainment and thought:
"The four assemblies, waiting for my arrival, are sitting and filling the entire monastery."
"Now it is time for me to enter the Dhamma-hall circle for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma.
Having risen from his seat and emerged from the fragrant Perfumed Chamber like a maned lion from a golden cave, or like a rutting, noble elephant approaching its herd,
he moved with a graceful gait free from bodily stiffness, his body radiant with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and adorned with the eighty minor characteristics.
Adorned with a radiant garland of banners, endowed with the graceful splendor of a halo extending a fathom,
and emitting the six-colored rays of a Buddha— blue, yellow, red, white, madder,
and brilliant gold— he approached the assembly hall, illuminating the entire monastery with his physical form, which was possessed of inconceivable power and incomparable Buddha-like grace.
Therefore it was said: "Then the Blessed One... [omitted] ...approached him.
Having approached in this manner and performed the customary duties, the Blessed One saw those monks sitting in silence.
Perceiving that "if I do not speak, these monks will not speak even for an eon out of reverence for the Buddha," he spoke in order to initiate the discourse: "By whom..."
“By what, monks? and so forth he said. Therein, *kāya nutthā* means “by what indeed do you exist here?
There is also the reading *kāya notthā*, which has the same meaning; some also read *kāya nvetthā*, for which the meaning is “by what indeed are you here?
The summary of the meaning therein is this: “Monks, by what kind of talk are you seated together here? By what [talk]?”

"And since your discussion regarding my arrival has not been concluded, I shall bring it to its conclusion"—thus he invited [them] by means of the invitation of the Omniscient One (*sabbaññupavāraṇā*).
"Na khvetan" means "it is not indeed this," or rather, this is the reading. They also read "Na khota";
the analysis of the words is simply "na kho etan. "Kulaputtānan" refers to sons of good family by birth and conduct. "Saddhā" means by faith, that is, by faith in the results of kamma.

And by means of faith in the Triple Gem. "From home" (*agārasmā*) means from the household; the sense is, from the state of being a householder. "To homelessness" (*anagāriyam*) means to the life of renunciation (*pabbajjā*).
"Of those who have gone forth" (*pabbajitānam*) means of those who have entered [the order]. "Yaṃ" is a reference to the action [of going forth]. Herein, this is the construction of the words:
"O monks, you have not gone forth having been led away by a king, nor led away by thieves, nor oppressed by debt, nor driven by the fear for your lives; rather..."
“Having gone forth from the home life out of faith into my teaching,
you should now engage in such idle chatter concerning kings; for such talk as this is neither fitting nor appropriate for you.”
Having thus rejected what is improper for those who have assembled as renunciants, he now, permitting their proper practice, said:
"Bhikkhus, when you have assembled, two things are to be done: either a discourse on the Dhamma or noble silence.
In this context, *vo* means "of you. For the word *karaṇīyaṃ* (to be done) is used here in relation to that [word].
This is a term for the agent (*sāmivacana*); therefore, the meaning is "by you. "Two things are to be done" means two things that ought to be performed.

"A discourse on the Dhamma" is a talk not departing from the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths; the meaning is a teaching of the Dhamma that illuminates both the round of existence (*pavatti*) and its cessation (*nivatti*).
For even a discourse on the Dhamma comprised of the ten bases of discourse is but a portion of that [Dhamma]. "Noble" (*ariya*) because it brings about absolute welfare.

Or, it is "noble" (*ariya*) because it is purified and supreme. "Silence" (*tuṇhībhāva*) refers to the state of not speaking, which consists of the cultivation of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
Some, however, say: "The second jhāna is noble silence, because it is the opposite of verbal formation (*vacī-saṅkhāra*).
Others say: "The fourth jhāna is noble silence. But this is the meaning here: "Monks,..."
For the purpose of cultivating seclusion of the mind, while dwelling in empty huts with bodies withdrawn into solitude,
if you should ever assemble, then having assembled in this way, you should— following the method stated as "making known what has not been heard or purifying what has been heard"—

engage in a discourse on the Dhamma connected with the impermanence and other characteristics of the aggregates and so forth, for the sake of mutual assistance and for the sake of non-harming one another.
"or one should dwell in the attainment of jhāna.
Therein, by the first statement regarding what is to be done, he shows the means for entering the Teaching for those who have not yet entered;
by the latter, the means for escape from saṃsāra for those who have already entered. Or alternatively, by the first he enjoins them to proficiency in the scriptures, and by the latter—
In the proficiency of realization. Alternatively, by the first [phrase] he illuminates the primary cause for the arising of right view, and by the second, the secondary one. For this has been said:
"Bhikkhus, there are these two causes, two conditions, for the arising of right view: the voice of another and wise attention within oneself."

The connection here should be understood as follows: by the former [phrase], he clarifies the root cause of mundane right view (*lokiya-sammādiṭṭhi*), and by the latter, the root cause of supramundane right view (*lokuttara-sammādiṭṭhi*).

"Having understood this matter" means having understood in every aspect that the attainment of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and so forth is more peaceful and more sublime than the excellence of sensual pleasures praised by those monks.
"He uttered this inspired utterance" (*udāna*) means he uttered this *udāna* which illuminates the power of the bliss of the noble abiding (*ariyavihāra*).

In that context, regarding the phrase "the sensual pleasure which the world seeks," the word "world" (*loka*) is used here in the sense of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), as in such passages as "the world of aggregates, the world of bases, the world of elements.
"As far as the moon and sun revolve,
The quarters shine with radiance..."
It occurs in the sense of *space* in such passages as: "The world extends for a thousandfold; therein your power prevails.
It occurs in the sense of *beings* in such passages as: "The Blessed One, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, saw... and so forth.
Furthermore, this should be understood here with respect to both the world of beings and the world of space.

Therefore, within this world, from the Avīci hell upwards to the Brahmā-world downwards, there is that pleasure accompanied by sensual desire (*kāmasahagata-sukha*) which arises by way of the defilement of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*) depending upon sense-objects (*vatthukāma*).
And as for "that which is heavenly pleasure" (*yadidaṃ dibbaṃ sukhaṃ*), it is that which exists in heaven (*divi*) and is obtainable by way of the divine abodes (*dibbavihāra*).
The bliss of the form-sphere attainments of both Brahmās and humans. Regarding "the bliss of the destruction of craving" (*taṇhakkhayasukha*):

that by resorting to which craving is destroyed—that is Nibbāna. Taking that as its object, the bliss of the fruition-attainment (*phalasamāpatti*) that occurs through the subsiding of craving is called "the bliss of the destruction of craving. Of that bliss of the destruction of craving:
the word *ete* (these) is a designation [for the former blisses] by means of a change in grammatical gender.
The meaning is "these are pleasures. Some, taking both [the preceding and following phrases] under the common category of "pleasure," read "etaṃ" (this);
for them, the reading should be "kalaṃ nāgghati" (it is not worth a fraction).
"Soḷasiṃ" means that which completes the sixteen. This is the summarized meaning here: beginning with the happiness of a wheel-turning monarch...
There is human happiness in the entire world of humans; there is the happiness to be experienced by nāgas, supaṇṇas, and others in their respective worlds;

and there is the sixfold sensual pleasure in the divine worlds beginning with those of the Four Great Kings—namely, whatever sensual pleasure arises in the elevenfold world of sense-desire, as well as that which arises among the gods of the fine-material and immaterial realms due to their attainment of the fine-material and immaterial jhānas, which constitute divine abodes.
“Divine” refers to the mundane jhāna-happiness that has received that name.

Taking both of those together and dividing them into sixteen parts, even one part—reckoned as a sixteenth part of the happiness known as the bliss of the destruction of craving, which is the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti)—is not worth a fraction of it.

And this commentary on the meaning is stated by way of the commonality of the attainment of fruition. Since the destruction of craving is mentioned in the text without distinction, even the mundane [happiness] is not worth a fraction of the bliss of the first attainment of fruition. For thus it is said:
“Better than sovereignty over the earth, better than going to heaven,
better than lordship over all the worlds, is the fruit of stream-entry.
This is also stated in the *Sotāpatti-saṃyutta*:
“Monks, even though a wheel-turning monarch, having exercised sovereignty, lordship, and dominion over the four continents,
at the breaking up of the body after death is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas; there,
surrounded by a host of nymphs in the Nandana grove, he is endowed with the fivefold divine cords of sensual pleasure.
He enjoys himself as one fully endowed [with sensual pleasures], yet he is not possessed of four qualities.

Consequently, he is indeed not liberated from hell, not liberated from the animal realm, not liberated from the sphere of hungry ghosts, and not liberated from the states of deprivation, the bad destinations, and the lower realms.
Monks, even though a noble disciple subsists on alms-food and wears rag-robes, he is [possessed of those four qualities].
“Endowed with which four qualities is he thus released from hell, released from the animal realm,
released from the sphere of hungry ghosts, and released from states of deprivation,
ill destiny, and perdition? Here, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Buddha...”

“He possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is indeed an arahant… [as above] …a Buddha, a Blessed One. He possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One… [as above] …to be realized by the wise for themselves.
He possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way… [as above] …the field of merit for the world.
He is endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken… [as above] …conducive to concentration. Endowed with these four qualities…”
"But, monks, whatever is the acquisition of the four continents, and whatever is the acquisition of the four [noble] states—
the acquisition of the four continents does not equal even a sixteenth part of the acquisition of the four states.
Thus the Blessed One distinguished all worldly happiness as surpassed and excelled, and supreme transcendental happiness alone as unsurpassed and preeminent.
The commentary on the second sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Daṇḍa Sutta: 13.
In the third [sutta], "children" (*kumārakā*) means young boys. Regarding the phrase "between Sāvatthī and the Jeta Grove," the word *antarā* [indicates the intermediate space].

In such passages as “Who could know that interval, other than a Tathāgata? and “People gather and deliberate; what is the difference between me and you?”, it occurs in the sense of a cause (*kāraṇa*).
In such passages as “Venerable sir, a certain woman saw me while she was washing a vessel by the light of a flash of lightning,” it occurs in the sense of a moment (*khaṇa*).

In such passages as “He in whom there are no anger from within,” it occurs in the sense of the mind (*citta*). [And] in the phrase “In the interval (*antarā*)... [it occurs in the sense of an intermediate state].

In such passages as "he reached the middle" (*vemajjhe*), it means the center. In such passages as "Moreover, monks, this Tapodā flows between two great hells" (*antarikāya*), it means an interval or opening (*vivare*).

Here, too, it should be understood as meaning an opening. Therefore, the sense here is to be understood as "in the opening between Sāvatthī and Jetavana. Furthermore, because of its connection with the word *antara*, the accusative case is used here.

“Between Sāvatthī and the Jeta Grove. In such instances, grammarians employ the word *antarā* only once, as in the expression “he goes between the village and the river,” which must then be construed with the second member as well.
However, in this case, it is stated by being repeated [and thus construed with both members].
“They strike the snake with sticks” means that having emerged from its hole, they pursue a hungry black snake as it goes out for its prey and beat it with sticks.
At that time, while the Blessed One was going to Sāvatthī for alms,
he saw those boys striking the snake with sticks along the way and said, “Why, young men, are you striking this snake with a stick?”
Having asked, "Are you killing them? and being told, "Out of fear of the gadflies, venerable sir," he felt a sense of spiritual urgency (*dhammasaṃvega*), thinking:

"These people, striking [the flies] with the thought 'We shall bring ourselves happiness,' will experience suffering in the place where they are reborn; oh, what skill in deceiving oneself through ignorance!
And because of that very spiritual urgency, he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*). Thus it is said: "Then the Blessed One... and so forth.

In this context, "having understood this matter" means: some explain it thus—"Having known that these children, by inflicting suffering on others for their own pleasure, will not themselves obtain happiness in the future.
For those who have practiced wrongly, the pursuit of pleasure leads to suffering in the future; for those who have practiced rightly, it leads exclusively to happiness.

Therefore, they say that the Teacher uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) precisely out of a sense of joy, thinking: "How truly fortunate are those who follow my instruction, for they are entirely free from harming others and partakers of ultimate happiness. Others, however, say:
"Having understood in every way the danger of such harm inflicted by those boys, [the Teacher spoke] regarding the harming of others..."
And out of compassion for others, he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) which analyzes the dangers and benefits in their proper order.
In that context: "Those who desire happiness" means those who are greedily attached to happiness because they exclusively long for their own well-being.

"Beings" refers to living creatures (*pāṇino*). Regarding the phrase "he who harms with a stick": here, "with a stick" is merely an illustration; it includes [injury] by means of a stick, or by clods of earth, weapons, blows with the hand, and so forth.

This is the meaning. Alternatively, "by means of a rod" (*daṇḍena*) means by means of punishment (*daṇḍanena*). This is what is intended: one who, toward all beings desiring happiness, [inflicts harm] through the "rod of speech" (*vacī-daṇḍa*) by way of striking them with birth and so forth;
or through the "rod of the body" (*kāya-daṇḍa*) by way of beating, striking, cutting, and so on, with the hands, mallets, weapons, and the like;
or through the "rod of wealth" (*dhanadaṇḍa*) by way of imposing fines of a hundred or a thousand [coins]. Among these rods—

By whatever means one harms, oppresses, or inflicts suffering upon another while seeking one’s own happiness, that person—seeking, searching for, and longing for their own happiness—does not obtain happiness after death;
in the world beyond, they do not obtain any of the three kinds of happiness: human happiness, divine happiness, or the happiness of Nibbāna.
The meaning is that, in truth, one receives nothing but suffering through that punishment.
"After passing away, he obtains happiness" refers to one who is endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion;

having reflected, "Just as I desire happiness and am averse to suffering, so it is for all beings," and being established in the abstinence from what is encountered and other virtues, according to the method described, [he does not harm] anyone by any means of punishment.
"He does not harm or oppress living beings; that person, having become a human in the next world, attains human happiness, and having become a deva, attains divine happiness;
transcending both, he attains the bliss of Nibbāna.
And here, the word "attains" (*labhate*) is used to show that, because such a person is certain to experience it, that happiness is as if present before them.
The same method applies to the previous verse as well.
The commentary on the third sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Sakkāra-sutta.

14. Fourth: At that time, the Blessed One was honored; indeed, by means of the honor and so forth that increased ever further—like a surge of effort born from the thought, "Beyond this, there is no room for me"—which was the fruit of the excellence of his accumulation of merit fulfilled over four incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand aeons, the Blessed One [was thus venerated].

He was honored. For, as the great Yamaka-clouds arise in all directions and produce a great flood, so too did all the perfections (*pāramī*), as if gathered together saying, "We shall give our fruition in a single existence," produce for the Blessed One a great flood of gain and honor.
Then, with food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, and so forth in their hands, the kshatriyas, brahmins, and others [approached].
Having arrived, they sought out the Blessed One, crying, “Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the God of Gods? Where is the Bull among Men?

Where is the Lion among Men? Bringing provisions by means of hundreds of carts, yet finding no space to enter, they stood and followed along, with the yoke of one cart touching the yoke of another for a distance of a league all around.
It is like the case of the Andhakavinda brahmins and others. All of that should be understood according to the method set forth in the Khandhaka and in various Suttas.
And just as it was for the Blessed One, so it was for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. For this has been said:

"Cunda, as far as any Saṅghas or groups have arisen in the world at present, Cunda, I do not see even a single Saṅgha that has attained such a pinnacle of gain and a pinnacle of fame as this Saṅgha of bhikkhus."

The gains and honors that arose for both the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus became, when combined, immeasurable like the flood of water from two great rivers. Therefore it was said: “At that time, the Blessed One was honored...
[and so on] ...with the requisites; the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was also honored... [and so on] ...with the requisites.”
But the sectarians (titthiyā), due to their lack of merit in the past and their wrong practice, were previously unhonored and held in low esteem;
however, with the arising of the Buddha, their splendor was especially ruined, like glow-worms at sunrise—devoid of radiance, lacking majesty, and deprived of gain and honor.
Unable to endure such gain and honor for the Blessed One and his Saṅgha, they became possessed by envy and said: "In this way..."
"Let us drive them away by harassing them with harsh words.
Thus, spitting out the poison of envy, they wandered here and there, abusing and reviling the bhikkhus. Therefore it is said:
"But the wanderers of other sects were not honored... [omission] ...of requisites. Then those wanderers of other sects..."
“Unable to endure the honor shown to the Blessed One, they see monks in the village and in the forest and revile, abuse, incense, and harass them with improper, harsh words.

In this context, “improper” (*asabbhāhi*) means unsuitable for a gathering (*asabhāyoggāhi*), unfit to be spoken in an assembly (*sabhāyaṃ*) or among a multitude of virtuous people; “harsh” (*pharusāhi*) means...
Meaning: "Harsh" means cruel and piercing to the vital organs. "Abusing" means they revile them by means of grounds for abuse such as birth and so forth.
"Insulting" means they threaten them, instilling fear by way of quarreling.
"Provoking anger" means they produce resentment by way of incitement so that another becomes angry. "Harassing" means they torment.
They cause discomfort in various ways.
But how did they direct insults and the like toward the Blessed One, who is serene on all sides, and toward the Saṅgha of bhikkhus?
Because their hearts were wounded by the loss of gain and honor since the appearance of the Blessed One, they dug into the earth and wallowed in it.

Just as one might cause a wound upon a flawless beryl gem, they persuaded the female wanderer named Sundarī to utter dispraise of the Teacher and the monks, and they proceeded to hurl insults and the like at them.
This account of Sundarī will appear later in the Pāḷi itself within the Sundarīsutta; therefore, whatever needs to be said regarding this matter, we shall explain it there.

The bhikkhus approached the Blessed One and reported that occurrence. Therefore it was said: “Then a great number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One... [they were] harassing him. This has the same meaning as what was stated before. “Having understood this matter”:
having understood in every aspect this misconduct of the sectarian teachers who were possessed by envy.

“This inspired utterance”: he uttered this inspired utterance which illuminates the state of being a *tādi* (one who is such) in the face of both the improper treatment performed by them and the assistance performed by others with confident hearts.

In that regard, "touched by pleasure and pain in the village or in the forest" means being touched by pleasure and pain anywhere—whether in the village or in the forest—experiencing pleasure and pains, or being endowed with their conditions.
"One should not perceive them as from oneself or from another" means: "I am happy, I am suffering; this is my happiness, this is my suffering; this [is another's]..."
"Do not establish that pleasure and pain as either yourself or another, thinking, 'Pleasure and pain have arisen for me. Why?
Because within this pentad of aggregates there is nothing whatsoever suitable to be viewed as 'I,' 'mine,' 'another,' or 'belonging to another';
rather, it is merely formations that, having arisen according to conditions, break up moment by moment."
And here, the mention of pleasure and pain is the heading for the teaching; the meaning should be understood by way of all worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*).
Thus the Blessed One elucidated the fourfold emptiness: "I am not anywhere, in anything, nor do I belong to anything; nor is there anything anywhere that belongs to me."
Now he shows the reason why that [feeling] does not burn, both for oneself and for others, with the words: “Contacts touch depending on the substrate (upadhi).
These contacts—namely, those to be experienced as pleasant and those to be experienced as painful—depend upon the substrate known as the five aggregates;
when that [substrate] exists, they touch their respective objects and indeed proceed therein. [As for those] neither-painful-nor-pleasant...
Since feeling, by its very nature of being peaceful, is included within happiness alone, this commentary on the meaning has been made solely by way of the two kinds of contact.
However, in order to show how those contacts do not actually touch [the Tathāgata], it is said: "By what means could contacts touch one who is without substrate (nirupadhi)?
For when there is an absolute absence of the substrate of the aggregates (khandhūpadhi), by what cause could those contacts touch him? They cannot.
There is a reason. For if you do not desire the pleasure and pain that arise by way of abuse and so forth, you should apply yourselves entirely to the state of being without substrate;
thus he concluded the verse with reference to the element of Nibbāna without residue.
In this way, by means of this Udāna, the cycle of existence and its cessation have been explained.
The commentary on the fourth sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Upāsaka Sutta: 15.
Regarding the fifth [sutta], "at Icchānaṅgala" refers to a certain brahmin village in the Kosala country named Icchānaṅgala; it was because he was residing there [that the Buddha spoke].

"Born there" means he was born in Icchānaṅgala; thus he is "of Icchānaṅgala. "A lay follower" (upāsaka) means one who has declared his status as a lay follower in the presence of the Blessed One by means of the three goings for refuge;
such a lay follower observes the five training precepts and holds the Buddha as his guide, the Dhamma as his guide, and the Saṅgha as his guide.
"On some business" means on some task that ought to be done, such as the clearing of a debt or similar matters.

“Having fulfilled” means having brought to completion. It is said that this lay follower used to approach and attend upon the Blessed One frequently in the past, but for some time he was unable to see the Teacher due to his many obligations.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “It has been a long time, lay follower, since you made the effort to come here.”
In this context, *cirassaṃ* means "after a long time. *Pariyāyaṃ* means "turn" or "occasion. *Yadidaṃ* is a particle; its meaning is "that which is this. What is meant is this:

"This turn that was made today for coming into my presence, you have taken a long time to perform, having created much delay (*papañca*). *Cirapaṭikāhaṃ* means "I am one who has waited long"; I [have been waiting] from a long time ago.
"Desirous of approaching" is the connection [of the phrase]. "By this or that" means by some or by others.

Alternatively, "by this or that" means by whichever or by those whomsoever; therein he shows respect. For one who has deep faith in the Teacher, there is no concern for anything else as much as for seeing the Teacher and hearing the Dhamma.
Regarding "duties and obligations": here, "duty" (*kicca*) refers to what must necessarily be done, while the other is...
*Karaṇīyaṃ* means that which ought to be done. *Kiccaṃ* is what must be done first; *karaṇīyaṃ* is what must be done later.
*Kiccaṃ* refers to a minor task; *karaṇīyaṃ* refers to a major one. *Byāvaṭo* means busily engaged or striving. *Evāhaṃ* means "in this manner" or "by this way," implying:
"I was unable to approach [the Teacher], not because I spoke with disrespect"—this is the intended meaning.

"Having understood this matter": having understood in every aspect this matter—that for beings, when the appearance of a Buddha is rare and the attainment of human birth is difficult, there is an obstacle to the wholesome because of their state of possessing something (*sakiñcana*) and their preoccupation with duties, whereas for one who possesses nothing (*akiñcana*), there is not;
[the Buddha] uttered this *udāna* as a mere illumination of that very meaning.

In this context, "Sukhaṃ vata tassa na hoti kiñci" means: for that person who has no "something"—not even a single object such as form—possessed by craving in the sense of "this is mine," for that person there is indeed happiness;
the meaning is, "Ah, it is truly happiness! There is also a reading "na hosī," which refers to the past tense.

It should be understood thus. However, some explain the phrase "there is nothing whatsoever" (*na hoti kiñci*) as meaning "one for whom there is no 'something' consisting of lust and so forth" (*rāgādikiñcana*);
that is not correct, because the teaching is presented here with reference to the phenomena that constitute objects of grasping (*pariggahadhamma*).

If the term "something consisting of lust and so forth" were included within the category of things to be grasped, then what was said would indeed be appropriate; or else, it refers to a person for whom there is "nothing" [to grasp].
Even the slightest "something" that constitutes an impediment does not exist for him precisely because of the absence of the "somethings" such as lust (*rāga*).
That state of his being "nothing" (*akiñcanatta*) is a "blissful condition" (*sukhavataṃ*) because it serves as a basis for happiness; the meaning is, "Oh, what bliss!

If one asks, "For whom is there no 'something'?", he says: "For the one who has understood the Dhamma and is well-versed in it. This refers to one who, through the four paths, has accomplished the sixteen functions.
He has fully understood the Dhamma and accomplished what was to be done; for that very reason, he is "learned" (bahussuta) through his proficiency in penetration.

Thus, having shown the benefit of being without anything (akiñcana), the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with "Behold one who possesses something" (sakiñcanaṃ passa) in order to show the disadvantage of possessing something.
