Its meaning is as follows: one who possesses something because of the existence of the "somethings" (kiñcana) of passion and so forth, as well as the "somethings" of material things.

Seeing that people are being tormented and fall into distress because they possess something— that is, because of their attachment— and because of the pursuit of sensual pleasures not yet obtained and the guarding of those already obtained,
and because of their sense of duty and obligation, and because of their grasping at things as "I" and "mine," the Teacher, having attained spiritual urgency (*dhammasaṃvega*),
speaks thus to his own mind: "A person is bound to another person"— meaning, while being one person himself...
In regard to another person, one who has become bound by way of craving, thinking "I am his" or "this is mine," is afflicted and falls into distress.
There is also the reading *paṭibaddhacitto*. And this is the meaning:
"The fool is afflicted, thinking, 'I have sons, I have wealth.'"
"One has no self belonging to oneself; how then can there be sons?
How can there be wealth?"—this is to be illustrated by such scriptural passages.
The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Discourse to the Pregnant Woman (Gabbhinīsutta) 16.
Regarding the sixth [discourse], "a certain wanderer": this refers to a wanderer who was a householder. "Young" means youthful.
"Maiden" (*māṇavikā*) is a designation for the daughter of a brahmin. "Pajāpati" means wife. "Pregnant" means having conceived a living being.

"Upavijañña" means that the time for childbirth has arrived today or tomorrow; this is the connection [of the phrase]. It is said that he was of brahmin birth and lived with his wife in the Vādapaṭṭha forest;
therefore, they addressed him by the designation "wanderer" (paribbājaka) together with his wife.
However, because his wife was of brahmin birth, he addressed her as "brahmin. "Oil" refers to sesame oil. By way of the term "oil,"...
And here, she commands: "Bring whatever is required for the relief of the pains of childbirth for one who has given birth, including ghee, salt, and so forth.
"Whatever will be for me when I have given birth" means whatever oil and such will be of benefit to her once the fetus has emerged from her womb.
There is also a reading, "for the female wanderer" (*paribbājikāya*). "From where? means from which place, namely, from her own family home.
The intention is: "There is no place for me to fetch oil and such from a friend's family.
The phrase "I am fetching oil" is stated using the present tense to indicate proximity to the present moment; the meaning is "I shall fetch oil.
In the expression "of a recluse or a brahmin, of ghee or oil," the word *vā* has a conjunctive sense, as in "from fire or from water... [and so forth].
[It is used] as in such passages as, "or [there may be] dissension of friends. In the phrase *sappissa vā telassa vā*, the genitive case (*sāmivacana*) expresses the sense of identity (*paccatte*).
The meaning is: "ghee and oil are given to be eaten or drunk to one's heart's content. However, others say:

"In *sappissa vā telassa vā*, the genitive expresses a relationship of part to whole (*avayavasambandhe*). For here, by the word 'to one's heart's content' (*yāvadattha*), a part of the aggregate consisting of ghee and oil is intended."
They say, "It is so called. "Not to be taken out" means it cannot be led outside by means of a vessel or by hand;
it is not given. "Having vomited" means having thrown up. The connection is: "What if I were to give? Indeed, this was his thought:
"I shall go to the king's storehouse, drink oil up to my throat, and immediately upon returning home, [place it] in a single vessel..."
“Having vomited it up just as it was drunk and placed it on the hearth, I shall cook it;
that which is mixed with bile, phlegm, and so forth will be consumed by the fire, but having taken the oil, I shall apply it to the work of this female wanderer.
To “make it go upward” means to bring it out upward by means of vomiting; but “not down” means not [to expel it] downward by means of purging.
But he was unable to expel it. For, thinking, "What has been drunk in excess will come out of the mouth by itself," he drank;

yet because his stomach lacked the natural capacity [to expel it], and because he neither knew nor obtained the proper methods for inducing vomiting or purging, he merely wallowed and rolled about, afflicted solely by painful sensations. "Dukkhāhi" means painful. "Tibbāhi" means...
"Thick" means sharp. "Harsh" means rough. "Bitter" means cruel due to being extremely disagreeable.
"Rolls about" means that without lying down in one place, he rolls his body here and there, dragging it along.
"Turns over" means that even when lying in one spot, he turns by tossing his limbs all around; [he turns] toward [the fire].
Turning, it revolves; turning all around, it turns back.

"Having understood this matter" means: having known in every aspect this matter—that "this arising of suffering is caused by the unreflective enjoyment of one who possesses something, whereas for one who possesses nothing, this does not exist at all"—[he spoke] the elucidation of that meaning.

He uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*). Therein, “O, how happy indeed! means: O, how happy indeed are the true persons (*sappurisa*). Who, then, are they? They are those who possess nothing (*akiñcana*).

By what absence are they "those who possess nothing"? By the absence of the "possessions" of passion (*rāga*) and so forth, as well as the "possessions" of grasping (*pariggaha*). To the question, "For whom is there no such possession? he said: "The knowers of the Vedas (*vedagu*)."

"Indeed, people are 'nothing' (akiñcana)" means those who have gone to, or attained, that which is called the Veda—namely, the knowledge of the Noble Path—or who have gone to Nibbāna by means of that Veda;

thus they are "Veda-gone" (vedaguṇo). Those noble persons, individuals whose taints are destroyed, are called "nothing" because all things such as greed and so forth have been completely eradicated by the Supreme Path. For when greed and other such things do not exist, how could there be the "thing" that constitutes possession?

Thus, having praised the Arahants with the first half of the verse, he spoke the words beginning with "One who possesses something" (*sakiñcanaṃ passa*) in the second half, censuring the blind worldlings (*andhaputhujjana*).
That has the same meaning as what was stated in the previous sutta. In this way, the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) are explained by this verse as well.
The commentary on the sixth sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Ekaputtaka Sutta:
Regarding the seventh [sutta], "an only son" (ekaputtaka) means one son; and he is called an "only son" in the sense of being worthy of compassion, and in the sense of being beloved.
*Piyo* means dear; *manāpo* means pleasing in the sense of increasing mental delight.

Alternatively, he is dear in the sense of being beautiful to behold due to the perfection of his physical splendor, and pleasing in the sense of possessing a virtuous nature due to the perfection of his moral conduct and behavior. *Kāla* means that which exhausts (*khapeti*) beings; it is death.

One who has undergone (*kata*) that is "one who has passed away" (*kālaṅkata*). Or, one who has been done away with (*kata*) by *kāla*, that is, by Death (*maccu*), and has perished or gone beyond sight, is "one who has passed away" (*kālaṅkata*); the meaning is "dead."
"A number of lay followers" refers to many lay followers residing in Sāvatthī who, out of shared grief for the lay follower whose son had died, followed him all the way to the cremation ground.
Having performed whatever duties were to be done for the deceased body, they turned back;
yet, dressed exactly as they were, they entered the water, bathed their heads, wrung out their clothes without even drying them, and put on one lower garment and one upper robe.
Having made him an upāsaka and placing him at their head, they approached the Blessed One with the thought, "We shall hear the Dhamma for dispelling sorrow from the presence of the Teacher.
Therefore it is said, "with wet hair," and so forth.
In that context, *allavatthā* means those whose clothes were soaked with water. *Divā divassa* means during the day of the day, that is, at midday.
The meaning is "the right time. Since the Tathāgatas ask even when they know, and do not ask even when they know;

since they ask having discerned the right time, and do not ask having discerned the right time—therefore, the Blessed One, though already knowing, asked for the purpose of initiating the discourse, saying, "What, indeed, are you doing, lay followers?
and so forth. Its meaning is: on other days, you lay followers...
"When you came to me previously, you arrived in the evening dressed in clean, dried clothes; but today you have come here at midday with wet clothes and wet hair.

What is the reason for this? "Because of that," [they replied], "because we were overcome by such intense grief born from the mental torment caused by the separation from our son, we approached you in this state."

"Having understood this matter": having known in every way that sorrow, pain, dejection, and so forth arise from the basis of what is dear, and that these do not exist at all when the basis of what is dear is absent—having understood this matter—he uttered this *udāna* (inspired utterance) to illuminate its meaning.

In this context, "those who are attached to the gratification of the form of what is dear" means those whose minds are bound and fettered by the relish of pleasant feeling toward the aggregates of form and so forth, which are of a dear nature.
For "gadhitāse" has the same meaning as "gadhitā"; or, "se" is merely a particle.
"Endearing forms" refers to the eye and so forth, as well as children, wife, and so on. For this has been said: "And what in the world is endearing and pleasant?
The eye in the world... [and so on] ...craving for phenomena in the world is endearing and pleasant.
"Fields, lands, or gold, cattle, horses, slaves, and men;"
And: "The woman’s kinsmen pursue various sensual pleasures; the man who lusts after them [is lost].

Therefore, the meaning is that they are greedy for, infatuated with, and addicted to those pleasant forms through their gratification. To show who those are who are "infatuated with the gratification of pleasant forms," he says:
"the hosts of devas and various humans. This refers to the many assemblies of devas, such as the Cātumahārājika gods and others, as well as those of Jambudīpa and so forth.

And there are many people. "Possessing ill-will" (*aghāvino*) means afflicted by physical and mental suffering. "Worn out" (*parijunna*) means fallen away from the excellence of youth, health, and so forth, due to misfortunes such as old age and disease.
Or rather, this meaning should be understood among gods and humans according to what they happen to obtain.
Alternatively, although suffering, old age, and disease do not occur for gods who are endowed with absolute happiness, because their very nature does not transcend that [state of suffering].

Furthermore, they are described as "full of suffering" and "worn out. Or rather, the occurrence of suffering and so forth should be understood for them as well, by way of the arising of premonitory signs, concealed aging, and mental disease.

They fall under the power of King Death because, due to not having abandoned craving for objects of affection, they enter the womb again and again, owing to their lack of mastery over the three elements.
They fall directly into the power of death, which is designated as the King of Māra.
Having thus far shown the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), he now shows the turning away from it (*vivaṭṭa*) with the verse beginning, "But those who, by day and night...
Therein, "those who are heedful by day and night" means that during the day, through walking and sitting, they [keep] the mind [free] from obstructive states.
In the manner described by the passage beginning with “he purifies,” they fulfill the practice of heedfulness with firm diligence during both the day and the night.

“They abandon what is dear”: having made the cultivation of the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths their primary concern, they abandon through the attainment of the Noble Path that which is dear, that which is of a dear nature—the dear objects such as the eye and so forth—by abandoning the desire and lust bound up with them.

These noble persons indeed dig up the root of evil—the bait of death that is difficult to overcome. This refers to the root of the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*), which is the "bait" because it is to be seized by death;
it is "difficult to overcome" because it cannot be turned back by any ascetics or brahmins outside of this [teaching].
Together with ignorance, they dig up craving with the hoe of the knowledge of the Noble Path.
They dig up [the roots], not leaving even a trace behind, uprooting them. This is the meaning:
"Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless; heedlessness is the path of death.
Those who are heedful do not die; those who are heedless are as if already dead."
It should be expanded upon by means of the initial phrases of the sutta.
The commentary on the seventh sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Suppavāsā Sutta.
18. In the eighth [case], *Kuṇḍikāyaṃ* refers to the city of the Koliyans named after that. *Kuṇḍadhānavane* means in the forest called Kuṇḍadhāna, not far from that city.
It is said that in the past, a certain yakkha named Kuṇḍa made his dwelling in that grove;
because he was satisfied by offerings consisting of a mixture of *kuṇḍadhāna*, they brought such offerings to him there, and for that reason, this grove [was so named].
It was indeed known as Kuṇḍadhāna. Not far from it, there was a certain village headman’s dwelling;
because it was situated in the place where that *yakkha* issued his commands and because it was protected by him, it was designated as "Kuṇḍikā.
Later on, the Koliya kings built a city there, which also continued to be called "Kuṇḍikā" according to its former designation.
It is said. And in that grove, the Koliyan kings established a monastery for the Blessed One and the community of monks; it too became known as the Kuṇḍadhāna Grove.
Then, while wandering on tour through the countryside, the Blessed One eventually arrived at that monastery and stayed there. Therefore it was said: "At one time the Blessed One..."
“He dwells at Kuṇḍadhāna’s Wood with his water-pot.
“Suppavāsā” is the name of that female lay follower. “Daughter of the Koliyas” means she was the daughter of a Koliyan king.

For she was the Blessed One’s foremost attendant and was placed by him in the foremost position among those female disciples who give excellent gifts; she was a noble female disciple who had attained the stream-entry fruit.
For whatever suitable solid food, soft food, or medicine belonged to the Blessed One, there was nothing else that needed to be prepared there;
he himself, having deliberated with his own wisdom, would carefully prepare and present it all.
And daily he provided eight hundred meals for the Saṅgha and individual meals for individuals. Whosoever the bhikkhu—
Or, when a monk or a nun has entered that family for alms, they do not depart with empty hands.
Thus, being free in their generosity, pure-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to begging, and fond of giving and sharing;
in her womb, a disciple-bodhisatta who had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and was in his final existence took rebirth. She [conceived] that embryo by means of...
Due to her evil karma, she carried [the child] in her womb for seven years, and for seven days she remained with a dead fetus. Therefore it is said:
“She bore the fetus for seven years and was with a dead fetus for seven days.
In this context, “seven years” means seven full years; and because this expresses an uninterrupted duration, it is used in the accusative case.
"She carries a fetus" means she bears a fetus; the meaning is that she is pregnant. "With a fetus confused for seven days" means with a fetus in distress for seven days.

For when a fetus has fully developed and it is time for birth, it is moved and turned by the winds born of karma (kammaja-vāta), becoming head-downward and feet-upward, facing the opening of the womb. Thus it is...
Not adhering to anything, it emerges outside. However, if it fails [to emerge], it closes off the birth canal by way of turning back and lies across, or the birth canal closes by itself;
being turned back and forth therein by the winds born of karma (*kammaja-vāta*), it is called "confused" or "a miscarried fetus. For that too, for seven days...
Because it was so, it is said: “For seven days she was with a confused womb.

And this embryo was the Elder Sīvali. How did he experience the suffering of dwelling in the womb for seven years, how did he undergo the state of being in a confused womb for seven days, and how did his mother, a noble female disciple who had attained the stream-entry (sotāpanna), likewise experience such suffering?

"How was it born? It is said: In the past, while Kāsika-raja was ruling in Benares, a king of Kosala arrived with a great army, seized Benares, killed that king, and made his chief queen his own chief queen.
However, the son of the King of Benares, at the time of his father’s death, fled through the gate of the latrine and [reached] his own...
Having gathered his kinsmen, friends, and relatives together and gradually assembled his forces, he arrived at Bārāṇasī.
Having established a great encampment not far away, he sent a letter to that king, saying: "Either give up the kingdom, or wage war.
When the prince’s mother heard the message, she said: "There is no need for war; [let there be] movement in all directions..."
“Having cut off [the supply], surround the city of Bārāṇasī;
then, exhausted by the depletion of wood, water, and food, the people in the city will hand over the king without even a battle,” he sent in a letter.
Having heard his mother’s message, he besieged the city for seven years, guarding its four great gates. In the city...
People would exit through the small gate to bring firewood and water, and to perform all their various tasks.
Then, when the prince’s mother heard of this situation, she sent a secret message to her son, saying:
“My foolish son does not know the proper stratagem; go, tell him to close the small gates and besiege the city.”
Thus, having heard his mother’s command, he acted accordingly for seven days.
The citizens, unable to go outside, took the head of that king on the seventh day and gave it to the prince. The prince entered the city and took possession of the kingdom.
At that time, due to the ripening of the karma of besieging the city for seven years, now for seven...

She dwelt for seven years in what was called the mother’s womb—a vessel of blood—and furthermore, for seven days she remained besieged in the city, and for seven days she experienced the state of a woman with a difficult labor. However, in the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*, it is said:
"Having besieged the city for seven days, by the outflow of her past deeds, she dwelt in a vessel of blood for seven years and experienced the state of a woman with a difficult labor for seven days."
It is said, "He attained [it]. Furthermore, by the power of the aspiration he made when he gave a great gift at the feet of the Perfectly Enlightened One Padumuttara, thinking,

"May I become the foremost among those who receive gains," and the aspiration he made during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī when he gave sugar-curd worth a thousand coins together with the city-dwellers, he became the foremost among those who receive gains.
Suppavāsā, too, because she had been sent with the command, "Seize the city by siege,
dear ones," carried the fetus in her womb for seven years and gave birth after being in false labor for seven days. Thus,
mother and son experienced such suffering as was appropriate to their own karma.
"By three kinds of thoughts" means by the three types of right thought associated with the recollection of the qualities of the Triple Gem.
"She endured" means she bore the suffering arising from being delirious in childbirth;

for she, while recollecting the Blessed One’s state of perfect enlightenment, the noble Saṅgha’s correct practice, and the fact that Nibbāna is the escape from suffering, [endured] the suffering arising within herself.
Having overcome them by means of non-attention (*amanasikāra*) alone, he endures them. Therefore it is said: “He endures through three kinds of thoughts.
The passage beginning with “Truly, he is a Perfectly Enlightened One” (*sammāsambuddho vata*) is a demonstration of the manner in which those thoughts arise. Its meaning is as follows:

He who, by reason of his blessedness (*bhagyavantatā*) and other such qualities, is the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*), the Lord of the World (*Lokanātha*), has rightly—that is, without error—personally and by himself awakened to all phenomena; oh, what a Buddha! [he thinks].

Thus the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the abandoning and the absolute non-arising and cessation of this very kind of suffering of the round—which is currently being experienced by me—and of all other such suffering; he teaches the Dhamma that is non-perverted.
For it is through the teaching of the non-perverted Dhamma that the Teacher’s attainment of perfect enlightenment is accomplished. Of him, who possesses the aforementioned qualities...

Because they were born at the conclusion of the Blessed One’s hearing of the Dhamma and because they are united by the commonality of virtue and view, this assembly of eight noble persons—known as the Saṅgha of Disciples—is indeed well-practiced; oh, how they have practiced rightly!
This Noble Saṅgha follows the path that does not turn back for the sake of abandoning such and such round-of-existence suffering, and for the sake of its non-arising and cessation.
"One who is practicing. "How truly blissful! Oh, what excellent bliss is Nibbāna, which is free from all conditioned things, wherein such suffering of the round of existence is not found!

And here, even those who are currently practicing are called "those who have practiced" because there is no turning back from the practice. Alternatively, the word *paṭipanna* (practicing) is used like the word *uppanna* (arisen).
The sense of the present tense should also be understood. For this very reason, it says: "one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.
"Her husband" means her own husband, the prince of Koliya. "Addressed" means she spoke.
"With my words, bow your head at the feet of the Blessed One"—that is, with my message, [bow] to those feet adorned with the marks of wheels, as beautiful as blooming lotuses.
"Pay homage to the Blessed One’s feet with your head"—the meaning is that you should perform a salutation with your highest limb.

Regarding the phrases beginning with "free from illness" (*appābādha*): "illness" (*ābādha*) refers to a discordant sensation; though it may arise in only one part [of the body], it seizes the entire body as if binding it with an iron band.
"Affliction" (*ātaṅka*) is a disease that makes life difficult. Alternatively, *ātaṅka* is a disease that must be endured.
The other is affliction (*ābādha*). It refers either to a minor illness or ailment, or to a severe affliction. Some, however, say:
"Affliction arises from within oneself, while ailment arises from without. He asks about the absence of both of these.
Furthermore, for one who is ill, even rising up is considered a great burden; there is no strength in the body. Therefore, [he asks] regarding freedom from illness.
He says, "Ask about the lightness of the body, which is reckoned as its quick transformation, and about bodily strength.
He says, "And ask about dwelling in comfort," meaning: ask about dwelling in happiness within the four postures—standing, sitting, walking, and lying down.
Then, showing the manner in which he should be questioned, she said, "Venerable sir, Suppavāsā... and so forth. And when he says, "Speak thus now... [the text continues].
This indicates the manner in which she should speak.
"Param" means the acceptance of the words. By this, she shows: "It is well, noble lady; I shall practice exactly as you have said.
"Koliyaputta" refers to Suppavāsā’s husband, the son of the Koliyan king. "May she be happy" [means] in the world with its devas...
The Teacher, the foremost recipient of offerings in the world, having accepted the salutation sent by Suppavāsā,
immediately thereafter personally manifested to her a bestowal of happiness that was characteristic of the Buddhas and indicative of his own abiding in loving-kindness;
furthermore, he bestowed upon her a further gift of happiness by way of warding off the suffering arising from the miscarriage of her son.
Showing [her this], he said: “May you be happy... may you be free from disease; may you give birth to a healthy son.
“Simultaneously with the words” means together with the Blessed One’s speech. At the very moment the Blessed One spoke thus, that karma also reached total exhaustion.
Observing its state of exhaustion, the Teacher [acted] accordingly.
He spoke. Others, however, say: "If the Teacher had not declared this, then that suffering would have persisted for her for some further time.
But because the Blessed One said, 'May she be happy and healthy, and may she give birth to a healthy son,' at the very moment those words were spoken, that fetus abandoned its state of distress."
She went outside as if in ease, and thus it was safe for both mother and son. For inconceivable indeed is the power of the Buddhas.
Just as Paṭācārā, having reached a state of madness through grief born of separation from her beloveds—“Both my sons are dead, my husband is dead on the road;”
“Mother, father, and brother— all burn upon a single funeral pyre. Having said this,
as soon as the Blessed One spoke the words, “Sister, regain your mindfulness,” the derangement of Suppiyā the laywoman—
who was wandering about with nothing but her own gold— subsided immediately due to the great wound she had inflicted upon her own thigh.

Unable to rise, she lay upon her bed; yet immediately after saying, "Come and pay homage to me," her wound was healed, and she went of her own accord to pay homage to the Blessed One—such instances are to be cited here.
"So be it, Bhante," [said Ānanda]. Bhante, just as the Blessed One, wishing to wish health upon his mother and her son, said:
“May she be happy and healthy, and may she give birth to a healthy son”—this is exactly so. For the word of the Blessed Buddhas never turns out otherwise;
this is the intended meaning. Some, however, say “evamatthū” (let it be thus), while others explain by bringing in the sense of the word “hotū” (let there be).
“Abhinanditvā” (having rejoiced) means with a Brahma-voice as sweet as the song of the karavīka bird.
While that speech was being spoken by the Blessed One, he rejoiced by facing it with the attainment of joy and gladness. "Having expressed his appreciation" means:
having subsequently generated gladness, or having delighted with the mind and expressed appreciation with words;
or having delighted in the excellence of the words and expressed appreciation for the excellence of the meaning. "He returned to his own home."

He returned to his own home. As for those who read "yena sakaṃ gharaṃ" (to where his own home was), although the word "tena" (by that) is indeed already expressed due to the correlative relationship between the words *ya* and *ta*, nevertheless, the elliptical reading "paṭiyāyitvā" (having prepared) must be supplied.
"Vijāta" means born; it has the sense of having given birth. "Acchariya" (marvelous) is constant, like a blind man’s climbing a mountain.
"It does not exist" is a marvel; this, first of all, is the method of etymology (*saddanaya*). In the Commentaries, however, it is said:
"A marvel (*acchariya*) is that which is worthy of a finger-snap (*accharā*)," meaning it is fit to be struck with a finger-snap. "Vata" expresses esteem; the sense is, "Oh, what a marvel!
"Bho" is an address concerning the Dhamma. "Abbhuta" means that which has become something never before been.
“Of the Tathāgata”: for eight reasons the Blessed One is a Tathāgata—he is a Tathāgata because he has come (āgata) in accordance with reality (tathā);

he is a Tathāgata because he has gone (gata) in accordance with reality; he is a Tathāgata because he has come to the true characteristic (tathalakkhaṇa); he is a Tathāgata because he has perfectly awakened to (abhisambuddha) the true dhammas as they really are;

he is a Tathāgata because of his seeing in accordance with reality; he is a Tathāgata because of his speaking in accordance with reality; he is a Tathāgata because of his acting in accordance with reality.
The Tathāgata is so called in the sense of overcoming.

How is the Blessed One the Tathāgata in the sense of having come thus? He is the Tathāgata because he has come in the same way that the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones came for the welfare of the entire world.
What is meant by this? It means that by the same resolute intention (*abhinīhāra*) by which those Blessed Ones came, [he too has come].
Endowed with the eight qualities, this Blessed One has also arrived. Just as those Blessed Ones, having fulfilled the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*),
and having fulfilled the thirty perfections— namely, the ten perfections (beginning with *sīla*, *nekkhamma*, *paññā*, *vīriya*, *khanti*, *sacca*,

*adhiṭṭhāna*, *mettā*, and *upekkhā*), the ten secondary perfections (*upapāramī*), and the ten ultimate perfections (*paramatthapāramī*)— and having performed the five great renunciations (*mahāpariccāga*):

Having completely renounced, fulfilled the practice of former associations, former conduct, the preaching of Dhamma, the conduct for the benefit of others, and so forth, and having reached the pinnacle of the practice of wisdom, they have come;
in that same way, this Blessed One has also come. And just as those Blessed Ones came after developing and cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness...
[pe] ...the noble eightfold path, in that same way, this Blessed One has also come. Thus...
Thus he has come, therefore he is the Tathāgata.

How is it that he has thus come, and so is the Tathāgata? Just as those Blessed Ones, immediately upon birth, stood with level feet upon the earth and proceeded seven steps toward the north while a white parasol was being held over them—all of them...
They surveyed the directions and uttered a lion’s roar, proclaiming their own status as the eldest and most excellent in the world;
and that departure of theirs was true, not false, serving as a precursor to many distinguished attainments.
Likewise, this Blessed One has departed, and how was his departure true? It was true in the very same way as those [former ones] regarding their distinguished attainments.
By way of being a precursor. Thus, he has gone thus (tathā-gata), therefore he is the Tathāgata.
Or alternatively, just as those Blessed Ones went forth by means of renunciation, having abandoned sensual desire; by means of non-ill will, having abandoned ill will;

by means of the perception of light, having abandoned sloth and torpor; by means of non-distraction, having abandoned restlessness and remorse; and by means of the discernment of phenomena, having abandoned doubt.

Having abandoned [the defilements] and departed—having shattered ignorance with knowledge, having dispelled discontent with gladness, and having abandoned each respective opposite by means of the eight meditative attainments, the eighteen great insights, and the four noble paths—he has gone;
thus this Blessed One also has "gone. In this way, he is a Tathāgata because he has "thus gone."
How is it that he is a Tathāgata because he has come to the characteristic of suchness? The earth element has the characteristic of hardness;
the water element has the characteristic of cohesion; the fire element has the characteristic of heat; the air element has the characteristic of distension;
the space element has the characteristic of non-obstruction; the characteristic of matter is its mutability; the characteristic of feeling is its being felt.
Perception has the characteristic of perceiving; formations have the characteristic of forming; consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing.

In this way, [one understands] the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the twenty-two faculties, the four truths, the twelvefold formula of conditions, and the four foundations of mindfulness.
Of the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers,
the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the seven purifications,
and Nibbāna which plunges into the deathless— thus, whatever is the specific characteristic of the intrinsic nature and essence of each respective phenomenon.
He is called the *Tathāgata* because he has come (*āgata*) by way of knowledge to that which is such, not otherwise, not different—that characteristic—having reached and attained it without failing.
Thus, he is the *Tathāgata* because he has come to the characteristic of suchness (*tathalakkhaṇa*).
How is he the *Tathāgata* because he has perfectly awakened (*abhisambuddha*) to the true nature of things (*tathadhamma*) as they really are? "True things" (*tathadhammā*) refers to the four...
The Noble Truths. As it is said: "Monks, these four are such, not otherwise, not different.
Which four? 'This is suffering,' monks—this is such, this is not otherwise, this is not different," and so on in detail.
And the Blessed One has fully awakened to them; therefore, because he has fully awakened to what is such (*tatha*), he is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the sense of being produced and brought about through birth as the condition for aging-and-death is such, not otherwise, not different;

…pe… the sense of being produced and brought about through ignorance as the condition for volitional formations is such, not otherwise, not different; likewise, the sense of ignorance as the condition for volitional formations is such, not otherwise, not different;
…pe… the sense of birth as the condition for aging-and-death is such, not otherwise, not different.
The Blessed One has fully awakened to all that; therefore, because he has fully awakened to suchness (*tathatā*), he is the Tathāgata. For here, the word *gata* has the sense of "fully awakened.
Thus, he is the Tathāgata because he has fully awakened to the true nature of phenomena (*tathadhamma*) as they really are.

How is he the Tathāgata by virtue of seeing things as they truly are? That which, in this world with its gods... [and so on] ...among the generation including gods and humans, in immeasurable... [and so on].
In the world-systems, there exists a visible object (rūpārammaṇa) that comes within the range of the eye-door of immeasurable beings;

the Blessed One knows and sees that in every aspect. Knowing and seeing it thus, he describes it by way of its desirable or undesirable nature, or by way of the terms applicable to what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized:
"What is that form which is the sphere of form (rūpāyatana)?"

Whatever form is derived from the four great elements, possessing color and luster, visible and impinging—whether it be "blue," "yellow," and so forth—it remains exactly as it is when analyzed through numerous names, thirteen sections, and fifty-two methods;
it is not otherwise. This same method applies to sounds and other objects that enter the range of the ear-door and the rest.
For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Bhikkhus, whatever in this world with its devas... including gods and humans, has been seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or explored by the mind—that I know; that I have directly known.”
“That which is known by the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata does not stand [in need of] that.
Thus, he is the Tathāgata because of seeing things as they truly are (*tathadassitā*). In this context, the derivation of the term *tathāgata* should be understood in the sense of “one who sees thus.
How is he the Tathāgata because of speaking what is true (*tathavāditā*)? On the night when the Blessed One fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment...

And whatever was spoken and uttered by the Blessed One during the interval of forty-five years between the night he was born and the night he attained final nibbāna through the element of nibbāna without residue—
all that, consisting of the suttas, geyyas, and so forth, is entirely pure, complete, a crusher of lust, pride, and the like,
uniform, true, and not otherwise. Therefore he said:
“Cunda, on the night when the Tathāgata awakens to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,
and on the night when he attains final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue— whatever he speaks, utters, or explains in the interval between these two nights,
all that is exactly so and not otherwise; therefore, he is called the ‘Tathāgata.’”
In this context, the word *gata* has the sense of "meaning. Thus, he is a *tathāgata* because of his speaking truthfully (*tathāvāditā*).

Furthermore, *āgada* means "speaking" (*āgadana*), which is to say "speech. Since his speech (*āgada*) is true (*tatha*), not false, and not perverted, by changing the letter *da* to *ta*, he is called a *tathāgata*. In this way, the derivation of the term should be understood here.
How is he a *tathāgata* because of his acting truthfully (*tathākāritā*)? For the Blessed One’s body conforms to his speech, and his speech likewise conforms to his body.
Therefore, he is one who acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts. For one such as this, the meaning is that his body proceeds in accordance with his speech.
And just as his body proceeds, so too his speech proceeds; thus he is the Tathāgata. Therefore it was said:
"Monks, the Tathāgata acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts. Thus, acting as he speaks and speaking as he acts, he is therefore called the 'Tathāgata'."
Thus, he is a Tathāgata by virtue of acting accordingly.

How is he a Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming? Because, having made the peak of existence above and the Avīci hell below his limits, he overcomes all beings throughout immeasurable world-systems across the horizontal expanse, both by means of his virtue and his concentration.
In wisdom, in liberation, and in the knowledge and vision of liberation, there is no measure or limit for him;

rather, he is incomparable, immeasurable, unsurpassed, the god of gods, the supreme among the Sakkas, the supreme among the Brahmas, the highest of all beings—therefore he is the Tathāgata. Thus it was said.

“Bhikkhus, in the world with its devas... [and so on] ...in the world with its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the conqueror, the unconquered, the all-seeing, the wielder of power; therefore he is called ‘Tathāgata.
Here is the etymological derivation of the term: it is like a medicine (*agada*); it is both the splendor of his teaching and the accumulation of his merit.
By means of that great majesty, like a physician with a divine elixir, he [overcomes] the snakes that are all rival teachers and the world with its devas.

He overcomes. Thus, because he possesses that very medicine which is true, not false, and not perverted regarding the overcoming of the entire world—as previously described—the letter *da* is changed to *ta*, and he should be understood as "Tathāgata. In this way, he is a Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming.

Furthermore, he is a Tathāgata because he has gone (*gata*) to suchness (*tathā*); he is a Tathāgata because he has gone to reality (*tathaṃ*). In that regard, by means of the full understanding through investigation of the entire world...

Thus he has gone, thus he has understood—therefore he is the Tathāgata. He has gone beyond, having abandoned the arising of the world through the full understanding of its abandonment—therefore he is the Tathāgata.
He has gone to, has attained, the cessation of the world through its realization—therefore he is the Tathāgata.
He has gone to, has entered upon, the true path leading to the cessation of the world—therefore he is the Tathāgata. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Monks, the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is detached from the world.
The origin of the world, monks, has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the origin of the world has been abandoned by the Tathāgata.
The cessation of the world, monks, has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the cessation of the world has been realized by the Tathāgata. The path leading to the cessation of the world...”
“Bhikkhus, the practice awakened to by the Tathāgata—the practice leading to the cessation of the world—has been developed by the Tathāgata.
Whatever, bhikkhus, in this world with its devas... [as above] ...all that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.
Therefore, he is called ‘Tathāgata.’”
Furthermore, for eight reasons the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, is called "Tathāgata": he is a Tathāgata because he has come (āgata) in accordance with reality (tathā);

he is a Tathāgata because he has gone (gata) in accordance with reality; he is a Tathāgata because he has attained (āgata) that which is real (tathāni); he is a Tathāgata because he has understood (gata) that which is real; he is a Tathāgata because he is such (tathāvidha);

he is a Tathāgata because he has proceeded (pavattita) in accordance with reality; he is a Tathāgata because he has not come from anything other than that (agatehi agata); and he is a Tathāgata by virtue of his state of having gone in accordance with reality.
How is it that he is a Tathāgata because he has come thus? When the Blessed One, having been Sumedha, was at the feet of the Daśabala Dīpaṅkara, [he made this aspiration]:
“Human birth, the perfection of gender, the cause, the sight of the Teacher, Renunciation, the perfection of virtues, the service, and zeal;”
“Through the combination of eight factors, the aspiration succeeds.
Thus it was said. By one who fulfills such an aspiration endowed with these eight factors, [it is resolved]: “I, having crossed over, shall help the world including the devas to cross;
being liberated, I shall liberate; being tamed, I shall tame; being at peace, I shall bring to peace; being comforted, I shall comfort.”
"I shall lead to final Nibbāna those who have attained final Nibbāna; I shall awaken those who are Buddhas"—thus was the great vow proclaimed. For it has been said:
"What need have I for this one man who has crossed over and perceives his own strength?
Having attained omniscience, I shall ferry across the world together with its devas."
“By this service rendered to the Supreme Person,
having attained omniscience, may I deliver the vast multitude of beings.
Having severed the stream of saṃsāra and shattered the three realms of existence,”
"Having boarded the ship of the Dhamma, I shall ferry across the world together with its devas.
What need have I for this disguise? Having realized the Dhamma here and attained omniscience, I shall become a Buddha in the world together with its devas."

Furthermore, having fulfilled without deception that great promise— which serves as the cause for the investigation, reflection, and undertaking of the entire collection of qualities that constitute a Buddha—
the Leader of the World, for four incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand great aeons,
diligently and continuously practiced the thirty perfections, such as the perfection of giving, in their entirety.
Having fulfilled [the perfections], having practiced the five great renunciations such as the sacrifice of his limbs, having cultivated the four foundations such as the resolution of truth,
having accumulated the provisions of merit and knowledge, having brought to excellence his prior application, former conduct, teaching of the Dhamma, and conduct for the welfare of others,
and having brought the practice of wisdom to its supreme pinnacle, he fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, that great promise of his was thus, not otherwise, and not different; there is not even as much as a hair’s tip of falsehood in it.

For indeed, the twenty-four Perfectly Enlightened Ones who appeared in succession—Dīpaṅkara the Ten-Powered One, Koṇḍañña, Maṅgala... [and so on] ...up to Kassapa the Blessed One—each prophesied, "He will become a Buddha. Thus, regarding these twenty-four...
He has come (āgata) as one who has received the prophecy in the presence of the Buddhas, having obtained those benefits which are to be obtained by Bodhisattvas who have made their resolution;
thus, because he has come to, or attained, the state of being perfectly enlightened (abhisambuddha) in accordance with that aforementioned great promise (mahāpaṭiññā), he is the Tathāgata.
Thus, "he is the Tathāgata because he has come in accordance with reality."

How is he the Tathāgata because he has gone thus? It is by means of that great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) with which the Lord of the World, seeing the multitude of beings beset by the pressure of great suffering, stirred his mind with the resolve: "There is no other refuge for them;
I alone shall liberate them from the suffering of *saṃsāra*," and thereby made the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*). And having made it according to his aspiration...
Having applied himself with zeal for the accomplishment of the welfare of the entire world, disregarding his own body and life,
he practiced extremely difficult and arduous conduct that would cause terror even to the minds of others merely by coming within the range of their hearing;

and he did so in such a way that his practice for Great Enlightenment was not conducive to decline, nor conducive to defilement, nor conducive to stagnation, but rather was exclusively conducive to ever-higher distinction.
Practicing in such a manner, he gradually fulfilled the requisites for enlightenment without exception and attained supreme awakening (*abhisambodhi*).
Thereafter, his mind impelled by that very same great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he abandoned the delight in solitude and the supreme, peaceful bliss of liberation;
instead, amidst a world filled with foolish people, he endured the various manifestations of honor and dishonor produced by them.
Without regard for the training of those yet to be trained, he brought the Buddha-activity to its absolute conclusion.
In this regard, the manner in which the Blessed One’s great compassion toward sentient beings was impartial will be revealed later.

And just as the Lord of the World possessed great compassion toward sentient beings once he had become a Buddha, so too did he possess it while he was a Bodhisatta, from the time of his Great Resolve onwards.
Because it is identical in all respects and at all times—thus, not otherwise, and not different—it is "Thusness" (*tathā*).

Therefore, because he has gone to, that is, proceeded toward, the welfare of the entire world by means of this Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) which is of a uniform flavor for all beings throughout the three states, he is a "Tathāgata.
Thus, he is a Tathāgata because he has gone to Thusness.
How is it that he is the Tathāgata because he has come to the "thus-nesses"? The "thus-nesses" (tathāni) are the four noble path-knowledges.

For these comprise all knowable phenomena by way of the four noble truths—the occurrence and cessation [of suffering] and their respective causes—thus: "This is suffering; this is the origin of suffering; this is the cessation of suffering; this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
The meaning of suffering is oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of burning, and the meaning of change;

the meaning of origin is accumulation, the meaning of source, the meaning of bondage, and the meaning of an impediment; the meaning of cessation is escape, the meaning of seclusion, the meaning of the unconditioned, and the meaning of the deathless;
and the meaning of the path is outlet, the meaning of cause, the meaning of seeing, and the meaning of predominance—along with such like divisions thereof.
By means of severing the defilement-side which obstructs the realization of the true nature of things as they are,

the Blessed One— being himself independent of others for his knowledge— himself [realized] those things as they are (tathā), not otherwise (avitathā), and not different (anaññathā), through a non-perverted mode of occurrence termed the clear comprehension of non-delusion therein, which has been attained by cutting off that obstruction; for he does not deceive regarding the specific individual essence, intrinsic nature, and characteristic marks of phenomena.
He has come and has attained; therefore, because he has thus come, he is the Tathāgata.

And just as with the knowledges of the path, so too are the Blessed One’s unimpeded knowledges regarding the three times, his four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), his four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*), his knowledge that delimits the five destinies, his six unique knowledges, and his knowledge that manifests the seven factors of enlightenment.
The knowledges of the analysis of the eight path factors, the knowledges of the nine successive dwellings and attainments, and the ten powers should be understood as being of such a nature.

Herein, this is the analysis: whatever—in immeasurable world-systems, among immeasurable beings divided by distinctions such as inferior and so forth, and in past aggregates, bases, and elements—there is the individual essence, function, and so on, the specific states, and so on, and the names, clans, and so on connected with the aggregates.
And it should be understood that even regarding those material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) not bound to the sense faculties—

those which are extremely subtle, concealed, or located in distant places— the specific distinctions of color, shape, odor, taste, touch, and so forth, as they arise from their respective conditions along with those very conditions,
are all directly and unimpededly perceived by the Blessed One, as if looking at an *āmalaka* fruit placed in the palm of his hand.
Knowledge proceeds regarding the past, and likewise regarding the future and the present; these are called the "unobstructed knowledges" (appaṭihata-ñāṇa) concerning the three times.

As it is said: "The Blessed Buddha’s knowledge regarding the past is unobstructed; the Blessed Buddha’s knowledge regarding the future is unobstructed; the Blessed Buddha’s knowledge regarding the present is unobstructed.
Furthermore, these [knowledges] are "suchnesses" (tathāni) because they do not contradict the individual essence, intrinsic nature, or characteristic of phenomena in each respective instance.
They are not false, they are not otherwise; the Blessed One attained them through his self-dependent knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*). Thus, because he has come to those that are such, he is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, there are four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*): the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*). Among these, [the first] is the capacity for discerning, clarifying, and defining the distinctions of meaning.
Knowledge that has reached the distinction of meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
Knowledge that has reached the distinction of phenomena and is capable of discerning, clarifying, and defining them is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*).

Knowledge that has reached the distinction of language and is capable of discerning, clarifying, and defining the distinctions within linguistic expression is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*). [And] knowledge that is capable of discerning, clarifying, and defining the distinctions of ingenuity...
Knowledge that has reached the differentiation of ingenuity is the analytical knowledge of ingenuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*).

For it is said: "Knowledge regarding the meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning; knowledge regarding the Dhamma is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma; knowledge regarding the expression of the terminology therein is the analytical knowledge of language; and knowledge regarding knowledges is the analytical knowledge of ingenuity.
And here, in brief, "meaning" (*attha*) refers to the cause and its fruit, because it is to be sought after and to be attained by following the cause.
As for the classification: whatever has arisen by way of condition, Nibbāna, the meaning of what was spoken, result, and functional [consciousness]—these five things are "meaning" (*attha*).
The knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding that meaning for one who is reviewing that meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
"Phenomenon" (*dhamma*) is, in brief, condition; for it is because it establishes this or that meaning that it is called *dhamma*.
It causes [the cycle] to proceed and it brings about [the result]; therefore it is called "dhamma.
By way of classification, however, any cause whatsoever that produces a fruit—namely, the Noble Path, speech, the wholesome, and the unwholesome—these five things are "dhamma.
For one who reflects upon that dhamma, the knowledge that has reached the specific distinctions within that dhamma is the discrimination of dhamma (dhammapaṭisambhidā). And this has also been said:

“Knowledge regarding suffering is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*); knowledge regarding the origin of suffering is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*); knowledge regarding the cessation of suffering is the analytical knowledge of meaning; knowledge regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering is the analytical knowledge of phenomena.
Alternatively, knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical knowledge of phenomena, and knowledge regarding the fruit of the cause is the analytical knowledge of meaning.
Knowledge regarding those phenomena that have been born, become, produced, brought forth, and manifested is the analytical knowledge of meaning.

Knowledge regarding those phenomena from which other phenomena are born, become, produced, generated, fully manifested, and made apparent, is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā).
Knowledge regarding aging and death is the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā); knowledge regarding the origin of aging and death is the analytical knowledge of phenomena.
Knowledge regarding the cessation of aging and death is the analytical knowledge of meaning; [knowledge regarding] the way leading to the cessation of aging and death...

Knowledge of the way is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā). Knowledge regarding birth, becoming, clinging, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and volitional formations is the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā); knowledge of the arising of volitional formations is the analytical knowledge of phenomena.

Knowledge of the cessation of volitional formations is the analytical knowledge of meaning; [knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations is the analytical knowledge of phenomena].
Knowledge of the way is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*).
“Here, a bhikkhu knows the Dhamma—the discourses (*sutta*), mixed prose and verse (*geyya*), … [and so on] … the expositions (*vedalla*); this is called the analytical knowledge of phenomena.
He knows the meaning of each of those statements: ‘This is the meaning of this statement; this is the meaning of that.’”
“The meaning of what has been spoken”—this is called the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
“Which phenomena are wholesome? At whatever time a wholesome mind of the sense sphere has arisen, accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, having a visible form as its object...
[or] mental phenomena as its object, or whatever else it may be directed toward—at that time...”

“At that time there is contact... [and so on] ...there is non-distraction... these states are wholesome. Knowledge regarding these states is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā);
knowledge regarding their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā). This is the detailed explanation.
Furthermore, as for the intrinsic terminology, the unerring convention, and the expression regarding this meaning and these phenomena—that is [the analytical knowledge of language].

The analytical knowledge of language (*niruttippaṭisambhidā*) is the knowledge that has reached a state of differentiation regarding correct and incorrect linguistic expression in the Magadhi language—the fundamental tongue of all beings—such that one knows: "This is correct linguistic expression; this is incorrect linguistic expression.

For one who reflects upon all that knowledge—whether it be the aforementioned types of knowledge taken as objects, or all such knowledge in its full extent according to its range and function—[this is the analytical knowledge of language].

The knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding that knowledge is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*). Thus, these four analytical knowledges were realized by the Blessed One himself;

because they proceed in an unerring manner with respect to their respective domains—such as meaning (*attha*) and phenomena (*dhamma*)—without contradiction, they are "thus" (*tathā*), "not otherwise" (*avitatha*), and "not different" (*anaññathā*). In this way, the Blessed One has come to what is thus; therefore, he is the Tathāgata.
Likewise, whatever is called "the knowable," all that has been known, seen, attained, and fully awakened to by the Blessed One in every aspect.
For thus have the phenomena to be directly known been directly known by him; the phenomena to be fully understood, fully understood;
the phenomena to be abandoned, abandoned; and the phenomena to be realized, realized.
The states to be developed are so called because they are to be developed, such that no ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra,
or Brahmā is able to challenge them with reason, saying, "These states have not been fully awakened to by you.
Whatever is to be abandoned has all been abandoned by the Blessed One without remainder right at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
It is a state that has already arisen; there is nothing further to be done for its abandonment.

For in him, greed, hatred, delusion, distorted attention, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, hypocrisy, lethargy, agitation, anger, enmity, contempt, domineering, envy, avarice, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, presumption, arrogance, conceit, intoxication, negligence, the various unwholesome roots, misconduct, unevenness, distorted perception, stains, discursive thoughts, conceptual proliferation, seeking, craving, the fourfold perversions, and the taints and fetters have been eliminated.

The fifteen hundred and fifty defilements— including the floods, yokes, bonds, cravings, clingings, fivefold delights, hindrances, mental obstructions, mental shackles, roots of dispute, underlying tendencies of beings,
eight wrong views, nine grounds for resentment, craving-based ten unwholesome courses of action, twenty-one modes of improper search, sixty-two types of speculative views,
and the eight hundred variations of craving— along with their latent dispositions (*vāsanā*), have been abandoned, cut off, and utterly destroyed; therefore, no one...
There is no ascetic, or even... Brahmā, capable of rightfully challenging him by saying, "These defilements have not been abandoned by you.

Furthermore, as for those things declared by the Blessed One to be obstacles—classified as the maturation of karma, the defilements, censurable conduct, and transgressions of the rules—they are indeed sufficient to act as absolute obstacles for one who indulges in them.
Therefore, no ascetic, or even... Brahmā, can say of him, "It is not enough for you..."
"There is no one capable of investigating according to the Dhamma [the claim] that 'for one who practices it,
there will be an obstacle. Furthermore, that unsurpassed, liberating Dhamma taught by the Blessed One— which consists of the sevenfold groupings of virtue, concentration,
and wisdom for the sake of escaping the entirety of the suffering of saṃsāra, is preceded by the Noble Path, and is divided into thirty-seven factors— is exclusively...
It leads out; for one who has entered upon it, it serves for liberation from the suffering of the round of existence, such that no ascetic or...
[as before] ...Brahmā is capable of challenging it with a reasoned argument, saying: "The Dhamma taught by you as leading out does not lead out.
For this has been said: "Regarding you who claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One, these things have not been fully realized by you."

The detailed explanation follows. Thus, because they realize the non-falsity of his own specific qualities of knowledge, abandonment, and teaching, the Blessed One’s four kinds of intrepidity-knowledge proceed in an unerring manner;
they are such, non-false, and not otherwise. In this way also, the Blessed One has come as one who is "such" (*tathā*);
thus he is the Tathāgata. Likewise, there are five destinies: the destiny of hell, the destiny of animals, the destiny of hungry ghosts, the destiny of humans, and the destiny of devas.

Within those [realms] are the eight great hells, such as Sañjīva; the sixteen secondary hells (ussadaniraya), such as Kukkuḷa; and the hell of the intermediate spaces between worlds (lokantarika-niraya).

All these are called "hells" (niraya) in the sense of being devoid of satisfaction due to their state of absolute suffering. They are called the "hellish destination" (nirayagati) because one must go there according to one's karma.
Even the hells of intense darkness and cold are included within these very same realms. [Also included are] the bodies of worms, insects, reptiles, birds, jackals, and so forth.
They are called *tiracchānā* because they move horizontally (*tiriyaṃ añchita-bhāvena*); that itself is their destination, hence *tiracchānagati*.

They are called *petā* because, due to being hungry and thirsty, they have gone away (*itā*) from manifest happiness because of the abundance of suffering—such as those who live on the gifts of others, those with parched thirst, and so forth;

that itself is their destination, hence *petagati*. The *asuras*, such as the *Kālakañjika*s and others, are also included within these very categories. [This was said] by the inhabitants of the small islands...

Together with those dwelling in the four great continents beginning with Jambudīpa, they are called "human beings" (*manussa*) because of the abundance of their mental activity; that which is their destination is the "human realm" (*manussagati*).

From the Cātumahārājika heaven up to those who have reached the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*), these twenty-six classes of deities are called "gods" (*deva*) because they play (*dibbanti*) by means of their own supernormal power (*iddhānubhāva*), sport, and shine; that which is their destination is the "divine realm" (*devagati*).

Since these destinies (gati) are, in their actual meaning, the aggregates of result (vipākakkhandha) and the matter produced by karma (kaṭattā-rūpa)—specifically the distinctions within the existence at rebirth (upapattibhava) brought about by various respective karmas—therefore it is said: "This particular destiny is born from this particular karma;
and because that karma is differentiated by such specific conditions, these groups of beings (sattanikāya) are likewise differentiated by such divisions."

The Blessed One’s knowledge proceeds by way of the specific grounds and causes through the determination of the distinction between their respective causes and fruits. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“Sāriputta, there are these five destinations. Which five? Hell, the animal realm, the sphere of hungry ghosts, human beings, and devas.
Sāriputta, I understand hell, the path leading to hell, and that which leads to hell.”
"...and I also understand the path, and how one who has practiced it, with the breakup of the body after death, reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, downfall, or hell.

These knowledges of the Blessed One are "thus" (tathā), "not otherwise" (avitathā), and "not different" (anaññathā), because they proceed in an unerring manner and are non-deceptive regarding their respective objects. Thus, the Blessed One is the "Tathāgata" because he has come (āgato) as one who is thus.

Likewise, there is the Blessed One’s knowledge of the relative strength of the faculties of others (*indriyaparopariyattañāṇa*), which proceeds in fifty modes by discerning the distinctions among beings—such as those with little dust in their eyes and those with much dust in their eyes—through the comprehension of whether they possess or lack the application of faith and the other faculties. For this has been said in detail:
"A person endowed with faith has little dust in their eyes; a person lacking faith has much dust in their eyes. [And so forth.]
And as for [the knowledge] that "this person has little dust in his eyes; this one holds the view of eternalism; this one holds the view of annihilationism;
this one stands in conformity with what is acceptable; this one stands in knowledge of things as they truly are; this one is inclined toward sensual desire, not toward renunciation and so forth;
this one is inclined toward renunciation, not toward sensual desire and so forth"—by such means [he knows], "The lust for sense-pleasures in this person is exceedingly firm, but..."
"Regarding aversion and so forth: for this person, aversion is exceedingly firm, not [the tendency toward] sensual lust and so forth";
and so on, up to: "For this person, the formation of merit is predominant, not the formation of demerit nor the formation of the imperturbable;

for this person, the formation of demerit is predominant, not the formation of merit nor the formation of the imperturbable; for this person, the formation of the imperturbable is predominant, not the formation of merit..."
Nor is there a formation of demerit. For this one, bodily good conduct is predominant; for this one, verbal good conduct; for this one, mental good conduct.
This one is of inferior inclination; this one is of superior inclination. This one is possessed of the obstruction of karma; this one is possessed of the obstruction of defilements;
this one is possessed of the obstruction of ripening; this one is not possessed of the obstruction of karma.

The Blessed One’s knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies (*āsayānusaya-ñāṇa*) is that which functions by discerning, as they truly are, the inclinations and other traits of beings, according to such passages as: “He is not possessed of an obstruction consisting of defilements; he is not possessed of an obstruction consisting of karmic fruition,” and so forth.
It is with reference to this that it was said:

“Herein, the Tathāgata knows the inclinations of beings, he knows their latent tendencies, he knows their conduct, he knows their dispositions, and he knows which beings are capable and which are incapable,” and so forth. Furthermore,

there is the emission of masses of fire and streams of water from the upper and lower parts of the body, from the front and back, from the right and left eyes, ears, nostrils, shoulders, hands, and feet,
from between the fingers and toes, and from the pores of the skin— an attainment not shared by others.
The Blessed One’s knowledge of the Twin Miracle is that which possesses the power to produce various transformations and emanations. With reference to this, it was said:
“Here the Tathāgata performs the Twin Miracle, which is not shared with his disciples;
from the upper part of his body a mass of fire issues forth, and from the lower part of his body a stream of water issues forth; from the lower part of his body a mass of fire issues forth...”
“Streams of water flow from his upper body,” and so forth.

Furthermore, there is the knowledge of the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇāsamāpatti-ñāṇa*), which serves as the condition for the Blessed One’s emergence of great compassion proceeding through various methods out of a desire to draw out the multitude of beings who are afflicted by numerous painful states such as passion and birth. As it has been said:
“What is the Tathāgata’s knowledge regarding the attainment of great compassion? Great compassion descends upon sentient beings for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as they perceive them in many ways.
Great compassion descends upon sentient beings for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as they perceive that the world-dwelling is ablaze.
[It descends] as they perceive it as being set in motion, as having set out, as having entered upon a wrong path, and as being led away.”
"The world is unstable; the world is without protection, without a lord; the world is ownerless; everything must be abandoned and departed from;
the world is deficient, unsatisfied, and a slave to craving"—seeing this, great compassion arises in the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, toward sentient beings.
"The dwelling of the world is without refuge, without shelter, without a resort, and has become a place of no resort. The world is agitated and unpacified, pierced by the arrow [of suffering]."
The world-dwelling is pierced by many arrows; shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, cast into the cage of the defilements, the world-dwelling has entered into ignorance.
It is like an egg, enveloped, born from a tangled web, born from a nest of reeds, born from *muñja* grass and *pabbaja* grass;
it does not transcend the states of loss, the miserable destinies, the lower realms, and saṃsāra. It is smeared with the poison of the corruption of ignorance, become a morass of the defilements.
Entangled in the tangle of lust, hatred, and delusion;

clothed in the cloak of craving, covered by the net of craving, swept away by the stream of craving, bound by the fetter of craving, permeated by the underlying tendency of craving, scorched by the fever of craving, and consumed by the burning heat of craving.

Clothed in the cloak of views, covered by the net of views, swept away by the stream of views, bound by the fetter of views, permeated by the underlying tendency of views, scorched by the fever of views, and consumed by the burning heat of views.
“Followed by birth, pursued by old age, overcome by sickness, struck down by death, established in suffering. “Suspended by craving,
enclosed by the wall of old age, hemmed in by the snare of Māra, bound by great fetters— bound by the fetter of lust, and bound by the fetters of hatred,
delusion, conceit, views, defilements, and misconduct— he has entered upon a path of great congestion.”
He is obstructed by great impediments; he has fallen into a great abyss; he has entered upon a great wilderness; he has entered upon the great cycle of saṃsāra;
he revolves in a great mountain pass; he is mired in a great mire. "The world-dwelling is struck down;
the world-dwelling is ablaze with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion, and with birth."
The world-dwelling is led away by aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
it is constantly being slaughtered—helpless, with the staff already in hand, doing its own deed, bound by the fetters of fault, standing at the execution ground.
The world-dwelling is without a protector, fallen into the utmost pitiness, overwhelmed by suffering, oppressed for a long time, clinging, and eternally thirsty.
“Blind, sightless, with ruined eyes, without a guide, he has entered upon a wrong path, strayed from the straight way, and plunged into a great flood.
He is obsessed by two types of views, practices wrongly through three types of misconduct,
is bound by four bonds, fettered by four ties, clings by means of four clingings, has ascended to the five destinations, and [is hindered] by five...”
He is stained by the strands of sensual pleasure; he is shrouded by the five hindrances; he disputes by means of the six roots of contention;
he is stained by the six classes of craving; he is obsessed by the six views; he is permeated by the seven underlying tendencies;
he is bound by the seven fetters; he is puffed up by the seven types of conceit; and he is whirled about by the eight worldly conditions.
He is led astray by the eight forms of wrongness; he is corrupted by the eight faults of a man; he is provoked to resentment by the nine grounds for malice;
he is puffed up by the nine kinds of conceit; he is stained by the nine states rooted in craving; he is defiled by the ten grounds of corruption;
he is provoked to resentment by the ten grounds for malice; and he is possessed of the ten courses of unwholesome action.
To those Buddhas who perceive the world as a dwelling place bound by ten fetters, driven out by ten forms of wrongness, possessed of wrong view with ten bases,
possessed of extreme views with ten bases, proliferated by the hundred and eight elaborations of craving,
and obsessed by the sixty-two types of speculative views— [this is how they see it].
Great compassion for beings arises in the Blessed Ones:
"I have crossed over, yet the world has not crossed over; I am liberated, yet the world is not liberated; I am tamed, yet the world is not tamed;
I am at peace, yet the world is not at peace; I am comforted, yet the world is not comforted."
“I am fully extinguished (parinibbuto), yet the world is not fully extinguished. I am indeed able—to have crossed over, to help others cross;

to be liberated, to liberate others; to be tamed, to tame others; to be at peace, to bring others to peace; to be comforted, to comfort others; to be fully extinguished, to lead others to full extinction.
Thus, as they see this, great compassion for beings arises in the Blessed Buddhas.
Thus, the analysis has been made in eighty-nine modes. Furthermore,
that which pertains to the extent of the element of phenomena (dhammadhātu)— the capacity to penetrate in every aspect everything that is to be known within it,
such as the conditioned and the unconditioned, independently of instruction from others, occurring in dependence upon mere desire, and not shared with others— [is the knowledge of omniscience].
The Blessed One’s knowledge is "all-knowing knowledge" (sabbaññutaññāṇa) because it awakens to all conditioned and unconditioned conventional truths in their entirety;
it is called "unobstructed knowledge" (anāvaraṇañāṇa) on account of its functioning without attachment due to the absence of any hindrance therein.
For that single knowledge is indeed taught in two ways by way of its engagement with its objects, for the purpose of showing its uniqueness compared to others.
Otherwise, the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutā-ñāṇa*) and the unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa*) would result in being identical and having the same object;
yet that is not tenable, even according to this very reasoning. Here is the scriptural passage (*pāḷi*) on this point:
"It is called the knowledge of omniscience because it knows all conditioned and unconditioned things without exception; therein, the obstruction..."
"There is no [obstruction]" refers to unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*). "He knows all that is past" refers to omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*);
because there is no obstruction therein, it is unobstructed knowledge. "He knows all that is future" refers to omniscience;
because there is no obstruction therein, it is unobstructed knowledge. "He knows all that is present" refers to omniscience; therein, there is no obstruction...
“There is not” is the knowledge of non-obstruction; such is the detailed explanation.

Thus, these six unique knowledges of the Blessed One are “thus” (tathā), “not otherwise” (avitathā), and “not different” (anaññathā), because they proceed in an unerring manner and are non-deceptive regarding their respective objects. In this way, the Blessed One has come (āgata) to what is thus; therefore, he is the Tathāgata. Furthermore—

“Bhikkhus, there are these seven factors of enlightenment: the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment, the energy factor of enlightenment, the rapture factor of enlightenment, the tranquility factor of enlightenment, the concentration factor of enlightenment, and the equanimity factor of enlightenment.

Thus they are stated by way of their specific characteristics. Furthermore, when they arise at the moment of the supramundane path, they counteract such things as lethargy and agitation, the bases for stagnation and distraction, the accumulation [of kamma], devotion to the pleasure of sensual indulgence and devotion to self-mortification, and adherence to annihilationism and eternalism.
The collection of states, such as mindfulness and the rest, which serves as the antidote to manifold calamities— that collection of states by means of which the noble disciple awakens,
rises from the sleep of the defilements, penetrates the Four Noble Truths,
or realizes Nibbāna itself— is called "awakening" (*bodhi*). The factors of that awakening are the "factors of awakening" (*bojjhaṅga*).
Alternatively, because the noble disciple awakens by means of the aforementioned harmony of the Dhamma, he is called "Awakening" (*bodhi*);

and since they are the limbs of that awakening, they are called "factors of awakening" (*bojjhaṅga*). Thus [they are defined] by way of their general characteristic. Furthermore: the mindfulness factor of awakening has the characteristic of establishing;

the investigation-of-phenomena factor of awakening has the characteristic of investigating; the energy factor of awakening has the characteristic of exerting; the [rapture factor of awakening] has the characteristic of pervading...

The enlightenment factor of rapture has the characteristic of joy; the enlightenment factor of tranquility has the characteristic of calm; the enlightenment factor of concentration has the characteristic of non-distraction;

the enlightenment factor of equanimity has the characteristic of reflective discernment. Thus [it is defined] by way of specific characteristics. In this regard, what is the enlightenment factor of mindfulness?
Here, a monk is mindful, possessing supreme mindfulness and circumspection.

Because it demonstrates the simultaneous occurrence of the seven factors of enlightenment through their mutual assistance, by such passages as: "Endowed with this, one remembers and recollects even what was done long ago and spoken long ago";
and because of [the Sutta passage]: "In that regard, what is the mindfulness factor of enlightenment?
There is, monks, mindfulness regarding internal phenomena; there is mindfulness regarding external phenomena," and so forth.
