Because it shows the occurrence [of the factors] through the classification of their objects; because it shows the method of development through such passages as: "In this regard, what is the enlightenment factor of mindfulness?
Here, monks, a monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment";
and because it shows the method of development through such passages as: "In this regard, what are the seven factors of enlightenment? Here, monks, at whatever time a monk..."
“He develops supramundane jhāna…” and so on, up to: “At that time there are seven factors of enlightenment:
the mindfulness factor of enlightenment… the equanimity factor of enlightenment. Therein, what is the mindfulness factor of enlightenment?

That which is mindfulness… non-forgetfulness,” and so forth—thus, through the analysis of ninety-six thousand methods, the Blessed One’s knowledges for the manifestation of the factors of enlightenment proceed in various modes.
Because they do not deceive regarding each respective meaning, they are "thus" (tathā), not otherwise, and not different.
In this way also, the Blessed One has come as that which is thus; therefore, he is the Tathāgata. Thus—
“In this context, what is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this very Noble Eightfold Path. That is to say:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration. Thus it is defined by its specific characteristics.

It is called “noble” (ariya) because it is remote from all defilements, because it produces the state of a noble one, and because it brings about the attainment of the fruit of a noble one; and it is eightfold for the sake of attaining Nibbāna.

And it is "eightfold" because its causes are exclusively [wholesome]. It is called the "path" (magga) from the perspective of its general characteristic (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*) in the sense that: it goes while slaying the defilements (*kilesa*);
it is sought out by those seeking Nibbāna; or it itself seeks out Nibbāna. Furthermore:
right view has the characteristic of correct seeing; right intention has the characteristic of correctly directing the mind; right resolve has the characteristic of correct embracing...
“Right speech has the characteristic of being well-spoken; right action has the characteristic of right origination; right livelihood has the characteristic of right purification;
right effort has the characteristic of right exertion; right mindfulness has the characteristic of right establishment;

and right concentration has the characteristic of right non-distraction”—thus [they are distinguished] by their specific characteristics. Furthermore, right view [is distinguished] from its own opposing defilements...
Together with it, one abandons wrong view, takes Nibbāna as its object, and— by dispelling the delusion that conceals it—
sees the associated states through non-delusion. Likewise, right intention and the others abandon wrong intention and so forth,
take Nibbāna as their object, and perform, respectively, the functions of correctly directing, embracing, originating, purifying, exerting, establishing, and concentrating the co-nascent states.

And they perform [their functions]—thus is it according to the analysis of their functions. Right view, having been at the prior stage (pubbabhāga) occurring at different moments with suffering and so forth as its respective objects, becomes at the time of the Path (maggakāla) a single-moment state, taking Nibbāna alone as its object;

by virtue of its function, it receives the four names beginning with "knowledge of suffering. Right intention and the others also, having been at the prior stage occurring at different moments with various objects, at the time of the Path...
They share a single moment and a single object.
Among them, right intention receives three names according to its function, such as "intention of renunciation" and so forth.

Right speech and the other two [right action and right livelihood]—which in the prior stage consist of the divisions of abstaining from false speech and so forth—are both abstinences (*virati*) and volitions (*cetanā*) at the moment of the Path.
The [factors] beginning with right effort and right mindfulness receive four names according to their function, by way of the right exertions and the foundations of mindfulness;
however, right concentration is different even at the moment of the path, by way of the first jhāna and so forth.
Thus, according to the distinction in their occurrence during the prior and subsequent stages, it is said: "Here, monks, a bhikkhu develops right view dependent on seclusion," and so on.
From the perspective of the method of cultivation: "In that regard, what is the eightfold path? Here, bhikkhu, at whatever time one cultivates supramundane jhāna...
when it is of difficult progress and sluggish direct knowledge, at that time there is the eightfold path:
right view, right intention," and so forth—thus [it is taught] in its many aspects through eighty-four thousand divisions of methods.

All the knowledges of the Blessed One for discerning the Noble Path, which have been set in motion, are "thus" (tathā), not otherwise, and not different, because they do not deceive regarding the goal.
Thus, too, the Blessed One has come to what is thus; therefore, he is the Tathāgata.
Likewise, in the sense that one should dwell in these—the attainment of the first jhāna up to the attainment of cessation—in their proper sequence, [he is the Tathāgata].

Furthermore, the Buddha’s knowledges—which function, as appropriate, by way of application through the attainment of the successive meditative dwellings (*anupubbavihārasamāpatti*) and by way of their accomplishment and review—exist exactly as they are for the fulfillment of that purpose;
they are such, not otherwise, and not different. Likewise, his knowledge that "this is the possible" and "this is the impossible" is unerring.

It is the knowledge of the causes and non-causes of that fruit; the knowledge, in its entirety and according to reality, of the various ripenings of the undertaking of kamma by those respective beings, distinguished by their past and other temporal divisions;
and, at the very moment of the accumulation [of karma], the knowledge, as it truly is, of the distinction between kamma with and without taints for each respective being, such that:
"This is the practice leading to hell... [and so on]... this is the practice leading to Nibbāna."

The knowledge of the diversity of elements (*dhātunānatta*) as it truly is— namely, the knowledge that within this world, which possesses many intrinsic natures and diverse natures such as the aggregates,
bases, and so forth, whether clung-to (*upādinnā*) or not clung-to (*anupādinnā*), "due to the predominance of this particular element,
this specific distinction arises in this continuity of phenomena"— and the knowledge, without exception, of the inferior and other inclinations and dispositions of sentient beings.

It is the knowledge of the sharpness and pliancy of the faculties such as faith; the knowledge of the distinctions of the jhānas, liberations, and so forth, together with their defilements and other attributes;
the knowledge, in its entirety and through its connection thereto, of the continuity of the aggregates in all the immeasurable births of beings in the past;
and the knowledge of death and rebirth-linking together with their classifications as inferior and so on—in the same manner as previously stated under the formula, "This is suffering," and so forth.

“Knowledge of the Four Truths”: these ten powers of knowledge of the Blessed One are called *tathā* (thus), *avitathā* (not otherwise), and *anaññathā* (not different) because they penetrate their respective objects without fail, accomplish the intended purpose, and function in accordance with reality. For it has been said:
“In this world, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible,” and so forth.
Thus also, because the Blessed One has come to suchness (*tathā*),

he is the Tathāgata. And just as it is by virtue of these knowledges, so too, by virtue of his specific types of wisdom (*paññā*)— such as the knowledge that discerns the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*) as previously described—
which are infinite and immeasurable in their divisions and are not shared with anyone else— the Blessed One has come to suchness.
He is the Tathāgata because he has come to, or attained, the knowledges. Likewise, he is the Tathāgata because he has come to what is thus (tathā).

How is it that he is the Tathāgata because he has gone thus? That which is the Blessed One’s noble birth, his full enlightenment, his proclamation of the Dhamma and Vinaya, and the element of Nibbāna without residue—that is "thus" (tathā).
What is meant by this? It is for the sake of that [Nibbāna] that the Lord of the World attained full enlightenment.
It is *tathā* (thus) because it is established and set in motion; because it is non-deceptive due to the absolute accomplishment of its purpose;
and because it functions with an unerring meaning. It is *avitathā* (not otherwise) and *anaññathā* (not different).

For indeed, this Blessed One, while still a Bodhisatta, having fulfilled all the causes for Buddhahood—such as the thirty perfections (*pāramī*) and other aforementioned distinctions—remained in the Tusita heaven [and heard] the proclamation of the Buddha.
Having heard this, the deities from ten thousand world-systems gathered together and approached him, saying:
"The time has come, O Great Hero, Deva; arise in the mother’s womb!
Delivering the world including the gods, awaken to the state of deathlessness."

Having been entreated and having perceived the previously arisen signs, he surveyed the five great contemplations and thought, "Now, having been born in the human womb, I shall attain full enlightenment.
On the full moon day of the month of Āsāḷha, he took conception in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā of the Sakyan royal family;
for ten months, he was carried with great honor by gods and humans.
On the full moon of Visākha, at the time of dawn, he attained his noble birth.
At the moment of his noble birth—just as at the moment of his conception—the thirty-two portents appeared.
Indeed, this ten-thousandfold world system quaked, trembled, shook, and vibrated; and throughout the ten thousand world-systems...
An immeasurable radiance pervaded [the world]; as if desiring to behold his glory, those born blind regained their sight, and the deaf heard sounds.

The mute spoke, the hunchbacked became straight-limbed, the lame regained the power of walking on their feet, and all beings who were in bondage were released from their fetters and chains. In all the hells...
The fire was extinguished; hunger and thirst were stilled in the realm of the hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*); fear no longer existed among the animals (*tiracchāna*);
the disease of all beings was pacified; all beings became sweet-spoken;
horses neighed with a melodious sound, elephants trumpeted, and all musical instruments emitted their respective notes even without being struck by humans.
Ornaments such as bracelets and the like resounded with a sweet melody; all directions became serene;
a soft, cool breeze blew, bringing happiness to sentient beings; unseasonable clouds rained down; water burst forth from the earth and overflowed;
birds abandoned their flight through the sky; rivers stood still without flowing; and in the great ocean...
The water became sweet; as soon as the sun was seen freed from its impurities, all the luminaries in the sky blazed forth;
with the exception of the deities of the formless realm (ārūpāvacara), all other deities and all beings in the hells became visible in their physical forms;
trees, walls, doors, mountains, and so forth, ceased to be obstructions; and there was no passing away or rebirth among sentient beings.
Having overcome all unpleasant odors, a divine fragrance wafted forth; all fruit-bearing trees became laden with fruit;
the entire surface of the great ocean was covered with five-colored lotuses;
and all flowers, both land-born and water-born, blossomed—stem-lotuses upon the trunks of the trees and [branch-lotuses] upon the branches.
Tree-lotuses blossomed upon the branches; creeper-lotuses blossomed upon the creepers;
on the surface of the earth, having split the stone slabs, there emerged what are called staff-lotuses, seven upon seven, one above the other; hanging-lotuses appeared suspended in the sky;
a rain of flowers fell on all sides; celestial musical instruments resounded in the air throughout the entire ten-thousandfold world system.
Like a garland-cluster that has been wound and then released, like a bound bouquet of flowers that has been pressed together,
and like a decorated throne prepared for adornment, she— adorned with a single garland, fanning herself with a shimmering yak-tail whisk,
and perfumed by the scents of flowers and incense— reached the pinnacle of supreme beauty; and those were the portents of the many distinguished attainments she would subsequently achieve.
They became merely the signs. And thus, this birth, adorned with the manifestation of many wonders,
came to be exactly so— unfailing and not otherwise— for the sake of that supreme enlightenment which he had aspired to attain.
Likewise, those who are to be disciplined by a Buddha—the kinsmen who are to be awakened—have all, without exception, been disciplined by the Blessed One himself.
And those who are to be disciplined by disciples or by the Dhamma, they too have been disciplined by the disciples and others; they have been disciplined, and they will continue to be disciplined.
Thus, for the sake of the absolute accomplishment of that purpose for which the Blessed One aspired to full enlightenment, [this has been achieved].
His perfect enlightenment is thus, not otherwise, and not different. Furthermore,

whatever intrinsic nature of each knowable phenomenon is to be awakened to, that very nature was perfectly and completely awakened to by the Blessed One through his own knowledge, which— dependent merely upon the act of adverting the mind— is as unerring as a myrobalan fruit placed in the palm of the hand.
Thus too, his full enlightenment is such, not otherwise, not different.
Having correctly observed the manner in which each respective Dhamma should be taught, as well as the underlying tendencies, temperaments, conduct, and inclinations of those various beings—
without ever deviating from the nature of phenomena (dhammatā)— he [proceeds] along the path of conventional designations, methods, and terminology.
And by the Blessed One— who did not overstep the nature of things, who clearly manifested that very nature, and who instructed according to the offense,
according to the disposition, and according to the Dhamma— the those to be trained were disciplined and brought to the plane of the Noble Ones;
thus, his proclamation of the Dhamma and Vinaya is likewise true, not false, and not otherwise, because it accomplishes that purpose and functions in accordance with reality.

Likewise, that which has been attained by the Blessed One—the element of the great deathless Nibbāna, which is free from the nature of form and non-form such as contact and feeling with respect to earth and so forth;
which transcends the nature of the world because it lacks the state of being subject to disintegration; which cannot be illuminated by anything because it is dissociated from darkness;

which, due to the very absence of the nature of the world, is devoid of states such as a destination; which is without foundation and without an object; and which pertains to those things designated as the aggregates—[is thus described].
It is called "without residue" (anupādisesa) because there is not even a trace of clinging remaining; with reference to this it was said:

"There is, monks, that base where there is neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air, nor the base of infinite space, nor the base of infinite consciousness, nor the base of nothingness, nor the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor this world..."
“There is no other world, nor both the moon and the sun. In that regard, monks, I say there is neither coming nor going, neither staying nor passing away nor being reborn.
This is without foundation, without occurrence, and without an object;
this indeed is the end of suffering.”
It is the subsiding of all aggregates of clinging, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions,
the pacification of all suffering, the eradication of all attachments, the cutting off of all rounds of existence, and it is characterized by ultimate peace;
thus it is "Suchness" (*tathatā*) because it never deviates from the aforementioned intrinsic nature, being non-false (*avitathā*).
Not otherwise. Thus, because he has gone to, approached, attained, practiced, and reached these [states] beginning with the higher births (*abhijāti*), he is the Tathāgata.
In this way, the Blessed One is the Tathāgata because he has "gone thus" (*tathā gata*).
How is he the Tathāgata because he is "of such a kind" (*tathā-vidha*)? Just as the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones were of such a kind, so too is this Blessed One.
"Of such a kind. What is meant? Just as those Blessed Ones were endowed with the virtue of the path and the virtue of the fruit—indeed, with all mundane and supramundane virtue;
with the concentration of the path and the concentration of the fruit—indeed, with all mundane and supramundane concentration;
and with the wisdom of the path and the wisdom of the fruit—indeed, with all mundane and supramundane wisdom; [and] with those things to be practiced daily...

In brief, [it is endowed] with the twenty-four hundred thousand millions of abidings in meditative attainments (*samāpatti-vihāra*), and with liberation by way of its constituent parts (*tadaṅga-vimutti*), liberation by suppression (*vikkhambhana-vimutti*), liberation by eradication (*samuccheda-vimutti*), liberation by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi-vimutti*), and liberation by escape (*nissaraṇa-vimutti*).
In detail, however, it is endowed with all the qualities of omniscience, which possess inconceivable power through infinite and immeasurable distinctions. This too is ours...
The Blessed One was of such a nature. For among all the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, there may be differences by way of these five differences:
difference in lifespan, difference in the size of the body, difference in lineage, difference in the practice of austerities, and difference in the rays of light;
but there is no difference in their purification, such as the purification of virtue and so forth, nor in their practice of serenity and insight. By himself...

Furthermore, there is no difference whatsoever among the qualities they have attained. Rather, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are indistinguishable from one another, like gold that has been refined in the middle.
Therefore, just as the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones were, so too is this Blessed One;
because he is "of such a kind" (*tathāvidha*), he is a *Tathāgata*. And here, the word *gata* has the sense of "being of such a kind."
For thus worldly people explain the word *vidhūta-gata* in the sense of "gone" (*pakāratthe*).

How is he the Tathāgata? Because the Blessed One is endowed with supernatural power (*iddhānubhāva*) not shared by others, and because of his attainment of unobstructed knowledge through reaching the highest perfection of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), such as the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
Because there is no obstruction anywhere for the activity of the body and so forth, he has gone (*gata*)—that is, his movement (*gati*) or proceeding—as he wishes;
thus, he whose bodily, vocal, and mental activities proceed in such a way is a *Tathāgata*. Likewise, he is a *Tathāgata* because he has proceeded in accordance with reality (*tathā*).

How is he a *Tathāgata* because he has not gone otherwise than reality (*tathā*)? In the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*), [he has not gone otherwise] regarding what is reckoned as the activity of their opposites...

There is no destination for him; thus he is "un-gone" (*agata*). Furthermore, this state of being un-gone is understood through those very knowledges that proceed in the manner of reflecting upon the disadvantages and advantages regarding stinginess, the perfection of giving, and so forth; therefore, he is a "Tathāgata" because he has gone by means of such knowledges.

Alternatively, [the term refers to one who] has gone to the cessation of the five aggregates, whether characterized as the occurrence of defilements and volitional formations, or simply as the occurrence of the aggregates themselves.
He is "Agata" (one who has not gone) because there is no further going for him among the realms of existence (*gati*).

This state of his being "not-gone" is due to his attainment of *nibbāna* with residue remaining (*saupādisesa*) and without residue remaining (*anupādisesa*) by means of those very same noble path-knowledges (*ariya-magga-ñāṇa*). Thus, the Blessed One is a "Tathāgata" because he is "Agata" by means of those [knowledges].
How is he a "Tathāgata" by way of having "gone thus" (*tathā-gata*)? Regarding the phrase "by way of having gone thus," it refers to the actual presence (*sabbhāva*) of the Tathāgata.
"Because of his existence" is the meaning. But who is this Tathāgata, because of whose existence the Blessed One is called "Tathāgata"?
It is the True Dhamma (Saddhamma). For the True Dhamma is first the Noble Path;

it has been "gone to" (*gata*) in the sense of its abandonment by complete eradication, insofar as it proceeds by means of the power of serenity and insight joined together, completely uprooting the faction of the defilements. Then there is the Dhamma of the Fruit (*phala-dhamma*).
Just as one must proceed according to one’s own path by means of subsiding and abandoning, so has he gone; thus he is "one who has gone" (*tathā-gata*).
Furthermore, the Dhamma of Nibbāna, having been gone to—that is, penetrated by wisdom—results in the subsiding of all the suffering of saṃsāra;

because it has been gone to and realized by the Buddhas and others in that way, he is the Tathāgata. The Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) is also [called *tathāgata*] because it was gone to by previous Buddhas...

He is called the Tathāgata because he has proceeded in accordance with the inclinations and dispositions of those to be trained, by way of the discourses (*sutta*), verses (*geyya*), and so forth, and by way of revealing the modes of conduct and so on;
or else, because he has likewise gone (*tathā gata*) and spoken (*gadita*) as we have been taught by the Blessed One.

Or, he is the Tathāgata because the disciples of the Blessed One have likewise gone to and understood (*avagata*) what was taught by the Blessed One. In this way, the entire True Dhamma (*saddhamma*) is also the Tathāgata.
Therefore Sakka, Lord of the Devas, said: “Let there be well-being as we pay homage to the Tathāgata, who is worshipped by gods and humans, and to the Dhamma.
He is called the Blessed One (Bhagavā) because he possesses that [quality].
And just as it is with the Dhamma, so too is the Noble Saṅgha, which is perfectly purified by those who have practiced for their own welfare and for the welfare of others.
Having placed the preliminary practice of serenity and insight (pubbabhāga-samatha-vipassanā) before him, he must proceed by whichever path is appropriate;

thus, because he has gone in that way, he is a Tathāgata. Or alternatively, because he has awakened to and spoken of the truths, dependent origination, and so forth, exactly as they were taught by the Blessed One, he is a Tathāgata. Therefore, Sakka, the king of the gods, said: "The Tathāgata..."
"We pay homage to the Saṅgha, honored by gods and humans; may there be well-being.
Because he has disciples who are "thus-gone" (tathā), the Blessed One is the Tathāgata. Thus, he is called the Tathāgata by virtue of his state as a Tathāgata.
And this is merely a brief introduction to the illumination of the Tathāgata’s state as a Tathāgata; however, in every respect, he is indeed the Tathāgata.
One might describe the state of a Tathāgata to a Tathāgata. For this "Tathāgata-word" possesses great significance, a great destination, and a vast scope;

thus, one who brings forth even the entire word of the Buddha contained in the Tipiṭaka through its logical connection and essential meaning—just as one would with a single word on heedfulness—is not to be called a "Dhamma-preacher who has leaped over a shallow ford."
Regarding this, it is said:
"Just as in the world the former great seers,
the sages, attained omniscience here;”
In the same way, this Sage of the Śākyas has also come;
therefore, he who possesses the eye is called a Tathāgata.
Having abandoned the stains of sensual desire and the rest without remainder,
Just as the ancient Conquerors, the Sage of the Śākyas, the bearer of radiance, went by means of the knowledges of concentration,
so has he gone; therefore he is considered a Tathāgata.
And thus, regarding the characteristics of the elements, bases, and so forth— from the distinctions of their individual essence, commonality, and classification—
this Victor has arrived through the knowledge of the Self-Existent One.
The Bull of the Sakyas is called the Tathāgata:
“The truths are such as they are by his all-seeing eye,
and so too is the conditionality of this [world] in every respect.”
He is not to be led by others, as he has been clearly manifested through the method;
therefore, the Victor is the Tathāgata.
Even in world-systems of manifold divisions...
Regarding the Victor’s range of experience—
the various and manifold objects such as the sphere of visible form— his vision is exactly as it is;
therefore, the Tathāgata is "All-Seeing."
But when one speaks of the Dhamma exactly as it is,
and acts in accordance with one’s own words,
one proceeds having overcome the world by means of one’s virtues.
The Tathāgata, the leader of the world,
by means of that very [knowledge], having fully understood thusness in every way,
declared the world and transcended its origin.
The Tathāgata has gone to Nibbāna through direct realization and has likewise gone by means of the Noble Path.
Because he has thus acknowledged everything as it truly is, in every way...
Because he has come for the welfare of the world,
the Protector always acts out of compassion;
therefore, he is the Conqueror, the Tathāgata.
“Because his knowledges are such as they are, from whence he has come,
through the awakening to objects according to their true nature;
because of such noble birth and so forth, he is the Tathāgata.”
He is the Tathāgata because he has accomplished that goal:
“Just as those former Great Seers were,
so am I likewise, according to my own resolve.”
Because his speech proceeds with a subtle state of mind,
the Tathāgata is called the Supreme Person.
Prior to this, through the ripening of the requisites for full enlightenment...
He has gone, yet he does not go to the realm of saṃsāra;
for the Protector who sees the end of existence, there is no further becoming.
Thus, because he has come in such a way, he is the Tathāgata.
“The Tathāgata, the supreme Dharma, and the Great Seer—
how the impurity that is to be abandoned is abandoned;
the Tathāgata, the Noble Assembly, and the Teacher.”
"The Tathāgata is so called because he is possessed of that.

Regarding "of great psychic power" (*mahiddhika*): it is the possession of great psychic power (*iddhi*), which consists in the capacity to produce the alteration of phenomena through the supreme mastery over the mind and the application of the various modes of psychic power (*iddhividha*). [This is] by means of that which has arisen long ago and whose opposite is very far removed...
Great power (*mahānubhāvatā*) is the possession of a great radiance of merit (*puññateja*), which serves as the cause for the accomplishment of one's desired goal.
"Yatra" is a particle used in the sense of the personal pronoun, signifying wonder, praise, curiosity, laughter, and clarity.

Because it is joined with that [particle], the expression "she will give birth" is a statement regarding the future time, yet the actual meaning refers to the past time alone. This is the meaning here: namely, she who...
Suppavāsā, who was thus submerged in suffering and fallen into distress, became happy and free from illness at the very moment she heard the Blessed One’s words, and she gave birth to a healthy son.
"Attamano" means "with a contented mind"; the meaning is that his mind was free from defilements through confidence in the Blessed One.
For a mind overwhelmed by defilements cannot be called "contented," since it cannot be brought under control.
"Attamanā" means one whose mind is seized by joy and gladness. "Pamudito" means endowed with rapture (*pāmojja*).
"Pītisomanassajāto" means one in whom powerful joy and gladness have arisen. "Atha" means afterwards, after some days have passed.
"Sattabhattāni" means meals to be given on seven days. "Svātanāya" means for the sake of future merit; that which [is to be given] tomorrow to the community headed by the Buddha...
"There will be merit for that purpose by way of giving to the Saṅgha and by way of paying homage.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Why did he address him?
For the sake of protecting the faith of Suppavāsā’s husband. However, Suppavāsā herself was already of unshakable faith; it was rather for the protection of the lay follower's faith [that he spoke].
This was the burden of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. Therefore he said, "He is your attendant. In that context, "tuyheso" means "he is yours.

Regarding the phrase "guarantor for three things": if the noble Mahāmoggallāna were the guarantor—that is, the surety—for the non-deprivation and non-destruction of my three things, namely my wealth and so forth, then after seven days have passed from now, my...
"If it is known by the Noble One that it is possible to give a gift," he indicated.
The Elder, seeing that during those days there was no misfortune regarding his wealth or his life, said: "Friend, I am a guarantor for two things:
for his wealth and for his life. But since faith is bound to the mind, placing the burden upon him alone—
"But you alone are the guarantor by means of your faith," he said. Furthermore, that lay follower was one who had seen the Truth (diṭṭhasacca);
since there could be no change in his faith, it was stated thus. For that very reason, the Blessed One said, "Convince him, saying, 'You will do it later.
And because of his reverence for the Teacher and the elders, as well as his easy speech and that merit, the lay follower...
Desiring prosperity, she gave her permission, saying, "Let Suppavāsā, the daughter of the Koliyas, provide the seven meals;

afterwards, I shall do so. And as for that child, having passed the eleventh day from the day of birth, and after feeding the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha for seven days thereafter, on the seventh day, that seven-year-old—
He had the boy pay homage to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. "Seven years for me" means seven years for me;

this is the accusative case used in the sense of absolute connection (*accantasaṃyoga*). "Dwelt in a copper pot" refers to the suffering of dwelling in the womb within his mother’s belly. "And other such as these, seven sons"—"others" [refers to...]
Where it should have been said, "seven such sons," it is stated as "such [sons]" (*evarūpāni*) due to a shift in grammatical gender. Thus, the meaning is:
"sons who arise after causing great suffering by way of carrying the fetus for seven years and by way of the confusion of the womb for seven days.
By this, he shows that there is no satiety for women through the acquisition of sons due to their greed for children.

"Having understood this matter": having understood at once this great suffering—which has occurred for seven years and seven days due to the carrying of the fetus and so forth—and having understood the matter spoken by her through her longing for a son; "this inspired utterance (*udāna*"):
[he spoke] this inspired utterance after deceiving heedless persons, who are as if intoxicated by mental pleasure, with a desirable form, [and thus] [of the moisture of craving].
He uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which illuminates the state of being a bringer of great harm.

In this context, "asāta" means not sweet, not beautiful, and undesirable. "In the form of the pleasant" (sātarūpena) means by way of a desirable nature. "In the form of the dear" (piyarūpena) means by way of a state that is to be cherished.
"In the form of pleasure" (sukhassa rūpena) means by way of the nature of happiness. This is what is meant: because it is unpleasant...

Although the entire range of conditioned phenomena within the cycle of existence is nothing but the disagreeable and painful, because one has not abandoned the distortions (vipallāsa), it appears through improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra) as if it were desirable, dear, and pleasant;
thus, by means of the lapse of mindfulness, it overcomes, masters, and overwhelms the heedless person. Therefore, [the Buddha spoke] again to this Suppavāsā.
"Seven times over, such unpleasant, disagreeable, and painful [experiences] are overwhelmed by a pleasure that is the opposite of pain—a pleasure consisting in the object of affection known as a son.
The commentary on the eighth sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Visākhā Sutta.

19. "In the Eastern Monastery" means in the monastery built to the east of Sāvatthī, in a place similar to the Uttamadevī Vihāra at Anurādhapura. "In the Palace of Migāra’s Mother" means in the palace of Migāra’s Mother.

Herein, this is the sequential narrative: In the past, at the end of a hundred thousand kappas, a certain laywoman saw Padumuttara, the One of Ten Powers, appointing another laywoman to the position of his chief attendant. Having seen this, she [made a vow] to the Blessed One...
Having invited [the Sangha] and given alms to one hundred thousand bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, she paid homage to the Blessed One and made this aspiration:
"In the future, may I become the foremost attendant of a Buddha such as you.
After wandering through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, at the time of our own Blessed One, she was born in the city of Bhaddiya.
She took rebirth in the womb of Queen Sumanā in the house of the merchant Dhanañjaya, the son of the merchant Meṇḍaka.
At the time of her birth, they gave her the name Visākhā.
When the Blessed One went to the city of Bhaddiya, she went out to meet him together with five hundred maidens; at that very first sight, she became a stream-enterer.
Later on, she went to the house of Puṇṇavaḍḍhana Kumāra, the son of the merchant Migāra in Sāvatthī.
There, her father-in-law, the merchant Migāra, established her in the position of a mother out of gratitude for her assistance; therefore, she is called Migāramātā.
Having relinquished her own means of livelihood as an elderly woman, she [provided] ninety million [pieces of gold] for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

For the purpose of dwelling, he had a palace built, adorned with a thousand chambers—five hundred on the upper floor and five hundred on the lower floor—on a plot of ground measuring a *karīsa* in area. Therefore it is said, "in the Migāramātupāsāda.
"Some purpose" means some specific motive. "Of the king" means of the queen. "Dependent" means subservient. [This refers to] Visākhā.
A certain kind of merchandise, such as gems and pearls, had been sent from her kinsmen’s family as a gift for her;
when it reached the city gate, the customs officers, instead of taking the appropriate duty, took an excessive amount.
Hearing this, Visākhā, wishing to inform the king of the matter, went to the royal palace with a suitable retinue.
At that moment, the king had gone to the inner apartments together with Queen Mallikā.
Unable to gain an audience, Visākhā thought, "I shall get it now, I shall get it now," and having let the mealtime pass, she departed with her meal cut short.
Although she went back and forth for two or three days in this manner, she still did not obtain an audience. Thus, the king—
Even though he had not reported [the matter], because he did not grant an opportunity for the decision on the case, it was said of him, "He does not fulfill his intention.
In this context, "according to his intention" means in accordance with his purpose. "Does not fulfill" means he does not bring it to a conclusion.
For the Great Laywoman’s intention was to give only the customs duty subject to the king to the king and have the rest released; since that [intention] was not seen by the king, [he spoke thus].
Thus it was not determined. *Handā* is a particle used in the sense of relinquishment or transition. *Divā divassa* means "during the day" of the day; the meaning is "at midday.
Because of some business or other, she went to the gate of the royal residence for two or three days;
since that matter remained unfinished, she approached [the king] in vain. However, her approaching the Blessed One—

"Because it is the cause for obtaining the unsurpassed vision and so forth, it is 'meaningful' (sātthaka)," thus thinking, Venerable Sir, "I have come here at this time," the Great Laywoman spoke these words beginning with "Here, Venerable Sir," demonstrating this very point.

"Having understood this matter" means having understood this matter characterized by the failure of one's purpose due to dependence on others. "He uttered this inspired utterance" (udāna) means he uttered this inspired utterance which illuminates the danger and the benefit in lives lived dependent on others and independent of others.

In this context, "everything under the power of another is suffering" means that whatever kind of matter or purpose is under the control of another—that is, dependent on another—is suffering and brings about suffering because it cannot be accomplished according to one's own wish.
"All sovereignty is happiness": sovereignty is twofold, mundane and supramundane. Of these, the mundane consists of royal sovereignty and so forth.
There is both the sovereignty of mind produced by mundane jhānas and higher knowledges (abhiññā),
and the sovereignty of cessation (nirodhissariya) characterized by the attainment of the supramundane paths and fruits. Among these,

although both the sovereignty among humans culminating in the state of a wheel-turning monarch, and the sovereignty consisting of lordship over various classes of deities such as Sakka and others, exist through the power of kamma—

It is "pleasure" because it is a sign of happiness due to the fulfillment of one's desires; however, it is entirely suffering because of the nature of the suffering inherent in change (*vipariṇāmadukkhatā*).
Likewise, the sovereignty of mind produced by mundane absorption (*lokiyajjhāna*) is impermanent and non-final;

but the sovereignty of cessation (*nirodhissariya*) alone is called "absolute pleasure" because it cannot be shaken by worldly phenomena (*lokadhamma*) and because its very nature is non-retrogression. As for that which is here...
In all cases, one obtains mental happiness through independence; with reference to this, the Teacher said, "All sovereignty is happiness.
"They are distressed when things are shared" is an explanation of the meaning of the phrase, "All that is under the control of others is suffering.
This is the meaning here: when a common purpose is to be accomplished, because it depends on others, it does not proceed according to one's own intention.
Because they cannot be brought to fulfillment, these beings are tormented, fall into distress, and become exhausted. Why? Because the bonds are difficult to transcend.

This means that since the bond of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*), the bond of existence (*bhavayoga*), the bond of views (*diṭṭhiyoga*), and the bond of ignorance (*avijjāyoga*) have been cultivated since beginningless time, they are difficult to transcend because they cannot be abandoned by those who have not accumulated a store of wholesome qualities (*kusalasambhāra*). Among these, the bond of views is to be transcended by the first path.
The bond of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*) is overcome by the third path; the others are overcome by the final path.

Thus, because the noble paths are difficult to attain, these bonds are hard to transcend. Therefore, the intention is this: through the bond of sensual desire and the rest, beings are afflicted by the failure to obtain what they desire;
however, when there is the uncommon sovereignty of mind and the sovereignty of cessation, affliction can never arise.
Alternatively, "all that is subject to another" refers to everything characterized by a mode of existence dependent on others;
all that is suffering because its intrinsic nature is impermanent, for it has been said: "What is impermanent, that is suffering.

"All sovereignty" refers to Nibbāna—which, because it is the state of sovereignty transcending all conditioned things, is given the name "sovereignty"—and this includes every division such as that with a residue of clinging (*upādisesa*) and so forth.
Happiness. For it has been said: “Nirvana is the supreme happiness. Regarding the phrase “in common”:

when suffering and happiness have been thus defined, these beings, having become submerged in causes of suffering that are largely shared in common, are tormented. Why? Because the bonds are difficult to transcend;
for since those bonds of sensual desire and so forth—which are the cause of their submergence everywhere—are difficult to transcend, therefore you too...
The intention is that, Viśākhā, you are distressed because you have sought an object dependent on others and failed to obtain it.
The commentary on the ninth sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Bhaddiya Sutta.
20. At Anupiyā: in a city of this name. At the Mango Grove: not far from that city there was a mango grove belonging to the Malla kings;
a monastery for the Blessed One was built there by the Malla kings, and it is called simply "the Mango Grove.
Having made Anupiyā his alms-resort village, the Blessed One dwelt there; hence it is said, "at Anupiyā."
“He dwells in the Mango Grove. Bhaddiya is the name of that elder. “Son of Kāḷīgodhā”:
Kāḷīgodhā was a Sākiyan lady, the queen of the Sākiya king, a noble disciple who had attained the fruits [of the path] and understood the teaching; he was her son.
The procedure for his going forth is already recorded in the Khandhaka. Having gone forth and established insight meditation (*vipassanā*), before long...
He attained the six direct knowledges and practiced by undertaking all thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).

Furthermore, the Blessed One placed him among the foremost disciples in the category of those from high-born families, declaring: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples of high birth, namely Bhaddiya, son of Kāḷīgodhā," thus including him within the circle of the eighty great disciples.
“Having gone to an empty place”: having excluded the village and its precincts, the remainder is called the forest (*arañña*).

Excluding the foot of a tree, any other dwelling place suitable for one who has gone forth—such as a mountain, a cave, and so forth—is intended here by the term “empty place,” because it is free from the crowding of people.
Alternatively, it is secluded because it is devoid of sounds, which are thorns to meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
Whatever house there may be, it should be understood as an empty house. He had gone to that empty house. "Frequently" means often.

"He uttered an inspired utterance": for that venerable one, whether he had gone to his daytime rest in the forest or had gone to stay there at night, he spent the time for the most part in the bliss of the attainment of fruition and the bliss of cessation; therefore, with reference to that bliss—

Having become disgusted with the royal pleasure previously experienced by himself—which was accompanied by fear and fever—he brings forth a surge of joy arising from knowledge and arising from rapture, accompanied by gladness, thinking, "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness! Regarding the phrase, "Having heard this, it occurred to them":
it occurred to those many bhikkhus that regarding that venerable one, "Oh, what happiness!"... [the rest of the passage follows].
Upon hearing the exclamation "O, what happiness! uttered by him, they thought: "Without a doubt, this one practices the holy life without finding delight [in it].
Those monks were worldlings; not knowing that the exclamation was made with reference to the venerable one’s bliss of seclusion, they conceived such thoughts.
Therefore it is said, "Without a doubt," and so forth. In that context, "without a doubt" means:
The meaning is "without doubt" or "certainly. Having cited the text, "Yaṃ so pubbe agāriyabhūto samāno," some explain the meaning by supplying the word *anubhavī* (he experienced);
others read it as "yaṃ sā. However, the text is actually "yaṃsa pubbe agāriyabhūtassa. In that context, "yaṃsa" means "yaṃ assa" (which was his);
for the elision of the vowels *a* and *sa* occurs by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), as in "evaṃsa te" or "pupphaṃsā."

As in the passages beginning with "it arose," the meaning is as follows: "Of him"—that is, of the venerable Bhaddiya—while he was still a householder and a layman prior to his going forth, there was a royal pleasure that had been experienced. "Recalling that" means:
he is now recollecting that pleasure by way of longing for it.

"Those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One": those many bhikkhus, whose nature was inclined toward flattery, said this to the Blessed One with the intention of favoring him, not out of a desire to criticize.
"A certain one": a single bhikkhu who was not well-known by name or clan. "Addressed": he commanded [him], desiring to inform those bhikkhus.
In this way, regarding the acceptance of the words, the meaning is "well said. Again, *evaṃ* (thus) refers to his assent.
By saying, "He uttered this exclamation repeatedly: 'Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss! he acknowledges his own exclamation, confirming that it was exactly as those bhikkhus had stated:
"It is so, it is just so. But why did the Blessed One ask, "But is it so for you, Bhaddiya? What was his [intention]?
“Does the mind not know? It is not that it does not know; rather, he asks in order to make those bhikkhus understand by having them state that very meaning themselves.
For this has been said: “Tathāgatas ask even though they know, and they do not ask even though they know,” and so forth.
*Atthavasam* means the reason.

"In the inner palace" (*antepure*) means within the royal residence, which serves as the place for the movement of the women's quarters (*itthāgāra*), where the king performs his bathing, eating, sleeping, and other activities.
"Guarded well" (*susaṃvihita-rakkhā*) means that protection has been properly arranged on all sides by guards and other men.
"Outside the inner palace" (*bahipi antepure*) refers to the parts of the royal residence situated outside the inner palace, such as the places for administering justice and so forth.

"Thus guarded and protected, being at peace"—meaning that while I was thus guarded and protected for my own sake, for the sake of fearlessness, and for the sake of dwelling in comfort, in many hundreds of well-arranged defenses, enclosures, and guards within and without the royal palace, the capital city, and the kingdom in numerous locations;
the words "frightened," and so forth, are synonyms for one another. Alternatively, "frightened" means...
"Fearing other kings" means being apprehensive. "Agitated" means shaken by the surge of fear arising even from one's own kingdom.

"Suspicious" means looking around with an upward gaze due to a lack of confidence in all matters—based on the saying, "A king must always remain distrustful"—and due to the suspicion regarding the conditions for various duties and obligations.

“Uttrāsī” means: he was terrified (*utrāsī*) by a fear that was capable of causing a trembling of the body, arising from the thought, “Perhaps some misfortune might happen to me even from those who dwell nearby, though they do not know [of my situation]. They also read it as “utrasto.
“Vihāsim” means: having become thus, I dwelt.
“Etarahī” means now, from the time of his going forth. “Eko” means alone; by this, he shows the state of having withdrawn the body.
The meaning of the words beginning with “abhīto” should be understood as the opposite of what was previously stated.
Because of the absence of both the grasping that takes fear and so forth as its sign, and the defilement that is that sign, he is “fearless” and so on. By this, he shows the seclusion of the mind.

"Free from anxiety" (*appossukka*) means being without concern for the protection of the body. "With hair standing on end" (*pannaloma*) means having the hair not bristling due to the absence of that trembling which causes horripilation.

By these two phrases, he demonstrates a life lived with ease (*serivihāra*). "Living on what is given by others" (*paradattavutta*) means subsisting on robes and so forth provided by others; by this, through the manner of illustrating the total absence of attachment, he shows the lack of every cause for fear.
He shows this by means of the phrase "with a mind become like a deer. This refers to a mind that has become like a deer's through its state of dwelling with confidence.
For a deer, while living in a forest on a path frequented by non-humans, stands, sits, lies down, and departs wherever it pleases with unimpeded movement, dwelling confidently;
thus he shows: "I too dwell in such a manner. For this was said by the Paccekabuddha:
"Just as a deer, unbound in the forest,
goes wherever it pleases for its range,
so does the wise man, looking toward freedom."
“One should wander alone like the rhinoceros’s horn.
Venerable sir, this is the benefit I see, venerable sir, namely, this supreme bliss of seclusion, this bliss of the attainment of fruition which I now possess;
seeing this very reason, [I think]: “Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!”
"He uttered this exclamation:

'Happiness!'"—having understood in every way this matter, which is beyond the sphere of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) and is known as the bliss of seclusion, concerning the Elder Bhaddiya. "He uttered this exclamation"—he uttered this exclamation which illuminates the power of the disappearance of fear and sorrow together with their causes.
In that regard, "for whom there is no anger from within": for that noble person (*ariyapuggala*), from within—that is, from his own interior—there is no anger.

Because they cause turbidity in the mind, the corruptions of lust and so forth are "disturbances of the mind" (*cittappakopa*). As for "wrathful disturbances" (*dosakopa*), these are indeed "wrath" (*kopa*) because they arise from various causes such as the bases of resentment (*āghātavatthu*);
however, since they have been abandoned by the Path, they do not exist and are no longer found.

Now, although this word *antara* is seen in the sense of "cause" in such phrases as "What is the difference between you and the bed?", it is also seen in the sense of "time" in such phrases as "during the period of snowfall known as *antaraṭṭhaka*."
In such passages as “in the middle,” it refers to an interval—as in “between the Jeta Grove and Sāvatthī”; in such passages as “fear born from within,” it refers to the mind;
here too, it should be understood as referring precisely to the mind. Therefore it is said: “from within, in one’s own mind.
And as for the phrase “transcending both ‘it is’ and ‘it is not’”: since “existence” (*bhava*) means success and “non-existence” (*abhava*) means failure, likewise, “existence” means...

"Becoming" (*bhava*) is increase, while "non-becoming" (*abhava*) is decrease. Or, "becoming" is eternalism (*sassata*), while "non-becoming" is annihilationism (*uccheda*). Or, "becoming" is merit (*puñña*), while "non-becoming" is demerit (*pāpa*).
Or, "becoming" is a happy rebirth (*sugati*), while "non-becoming" is an unhappy rebirth (*duggati*). Or, "becoming" is small, while "non-becoming" is great.
Therefore, that which consists of success and failure, increase and decrease, eternalism and annihilationism, merit and demerit, happy rebirth and unhappy rebirth—
"By way of minor and major states of rebirth," thus it is said that "becoming this or that" (*itibhavābhavatā*) is of many kinds.

By means of each of the four noble paths, according to their respective possibilities and by various methods, one has transcended and gone beyond that "becoming this or that. The case ending should be modified for the sake of the sense.
"That which is free from fear" (*vigatabhayaṃ*): that which is of such a nature, endowed with the qualities as previously described.

One whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) is "free from fear" (*vigatabhaya*) because of the absence of mental agitation and because of having transcended "this state of being and that state of being," thereby removing the causes of fear;
one is "happy" (*sukhi*) through the bliss of seclusion and the bliss of the supreme fruit; and precisely because of being free from fear, one is "without sorrow" (*asoka*).

The phrase "the gods do not experience [him] for the sake of seeing" means that, setting aside those who have attained the Path, even all the gods born in the realms of rebirth, though they strive, cannot perceive the movement of his mind.
They are unable to see, to behold, to experience, or to reach [him], let alone human beings.
For even those in training (*sekkhā*) do not know the movement of the mind of an Arahant, just like worldlings (*puthujjana*).
The commentary on the tenth sutta is concluded.
The commentary on the Mucalinda Chapter is finished.
3. The Nanda Chapter: 1.
Commentary on the Kammavipākaja Sutta.
21. In the first sutta of the Nanda-vagga, "a certain bhikkhu" refers to a certain bhikkhu whose name and clan were not well-known, one whose taints were exhausted.
It is said that he was a son of good family living in Rājagaha who, having been stirred by the Elder Moggallāna and seeing the defects of *saṃsāra*, went forth in the presence of the Teacher.
Having purified his moral conduct and taken up the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths, before long he attained insight.
Having exerted himself, he attained arahantship. Later on, a severe illness arose in him;
dwelling in reflective contemplation, he endured it. For those whose taints are destroyed, there is indeed no mental suffering, yet physical suffering certainly exists.
One day, while the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma, he remained at a place not far away, enduring his pain.
He sat cross-legged. Therefore it was said: "He sat not far from the Blessed One," and so forth.
In that context, *pallaṅka* means a seat with the thighs bound all around. *Ābhujitvā* means having bound [the legs].
*Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāyā* means having placed the upper body straight, setting the tip of one vertebra against the tip of the next among the eighteen spinal vertebrae.
For one sitting in this way, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not bend; therefore, he sits in such a manner.
"Born of the ripening of past karma" means born by way of the result (*vipāka*) of karma performed in the past;

or, it means born as a constituent part of the mass of results consisting of the cycle of results (*vipākavaṭṭa*), which takes the form of pleasure and pain within the ripening of past karma. What is that? Suffering. "Born of the ripening of past karma."
And by this, showing that the illness originates from karma, he rejects its being caused by external injury, seasonal change, and so forth.
"Painful" (*dukkha*) means that which cannot be endured by ordinary people. "Sharp" (*tibba*) means acute, or intense due to its overwhelming occurrence.
"Harsh" (*khara*) means rough. "Bitter" (*kaṭuka*) means unpleasant. "Enduring" (*adhivāseto*) means dwelling upon it, bearing it, and tolerating it.
“Mindful and clearly comprehending” means being mindful and clearly comprehending by way of mindfulness and clear comprehension that grasp the feeling.
This is what is meant: “This so-called feeling, having come to be, is impermanent in the sense of non-existence;
it is dependently arisen because it has arisen in dependence on conditions such as undesirable objects; and it is subject to destruction because its nature is to break up once it has arisen.”
"Subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation"— having thus become mindful by means of the careful observation of the characteristic of impermanence regarding feeling,
and having become clearly comprehending by means of penetrating its true nature without error; or alternatively,

being "mindful" (sato) due to the excellence of mindfulness attained through the thorough establishment of mindfulness toward the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena in all respects, and likewise [clearly comprehending] due to the excellence of wisdom attained.
Being fully aware through the state of having grasped the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). "Without being afflicted" means that, unlike the blind worldling of whom it is said:

"Bhikkhus, when the uninstructed worldling is touched by this or that painful phenomenon, he sorrows, languishes, laments, beats his breast, and falls into confusion," he is not afflicted like that blind worldling, but proceeds by way of the Path itself.
Because he had eradicated [the defilements], he sat as if having entered meditative absorption, enduring only the bodily pain born of the ripening of karma without producing any mental suffering.
"He saw" means that he beheld that venerable one sitting in such a manner through his endurance and patience.

"Having understood in every aspect this meaning"— that is, having fully comprehended the meaning characterized by the fact that those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) remain unstained by worldly conditions (lokadhamma), which is the reason why they do not strive for the medical treatment of even such a disease as that mentioned;

"he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna)"— he uttered this inspired utterance which elucidates the attainment of non-affliction (avighātapatti) through any of the various painful states (dukkhadhamma) among conditioned phenomena (saṅkhatadhamma).

In this context, "of one who has abandoned all karma" means one who has relinquished all wholesome and unwholesome karma. Indeed, from the moment the supreme path (agga-magga) arises, all the wholesome and unwholesome karmas of an Arahant are said to be abandoned, because they are no longer capable of producing rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi);
it is for this reason that noble path-knowledge is called the "exhauster of karma. "A bhikkhu" refers to one who is a bhikkhu by virtue of having shattered the defilements (kilesa).

"Shaking off what was done before": they "cling"—that is, they are stained by the dust of passion and so forth—to karma performed prior to attaining *arahantship*, which has received its name because it is to be experienced as suffering;
[the verse refers to] one who shakes off and destroys that [karma] through the experiencing of its result.
However, after the attainment of *arahantship*, there is simply no possibility for the occurrence of any blameworthy action.
And because the root of existence has been cut off, blameless action—due to the absence of any capacity to yield fruit, like a flower whose roots have been severed—is merely action alone.

"Of one who is without 'mine'" means of one who is free from the sense of "mine" because there is no grasping at anything as "mine" among form and so forth; of one who is devoid of the conceit "mine. Of whom...
For there is "mine-making" (mamankāra) in me; through attachment to self, one has physicians and others attend to the body. But the Arahant is "without mine" (amama);
therefore, he is indifferent even regarding the care of the body. "Of one who stands" means of one who, having crossed over the fourfold flood, stands on the dry land of Nibbāna;
or, it means standing because of the absence of running about by way of taking rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).

For learners (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*), because they have not abandoned the defilements (*kilesa*) and volitional formations (*abhisankhāra*), they are said to "run" through the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) by way of death and rebirth;

however, the Arahant is called "steadfast" because of the absence of those [defilements]. Alternatively, it refers to one who is established in the tenfold noble Dhamma characterized by the destruction of the taints (*khīṇāsava*).
"Such-like" (*tādino*) means, according to the method beginning with, "He dwells perceiving the repulsive in the non-repulsive," and so forth.

One who possesses the fivefold noble psychic power (*ariyiddhi*) described above, who is unshakable by the eight worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*), and who is endowed with the sixfold equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*);
such a one is "one who is thus" (*tādī*) because of the state of being "thus" (*tādibhāva*), which is defined as being the same toward the desirable and so forth.
For such a one, there is no purpose in addressing people, meaning there is no need for the motive to speak to or address people by saying, "Prepare medicines and so forth for me."

Because of their state of indifference toward the body. For the intention of those whose taints are exhausted is: "Let this body, like a withered leaf detached from its stalk, break up and fall of its own accord. Indeed, it has been said:
"I do not long for death, nor do I long for life..."
"And I await my time, like a wage-earner awaiting his wages.
Alternatively, there is no need for one whose taints are exhausted to display any sign whatsoever and then speak to people, saying, "What does the Noble One desire?
in order to have them speak [of offerings] by way of inviting them with the requisites; for such a wrong livelihood is itself a path [to ruin].

The meaning is "because it has been eradicated. Thus, the Blessed One revealed the reason for the Elder’s refusal of medical treatment to those who were thinking, "Why is this elder sitting not far from the Blessed One after having his own illness neglected by physicians?
The commentary on the first sutta is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Nanda Sutta 22.

In the second [sutta], "Nanda" is his name. For he was born bringing joy (*nandayanto*) to his parents, along with their retinue and his entire circle of kinsmen, because he was endowed with the marks of a wheel-turning monarch; thus he received the name "Nanda. He was the Blessed One’s brother.
He was the brother of the Blessed One by virtue of having the same father. For no uterine brothers of the Blessed One were born;
therefore it is said, "the son of his maternal aunt," meaning the son of his younger mother. For he was the son of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. "Dissatisfied" means not satisfied.
"The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) refers to the conduct that is holy, supreme, and excellent: sitting alone, sleeping alone, and abstaining from sexual intercourse.
"To maintain" means to bear, to cause to proceed, and to keep perfectly complete and pure from the first moment of consciousness until the final moment of consciousness.
Furthermore, by the second term, "the holy life" (*brahmacariya*), it should be understood that the "noble holy life" (*magga-brahmacariya*) is also included.
"Having renounced the training" refers to that which was undertaken at the time of full ordination (*upasampadā*) together with the state of a monk, as something to be realized.
"Having rejected the threefold training that had been undertaken"—the meaning is "having abandoned it. "To the low life" means to the state of a householder.
"I shall turn back" means I shall return.
But why did he announce this? Herein is the sequential account: the Blessed One, having set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma...

Having gone to Rājagaha and staying in the Veḷuvana grove, ten messengers— each accompanied by a retinue of a thousand followers— were sent by King Suddhodana with the command, "Bring my son here and show him to us.
When these messengers had all attained Arahatship along with their retinues,
Kāḷudāyi Thera, who was the very last to go and had likewise attained Arahatship, perceived the time for departure and [began] describing the path.
Having praised [the city] and being requested to go to his birthplace, he went to the city of Kapilavatthu accompanied by twenty thousand *khīṇāsava* (arahants).

At the assembly of his kinsmen, he established the origin story (*aṭṭhuppatti*) of the *Pokkharavassa Jātaka*, and after recounting the *Vessantara Jātaka*, on the following day, as he entered for alms, he established his father in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) with the verse: "Arise! Do not be negligent!"

Having established her in the refuges, he went to his residence and, with the verse beginning "One should live according to the Dhamma," he established Mahāpajāpatī in the fruit of stream-entry and the king in the fruit of once-returning.
At the conclusion of the meal, however, based on a discourse regarding the virtues of Rāhula’s mother, he related the Canda-kinnarī Jātaka.

On the third day, while the auspicious ceremonies for Prince Nanda’s entry into the palace for his consecration and marriage were underway, [the Blessed One] entered for alms, placed his bowl in Prince Nanda’s hand, and after pronouncing a blessing, rose from his seat and departed;
yet he did not take the bowl from the prince’s hand. Out of reverence for the Tathāgata, the prince said, “Venerable Sir, please take your bowl.”
He was unable to speak. However, he thought, "The Teacher will take the bowl at the top of the stairs," but the Teacher did not take it there.
He thought, "He will take it at the foot of the stairs," but the Teacher did not take it there either.
He thought, "He will take it in the royal courtyard," but the Teacher did not take it there either. The prince then desired to turn back.
Going against his will, out of respect he was unable to say, "Take the bowl";
he went along thinking, "He will take it here; he will take it there.
At that moment, they pointed out the Janapadakalyāṇī to him, saying, "Noble lady, the Blessed One is going along taking King Nanda with him."

“Without you, he will do it. With her hair half-combed and dripping with drops of water, she hurriedly ascended the palace, stood at the door of the lion-window, and said, “My noble son, please come quickly!
Those words of hers fell across his heart as if they were engraved there. The Teacher [then] took them from his hand...
Without even taking the bowl, he led him to the monastery and said, "Nanda, will you go forth?
Out of reverence for the Buddha, he did not say, "I will not go forth," but replied, "Yes, I will go forth.

The Teacher, saying, "In that case, let Nanda go forth," went to the city of Kapilavatthu and on the third day ordained him. On the seventh day, having been adorned by his mother, [he was brought before the Buddha].
Having been sent with the message, "O ascetic, give me my inheritance," he caused Prince Rāhula—who had come to the monastery with him—to go forth.
On another day, after recounting the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka, he established the king in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
Thus, having established Mahāpajāpatī in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) and his father in the three fruits, the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, [proceeded].
Having gone back once more to Rājagaha, he gave his promise to Anāthapiṇḍika to come from there to Sāvatthī;
and when the great monastery of Jetavana was completed, he went there and took up residence.
While the Teacher was thus dwelling at Jetavana, the Venerable Nanda—who had gone forth against his own will—seeing no danger in sensual pleasures, [fell in love] with Janapadakalyāṇī.
Recalling those words spoken, he became dissatisfied and informed the monks of his lack of enthusiasm for the religious life.
Therefore it is said: "At that time, the Venerable Nanda... [and so on] ...I shall return to the lower life.
But why did the Blessed One ordain him in this way? [It was because] he had already shown him the danger of sensual pleasures beforehand.
"It is not possible to separate her [now]; however, having ordained her, I shall use a skillful means to separate her from that [attachment] and bring about higher distinction.
Thus the Teacher, skilled in taming those to be converted, first ordained her.
"Sākiyānī" means the daughter of the Sakya king. "Janapadakalyāṇī" means beautiful in the country; she was supreme in physical form and free from the six bodily defects.

She is endowed with five kinds of excellence. Because she is neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too stout, and neither too dark nor too fair—thus surpassing human appearance yet not having attained divine appearance—she is therefore free from the six defects of the body.
These five [excellences] are: excellence of skin, excellence of flesh, excellence of nails, excellence of bones, and excellence of age.
They are endowed with beautiful qualities.
In this regard, she creates light within a space of ten or twelve cubits by means of the radiance from her own body;
she is like the *piyaṅgu* flower or like gold—this is her beauty of complexion. Furthermore, her four hands and feet, as well as the area ending at her face, [are beautiful].
It is like red coral or red woolen cloth treated with lac-dye; this is its excellence of flesh.
The twenty nail-leaves, where they do not emerge from the flesh, are as if smeared with lac-dye, while where they do emerge, they resemble streams of milk;
this is its excellence of nails. The thirty-two teeth are very smooth, resembling a row of pure coral.
They appear like rows of diamonds; this is her excellence of bone. Although she is one hundred and twenty years old, she appears as if she were sixteen years of age, being devoid of grey hair;
this is her excellence of age. She is beautiful and endowed with such qualities;
therefore it is said, "the most beautiful woman in the land."
“Of one departing from the house”: this is a term of address used in a sense of disregard; the meaning is “departing from the house. They also read it as “nikkhamantaṃ gharā. “With hair half-shorn”:
this is an instrumental expression used as a characteristic mark of a state (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa);
the meaning is “characterized by hair that has been incompletely shorn. They also read it as “aḍḍhullikhitehi. And “shaving” (ullikhana) refers to [the act performed] with razors and such.
"Styling the hair"—some also call it "the arrangement of half-locks.
"Having looked back" means having looked as if binding [her] with a sidelong glance that reveals the diffusion of the essence of affection.
"'Sir, me'—having previously said 'me,' because his mind was agitated by longing, he spoke again: 'He said this to me. "Quickly" means swiftly. "Recalling that" refers to those words of hers.
Or, as he was recollecting her words along with their context,
the Blessed One, having heard his speech, thought, "I shall pacify his lust through a skillful means. By the power of his supernormal might,
while leading him toward the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, he saw on the way, at the top of a charred stump in a burnt field, a man sitting there whose ears, nose, and thumbs had been cut off.
Having shown him a single monkey that had leaped away, he led him to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

In the Pāḷi, however, it is stated as if the Teacher had gone to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a single moment; that journey was not mentioned there, but rather what was said refers to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven itself.
For while the Blessed One was indeed traveling, on the way to the venerable Nanda’s home, he [showed] that leaping monkey.
...he shows. If this is so, how is the demonstration of bending and so forth to be understood? It should be taken as a demonstration of their disappearance.

Thus the Teacher, having led her to that Tāvatiṃsa heaven, showed her the five hundred celestial nymphs with peacock-feather feet who had come to wait upon Sakka, the king of the gods, and were standing after having paid homage to him; [he showed her] those five [nymphs] of Janapadakalyāṇī.
He asked about the distinction based on the excellence of the form of hundreds of nymphs. Therefore it was said:
“Then the Blessed One, taking the Venerable Nanda by the arm… [and so on] …like the feet of a cock.
Therein, “taking by the arm” means as if taking him by the upper arm. For at that time the Blessed One performed such a feat of psychic power (*iddhi-abhisankhāra*).
He performed a supernormal feat such that the Venerable Nanda felt as though he were being led by the Blessed One by the hand.

And there, if the Blessed One had intended for that Venerable one merely to see or enter the Tāvatiṃsa deva-world, He would have shown him that world while he remained seated, just as He did during the manifestation of the worlds. To that very effect:

Or he might have sent him there by means of psychic power (*iddhi*). However, because he wished to show that monkey on the way—desiring that the inferior and loathsome nature of the human state compared to his divine existence be easily grasped—and because he wished to display the splendors and riches of the celestial realms after having immersed himself in them, he took the monkey and went there. For it was for this purpose that he acted.
"There will be a special delight in living the holy life (brahmacariya).

"Kakuṭapādā" means those whose feet are like those of a pigeon due to their reddish color. It is said that all of them came to have such delicate feet through the gift of foot-unguent oil given to the disciples of the Blessed One Kassapa. "Do you see? means "Do you see?"
Now, "more beautiful" means having a more distinguished form. "More lovely to behold" means more worthy of being seen in the sense that even those who look upon them for days would never be satiated.
"More pleasing" means bringing greater serenity from all sides due to the beauty of every limb.
But why did the Blessed One have the Venerable Nanda, whose mind was lustful, look at the nymphs? It was so that he might easily [attain liberation].

In order to expel the defilements. For just as a skilled physician, treating a person with aggravated humors, first causes those humors to rise by means of an oily drink and so forth, and subsequently has them expelled properly through emetics and purgatives;

even so, the Blessed One, who is skilled in training those to be disciplined, having shown celestial nymphs to the Venerable Nanda whose passion was aggravated, caused it to rise and then expelled it by means of the medicine of the Noble Path.
"It should be understood that he wishes to extract [the faults] without remainder.
"A scorched female monkey" means a female monkey whose limbs and members have been singed. "In just this way," venerable sir, means:
just as that scorched female monkey with severed ears and nose whom you showed me was compared to the most beautiful woman in the land, even so...

"Janapadakalyāṇī [is superior] taking these five hundred celestial nymphs as the standard"—this is the meaning. In the phrase "of the five hundred celestial nymphs," the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative;
thus, the meaning is "five hundred celestial nymphs. Alternatively, this genitive expresses a relationship of parts (avayava-sambandha);
therefore, the intended sense is "in comparison with the physical beauty of the five hundred celestial nymphs. Regarding the word *upanidhāya*:
"And having placed near" means "taking as a basis. "Number" refers to the calculation of "woman. "A fraction of a fraction" (*kalabhāga*):

even a part of a part; having divided [a unit] into sixteen portions and taken one portion from those, when that is further divided sixteenfold, each individual portion therein is intended here as a "fraction of a fraction.
He says that even such a fraction of a fraction does not approach [the magnitude of the Buddha's qualities].
“Upanidhi” means taking something as a comparison by way of its similarity, thinking, “This is like that,” and placing it nearby.
Since the holy life (*brahmacariya*) in which he finds no delight has already been mentioned and is well known, the Buddha does not refer to it directly;
rather, in order to generate a sense of urgency for delighting in that [holy life], he says, “Delight, Nanda! Delight, Nanda! using reduplication (*āmeḍita*).
When the Blessed One said, “I am your guarantor,” why did he, desiring his dwelling in the holy life (*brahmacariya*), offer himself as a guarantor for a non-holy life?
He offered himself as a guarantor so that, by transferring [the disciple’s] passion—which was firmly settled upon its original object—to a new object, it might be abandoned with ease.
In this gradual discourse, there is the talk of heaven (*saggakathā*).
This is an illustration of this meaning.

"They heard"—how did they hear it? For at that time, after the Blessed One had shown the Venerable Nanda his duties and had gone to his own daytime resting place, he related that occurrence to the monks who had come for attendance, just as a skilled man [would do].
Just as one who, having recognized that a wedge has not yet been removed, extracts it with another wedge and then moves it away by shaking it again with his hands and so forth;

even so, desiring to remove the lust for that accustomed object by extracting it with an adventitious object, and then further removing even that [adventitious object] by making it a cause for grasping the path of the holy life, he said:
"Come, monks, address the bhikkhu Nanda with the term 'hireling' and the term 'servant'..."

"...and act accordingly," he commanded; thus did the bhikkhus hear. However, some say that the Blessed One performed such a feat of supernormal power (*iddhi-abhisaṅkhāra*) that those bhikkhus came to know the matter.
"By the term 'hireling' (*bhataka-vādena*)" means by the expression "hireling. For one who performs work for wages is called a hireling.
"This venerable one, too, while practicing the holy life for the sake of enjoyment with celestial nymphs, is like a hireling"; thus it is said by the term "hireling.
Regarding the term "purchaser": one who buys something with coins such as kahāpaṇas is called a "purchaser.
This venerable one, too, purchases his own holy life for the sake of celestial nymphs; therefore, he is called a "purchaser."

Thus it is by means of this word. Alternatively, because he maintains his life—which consists of living the holy life (brahmacariya)—as a service consisting of the enjoyment of celestial nymphs (accharā) by the command of the Blessed One, he is as if being supported by that service;
