thus he is called "one who is supported" (bhatako). Likewise, having made the enjoyment of celestial nymphs a commodity to be sold, [he acts] upon the instruction of the Blessed One.
"Standing there, he was as if branded by that sale by the Blessed One"; thus it is said, "branded. "Distressed" means being oppressed, being made to suffer.
"Ashamed" means feeling bashful. "Disgusted" means perceiving [the situation] with revulsion. "Alone" means without a companion.
"Withdrawn" means [withdrawn] from sense-pleasures of the objects and sense-pleasures of the defilements, both in body and mind.

And “withdrawn” means secluded. “Diligent” means not abandoning mindfulness regarding the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). “Ardent” means one who is ardent through the ardor of physical and mental energy;
*ātāpa* is that which burns away or consumes the defilements, which is energy (*vīriya*).

“Resolute” means one whose self is directed toward—having relinquished attachment for body and life—or one whose mind is directed toward Nibbāna. “Before long” means from the commencement of the meditation subject.
Not long at all. "For whose sake" means for the purpose of whom. "Noble sons" (*kulaputta*) are of two kinds: noble sons by birth and noble sons by conduct;
this one, however, is a noble son in both respects. "In the right way" means by means of the cause and the reason.
"From the home" means from the house. "The homeless state" means the going forth (*pabbajjā*). For agriculture, trade, and such activities are beneficial to the home.
"Household life" means that which exists there; since that is not present here, "going forth" is called "the homeless state.

"They go forth" means they approach it. "That unsurpassed" means that which is unsurpassed. "The consummation of the holy life" refers to the fruit of arhatship, which constitutes the consummation of the holy life of the path.
It is for the sake of this that sons of noble family go forth here. "In this very life" means in that very [existence].
"In his own person. "Having realized it through direct higher knowledge" means having made it personally evident through his own wisdom;
the meaning is that he knew it by himself, not dependent on another. "Having attained and dwelt [in it]" means he dwelt having reached or having accomplished it.
While dwelling thus, "birth was exhausted... [and] he directly knew," by this his stage of reviewing is shown.

Regarding the phrase "birth is exhausted" (*khīṇā jāti*): it is not that his past birth is exhausted, because it was already exhausted previously; nor is it the future birth, because it is yet to come;

nor is it the present birth, because it currently exists. Rather, it refers to that birth—which is differentiated by one, four, or five aggregates within one, four, or five-aggregate existences—that would have arisen had the Path not been cultivated; [that birth] has reached the state of non-arising due to the cultivation of the Path.

They are exhausted by way of their occurrence. Having reviewed the defilements abandoned through the cultivation of the path, he directly knew—by means of knowing that even though karma still exists due to the absence of defilements, it will not lead to rebirth in the future—that "it has been lived" (*vusita*).

"Lived" (*vuttha*) means dwelt upon, fully dwelt upon, performed, and practiced; the sense is that it has been brought to completion. "The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) refers to the holy life of the Path.

Indeed, together with the virtuous worldling (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*), the seven types of trainees (*sekkha*) are said to "dwell in the holy life" (*brahmacariyavāsa*); one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) has completed that dwelling.
Therefore, reviewing his own dwelling in the holy life, he directly knew: "The holy life has been lived.

"What was to be done has been done" means that, regarding the four truths, [the tasks] have been accomplished by way of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing through the four paths.

The sixteenfold duty has been brought to completion. For while those such as the "virtuous worldlings" (puthujjanakalyāṇaka) are said merely to perform that duty, the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) has already accomplished what was to be done; therefore, reflecting upon his own task, he directly knew: "What was to be done has been done.
Regarding the phrase "there is nothing further of this nature": "now there is no more returning to this state of being, that is, to the state of performing these sixteen duties."
He directly knew: "I have no further task to perform for the destruction of the defilements or for the cultivation of the path.

Regarding the phrase "there is nothing further of this nature": "From this present state—namely, from this current continuity of aggregates of such a kind—there is no further continuity of aggregates for me;
these five aggregates, however, remain fully understood, like trees whose roots have been cut."
He understood: "With the cessation of their final consciousness, they will be extinguished like a fire without fuel, reaching the state of being indescribable.
"A certain one" (aññatara) means one; the meaning is that he was one great disciple among the Blessed One’s disciples who were arahants.
"A certain deity" refers to a single Brahma-deity who had attained the Path. For she, being an *asekha* (one beyond training), directly knew that which is the domain of the *asekhas*.
Indeed, those in training (*sekkhā*) know their respective domains of training, and worldlings (*puthujjanā*) know only their own domain as worldlings.
"When the night was far spent" means when the night was exhausted; the meaning is "in the middle watch. "Of surpassing beauty" (*abhikkantavaṇṇā*).
Of exceedingly sublime complexion. "Kevalakappaṃ" means entirely and on all sides.
"Obhāsetvā" means having made Jetavana a single expanse of light with his own radiance, like the moon or the sun.
"Tenupasaṅkami" means that, having understood the Venerable Nanda’s attainment of Arahatship, he approached, filled with joy and gladness, thinking, "I shall inform the Blessed One."

Regarding the phrase "the destruction of the taints" (*āsavānaṃ khayo*): here, they are called *āsava* because they flow (*āsavanti*). The meaning is that they proceed through the doors of the eye and so forth.
Alternatively, they are called *āsava* because they flow as far as the stage of "change-of-lineage" (*gotrabhū*) or as far as the peak of existence (*bhavagga*).

The meaning is that they proceed by making these phenomena and this spatial range their limit. They are called *āsava* because, in the sense of having been stored for a long time, they are like fermented liquor and the like. "Bhikkhus, the former... [etc.]
Their state of having been stored for a long time is to be understood from such statements as, “No limit of ignorance is discerned.
Alternatively, they are called *āsava* because they flow (*savanti*) and pour forth (*pasavanti*) the far-reaching suffering of *saṃsāra*.

Herein, the former meaning applies to the defilements (*kilesa*), while the latter applies to both defilements and kamma. Furthermore, it is not only kamma and defilements that are *āsava*, but various other things as well.

There are also calamities. For instance, in the passage: “Cunda, I do not teach the Dhamma merely for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life,” it is the defilements that constitute the root of dispute which are referred to as “taints. And:
“By which one may be reborn as a god, or as a gandhabba, or a bird-farer...”
“Those by which one might go to the state of a *yakkha*, or fall into the human state—those taints (*āsava*) of mine are exhausted, shattered, and rendered baseless.
Here, it is stated that the *āsava* consist of karma pertaining to the three planes of existence and all remaining unwholesome states (*akusala-dhamma*). “Of those pertaining to the present life...”

"For the restraint of the taints, for the warding off of the taints pertaining to future lives"—this refers to various kinds of calamities, such as remorse for harming others, killing, binding, and so forth, as well as the sufferings of the states of deprivation (apāya).
Furthermore, these taints are addressed in the Vinaya: "For the restraint of the taints pertaining to the present life, and for the warding off of the taints pertaining to future lives..."
In the *Saḷāyatana-vagga*, it is presented in two ways as: "Friends, there are these three taints (*āsava*): the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance.
It appears likewise in other discourses (*suttanta*). In the Abhidhamma, those same three are presented in four ways by adding the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*).
In the *Nibbedhika-pariyāya*, it is stated: "Bhikkhus, there are taints leading to hell," and so forth.
They appear in five ways. In the *Chakkanipāta*, they appear in six ways by way of the passage beginning, “Bhikkhus, there are taints to be abandoned through restraint,” and so forth.
In the *Sabbāsavapariyāya*, those same [taints] appear in seven ways together with those to be abandoned by vision.
However, here, according to the method of the Abhidhamma, four taints are to be understood.

In this context, however, the term *khaya* (destruction) refers to the destruction of the intrinsic nature (*sarasabheda*) of the taints (*āsava*), as in such passages as: "The destruction, breaking up, and disintegration of the taints.
In such passages as: "Bhikkhus, I declare the destruction of the taints for one who knows and sees," it refers to the non-arising of the taints in the future.
“In the case of one in training, one who is still practicing, following the straight path—the first knowledge is regarding destruction, and immediately after that comes full realization.

In such passages as these, the path is called the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*). In such passages as “Through the destruction of the taints, one becomes a recluse,” it refers to the fruit.
"In one who constantly observes the faults of others and is always prone to criticism, the taints increase; he is far from the destruction of the taints.
In such passages as these, "nibbāna" is meant. But here, the absolute destruction or non-arising of the taints, or the path [leading thereto], is called "the destruction of the taints."

"Free from taints" (*anāsava*) means that all taints have been entirely abandoned by way of complete subsiding. "Liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*) refers to the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship.

"Liberation by wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*) refers to the wisdom of the fruit of Arahantship. The mention of both is for the purpose of showing that, just as on the path, serenity and insight are conjoined even in the fruit.
"Knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) refers to the knowledge of omniscience. Immediately after the utterance of the deity...
As the Blessed One was reflecting, "How indeed [did this come to pass]?", knowledge arose in him: "Nanda has realized arhatship.
For that venerable one, being thus mocked by his fellow monks, had thought:
"Alas, a grievous thing I have done, in that having gone forth in such a well-proclaimed Dhamma and Vinaya, I have stood as a guarantor for the Teacher regarding the acquisition of celestial nymphs."
Thinking, “I have done it,” he was stirred with a sense of urgency; having established shame and fear of wrongdoing, and striving with diligence, he attained arahantship and thought:
“What if I were to release the Blessed One from this promise?
He approached the Blessed One and informed the Teacher of his intention. Thus it is said: “Then the Venerable Nanda... [and so on].”

"From this promise. In this context, "promise" (*paṭissava*) refers to a promise of surety (*pāṭibhogappaṭissava*), by means of the declaration: "I am the guarantor for the obtaining of celestial nymphs.
Then the Blessed One [thought]: "It is known to me that another [deity] was propitiated by you; even the deity has informed me."
"Therefore, I am not to be released from my promise now, because I have already been released by the attainment of Arahatship," he said. Thus it was said: "Nanda, at the very moment... and so forth.
In this context, *yadeva* means "at which very time"; *te* means "your"; *mutto* means "released.
This is what is meant: at the very time your mind was liberated from the taints (*āsava*), immediately thereafter I [was released].
"Then he was released from his surety.

That venerable one, at the very time of practicing insight (vipassanā), gave rise to such exertion, thinking: "Whatever misconduct I have fallen into due to lack of restraint over the sense faculties, that very thing I shall thoroughly subdue.
He possessed powerful moral shame (hiri) and moral dread (ottappa), and because he had previously performed meritorious service in that regard, he was intent upon it.
He even reached the highest level of practice regarding the restraint of the sense faculties. For it has been said:
"Bhikkhus, if Nanda must look toward the eastern direction, he looks toward the eastern direction having fully concentrated his entire mind, thinking:
'Thus, as I look toward the eastern direction, may no covetousness or mental distress arise in me.'"
“May evil, unwholesome states flow in upon me”—thus he is fully aware in that regard.
“If, monks, Nanda must look toward the west... the north... the south... above... below...

or the intermediate directions, having brought his whole mind to bear, Nanda looks toward the intermediate direction, thinking: ‘In this way may my [unwholesome states] not flow in... thus he is fully aware.”

For that very reason, the Teacher placed that venerable one in the foremost position, saying: "Bhikkhus, among my disciples, the bhikkhus who guard the doors of the sense-faculties, Nanda is the foremost.

"Having understood this matter" means: having understood in every aspect this matter consisting of the venerable Nanda’s exhaustion of all taints (āsava) and his attainment of equanimity (tādibhāva) regarding pleasure and so forth. "He uttered this inspired utterance" means: he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which elucidates that meaning.
In that regard, "by whom the mire has been crossed over" refers to that noble person by whom the entire mire of views has been crossed over by means of the bridge of the Noble Path.
He has indeed crossed over the mire of saṃsāra by reaching the further shore of nibbāna. He has crushed the thorn of sensual desire (*kāmakaṇḍuka*), because it pierces sentient beings.
All defiled desire, which is named "the thorn of sensual desire" and is the entire sting of sensual craving, has been crushed, broken, and completely ground away by the staff of supreme knowledge.
Having thus attained the destruction of delusion, he [has transcended] the object of suffering and so forth.
By the destruction of all delusion, he has attained the exhaustion of delusion; he has reached the fruit of arhatship and Nibbāna.

"That bhikkhu does not tremble amidst pleasure and pain": that bhikkhu, having shattered the defilements, does not tremble or waver when pleasure arises from contact with desirable objects, nor when pain arises from contact with undesirable objects.
He does not undergo that sign or mental transformation. Furthermore, the phrase "in pleasure and pain" is merely an illustration;
it should be understood that he does not waver even in the face of all worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*).
The commentary on the second sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Yasojasutta 23.

Regarding the phrase "headed by Yasoja" in the third [sutta]: here, *Yasojā* is the name of that elder. Because those five hundred bhikkhus went forth and wandered about with him as their leader, they are called "headed by Yasoja.
This was their past connection: it is said that in the past, during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, there was a certain forest-dwelling bhikkhu.

He was dwelling in a leaf-hut built upon a rock in the forest. At that time, five hundred thieves, having committed acts such as plundering villages and living by robbery, were pursued by the people of the countryside while fleeing from their criminal deeds.
Having entered the forest and finding no hiding place or refuge there, they saw that monk not far away on the rock.
Seeing him seated, they paid homage to him, related their situation, and entreated him, saying, "Venerable sir, please be our refuge.
The Elder said, "There is no refuge for you equal to virtue; all of you, undertake the five precepts.
They accepted, saying, "Very well," and undertook the precepts. The Elder said, "Now that you are established in the precepts..."
“Do not let your mind become corrupted even when they are destroying your own lives,” he said, and explained the method of the simile of the saw.

They accepted this, saying, “Very well. Then those country folk, having arrived and searching here and there, saw those thieves and deprived them all of their lives. Yet, without harboring even the slightest corruption of mind toward them, they remained of unbroken virtue.
Having passed away, they were reborn among the gods of the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*). Among them, the eldest thief became the eldest son of a god, while the others became his attendants.
Wandering from one state to another, they spent an entire interval between Buddhas (*buddhantara*) in the world of the gods, and then, during the time of our Blessed One...

Having descended from the world of the gods, the eldest son of the devas was reborn in the village of Keṭaka at the gate of the city of Sāvatthī as the son of the head of five hundred families among the fishermen; they gave him the name Yasodatta.
The others were also reborn as the sons of the remaining fishermen. Because of their previous association, they all became companions and played together in the dust.
Playing together, they gradually reached maturity, and Yasoja was their leader.
They all joined together, took up their nets, and roamed about catching fish in rivers, ponds, and other waters.
Then one day, when a net had been cast in the Aciravatī River, a golden-colored fish entered within the net.
Seeing this, all the fishermen were delighted and joyful, thinking, "While catching fish, our sons have caught a golden-colored fish!
Then those five hundred companions placed the fish in a boat, hauled it up, and presented it to the king.
When the king saw it, he thought, "The Blessed One will know the cause of its golden color."

Having had a fish caught, he showed it to the Blessed One. The Teacher said, "This man, having gone forth during the declining period of the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, practiced wrongly and caused the teaching to decline;
he was reborn in hell, and after being cooked in hell for the duration of one interval between Buddhas, he passed away from there and was reborn as this fish in the Aciravatī River. Thus he spoke.
Having had his mother, his sisters, and his brother— the Elder— speak of their respective births in hell and his own final passing away (parinibbāna),
he taught the Kapila Sutta on this occasion.
Upon hearing the Teacher’s discourse, those five hundred sons of fishermen were moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and [approached] the presence of the Blessed One.
Having gone forth and received full ordination (*upasampadā*), they lived in seclusion and then came to see the Blessed One.
Therefore it is said: "At that time, there were about five hundred bhikkhus headed by Yasoja," and so forth.
In this context, *tedha* means "they here. *Nevāsikehi* means by those living in permanent residence. *Paṭisammodamānā* means...
When the resident bhikkhus had performed greetings as a form of hospitality, saying, “Is it bearable, friends?
and so forth, [the newcomers] replied, “Yes, friends, it is bearable,” and so on; thus, greeting them in return, they shared in the joy that arose together with them.
“Arranging the lodgings” means having asked for lodgings that would fall to their teachers, preceptors, and themselves, by those [resident bhikkhus].
The resident monks, having assigned lodgings for them by saying, "This is for your teachers; this is for your preceptors;

this reaches you," and having gone there themselves, opened the door-panels, removed the beds, stools, mats, and so forth, shook them out, and arranged them by placing them back in their proper places.

"Storing away their bowls and robes" means: "Venerable sir, please set aside this bowl for me, this robe, this alms-bowl, this water-pot, and this walking-stick"—thus they are guarding their requisites for the ascetic life.
"Loud noises, great clamor" means: those whose sound has gone upward (*uddha-gata*) in the sense of being high are "loud noises"; [this is] the substitution of *ākāra* for the vowel *a*.
Having done so. They are "loud-voiced" (*mahāsaddā*) because they possess a great sound that spreads in every direction.
"As if fishermen were plundering fish" means as if in the act of plundering fish like fishermen.

Just as those who earn the name "fishermen" (*kevaṭṭā*) because they move about in the water for the purpose of catching fish—those fishers who, for the sake of catching fish, cast a net into the water—so too [is it here].
They raised a great clamor and loud noise, saying things such as, "He has entered! He has not entered! He has been caught! He has not been caught!
And just as those [fishermen] went among the great crowd at the place where the fish-trays and other goods were set out, plundering while saying, "Give me one fish!
Give me one fish-spear! What was given to so-and-so is large; what was given to me is small," and so forth.
He shows that these monks are thus characterized by loud noise and great clamor through their refusal [to comply] and so forth.
"Tete" means "those very ones. "Kiṃnū" means "for what reason indeed?"—the sense being "for what purpose indeed. "Temeti" means "these ones.
"Paṇāmemī" means "I am expelling. "Vo" means "you. "Na vo mama santike vatthabban" means "you must not dwell in my presence."
By saying, "Since you have come to the dwelling place of a Buddha such as I and made such a great noise, what propriety is there in living according to your own nature?
There is no need for those like you to dwell in my presence," he demonstrates that they have been dismissed.
And when they had thus been dismissed by the Blessed One, not even a single bhikkhu [thought], "The Blessed One [dismissed us] merely because of our loud noise..."

Without saying "We pay homage to you" or any other reply, out of reverence for the Buddha, they all accepted the Blessed One’s words, saying, "So be it, venerable sir," and departed. However, this thought occurred to them:
"We came thinking, 'We shall see the Teacher, we shall hear the Dhamma, and we shall dwell in the presence of the Teacher'; yet such [a person as this]..."
"But it was because we came into the presence of our venerable Teacher and made a great noise that this fault was ours;

we were expelled from there and did not obtain the opportunity to dwell in the Teacher's presence, to behold his all-beautiful, golden-hued body, or to hear the Dhamma taught with his sweet voice. Having become deeply dejected, they departed.
“Having composed himself” means having made himself well-guarded. “The Vajjis” refers to a country of that name;

the princes of the realm are called the Vajjis, and the country where they dwell—though it is but one—is also called “the Vajjis” by way of conventional usage. Therefore it is said, “among the Vajjis.
“The Vaggumudā” is a certain river so named, esteemed by the world as meritorious. There is also a reading, “Vaggamudā. “By one desiring welfare” means...

By one who desires only the welfare, regardless of any personal motive; by one who "desires welfare" (*hitesinā*), meaning by one desiring the welfare [of others], possessing the habit of seeking that which is beneficial (*hita*)—which is either the welfare itself or the cause of that welfare—thinking, "How might my disciples be liberated from the suffering of saṃsāra?
And for that very reason, disregarding even physical exhaustion of his own body, he approaches those to be trained (*veneyya*) even from afar.
Having gone there out of compassion, we were sent away by that compassionate one.
We were dismissed not because of any expectation of personal service or the like, but because the Blessed Buddhas, who are reverent toward the Dhamma, must be honored solely through right practice;
for they dismiss us even at the mere sound of a loud noise. Therefore, friend, let us go to such a dwelling...

We conduct ourselves and dwell everywhere by means of mindfulness and clear comprehension, fulfilling the unerring course of practice, bringing the meditation subject we have undertaken to its culmination, and conducting ourselves while dwelling in the four postures. "In such a way that we might dwell" means:
so that while we are dwelling thus, the Blessed One would be pleased, being gratified by our worshipful right practice—this is the meaning.
"Within that very same year" means, without even exceeding that very year of the Great Invitation (*mahāpavāraṇā*).

"All have realized the three knowledges" means that all those five hundred bhikkhus realized these three: the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*), and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*). [These are the knowledges] of the aggregates of delusion and so forth that conceal the aggregates of past existences...

They made these two [knowledges] their own direct experience in the sense of piercing through. Among the mundane higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), it is precisely these two that are of great assistance for the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*);
the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledge of supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) are not so helpful.

It is for the purpose of showing this that only the three true knowledges (*vijjāttaya*) are mentioned here by way of demonstrating what those bhikkhus attained. For thus it is said in the Verañja Sutta:

The Blessed One, demonstrating his own attainment to the Brahmin of Verañjā, taught only the threefold clear knowledge (*vijjā-ttaya*), because he lacked such things as the divine ear-knowledge (*dibba-sota-ñāṇa*).

Likewise, although those monks also possessed the divine ear-knowledge and other such powers, they were not mentioned; for those monks were possessors of the six supernormal knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*).
And having done so, [the Buddha] vanished from the bank of the Vaggumudā River and appeared in the Gabled Hall in the Great Forest.
He will speak of the exercise of psychic power (*iddhivikubbana*) by those bhikkhus when they appeared in the presence of the Blessed One.
"According to their pleasure" (*yathābhirantaṃ*) means according to their delight (*yathābhiratiṃ*) or according to their inclination (*yathājjhāsayaṃ*).

For indeed, even for Buddhas dwelling in one place, dissatisfaction may arise due to a deficiency of shade or water, an uncomfortable lodging, or because of the lack of faith and other such qualities in people.
There is no such thing as "living at ease" for those who lack these attainments, nor is there any long-term residence for them.
However, wherever the Blessed One dwells, people either take refuge, undertake the precepts, go forth into homelessness, or reach the path of stream-entry and so on;
the Teacher resides there for the purpose of establishing them in those attainments.
In the absence of that [reason], he sets out on his journey. For at that time, there was no Buddha-work to be done in Sāvatthī. Therefore it is said:
"Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Sāvatthī as long as he pleased, set out on a walking tour toward Vesālī.
"Walking on a walking tour" means traveling along a road. And this walking tour of the Blessed One is of two kinds: the hurried walking tour and...

"Without haste in wandering. In this context, "hurried wandering" (*turitacārikā*) refers to going quickly even over a long distance upon seeing a person capable of being enlightened, for the purpose of awakening them;

this is to be seen in instances such as Mahākassapa’s meeting [the Buddha] halfway. However, when one travels day by day through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, covering two or three *yojanas* at a time, supporting the world through the practice of alms-gathering and so forth, [this is not hurried wandering].
This is called "the unhurried journey," and this alone is intended here. *Tadavasarī* means he went by means of that, or he approached that, or he stayed there;
the meaning is that he entered. *Tatra* means in that [place].
*Sudam* is merely an expletive particle. *Vesāliyam* is so called because it has become vast (*visālībhūta*) three times.
In the city of the Licchavi kings, which has acquired its name [Lumbinī]. "Mahāvana" refers to a great forest named Mahāvana that is self-grown, not planted, well-defined, and extensive.

However, the Mahāvana in the vicinity of Kapilavatthu is connected as one with the Himalayas, being undefined and reaching as far as the great ocean. This [forest] is not like that; it is well-defined.
They frequent a great forest; thus it is "in the great forest. In that great forest, in the monastery built for the Blessed One, there was a gabled hall (*kūṭāgārasālā*).

Within that gabled hall was the Perfume Chamber (*gandhakuṭi*) of the Buddha, the Blessed One, which was constructed with a gabled roof and covered with a *haṃsavaṭṭaka* (swan-patterned) roof, perfect in every respect. It is called the "Gabled Hall" because the gabled chamber is situated within it. "Of those dwelling on the banks of the Vaggumudā River... [is the meaning].
"Of those dwelling on the banks of the Vaggumudā. "Having encompassed their minds with his own mind and attended to them" means: having discerned their minds with his own mind and attended to them;
or, having known the specific distinctions attained by them through either the knowledge of penetration of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*) or the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*).
"As if light were born" means as if light had arisen. The other [phrase] is a synonym for that very same thing, [as if there were] a thousand moons and a thousand suns.

The meaning is "as if illuminated. Because those five hundred bhikkhus, headed by Yasojappa, dwell having become like light and like radiance through the complete dispelling of the darkness of ignorance, therefore the Blessed One praises those bhikkhus by way of expressing praise for the direction where they stand, saying:
"Ānanda, this direction has, as it were, become luminous for me," and so forth. By that...
It is said: “In whatever direction the bhikkhus from the banks of the Vaggumudā dwell. “Not repulsive” means not loathsome;

the meaning is that they are pleasing and heart-captivating. For in whatever place great seers endowed with virtues such as moral discipline dwell, even if that location has uneven, rugged, and difficult terrain, it is nevertheless delightful and beautiful. Indeed, this has been said:
“Whether in a village or in the forest, whether in a valley or on high ground—wherever the Arahants dwell, that place is delightful.
“Pahiṇeyyāsī” means you should send. “The Teacher desires to see the venerable ones” means [he desires to see] those bhikkhus.

The demonstration of the manner of sending away. Thus, seeing that the purpose for which the Blessed One had sent those bhikkhus had reached its consummation, he became joyful in heart and informed the Elder of their desire to see him. For this was his thought:
"I shall send these away for making loud noises and great clamor; then they will be like noble thoroughbred horses struck by a whip."
"Urged by him, they will attain a sense of spiritual urgency; having entered the forest for the sake of pleasing me, and striving with diligence, they will soon realize Arahantship.
Now, seeing that they had attained the supreme fruit, his heart was gladdened by their attainment of Arahantship, and desiring to see them, he thus commanded the Treasurer of the Dhamma:
"Thus, O monks"—this was addressed by the Elder Ānanda to a certain monk endowed with the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiñña). "In front" means in his presence.

"By means of imperturbable concentration" (āneñjasamādhinā) refers to the concentration of the supreme fruit (aggaphala) based on the fourth jhāna; some also say it is based on the formless jhānas (arūpajjhāna).
There is also a reading: "by means of immovable concentration" (āneñjena samādhinā). But why did the Blessed One [wait for] the arrival of those monks?
Did he enter meditative attainment without offering a welcome despite knowing [their arrival]? It was for the purpose of entering the same attainment as those who had already entered it;
for the purpose of showing that he now shares the same enjoyments with those who were previously dismissed; for the purpose of manifesting his power;
and for the purpose of demonstrating a way of answering others without uttering a word. Others, however, say: "Previously..."
“In order to perform a hospitality that is not shared by others, by producing unsurpassed happiness for those who have been sent away and have now returned to his presence.
Those venerable ones, having understood the Blessed One’s intention, entered into that very attainment. Therefore it was said:
“In what dwelling, indeed, does the Blessed One dwell at present? and so forth.

And here, because the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere is very far removed from such obstructive states as indolence, and because it is endowed with the sixteen factors of purification—beginning with non-slouching—which are the roots of psychic power, it has reached imperturbability;
thus, in the sense of being itself unshakable, it is called "imperturbable" (*āneñja*). For this has been said:
“A mind that is not depressed does not waver in sloth; thus it is imperturbable (*āneñja*). A mind that is not elated does not waver in agitation;
thus it is imperturbable. A mind that is not delighted does not waver in lust; thus it is imperturbable. A mind that is not repelled does not waver in ill-will;
thus it is imperturbable. A mind that is independent does not waver in views; thus it is imperturbable. A mind that is unattached...”
It is "unshakable" (āneñja) because it does not waver in the face of desire and lust. It is unshakable because the liberated mind does not waver in the face of sensual passion.

It is unshakable because the disjoined mind does not waver in the face of the defilements. It is unshakable because the mind that has broken down its barriers does not waver in the face of the barriers of the defilements.
It is unshakable because the mind that has attained unity does not waver in the face of the diversity of defilements. [This is] through faith...
A mind embraced by faith does not waver in lack of faith; thus it is "unwavering" (*āneñja*).
A mind embraced by energy does not waver in laziness; thus it is "unwavering. A mind embraced by mindfulness does not waver in negligence; thus it is "unwavering.
A mind embraced by concentration does not waver in agitation; thus it is "unwavering. [A mind] embraced by wisdom...
"The mind does not waver because of ignorance; thus it is 'imperturbable' (āneñja). The mind that has reached illumination does not waver in the darkness of ignorance;

thus it is 'imperturbable. Only the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), when practiced by way of the development of dispassion toward matter, and the fourfold immaterial-sphere jhāna (arūpāvacara) distinguished by their objects—these five jhānas receive the designation "imperturbable. Of these, that which...
The ancients say that the attainment of the fruit of arahantship, having made something its basis, is "imperturbable concentration" (*āneñjasamādhi*).
"When it had passed" means when it was past. "When it had departed" means gone out; the meaning is "departed.
"He became silent" means the Blessed One became silent with noble silence. "When the dawn had risen" means when the dawn had broken; "dawn" refers to [the light] in the eastern direction.
The light that has arisen is prior even to the rising of the sun. "Nandimukhiyā" means:
because the dawn of the night has broken, the night—as if its face were made joyful by the radiance of the dawn which brings joy to beings who subsist on the light of the sun—has become bright;
this is the meaning.
"Having emerged from that concentration" means having arisen from that unshakable concentration, which is the attainment of the fruit of arahantship, according to its predetermined limit.
"If you, Ānanda, were to know" means, O Bhagavā, if you, Ānanda, were to know: "These bhikkhus have spent this much time in this kind of bliss of meditative attainment. Even this much...

“They would not have occurred to you” refers to worldly greetings; that is to say, even that inspired speech of yours which arose three times in the form of “The night has passed, venerable sir,” and so forth—this would not have occurred to you.
And because you, Ānanda, are still in training (*sekha*) and do not know the attainment-dwelling of one beyond training (*asekha*), therefore [I said this] to me...
He made an effort to exchange worldly greetings with these monks.

But the Blessed One said, "Ānanda, both I and these five hundred monks sat down together in unshakable concentration (āneñjasamādhi)," showing that he spent the entire three watches of the night exchanging only supramundane greetings with these monks.
"Having understood this matter": having understood in every aspect this state of mastery, which consists in those bhikkhus' own capacity to attain immovable concentration equal to his own.
"He uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*)": he uttered this *udāna* which illuminates the essential nature of those bhikkhus' complete abandonment of passion and the other defilements.
In that context, "for whom the thorn of sensual desire is conquered": sensual desire as a defilement is like a thorn in the sense that it pierces the side of what is wholesome.
By the noble person (*ariyapuggala*) who has conquered and abandoned it without remainder, he demonstrates the absence of attachment (*anunaya*).

There is also a reading, “*gāmakaṇṭako*. Its meaning is: for whom the entire sensual desire for the basis of existence (*vatthukāma*), which is like a thorn in a village—a source of irritation—is conquered.

And this victory should be understood as occurring precisely through the abandonment of the desire and lust (*chandarāga*) bound to that [sensual desire]; by this, the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*) is stated.
"...there is. 'Insult is conquered'—this is the connection. 'Killing and bondage'—here too the same method applies.
Among these, by the conquest of insult, the absence of verbal misconduct is shown; by the other [conquests], the absence of bodily misconduct is shown.

By that, through the complete abandonment of ill will (*vyāpāda*) caused by those [misconducts], the third path is stated. Alternatively, by the statement regarding the conquest of insults and so forth..."
The third path has been stated; therein, the absolute forbearance toward abuse and the like is explained.
Thus, in both ways, he demonstrates their lack of contradiction. He stands immovable like a mountain: "ejā" refers to the obstacle of restless defilements (*kilesa*);

because of the absence of the remaining defilements that are the causes of *ejā*, he is "unshaken" (*aneja*). Precisely because of this unshakeability, from all defilements and from the winds of opposing doctrines...

And because of his unshakability, he stands like a solid, single mass of rock. "That bhikkhu does not tremble in pleasure or pain"—the meaning of this phrase, "that bhikkhu who has destroyed the defilements does not waver at the sign of pleasure or pain," should be understood in the same manner as explained below.
Thus, by means of the attainment of Arahantship, the Blessed One [described] the arrival at the state of equanimity (*tādibhāva*) for those five hundred bhikkhus.
Having brought them together, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) concerning a single individual.
The commentary on the third sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta.
24. "Having established mindfulness facing the front" means having placed mindfulness directed toward the object, having brought it near to the face. For thus it is said in the *Vibhaṅga*:
"This mindfulness is established, well-established, either at the tip of the nose or on the sign of the mouth; therefore it is said, 'having established mindfulness facing the front.
Alternatively: "The prefix *pari-* has the sense of embracing (*pariggaha*); *mukha* has the sense of outlet (*niyyāna*); *sati* has the sense of establishment (*upaṭṭhāna*); therefore it is said..."
‘Mindfulness facing the face. Thus the meaning here should be understood according to the method stated in the *Paṭisambhidā*.
In brief, the meaning is this: “having established mindfulness that has discerned the way out.
And “the way out” (niyyāna) should be seen as the object to be penetrated by mindfulness. Here, the first and the last meanings are inclusive of all [aspects], while the other...
It should be understood by way of the preliminary mental application (*pubbabhāga-samannāhāra*) to the attainment (*samāpatti*).

Alternatively, "mindfulness" (*sati*) is stated as a designation for the jhāna, as in such passages as, "those who enjoy mindfulness directed to the body" (*kāyagatāsati*). But what is that jhāna? It is the jhāna of the fruit of Arahantship attained by taking the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) as its basis.
How, then, is this to be known? By means of its association with imperturbable concentration (*āneñja-samādhi*).
The Blessed One uttered this *udāna* while illustrating with the simile of a mountain the Elder’s exceptional state of immovability and his unshakability by anything;

this meaning is understood from the verse itself. Furthermore, this sitting was not for the sake of the Elder’s penetration of the Truth (*sacca*), but rather for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*).
For previously, at the Sūkarakhatā Cave, [the Buddha had already taught] his own nephew...
While the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the wanderer Dīghanakha, this Great Elder brought the task of penetrating the Truths to its ultimate conclusion.

"Having understood this matter"—that is, having understood in every aspect the meaning characterized by being unshakable by anything due to the Elder’s attainment of the state of suchness (*tādibhāva*) through the power of imperturbable concentration (*āneñjasamādhi*)—"he uttered this *udāna* (inspired utterance) to elucidate that meaning.
In that context, 'just as a mountain of rock' means just as a mountain consisting of solid rock, a single mass of stone, and not a mountain of loose earth."
The meaning is "not a mountain of mixed [elements]. "Immovable and well-established" means that its roots are firmly established; it is immovable and unshakable by natural winds.
Thus, through the destruction of delusion, the bhikkhu does not waver like a mountain.
This means that because all unwholesome states have their root in delusion, the bhikkhu who has abandoned all unwholesome states—just as that mountain [is unshaken] by natural winds—does not tremble.
Thus, he does not waver or tremble because of the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*).

Since "the destruction of delusion" (*mohakkhaya*) refers both to Nibbāna and to Arahantship, the intended meaning is that—because of having attained Nibbāna or Arahantship, which are the causes for the destruction of delusion—one is well-established in the Four Noble Truths;
even at a time when one has not yet entered meditative absorption, one does not waver due to anything, just like the aforementioned mountain, let alone at a time when one has entered absorption.
The commentary on the fourth sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Mahāmoggallāna Sutta: 25.

In the fifth [sutta], "by means of mindfulness directed to the body" means by means of mindfulness that has gone to the body—that is, mindfulness having the body as its object—by way of the contemplation of the body.
This is an instrumental expression used in the sense of a characteristic of a state already attained (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇe*). "Internal" (*ajjhatta*): here, "internal" means one's own internal;

therefore, the meaning is "in oneself" or "in one's own continuity. Alternatively, since the collection of thirty-two parts beginning with head-hairs, which constitutes the meditation subject, is intended here as the "body," the meaning of the word "internal" should be understood as "internal as an object" (*gocarajjhatta*).

"By being well-established" means by being well-established in the body, which constitutes either one's own internal domain (*niyakajjhatta*) or the objective domain (*gocarajjhatta*). What, then, is this mindfulness that is said to be "well-established internally"?

It is the attention directed toward repulsiveness regarding that body consisting of the thirty-two aspects—beginning with head-hairs and body-hairs—which was described by the Blessed One as follows: "In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs... and so forth. In that regard, [it is the mindfulness] through the application of attention to repulsiveness...
The mindfulness established in the body through the development of access and absorption concentration is called "mindfulness directed to the body" (*kāyagatā sati*).
Just as this is so, so too, for one who applies attention by way of mindfulness of breathing, the four postures, and clear comprehension, or by way of the bloated, the livid, and so forth,
the mindfulness established in the body through access and absorption concentration as appropriate is "mindfulness directed to the body."

It is called "mindfulness. Here, however, "mindfulness directed to the body" (kāyagatā sati) is intended to mean the mindfulness associated with insight (vipassanā) that has been established by defining, through any one of the various modes—such as the brief summary of the constituent parts—the four elements beginning with earth within the internal body, by means of observing their characteristics such as impermanence. But the Elder [said] thus...
Having practiced insight, he sat down after entering into the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) himself.
Here too, the meaning of this verse should be understood according to the method stated in the passage beginning with "And this sitting," and so forth.
"This matter" refers to the Elder’s establishment of mindfulness through the contemplation of the body by way of the analysis of the four elements (catudhātuvavatthāna).
Having plunged into insight (vipassanā) and having realized the goal known as the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna).
This inspired utterance reveals the attainment of Nibbāna through the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna).
Therein, "mindfulness directed to the body is established" refers to the mindfulness previously defined, which is preceded by faith and accompanied by concentration, energy, and wisdom.
Because they have attained the state of being companions by accomplishing their respective functions, and because their opposites have been abandoned, they—

having become sharp and clear, and having approached and remained while discerning the unerring nature through the aforementioned restraint of the body and through their convergence on a single purpose—
[serve] for the four elements known as the body and for the derived matter (upādārūpa) dependent upon them.

Having defined the conditions by way of their specific characteristics, he shows the succession of knowledge that proceeds by way of discerning the characteristics of impermanence and so forth in those [conditions], which is [itself] mindfulness;
or, under the heading of "mindfulness," he shows the very succession of knowledge associated with it that is included within the threefold full understanding (*pariññā*).
"Restrained in the six bases of contact" means being endowed with the mindfulness established in the body as previously described.
Regarding the six doors consisting of the eye and so forth, which serve as the causes for contact:

when bodily contemplation has not been developed, covetousness and other such states are liable to arise; but because that [contemplation] has been developed, one who realizes the occurrence of knowledge while closing those [doors] is said to be "restrained therein.
By this, he demonstrates the restraint of knowledge (*ñāṇasaṃvara*).
"A bhikkhu who is constantly concentrated": that bhikkhu, with mindfulness thus established and restrained in every way,
not casting his mind toward diverse objects, but comprehending by way of impermanence and so forth, and having brought insight to its peak, while knowledge is sharp, keen, and flowing,
is "constantly and continuously concentrated" by means of insight-concentration (vipassanā-samādhi) until, immediately after the knowledge of conformity (anuloma-ñāṇa), [the path arises].
From the moment the knowledge of the lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) arises, one should know Nibbāna as "the self" because it is not within the range even of dreams for other worldlings (puthujjana),
and because it is the exclusive domain of the noble ones (ariya)— being like their own selves—
and because it is the preeminent object of the knowledge of the path and fruit which has acquired the conventional designation "self. Thus, Nibbāna brings absolute happiness.
“The unconditioned element is called ‘one’s own’; one should know that, which is Nibbāna—one should understand it, penetrate it through the knowledge of the path and the fruit, and realize it.
This is the meaning. By this, he shows the Noble Ones’ inclination toward Nibbāna.

For the Noble Ones, even at the time of the activity of higher consciousness (*adhicitta*), dwell with a state of being exclusively inclined, leaning, and tending toward Nibbāna. And herein, for whom mindfulness is directed toward the body...
The connection between the lines of this verse should be understood as follows: "Being established [in mindfulness], that bhikkhu is restrained in the six bases of contact;
therefore, being constantly concentrated, he shall know Nibbāna for himself by means of personal realization.
In this way, the King of Dhamma shows the path of deliverance leading up to Arahantship for a single bhikkhu, by way of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body.
Another method: by the phrase "mindfulness established as directed toward the body," he shows the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body.
"Restrained in the six bases of contact" (*phassāyatanesu saṃvuto*): those for which contact is the base, that is, the cause, are the "bases of contact"; [he is restrained] in those bases of contact.
That is, in the six types of experienced feeling born of eye-contact and so forth, which have contact as their cause and are produced with contact as their condition.
"Restrained by the non-occurrence of craving and the rest"—by this he shows the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of feelings.
"The bhikkhu is constantly concentrated": the bhikkhu is constantly, at all times, and uninterruptedly concentrated due to the absence of distraction.
And this non-distraction occurs when the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness has reached its ultimate consummation. Contemplating...
For he comprehends by way of full inclusion the five aggregates of clinging, which are divided into the distinctions of past and so forth.
By this, he shows the remaining foundations of mindfulness. "One should know:

'I am merely Nibbāna'"—thus, having brought the development of the four foundations of mindfulness to its culmination, the bhikkhu whose defilements are destroyed reflects upon his own Nibbāna of defilements through the knowledge of reviewing.
The meaning is: "one should know for oneself.

Alternatively, by stating that mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatā sati*) is established, the Elder’s attainment of perfection in mindfulness is illustrated through the demonstration of his thorough understanding (*pariññā*) of the true nature of his own and others' bodies.
"Restrained in the six bases of contact" refers to the six [bases] beginning with the eye.

By demonstrating absolute restraint at the doors [of the senses], the Elder’s attainment of the abundance of wisdom—which manifests clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) through his mode of constant abiding—is illustrated.

With the phrase "The bhikkhu is constantly concentrated," the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling (*anupubbavihārasamāpatti*) are shown by way of demonstrating his great frequency of attaining them.
Furthermore, such a bhikkhu "should know Nibbāna alone" because he has performed his duty and there is nothing further to be done.
The intention is that he should know and contemplate only his own *nibbāna* without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*), and there is nothing else for him to contemplate.
The commentary on the fifth sutta is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Pilindavaccha Sutta.
26. Regarding the sixth [case], "Pilindavaccha": Pilinda is the name of Atissa, while "Vaccha" is how they recognize the Thera by way of his clan (gotta).
"He addresses them with the word 'outcaste'" means that he speaks to and addresses the monks with the term "outcaste," saying such things as, "Come, outcaste! Go away, outcaste!
"A number of monks" means many monks. They [addressed] the Thera as he was thus addressing them.

Seeing this, and not knowing that "even though he is an arahant, he speaks thus because his latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not yet been abandoned," they thought, "I suspect this elder speaks in this way because of some inner malice.
With the intention of exposing him, they reported it to the Blessed One so as to have him removed from there.
Therefore it was said: "Venerable sir, the Venerable Pilindavaccha addresses the bhikkhus with the term 'outcaste' (*vasala*)."
But some say: "The monks perceive this elder as an 'Arahant,' yet they treat him in this way with harsh words.

Not knowing that such treatment was due to his latent disposition (*vāsana*)—thinking, 'Could it be that no superhuman quality (*uttarimanussadhamma*) exists in him?'—and lacking faith in his noble state, they reported this to the Blessed One with a sense of reproach."
“They reported that matter. Desiring to demonstrate the elder’s lack of internal ill-will, the Blessed One had a certain monk summoned and, in his presence, said to him:
“He behaves in this way toward you due to his former habituation; it is not with the intention of harsh speech.
Therefore it was said: “Then the Blessed One addressed a certain monk,” and so forth.
In that regard, having called to mind his former lives, the Teacher asked the Elder, "Is it true, Vaccha, that you address the bhikkhus with the word 'outcaste'?
When the Elder replied, "It is so, Bhante," he thought, "This Vaccha does not abandon the term 'outcaste' due to the latent tendencies of defilement;
was he perhaps born into the brahmin caste even in past existences?"

Reflecting by means of the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*) or the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), he brought to mind the continuity of aggregates (*khandhasantāna*) in which that person had dwelt in past births;

having brought it to mind for himself by way of making it directly present—like an *āmalaka* fruit placed in the palm of his hand—he addressed the bhikkhus. He spoke to those bhikkhus in order to inform them; he conversed with them. By that...
It is said: “Do not you, O bhikkhus,” and so forth.
Therein, *mā* is a particle used for prohibition; its connection is with the word *ujjhāyittha*.
“Do not *ujjhāyittha*” means do not think with contempt, that is, do not look down upon it. And [the phrase] “of the bhikkhu Vaccha” refers to the act of censuring.
The word "sampadāna" (recipient) is used because of the sense of envy. Now, showing the reason why he should not be disregarded, [the Buddha] said:
“Monks, this calf does not address the monks with the term ‘outcaste’ while harboring hatred within. Its meaning is as follows:
Monks, this calf, harboring hatred—that is, being possessed of a hateful mind, his mind defiled by malice—does not address the monks with the term “outcaste.”

It does not manifest; indeed, ill-will has been eradicated by the Path itself. Thus, even though he was free from hatred (*adosantara*), the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with "Monks, regarding the calf" in order to show the cause established in previous births for such a manifestation [of affection].
Therein, "uninterrupted" (*abbokiṇṇāni*) means not mixed with other castes such as the Khattiyas, being continuous. Five hundred births.
"Reborn in brahmin families" means that all those five hundred births of Vaccha occurred successively in brahmin families alone;

this is the meaning. "That speech of 'outcaste' was long practiced by him" means that this speech of "outcaste" uttered by the bhikkhu Vaccha—which continues even now, though he is one whose taints are destroyed—was practiced by him for a long time.
From this birth onwards, for a period of about five hundred births, he habitually and customarily behaved as a brahmin by virtue of his high status.
For brahmins, stiff with pride established by birth, treat others with the term "outcaste.
They also read the word as *ajjhāciṇṇo*, which has the same meaning. *Tena* means: by that [habitual behavior] over a long period of time in such a manner.
By the phrase "through the state of habitual practice" (*samudāciṇṇabhāvena*), he shows that the cause of such conduct is *vāsanā* (latent predisposition).

What, then, is this so-called *vāsanā*? It is a mere capacity deposited by defilements cultivated since beginningless time, which exists within the continuum even of one free from defilements and serves as the cause for conduct resembling the conduct of those with unabandoned defilements; they call it a "tendency toward such [conduct]."
Now, this [obscuration] exists in the mental continuum of disciples and paccekabuddhas in those instances where the defilements have not been abandoned in such a way;

however, because of the perfection of his resolve and the abandonment of the cognitive obscurations (*ñeyyāvaraṇa*), wherever the defilements have been abandoned, that [obscurations] does not exist in the Blessed One’s continuum.
Therefore, only the Tathāgata possesses unobstructed knowledge and vision (*anāvaraṇañāṇadassana*).
"Having understood this matter": having understood this matter—namely, that although the Venerable Pilindavaccha had been addressed as "outcaste," he was nonetheless devoid of internal hatred.
"He uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*)": he uttered this *udāna* which clarifies his attainment of the supreme fruit.
In that context, "in whom neither deceit nor pride dwells" refers to that noble person in whom there is no concealment of existing faults.
Neither illusion (*māyā*)—which functions through the mode of grasping as "I am superior" and so forth and is characterized by arrogance (*uṇṇati*)—nor conceit (*māna*) dwells there;

because it has been eradicated by the Path, it neither proceeds nor arises. Furthermore, he who is free from greed, without the sense of "mine," and without expectation is so because greed—which functions through its synonyms such as lust (*rāga*) and is characterized by the apprehension of an object—has entirely disappeared.

Free from greed (*vītalobho*), and for that very reason, because there is no sense of "mine" toward anything such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, he is without "mineness" (*amamo*) and without possessiveness (*apariggaho*);
because he has no longing even for future existences (*bhava*), he is without expectation (*nirāso*). With anger dispelled (*panuṇṇakodho*):

because anger, which is characterized by being prone to wrath, has been entirely abandoned through the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*), his anger is dispelled and his malice (*aghāta*) is utterly cut off. As for "being extinguished" (*abhinibbutatto*): this refers to one who, in this way, [is free from] deceit, pride, greed, and anger...

Because all factors on the side of defilement have been thoroughly abandoned through their eradication and the removal of those associated with them, his mind is completely extinguished by the final nibbāna of the defilements;
he has become cooled. Such a one is a brahmin, such a one is a recluse, such a one is a bhikkhu.
He is a brahmin because he has entirely banished evil; he is a recluse (*samaṇa*) because he has stilled evil and because of his even conduct; he is likewise [a bhikkhu].
And because his defilements have been entirely destroyed, he is called a "bhikkhu. Being such as this, O monks, how could that Vaccha engage in any bodily action or the like with internal hatred?
Rather, it is solely because the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not yet been abandoned that he addresses him with the term "outcaste" (*vasala*).
The commentary on the sixth sutta is concluded.
7. Commentary on the Sakkudāna Sutta. 27.
Regarding the statement, "For seven days he remained seated in one cross-legged posture, having attained a certain concentration," some first say:
"The concentration of the fruit of arahantship is intended here by the phrase 'a certain concentration.'"

For that venerable one frequently enters that attainment for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life, and he is able to spend even seven days in the attainment of fruition. Thus it was said by the Blessed One:

"Bhikkhus, as long as I wish, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states... I dwell [in the first jhāna]. Kassapa too, bhikkhus, as long as he wishes, secluded from sensual pleasures... dwells [in the first jhāna]."
By the word "etcetera," he is placed in a position equal to himself among the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) distinguished by the nine successive dwellings,

the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā), and so forth; nor should it be said here, "If that were so, the Elder would have performed even the Twin Miracle," because what is intended are only the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and other qualities shared with disciples.
The Ancients, however, said: "Having attained a certain concentration" means having attained the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
But how is the attainment of cessation called "concentration"? In the sense of being composed (*samādhāna*).

What, then, is this sense of being composed? It is the state of being properly composed. For that which is unshakable by contrary states due to the attainment of strength is the power of serenity (*samathabala*).
"Insight power" refers to these two powers: by means of the sixteen modes of knowledge— namely,

the four path-knowledges and the four fruition-knowledges consisting of the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, non-self, disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, relinquishment, and turning away—
and by taking together as one the eight types of concentration beginning with the first jhāna-concentration, these [are included].
By means of these nine types of concentration— including access concentration—
one who desires to dwell thus through the subsiding of the three formations— namely, the bodily formation, the verbal formation, and the mental formation—
by way of these nine modes of practice in concentration, must be an Arahant or a Non-returner who has attained mastery in the aforementioned states.
The meaning of "concentration" (*samādhāna*) here refers to the proper non-occurrence of the continuum of consciousness and mental factors for as long as intended;
it is because this [continuum] must be concentrated in that way that this abiding is called "concentration," not in the sense of non-distraction (*avikkhepa*).

By this, it should be understood that its meaning of "attainment" (*samāpatti*) is also expressed. For, with reference to this attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is said in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*:

“‘How is there knowledge of the attainment of the cessation of perception through the subsiding of the three formations by means of being endowed with two powers, through sixteen modes of knowledge-conduct, and through mastery over nine modes of concentration-conduct?
Having thus asked, [the answer is given: ‘By two powers’—that is, the power of serenity (*samatha*) and the power of insight (*vipassanā*), in detail.
This discussion of the attainment of cessation has indeed already been explained in the *Visuddhimagga*. But why did this Elder [not attain] the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*)?
Did he enter cessation without first entering the other attainments? Out of compassion for sentient beings.
For this great elder makes use of all the attainments, yet for the sake of benefiting beings, he mostly enters cessation.
This is because for one who has emerged from that attainment, even a small act of honor becomes especially fruitful and of great benefit.

"He emerged" means he emerged through the arising of the consciousness of the fruit of Arahantship. For when an Arahant who has attained cessation emerges by the arising of the fruit of Arahantship, or a Non-returner by the arising of the fruit of Non-returning, he is said to have "emerged.
Now, at that time, Sakka, the lord of the devas, desired to give almsfood to the Venerable Mahākassapa.
How did this desire to give arise in him? It was those "five hundred deities" who were mentioned.
Those female attendants of Sakka, the king of the gods, who had previously been sent by Sakka with the instruction, “The venerable Mahākassapa is entering Rājagaha for alms;
go and give an offering to the Elder,” approached him desiring to give divine food.
Having been refused by the Elder, they returned to the world of the gods. Now, reflecting upon that previous refusal, they [approached again].
“Perhaps he might accept it”: wishing to give alms to the Elder who had emerged from meditative attainment, they came of their own accord without informing Sakka and presented divine foods;
being refused by the Elder in the same manner as before, they returned to the world of the gods and, when asked by Sakka, “Where have you been?
they reported the matter to him, saying, “The alms-food was given to the Elder by you.”
When Sakka said, "He does not wish to accept it," [the Elder] asked, "What did he say? "He said, 'O gods, I shall provide for those who are ill-fated,'" [Sakka replied].
"In what manner did you go there? "In this very manner, O gods. Sakka asked, "How could someone like you give alms-food to an elder?
[The Elder replied,] "I myself wished to give; I am worn out by old age, with broken teeth, gray hair, and a stooped body."
Having become an old weaver, Sakka likewise made Sujā, the daughter of the Asuras, an old woman;
he established a weavers’ street and sat spinning thread, while Sujā filled the shuttle. Thus it was said:
“At that time, Sakka, lord of the devas... [and so on] ... Sujā filled the shuttle.”
Therein, "he weaves the warp" means he is like one weaving outstretched threads. "He fills the shuttle" means as if increasing the shuttle-rod.

"He approached the residence of Sakka, lord of the devas" means that the Elder, having dressed himself and taken his bowl and robe, was walking toward the city with the thought, "I shall provide for the poor," when, outside the city—

Having entered the weavers’ street built by Sakka and looking about, he saw a dilapidated and ruined old hall, and there he saw that husband and wife working at their weaving in the manner previously described. Seeing them, he thought:
"They are still working even at this advanced age. I imagine there are none more destitute in this city than these two. By means of these [two],...
“Having taken even a small amount of vegetables that have been given, I shall provide for these people.
He set out toward their house. Seeing him approaching, Sakka said to Sujā: “My lady, my master is coming this way;
sit there in silence as if you did not see him. We shall deceive him in an instant and give him alms-food. Thus spoke the Elder.
Having gone there, he stood at the door of the house. They, as if not seeing him, continued with their own work and waited for a short while.
Then Sakka said, "There appears to be an elder standing at the door; go and look for him. "Master, you yourself should go and look," they replied.
He went out from the house, prostrated himself before the elder with the fivefold greeting, and said:
Supporting himself on his knees with both hands and groaning, he stood up and asked, "Which elder is this, noble sir?
Stepping back a little, he said, "My eyes are smoking," and placing his hand on his forehead, he looked upward and thought, "Alas, what suffering!
Noble sir, it must be the Elder Mahākassapa; it has been a long time since he last came to the door of my hut. Is there perhaps..."
“Is there anything in the house? he asked. Sujā, appearing somewhat distressed, replied, “There is, Master.
Sakka said, “Venerable sir, do not consider whether it is coarse or refined; please show us favor,” and he took the bowl.
As the Elder gave him the bowl, he thought, “I must show favor to these very people who are poor and worn out by old age.”
Thus, having entered within, he drew out what is called "pot-rice" (ghaṭiodana)—rice that had been prepared in a pot—and filling his bowl, he placed it in the Elder’s hand.
Therefore it is said: “Sakka, lord of the devas, saw... [and so on]... and gave it.
Therein, *ghaṭiya* means prepared in a food-pot (*bhattaghaṭita*). There is also the reading *ghaṭiodana*; regarding that, *ghaṭiodana* refers to the rice of the devas.
Some say the meaning is "a particular kind of food. "Having taken out" means having taken it out from some vessel.
That very food, though consisting of many soups, appeared like the coarse food that suffices for the poor at the time when it was placed in the Elder’s hand after being put into his bowl;
but as soon as it was placed in his hand, it remained by its own divine nature. "Consisting of many soups" means...

"Various soups" refers to soups made from green gram, black gram, and so forth, as well as various kinds of snacks. "Various condiments" means diverse types of *uttaribhaṅga* (curries or side dishes).
"Condiments of many flavors" means that which manifests the sweet and other primary tastes, as well as blended flavors, through numerous soups and condiments;
the meaning is "condiments and soups of various excellent flavors."
It is said that when the alms-food was placed in the Elder’s hand, the city of Rājagaha was completely overwhelmed by its own divine fragrance.
Then the Elder thought: “This man is of little power, yet this alms-food is exceedingly refined, like the food of Sakka.
Who could this be? Having realized it was Sakka, he said: “This is a heavy burden.”

“Kosiya, you have performed a deed that robs those in misfortune of their prosperity; by giving this gift to me today, some person in misfortune might even obtain the position of general or the position of a wealthy merchant.
“Who, venerable sir, is more miserable than I? “How can you be miserable while experiencing the glory of divine sovereignty? “Venerable sir, it is thus:”
"This is not it; however, when a Buddha had not yet appeared, I performed wholesome deeds, and while the appearance of a Buddha was currently taking place, I performed meritorious deeds.

Consequently, three sons of gods—Cūḷaratha-devaputta, Mahāratha-devaputta, and Anekavaṇṇa-devaputta—were reborn in a place near me, possessing even greater majesty than I. Among those sons of gods, I..."
“‘We shall play at the festival of the constellations,’ thinking thus, I would take my female attendants and descend into the middle of the street; then, fleeing, I would enter my house.
For the heat from their bodies overwhelms my body, while the heat from my body does not overwhelm theirs.
Who, venerable sir, is more wretched than I? “Even so, from this point forward—”
“Do not deceive me thus by giving alms,” he said. “If you have deceived me and given alms to you, is there merit for me or not?

“There is, friend. “If that is so, venerable sir, the performance of merit is my burden,” he said, and having paid homage to the Elder, he took the hall, circumambulated the Elder, and rose up into the air.
“O, what a gift! What a supreme gift! Well-established in Kassapa!”—thus he uttered this inspired exclamation three times.
Therefore it is said: “Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahākassapa,” and so forth.
In that context, “Kosiya” is an address to Sakka, the lord of the devas, by way of his clan name. “Puññena attho” means having a need for merit.
The word “is” (*atthi*) is understood as the remainder of the sentence. “Having ascended into the air” (*vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā*) means having risen up from the earth into the air.
“In the sky, in the atmosphere” (*ākāse antalikkhe*): they say that *ākāsa* itself is expressed by the synonymous term *antalikkha*.

Alternatively, he speaks thus to specify that it is the sky known as the *antalikkha*, and not the space cleared by a *kasiṇa* or other such [meditative objects]. “Oh, the gift!”—here, “oh” (*aho*) is used in the sense of wonder.

This is a particle of emphasis. For Sakka, lord of the devas, [thought]: "Since this divine gift of food was given by me—preceded by right view—at the proper time, respectfully with my own hands, having honored the Venerable Elder Mahākassapa who had emerged from cessation, not casting it aside and without harming others;
therefore, there is perfection of the field and perfection of the object of offering."
Regarding "perfection of mind": because he was endowed with all three kinds of perfection, he thought, "Oh, a gift complete in every respect has been bestowed by me!
At that moment, giving voice to the joy and gladness within his heart, he exclaimed, "O, what a gift!
and [recognized] that gift’s status as a supreme gift and its status as having reached a worthy field, according to the method already described.
Proclaiming this, he uttered the inspired utterance: “The supreme gift is well-established in Kassapa.
As Sakka was thus uttering this inspired utterance, the Blessed One, standing right there in his dwelling, heard the sound with his divine ear and said to the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, behold Sakka, lord of the devas, as he proceeds through the air after uttering this inspired utterance!”
When they asked him, "But what, venerable sir, did he do?", he replied, "He deceived my son Kassapa and gave a gift;
and being pleased by that, he uttered an exclamation. Thus it was said: "The Blessed One heard with his divine ear-element," and so forth.
In this context, "with his divine ear-element" means it is called "divine" because it resembles the [hearing] of the devas. For it is produced by the well-performed karma of the devas.
The divine ear-element (*dibba-sotadhātu*), being unobstructed by bile, phlegm, blood, and so forth, and being free from defilements, is capable of grasping an object even at a distance.
This ear-element of the Blessed One, produced by the power of the cultivation of energy and consisting of knowledge, is exactly like that;
thus, it is called "divine" because it resembles the divine. Furthermore, it is called "divine" because it is obtained through the practice of the divine abidings (*dibba-vihāra*).
It is "divine" (*dibba*) because it is based on a divine abiding (*dibbavihāra*).

It is the "ear-element" (*sotadhātu*) in the sense of hearing and in the sense of maintaining its own nature; and because it performs the function of the ear-element, it is like the ear-element itself—thus, "by means of that divine ear-element.
"Purified" (*visuddhā*) means completely cleansed and free from defilements. "Transcending the human" (*atikkantamānusikā*) refers to [the range] beyond the human sphere.
"Having transcended" means having transcended the human faculty of hearing by means of hearing sounds.

"Knowing this matter": knowing that "even gods and humans, filled with reverence, greatly yearn for a superior person established in the specific virtues of right practice," he uttered this *udāna* which illustrates that meaning.
Therein, "of one who lives on alms-food" refers to one who has undertaken the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) known as the alms-gathering practice and has fulfilled it.
But surely this verse was spoken with the Venerable Mahākassapa as its specific reference;

and since the Elder is the foremost of all those who advocate the ascetic practices (*dhutavāda*) and the bearer of thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), why is he praised here by means of only one ascetic practice?

This exposition is given by way of the occasion for the teaching (*aṭṭhuppatti*). Alternatively, this is merely a sample of the teaching; under this heading of the teaching, all his ascetic practices are indeed stated.

It should be understood. Alternatively, it is said "of one who lives on alms-food" (piṇḍapātikassa) in order to demonstrate his preeminent practice therein—having remained unbroken in every duty of an alms-collector through supreme fewness of wishes and compassion for families—in accordance with the method stated in the verse beginning, "Just as a bee from a flower.
And the word "of one who lives on alms-food" (piṇḍapātikassa) is used in relation to the word "they desire" (pihayanti).
The word *sampadāna* (recipient) should be understood here in the sense of "utilization. *Attābharassa*:
for one who supports only oneself with the four requisites that are described as being "few, easily obtained, and blameless.
*Añaññaposino*: not supporting others, because of having no desire to support other disciples and so forth by means of gathering material goods.

By means of these two lines, he demonstrates his light livelihood, easy maintenance, and supreme contentment, as he wanders about with a robe that merely suffices for his body and almsfood that merely suffices for his belly. Alternatively, through the singular number in the word *attabharassa*,
it means that he maintains this one self known as the individual existence (*attabhāva*) alone, and nothing beyond this.
"Self-supporting" (*attabharo*); and for that very reason, because there is no other to be supported by him, he is "not supporting others" (*anaññaposī*).
By these two phrases, he demonstrates through the state of having exhausted the taints (*khīṇāsava*) his non-clinging in the future.
"The gods envy... [the mindful one]"—by the attainment of the supreme fruit, [he is free] from all the distress and fever of the defilements.

The gods, such as Sakka and others, long for and yearn for one who is tranquil through subsiding and pacification, who is mindful due to constant mindfulness and the attainment of fullness of mindfulness,
