Furthermore, he may be naturally weak, or overcome by illness and old age, such that when putting on a heavy robe, he becomes exhausted.
Having exchanged that [robe] with a monk of similar standing, even while making do with something light, he remains content;
this is his contentment regarding robes according to his strength. Another, having obtained a costly robe such as one made of fine cloth (*paṭṭacīvara*) or the like, thinks:
"This is for the elders who have long been gone forth; this is suitable for those of great learning; this is for the sick."
Thinking, "Let this be for those who are weak, or for those who have little gain," he gives it to them;
and even when he himself gathers rags from rubbish heaps and so forth to make a robe, or takes their old robes to wear,
he remains content— this is his contentment with robes as they happen to be suitable.
Furthermore, here a bhikkhu receives almsfood, whether coarse or refined; he sustains himself with that alone and does not long for anything else.
Even if he obtains other food, he does not accept it. This is his contentment with whatever almsfood is obtained.
Then, however, he becomes ill; having eaten almsfood that is coarse, or naturally incompatible, or contrary to his illness—

He falls into severe illness; yet, having given that almsfood to a bhikkhu of similar standing and having eaten suitable food from his hand, he remains content even while practicing the duty of a recluse. This is his contentment with almsfood according to his strength.
Another bhikkhu receives exquisite almsfood; he thinks, "This almsfood is suitable for those who have been long gone forth," etc.
Whether he gives them his own robe, takes what belongs to them, goes for alms himself, or partakes of mixed food, he remains content.
This is his contentment with almsfood as is appropriate.
Furthermore, whatever lodging a bhikkhu obtains—whether pleasant or unpleasant, even if it is merely a grass hut—[he remains content].
Even if he receives only a grass mat, he is content with that; yet if he later obtains something more beautiful, he does not take it—this is his contentment with whatever lodging is obtained.
Furthermore, if he becomes ill or weak, and he receives a lodging that is contrary to his illness or contrary to his constitution, such that while living there...

He becomes uncomfortable; yet, having given that [lodging] to a bhikkhu of similar standing and staying in a suitable dwelling belonging to him while practicing the ascetic’s duty, he remains contented.
This is his contentment with lodging according to his strength.
Another, even when obtaining a beautiful lodging, does not accept it, thinking, "Luxurious lodgings are a basis for negligence," due to his great merit.
Or he may obtain excellent lodgings such as caves, pavilions, or gabled houses;
having given these away like robes and other requisites to those who have long been ordained and others, he remains content wherever he dwells—this is his contentment with a suitable lodging.
Furthermore, in this case, a bhikkhu receives medicine, whether coarse or refined, and he is satisfied with that alone, not seeking another.
He does not crave for it, and even if he obtains it, he does not take it; this is his contentment with whatever is obtained regarding the requisite of medicine.

Furthermore, if one who needs oil obtains molasses, he gives that to a fellow monk, takes oil from his hand, prepares medicine, and while practicing the duty of a recluse, he remains truly content; this is his...
Contentment with whatever medicinal requisites one receives according to one’s strength. Another person of great merit obtains abundant high-quality medicines such as oil, honey, and molasses;

yet, having given these away like robes and other requisites to those who have been ordained for a long time and others, he remains content even when preparing his own medicine from whatever is brought back by them.
Furthermore, if there is gall-nut (*muttaharītaka*) in one vessel and...
When told, "Set aside the four sweets; take whatever you wish, venerable sir," if his illness should be relieved even by one of those [other medicines], he should reflect on the words:
"The 'urine-harītaka' is praised by the Buddha and others; the going-forth depends upon fermented urine as medicine;
therefore, you must exert yourself in that regard for as long as life lasts," and thus [reject] the four sweets.
Having refused [other medicines], one who prepares medicine with urine and harītaka is exceedingly content;
this is his contentment with what is suitable regarding the requisite of medicine.
All such varieties of contentment are called "contentment" (santuṭṭhi). Therefore it was said: "In meaning, it is contentment with the various requisites."

The "discourse on contentment" is a discourse that proceeds by way of demonstrating the benefits through the method of teaching and so forth along with contentment with whatever one has, and by way of demonstrating the dangers of being dominated by desire, which consists of such states as excessive greed—the opposite of that contentment.
This same method applies to the subsequent discourses as well; we shall mention only the specific differences.
Regarding the "discourse on seclusion": here there are three kinds of seclusion—seclusion of body, seclusion of mind, and seclusion from acquisitions (*upadhiviveka*).
Among these, one goes alone, one stands alone, one sits alone, one lies down alone;
one enters the village for alms alone, one returns alone, one advances alone, one undertakes the walking meditation alone, one wanders alone, and one dwells alone.
Thus, in all postures and in all activities, abandoning association with crowds and living in seclusion is called bodily seclusion (*kāyaviveka*).
The eight attainments (*samāpatti*), however, are called mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*). Nibbāna is called seclusion from the substrata (*upadhiviveka*). For it has been said:

"Bodily seclusion belongs to those who dwell secluded in body and delight in renunciation; mental seclusion belongs to those whose minds are purified and have attained supreme clarity; and seclusion from the substrata belongs to persons who are without substrata and have reached the unconditioned (*visaṅkhāra*)."
Seclusion itself is *paviveka*; talk connected with seclusion is "talk on seclusion.

Regarding "talk on non-association," there are five kinds of association here: association by hearing, association by seeing, association by conversing, association by sharing [possessions], and physical association. Among these, a certain monk here hears: "In such-and-such a village or town..."
Or, having heard that "there is a woman who is beautiful, lovely, pleasing, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion," he becomes dejected and dispirited;
he is unable to maintain the holy life, renounces the training, and returns to the lower life.
Thus, the intimacy of hearing consists in the association with defilements arising from hearing about an unsuitable object.

It is called [the first]. Furthermore, monk, it is not that he hears [of such a thing], but rather he himself sees a woman who is beautiful, lovely, pleasing, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion;

having seen her, he becomes despondent and discouraged, unable to maintain the holy life, and having renounced the training, he reverts to the lower state—thus, by seeing an object of a dissimilar nature.
The intimacy of defilements arising from seeing one another is called "contact through sight.

However, the intimacy of defilements arising through mutual conversation and chatter after having seen one another is called "contact through conversation. This also includes laughing together and so forth.
Furthermore, giving whatever belongs to oneself to a woman—whether she has given anything in return or not—such as forest-gathered fruits and the like, [constitutes contact].

The intimacy of defilements arising through the use of shared objects is called "association by enjoyment. The intimacy of defilements arising through holding a woman’s hand and so forth is called "physical contact. Furthermore, there is this:

"He dwells in association with householders, in an improper kind of association; he shares their sorrows and joys, being happy when they are happy and miserable when they are miserable; and when there are duties or tasks to be performed, he himself undertakes to carry them out."

When this has been said, having abandoned all such unwholesome association with householders, as well as any association even with fellow celibates that serves as a cause for the arising of defilements—
one should cultivate that which is a firmer sense of urgency regarding saṃsāra, a keen perception of fear toward conditioned formations (saṅkhāras),
a perception of repulsiveness toward the body, and a sense of shame and dread of blame (hirottappa) preceded by disgust for all unwholesome states.

"Mindfulness and clear comprehension in all activities" means that, having established [these qualities] in everything, one remains unattached in all circumstances like a water droplet on a lotus leaf;
this is "non-association" because it is the opposite of all forms of association. Discourse connected with that is "discourse on non-association."
Regarding the phrase "discourse on the arousal of energy" (*vīriyārambhakathā*): here, energy (*vīriya*) is either the state of a hero (*vīra*), or it is energy because it is an action;

or it is energy because it is that which should be impelled or set in motion according to the proper method. Furthermore, this "arousal of energy" (*vīriyārambha*) is the exertion for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states. This [energy] is twofold: physical and mental.

It is threefold as the element of initiative (*ārambha-dhātu*), the element of exertion (*nikkama-dhātu*), and the element of striving (*parakkama-dhātu*); it is fourfold by way of the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*).

All of this refers to that monk who does not allow a defilement arisen while walking to reach standing, nor one arisen while standing to reach sitting, nor one arisen while sitting to reach lying down, but [subdues it] right there on the spot like a calf with its tether.
Just as one who seizes a black snake after squeezing it with a stick, or as one striking an enemy in the neck with a sharp sword,
does not allow him to lift his head but suppresses him by the power of effort—
this is how it should be understood through the influence of one who has thus initiated energy. Discourse associated with that is "discourse on the initiation of energy."
Regarding the discourses on virtue and so forth, there are two kinds of virtue: mundane (*lokiya*) and supramundane (*lokuttara*).

Among these, the mundane consists of the fourfold purification of virtue, beginning with the restraint of the *pātimokkha*; the supramundane consists of the virtue of the path (*maggasīla*) and the virtue of the fruit (*phalasīla*).

Likewise, the mundane concentration (*samādhi*) comprises the eight attainments together with access concentration, which serve as the foundation for insight (*vipassanā*); whereas the supramundane concentration here is that associated with the path.

"Concentration" (samādhi) refers to this. Likewise, "wisdom" (paññā) includes both mundane wisdom consisting of what is heard (suta-maya), what is reflected upon (cintā-maya), that associated with meditative absorption (jhāna-sampayutta), and the knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa).

Specifically, however, it is the wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā) that should be understood here, as well as the supramundane wisdom of the path (magga-paññā) and the wisdom of the fruit (phala-paññā).

"Liberation" (vimutti) also refers to the liberation of the noble fruits (ariya-phala-vimutti) and Nibbāna. Others, moreover, [include] the liberations by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-vimutti), suppression (vikkhambhana-vimutti), and eradication (samuccheda-vimutti).
In this context, they explain the meaning by way of the "basis. The knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuttiñāṇadassana*) is also nineteenfold reflective knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*).

Thus, the discourse that proceeds by means of the method of demonstration and so forth regarding these [factors] beginning with virtue (*sīla*), through the manifestation of their manifold aspects and modes of benefit, and through the manifestation of the dangers of their opposites such as immorality (*dussīlya*), and which is connected therewith—
Or, "discourse" refers to discourse on virtue and so forth.

And here, because of such statements as, "He himself is of few desires and is a speaker of discourse on fewness of desires to others," and "He is content with any kind of robe and is a speaker in praise of contentment with any kind of robe," [it follows that] he himself...

Such discourse as is endowed with qualities such as fewness of wishes and is practiced with the aspiration for the welfare and benefit of others for that same purpose—this is what should be understood here as "discourse on fewness of wishes" and so forth, distinguished by its nature of being austere (*abhisallekhika*) and so on.
For it is specifically the discourse of the one who acts that accomplishes the intended goal. Thus he will say: "This is for one who has a virtuous friend..."
“Meghiya, it is to be expected for a bhikkhu... [and so on] ...to be one who gains without difficulty.
“Of such a kind” means of this sort, as previously described. “One who gains at will” means one who gains according to his wish, according to his preference;
one who, at all times, is able to hear and investigate these discourses as he pleases. “One who gains without hardship” means one who gains without suffering.
"One who gains with difficulty" means one who gains abundantly.

"Aroused in energy" means having exerted energy. "For the abandoning of unwholesome states" means for the sake of abandoning unwholesome, evil states in the sense that they have arisen through lack of skill.
"Of wholesome states" [is used] in the sense of flowing away from what is base, and so forth.
And in the sense of being blameless, it refers to the states of the path and fruit together with insight, which are wholesome.
"Upasampadāya" means for the sake of attainment, that is, for the sake of producing [them] within one's own continuum.

"Thāmavā" means endowed with the power of energy (vīriya-thāma) characterized by exertion (ussoḷhi). "Daḷhaparakkamo" means firm in effort, possessing unslackened energy. "Anikkhittadhuro" means one who has not cast off the yoke, one whose energy is not abandoned.

"Endowed with wisdom" means endowed with the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*). "Leading to arising and passing away" means that which penetrates the arising and the passing away of the five aggregates.
"Noble" means standing far removed from, at a distance from, defilements by way of suppression, and being stainless.
"Penetrative" means conducive to penetration. "Rightly leading to the destruction of suffering" refers to the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*).

To her who proceeds rightly by means of the cause and the method toward the Noble Path—which has received the name "the destruction of suffering" because it exhausts [defilements]—among these five factors, virtue, energy, and wisdom are the internal factors for the practitioner, while the other two are external factors.
Nevertheless, the remaining fourfold [set] succeeds only through reliance on a spiritual friend; for it is the spiritual friend alone who is essential here.
Showing the great benefit [of a good friend], the Teacher expands the teaching with the words: “Meghiya, it is to be expected for a bhikkhu who has a good friend,” and so forth.
In this context, *pāṭikaṅkha* means that which is to be expected as a certainty; the meaning is that it is bound to happen.
*Yaṃ* is a reference to the action. This is what is meant: regarding the statement “he will be virtuous,” that which belongs to one who has a good friend—

The "cultivation" (*bhavana*) for a bhikkhu consists in the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampannatta*) through his possession of virtue. Because that bhikkhu possesses virtue, it is "to be expected" (*pāṭikaṅkha*) of him;
the intended meaning is that its occurrence is inevitable and that he is directed toward it with absolute certainty.
This same method applies to the phrases "he will dwell restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha," and so forth.

Thus the Blessed One, having shown the entire excellence of the Dispensation through the venerable Meghiya’s possession of good friends and other qualities— despite the latter having entered that forest grove and fallen into such a state of misfortune by disregarding the words of the Buddha himself, who is reckoned as the supreme spiritual friend in the world with its devas—
now, as he had developed a sense of urgency regarding that matter, [addressed him] concerning those former thoughts of sensual desire and so forth.
Because he was afflicted, his meditation subject did not succeed; and because they were directly opposed to him, [the Buddha] explained the method of development to him.
Thereafter, while announcing the meditation subject for Arahantship, he said:
"But, Meghiya, having established himself in these five qualities, four further qualities must be developed," and so forth.

In this context, "by that" means by one who, through reliance on a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta), is endowed with the qualities of virtue and so forth as previously described. For this very reason it is said: "having established oneself in these five things.

"Further" means that if dangers such as lust (rāga) should arise for one who has begun the tender stage of insight (vipassanā), then for the sake of purifying them, four further things must be developed, produced, and increased beyond that.
“Foulness” refers to the development of foulness in any one of the eleven subjects of meditation on foulness, as appropriate.
“For the abandoning of lust” means for the purpose of abandoning sensual lust. This meaning should be clarified by the simile of the rice-gatherer:
suppose a man, taking a sickle, begins at the edge and reaps the rice in a rice field; then, for him—

Having broken down the fence, the cows entered. He set aside the sickle, took up a staff, drove the cows out by that same path, restored the fence to its original state, and then took up the sickle again to reap the rice. In this context, the field of rice should be regarded as the Buddha’s teaching;
the rice-reaper as the practitioner of yoga (yogāvacara); the sickle as wisdom (paññā); and the time of reaping as [the time for practice].
The time for performing the work of insight (vipassanā) is like the post; the meditation subject on the foul (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) is like the fence; restraint (saṃvara) is like the enclosure.
Just as when cows break through the fence and enter [the field], so too is the sudden arising of lust due to negligence, coming from a lack of reflection.
Having set aside the fodder, taken up the post, and having driven the cows back out by the very path they entered, [one repairs] the fence.

Having restored it to its original state, one suppresses lust by means of the meditation subject on the foul (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna), starting again from the place where it was originally situated—just like the draining away of water—and then it is time to perform the work of insight (vipassanā). This is the correlation of the similes here.
It is with reference to such a method of development that it is said: "The foul should be developed for the abandoning of lust."

"Loving-kindness" refers to the meditation subject of loving-kindness (*mettā-kammaṭṭhāna*). "For the abandoning of ill will" means, in the manner already stated, for the purpose of relinquishing arisen anger.

"Mindfulness of breathing" refers to mindfulness of breathing with its sixteen bases. "For the cutting off of applied thought" means, in the manner already stated, for the purpose of severing arisen applied thoughts.
"For the uprooting of the conceit 'I am'" refers to the ninefold [conceit] that arises as "I am."

For the purpose of the total eradication of conceit. "Perceiving impermanence" means: because of non-existence after having been, because of possessing arising and passing away, because of being subject to dissolution, because of being temporary, and because of being the opposite of permanence, they perceive impermanence by way of the contemplation of impermanence thus: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
"The perception of non-self becomes established" means: because of being without essence, because of lacking mastery, because of being other, and because of being empty and void.
And the perception of non-self—consisting of the contemplation of non-self that occurs as "All phenomena are non-self" within the void—is established in the mind;
it becomes firmly rooted. For when the characteristic of impermanence is seen, the characteristic of non-self is indeed seen.
Indeed, when one of the three characteristics is seen, the other two are necessarily seen as well. Therefore...
It is said: “For one who perceives impermanence, Meghiya, the perception of non-self becomes established.
When the characteristic of non-self is seen, the conceit “I am,” which arises, is easily abandoned; thus it is said: “One who perceives non-self reaches the uprooting of the conceit ‘I am.
“Nibbāna in this very life” means the unconditioned final Nibbāna in this very life, in this very personal existence.

He attains [this]. This is the summary here; however, the method for the development of the foul (asubha) and so forth should be understood in detail according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Having understood this matter" means having known this matter—the theft of the merchant's goods of the wholesome by the thieves of wrong thoughts—concerning the Venerable Meghiya.
"This inspired utterance" means he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which illuminates the danger in not dispelling and the benefit in dispelling sensual thoughts and the rest.
In this context, "trifling" (*khudda*) means inferior and base. "Thoughts" (*vitakka*) refers to the three unwholesome thoughts, beginning with sensual desire.
For these are called "trifling" here because they are the most contemptible among all thoughts, as in such passages as "one should not practice what is trifling.

"Subtle" (*sukhuma*) refers to thoughts concerning relatives and so forth. These include thoughts of relatives, thoughts of one's native land, thoughts of immortality, and those associated with compassion for others.
"Applied thought" (*vitakka*) refers to thought associated with gain, honor, and fame, and thought associated with not being despised.
These thoughts are called "subtle" because they are not coarse by nature, unlike the thoughts of sensual desire (*kāmavitakka*) and so forth.
"Accompanied" (*anugata*) means followed by the mind; for when applied thought arises, the mind follows it accordingly.
It exists because it directs the mind toward its object. There is also a textual reading, "anuggatā," which means "not arisen.
"Uppilāvā of the mind" means producing a state of elation in the consciousness.
One who is ignorant reflects upon these thoughts of the mind—these thoughts of sensual desire and so forth—from the perspective of their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them.
One who does not know things as they truly are through the full understandings of knowing, scrutinizing, and abandoning, has a wandering mind;

because of not having abandoned lustful thoughts, his mind is unsettled and he runs and wanders from object to object—sometimes toward forms, sometimes toward sounds, and so forth—by way of relishing them and the like.
Alternatively, "from place to place" (hurā huraṃ) [means...]
"He runs with a wandering mind" means that because he has not fully understood his thoughts, his mind wanders under the influence of ignorance and craving regarding those signs;
thus, from this world to the next, he runs and transmigrates through successive acts of grasping and letting go.
And "the wise man understands these thoughts of the mind" refers to these aforementioned varieties of mental thoughts, beginning with sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*).
Knowing [the nature of thoughts] as they truly are, beginning with their gratification (*assāda*); "ardent" (*ātāpī*) means possessing energy; "restrains" (*saṃvarati*) means he shuts them out;
"mindful" (*satimā*) means endowed with mindfulness; "not arisen" (*anuggate*) means not yet produced because they are difficult to obtain. This is what is meant:

the wise one, knowing these aforementioned types of mental thoughts—such as sensual thoughts (*kāmavitakka*) and so forth—as "agitations of the mind" (*manassa uppilāve*) because they are causes for the mind's agitation, by means of wisdom associated with insight (*vipassanāpaññā*),...
Knowing correctly through the wisdom of the path, and because of the presence of right effort and mindfulness which act as its companions, he is ardent and mindful;

at the very moment of the path, before those [defilements] that would otherwise arise in the future have even emerged, he restrains them, closes them off by means of the restraint of knowledge, and cuts off their path of arrival. And being thus constituted, through the awakening to the Four Noble Truths—
The Buddha, the noble disciple, through the attainment of Arahatship, has abandoned and utterly eradicated these thoughts of sensual desire and so forth, leaving nothing behind.
Here too, some read the word “anugate”; its meaning has already been explained above.
The commentary on the first sutta is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Uddhata Sutta 32.
Regarding the second [sutta], "at Kusinārā": this refers to the city of the Malla kings named Kusinārā. "In the Mallans' Sal Grove at Upavattana":
just as Thūpārāma was to Anurādhapura, so too was this park located to the south-west of Kusinārā.

It is as follows: just as the road from the Thūpārāma entering the city by the southern gate goes eastward and then turns northward, so too the row of *sāla* trees from the park goes eastward and then turns northward;
therefore, it is called "Upavattana" (the Turn). In that Upavattana, in the *sāla* grove of the Malla kings. "In a forest hut" means not far from the row of *sāla* trees.
A small hut built in a place overgrown with trees and shrubs—referring to that, it is said: “He dwells in a forest hut.
However, those bhikkhus were devoid of reflective discernment, had abandoned their energy, and lived negligently; therefore, it is said: “They were agitated,” and so forth.
Therein, they were “agitated” because their minds were unpacified due to an abundance of restlessness. Because of its emptiness, pride is like a reed.
*Unnaḷā*: "Naḷa" means pride; those in whom this lofty *naḷa*—that is, haughty pride—is present are called *unnaḷā*. The meaning is "those with loftily empty pride. *Capalā*:

They are fickle because they are possessed of fickleness regarding the adornment of bowl and robes, or because of their great abundance [of such things]. *Mukharā*: They are "mouthy" because their mouths are harsh due to their use of abusive speech. *Vikiṇṇavācā*:

They are "loose-tongued" because their speech is scattered or confused due to an abundance of frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*). *Muṭṭhassatino*: They are "forgetful" because mindfulness (*sati*) has been lost or destroyed in them.
The meaning is: "devoid of mindfulness" means they dwell in negligence. They are "unaware" because of the total absence of clear comprehension in every respect.
They are "unconcentrated" because of the absence of mental composure for even the duration of a cow’s snort.

They are "of wandering minds" because, due to their fickle nature, they resemble startled deer. [They are so] because of the lack of restraint over the six sense faculties, with the mind as the sixth.
"Those with uncontrolled faculties have their faculties exposed.
Having understood this matter means: having known that those bhikkhus were dwelling in negligence due to restlessness and other such factors.
"He uttered this inspired utterance" means: he uttered this inspired utterance which, respectively, clarifies the danger in dwelling in negligence and the benefit in dwelling in diligence.
In this context, "unprotected" means being unguarded due to the absence of the protection of mindfulness. "By the body" refers to the group of consciousnesses beginning with tactile consciousness;

for after seeing a form with visual consciousness, if one grasps at its signs and secondary characteristics, covetousness and other defilements arise because the door of consciousness has not been protected by mindfulness.
The same principle applies to auditory consciousness and the others as well. Thus, [it refers to] the unprotected state of the group of consciousnesses beginning with tactile consciousness.

He said this with intentional meaning: “with an unguarded body. Some, however, state the meaning as “by means of the body”; for them too, the application of the meaning would be appropriate provided it follows the method already explained.
Others, moreover, read “with an unguarded mind,” and for them also, the meaning is precisely the same method already explained.
“Stricken by wrong view” means corrupted by a false adherence to eternalism and so forth. “Overcome by sloth and torpor” means...

Being overwhelmed by *thina* (sloth), which has the characteristic of unwholesomeness of mind, and by *middha* (torpor), which has the characteristic of unwholesomeness of body—thereby, the connection is either with that body or with that mind.

"He goes under the power of Māra" means he comes under the sway of all Māras, beginning with the *kilesamāra* (the Māra of defilements), such that they may do with him as they wish; the meaning is that he does not transcend their domain.
For by this verse, the Blessed One [describes those] whose minds are entirely unguarded due to the absence of the protection of mindfulness;
who, because of the lack of wisdom—which is the cause of wise attention—grasp at perversions such as "eternal" through unwise emergence;
and who, for that very reason, being overcome by indolence due to the absence of the exertion of energy toward wholesome deeds, [are submerged] within the cycle of saṃsāra.

“They will not cast [him] out”: having shown the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) by way of censuring those monks who dwell in negligence, he now spoke the second verse, beginning with “Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded,” in order to show the turning away from that cycle (*vivaṭṭa*).
Therein, “therefore, for one whose mind is guarded” means: because one whose mind is unguarded becomes subject to Māra’s doing as he pleases.
It exists only within saṃsāra; therefore, by guarding and closing off the six faculties with the mind as the sixth through the restraint of mindfulness, one should have a guarded mind.
For when the mind is guarded, the eye and other faculties are indeed guarded.

"Having right intention as its domain" means that because one who has wrong intention as their domain, having applied inappropriate thoughts in various ways, [engages in] manifold kinds of wrong views...
One who takes it up with a mind struck by wrong view becomes subject to Māra’s doing with him as he pleases;

therefore, performing his work with wise attention (yonisomanasikāra), he should have the domain of right intention such as the intention of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa) and so forth, and he should make right intention associated with jhāna and so on the very sphere of activity for his own mind. "Having right view as his foremost" means because of having right intention as his domain.

Having first shaken off the view of desire, and having placed before him right view characterized by the understanding that one is the owner of one's own karma and the knowledge of things as they truly are,
he applies himself and exerts himself in virtue and concentration according to the method previously described;
then, having begun insight and comprehending formations, knowing their arising and passing away within the five aggregates of clinging, [he contemplates] the fifty-fold...

Having defined arising and ceasing by way of their modes and attained the knowledge of rise and fall, and thereafter having further intensified insight through the contemplation of dissolution and so forth,
the bhikkhu who has overcome sloth and torpor abandons all miserable destinies as he gradually attains the noble path;
thus, even before [the final path], he first [abandons] those defilements to be abandoned by the lower paths.
Because he has abandoned the stiffening and torpor that arise in mental states associated with greed but dissociated from views by means of the path of Arahantship—
which has been attained— and because he has also abandoned pride and other defilements associated with those states,

the bhikkhu, whose taints are exhausted and whose defilements are entirely shattered, has cut off all destinations known as the miserable realms due to the uprooting of the source of existence through the three types of suffering.
"Should abandon"—this means that after those [fetters], one should be established in *nibbāna*.
The commentary on the second sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Gopālaka Sutta.
33. "In the third [case], 'among the Kosalans' (*kosalesu*): the Kosalans are the princes of a certain territory;
the territory inhabited by them is also called 'the Kosalans. Among those Kosalans means in that Kosala country.

'He wanders on tour' (*cārikaṃ carati*) means he wanders through the countryside by way of a non-hurried tour. 'A great [assembly]' (*mahatā*): it is great both by greatness of virtue and by greatness of number, because its count is unlimited."
"With a great community of bhikkhus" means with a multitude of recluses united by commonality of view and virtue. "Together with" means in one place.

"Having stepped off the path" means having departed from the road. "To the foot of a certain tree" means to the vicinity of the root of a large tree endowed with thick leaves, branches, and foliage, and possessing dense shade.
"A certain cowherd" refers to a single protector of a herd of cattle; by name, however, he was called Nanda. It is said that he was wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments.

Just as the matted-hair ascetic Keṇiya [was supported] by means of his renunciation, so too, while guarding Anāthapiṇḍika’s herd of cattle, he protected his own family by acting as a cowherd and thereby warding off royal oppression. From time to time, he would [provide] five...
Having taken the cow’s milk and returned to the presence of the great merchant, he delivered it;
then, going into the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher and heard the Dhamma. He requested the Teacher to let him go so that he might return to his own dwelling place.
The Teacher, awaiting the full ripening of that very person's knowledge, did not go, but at a later time, together with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus...
While wandering on a journey through the countryside surrounded by his retinue, [the Buddha],
knowing that "now his knowledge has reached maturity," left the road not far from Nanda’s dwelling place and sat down at the foot of a certain tree, waiting for him to arrive.
Nanda, too, having heard that "the Teacher is indeed coming this way while wandering through the countryside," was joyful and elated.
Having gone with speed, he approached the Teacher, paid homage, and after exchanging greetings, sat down to one side;
then the Blessed One taught him the Dhamma. Having established himself in the fruit of stream-entry, he invited the Blessed One and gave an offering of milk-rice for seven days.
On the seventh day, the Blessed One, having given a blessing of thanksgiving, departed. By him—
It is said: “The Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the cowherd as he sat to one side with a discourse on the Dhamma… [and so on] … then, rising from his seat, he departed.

In that context, “instructed” means [he taught] by way of such statements as, “These phenomena are wholesome; these phenomena are unwholesome,” and so forth, concerning the wholesome and other phenomena.
Demonstrating the ripening of kamma in this world and the next through direct perception, he correctly showed the Four Noble Truths at the conclusion of his gradual discourse.

He "incited" (samādapesi) them by having them properly undertake the factors of virtue and so forth, thinking, "For the attainment of the Truths, these specific qualities must be generated within yourselves," and thereby established them therein. He "aroused enthusiasm" (samuttejesi) for those qualities once they had been undertaken.
Being developed in due course, they become conducive to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*) and, becoming sharp and keen, bring about the Noble Path very quickly;
in that way, he properly encouraged them and properly inspired them.

"He gladdened" means he thoroughly gladdened them by causing joy in their minds through showing the progressive distinction between earlier and later stages of development. Furthermore, herein, regarding wholesome and unwholesome phenomena...
It should be understood that there is "showing" by dispelling delusion regarding suffering and the other truths;
"encouraging" by removing negligence from right practice; "inspiring" by dispelling the mind's lack of ardor; and "gladdening" by the accomplishment of right practice.
Thus, through the Blessed One’s uniquely exalted teaching of the Dhamma, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

“He consented” means that, having been invited by that seer who had seen the Truth with the words, “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One consent for me,” etc., he consented and accepted with his mind alone, without moving any part of his body or speech. For this very reason, it says, “by way of silence.
“Rice porridge without water” means rice porridge prepared without water. “Having had it prepared” means having had it cooked and set out. And “fresh ghee.”
Having taken fresh butter, he had fresh cream-ghee prepared right then and there.
"With his own hand" means, out of reverence, serving with his own hand. "He satisfied" means he fed them with the food that had been prepared.

"He regaled" means he had them decline further by saying, "Enough, enough. "Those who had finished eating" means those who had completed the task of eating. "Those who had removed their bowls from their hands" means...
"With hand removed from the bowl" (*pattato apanītapāṇi*); there is also the reading "with hand having washed the bowl" (*dhotapattapāṇi*), which means "with hand having washed the bowl.
"Low" means taking a seat that is not high; sitting on the very seat is the custom of those dwelling in the Noble Land (Ariyadesa).
However, he sat near the wooden plank seat prepared for the sake of formal etiquette in the presence of the Teacher. "With a discourse on the Dhamma," and so forth.
This was said with reference to the thanksgiving (anumodana) performed on the seventh day.
It is said that he had the Blessed One and the community of monks dwell there for seven days and provided a great almsgiving; however, on the seventh day, he gave an offering of waterless gruel.
Because, in that particular existence, he lacked the ripening of knowledge for the sake of the higher paths, the Teacher merely performed the thanksgiving and departed.
“Between the boundaries” means within the boundary; that is, the interior of that village. It is said that the villagers, relying on a certain pond, quarreled with him.
Having overcome them, he took possession of that pond.
A man who harbored a grudge against him took the Teacher’s bowl and followed after him for a long distance. When [the Teacher] said, “Turn back, lay follower,” [he replied:]

Having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him, and having extended his joined palms in salutation to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he raised his hands—resplendent with the ten nails joined together—to his head until they passed beyond the range of sight.
Then, turning back, he shot and killed him with an arrow as he was walking alone in a forest region between two villages. Thus it was said: "Not long after he had departed... and so forth.
"...he left [the group]. Having been delayed by some business, the bhikkhus who were walking behind saw him dead in that manner and reported the matter to the Blessed One;
it is with reference to this that it is said, "Then a number of bhikkhus," and so forth.
"Having understood this matter" means: because by the man who was killing Nanda, a noble disciple endowed with right view...
"Having understood that the immediate karma (*ānantariya-kamma*) is abundant and flows with demerit (*apuñña*),
and that for this reason these beings' minds are wrongly directed— doing even more terrible things than what thieves and enemies would do—
he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) to illuminate that meaning."
In this context, "seeing one another" means the defiler seeing the defiled, the thief seeing the thief; "having seen" is the ellipsis of the verb.
"Whatever he might do" refers to whatever harm or ruin he might inflict upon the other; the same method applies to the second phrase as well. This is what is meant:

a single person, being treacherous toward his friend like a thief, while not offending against his own children, wife, fields, lands, cattle, buffaloes, and so forth, [offends] against that very person whom he offends.
Seeing even such a thief who has offended against him in that same way, or seeing an enemy with whom he has a settled enmity for some reason,
one might— due to one's own harshness and cruelty— inflict upon them misfortune and ruin, or oppress their wife and children,
or destroy their fields and so forth, or deprive them of life; [all these actions fall] among the ten courses of unwholesome action.
Because it is wrongly directed, a mind that is wrongly aimed would make him worse than that; it would make that person more evil than he already is.
For a foe of the kind described—whether an enemy or one who harbors enmity—might produce suffering for the enemy or the hater in this very life, or might even bring about the end of his life.
But this [mind], when wrongly directed among the unwholesome courses of action, is far worse.

"The mind brings about ruin and disaster even in this very life; having cast one into hundreds of thousands of individual existences and into the four states of misery, it does not allow one's head to be raised again.
The commentary on the third sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discourse on the Yakṣa’s Blow (Yakkhapahārasutta) 34.
In the fourth [discourse], "at Kapotakandarā" means in a monastery of that name.
It is said that in former times many pigeons lived in that mountain cave; therefore, that mountain cave was called "Kapotakandarā. At a later time...
There, even the dwelling was known simply as “Kapotakandara. Therefore it is said: “In Kapotakandara, that is, in the monastery of that name.
“On a moonlit night” means on a night of the waxing moon. “With newly grown hair” means with hair recently shaved;
here the instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (itthambhūta-lakkhaṇa). “In the open air” means where—
There was no roof or enclosure there, only such an open space in the sky.
In that place, the Venerable Sāriputta was golden-colored, while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was the color of a blue lotus.
Both of those great elders were born as brahmins of the northern region and had spent one incalculable aeon plus a hundred thousand aeons [in the practice of virtue].
Endowed with their original resolve, having attained the six direct knowledges and the analytical insights,
being great ones whose taints were exhausted and who had gained mastery over meditative attainments, they reached the pinnacle of the sixty-seven perfections of a disciple’s knowledge;
thus adorning this Kapotakanda Vihāra, they entered a golden cave like two lions, descended upon a stretch of ground for stretching like two tigers, and [entered] a grove of Sāla trees in full bloom.
They were like two Chaddanta elephant-kings who had entered [the same lake], like two Supaṇṇa kings who had entered the same Simbali forest,
like two Vessavaṇas mounted on the same Naravāhana vehicle, like two Sakkas seated upon the same Paṇḍukambala stone throne,
like two Mahābrahmās gone into the interior of the same celestial palace— within that one [place].
They shone like two moon-disks or two sun-disks stationed in the sky.
Among them, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna sat in silence, while the Venerable Sāriputta entered into meditative absorption. Therefore it is said:
"Having entered into a certain concentration."

Therein, "one or other concentration" refers to the attainment of the divine abode of equanimity (*upekkhā-brahmavihāra*). Some say it is the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*);

others, however, say it is the attainment of fruition (*phala-samāpatti*) that serves as the basis for the formless attainments (*āruppa*). For these three attainments alone are capable of protecting the body.
Among them, the application of the term "concentration" (*samādhi*) to the attainment of cessation has already been explained above; [the same applies to] the latter one.

However, the teachers explain it thus: "Going from the northern direction to the southern direction" means that having gone to the assembly of yakkhas in the northern direction, they go toward the southern direction in order to return to their own abode. "It occurs to me" (*paṭibhāti maṃ*):
here, *maṃ* is the accusative case used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmī*) due to its connection with the word *manti*; [it refers to] "on his head."
The meaning is: "the thought of giving a blow arises in me. It is said that in a previous birth he had harbored a grudge against the Elder;
therefore, upon seeing the Elder, such a thought occurred to him with a corrupted mind. But the other was of a wise nature;
thus, restraining him, he said, "Enough, friend," and so forth. In that context, "do not attack" means do not strike, do not give a blow.
"Give me," is what was said. "Exalted" means endowed with exalted, supreme qualities such as virtue (sīla) and so forth.
"Without taking [it to heart]" means without showing respect, that is, not accepting his words.
Since one who does not accept another's words is indeed one who does not take them to heart, it is therefore said: "without taking that yakkha to heart. [He struck him] on the head.
"Adāsī" means that, generating effort with all his might, he gave a blow upon the head while still standing in the air;
the meaning is that he struck a fist-blow upon the crown of the head. "Tāva mahā" means that by reason of the greatness of its strength, the blow was so great.
"Tena pahārena" means by means of that blow acting as the instrument. "Sattaratanam" refers to [the height] of a man of medium stature.
“With a jewel” means with a seven-jeweled [chariot]. “An elephant” means a noble elephant (*nāga*). “He would sink it” means he would cause it to sink into the earth, to submerge.
There is also a reading, “he would cause it to enter” (*osāreyya*), which means he would reduce it to powder and fragments.
“Seven and a half ratanas” means those that complete eight by adding half; thus, they are “seven and a half. That whose measure is seven and a half *ratanas* is “seven and a half *ratana*.”
That [body] was seven and a half cubits in height. "A great mountain peak" means a vast mountain summit, equal in size to the peak of Mount Kailāsa.
"He would split it" means he would break it into pieces like shards. The connection is: "he might even sink it, he might even split it.
At that very moment, a great fever arose in his body; afflicted by that pain, he was unable to remain standing in the air.

He fell upon the ground; at that very moment, the Great Earth—supporting Sineru, the king of mountains, which rises one hundred thousand and sixty-eight thousand yojanas high, and is two hundred thousand and forty-four thousand yojanas thick—gave way as if unable to bear that evil being, opening up a chasm.
Flames rising from the Avīci hell enveloped him even as he cried out.
They seized him; he fell down, weeping and wailing. Therefore it is said: “But then that yakkha, having cried out, ‘I am burning!
I am burning! right there fell into the Great Hell. In this context, *apatāsi* means he fell.
But did he go to hell in his very state as a yakkha? He did not go. For that which is to be experienced here and now (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*)—
There was an evil deed; by its power, he experienced great suffering in his state as a *yakkha*.
However, because of that *ānantariya* karma, which is to be experienced upon rebirth, he arose in hell immediately after his death.
But for the Elder, whose body was supported by the power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), no transformation whatsoever occurred. At the time when he had not yet emerged from that attainment—
Indeed, that yakkha struck him; seeing him striking thus with his divine eye, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached the Dhammasenāpati.
At the very moment he approached, the Dhammasenāpati arose from meditative absorption.
Then Mahāmoggallāna asked him about his physical condition, and he explained it to him as well; therefore, it was said:
—“The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw... [and so on] ...‘However, my head is slightly pained.
In this context, “slightly pained” means that my head is pained to a slight, minor degree, as if it were sweet;
the sense is that it has reached a state of pain. For when the head is the basis for pain, it is said to be “pained. It is also said: “There is slight pain in the head.”
[This is] the reading. But how was it that even a slight pain arose in the Elder’s head when his body had been sustained by the power of attainment?

Because he emerged from it very shortly. For the pain that is not perceived during the attainment becomes slightly perceptible upon waking—due to its dependence on the body—just like the pain caused by mosquitoes and the like to one who has fallen asleep and then awakens.
When the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having conceived a sense of wonder and amazement at the thought, “Even though his body was struck by the yakkha Mahābala with such total exertion,

there was no sign of injury,” had thus manifested the Great Leader’s (Dhammasenāpati) majesty by saying, “It is wonderful, friend Sāriputta,” [Sāriputta] in turn revealed the greatness of Moggallāna’s power of psychic potency by saying, “It is wonderful, friend Moggallāna,” and so forth.
This demonstrates that his own stains—envy, stinginess, ego-conceit, and so forth—were thoroughly abandoned.
"We do not see even a dust-demon" means we do not see even a minor *preta* wandering among rubbish heaps and the like.

Thus, the Great Elder, who was the foremost among those with few desires regarding attainments, spoke with reference to their invisibility at that time due to a lack of mental advertence (*anāvajjana*). For this very reason, he said, "At present."

But the Blessed One, standing in the Veḷuvana grove, heard this conversation between the two chief disciples with his divine ear. Therefore it is said: "The Blessed One heard," and so forth; the meaning of that has already been explained.

"Having understood this matter" means having understood this greatness of the power of psychic potency attained through the strength of the Venerable Sāriputta’s meditative absorption. "This inspired utterance" means he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which illustrates the attainment of his state of imperturbability (tādibhāva).

In this context, regarding the phrase "whose mind is like a rock, steady and unshaken": for that one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), the mind is like a mountain made of solid, single-piece stone;
because all agitation has ceased and because it has attained mastery, it is steady and is not shaken or disturbed by any of the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*).
Now, in order to show the manner of its immovability along with its cause, the words beginning with "dispassionate" (*viratta*) are spoken.

In that context, "dispassionate toward things that provoke passion" means it is dispassionate—by means of the Noble Path known as dispassion—toward all phenomena of the three planes that are provocative of passion and serve as causes for the arising of lust;
the meaning is that passion has been entirely cut off therein.

"Toward things that provoke anger" means that toward everything that serves as a basis for aversion, every ground for resentment, it does not become angry, does not feel ill will, and does not undergo a transformation [of mind].

"Of him whose mind is thus developed": of that noble person (ariyapuggala) as previously described, the mind has been developed in the manner stated by way of bringing about the state of suchness (tādibhāva). "From where will suffering come to him?":
from where—whether from a sentient being or from formations (saṅkhāra)—will suffering approach that supreme person? The meaning is that for one such as this, suffering does not exist.
The commentary on the fourth sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Nāga Sutta: 35.
Regarding the fifth [sutta], it is called "Kosambī" because it was established at the site where the seer named Kusumba had lived.
In the city named after this, in the Ghosita Monastery—a monastery built by the merchant Ghosita—the Blessed One dwelt crowded.
"The Blessed One dwelt crowded" means that the Blessed One dwelt having reached a state of congestion. But does the Blessed One have any congestion or social entanglement?
No, he does not. For no one is able to approach the Blessed One against his will; indeed, he is difficult to approach.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are entirely unstained by anything whatsoever. Nevertheless, out of affection for beings and motivated by compassion,

they consent to the approach of the eight assemblies from time to time— crossing over the four floods in accordance with their promise, "Having been liberated, I shall liberate others"— and they themselves, impelled by great compassion, know the proper time.

Having offered [the sacrifice], he approaches that place; this is the established practice of all Buddhas, and it is this which is intended here by the term "living in a crowded state" (*ākiṇṇavihāra*).

On this occasion, however, when the monks of Kosambī had fallen into quarreling, the Teacher brought forward the case of King Dīghīti of Kosala and gave them this exhortation beginning with, "For never in this world are enmities stilled by enmity," and so forth, on that day.
While they were still quarreling, the night turned into dawn. On the second day as well, the Blessed One spoke on that very same subject;
while they were still quarreling, the night turned into dawn. On the third day too, the Blessed One spoke on that very same subject.
Then a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One: “Be at ease, sir.”
“Venerable Blessed One, may you dwell devoted to the blissful abiding in this very life;
we shall be known by this quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute. The Teacher thought, “These foolish men have their minds completely consumed;
they cannot now be persuaded, and there is no one here to be persuaded. What if I were to live in solitary wandering?”
He thought, "If I were to dwell [here], these monks would cease their quarreling.
Thus, because it was impossible for him to lead a life in a single dwelling together with those quarrelsome monks, he visited lay followers and others, making his dwelling crowded;
this is why it is said: "At that time, the Blessed One dwelt in a crowded place," and so forth.
In this context, "suffering" means not happiness; the meaning is that it is not desirable because the mind is not satisfied.
For this very reason, he said, "I do not dwell in comfort. "Withdrawn" means situated in seclusion, having become distant [from the crowd].
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One, after attending to his body early in the morning and walking for alms in Kosambī, went alone, without a companion, without informing anyone.
Having gone to the Kosala country, he dwelt at the foot of a *bhaddasāla* tree in the Pālileyyaka forest grove.
Therefore it is said: “Then the Blessed One, in the morning time... [omitted] ...at the foot of a *bhaddasāla* tree. In that context, *sāmaṃ* means “himself. *Saṃsāmetvā* means “having adjusted.
Regarding the phrase “taking his bowl and robe,” here too the word *sāmaṃ* (“himself”) should be brought forward and connected. *Upaṭṭhāke* means...

Without taking leave of his attendants, such as the merchant Ghosita and others residing in the city of Kosambī, nor of the Venerable Ānanda, who was the foremost attendant at the monastery, the Teacher departed.
When the Teacher had thus gone, five hundred bhikkhus said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Friend Ānanda, the Teacher..."

"He has gone alone; we shall follow after him. "Friend, when the Blessed One, having himself tidied his lodging, taken his bowl and robes, and gone forth without taking leave of his attendants or informing the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, goes without a companion, it is the Blessed One’s intention to wander alone.
A disciple, indeed, should act in accordance with the Teacher’s intention."
"One must proceed [in this manner]; therefore, the Blessed One should not be followed for these days," he said, and thus he prevented him, and he himself did not follow after him either.

"By stages" means by gradual succession; while wandering on his alms-tour through the sequence of villages and market towns, thinking, "I shall see a bhikkhu living in solitary retreat," he went to the village of Bālakaloṇakāra and there [met] the Elder Bhagu.
Having explained the benefits of dwelling alone during the entire period after the meal and for three watches of the night,
on the following day, that junior attendant went for alms, turned back right there, and thinking,
"I shall see those three sons of noble family living in harmony," he went to the Pācīnavaṃsa Deer Park; there too, throughout the entire night, [he observed] their living in harmony.
Having explained the benefits, he sent them back to that very place and arrived alone at Pālileyyagāma.
The inhabitants of Pālileyyagāma went out to meet the Blessed One, gave him alms, and near Pālileyyagāma there was a protected grove named Rakkhitavanaṣaṇḍa;
having built a leaf-hut for the Blessed One there, they requested, "May the Blessed One dwell here," and so they provided him with lodging.
As for "Bhaddasāla," there was a certain beautiful and auspicious *sāla* tree there; the Blessed One, depending on that village, dwelt at the foot of that tree near a leaf-hut in a grove of woods.
Therefore it is said: "He dwelt at Pālileyyaka, in the protected grove of woods, at the foot of the Bhaddasāla tree."
"An elephant" means a great elephant, the leader of the herd. "By elephant calves" means by the young elephants.
"By elephant cubs" means by the very young elephant calves who are still nursing, who are also called "bhiṅkas.
"With tips broken off" means he eats what remains after being chewed—stumps like posts—with those elephants and others going ahead and ahead.
"Broken here and there" means that it was broken and broken down from its high places by that noble elephant and then felled.
"Its broken-off branches" means they eat the broken-off branches belonging to this [tree].
"Turbid" means he drinks waters mixed with mud, which have become turbid because they were stirred up by them as they descended first and drank. "From the ford" means from the bathing place.
“Ogāhan”ti is also a reading in the text. “Assā” means of the elephant-nāga. “Upanighaṃsantiyo” means rubbing against;
even while being rubbed against, he did not become angry because of his own noble nature, and for that reason they continued to rub against him. “Yūthā” means a herd of elephants.
“Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamī” means that it is said that the elephant-nāga, being weary of living in the herd, [went] to that forest grove where the Blessed One was.
Having entered there and seen the Blessed One, he became as if extinguished— his fever quenched by a thousand pots of water—
and stood before the Blessed One with a serene mind. From that time forth, taking his place at the head of the duties,
he cleared the area around Bhaddasāla’s leaf-hut of all weeds and swept it with broken branches for the Blessed One.
He provided water for washing the face, brought water for bathing, gave tooth-sticks, and having brought sweet fruits from the forest, he presented them to the Teacher;
the Teacher consumed them. Therefore it was said:
"In that place where the Blessed One dwelt, that noble elephant made the area free of green grass, [using] his trunk..."
“He prepares drinking water and water for bathing for the Blessed One.

Having brought wood with his trunk, struck it against another piece to produce fire, and ignited the wood, he heated stone fragments therein, rolled them along with sticks, and cast them into the trunk.
Knowing that the water had reached the proper temperature, he approached the presence of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One remains there, thinking, “The elephant-nāga wishes for my bath,” and having gone there, he performs the act of bathing;
the same applies to drinking water. When that [water] has become cool, he approaches; with reference to this, it is said:
“With his trunk, he presents the Blessed One with drinking water and water for use.”
Now, the passage beginning with "Then, when the Blessed One had gone into seclusion," etc., shows the two Great Nāgas reflecting upon the bliss of solitude;
its meaning is exactly as stated. "Having known his own seclusion" means having understood the physical seclusion obtained by being undisturbed by anyone;
however, the other types of seclusion are present in the Blessed One at all times.

"This inspired utterance" means that he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which illuminates the fact that his own disposition regarding delight in solitude was identical to that of his noble elephant.

Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: "The mind of this noble elephant, whose tusks are like the poles of a chariot, accords with and merges with the mind of the Buddha-noble-one. How does it accord? 'When one delights in the forest... [and so forth].
Just as the Buddha-elephant, having felt revulsion for his former crowded dwelling, thinking, "In the past, indeed, I lived crowded," and cultivating seclusion,
now delights and rejoices alone and without a second companion in the forest and the wilderness;
even so this elephant-king, having felt revulsion for his former crowded dwelling with other elephants and the like, and cultivating seclusion—
Now, he delights and finds joy in the forest and wilderness alone, without a companion. Therefore, his mind is "equal to that of a Nāga";
having made it so that his mind is equal to theirs, the meaning is that it becomes identical with them through the delight in solitude.
The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Piṇḍola Sutta 36.
Regarding the sixth [sutta], "Piṇḍolabhāradvāja": he is called Piṇḍola because he went forth as one who "searches for" (*ulamāna*) or seeks alms (*piṇḍa*).
It is said that he was a brahmin whose wealth had been exhausted; having seen the great gain and honor received by the Saṅgha of monks, he...
Having gone forth after departing for the sake of alms-food, he wandered about carrying a large bowl as his "alms-bowl.
He drank rice-gruel until the bowl was full, ate solid food, and consumed cakes and snacks. Then they reported his habit of eating so expensively to the Teacher.
The Teacher did not permit him to have an alms-bowl bag; instead, he turned the bowl upside down beneath his bed.
He set it down; even while setting it down, he did so by striking it and pushing it aside, and even while taking it up, he did so by pulling it along after striking it.
As time passed, it became worn out from being struck until it was capable of holding only a measure of rice from a *nāḷi* measure.
Then they informed the Teacher, and the Teacher permitted him an alms-bowl bag (*pattatthavika*). The Elder—
At a later time, while cultivating the development of the faculties, he was established in the supreme fruit of Arhatship.

Thus, because he previously went about for alms in a distinguished manner, he was called "Piṇḍola" (Alms-gatherer); and since his clan name was "Bhāradvāja," the two combined together he is called "Piṇḍolabhāradvāja."
*Āraññaka*: One who dwells in the forest by rejecting dwellings within the vicinity of a village is an *āraññaka*;
this is the name for one who lives having undertaken the forest-dweller’s ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*).

Likewise, *piṇḍapāta* refers to the "falling" (*pāta*) of morsels of food (*piṇḍa*)—meaning the falling of morsels given by others into one's bowl. One who gathers (*uñchati*) such alms-food from various families is a *piṇḍapātika*.
One who approaches and seeks [alms] is a *piṇḍapātī*; or, one whose practice (*vata*) is to fall upon or wander for alms-food (*piṇḍa*) is a *piṇḍapātī*;
thus, being a *piṇḍapātī* indeed, he is a *piṇḍapātika*. Because it stands upon dust on rubbish heaps and the like, it is like something that has emerged;
thus it is *paṃsukūla*. Or, because it goes toward (*ulati*) a state of worthlessness (*kucchita-bhāva*) like dust (*paṃsu*), it is *paṃsukūla*.
*Paṃsukūlika*: wearing refuse-rags (*paṃsukūla*) is *paṃsukūla*; one whose virtue (*sīla*) consists of that is a *paṃsukūlika*. *Ticīvarika*:

the three robes consisting of the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*), the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), and the inner garment (*antaravāsaka*) are called the "three-robes" (*ticīvara*); wearing those three robes is *ticīvara*; one whose virtue consists of that is a *tecīvarika*.
The meaning of the terms beginning with "one of few desires" (*appiccha*) has already been explained above.

"One who speaks on the ascetic practices" (*dhutavāda*): here, "ascetic" (*dhuta*) refers to a person whose defilements have been shaken off, or to the state of shaking off defilements. In this regard, one should understand the following fourfold classification:

there is one who is ascetic but does not speak on the ascetic practices; there is one who is not ascetic but speaks on the ascetic practices; there is one who is neither ascetic nor speaks on the ascetic practices;
and there is one who is both ascetic and speaks on the ascetic practices. Among these, he who has himself undertaken the ascetic qualities...
He himself practices [the ascetic virtues] but does not encourage others to do so for that purpose—this is the first.
He who himself does not undertake the ascetic virtues but encourages others to do so—this is the second. He who lacks both—this is the third.
But he who is accomplished in both—this is the fourth. And such was the venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja. Therefore it was said:
“An exponent of the ascetic practices (dhutavāda)”: this designation is by way of a partial *ekasesa* (single-remainder) compound, just as in the case of “name-and-form” (*nāmarūpa*).

Regarding the phrase “devoted to higher consciousness” (*adhicittamanuyutta*), here the state of being “higher consciousness” should be understood as the mind’s association with the eight attainments or its association with the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship;
however, in this context, they say it refers specifically to the “consciousness of the fruit of Arahantship.”
In the various attainments (*samāpatti*), concentration (*samādhi*) itself is "higher mind" (*adhicitta*); however, here it should be understood as the concentration of the fruit of arahantship.

Some, however, [interpret] it as "the mind of serenity and insight (*samatha-vipassanā-citta*) is the higher mind," as in the *Adhicitta Sutta*: "Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind should from time to time attend to three signs."
Some say that what is intended here is [a specific practice], but that is not correct; the former meaning alone should be accepted.

"Having understood this matter" means having understood in every aspect this matter of Venerable Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja’s perfection in the equipment of resolute determination, which is designated as the pursuit of higher consciousness (*adhicittānuyoga*). Thus: "The pursuit of higher consciousness is my fulfillment of the Dispensation."
Illuminating this, he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*).
Therein, "non-reproach" (*anūpavāda*) means not reproaching anyone by way of speech. "Non-harming" (*anūpaghāta*) means not causing harm to anyone by way of body.
Regarding the term *pātimokkha*: the meaning of the word *pātimokkha* has been explained in various ways below; [it refers] to that *pātimokkha*.
Restraint (*saṃvara*) is characterized by the non-transgression of the seven classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*).

"Knowing the proper measure" (*mattaññutā*) means knowing the limit in terms of receiving and using [alms-food]. "A secluded lodging" (*pantañca sayanāsanaṃ*) refers to a dwelling place that is isolated and free from disturbances.
"Exertion in higher consciousness" (*adhicitte ca āyogo*) is the application of cultivation for the attainment of the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Another method: "Non-reproach" (*anūpavāda*) means not speaking anything that would obstruct anyone;
by this, all verbal virtue (*vācasika-sīla*) is included. "Non-harming" (*anūpaghāta*) means not inflicting harm or injury upon anyone through the body;
by this, all bodily virtue (*kāyika-sīla*) is included. Furthermore, both of these are contained within the teaching of the Buddhas.
In order to show that [restraint] exists, it is said: “And restraint in the Pātimokkha. The word *ca* (and) is a mere particle.
“And restraint in the Pātimokkha” means that which constitutes the restraint of the Pātimokkha, namely, non-reproach and non-harming.
Alternatively, *pātimokkhe* is used in the locative case to denote the locus: restraint [exists] in the Pātimokkha, which serves as its support. But what [is it]?
What is that? It is non-reproach and non-harming. For at the time of full admission (upasampadā), the Pātimokkha virtue is indeed undertaken without distinction;
for one established in that Pātimokkha, the restraint consisting in the non-commission of reproach and harming thereafter is called "non-reproach" and "non-harming."

Alternatively, in the term *pātimokkha*, the locative case is used in the sense of that which is to be accomplished, as in: "The non-pacification of the mind has unwise attention as its proximate cause.
By means of that *pātimokkha*, there is to be achieved non-reproach and non-harming; the meaning is precisely that non-reproach and non-harming are comprised within the restraint of the *pātimokkha*.
Furthermore, by the word "restraint" (*saṃvara*), one refers to the restraint of mindfulness, the restraint of knowledge, and the restraint of patience.
"Restraint through energy" refers to the undertaking of these four types of restraint; this is the tetrad of restraints accomplished by the *pātimokkha*.
"Knowing moderation regarding food" means knowing the proper measure in eating by way of seeking, receiving, consuming, and relinquishing.
"A secluded lodging" refers to a dwelling place such as a forest, the foot of a tree, or other remote locations that are conducive to meditation (*bhāvanā*).

"And application to higher consciousness" (*adhicitta-āyoga*) means that because it is superior and supreme among all states of consciousness, when the consciousness known as "higher consciousness"—namely, the fruit of arahantship—is to be accomplished, there is application by way of the cultivation of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) for the purpose of its production. "This is the teaching of the Buddhas" refers to this:
not reviling others, not harming others, restraint according to the Pātimokkha, and [proper conduct] regarding seeking and receiving alms, and so forth.
The meaning is that moderation, dwelling in seclusion, and the pursuit of the aforementioned higher mind constitute the teaching, the exhortation, and the instruction of the Buddhas.
Thus, it should be understood that the three trainings are explained by this verse.
The commentary on the sixth sutta is concluded.
7. Commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta 37.
In the seventh [verse], there is nothing new. Regarding the phrase *adhicetaso*: it means "of one possessing higher consciousness" (*adhicitta*);

the sense is "of one endowed with the fruit-of-Arahantship consciousness, which is superior to all other states of consciousness. Regarding *appamajjato*: it means "not being negligent," that is, by means of diligence (*appamāda*).
This means: "of one who is endowed with constant practice regarding blameless states. Regarding the term *muni*:
as it is said, "He who understands both worlds is therefore called a muni," thus *mona* refers to knowledge (*ñāṇa*) by virtue of understanding both worlds;
or, because he is endowed with that knowledge known as the fruit of arahantship, the one whose taints are destroyed is called a *muni*. [The phrase] "of that muni" refers to him.

"Training in the paths of *mauna*": this means training in the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*), which are the paths of *mauna*—defined here as the knowledge of *arahantship*—or else training in the three trainings (*sikkhā*). This is stated by way of taking up the preliminary practice (*pubbhāgappaṭipada*). For an *arahant* has already completed his training;
therefore, it refers to one who "is thus training," who has attained the state of a sage (*muni*) through this training—it is in this sense that he is called a "sage" (*muni*) here.

The meaning must be seen. And because it is precisely this, therefore the meaning of these three terms is indeed appropriate: as "one of developed mind" (*adhicetasa*) by way of the minds of the lower paths and fruits;
as "one who is diligent" (*appamajjato*) by way of diligence in the practice leading to the awakening to the Four Truths;
and as "a sage" (*munī*) by way of being endowed with path-knowledge. Alternatively, [it may be understood as] "of one who is diligent and training."
The meaning of the words should be understood as follows: "for the sake of non-negligence" and "for the sake of training" refers to *adhicetaso*.

"Sorrows do not exist for such a one" (*sokā na bhavanti tādiso*) means that within such a sage whose taints are destroyed, sorrows—that is, mental torments—caused by factors such as separation from the beloved, do not arise.
Alternatively, "such a one" (*tādino*) refers to one endowed with the characteristic of suchness (*tādilakkhaṇa*), being of this kind.
“Sorrow does not exist for the sage”—this is the meaning here. “For one who is tranquil” means for one who is tranquil through the absolute pacification of lust and the other defilements.
“Always mindful” means for one who is never devoid of mindfulness due to having attained the fullness of mindfulness.

And herein, by the term “of heightened mind,” the training in higher consciousness (adhicitta-sikkhā) is indicated; by the term “for the heedful,” the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) is indicated.

By the words “of the sage training in the paths of sagehood,” the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā) is indicated. Alternatively, by the word “of the sage” (munino), the training in higher wisdom is shown;
by the phrase “training in the paths of sagehood,” the preliminary practice for those supramundane trainings is shown;

and by the words “sorrows do not arise,” etc., the benefit resulting from the fulfillment of those trainings is made manifest—this is how it should be understood. The remainder is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the seventh sutta is concluded.
8. Commentary on the Sundarī Sutta: 38.

The meaning of the words "honored" (*sakkata*) and so forth in the eighth [sutta] has already been explained above. "Not enduring" (*asahamānā*) means not being able to endure; the sense is that they were envious. The connection is: "not enduring the honor shown to the community of bhikkhus."

"Sundarī" was her name. It is said that at that time she was the most beautiful, lovely, and pleasing among all female wanderers, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion; for that very reason, she was known as "Sundarī.
And she was still in the prime of youth, yet her conduct was unrestrained; therefore, they [committed] evil deeds against the female wanderer Sundarī.

They incited [him]. For those followers of other sects, having seen that from the time of the Buddha’s appearance onwards their own gains and honor had declined, while—as described in the commentary on the Akkosasutta below—the Blessed One and his Saṅgha of bhikkhus were receiving vast and immeasurable gain and honor, became possessed by envy;
they gathered together and deliberated: "We [shall act] against the ascetic..."
"From the time Gotama appeared, our gains and honor have been lost; no one even acknowledges our existence anymore.
On what basis, then, is the world so deeply devoted to the ascetic Gotama and offers him such sublime honor and respect?
Thereupon, one said: "He is born of a high-born family, descended from the unbroken lineage of the Great Elect (Mahāsammata)."
Another [said], "Many wonders appeared at his birth";
another, "When he was brought to pay homage to Kāḷadevila, his feet turned around and rested upon the matted locks of that man";
and another, "At the time of the auspicious plowing ceremony, although midday had passed, the shade of the rose-apple tree did not shift and remained fixed while he lay within it."
One [person] says, "He is handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and perfected in physical form";

another says, "Having seen the signs of old age, sickness, death, and renunciation, he was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and went forth, abandoning his future sovereignty as a wheel-turning monarch.
Thus, the Blessed One’s equipment of merit and knowledge—accumulated over immeasurable time, not shared with others, and having reached the pinnacle of excellence—is peerless.
Not knowing the practice of self-effacement (*sallekha*), the unsurpassed power of the Buddhas such as the perfection of knowledge and abandonment,
and [merely] praising whatever reasons they themselves had seen or heard for their great respect toward the Blessed One while he was still living—
yet failing to find any reason for lack of respect— they thought: "By what means might we bring disrepute upon the ascetic Gotama?"
"We shall destroy his gain and honor. Among them, one sharp-witted man spoke thus:
"Friends, in this world of beings there are no beings who are not attached to the pleasure of women. This ascetic Gotama is handsome, god-like, and young;
having obtained a woman suitable for himself, he would surely become infatuated. Even if he were not to become infatuated, he would still be an object of suspicion to the people."
