“If this were to happen, come now, let us incite the female wanderer Sundarī in such a way that the ascetic Gotama’s ill repute shall spread across the earth.
When they heard this, the others said, “This has been well conceived by you; for if this is done, the ascetic Gotama will be overwhelmed by infamy.”
“Being unable to lift his head, he will flee in whatever direction possible.
Thinking thus, they all became of one mind and went into Sundarī’s presence to send her away in that manner. Seeing them, she asked, “Why have you come here together?
The non-Buddhist ascetics (titthiyas), remaining silent, sat down in a concealed spot at the edge of the monastery grounds. She went there.
Calling out again and again, she received no reply and asked, "What offense have we committed against you?
Why do you not give us an answer? For indeed, you look on with indifference while we are being harassed. She asked, "Who is harassing you?
[They replied,] "Do you not see, ascetic Gotama, who is harassing us and depriving us of our gains and honor?"
Having said, "We are wandering about," when it was asked, "What should be done by me there?
they replied, "In that case, you should go frequently to the vicinity of Jeta’s Grove and speak thus and so to the great multitude. She accepted this, saying, "Very well.
Therefore it was said: "The wanderers of other sects, unable to endure the honor shown to the Blessed One," and so forth.
In this context, *ussahasī* means "you are able. *Atthaṃ* means benefit or duty. *Kyāhaṃ* means "what am I?
Because those heretics, although they were strangers to her, acted as if they were relatives in order to win her over through the mere bond of ordination, they said:
"Sister, you are able to do what is beneficial for your relatives. Therefore, she [spoke to] the deer-creeper...
“Just as [a branch] clings to the foot, so too have I renounced even my life for the sake of my kinsmen,” she said.

To this he replied, “In that case”: “Since you say, ‘I have renounced even my life for your sake,’ and since you are in the prime of youth, beautiful and possessed of great fortune, therefore, by depending on you, [you may lead] the ascetic Gotama...”
Having said, "If misfortune should arise, you must act accordingly," they dismissed her with the words,
"Go frequently to Jetavana. That foolish woman, as if wishing to play a game of flower-garlands with a saw-toothed comb,
as if touching a fierce elephant in rut with her trunk, and as if grasping Death by the forehead, accepted the words of the sectarians.

Having taken garlands, perfumes, ointments, betel, mouth-fresheners, and so forth, she went toward Jetavana at the time when the great multitude was entering the city after hearing the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse. When asked, "Where are you going?
she replied, "To the presence of the ascetic Gotama; for I dwell with him in the same fragrant chamber. Thus she spoke in a certain place.
Having stayed in the monastery of the non-Buddhist sects, she descended early in the morning onto the path to Jetavana and was coming toward the city.
When asked, "Sundarī, where have you been? she replied, "I have come after staying with the ascetic Gotama in a single fragrant cell and delighting him with the pleasures of the defilements.
Thus it is said: "‘So be it, noble lady,’ said Sundarī."
Having heard this from those wanderers of other sects, the female wanderer went frequently to Jeta’s Grove.
After a few days had passed, the heretics gave money to some ruffians and said, "Go, kill Sundarī,
place her in a heap of flower refuse not far from the Perfumed Chamber of the ascetic Gotama, and then return."
They did exactly as instructed. Then the heretics, raising a clamor because they could not find Sundarī, informed the king.
When the king asked them, "Where do you suspect she might be? they replied, "In these days she has been staying at Jetavana;
we do not know her whereabouts there. "In that case, go and search for her there," the king commanded, and they were granted permission.
Taking his own attendants, he went to Jetavana; acting as if searching for her, he gathered the flower refuse, placed Sundarī’s body upon a bier, and brought it into the city, saying:
"The disciples of the ascetic Gotama, thinking, 'We shall conceal the evil deed committed by our Teacher,' have killed Sundarī and buried her among the flower refuse."
They informed the king. Without investigating the matter, the king said, "In that case, go and roam through the city.
They wandered through the streets of the city saying such things as, "Behold the deed of the recluses, the sons of the Sakyans," and then returned once more to the gate of the king's palace.
The king [saw] Sundarī’s body in the raw charnel ground.

Having raised a scaffold, he had it guarded. With the exception of the noble disciples, the majority of the inhabitants of Sāvatthī wandered about, both inside and outside the city, reviling the bhikkhus while saying such things as, "Behold the work of the recluses, the sons of the Sakyans!
Therefore it was said: "When those wanderers of other sects knew, 'Sundarī has indeed been seen [dead]'... and so forth.
In that context, *aññiṃsu* means they knew. *Vodiṭṭhā* means she was pointed out;
specifically, she was seen coming to and going from Jetavana, meaning she was frequently seen. *Parikhākūpe* means in the moat or ditch.
"That woman, O Great King, who is called Sundarī"—O Great King, she who is well-known and famous in this city for her beauty of form as "Sundarī."
The female wanderer. "She is not seen by us" means she, who was as dear to us as our own eyes or our very life, is now no longer seen.
"Just as she was placed" means having ordered men [to search], she was herself placed within the refuse of the flower-garden.
There is also a reading, "yathānikhātaṃ," which means the manner in which she was buried in the earth.
"From street to street" means from one road to another. "Road" (*vīthī*) refers to a thoroughfare that penetrates through. "Crossroads" (*siṅghāṭaka*) refers to a three-way junction.
"Those without shame" (*alajjino*) means those who do not feel shame; the meaning is that they are devoid of disgust for evil. "Immoral" (*dussīlā*) means lacking virtue.
"Of evil nature" (*pāpadhammā*) means having a base character and inferior conduct. "Liar" (*musāvādino*) means those who, while being immoral, claim, "We are virtuous."

“Liespokers” means those who speak falsehoods. “Unchaste ones” (abrahmacārino): they say this in derision, thinking, “These are indeed those who practice what is not noble by engaging in sexual intercourse.

“Practitioners of the Dhamma” (dhammacārino) means practitioners of wholesome states (kusala-dhamma). “Practitioners of equanimity” (samacārino) means those whose bodily actions and so forth are practiced with equanimity.

“Of beautiful nature” (kalyāṇadhammā) means having a lovely character; the connection [of the phrase] is “they will indeed claim to be [such]. This is due to its association with the word *nāma* (indeed/so-called).

"Indeed, they will acknowledge this here"—this is a statement referring to the future time. "Asceticism" (*sāmañña*) means the state of being an ascetic (*samaṇa*), the quality of having stilled evil.
"Brahminhood" (*brahmañña*) means the state of being excellent, the quality of having banished evil. "Why? means for what reason. "Departed" (*apagatā*) means gone away or fallen away.
They say "the duty of a man" with reference to the practice of sexual intercourse.

Then the bhikkhus reported that matter to the Blessed One. The Teacher said, “In that case, bhikkhus, you too should rebuke those men with this verse,” and he spoke the verse beginning with “A speaker of what is untrue. It was with reference to them that it was said:
“Then indeed, many... [omitted] ...men of low deeds for the sake of another. In that regard, bhikkhus, this is not... [omitted].
"The sound will endure for a long time"— this the Teacher said, knowing through his omniscience the eventual outcome of that infamy,
in order to comfort the monks. In this verse,
"one who speaks what is untrue" refers to one who, having not seen another's fault, utters a falsehood, speaking untruthfully and inaccurately of another.
"Speaking falsely": or "he who, having committed [an evil deed]," means one who, after having performed an evil deed, says, "I did not do this.
"After passing away they become equal" means that both these persons, having gone from here to the world beyond, become equal in their destination by way of entering hell.
For their destination alone is determined, but their lifespan is undetermined; for much indeed is the evil [they have done].
Having performed [great deeds], one is cooked in hell for a long time; having performed only a limited and trifling amount, one is cooked for only a very short time.
However, because the karma of both these [types of people] is inferior, it is said: "Inferior in their actions, O men, after passing away.
Furthermore, the word "after passing away" (*pecca*) connects with the preceding word "in the next world" (*parattha*); thus, "after passing away, in the next world."
The meaning is: having gone from here, those of inferior deeds become equal in the world beyond.
"Having mastered" means having learned. "Non-doers" means not doers of an offense.
"This was not done by these"—thus, it seems, this thought occurred to them: "Surely that evil deed was not committed by these ascetics, the sons of the Sakyans."
The followers of other sects, having made a proclamation, wandered throughout the entire city, thinking:
"Since these men show no sign of agitation even though we thus slander them with such unseemly and harsh words, and do not abandon their patience and gentleness,
but merely utter the Dhamma itself, saying 'the speaker of falsehood goes to hell,' they are merely swearing an oath."
"These recluses, sons of the Sakyans, without having investigated us, slander us; they speak as if they were swearing, uttering oaths.

Or rather, the meaning is: 'These people swear by making an oath against us in order to make known their own state of non-doers,' as it is said: 'He who, having done [an act], says "I did not do it," swears.'"

For as soon as those people heard the verse spoken by the Blessed One, through the power of the Buddha, trepidation overcame them and a sense of spiritual urgency arose: "This has not been seen by us with our own eyes;
yet what is heard may be so, or it may be otherwise. Moreover, these followers of other sects wish ill and harm upon them. Therefore...
“Out of faith, we should not say this; for ascetics are difficult to know. From that time forth, they desisted from that practice.
The king, for the purpose of discovering those by whom Sundarī had been killed, issued orders to his men.
Then those rogues, drinking liquor with those coins, began to quarrel with one another. Among them, one said to another: “You—”
“Having killed Sundarī all at once and thrown her among the flower-waste, you drink liquor with the coins obtained from that;
let it be, let it be! When the king’s men heard this, they seized those scoundrels and presented them to the king.
The king asked the scoundrels, “Was she killed by you? “Yes, Your Majesty. “By whom was she caused to be killed? “By the followers of other sects.”
“Sire,” they replied. The king summoned the heretics, had them confess the matter, and commanded:
“This Sundarī was caused to be killed by us who desired to bring disrepute upon that ascetic Gotama. There is no fault in Gotama, nor in his disciples;
the fault lies with us alone. Proclaim this as you wander through the city. They did so.
They did so. The great multitude believed it perfectly. They reviled the sectarians, and the sectarians incurred the punishment of death for their crimes against men.
From that time forth, the honor and respect shown to the Buddha and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus became exceedingly great.
The bhikkhus, filled with a sense of wonder and amazement, paid homage to the Blessed One and, being uplifted in mind, reported this to him.
Therefore it was said: “Then a great many bhikkhus... ‘That sound, venerable sir, has vanished.
But why did the Blessed One not inform the bhikkhus, “This is the work of the sectarians”? There is no purpose in informing the Noble Ones;
however, among worldlings, for those who might not believe it, that [informing] would lead to their long-term harm.
"It would lead to harm and suffering," he did not report it. Moreover, it is not the practice of the Buddhas to announce such a future matter.
For the Blessed One reveals the side of defilement only when prompted by others;
and since an action once committed cannot be undone, the Blessed One remained equanimous, overlooking both the false accusation and its cause.
He sat down. For this has been said:
"Not in the sky, nor in the midst of the ocean, nor by entering a cleft in the mountains,"
"There is no place in the world where one,
while remaining there, could be released from evil karma.
Having understood this meaning— that even harsh words uttered by foolish people for the sake of cutting through one's vital points [do not affect] one who is endowed with the power of patience—
Having understood in every way this meaning—that for the wise man there is nothing called "difficult to endure"—he uttered this *udāna*, which elucidates the power of patience through endurance.
In that regard: "Unrestrained people pierce with words, like arrows piercing an elephant gone into battle," [refers] to physical restraint and so forth.

Due to the absence of any restraint, undisciplined and untrained foolish people strike and pierce with the arrows of speech, like those who combat an elephant-nāga in battle when it has entered the fray with its own shafts and missiles;
this is their nature. Having heard harsh words uttered, a bhikkhu should endure them with an undisturbed mind.
Furthermore, a bhikkhu— removing that harsh speech uttered by those foolish people,
which was spoken by striking at his vital points and was untrue though presented as true— should, recollecting my "Saw Simile" instruction,
remain even slightly free from ill will and endure it, being one who perceives the fear inherent in saṃsāra, thinking, "This is the very nature of saṃsāra."
The meaning is that he should forgive by standing firm in the patience of forbearance.

Here it is asked: "But what was that deed, such that even the Teacher—who had diligently accumulated a vast store of merit over an immeasurable period of time—encountered such a cruel false accusation?
It is said in reply: This Blessed One, while still a Bodhisatta...
In a past birth, having been a rogue named Munāli, he lived as a companion to wicked people, wandering about with an abundance of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
One day, he saw the Paccekasambuddha named Surabhi putting on his robe to enter the city for alms.
At that moment, a certain woman was passing by not far from him. The rogue [thought], "He is unchaste..."

"He is this ascetic," he falsely accused him. Having been boiled in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years by that karma, and as a remainder of the ripening of that very same karma, even now, though he has become a Buddha, he has incurred false accusations on account of Sundarī.
Just as this was the case, so too were the false accusations against the Blessed One by Ciñcā Māṇavikā and other depraved women.
The sufferings encountered are all the remaining results of karma performed in the past, which are called "the remnants of karma.
For this has been said in the Apadāna:
"Near the Anotatta Lake, upon a delightful stone slab..."
In that place, radiant with various jewels and filled with various fragrant woods,
the Leader of the World sat surrounded by a great community of monks and there explained his own past karmas.
“Listen, O monks, to me regarding the deed that was performed by me;
even in my state as a Buddha, the fruit of that rag-like deed matures.
In former births, I was a rogue named Munāḷi.”
I falsely accused the fragrant Paccekabuddha, though he was innocent.
By the ripening of that kamma, I wandered for a long time in hell;
for many thousands of years, I experienced painful sensations.
“By the remainder of that karma, in this my final existence,
I received a false accusation on account of Sundarī.
There was a disciple named Nanda belonging to the Buddha Sabbābhibhū.”
Having falsely accused him, I wandered for a long time in hell.
For ten thousand years I wandered for a long time in hell;
having attained human status, I received much false accusation.
“By the remainder of that karma,
Ciñcā Māṇavikā falsely accused me with untruth before the assembly of people.
‘I was a learned brahmin, honored and revered.’”
In the Great Forest, I was teaching the mantras to five hundred students.
There, the terrifying seer Āgata, possessed of the five super-knowledges and great psychic power, arrived;
and seeing him, though he was innocent, I slandered him.
Then I said to my students, "This seer is a seeker of sensual pleasures.
Even as I spoke, the young brahmins gave their approval.
Then all those young brahmins followed him as he went begging from family to family.
They said to the great multitude, "This seer was a seeker of sensual pleasures.
By the ripening of that karma, all these five hundred bhikkhus received false accusations on account of Sundarika.
“In the past, for the sake of wealth, I killed my half-brother;
I threw him into a treacherous mountain ravine and crushed him with a stone.
By the ripening of that karma, Devadatta hurled a rock.”
“The thumb on my foot was crushed by a pebble from a stone.
‘Long ago, when I was a young boy playing on the great highway,
I saw a Paccekabuddha and threw a clod of earth onto his path.’”
“By the ripening of that karma, in this final existence,
Devadatta incited me to be assassinated for the sake of killing.
In the past, I was an elephant trainer [who killed] the supreme Paccekabuddha.”
As he was wandering for alms, I assailed him with an elephant.
Through the ripening of that karma, the elephant Nāḷāgiri,
becoming fierce, rushed toward the excellent city of Giribbaja.
“I was once a king, a ruler of the earth, and I struck men with a spear.
Through the ripening of that karma, I suffered intensely in hell.
By the remaining residue of that karma, now my entire [body]—”
He restored the skin on his foot, for indeed, karma does not perish.
“In the village of Kevaṭṭa, I was once a fisherman’s son;
seeing fish being killed, I felt a sense of joy.”
“By the ripening of that karma, there was pain in my head;
and all the Sakkas were slain when Viṭaṭūbha slaughtered them.
In the dispensation of Phussa, I reviled his disciples.”
"Eat and consume barley, but do not eat with attachment.
By the ripening of that karma, I ate barley for three months;
invited by a brahmin, I then dwelt in Verañjā.
“While wrestling was taking place, I struck down a son of the Mallas;
by the ripening of that deed, there was pain in my back.
I was once a physician and gave a purgative to the son of a merchant;”
Through the ripening of that kamma, I have this dysentery.
At that time, Jotipāla said to the Sugata Kassapa:
"Whence indeed is enlightenment for one who is shaven-headed? Enlightenment is exceedingly difficult to attain."
“By the ripening of that karma, I practiced many difficult austerities for six years at Uruvelā;
thereafter, I attained enlightenment.
It was not by this path that I attained supreme enlightenment.”
I sought the way by a wrong path, but was held back by my former karma.
"With merit and evil exhausted, free from all burning fevers,
sorrowless and without despair, I shall attain Nibbāna, free from taints."
“Thus the Conqueror prophesied, at the head of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,
having attained all the powers of direct knowledge, at the great lake Anotatta.
The commentary on the eighth sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Upasena Sutta 39.

Regarding the ninth sutta, "Of Upasena": here, *Upasena* is the name of that elder; however, because he was the son of the brahmin Vaṅganta, they also address him as "Vaṅganta-putta" (the son of Vaṅganta).
For this elder was the younger brother of the Venerable Sāriputta; having gone forth in the Dispensation, before the training rule had been laid down...
Having been a preceptor for two years since his own full ordination, he ordained a certain bhikkhu and went with him to attend upon the Blessed One.
When the Blessed One asked that bhikkhu about the status of his student, he replied according to the method set forth in the Khandhaka:
"Truly too quickly, foolish man, have you turned back toward abundance, namely, by forming a group."
Reproached like a noble steed struck by a goad, his mind filled with agitation, he thought:

"If I have now been reproached by the Blessed One on account of the assembly, may I yet become worthy of praise by relying on that very same assembly. With such zeal born within him, he undertook and practiced all the ascetic qualities (*dhutadhamma*);
having begun insight meditation (*vipassanā*), before long he became one possessed of the six supernormal knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*).
Having attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and become one whose taints were greatly exhausted, he made only those who maintained the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) his dependents;

together with them, he approached the Blessed One and, as described in the rule regarding sitting mats (*santhatasikkhāpada*), received praise from the Blessed One on account of his assembly, saying, "Upasena, this assembly of yours is indeed inspiring. [The Buddha declared: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost..."
"He has been placed in this foremost position among my disciples, the monks who are serene on all sides, namely Upasena Vaṅgantaputta," he was thus ranked among the eighty great disciples.
One day, having returned from his alms round after the meal, while his own pupils were each at their respective daytime resting places...
At the city gates, he took water from a water-pot, washed his feet, and cooled his limbs.
Spreading out a piece of leather, he sat for his midday rest in a daytime shelter and reflected upon his own virtues.
To him, those hundreds and thousands of qualities appeared in rapid succession, one after another. He thought, "While I am but a disciple, such as these are my virtues..."
“What kind of qualities does my Teacher possess? Thus he directed his attention toward the qualities of the Blessed One.

Thousands of millions of those qualities appeared before him in accordance with the power of his own knowledge. He reflected: “Such is the virtue of my Teacher; such is his Dhamma; such is his wisdom;
such is his liberation,” and so forth, as well as: “Thus indeed is that Blessed One: an Arahant, perfectly enlightened.”

And having recollected the virtues of the Teacher in accordance with their manifestation, he then recollected the virtues of the Dhamma by means of the words beginning with "well-expounded," and the virtues of the Noble Saṅgha by means of the words beginning with "well-practiced.
Thus the Great Elder sat, his mind delighted and gladdened as the manifold qualities of the Triple Gem became manifest, experiencing sublime joy and happiness. Regarding this matter:
In order to show this, it was said: “When the Venerable Upasena Vaṅgantaputta had gone into seclusion,” and so forth.
Therein, “gone into seclusion” (*raha-gatassa*) means having gone to a private place. “Retired” (*paṭisallīnassa*) means having become solitary.

“Thus a reflection arose in his mind” (*evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi*) means that a thought of the mind arose in this manner, which is now about to be described. “It is a gain for me indeed” (*lābhā vata me*): those which are these...
Human birth, the appearance of a Buddha, the attainment of faith, and so forth—“Oh, how great are these gains for me! Truly well-gained by me!

Whatever I have obtained within the Blessed One’s dispensation, such as going forth, full ordination, the Three Jewels, and attendance upon them—that has indeed been very well gained by me. Regarding this, he states the reason with the words, “And the Teacher is mine,” and so on.

In this context, he is called the Teacher (*satthā*) because he instructs beings as appropriate according to the truths pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal (*paramattha*).

He is the Blessed One (*bhagavā*) for reasons such as his possessing good fortune (*bhāgyavantatā*). He is the Worthy One (*arahant*) because he is far removed (*āraka*) from defilements, because he has slain the enemies that are the defilements, or because he has slain the spokes (*ara*) of the wheel of saṃsāra;

because he is worthy of receiving requisites and so forth (*paccayādīnaṃ arahattā*); and because he is devoid of secrecy (*rahābhāva*) regarding the performance of evil. He is the Fully Self-Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*)...

"Because he has awakened to all phenomena, he is the 'Perfectly Self-Awakened One' (Sammāsambuddho)"—this is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, should be taken from the description of the Recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*) in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Well-expounded" (*svākkhāto*) means well-proclaimed, spoken having made it exclusively leading to liberation. "Dhamma and Vinaya" refers to the teaching (*pāvacana*).

For it is called the *Dhamma-Vinaya* because it upholds those who practice according to the instructions from falling into the suffering of *saṃsāra*, and because it subdues the defilements such as lust.

"Fellow-practitioners" (*sabrahmacārino*) means those who walk together with, that is, practice the Noble Path—the Blessed One’s teaching—which is reckoned as "Brahma" in the sense of being supreme. "Virtuous" (*sīlavanto*)...
They are virtuous by virtue of the morality of the paths and fruits (*maggaphala-sīla*).

They are "possessors of noble qualities" (*kalyāṇadhamma*) because they possess noble, beautiful qualities such as concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; thus they are *kalyāṇadhamma*. By this, he demonstrates the excellent practice of the Saṅgha.
And by saying, "I too am one who fulfills the precepts," he shows: "Having gone forth myself, I am not one who engages in frivolous talk."

"Having been one who abounded in physical strength, I nevertheless fulfilled the fourfold virtue—beginning with restraint according to the Pātimokkha—making it unbroken, flawless, unspotted, untarnished, liberating, praised by the wise, and unadulterated;
thus I brought myself to the Noble Path itself. By this, [he shows] his attainment of the two lower fruits.
He illuminates [this]. For stream-enterers and once-returners are those who fulfill their duties regarding the precepts.

By the words "I am well-concentrated with a one-pointed mind," he shows that he is concentrated in every respect through concentration—distinguished as access and absorption—and that his mind is undistracted.
By this statement of fulfilling concentration, he illuminates his attainment of the third fruit. For non-returners...
"I am one who has brought concentration to fulfillment. I am an *arahant* whose taints are destroyed;

because the taints of sensual desire and the rest have been entirely destroyed, I am "one whose taints are destroyed" (*khīṇāsava*). For that very reason, with the fetters of existence completely exhausted, I am an *arahant* in the world with its devas due to being the most worthy of offerings.
By this, he shows that his task has been accomplished. "I am of great psychic power and great majesty" refers to the supernormal powers such as resolve and transformation.

Because I am endowed with mastery over the great [powers], I am possessed of great supernormal power (*mahiddhika*), and because of the attainment of the majesty of sublime merit and the majesty of noble qualities, I am possessed of great majesty (*mahānubhāva*).
By this, he illuminates his own possession of mundane higher knowledge (*abhiññā*) and the practice of the successive attainments of meditative dwelling (*anupubbavihārasamāpatti*).

For by mastery over the higher knowledges, the Noble Ones are possessed of great supernormal power through the accomplishment of whatever they desire; and by the excellence of their prior supporting conditions...
And because their mental continuums have been purified through various abidings and attainments, they possess great majesty.
"My life is auspicious": for one endowed with such virtues as virtue (sīla) and so forth, as long as this body endures, the welfare and happiness of beings increases;
thus, even my life is auspicious because it serves as a field of merit (puññakkhetta).

"Beautiful! A fortunate death!"—if this fivefold aggregate were to go out today, or even at this very moment, like a fire without fuel, then even that death known as final Nirvana without rebirth would be "fortunate" for me;

thus he demonstrates his state of equanimity in both circumstances. In this way, because the Great Elder was still saturated by the latent tendencies of joy and elation that had not yet been abandoned, [he spoke].
Filled with sublime joy through his great reverence for the Dhamma and his experience of the rapture of the Dhamma, he reflected.

While seated in the Fragrant Chamber, the Teacher, knowing this through his omniscient knowledge, uttered this *udāna* that reveals the state of equanimity regarding both life and death. Thus it is said: "Then the Blessed One... [omitted] ...uttered this *udāna*.
In that context, "that life does not burn" refers to the person whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), in regard to the future manifestation of the aggregates.
Because it is entirely non-existent, it does not burn or afflict;

or rather, even while life is currently proceeding, because all things are conditioned (*saṅkhata*), and because one has attained the abundance of mindfulness and wisdom, one is not afflicted due to being endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension in every respect.

For the blind worldling who associates with evil people, who is full of improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), who has not performed what is wholesome, and who has not made merit, [is tormented] by such thoughts as, "Alas, I have not done what is beautiful," and so forth.
"One who is tormented by remorse—his life is said to be tormented by that.

However, others—those who have not committed evil, those who have performed merit, the virtuous worldlings together with the seven types of trainees (sekha)—do not burn with subsequent regret because they have avoided the states that cause remorse and are endowed with the states that do not cause remorse;
thus, their lives are not tormented. As for those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), it need only be stated [that their lives are not tormented].
The commentary on the meaning has been made by way of the suffering of the process of existence (*pavatti-dukkha*) with respect to the phrase "it does not exist.

Regarding the phrase "he does not grieve at the end of death": at the end or conclusion known as death, or in the vicinity of death, he does not grieve because sorrow has been completely eradicated by the very path of non-returning (*anāgāmi-magga*).
He is indeed a wise one who has seen the state; he does not grieve in the midst of sorrow—such a person [possesses] non-covetousness and the other [virtues].
Because he has seen Nibbāna itself as the goal of the four Dhamma-footings, he is one who has "seen the path" (diṭṭhapada). Because he is endowed with steadfastness, he is "wise" (dhīra).

Although he stands in the midst of those beings who have not yet abandoned passion—who are called "sorrows" (sokā) because they are subject to grieving—or in the midst of the worldly conditions that cause sorrow, he does not grieve.
Now, in order to illustrate the complete absence of all causes for sorrow, he said:

“For one whose craving for existence is cut off,” and so forth. Therein, he for whom the craving for existence has been entirely cut off by the supreme path is “one whose craving for existence is cut off.
For that bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted and whose mind is peaceful through the total subsiding of the remaining defilements, “the wandering in birth is exhausted” refers to birth and the rest—
“The succession of the aggregates, and of the elements and sense-bases, occurring without interruption, is called ‘saṃsāra.
Saṃsāra, characterized as described above, has been specifically exhausted. Therefore, there is no further becoming for him, because of that.
For such a noble person (ariyapuggala), there is no future renewed existence; therefore, their wandering through births (jātisaṃsāra) is exhausted.
Why, then, is there no renewed existence for them? Because they have cut off craving for existence and possess a peaceful mind—it should be stated by turning the argument back in this way.
Alternatively, the meaning should be construed as: "The wandering through births is utterly exhausted; for that very reason, there is no renewed existence for them."
The commentary on the ninth sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Sāriputta-upasama-sutta:

In the tenth [sutta], "they become peaceful for themselves" refers to the complete subsiding of one's own defilements by means of the supreme path, which serves as the cause for reaching the pinnacle of the perfections of a disciple.
For the Venerable Sāriputta, having personally witnessed the suffering, distress, and fever born of the defilements such as lust in beings whose defilements are not yet stilled—
as well as the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, and so forth, which have the formations of defilement as their cause—

and having weighed against this the suffering rooted in the cycle of existence for those same beings in the past and future, he felt compassion; and even while he himself was still an ordinary person (*puthujjana*),...
Or, having recollected the signs of defilement experienced or the no small amount of suffering endured, he frequently reflects upon the subsiding of his own defilements, thinking:
"The defilements that were the cause of such great suffering have now been well-abandoned by me. And while reflecting, he considers:
"So many of these defilements have been stilled by the path of stream-entry; so many by the path of once-returning..."

"so many have been stilled by the path of non-returning, so many by the path of arahantship"—thus he reviews the specific state of the defilements having been stilled by the respective knowledges of those paths. Therefore it is said: "reviewing his own peace. Others say:
"The Elder, having attained the fruition attainment of arahantship and reviewed it, [thought]: 'Indeed, this... "

Others, however, say: "He frequently contemplates peace thus: 'The state of being cooled arises from the object of the unconditioned element which is absolute peace, and because of the complete subsiding of the defilements within himself. Still others say:
"'Peace' here refers specifically to the supreme fruit (agga-phala) born at the conclusion of the subsiding of all defilements without exception; he sits contemplating that."
"Having understood this matter": having understood in every aspect the meaning— namely,

the abandonment of defilements or the fruit of the highest attainment (aggaphala), which is unique among disciples and not shared by others, and which serves as the cause for the Venerable Sāriputta’s great wisdom and so forth,
and which is described here by way of tranquility (upasama)— he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) that illuminates its power.

In this context, "one whose mind is tranquil and peaceful" (*upasantasantacitta*) means one whose mind has become peaceful precisely because it is tranquil; thus, he is "one whose mind is tranquil and peaceful.

For although the mind is tranquil due to the suppression of defilements by meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), it is not called "tranquil and peaceful" in an absolute sense, because that tranquility is not final.
It is not so, however, in the case of the supreme path (*aggamagga*). By that [path], it is indeed absolutely...
Because the defilements have been utterly eradicated, the mind of the Arahant has already been stilled by the lower paths of serenity and insight through the non-recurrence of defilements;
it is therefore called "peacefully peaceful" (*upasantasanta*) precisely because of its state of ultimate peace. Thus it is said:
"His mind is peaceful and, having become peaceful, is calm; thus he is 'one whose mind is peacefully peaceful'. Alternatively, *upasantam*...
“Upasama” (calming) is so called; therefore, the phrase “of one whose mind is calmed and tranquil” means “of one whose mind is tranquil through absolute calming.

Alternatively, although there is a complete subsiding of all defilements for all those whose taints are destroyed, the specific subsiding of defilements belonging to the General of the Dhamma is distinguished by being unique among disciples and serving as the cause for reaching the pinnacle of disciple-perfection-knowledge.
To demonstrate this, the Teacher spoke, distinguishing it by the term "tranquil" (*upasanta*):

“of one whose mind is tranquil and peaceful” (*upasantasantacittassa*). Herein, this is the meaning: that which is exceedingly or firmly peaceful is "tranquil" (*upasantam*); being tranquil through that very tranquility, it is "peaceful and tranquil" (*upasantasantam*);
one who possesses such a mind is [described as] "one whose mind is tranquil and peaceful"—the rest is exactly as before. For it is thus:

The Blessed One has praised and extolled Sāriputta in many ways, saying: “Bhikkhus, Sāriputta is of great wisdom, of broad wisdom, of joyful wisdom, of swift wisdom, of sharp wisdom, and of penetrative wisdom,” and so forth. “Of one whose guide is severed”:

the “guide” (netti) is called the craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*), because it leads one through the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*); he by whom that guide is severed is “one whose guide is severed. Of him...

"Of one whose net is cut" means one who has abandoned craving. "He is freed from Māra’s bonds": such a person, having thus completely exhausted the fetters of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*), is liberated from all of Māra’s bonds;
there remains nothing further for him to do for the sake of being released from Māra’s bonds.
Therefore, the General of the Dhamma reflects upon his own peace. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the Tenth Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Meghiya Chapter is also finished.
5. The Soṇa Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Piyatarasutta 41.
Regarding the phrase "together with Queen Mallikā": it means together with his chief queen named Mallikā.

"Having gone to the top of the excellent palace" means having gone to the upper story of the excellent palace. "Is there anyone dearer than himself? means: is there anyone at all who is dearer than himself?
"Is there anyone dearer to you than yourself?"—he asks the queen, "What do you have?
Why does he ask? For she was the daughter of a poor garland-maker in Sāvatthī.
One day, having taken some cakes from a shop, she was going toward the flower garden thinking, "I will eat them," when she encountered [the Buddha] on the path, surrounded by the community of monks.
Seeing the Blessed One entering for alms, she, with a heart full of faith, gave it to him.
The Teacher indicated that he wished to sit in such a place. The Elder Ānanda spread out a robe and offered it to him.
The Blessed One sat there, ate the cake, rinsed his mouth, and manifested a smile. The Elder—
“Venerable sir, what will be the result of this gift? she asked. “Today, Ānanda, she has given the first meal to the Tathāgata;
today itself she will become the chief queen of the King of Kosala, beloved and pleasing.
And on that very day, the king, having fought with his nephew at Kāsigāma and being defeated, fled.
Having arrived and entering the city, thinking, "I shall wait for the arrival of the army," he entered that flower garden.
Seeing that the king had come, she performed her duties for him.
The king, being pleased with her service, summoned her father, granted him great authority, had him installed in the inner apartments, and appointed her to the position of chief queen.
He established her [in that position]. Then one day the king thought: "I have granted her great authority;
what if I were to ask her, 'Who is dear to you? If she says, 'You, Great King, are dear to me,' and then asks me in return, I shall say to her, 'You alone are dear to me as well.
Thus he intended to create mutual confidence between them.
Engaging in friendly conversation, he questioned her.

But the queen was wise, a devotee of the Buddha and a devotee of the Saṅgha; thinking, "This question must not be answered by looking to the king's face," she spoke exactly as it was: "Great King, there is no one else for me..."

"More dear," he said. Having spoken thus, desiring to bring the matter she had explained into the King's direct experience through a skillful means, she questioned the King in the same manner as she had been questioned herself:
"But, Great King, is there anyone else more dear to you than yourself?
The King, unable to turn back because her speech was characterized by such eloquence and grace, replied:
He too, speaking according to the very characteristics of his own body, gave an answer exactly as the queen had given hers.
Having answered, because of his weakened physical constitution, he thought thus: "I am a king, a lord of the earth, who dwells having conquered a vast circle of the earth;
for me, it is indeed appropriate to say, 'I see nothing else dearer than myself.'"
But this low-born woman, having been placed by me in a high position, does not love me as her master;
she says in my very presence, ‘I am dearer than myself. How hard-hearted she is! Being thus displeased, he rebuked her, saying, “Are not the Three Jewels dearer to you?
The queen replied, “O King, even the Three Jewels are [dearer] to me than myself.”
“I cherish [others] because I desire the happiness of heaven and the happiness of liberation; therefore, my own self is dearer to me,” he said.
Indeed, this entire world cherishes others solely for its own sake: even when desiring a son, one desires him thinking, “He will support me in my old age”;
a daughter, thinking, “She will expand my lineage”; and a wife, thinking, “[She will serve] my feet.”
“...will attend upon me,” and likewise other relatives, friends, and kin according to their respective duties;
thus, perceiving only his own self-interest, the world holds others dear. This was the queen’s intention.
Then the king thought: “This Mallikā is skillful, wise, and discerning; she says, ‘I am indeed dearer to me than myself.’”
“Even for me, my own self appears as something more dear; well then, I shall inform the Teacher of this matter, and I will hold to it exactly as the Teacher explains it.
Having reflected thus, he approached the presence of the Teacher and reported that matter to him. Therefore it was said: “Then King Pasenadi of Kosala... [more dear].”

"Having understood this matter": having fully realized this matter spoken by the king—that "in the world, for all beings, one's own self is dearer than anything else"—he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) which elucidates that very point.
Therein, "having traversed all directions with his mind" means having followed all ten directions without exception with his consciousness by way of searching.
"He did not find anywhere anyone dearer than himself" means he found no other who was more exceedingly dear than himself.
Suppose a man, searching with all his effort in every direction and in every place, were to neither find nor see [anything].
Thus, because one’s own self is dear to each individual, and because no one is found to be dearer than oneself, the self alone is dear to each and every being individually and separately.
Therefore, "one who desires their own self should not harm another."
Since every living being thus loves themselves, desiring their own happiness and being averse to suffering,
therefore one who desires their own welfare and seeks their own benefit and happiness should not harm, nor kill, nor even afflict another being— down to a tiny ant or a termite—
with hands, clods of earth, sticks, or other means. For when suffering is inflicted upon another by oneself...
As it were, that [kamma] moves from there and reappears within oneself at a later time. For this is the natural law (*dhammatā*) of kamma.
The commentary on the first sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Appāyuka-sutta*.
42. "The second 'wonderful thing,' venerable sir": this too should be understood as being by way of the wonder of censure, just as in the *Meghiya-sutta*.
"As long as [their] lifespan is short" means however much their life is limited; the sense is that their life is exceedingly brief.
"Seven days old" (*sattāhajāta*): one born after seven days is "seven-days-old. In "at that seven-days-old [time]," the meaning is on the seventh day of the one who was born. "The Tusita realm..."
"He was reborn" means he was reborn into the Tusita host of devas by way of taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

It is said that one day, after his meal, while the Elder was sitting in his daytime meditation place, he brought to mind the glory of the Blessed One’s physical body—the supreme object of sight, adorned with the primary and secondary marks and having attained the pinnacle of beauty—and thought: "O!"
Experiencing a sublime sense of rapture and joy, thinking, "The perfection of the Buddhas' form-body is beautiful to behold, serene on all sides, and heart-stealing," he reflected thus:
"Even a son who is ugly becomes pleasing and attractive to his mother as soon as he is born;
what kind of beauty would the Blessed One possess if Queen Mahāmāyā, the mother of the Buddhas, were still alive?"
“If joy and gladness had arisen at the sight of his form, it would have been a great loss for me, my noble mother the queen,
that she passed away when the Blessed One was only seven days old. Having thought thus, he approached the Blessed One and,
reporting his own reflections while censuring her death, said, “It is wonderful, Bhante,” and so forth.
However, some say: "Although Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī requested the Blessed One for the going forth with great effort, she was refused;

but when she requested it through me by means of a stratagem, the Blessed One granted her the going forth and full ordination on the condition that she accept the eight weighty rules (garudhamma). Having accepted those rules, she obtained the going forth and full ordination."
Having produced a second assembly for the Blessed One, she became the condition for a fourth assembly.
If, however, the Blessed One’s mother, Queen Mahāmāyā, were still living, then these two noble sisters of the Khattiya clan, being together, would have graced this Dispensation;
and the Blessed One, out of great reverence for his mother, would have granted the going-forth into homelessness in the Dispensation for women.
“[The Elder said: ‘He would have permitted full ordination quite easily; however, because of her short lifespan, it was accomplished with difficulty.
It was with this intention that the Elder spoke to the Blessed One, saying, ‘It is wonderful, venerable sir,’ and so forth. This is not the reason.
For when the Blessed One permitted the going forth into his own dispensation for his mother or for any other woman, he did so only as something weighty.
Having done so, he grants permission; it is not for the sake of making light [of the offense], but out of a desire for its long endurance.

Others, however, say: "The Elder, having brought to mind the infinite and immeasurable qualities of a Buddha—such as the ten powers and the four grounds of self-confidence—which are not shared by others, [reflected]:
'How can one carry in one's womb the Teacher, the foremost person in the world, who possesses such great majesty?'"
"It is improper to think that the Mother of the Buddha, having carried him for ten months, will become an attendant to anyone else. Why?
Because this is entirely worthy of the Teacher’s virtues: that seven days after the Blessed One was born, his mother passed away, and having passed away, she was reborn among the Tusita devas.
Having thus conceived a sense of wonder and amazement, he [the Bodhisatta] reflected upon this thought of his own.
“Reporting to the Blessed One, he spoke these words beginning with, ‘It is wonderful, Bhante.

But because it is a natural law (*dhammatā*) that the Bodhisatta’s mother passes away seven days after the Bodhisattas are born, the Teacher, wishing to illustrate that natural law, said, ‘It is even so, Ānanda,’ and so forth. And this is the natural law:”
Because all Bodhisattvas, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), are reborn in the Tusita heaven;

and having remained there for the duration of their lifespan, at the end of that life, they are requested by the devas of the ten thousand world-systems who have assembled together to take rebirth in the human world in order to attain full enlightenment—
just as [they choose] the time, the island, the country, and the family— [the Bodhisatta] likewise chooses the lifespan of his mother.

Having observed these, they take rebirth; likewise, this Blessed One, while still a Bodhisatta dwelling in the Tusita heaven, performed the five great observations and, determining that his mother’s lifespan was limited to ten months plus seven days, thought:
"This is the time for me to take rebirth; it is now fitting to be born."
Having known [the time], she took rebirth; therefore, this should be understood as being according to the established custom of all Bodhisattvas.
Thus the Blessed One said: "For, Ānanda, the mothers of Bodhisattvas have short lifespans," and so forth.
In that context, "passing away" means they pass away solely through the exhaustion of their aforementioned lifespan, not due to the conditions of childbirth.
A place where Bodhisattas have dwelt during their final existence is like a shrine-house; it is not fit for the use of others.
Furthermore, it is impossible to remove the Bodhisatta’s mother and install another in the position of chief queen;
therefore, the lifespan of the Bodhisatta’s mother is exactly that long, and thus she passes away at that time. Indeed, this is the very meaning [of the passage].
Having made this resolve, the great Bodhisattvas perform the fifth great observation.
At what stage of life, then, do they pass away? It is at the middle stage of life. For in the first stage of life, beings' desire and lust for their own personal existence (*attabhāva*) are powerful;
consequently, women who have conceived at that time generally find it difficult to protect the fetus.
They are not able [to conceive]. If they were to conceive, the pregnancy would be fraught with many complications.

However, when two-thirds of middle age have passed and one enters the third stage, the physical basis (*vatthu*) becomes clear; when the physical basis is clear, the children born therein are free from disease.
Therefore, the mothers of Bodhisattvas, having experienced prosperity during their early years, [conceive] in the third stage of middle age.
"Having given birth, they pass away.

"Having understood this matter" means: having understood that for the mother of a Bodhisatta and for all other beings, the individual existence (attabhāva) ends in death at the conclusion of its lifespan;
and by way of elucidating that point, [the Blessed One spoke] to inspire enthusiasm for the practice of blameless conduct.
He uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*).
In that context, "whosoever" (*ye keci*) is an indefinite designation. "Have arisen" (*bhūtā*) means those who have been reborn. "Will arise" (*bhavissanti*) means they will be reborn in the future.
The word *vā* has the sense of an alternative; the word *api* has the sense of inclusion. By these, it includes those who are currently being reborn as well. To this extent—
It encompasses beings included within the three periods of time—past, present, and future—without exception.
Furthermore, womb-born beings are called "existent" (*bhūta*) from the moment they emerge from the womb; prior to that, they are called "will-be" (*bhavissanti*).

Moisture-born and spontaneously born beings are called "existent" after the moment of rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-citta*); prior to that, they are called "will-be" by virtue of the state of existence in which they are to arise.

"Named. Or alternatively, all those who have come into being by way of a present existence are "named as having been," while those who will exist by way of renewed existence in the future are "named as about to be.
Those whose taints are exhausted are "named as having been," for they have truly come to be and will not exist again; others besides them are "named as about to be.

"All shall go, leaving the body behind"—all, according to the aforementioned divisions, by way of all existences, birth-sources, destinations, stations of consciousness, abodes of beings, and so forth.
Beings, divided into many different classes, will abandon and cast off their own bodies and go to the next world;
but the Asekhas [attain] Nibbāna. Here he shows that there is no one who is not subject to death.
"The skillful one, knowing that to be the ruin of all beings"—that is, the ruin, the loss, the death of every single being. Or rather, of every being...

"Having known destruction, dissolution, and perishability"— that is, having understood this through the recollection of death (*maraṇānussati*) or through the mental attention to impermanence (*aniccatāmanasikāra*),
one who is skilled and wise; "should live the holy life ardent (*ātāpiyo*)"— meaning that while performing the work of insight (*vipassanā*),
being endowed with the energy termed "ardent," having initiated vigor by means of the fourfold right effort (*sammappadhāna*), [one should practice] the means for completely transcending death.
The meaning is that one should practice the holy life of the path; one should proceed [upon it].
The commentary on the second sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Suppabuddha the Leper Sutta.
43. Regarding the third [case]: "In Rājagaha there was a leper named Suppabuddha. There was a certain man named Suppabuddha in Rājagaha;
he was a leper whose body was severely disfigured by the disease of leprosy.
"A poor man among men" means that among all the people in Rājagaha, he was the most destitute. For he [lived on] scraps of rags discarded by people in places such as rubbish heaps and cesspools.

Having sewn [rags] together, he wears them; taking an alms-bowl, he goes from house to house and lives depending on the dregs of rinsings and leftover food obtained there, yet even that he does not obtain in sufficient quantity due to the condition of his past deeds. Therefore it is said:
"a poor human being. A wretched human being (*manussakapaṇo*) is one who has reached the state of extreme wretchedness among humans. A miserable human being (*manussavarāko*)...
He was exceedingly dejected due to being despised and insulted by people. "In a great assembly" means in a great assembly of both monks and lay followers.
It is said that one day, the Blessed One, surrounded by a great community of monks, entered Rājagaha for alms; then, among the monks—
Having made alms-food easy to obtain, he returned from his alms-round after the meal and set out accompanied by a few bhikkhus.

Waiting for the arrival of those lay devotees who had given the gift as well as the remaining bhikkhus, he stood in a certain delightful spot within the city itself. At that very moment, bhikkhus arrived there from various directions.

They surrounded the Blessed One. The lay followers (*upāsaka*) also approached the Blessed One, thinking, "Having heard the expression of appreciation (*anumodanā*), we shall pay our respects and return.
There was a great assembly. The Blessed One made a gesture indicating that he wished to sit down.

Immediately, they prepared a seat worthy of a Buddha. Then the Blessed One [sat] upon it, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*) and embellished by the eighty minor characteristics (*anubyañjana*).
Shining with a halo of fathom-wide radiance, emitting the six-colored rays of a Buddha—
blue, yellow, red, white, orange, and brilliant— through his incomparable glory of physical form,
he illuminated that entire region like the full moon surrounded by a host of stars; thus, seated upon the excellent Buddha-throne prepared for him, he was surrounded by a multitude of bhikkhus.
Having sat down upon the surface of the ruby, like a maned lion letting out a lion’s roar, he taught the Dhamma with a Brahma-voice as melodious as the song of the karavīka bird.
The bhikkhus there were also few in desire, contented, secluded, unattached, energetic, resolute, reprovers of evil, censurers of sin,
speakers of truth, patient in speech, and endowed with virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation.
Endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation, they donned robes made of rags from the dust-heap that were the color of a cloud;
like well-trained scent-elephants, they surrounded the Blessed One and listened to the Dhamma with attentive ears.

The lay followers as well, dressed in clean lower garments and clean upper robes, having offered great alms-giving in the morning, honored the Blessed One with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.

Having honored and paid homage to the Blessed One, having shown their reverence to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and having surrounded the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, they listened to the Dhamma with great care, their hands and feet restrained and their ears attentive. Therefore it was said:
“At that time, the Blessed One was seated, teaching the Dhamma, surrounded by a large assembly.”
But Suppabuddha, overcome by the weakness of hunger, while wandering in search of food, entered a street;
seeing from afar that great gathering of people, he thought, "Why has this great multitude gathered?
Surely food is being distributed here, I think; perhaps if I go there, I might find something to eat or drink."

Thinking, "Could it be obtained? he developed a longing and went there; there he saw the Blessed One—inspiring, beautiful to behold, serene, having attained the highest self-mastery and tranquility, tamed, guarded, with senses calmed, well-composed, surrounded by that assembly, teaching the Dhamma.
Having seen him, [he was moved] by the ripening of the merit accumulated in previous births.
Being urged by the excellence of the supporting conditions (*upanissaya-sampatti*), he thought, "What if I too were to listen to the Dhamma? and sat at the edge of the assembly.
It was with reference to him that it was said: "Suppabuddha the leper saw [them]... [and so on]... and sat down right there to one side, thinking, 'I too shall hear the Dhamma.'"
"Sabbāvantam" means "possessing all," that is, possessing all types of persons, such as those who are inferior and so forth; the meaning is that he leaves nothing therein unexhausted.
They also read it as "sabbavantam. "By the mind" (cetasā) means by the consciousness associated with the Buddha-eye.

For knowledge is indicated here by way of the headword "mind"; therefore, the meaning is: by the knowledge of the underlying tendencies (*āsaya-anusaya-ñāṇa*) and by the knowledge of the degrees of the faculties in others (*indriya-paropariyatta-ñāṇa*).
“He encompassed their minds with his own mind” means that he mentally attended to the minds of that assembly one by one, delimiting them individually;
he scrutinized them. “Capable of understanding the Dhamma” means capable of attaining the Dhamma of the path and its fruits;

the meaning is that he was endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*). “This thought occurred to him”: although this Suppabuddha had indeed offended the Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhin...
He has become such a person; however, the support for the path and its fruits shines within his heart alone, like a gold coin covered by dust.
Therefore, it was said that he is "easily made to understand. Thus he said: "This one here is capable of understanding the Dhamma.
"Graduated discourse" means: after giving comes virtue, after virtue comes heaven, and after heaven comes the Path.

Such is the discourse on the successive order. For the Blessed One, having first shown the gratification together with its cause, then—in order to detach beings from it—reveals the danger through various methods;
and for those whose hearts are agitated by hearing of that danger, he shows the turning away (vivaṭṭa) by way of elucidating the qualities of renunciation.

"Discourse on giving": this is indeed the source of all happiness, the root of all prosperity, the foundation of all wealth, the refuge, the shelter, the destination, and the ultimate resort for one who has fallen into adversity.

In both this world and the next, there is no support, foundation, prop, refuge, shelter, destination, or ultimate resort equal to giving. For in the sense of being a support, it is like a lion-throne made of jewels.
In the sense of being a foundation, it is like the great earth; in the sense of being an object of support, it is like a supporting rope;

in the sense of crossing over suffering, it is like a ship; in the sense of providing consolation, it is like a hero in battle; in the sense of protection from fear, it is like a city surrounded by a moat;

in the sense of being unsullied by the stains of stinginess and so forth, it is like a lotus; in the sense of consuming those [stains], it is like fire; and in the sense of being difficult to assail...
It is a venomous serpent in the sense of being free from fear; a lion in the sense of possessing strength; a white bull in the sense of being considered auspicious;

and the king of horses, Valāhaka, in the sense of bringing one to the land of security. For in this world, giving bestows royal glory, the prosperity of a wheel-turning monarch, the prosperity of Sakka, the prosperity of Māra, the prosperity of Brahmā, the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple, and the knowledge of the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha.
He spoke a discourse connected with the virtues of giving, such as "it bestows the knowledge of perfect enlightenment.
Since one who gives a gift is able to undertake moral discipline (*sīla*), he spoke on the discourse of moral discipline immediately after the discourse on giving.
Regarding the discourse on moral discipline: this moral discipline is indeed a refuge, a foundation, a support, a protection, and a shelter for sentient beings.

It is the ultimate refuge. Indeed, for the attainments of success in this world and the next, there is no support, foundation, object of reliance, shelter, cave, goal, or ultimate resort equal to virtue (*sīla*);
there is no ornament equal to the ornament of virtue; there is no flower equal to the flower of virtue;
there is no fragrance equal to the fragrance of virtue. For that which is adorned with the ornament of virtue and bedecked with the flowers of virtue—
"Even the world with its gods never tires of gazing upon one who is anointed with the fragrance of virtue"—speaking thus, he delivered a discourse connected with the qualities of virtue (*sīlaguṇa*).
Furthermore, in order to show that this heaven is obtained by relying on this very virtue, he spoke next on the subject of heaven (*saggakathā*).
Regarding "the subject of heaven": heaven is indeed desirable, lovely, and pleasing; here there is constant play and constant prosperity is obtained.
The Cātumahārājika devas obtain divine pleasure and divine prosperity for nine million years;
the Tāvatiṃsa devas [obtain it] for thirty-six million years—such is the discourse connected with the qualities of heaven.
Indeed, the mouth of the Buddhas never tires of speaking of the excellence of heaven. And this has been said: "In many ways..."
“Monks, I would indeed speak a discourse on heaven,” and so forth.
Having thus enticed him with a discourse on heaven together with its cause, he then—like one cutting off the trunk of an elephant that has been decorated—spoke in order to show:
“This heaven, too, is impermanent and unstable; no craving or passion should be placed therein.”
“Sensual pleasures have little gratification, much suffering, and much despair;
herein the danger is greater”—in such a manner he spoke of the danger (*ādīnava*), the wretchedness (*okāra*), and the defilement (*saṅkilesa*) of sensual pleasures. Therein, "danger" means fault.
"Wretchedness" means a base nature; the meaning is that it is practiced by the inferior and not practiced by the superior, being of a lowly nature. "Defilement" means...
By these [defilements], there is the defiling of beings in saṃsāra. Therefore he said: “Alas, beings are indeed defiled!
Having thus threatened them with the danger of sensual desire, he revealed the advantage in renunciation and illuminated and praised the virtues of going forth, of the jhānas, and so forth.
Regarding the phrases beginning with “with a ready mind”: “ready mind” means a mind that is workable; this is because of the teaching that had proceeded previously.
Because of the absence of mental defects such as lack of faith (*assaddhiya*), the mind is "workable" (*kammaniya*) by way of becoming a fit vessel for the higher instructions;
the meaning is that it is a mind capable of performing the task. Because of the disappearance of defilements such as wrong view and conceit, the mind is "pliable" (*mudu*).

Because of the absence of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and so forth, the mind is "unobstructed" (*vinīvaraṇa*). Through the application of sublime rapture and gladness (*pīti-pāmojja*) in right practice, the mind is "exultant" (*udagga*). In this context, through the perfection of faith...
The connection is: "when the Blessed One knew that his mind was serene.

Alternatively, "a ready mind" (*kallacitta*) means a healthy mind due to the departure of sensual desire. "A pliant mind" (*muducitta*) means a mind that is not rigid due to loving-kindness, owing to the departure of ill-will.
"An unobstructed mind" (*vinīvaraṇacitta*) refers to its state of non-distraction due to the departure of restlessness and remorse.
"Not with a closed mind. "Exalted mind" means a mind that is not dejected due to the removal of sloth and torpor, by way of being uplifted.
"Serene mind" means a mind inclined toward right practice due to the removal of doubt.
"Then" means afterwards. "Self-proclaimed" means proclaimed by oneself, taken up after having been raised up by oneself; [it is] by means of self-existent knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*).
"Seen by oneself" means not shared with others. And what is that? It is the teaching on the Noble Truths.
For this very reason it is said: "Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. This is indeed the demonstration of the true nature of the truths;
therefore, the Noble Truths should be explained in this place. These have been stated in full detail in all their aspects in the *Visuddhimagga*.
These points are to be understood according to the method already stated.
By the passage beginning with "Just as if," etc., he demonstrates Suppabuddha’s abandonment of the defilements and the arising of the Noble Path by means of a simile.
"Apagatakāḷakaṃ" means free from blackness. "Sammadeva" means indeed thoroughly. "Rajanaṃ" refers to the various kinds of dye, such as blue, yellow, red, madder, and so forth.
"Should receive" means he would take it up; he would become radiant. "In that very seat" means in that very sitting posture.
By this, his state of swift insight, his possession of sharp wisdom, his pleasant path of practice, and his quick direct knowledge are demonstrated.

"Dustless and stainless" means dustless due to the absence of the dust of passion and so forth that leads to rebirth in the states of misery, and stainless due to the departure of the stains of views and doubt without remainder.

“Free from stain” (*vītamala*): It is “dustless” (*viraja*) by virtue of being free from the dust of defilements to be abandoned by the first path, and it is “free from stain” by virtue of the departure of the fivefold stains of immoral conduct.
By “the Dhamma-eye” (*dhammacakkhu*), the path of stream-entry is intended.
To show the manner of its arising, it is said: “Whatever is subject to origination, all that is subject to cessation. For that [path] has cessation as its object.
It arises penetrating conditioned phenomena precisely by way of their functions.
Herein, this is the correlation with the simile: the mind should be regarded as like a cloth;

the state of the cloth being defiled by adventitious stains is like the state of the mind being defiled by the stains of lust and so forth; and the washing-board is like the progressive discourse (*anupubbikathā*).

Faith is like water; just as one who washes a cloth first thoroughly wets it with water and then rubs it with cow-dung lye to remove stains, so too, having moistened the mind with the water of faith and loosened its defects by means of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, one exerts energy in purifying the mind through the method of faith and the other factors. By that application, the stains depart from the cloth.
The suppression of defilements through the exertion of energy is like the removal of dye; the Noble Path is like the dye itself;
and the cleansing of the mind whose defilements have been suppressed by means of the Path is like the brightening of a clean cloth by that dye.
Thus, Suppabuddha, sitting at the edge of the assembly, heard the teaching of the Dhamma and attained the fruit of stream-entry.

Having realized the qualities he had attained within himself, wishing to announce them to the Teacher but unable to venture into the midst of the assembly, he followed the Teacher after the multitude had paid their respects and turned back;
when the Blessed One had entered the monastery, he too went to the monastery.
At that moment, Sakka, the king of the gods, thought: "This leper Suppabuddha has [attained] through himself..."
Knowing that he wished to make manifest the virtues he had acquired in the Teaching, [the deity] thought, "I shall test him," and having gone there, stood in the air and said this:
"Suppabuddha, you are a poor man, a wretched man, a miserable man.
I will give you immeasurable wealth; [but tell me: 'The Buddha is not the Buddha, the Dhamma is not the Dhamma, the Saṅgha is not the Saṅgha.'"
“Say: ‘I have no need for the Buddha, I have no need for the Dhamma, I have no need for the Saṅgha.
Then he said to him, “Who are you? “I am Sakka, king of the gods. “You blind fool, you shameless one!
You are not fit to converse with me, you who speak what should not be spoken; moreover, you call me ‘one who is miserable, poor, and wretched.’”
"Why do you say this? Am I not the legitimate son of the Lord of the World? I am neither miserable, nor poor, nor wretched;
rather, having attained happiness through supreme bliss, I am one who possesses great wealth. Having said this, he spoke:
"The wealth of faith, the wealth of virtue, and the wealth of moral shame and dread of blame;"
“Learning, wealth, and generosity, and wisdom is indeed the seventh treasure.
Whoever possesses these treasures—whether woman or man—is called ‘not poor’; their life is not in vain.”
“In this regard, I possess these seven noble treasures. For those who possess these treasures are certainly not called ‘poor’ by the Buddhas or the Paccekabuddhas.
Having heard his words, Sakka left him on the road and went into the presence of the Teacher, where he reported all of that speech and its reply.
Then the Blessed One said to him: “Sakka, it is not possible for such as those—”
“Even for a hundred or a thousand pieces of gold, you should cause the leper Suppabuddha to declare: ‘The Buddha is not the Buddha; the Dhamma is not the Dhamma; the Saṅgha is not the Saṅgha.
Then the leper Suppabuddha went into the presence of the Teacher, and after being greeted by the Teacher, he reported the qualities he had attained. Thus it is said: “Then Suppabuddha...”
“A leper who has seen the Dhamma,” and so forth.
Therein, “one who has seen the Dhamma” (*diṭṭhadhammo*) means one by whom the Dhamma of the Noble Truths has been seen; thus he is “one who has seen the Dhamma.
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. In this context, the word *dhamma* in the phrase “one who has seen the Dhamma” is used in its general sense. As for “seeing” (*dassana*):
To exclude the possibility that there might be something other than knowledge and vision, it is said "one who has attained the Dhamma.
Since there is also an attainment other than the attainment of knowledge, it is said "one who has understood the Dhamma" in order to distinguish it from that.

However, since this state of having understood the Dhamma can occur even with respect to only a portion of phenomena, it is said "one who has fathomed the Dhamma" to show the state of having understood it without exception.
This has been said. This statement illuminates precisely his aforementioned perfect awakening to the Truths.

For it is the knowledge of the Path (*magga-ñāṇa*), by means of its single act of realization, which accomplishes the tasks of full understanding (*pariññā*) and so forth; it is this alone that is called "having plunged all around" into the phenomena to be fully understood without exception, and no other knowledge.
Therefore it was said: "The noble Truth-dharma has been seen by him, thus he is one who has 'seen the Dharma' (*diṭṭhadhammo*)."
For this very reason, it says, "one who has crossed over doubt," and so forth.

In that context, one is called "one who has crossed over doubt" because by means of this [knowledge], one has crossed over the sixteen-based and eight-based doubts, which are like a terrifying wilderness.
Precisely for that reason, regarding the process of existence and so on, there no longer occurs such a state as "Is it thus? Or is it not? which had previously arisen.
"Free from doubt" (*vigata-kathaṃkatho*) means one for whom uncertainty has departed and been utterly cut off.

Because he has abandoned those evil qualities that cause trepidation and because he is well-established in the opposing virtues such as morality (*sīla*), he has attained "intrepidity" (*vesārajja*), which is the state of being confident and proficiency;
thus he is "one who has attained intrepidity. For him there is no other condition, nor does he rely here upon the faith of another.
"It proceeds" means it is not dependent on another. To the question "Where?", he says: "In the Teacher’s Dispensation.

Although this word *abhikkanta* is seen in many senses—such as destruction, beauty, loveliness, and rejoicing—it should here be understood in the sense of rejoicing. For that very reason, by way of serene confidence...
It is stated twice by way of praise; thus it means, "Excellent, excellent, venerable sir.
Alternatively, *abhikkanta* means "exceedingly lovely," "exceedingly desirable," "exceedingly agreeable," or "exceedingly beautiful"—this is the meaning.
In this context, with one instance of the word *abhikkanta*, he praises the Blessed One's teaching, and with the other, his own state of serene confidence (*pasāda*).
This is the intended meaning here: "Excellent, venerable sir, is this teaching of the Dhamma by the Blessed One;
excellent, venerable sir, is this teaching of the Dhamma by the Blessed One, for it has brought about confidence in me.

Or else, the words of the Blessed One themselves are "excellent" because they destroy faults, they are "excellent" because they lead to the attainment of virtues, and likewise because they increase faith and generate wisdom.

Praising it in such ways as: "It is meaningful," "it is well-phrased," "its words are clear," "its meaning is profound," "it is pleasant to the ear," "it is heart-stirring," "it does not exalt oneself," "it does not disparage others," "it is cooled by compassion," "it is purified by wisdom," "it is delightful upon first hearing," "it withstands scrutiny," "it is pleasant while being heard," and "it is beneficial when investigated"— he spoke these two lines of verse.
Beyond that, he further praises the teaching itself by means of four similes. In this context: "upturned" (*nikkujjita*) means placed face-downward or having its opening turned downward;

"one would turn it upward" (*ukkujjeyya*) means one would make its opening face upward. "Covered" (*paṭicchanna*) means concealed by grass, leaves, and so forth; "one would uncover it" (*viva- reyya*) means one would remove the covering.
"Of one who is lost" (*mūḷhassa*) means of one who is confused about the directions; "one would point out the path" (*maggaṃ ācikkheyya*) [means] with the hand...
Having taken [the lamp], he would point out the path, saying, "This is the way. "In darkness" means endowed with the four factors. This, first of all, is the literal meaning (*padattha*).

This, however, is the application of the underlying intention (*adhippāyayojanā*): just as someone might set upright what was overturned, so too, by raising me up from unrighteousness—me who am turned away from the true Dhamma and established in unrighteousness—just as one might uncover what was concealed, [so has this been done].
Thus, from the time of the disappearance of the Blessed One Kassapa’s dispensation onwards, by revealing the teaching that had been shrouded by the thicket of wrong views—
just as one might point out the path to one who is lost— and by disclosing the way to heaven and liberation to me, who was traveling along a bypath and a false path—
just as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness— [he revealed it] in the darkness of delusion.
For me, who was submerged and unable to see the forms of the jewels beginning with the Buddha,
the Dhamma has been elucidated by the Blessed One in many ways and through various methods,

by means of holding aloft the lamp of the teaching that destroys the darkness of delusion which conceals them. Having thus praised the teaching, and manifesting his state of serene confidence toward the Triple Gem through that very teaching:
He said, “Esāhaṃ,” and so forth. Therein, “Esāhaṃ” means “this I. “I go for refuge to the Blessed One” means:

with the intention that “the Blessed One is my refuge and my ultimate resort, the destroyer of suffering and the provider of welfare,” I go to, I resort to, or I recognize and understand the Blessed One in this way.
For of those verbal roots whose meaning is “going,” there is also the sense of “understanding.”

"Of them, the goal": "Dhamma" means that which sustains (dhāreti) those who have attained the path, realized cessation, and are practicing according to the instructions, preventing them from falling into the four states of misery; thus it is called "dhamma. In its essential meaning, this is both the Noble Eightfold Path and Nibbāna. For it has been said:
"Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are conditioned phenomena, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared to be the foremost among them."
“Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (*virāga*) is declared to be the foremost among them.
