Thus, it is not only the Noble Path and Nibbāna, but also the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyattidhamma*) together with the Noble Fruits. For this has been said:
“The Dhamma that is the fading away of lust, immovable, sorrowless, unconditioned, and non-repulsive;”
"Come for refuge to this Dhamma, which is sweet, skillful, well-analyzed.

Herein, "the fading away of lust" refers to the Path; "the unshakable, sorrowless" refers to the Fruit; "the unconditioned" refers to Nibbāna; and "this sweet, skillful, well-analyzed [Dhamma] that is not repulsive" refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma).
"The Saṅgha of bhikkhus" refers to the assembly of the eight noble persons (ariya-puggala) who are united by the commonality of view and virtue. Up to this point—

Suppabuddha declared the threefold going for refuge. “May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward (*ajjatagge*) for as long as life lasts (*pāṇupetaṃ*);
here, *ajjatagge* means beginning from today (*ajjataṃ ādiṃ katvā*). There is also a reading *ajjadagge*;

in that case, the letter *da* serves to facilitate the euphonic junction (*padasaṃdhi*), meaning “today at the head” or “beginning from today. *Pāṇupetaṃ* means [for as long as] the vital breaths (*pāṇehi*).
The meaning is: "May the Blessed One consider and recognize me as one who has approached [the Buddha], as long as my life continues;

as one who has gone for refuge through the three refuges with no other teacher; as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) because of his attendance upon the Triple Gem; and as one who performs what is appropriate.
Furthermore, this going for refuge was accomplished only by the attainment of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), [and it was done] out of [his] underlying intention...
But revealing [his intention], he spoke thus:

"Having rejoiced and expressed appreciation for the Blessed One’s speech" means having mentally rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words and, making manifest that very state of rejoicing, having expressed appreciation with speech in the manner described. Having paid homage, [he departed] keeping [the Blessed One] to his right.
"Having done so, he departed": having paid homage to the Blessed One by prostrating himself with the five points of the body, and having circumambulated him three times,
with his mind inclined toward the virtues of the Teacher, he departed while gazing only at the Blessed One until the latter passed from the range of his vision,
keeping his hands joined in reverence and paying homage.

And having departed, overcome by leprosy— with his hands, feet, and fingers severed, his body ablaze, with secretions oozing from all sides, tormented by itching, foul-smelling, utterly loathsome, and having reached a state of supreme pitiability—
he, through a resolve arisen [in him], thinking: "This body is not fit to be a vessel for this most peaceful and most sublime Noble Dhamma," [renounced it].

When space had been made by a meritorious deed conducive to heaven, he was urged on by an accumulated evil deed conducive to a short life that acted as an interruption; thus, having rushed upon a cow with a young calf, he was killed.
Therefore it was said: “Then, not long after Suppabuddha the leper had departed, a cow with a young calf rushed at him and took his life.”
It is said that in the past, having been the son of a merchant, while playing with three other sons of merchants who were his companions, he took a city beauty—a courtesan—to a park.
After they had enjoyed their prosperity there throughout the day, when the sun had set, he said this to his companions:
"In her hand [are] a thousand kahāpaṇas and much gold, as well as costly [jewels]."
“Means of execution are available; there is no one else in this forest, and night has fallen.
Come, let us kill him, take all his wealth, and go. Those four men, being of one mind, set about to kill him.
As she was being killed by them, she said: “These shameless and pitiless ones—me with...”
"Having formed an intimacy with the defilements, they kill me—who am entirely innocent—merely out of greed for wealth. Let them kill me this once;
however, having become a *yakkhinī*, I shall be capable of killing them many times over.
Having made this aspiration, she passed away. It is said that among those [companions], one was the noble son Pakkusāti, and the other was Bāhiya Dārucīriya.
One was the copper-toothed executioner, and the other was Suppabuddha the leper;
thus, having been reborn in that yakṣa womb through hundreds of existences as these four individuals, she took the life of a cow.
Due to the outflow of that karma, they met with untimely death in various places. Such was the case for Suppabuddha the leper.
His death occurred suddenly; therefore it was said: “Then, not long after he had departed... he deprived him of life.

Then a number of bhikkhus, having informed the Blessed One of his passing away, asked about his future destiny. The Blessed One explained it. Therefore it was said: “Then a number of bhikkhus,” and so forth.
In that context, “the complete destruction of the three fetters” refers to personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), and adherence to rites and rituals (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*).

It is by means of the complete eradication of these three bonds of existence that one is an *sotāpanna*. One is an *sotāpanna* because one has entered (*panna*) the Noble Eightfold Path, which is designated as the "stream" (*sota*). For this has been said:
"Friend Sāriputta, 'the stream, the stream'—this is what is said. But what, friend, is the stream? It is precisely this Noble Eightfold Path," and so forth.
"Avinipātadhammo" means "one whose nature is not to fall into ruin. *Vinipāta* is falling into ruin;

one for whom ruin is not his nature is "avinipātadhammo," meaning one whose essential character is not to fall into the four states of misery (*apāya*). "Niyato" means fixed by the fixedness of the Dhamma, fixed by the fixedness of rightness (*sammatta-niyāma*).
"Sambodhiparāyaṇo" means one for whom the goal (*para*) and destination (*ayana*) is enlightenment (*sambodhi*), which consists of the three higher paths.
"Refuge is inevitably to be attained"—thus he is one whose ultimate goal is perfect enlightenment (*sambodhi*).
By this, the answer to the question, "What is his destination? What is his future state? is shown: Suppabuddha’s destination is indeed auspicious, not evil.
However, that destination has not yet been reached by him; rather, desiring to reveal it through the connection of the inquiry, the King of Dharma [the Buddha] stated only this much.

He spoke thus because the Blessed One foresaw: "When I have spoken this much, a certain monk skilled in the connection of the discourse will ask, within this very assembly, about the cause of Suppabuddha’s leprosy, poverty, and wretchedness;
then, having revealed that cause to him through the sequence of his question, I shall bring the teaching to its conclusion."
For this very reason it says: “When this was said, a certain bhikkhu,” and so forth. In that context, *hetu* (cause) is the uncommon cause, whereas *paccaya* (condition) is the common cause;
this is the distinction between them. “By which” means by whichever cause and by whichever condition.
“In former times” (*bhūtapubba*) means having occurred previously. To show that it arose in the past, it is said: “Suppabuddha,” and so forth.
But when did it come to be? It is said that in the past, before the Tathāgata had appeared, in a village near Bārāṇasī, a daughter of a noble family was guarding a field.
Seeing a Paccekabuddha, she offered him a lotus flower together with five hundred handfuls of parched grain with a devout heart, and she made a wish for five hundred sons. In that very [existence]...
At that moment, five hundred deer-hunters gave sweet meat to the Paccekabuddha and made this aspiration:
"May we become her sons, and may we attain the distinguished state reached by you. Having lived out her full lifespan, she was reborn in the world of the devas.
Passing away from there, she was reborn within the calyx of a lotus in a certain lake. A certain ascetic, seeing her—
She looked after him. As she walked about, lotuses rose up from the ground at every step.
A forest-dweller saw her and informed the King of Bārāṇasī. The king brought her and made her his chief queen.
A fetus was established in her womb. The Prince Mahāpaduma dwelt in her womb, while the others were merely the impurities of the womb.
Born in dependence [upon that lake], they reached maturity and, while sporting in a lotus pond in the garden, each sat upon a single lotus.

Having established the contemplation of the destruction and vanishing of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), they attained the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha. Their verse of proclamation was as follows:
“Born from the petals and leaves of the lotus in the lake, ...”
A lotus in full bloom, frequented by swarms of bees;
having understood its impermanence, its decay, and its passing away,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Thus, among those five hundred paccekabuddhas who had attained paccekabodhi, the paccekasambuddha named Tagarasikhī,
having entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) for seven days on the Nandamūla cave of Mount Gandhamādana,
emerged from cessation at the end of those seven days and arrived by way of the air at Isigili Mountain.
Having descended, he dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms.

At that time, a merchant’s son in Rājagaha, departing from the city with a large retinue for a pleasure excursion to the park, saw the Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī and thought, "Who is this clothed in shaven saffron robes? He must be a leper. Thus...
“Indeed, he goes about having covered his body with the robe of a leper,” he spat, turned his left side toward him, and departed.
With reference to this, it is said: “The leper Suppabuddha, right here in Rājagaha... [etc] ...departed. In that passage, *kvāyan* means “who is this?
He speaks by way of contempt. There is also a textual reading, *kovāyaṃ*. *Kuṭṭhī* means one who is not a leper.
The merchant spoke thus, using the leprosy as a pretext for his abuse. "With the rags of a leper" means with the clothing of those suffering from leprosy.

For generally, a leper—either to ward off gadflies, mosquitoes, snakes, and reptiles, or to conceal the disease—puts on whatever scraps of cloth he can find; it is to show that this man was likewise so. This is because he wore robes made of discarded rags (*paṃsukūla*).
Because of the multicolored nature of his sores, he was like a body afflicted with leprosy; thus, treating him with contempt, [the man] said, "with the robe of a leper.

"Having spat" means having dropped saliva. "Having kept to the left" means that when wise people see such a Paccekabuddha, they pay homage and circumambulate him keeping him to their right; however, this man, out of ignorance and disdain, kept him to his left.
Having placed himself to the left and having circumambulated [him] counter-clockwise, he departed. There is also a reading: “*apasabyāmato*. “Of that karma” means:
of the evil karma committed by reviling the Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī with the words “Where is this leper?

and by spitting upon him and acting counter-clockwise. “He was boiled in hell” means: he was consumed by the fires of hell. There is also a reading: “*paccitvā nirayagginā*” (having been boiled by the fires of hell).
They recite [the following]: "By the remaining result of that very same karma. That karma by which he took rebirth in hell does not yield its result in the human world.

However, his volition—which was asynchronous (nānakkhaṇika), having arisen through the act of wrong conduct toward the Paccekabuddha, and which is to be experienced in a subsequent life (aparāpariyavedanīya)—[yields its result] precisely as something to be experienced in a subsequent life.

By means of a meritorious deed, having received a rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) with three roots among human beings, he brought about the state of being a leper, poverty, and extreme wretchedness during his course of existence (pavatti).
With reference to this, it was said by way of the similarity of the action: “by the remainder of the ripening (vipāka) of that very same action.
For even when things are similar, such usage is seen in the world, as in the expressions: “that is the very same partridge,” or “those are the very same medicinal herbs.”
Having thus answered the question asked by that bhikkhu, “What, venerable sir, is the cause?
he now spoke the words beginning with “He has been proclaimed by the Tathāgata” in order to answer the question previously asked by the bhikkhus, “What is his destination?
What is his future state? Therein, “proclaimed by the Tathāgata” means by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata.
"Taught, declared, and made manifest" means proclaimed by the Tathāgata. "Having approached" (āgamma) means having attained, relied upon, or known.
There is also a reading: "In the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata. "He undertook faith" (saddhaṃ samādiyī) means he took refuge in the Triple Gem:
"The Blessed One is the Perfectly Enlightened One; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good path."
He correctly undertook both types of faith: that of the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga-saddhā*) and that which transcends the world (*lokuttara-saddhā*).

He took them up in such a way that they would not need to be undertaken again; the meaning is that he produced them within the continuum of his own mind until the destruction of existence (*bhavakkhaya*).

The same method applies to the phrases "he undertook virtue" (*sīlaṃ samādiyi*) and so forth. Here, "virtue" (*sīla*) refers to the virtue of the Path (*maggasīla*) together with the virtue of the preliminary stage.

And the virtue of fruition (*phala-sīla*). "Learning" (*suta*) refers to both types of learning: the learning of the scriptures (*pariyatti-bāhusacca*) and the learning of penetration (*paṭivedha-bāhusacca*).
For even the teachings of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) are, at the time of hearing the Dhamma, heard by disciples in the manner they have received them for the sake of penetrating the Truths;

they are mastered, examined by the mind, and well-penetrated by right view. "And generosity" (*cāga*) refers to the formative volitions (*abhisaṅkhāra*) regarding the defilements to be abandoned by the first path.
"Relinquishment" (*vossagga*) refers to generosity (*cāga*), by means of which noble disciples become free-handed in regard to things to be given, pure-handed, and delighting in relinquishment.
"Wisdom" (*paññā*) includes both the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*) as well as the wisdom of the path (*magga-paññā*) and the wisdom of the fruit (*phala-paññā*).

"With the breakup of the body" (*kāyassa bhedā*) means the discarding of the aggregates that have been clung to. "After death" (*paraṃ maraṇā*) means the grasping of the newly produced aggregates immediately following that.
Alternatively, "with the breaking up of the body" means with the cutting off of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). "After death" means after the moment of death (*cuti*).

By all three terms—"a happy destination," "the heavenly world," and "the world"—he refers specifically to the world of the devas. For that world is called a "happy destination" (*sugati*) because it is a beautiful (*sundara*) state due to its excellence;
it is called "heaven" (*sagga*) because it is a supreme (*agga*) place by way of its distinguished qualities such as form and so forth; and because there is only happiness at all times therein.
It is called "the world" (*loka*) because it dissolves or it breaks apart. "Reborn" (*upapanna*) means having approached by way of taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"Companionship" (*sahabyatā*) means the state of being together. As for the etymological meaning: one who exists or dwells together is a "companion" (*sahabya*);
that is, one who stays together or dwells together. The state of such a person is "companionship. "Outshines" (*atirocati*) means surpassing and overcoming.
It shines and glows. "By beauty" means by the perfection of form. "By glory" means by its retinue.
For he is like one who, having discarded a worn-out earthen vessel smeared with filth, takes up a pure vessel of Jambu-river gold, variegated with many jewels and enveloped in a web of radiant rays;
so too, having cast off this body here of the aforementioned kind, in a single moment of consciousness, he [assumes] that which has been described.
"He regained a divine body together with a great retinue.

Having understood this matter—having understood in every way both the disadvantage in not avoiding evil deeds and the benefit in avoiding them—he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) which elucidates that meaning.
This is its summary meaning: just as a man with sight, while physical energy and bodily vigor are present, [would exert himself...]
Just as one who travels avoids uneven precipices and other dangerous places out of a sense of caution, avoiding wild elephants, horses, snakes, dogs, oxen, and so forth;

even so, in this world of living beings, in this world of creatures, a wise and intelligent person, knowing what is for his own welfare through that very intelligence, should avoid evil, base, and immoral conduct. For it was in this way that Suppabuddha—
The intention is: "Just as [the king] fell into great ruin and calamity by not avoiding evil toward the Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī, so too might another fall;

or, just as the leper Suppabuddha, having come to my teaching of the Dhamma, has now attained a state of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), avoids evils, and achieved a sublime distinction (*visesa*), so too might another achieve a sublime distinction."
The intention is that one who desires [to avoid suffering] should avoid evil deeds.
The commentary on the third sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Kumāraka* Sutta.
44. "Young boys" (*kumāraka*) in the fourth [verse] refers to young persons. Those who understand the meaning of what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken are intended here by the term "young boys.
For these beings are called "young boys" and "fools" from the day of their birth until they reach fifteen years of age; thereafter, for twenty years, they are called "youths. As for the fish...

“They harass” means that, near the road, when the water in a certain pond has dried up during the hot season, they draw out the water remaining in the low-lying places, catch the small fish, and kill them, thinking, “We shall cook and eat them.
“He approached” means that he stood having passed slightly beyond the pond from the road; therefore, it says “he approached.”
But why did he approach them? He approached in order to inspire confidence in those boys. In the phrase *bhāyatha vo*, the word *vo* is merely a particle.
In *dukkhassa*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative; the meaning is "from suffering. In *appiyaṃ vo dukkhaṃ*, he asks:
"Is the suffering that arises in your bodies unpleasant and undesirable to you?"

"Having understood this matter": having understood in every aspect this matter—that these beings, while not desiring their own suffering, by engaging in the cause of suffering, come as it were to desire it for themselves;
he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*), which is a prohibition against unwholesome action and an exposition of its danger.

The meaning of this is as follows: If all the suffering pertaining to the states of misery, as well as the suffering in the happy destinies—such as short life spans, physical deformity, and so forth—is unpleasant and undesirable to you; if you fear that [suffering];

and if, whether openly before others in a manifest manner without concealment through body or speech, or in secret in a non-manifest manner, you refrain from the various types of misconduct such as killing living beings and the like; [then...]
Having concealed [the mind], do not commit even the slightest evil or base state, such as covetousness and the like, within the mind-door itself;

do not do it. Furthermore, if you are committing that evil deed now, or will commit it in the future, then while fleeing here and there from the suffering that is its fruit in the four states of deprivation beginning with hell, and among human beings—
Even if one approaches and then flees with the intention, "He will not pursue us," there is no liberation or release for you from that [kamma].
This shows that it will certainly ripen when other conditions, such as the time of death and the destination, come together.
Some also read "palāyane" (in fleeing); the meaning is: "when there is going or departing anywhere," according to the method already stated. And this is the meaning:
This is to be illustrated by the verse: “Neither in the sky, nor in the midst of the ocean… [etc.
…by evil deeds. The commentary on the fourth sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Uposatha Sutta.
45. *Pañcame tadahūti*: on that day, on that very day. Regarding the term *uposatha*: here, it is called *uposatha* because they dwell (*upavasanti*) therein.
"They dwell" means they live having become endowed with either virtue (*sīla*) or fasting (*anasana*).
Indeed, this word *uposatha* occurs in reference to virtue in such passages as: "I observe the *uposatha* endowed with the eight factors. "The *uposatha*..."
In such passages as "the *pātimokkha* recitation or the *pavāraṇā*," it refers to the disciplinary acts (*vinayakamma*) such as the recitation of the *pātimokkha*.

In such passages as "the cowherd’s *uposatha*, the Nigaṇṭha’s *uposatha*," it refers to the observance day (*upavāsa*). In such passages as "there was a king of serpents named *Uposatha*," it refers to a designation (*paññatti*). In such passages as "Today is the *uposatha*, the fifteenth day," it refers to the day.
Here too, it should be understood as referring to the day; therefore, in the phrase "on that very *uposatha* day" (*tadahuposathe*), it means on that which constitutes the *uposatha* day.
The meaning is "on the day. "He was seated" means he was seated surrounded by a great community of monks in order to recite the Pātimokkha of exhortation.
However, while seated and observing the minds of the monks, seeing one person of immoral conduct, [he thought]:
"If I were to recite the Pātimokkha to this person while he is still sitting right here, his head would split into seven pieces."
“It will bear fruit,” he thought, and out of compassion for him, he remained silent.

And here, although the dawn had already broken—meaning that sunrise had occurred—the Elder requested the Blessed One to recite the Pātimokkha, saying, “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha for the monks. At that time, [the Buddha said], “Monks, not...
Because the training rule, "The Uposatha should be performed on the Uposatha day," had not yet been promulgated.

Since the assembly was impure, Ānanda—when explaining the reason for the non-recitation after the Elder had requested the recitation of the Pātimokkha three times—said, "Ānanda, the assembly is impure," rather than saying, "Such-and-such a person is impure. But why did the Blessed One [wait] through the three watches of the night?
In this way he passed the time. From that point on, desiring not to recite the *ovāda-pātimokkha*, he wished to make the matter public.

"He saw"—how did he see it? By means of his knowledge of the minds of others (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*), while thoroughly understanding the minds of the bhikkhus in that assembly, he perceived the mind of immorality in that foolish person. For when the mind is seen, the person possessing that mind is [also] seen.
It is said to be "seen"; therefore, it was stated: "The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw that person as one of immoral conduct," and so forth.
For just as one who has attained the knowledge of penetration of minds (cetopariyañāṇa) knows the minds of others occurring during the seven future days, so too does he know them in the past.
"Immoral" (dussīla) means devoid of virtue; the meaning is "deprived of moral discipline. "Of evil nature" (pāpadhamma).
Because of immorality and a base disposition, it is of a lowly nature. It is "impure" because it is possessed of impure bodily actions and so forth;

it is not pure. It is "of suspicious conduct" because its behavior must be remembered with suspicion due to being suspected by others upon seeing some unsuitable act, thinking, "This must have been done by this person. Furthermore—
Or, seeing monks deliberating on some business or other, he thinks, "Could it be that these [monks] are deliberating because they know of the deed I have committed?
Thus, due to his own suspicion, he must conceal his conduct.
Because his course of action is to be concealed due to its shameful nature and because it is a cause for hiding, he is one whose course of action is concealed (*paṭicchannakammanta*).
Because he wears the robes of a recluse while being corrupt, he is not a recluse; thus, he is a non-recluse (*assamaṇa*).

Because he makes the false claim of being a recluse—both by being counted among the recluses during the distribution of voting sticks and the like when people ask, "How many recluses are there?", and by declaring, "I too am a recluse"—he is one who professes to be a recluse (*samaṇapaṭiñña*).

Because his conduct is not noble, he is one who does not live the holy life (*abrahmacārī*). While other recluses are well-clad, well-dressed, well-robed, and wander for alms in villages, market towns, and so forth...
"Claiming to be a practitioner of the holy life" (*brahmacāripaṭiñña*) refers to one who, while not actually living the holy life, sees others making their livelihood by practicing it;
thus, adopting a similar outward appearance himself, appearing at the observance days (*uposatha*) and other such occasions, he gives the declaration, "I too am a practitioner of the holy life.

"Putrid within" (*antopūti*) is so called because of being internally corrupted by a rotten deed through a failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*). [It is also so called] because of the raining down of defilements such as lust through the six sense-doors.

It is "corrupted" because it is defiled by lust and other passions. It is "putrid" because it has become a refuse-heap due to the accumulation of passion and the like, and because it must be discarded by those possessing virtue.
"Seated in the midst of the Bhikkhu-saṅgha" means seated within the Bhikkhu-saṅgha as if included among its members.
"You have been seen" means that you have been seen by the Blessed One as one who is not a regular member (pakatatta). And because you have been seen in this way, therefore—
"There is no communal living for you with the bhikkhus, such as performing formal acts together (*ekakamma*) and so forth.
Since that communal life does not exist for you, therefore arise, friend!"—thus should the construction of the words here be understood.
"And for a third time that person remained silent," meaning that even after the Elder had spoken many times, [the person remained silent] because he was himself weary [of the world].
He remained silent either with the intention, "He will speak later," or with the thought, "Now I shall see their conduct.
Regarding the phrase "having taken him by the arm": [the Buddha thought], "He has been seen by me and by myself exactly as he is; though told three times, 'Arise!', he does not arise.
Now is the time to expel him, lest there be an obstruction to the Saṅgha's Uposatha. Thus, taking him by the arm—
He seized him; having seized him in that manner. "Having led him out from the gatehouse" means having led him outside the hall that serves as the gatehouse.

The word "outside," however, indicates the location to which he was led; alternatively, "from outside the gatehouse" means having led him out even from the exterior of the gatehouse, and not from within the gatehouse—thus, in either case, the meaning is that he was placed outside the monastery.
"Having inserted the bolt and the upper pin" means having fixed both the door-bolt and the upper latch; the sense is that he had firmly closed the door.

"Even to the point of seizing him by the arm"—by this [phrase], it is implied that upon merely hearing the words, "Ānanda, the assembly is not pure," he ought to have departed; yet, instead of departing, he remained even until he was seized by the arm.
He shows that it is indeed marvelous how that foolish man will endure [the consequences]. This too should be understood as a marvel of censure. Then the Blessed One thought:
"Now the community of monks has become infested with maggots; impure individuals are coming to the Uposatha.
Yet the Tathāgatas do not perform the Uposatha with an impure assembly; [they do not recite] the Pātimokkha..."

"Since the Uposatha of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is interrupted both when they recite [the Pātimokkha] and when they do not recite it, what if, from now on, I were to authorize the bhikkhus themselves to recite the Pātimokkha?
Having reflected thus, he authorized the bhikkhus themselves to recite the Pātimokkha.
Therefore it was said: "Then the Blessed One... 'you should recite the Pātimokkha.'"
In this context, the phrase "I shall not give" is connected individually with each negative particle (*na*) as follows: "Now I shall not observe the Uposatha; I shall not recite the Pātimokkha.
For the Pātimokkha is of two kinds: the Pātimokkha of the injunction (*āṇā-pātimokkha*) and the Pātimokkha of the exhortation (*ovāda-pātimokkha*).
Among these, the Pātimokkha of the injunction—beginning with "Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me"—is recited only by disciples, not by Buddhas.
This [text] is recited every half-month. These three verses—“Patience is supreme… [etc. …the non-doing of all evil… [etc. …non-reproach and non-injury… [etc.
…this is the teaching of the Buddhas”—are called the *ovāda-pātimokkha* (Exhortation Pātimokkha).
Only Buddhas recite it, not disciples; they recite it at the end of six years. For among the long-lived Buddhas, [it is recited...]
During his own lifetime, this very recitation of the Pātimokkha was performed; however, for Buddhas of short lifespan, it occurs only during their first enlightenment.
After that, the other [recitation] takes place, and it is the monks themselves who recite it, not the Buddhas.
Therefore, our Blessed One also, having recited the Pātimokkha of exhortation for about twenty years, saw this obstacle and did not recite it thereafter.
“An impossibility” (*aṭṭhāna*) means a non-cause. “No occasion” (*anavakāsa*) is a synonym for that very term.
For just as a cause is called a “possibility” (*ṭhāna*) because the fruit stands there [within it] by virtue of being dependent upon it, so too it is called “no occasion.
The word “that” (*yaṃ*) is a reference to the action; it should be construed according to the method explained below.
What is the connection (*anusandhi*) for this statement: "Bhikkhus, there are these eight qualities of the great ocean"?

It is intended to show that the recitation of the *Pātimokkha* before an impure assembly—which was previously mentioned—is a wonderful and marvelous quality (*acchariya abbhuta dhamma*) within this Dhamma and Vinaya;
thus, wishing to explain it by means of seven other wonderful and marvelous qualities, [the Buddha] first presents them as its analogies.
Showing the eight wonderful and marvelous qualities of the great ocean, the Teacher said, "Bhikkhus, these eight [qualities] of the great ocean," and so forth.
They are called *asuras* because, unlike natural deities (*pakatideva*), they do not laugh, they do not exult, and they do not shine;

or alternatively, they are *asuras* because they are the adversaries of the *suras*—the *suras* being the gods—and they include Vepacitti, Pahārāda, and others. Their abode is at the lower portion of Sineru.
Entering and exiting there, they create pavilions and other structures at the foot of Sineru and take delight while sporting.
Regarding their enjoyment there, it was said: "Having seen these qualities again and again, the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
In this context, "take delight" means they find pleasure; the sense is that they dwell there without longing for anything else.
"Gradually sloping," and so forth—all these are synonyms for the state of being inclined in successive order.
"Not steep from the very beginning" means it does not fall precipitously from the start like a great waterfall from a sheer cliff.
For that [ocean] becomes deep starting from the shore by degrees—by one finger-breadth, two finger-breadths, a span, a cubit, a fathom, a usabha, half a gāvuta, a gāvuta, half a yojana, and so on.
It shows that as it flows on and on, it comes to stand at the foot of Sineru with a depth of eighty-four thousand yojanas.
"Of stable nature" (ṭhitadhammo) means having a stable character, a constant character.
"It does not dwell with a dead corpse" means it does not dwell together with any carcass whatsoever, such as those of elephants or horses. "It carries the bank away" means it washes the bank away.
"He hurls onto the dry land" means that he casts it onto the land by the very force of the wave, as if grasping it with his hand.

Regarding the Ganges and Yamunā: at the place where the river emerging from the southern mouth of Lake Anotatta flows forth in five streams, they come to be designated by the five names beginning with "Ganges."
In this regard, here is the account of the origin of these rivers starting from the beginning: This Jambudīpa is ten thousand yojanas in extent;
of that, an area measuring four thousand yojanas is submerged by water and is reckoned as the ocean;
three thousand yojanas are inhabited by humans; and three thousand yojanas are occupied by the Himavat mountain range.
Five hundred yojanas in height, adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks, and variegated by five hundred rivers flowing from all sides—
therein lies Lake Anotatta, fifty yojanas in length, breadth, and depth, and one hundred and fifty yojanas in circumference;
as well as Lake Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Lake Rathakāra, Lake Chaddanta, Lake Kuṇāla, and Lake Mandākinī.
There are seven great lakes established there, including the Siṃhapapāta lake.
Among them, Lake Anotatta is surrounded by these five mountain peaks: Sudassana Peak, Cittakūṭa, Kāḷakūṭa, Gandhamādana Peak, and Kelāsa Peak.
Therein, Sudassana Peak is made of gold and is three hundred yojanas in height.
The inner curve is shaped like a crow’s beak and stands concealing that very lake. Cittakūṭa is composed of the seven precious gems.
Kāḷakūṭa is composed of collyrium. Gandhamādana-kūṭa is composed of masāragalla stone and is green inside like a mung bean;
it possesses the fragrance of roots, the fragrance of heartwood, the fragrance of sapwood, the fragrance of bark, the fragrance of shoots, and the fragrance of the trunk.
It is abundant with these ten kinds of fragrance—the scent of sap, the scent of flowers, the scent of fruits, and the scent of leaves—and is covered with various medicinal herbs.
On the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, it stands blazing like a glowing ember set on fire.
Kelāsakūṭa is made of silver. All of these are equal to Sudassana in height and shape.
They stand there concealing that very lake. There, by the power of the devas and the power of the nāgas, the rain falls and the rivers flow;

all that water enters into Anotatta itself. When the moon and sun pass either to the south or to the north, they create a radiance there through the mountain range, but when they pass directly [overhead], [they do not].
Because they do not cause [the water] to be heated, for that very reason the designation "Anotatta" (Unheated) arose for it. Therein,
bathing places produced by the kamma of the beings who enjoy them exist— having stone floors with agreeable staircases made of jewels,
free from fish and turtles, resembling crystal, and possessing stainless water— wherein Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas [bathe].
Powerful disciples and seers perform their ablutions and other rites there; gods, yakṣas, and others sport in the water.
On its four sides are four outlets for the water—lion faces, elephant faces, horse faces, and bull faces—from which four rivers flow. On the bank of the river issuing from the lion face...
The lions with manes are more numerous; likewise, from the elephant-mouths and other [outflows], there are elephants, horses, and bulls.

The river that issues from the eastern direction circles the Anotatta lake three times clockwise, and without joining the other three rivers, it enters the great ocean by way of the eastern Himālaya mountains, which are a path frequented by non-humans. From the western direction and from the northern direction...
And the rivers issuing from the [other] three directions likewise circumambulate it to the right,
and having entered the path of non-human beings via the Western Himālaya and the Northern Himālaya respectively, they flow into the great ocean. However,
the river issuing from the southern direction, after circumambulating it three times to the right, flows straight toward the south.
Having traveled sixty yojanas as if on a stone surface and struck a mountain, it rose up and became a stream of water measuring three gavutas in circumference;
traveling sixty yojanas through the air, it fell upon a rock named Tiyaṅgala. The rock was split by the force of the water's impact.
Thereupon, a lotus pond named Tiyaṅgalā, measuring fifty yojanas, was formed. Of that pond—
Having broken through the bank and entered the rock, it travels sixty yojanas; then, having broken through the solid earth,
it travels another sixty yojanas by way of a subterranean passage, strikes the transverse mountain named Viñjha,
and proceeds forth as five streams resembling the five fingers on the palm of a hand.
Having circumambulated Anotatta three times, the place where she went is called the "Āvaṭṭagaṅgā";
the place where she went straight for sixty yojanas over the surface of the rocks is called the "Kaṇhagaṅgā"; the place where she went through the air for sixty yojanas is called the "Ākāsagaṅgā";
and the fifty-yojana area situated upon the Tiyaṅgaḷa rock is called the "Tiyaṅgaḷapokkharaṇī."
Having broken through the bank and entered the rock, it is called the "Thick Gaṅgā" at the place where it has traveled sixty yojanas;
it is called the "Umaṅga Gaṅgā" at the place where it has traveled sixty yojanas by way of a subterranean passage;
and at the place where, having struck the mountain named Viñjha—a cross-mountain—it proceeds as five streams, they are called the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī.
They have come together in five ways. Thus it should be understood that these five great rivers flow forth from the Himālaya.
In this context, "river," "stream," and so forth, refer to their genus (*gotra*); "Ganges," "Yamunā," and so forth, refer to their names.
"Flowing" refers to whatever great rivers or small streams go along, flowing and streaming. "Enter" means they adhere to and flow into [the ocean].
“Stream” (dhārā) means a stream of rain. “Fullness” (pūratta) means the state of being full. For this is the nature of the great ocean:
it is not possible [for one to think], “At this time the rain has become light; we shall take up our nets and so forth to catch fish and turtles,” or “At this time the rain is too heavy;
shall we not find a place to stretch out our backs? It is simply not possible.

To speak: from the time of the first aeon onwards, whatever rain has fallen and the water that remains touching the girdle of Sineru does not descend even a single finger’s breadth further, nor does it rise even a single finger’s breadth higher.
"Of one taste" means its flavor is undifferentiated. "Pearls" refers to many kinds of pearls, distinguished as small or large, round or long, and so forth.

"Maṇi" refers to various kinds of gems, such as the ruby, sapphire, and so forth. "Veḷuriya" (cat's-eye) refers to various kinds distinguished by their bamboo-like color, the hue of the sirīsa flower, and other shapes.
"Saṅkha" (conch) refers to various kinds, such as the right-spiraling conch, the copper-colored conch, the *kadhamana* conch, and others.

"Sila" (rock crystal) refers to various kinds distinguished by colors such as white or black like a mung bean, and so forth. "Pavāḷa" (coral) refers to various kinds, such as small or large, pale red or deep red, and so on.
It is of many kinds. *Lohitaṅga* refers to various types such as the red-lotus-colored gem and so forth; *masāragalla* is the variegated gem (*kabara-maṇi*).
Some also call it *cittaphalika*. "Of great beings" means of great creatures. *Timitimiṅgala* and the others are three species of fish. [The text mentions] the *timi*...
“Timiṅgalas” are those capable of swallowing a *timi*; and those capable of swallowing both a *timi* and a *timiṅgala* are called “*timitimiṅgalas*.
“Nāgas” refers to both those who dwell on the backs of waves and those nāgas who reside in celestial palaces (*vimānas*).
“In the very same way” means that although the Teacher [has taught] sixteen, thirty-two, or even more [qualities] in this Dhamma and Vinaya...
When he is able to analyze and demonstrate the marvelous and wonderful qualities, then,
in order to show those eight corresponding qualities that serve as the basis for the eight similes already presented,
he says: "In this very Dhamma and Discipline, monks, there are eight marvelous and wonderful qualities," and so forth.
Therein, by "gradual training" (anupubbasikkhā), the three kinds of alms-gathering (bhikkhā) are included; by "gradual practice" (anupubbakiriyā), the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga-dhammā);

and by "gradual path" (anupubbapaṭipadā), the seven contemplations (anupassanā), the eighteen great insights (mahāvipassanā), the thirty-eight analyses of objects (ārammaṇavibhattiyo), and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhammā) are included.
It is not through mere prolixity that there is penetration of higher knowledge (aññāpaṭivedha); [this is] like the frog.
Just as there is no flying up [into the air] from the very beginning, so too there is no realization of Arahatship without first fulfilling virtue (*sīla*) and the other stages;
rather, the meaning is that one attains Arahatship only after having fulfilled virtue, concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*) in their proper sequence.

"My disciples" refers to the noble persons (*ariyapuggala*), such as stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and the rest. "He does not dwell together" means by way of performing the Uposatha ceremony and other such duties.
He does not associate with them. "He casts out" means he removes them. "Far away" means at a great distance. "Neither by that is there a deficiency nor a fullness in the element of Nibbāna":

even if Buddhas do not arise for incalculable great aeons (*asaṅkhyeyya-mahākappa*) such that not a single being is able to attain final Nibbāna, even then it cannot be said that "the element of Nibbāna is empty"; this is so both during the time of a Buddha and [when no Buddha has arisen].
Furthermore, in each single assembly, even incalculable beings attain the Deathless; even then, it cannot be said that "the element of Nibbāna is full.

"The flavor of liberation" means the flavor of being liberated from the defilements. For every success of the Dispensation results solely in the liberation of the mind from the taints through non-clinging.

The "jewels" (ratanāni) are so called in the sense of producing delight (ratijanana). For when the foundations of mindfulness and the other [factors] are cultivated, they produce no small measure of rapture and gladness even in the prior stage, let alone in the subsequent stage. Indeed, it has been said:
"From whatever [aspect] one contemplates The arising and passing away of the aggregates, One gains rapture and gladness; That is the deathless for one who understands."
Furthermore, the meaning that the joy and gladness [derived from] worldly gems does not merit even a fraction of this has already been shown above.
Moreover: “Wondrous, of great value, incomparable, rare to behold, To be enjoyed by beings who are no ordinary—such is called a ‘gem.’”
And if something is called a "jewel" by virtue of being honored and so forth, then the status of being a jewel belongs truly only to the foundations of mindfulness and the like.

For it is the power of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhammā) that disciples attain the knowledge of disciple-perfection, pratyekabuddhas attain the knowledge of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas attain perfect enlightenment; this is because they are the proximate causes.

For the indirect cause (*paramparakāraṇa*)—namely, the decisive support (*upanissaya*) such as giving—is the reason why the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*) possess the status of "jewels" (*ratana*) in the sense of producing delight and in the sense of being honored;
this quality of being a jewel is especially prominent in them. Therefore it was said: "In this regard, these are the jewels, namely, the four foundations of mindfulness," and so forth.
In this context, it is a "foundation" (*paṭṭhāna*) in the sense of being established upon an object; mindfulness itself is the foundation, thus it is "foundation of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
Because the object is fourfold—consisting of the body and so forth—it is said, "the four foundations of mindfulness.

For, by abandoning the perceptions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self with respect to the body, feelings, mind, and mental phenomena, one grasps them as foul, painful, impermanent, and non-self.
And their state as "contemplation of the body" and so forth is analyzed [in the respective sections].
One strives rightly by means of this; or it itself strives rightly; or one strives in a way that is praised or beautiful—thus it is "right striving" (*sammappadhāna*).
Or, because it brings about the state of right striving in a person, it is "right striving. This is a term for energy (*vīriya*).
It is a designation. That too is called "the four right endeavors" (cattāro sammappadhānā) because they perform four functions:

by way of the non-arising and abandoning of unwholesome states that have arisen or have not yet arisen, and by way of the arising and cultivation of wholesome states that have arisen or have not yet arisen.

It is called *iddhi* because it succeeds (*ijjhati*); the meaning is that it is accomplished (*samijjhati*) and brought to fruition (*nipphajjati*). Or else, beings succeed (*ijjhanti*) by means of this; thus they are successful (*iddhā*) and prosperous (*vuddhā*).

"Supernormal power (*iddhi*) is that which has reached the highest excellence. Thus, according to the first sense, *iddhipāda* means "the foot of supernormal power," which is to say, a constituent part of supernormal power.

According to the second sense, it is the "foot" (basis) or the "means of attainment" for supernormal power; for by means of it, one goes to—that is, reaches—supernormal power, which consists of successive stages of distinction.
And this "foot of supernormal power" is, because of the four dominant factors beginning with desire (*chanda*), etc.
Because it arises having been made the foremost, it is therefore called "the four bases of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*).

"The five faculties" (*pañcindriyāni*) refers to the five faculties beginning with faith (*saddhā*). Among these, that which exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*) in the characteristic of resolution (*adhimokkha*) by overcoming lack of faith is the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*);
that which exercises lordship in the characteristic of exertion (*paggaha*) by overcoming sloth (*kosajja*), and [in the characteristic of non-forgetfulness] by overcoming negligence (*pamāda*)...

It exercises lordship over its associated states by overcoming dullness through the characteristic of presence, by overcoming distraction through the characteristic of non-distraction, and by overcoming ignorance through the characteristic of seeing; thus it is the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*).

These same factors should be understood as "powers" (*balāni*) in the sense of being unshakable because they cannot be overcome by lack of faith and the rest, and in the sense of stability among associated states.

"The seven factors of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅga*) means they are the limbs (*aṅga*) of enlightenment (*bodhi*), or the limbs of one who possesses enlightenment. For this is that harmony of states (*dhammasāmaggī*) which,
when arising at the moment of the supramundane path, serves as the antidote to numerous calamities— namely, the foundations of lethargy and agitation, the exertion of striving,

the pursuit of sensual pleasure and self-mortification, and the dogmatic adherence to annihilationism and eternalism— and consists of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.

The noble disciple awakens through the harmony of the Dhamma; he rises from the sleep of the defilements, penetrates the Four Noble Truths, or realizes Nibbāna itself—thus it is called "awakening" (*bodhi*).

The factors of that awakening, which is defined as the harmony of the Dhamma, are the "factors of awakening" (*bojjhaṅga*), just like the "factors of jhāna" (*jhānaṅga*) or the "factors of the path" (*maggaṅga*). And this [harmony] of the aforementioned kind of harmony of the Dhamma...

Because he awakens, the noble disciple is called "one who has awakened" (*bodhi*); and because they are factors of that awakening, they are called "factors of awakening" (*bojjhaṅga*), just as there are factors of an army or factors of a chariot.
Thus the ancients said: "They are factors of the person who is awakening; hence they are 'factors of awakening'.
Furthermore, the meaning of "factor of awakening" for the *bojjhaṅgas* should be understood by such methods as: "They lead to awakening; hence they are 'factors of awakening.'"

The Noble Eightfold Path (*ariya-aṭṭhaṅgika-magga*): It is "noble" (*ariya*) because it is remote from the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path, because it brings about the state of a noble one, and because it effects the attainment of the noble fruits.
It possesses eight factors, such as right view and so forth; or, it is "eightfold" (*aṭṭhaṅgika*) simply because its factors are eight.
It is called a "path" (*magga*) because it goes while slaying the defilements, because it is sought after by those seeking Nibbāna, or because it itself seeks out Nibbāna.
In this way, the analysis of the meaning of these [factors], such as the foundations of mindfulness, should be understood.
"Stream-enterer" (*sotāpanna*) means one who has entered, reached, and stands within the stream known as the Path;

the sense is "one established in the fruit of stream-entry. "One practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry" means for the sake of making the fruit of stream-entry personally manifest.

One who is practicing [the path] is one standing on the first path, who is also called the "eighth person" (*aṭṭhamaka*). A "once-returner" (*sakadāgāmī*) is one whose nature it is to come back to this world only once more by way of taking rebirth;
he is one standing on the second fruit. A "non-returner" (*anāgāmī*) is one whose nature it is not to return to the sense-sphere world by way of taking rebirth;

he is one standing on the third fruit. Furthermore, there are those who are followers by faith (*saddhānusārī*), followers by Dhamma (*dhammānusārī*), and those who have only one seed remaining (*ekabījī*).
This classification of noble persons (ariyapuggala) beginning with these [terms] is the very distinction among them. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
"Having understood this matter" means having understood this matter, namely, the non-dwelling together with a person of immoral conduct who is like a corpse in one's own Dhamma and Vinaya.

"He uttered this inspired utterance" (udāna) means he uttered this inspired utterance which elucidates the reasons for distinguishing between those worthy of not dwelling together and those worthy of dwelling together.
In this context, "the rain pours down upon what is covered" means that one who, having committed an offense, conceals it, commits another new offense, and then yet another beyond that;
thus the rain of offenses and the rain of defilements pour down excessively.

"The rain does not pour down upon what is uncovered" means that one who has fallen into an offense, instead of concealing it, reveals it and makes it known to his fellow celibates, acting in accordance with the Dhamma.
When one makes amends according to the discipline, confesses, and emerges from the offense, one does not incur another new offense;
therefore, for such a person, the rain of offenses that had been covered over—the rain of defilements—does not fall again.
Since this is so, you should uncover and reveal the offense that was concealed. In this way, it will not rain upon you; for when this is done, that person who incurred the offense [is freed].
Having pierced through the personal existence of a person who has fallen [into defilement], the rain of defilements does not fall upon him nor drench him.
Thus, being unsullied by defilements and possessing pure virtue, he becomes concentrated;
having established insight and practicing comprehension, he gradually reaches Nibbāna—this is the intended meaning.
The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Soṇa Sutta: 46.
In the sixth [sutta], "in Avantī" means in the kingdom of Avantī; "at Kuraraghara" means in the city of that name; "on Mount Pavatta."
On the mountain named Pavatta (some also read "Papāta"). The lay follower Soṇa was known by the name Soṇa;
he was a lay follower (*upāsaka*) because he had declared his status as such through the threefold taking of refuge.
He was renowned as "Koṭikaṇṇa" (Ear-of-a-Crore) because he wore an earring worth a crore, though he should have been called "Koṭikaṇṇa," he was thus known as "Kuṭikaṇṇa."
The meaning is not that he was delicate or soft. For this man, having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, became deeply devoted to the Teaching;

established in the refuges and the precepts, he had a monastery built at Pavatta Mountain—a place endowed with shade and water—and having settled the Elder there, he attended upon him with the four requisites. Therefore it was said.
“He was the attendant of the Venerable Mahākaccāna.
From time to time he would go to attend upon the Elder, and the Elder would teach him the Dhamma.

Thereby, filled with a sense of spiritual urgency and inspired with zeal for the practice of the Dhamma, he lived his life. On one occasion, he traveled with a caravan for the purpose of trade to Ujjenī.
While traveling, he fell asleep on one side after moving away from the caravan that had halted in the wilderness during the night, out of fear of being crowded by people.
When the caravan rose and departed at dawn, not a single person woke Soṇa; they all went on, having forgotten him.
When the night had turned to day, he woke up, arose, and seeing no one, [realized what had happened].
Following the path taken by the sword, he proceeded very quickly and came upon a banyan tree.
There he saw a man of massive body and hideous appearance walking along, who was standing and eating his own flesh that had fallen off by itself.
Having seen him, he asked, "Who are you? "I am a peta, venerable sir," he replied. "Why?"
“Is this what you are doing? “It is because of my own past karma. “But what was that karma? “In the past, while living in the city of Bhārukaccha, I was a fraudulent merchant;
I deceived others and consumed their property. When ascetics came for alms, I reviled them, saying, ‘Eat your own meat!
Because of that karma, I am now experiencing this suffering. Thus he spoke.
Upon hearing this, Soṇa was overcome with extreme spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
As he proceeded further, he saw two *peta* children with black blood trickling from their mouths;
he questioned them in the same manner, and they too told him of their own karma. It seems that, while they were children in the city of Bhārukaccha, they had engaged in the trade of perfumes.
While making their living, they went to the house of their own mother—who had invited and was feeding an arahant monk—and reviled her, saying, "Why do you give what belongs to us to these ascetics?
May black blood flow from the mouths of those ascetics who eat the food given by you!
Having been boiled in hell for that deed, as a remainder of its karmic result, they were reborn in the womb of hungry ghosts (petas).
Having been reborn, they then experience this suffering. Upon hearing that as well, Soṇa was filled with extreme spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Having gone to Ujjenī and completed his business, he returned to his family home; there, having approached the Elder and exchanged greetings, he reported the matter to him.
The Elder [explained] to him the dangers and benefits regarding worldly involvement and renunciation.
He taught the Dhamma while analyzing it. Having paid homage to the Elder, he went home; after eating his evening meal, he retired to his bed.
Having slept only a little, he woke up and sat upon the surface of the bed, beginning to reflect upon the Dhamma exactly as he had heard it.
As he reflected on that Dhamma and recollected those states of existence as a peta, the suffering of *saṃsāra* [assailed him].
It appeared to him as exceedingly terrifying, and his mind inclined toward the going-forth.
When the night had turned to dawn, he attended to his bodily needs, approached the Elder, declared his aspiration, and requested the going-forth.
Thus it is said: "Then, while the lay follower Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa was alone in seclusion... [omitted] ...please let me go forth."
“Venerable sir, may the noble Mahākaccāna [teach] me.
In this context, the brief meaning of the words beginning with “in whatever way” is as follows:
in whatever manner the noble Mahākaccāna teaches, declares, makes known, establishes, reveals, analyzes, clarifies, and elucidates the Dhamma—

As I examine it in this way, it occurs to me: this holy life of the three trainings, having been practiced without breach for even a single day, must be brought to the final moment of consciousness as something absolutely complete;

having been made unstained by the impurity of defilements for even a single day, it must be brought to the final moment of consciousness as something absolutely pure; and it is "well-calcified," meaning it is like a well-burnt shell.
One should conduct oneself like a polished conch shell. It is not easy for one living in a household, dwelling in the midst of a home, to conduct oneself in this way—perfectly complete...

[and so forth]... What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, pull out my hair, and, having dyed them with the color of yellow ochre, put on the saffron robes suitable for those leading the holy life?
Having dressed myself, having put on my lower garment, and having wrapped myself in my upper robe, I would go forth from the home life into homelessness.

Since the work such as farming and trade that is beneficial to the household is called "the state of the householder" (*agāriya*), and since that does not exist for one who has gone forth, therefore going forth is called "the state of the homeless" (*anagāriya*). That state of the homeless, that going forth, I would go forth into; I would enter upon it.
The meaning is: "one should practice.
Having thus reported what he had thought in private to the Elder, the lay follower Soṇa, desiring to practice accordingly, said:
"Venerable sir, may the noble Mahākaccāna ordain me. But the Elder [thought], "How can his wisdom reach maturity yet?"
Having reflected thus and awaiting the ripening of his knowledge, he restrained his desire for renunciation with the words, "It is indeed difficult," and so forth.

Therein, "eating one meal" refers to the abstinence from eating at improper times, as stated in the passage: "He eats one meal a day, refraining at night and abstaining from eating outside the proper time.
"Sleeping alone" means sleeping without a companion. And here, by the term "sleeping" (seyyā),...

By the method beginning with “He stands alone, he walks alone, he sits alone,” it indicates physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*) among the four postures (*iriyāpatha*) thus described, not merely lying down by oneself.

“The holy life” (*brahmacariya*) refers either to the holy life consisting in abstention from sexual intercourse, or to the holy life of the Dispensation (*sāsana-brahmacariya*), which is characterized by devotion to the three trainings (*sikkhattaya*). “Come now” (*iṅgha*) is an exhortative particle. “Right there” (*tattheva*)—

"Only at home": apply yourself to the teaching of the Buddhas, which consists of the fivefold, eightfold, and tenfold moralities such as the constant morality and the Uposatha morality, as well as the cultivation of concentration and wisdom corresponding thereto.
For this is what is called "the teaching of the Buddhas" that should be applied to by a lay follower in the preliminary stage.
Therefore he said: "Eating at the proper time, eating once a day, and the noble life."
In this context, "joined with the proper time" means joined with the time known as the fourteenth, fifteenth, eighth, or the fortnight of miracles;
or it means that for one who applies himself at the aforementioned times, it is appropriate, fitting, and possible—meaning that renunciation is not [possible] at all times.
All of this is because his knowledge is not yet mature and because those sensual desires are difficult for him to abandon.
He says this in order to have [the youth] made fit for right practice, not to deter his desire for the going-forth.

"The volitional formation of going-forth" (*pabbajjābhisaṅkhāra*) means the undertaking or effort to go forth. "It subsided" (*paṭipassambhi*) means it was pacified because the faculties were not yet mature and the sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) was not too intense.
Even though it subsided, while following the procedure stated by the Elder...
From time to time, having approached the Elder and paid him homage, he listened to the Dhamma.
In the same manner as previously described, a second thought for the going-forth arose in him, and he informed the Elder. A second time, the Elder refused.
But on the third occasion, perceiving that his knowledge had reached maturity and thinking, "Now is the time to ordain him," the Elder—
He granted him the going-forth; and having let three years pass for him once he had gone forth, he sought out a group and granted him full ordination.
It was with reference to this that it was said: "A second time, Soṇa... [etc. ...granted him full ordination.
In this context, "one with few bhikkhus" means one who has only a few bhikkhus. At that time, it seems, the bhikkhus were for the most part in the Middle Country.
Thus they lived. Therefore, there were only a few there, and they lived separately—one in one town and two in another, and so forth.
"With difficulty" means with suffering; "with hardship" means with exhaustion. "From here and there" means from this or that village or town.
For when the Elder had brought a few monks and others were being brought, [he thought:]...
Those who had been brought previously departed on some business; after waiting for some time, when they were being brought back again, others departed.
Thus, through this repeated bringing and going, the assembly was formed only after a long time, and at that time the Elder was living alone.
"Having assembled a community of monks consisting of a group of ten" means that at that time, even in the border regions, by the Blessed One...
Full ordination was authorized by a Saṅgha of ten members. Indeed, because of this matter, when requested by the Elder, the Saṅgha authorized full ordination in border regions by a group of five.
Therefore it is said: “Having assembled those who have completed three years...
etc. “Of one who has spent the rains” means: of one who, having been fully ordained, has entered upon and completed the first year of residence. And such as this, and such as this...

"Such and such is his name; he is endowed with such and such perfection of the mental body and the physical body, and he is endowed with such and such perfection of the Dhamma-body"—thus has that Blessed One been heard of by me alone.
"I have not seen that Blessed One face-to-face"—by this, the Venerable Soṇa desired to see the Blessed One through the very faith of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).

Later, however, having lived together with the Teacher in the same fragrant chamber, he was requested at the time of dawn to recite the sixteen chapters of the *Aṭṭhakavagga* in the presence of the Teacher.

Having established the meaning, attended to it, and applied his whole mind to it, and being sensitive to both the meaning and the Dhamma, he spoke while remaining concentrated through the gateway of joy associated with the Dhamma; and at the conclusion of his recitation,
Having established insight and contemplating formations, he gradually attained Arahantship.
For it is said that it was for this very purpose that the Blessed One commanded him to dwell together with Him in the same Perfumed Chamber.
However, some say that the statement, "I have not seen that Blessed One face-to-face," refers specifically to the sight of His physical body (rūpakāya).
It is said: For the Venerable Soṇa, having gone forth and received a meditation subject from the Elder, while striving and exerting himself, became a stream-enterer even before his full ordination.
After being ordained, he thought, "The lay followers have become stream-enterers, and I too am a stream-enterer; what is there to worry about here?
Thus, for the sake of the higher paths, he developed insight and dwelt within the rainy-season residence itself.
Having become one possessed of the six direct knowledges, he offered the invitation of purification. For by the vision of the Noble Truths, the Dhamma-body of the Blessed One is truly seen.
Indeed, this has been said:
"Vakkali, whoever sees the Dhamma, he sees me; whoever sees me, he sees the Dhamma."
Therefore, his vision of the Dhamma-body was already accomplished; however, after the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), he desired to see the physical body (*rūpakāya*).
There is also a reading: "If my preceptor permits me. But they write "Venerable Sir" (*bhante*). Likewise, there is a reading:
"Excellent, excellent, friend Soṇa; go you, friend Soṇa. However, in some manuscripts, it says "friend" (*āvuso*).
There is none. Likewise, there is also the reading: “‘So it is, friend,’ said the Venerable Soṇa.

For during the time of the Blessed One, it was the custom for monks to address one another simply as “friend” (āvuso). The meaning of the phrases beginning with “the Blessed One is inspiring” has already been explained above.
"Is it endurable, monk? means: "Monk, regarding this body of yours with its four wheels and nine gates, is it endurable?
Is it possible to endure, to bear, and to maintain it? Does the burden of suffering not overwhelm you? "Is it sustainable? means:
"Is it possible to sustain or carry out your various duties? Is there no obstacle whatsoever? Thus he shows this.
"Have you come without fatigue? means: "Have you come this far without exertion? "This thought occurred to him" means:
as the Venerable Ānanda was recollecting the practice customary for Buddhas, this thought—which is now being stated as "For whom the Blessed One...
and so forth—occurred in his mind as a habitual inclination. "In a single dwelling" means: in a single fragrant hut (*gandhakuṭī*). For the fragrant hut...
"Here" refers to the dwelling. "Abode" means for the purpose of residing.

Regarding the phrase "having passed the time sitting": here, because the Blessed One was providing a hospitable welcome to the Venerable Soṇa by entering all the meditative attainments (samāpatti) common to his disciples, both in direct and reverse order; [it is said that he passed the time sitting].

For a great part of the night... [as before] ...he entered the monastery; therefore, some say that the Venerable Soṇa, having understood the Blessed One’s intention and entering into all those meditative attainments accordingly, "for a great part of the night... [as before] ...entered the monastery.
And having entered, with the permission of the Blessed One, he made his robe serve as a screen even for the Blessed One.
He spent the time sitting at the foot of a tree. *Ajjhesī* means he commanded. *Paṭibhātu taṃ bhikkhu dhammo bhāsituṃ*:

"O monk, may the Dhamma manifest itself to you for speaking"—the meaning is: "May knowledge arise before you so that you may speak the Dhamma as you have heard it and as you have mastered it; speak the Dhamma."
"The sixteen *Aṭṭhakavagga* discourses" means the sixteen discourses beginning with the *Kāmasutta*, which constitute the *Aṭṭhakavagga*.
"He recited them with melody" means he spoke using the melodic intonation for rehearsing discourses; the sense is that he delivered them by way of *sarabhañña* (melodic chanting).
"At the conclusion of the *sarabhañña*" means at the end of the rehearsal. "Well-learned" means properly mastered. "Well-attended to" means thoroughly kept in mind.

A certain person, although having correctly grasped [the teaching] at the time of learning, later, at the time of mental attention through methods such as recitation, either misrepresents the phrasing or distorts the sequence of the words; this is not so for him.
Rather, he has attended to them exactly as they were correctly grasped. Therefore it is said: "well-attended to" means "properly attended to."
"Well-considered" means well-reflected upon even in their meaning; for when the meaning is well-reflected upon, it is possible to recite the text correctly.

"Endowed with lovely speech" means he was endowed with refined speech that is complete in its words and syllables and perfect in its structure, through speech that is neither too loose nor too harsh, according to the rules. "Lucid" means liberated.
This shows his state of being one who speaks with liberation. *Anelagaḷāya*: "Elā" is said to mean fault (*dosa*); that which does not leak out (*paggharati*) such [fault] is *anelagaḷā*.

The meaning is: by means of that which is faultless. Alternatively, *anelagaḷāya* means both *anelā* and *agaḷā*; that is, by means of that which is faultless and non-leaking—that is, by means of words and phrasing that have not leaked away, meaning words and phrasing that are not deficient.
For it was thus that the Blessed One declared of her: "This is the foremost..."
“Bhikkhus, among my disciples who are bhikkhus of beautiful speech, this Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa stands foremost”—thus he placed him in that rank.
“In order to make his meaning known” means: capable of making known the intended meaning. “How many years [had he been ordained]?
It is said that he was situated in the third division of middle age and was endowed with proper deportment, and for others...
He appears as if he had gone forth a very long time ago. Some say that the Blessed One asks this with reference to him, but that is not the reason.
If that were the case, [the Teacher] would have further questioned him, saying, "Since you are fit to experience the bliss of concentration, why have you fallen into negligence for so long?
It is for this reason that the Teacher asks him, "How many years have you been ordained? Thus he said: "But why, monk..."
"Thus he acted for a long time.
In this context, "why" (*kissa*) means for what reason. "Thus he acted for a long time" means he delayed thus;

the meaning is: for what reason did he dwell in the midst of the household life instead of entering the going-forth for such a long period? "Seen after a long time" (*ciraṃ diṭṭho me*) means after a long duration, after a long time.

"I have seen it. Regarding "in sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu*): this refers both to defilement-sensualities (*kilesa-kāma*) and object-sensualities (*vatthu-kāma*). "Disadvantage" (*ādīnava*) means a fault.
Furthermore, even though the disadvantage in sensual pleasures had been seen by me in some manner, I was still unable to go forth from the household life.
Why? Because the household life is cramped, crowded with various duties and obligations; such is the state of being a householder. Therefore he said:
—“He has much to do, he has much to attend to.

Having understood this meaning: that for one who sees the danger in sensual pleasures as it really is, the mind does not settle there even after remaining for a long time, but rather turns away entirely like a drop of water on a lotus leaf—having understood this meaning in all its aspects...
Having understood: knowing correctly both the process of occurrence (*pavatti*) and the process of cessation (*nivatti*), he never finds delight in occurrence nor in its causes;
thus, illuminating this meaning, he uttered this *udāna*.

Therein, "having seen the danger in the world" means having seen that in the entire world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-loka*), it is "impermanent, suffering, and subject to change," and so forth.
"Having seen the danger and the fault with wisdom. By this, the section on insight (*vipassanā*) is explained. "Having known the Dhamma that is without substrate (*nirupadhi*).

Because it is the relinquishing of all substrates, one knows the Dhamma of Nibbāna—which is without substrate—as it truly is; having penetrated it through path-knowledge as being by nature the escape, seclusion, the unconditioned, and the deathless.
Regarding these two phrases, "having seen" and "having known," [the commentary says]: "Just as strength comes from drinking ghee..."
In passages such as, "Fear arises upon seeing a lion; upon seeing wisdom, the taints (āsava) are completely destroyed," it should be understood as having the sense of a cause.
An *ariya* does not delight in evil because he is far removed (*āraka*) from defilements; thus an *ariya*, a true person, does not delight even in the slightest evil.
Why? Because he does not delight in evil, he is "pure" (*suci*), meaning a person who is purified by means of perfectly pure bodily conduct and so forth.
Like a royal swan, he does not delight in nor take pleasure in evil, defiled states, which are like a dungheap.

There is also a reading: “The wicked man does not delight in the pure. Its meaning is this: the wicked person, a person of evil, does not delight in what is pure, blameless, or a state of purification;
rather, like village pigs and the like, he delights only in what is impure and defiled, such as a dungheap.
"Delights" (ramati) thus turns the teaching from its opposite.

When the Exalted One had uttered this Udāna, the Venerable Soṇa rose from his seat, paid homage to the Exalted One, and at the word of his own preceptor, requested the five matters beginning with full ordination for the border regions by means of a group of five. The Exalted One, too—
He authorizes those [rules]; all of that should be understood according to the method presented in the Khandhaka.
The commentary on the sixth sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Kaṅkhārevata Sutta.
47. Regarding "Kaṅkhārevata": this is the name of that elder. For after going forth in the Dispensation and receiving full ordination, he lived as one possessed of virtue and good qualities;

yet, he was full of doubt characterized as scruples regarding the Vinaya, thinking such things as, "Green gram is not allowable; green gram is not fit to be consumed," and "Sugar is not allowable. Therefore, he is called Kaṅkhārevata.

He appeared. Later on, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher and striving with diligence, he realized the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*) and spent his time in the bliss of jhāna and the bliss of fruition.
However, for the most part, he honored and reflected upon the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) he had attained himself. Therefore it was said: "His own purification by overcoming doubt..."
"Reflecting thus": for path-wisdom (*magga-paññā*) crosses over all doubts without exception—namely, the sixteen-based doubts occurring in the manner of "Was I indeed in the past?
and so forth, as well as the eight-based doubts spoken of as "He is doubtful about the Buddha... [and so on]...
he is doubtful about dependently arisen phenomena"—let alone the other types. Thus, it is because it transcends all doubts in their entirety.

Because it involves transcending and because it is absolutely purified of the defilements that one must abandon oneself—more so than other [purifications]—it is here intended as "purification by overcoming doubt.

For this venerable one sat reflecting with reverence, thinking: "Having attained this state of the Path, these doubts of mine have been abandoned without remainder," since he had long been dominated by doubt; it was not, however, a vision of name-and-form together with their conditions.
Because that crossing over of doubt is final and not subject to recurrence.

"Having understood this meaning" means: having understood this meaning—which is defined as the complete crossing over of all doubts by means of the Noble Path—he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) which illuminates that very meaning.
In this context, "whatever doubt there may be, either here or hereafter": "here" refers to this present personal existence (*attabhāva*), [thinking] "I..."
Doubts that arise regarding past or future personal existences (attabhāva), such as "Am I now? Am I not now? or "Did I exist in the past time?
and so forth; or "experienced by oneself" (*sakavediya*) or "experienced by another" (*paravediya*):
these, in the manner already described, are "experienced by oneself" because they are to be obtained through the occurrence [of consciousness] by way of their own personal existence as the object.
Or whatever doubt or perplexity there may be regarding what is to be obtained in another’s personal existence— such as "Is he a Buddha, or is he not?"—
or regarding the activity to be obtained in another's supreme exertion, or whatever is to be experienced by another;
all these the meditators abandon, being ardent and leading the holy life, through their close contemplation of the object.
By means of contemplation on the characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*), those meditators who have brought insight (*vipassanā*) to excellence,
being ardent through the fulfillment of the fourfold right exertion (*cattāro sammappadhānā*) and practicing the holy life of the path, reach the state of individuals established in the first path—
such as the faith-follower (*saddhānusārī*) and others— and at the moment of the path, they abandon and utterly sever all those doubts. Thereafter, however, they...
They are said to be "abandoned"; therefore, the intention is that there is no other absolute abandonment of them than this.

Thus, the Blessed One, praising the Venerable Kaṅkhā-Revata’s attainment of the Noble Path by way of the jhānas—specifically under the heading of his jhāna—uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) as a form of praise.
