And for that very reason, he addressed him: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my [disciples]..."
"He places Kaṅkhārevata at the foremost among his disciples, the bhikkhus who are meditators (jhāyī), on account of his state as a meditator.
The commentary on the seventh sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Saṅghabhedasutta.
48. Regarding the statement, "He said this to the Venerable Ānanda":

having employed Abhimāra, having released Nāḷāgiri, and having hurled a rock, being unable to cause harm to the Blessed One, he spoke these words beginning with "From this day forward," with the intention: "I shall split the Saṅgha and bring about a schism in the Wheel. "Apart from the Blessed One" means...
"Without the Blessed One" means without making him the Teacher. "Apart from the Saṅgha of bhikkhus" means without the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

"I shall perform the Uposatha and the Saṅgha formal acts" means setting aside the Saṅgha of bhikkhus who follow the instruction of the Blessed One, [to perform] the Uposatha and the Saṅgha formal acts independently with those bhikkhus who follow me.
And the meaning is: "I shall do it. Regarding the statement "Devadatta will split the Saṅgha":
because all those who cause a schism are prepared by Devadatta, Devadatta will today certainly split the Saṅgha—that is, he will divide it into two.
For, among the eighteen bases for causing a schism, such as "what is non-Dhamma is Dhamma," having demonstrated even a single one of those bases, by that...

For that reason, when one has persuaded others by saying, “Take this; approve of this,” and having had voting tickets distributed, a formal act of the Saṅgha is performed separately, the Saṅgha is split. For it has been said:
“Upāli, the Saṅgha is split in five ways: by formal act, by recitation, by discussion, by proclamation, and by the distribution of voting tickets.”
In this context, "by means of a formal act" (*kammena*) refers to any one of the four types of formal acts, such as the act of obtaining permission (*apalokana-kamma*).

"By means of a recitation" (*uddesena*) refers to any one of the five recitations of the *Pātimokkha*. "Speaking" (*voharanto*) means demonstrating the eighteen grounds for schism, such as "what is not Dhamma is Dhamma," by means of various specific instances.
"By means of a proclamation" (*anussāvanena*) refers to [the proclamation]: "Do you not know?"... [and so forth].

"Is it even fitting for you to entertain such a thought as: 'How could someone like me—one who has gone forth from a high-born family and is so learned—ever lead another into what is contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya? Do I not fear the states of misery?
Having spoken thus in his ear, he made the proclamation by means of a vote (*salākaggāha*). "Having thus proclaimed... [and so on].
Having steadied their minds and made them of a nature not to turn back, he says, "Take this voting ticket," by means of the taking of the voting tickets (*salākaggāha*).

In this context, the formal act (*kamma*) itself or the proclamation (*uddesa*) is the criterion; however, the preliminary stages consist of the announcement (*vohāra*), the proclamation (*anussāvana*), and the taking of the voting tickets (*salākaggāha*).
For, while announcing by way of illustrating the eighteen grounds, one proclaims there for the purpose of generating consent, and then [proceeds] with the voting ticket.

Even when the voting sticks have been distributed, the Saṅgha remains undivided. However, when four or more monks, having thus distributed the voting sticks, perform a separate recitation or a formal act (*kamma*), then the Saṅgha is said to be split.
And Devadatta, having completed all the preliminary stages for a schism in the Saṅgha, [thought]: "Today, by one means alone, [I shall perform] a separate Uposatha."
Thinking, "And I shall perform a formal act of the Saṅgha," he spoke the words beginning with "From this day forward. Therefore he said:

"Venerable sir, today Devadatta will split the Saṅgha. As for what we said—"Because all those who cause schism have been instigated by Devadatta"—having understood this matter, [he realized] that it leads to rebirth in the great Avīci hell, lasts for an eon, and is incurable.
Having understood in every aspect the act of schism being brought about by Devadatta, he uttered this *udāna*—that is, he uttered this inspired utterance to clarify its meaning as follows:

"Among the wholesome and unwholesome, according to their respective order, through the practice that is either concordant or discordant with the nature of true men and untrue men, [the wholesome is] most wholesome. Thus he spoke this *udāna*.
In this context, one who accomplishes what is beneficial for oneself and others is called "good" (*sādhu*), meaning one who has entered upon the right path.

By such a good person—whether they be a disciple like Sāriputta and others, a Paccekabuddha, a Fully Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*), or any other worldly good person—it is easy (*sukara*) to perform that which is good, beautiful, and auspicious, bringing about welfare and happiness for both oneself and others. It is possible to do so with ease.
"Good is what is difficult for the wicked to do": this refers to the characteristic already mentioned;
it is good that what is difficult to perform cannot be done by a wicked person such as Devadatta or others—the meaning is that he is not able to do it.
"Evil is easy for the wicked to do": evil, which is unwholesome and brings harm to oneself and others, is easy to do for a wicked person as previously described.

One would be able to do it with ease. "Evil is difficult for the Noble Ones": however, for the Noble Ones—such as the Buddhas and others—that respective evil is difficult to perform and hard to accomplish.
For the Teacher explains that for them, there is indeed the destruction of the bridge.
The commentary on the eighth sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Sādhāyamāna Sutta 49.
In the ninth [verse], "young men" (*māṇavaka*) means those who are youthful. In the first [verse], it refers to Brahmin youths established in their prime.
"Acting in a mocking manner" (*sadhāyamānarūpa*) is said with reference to speech that is of a teasing nature. Others mock when they "sādh" (applaud).
The meaning is: "those whose nature is to speak of that [meaning]. This is its etymological analysis: *sadha* means "with proof" (*sadhana*);

those who explain that are called *sadhayamānā*, though it should have been said *sadhāyamānā* with a long vowel. Alternatively, they are called *sadhāyamānā* because they cause themselves to be heard as if accompanied by proof (*sa-sedha*) in a specific sense.
Because they possess such a nature, they are described as "having the form of being accompanied by proof" (*sadhāyamānarūpā*).
There is also a reading, “*saddāyamānarūpā*,” meaning they were making loud noises and great clamor.
“Passing by not far from the Blessed One” means they went by while speaking whatever had come to their lips within the range of the Blessed One’s hearing.
“Having understood this matter” means having recognized their lack of restraint in speech, he uttered this *udāna* out of a sense of spiritual urgency (*dhammasaṃvega*) to illuminate that very point.
In this context, "forgetful" means sluggish and of muddled mindfulness. "Appearing wise" means resembling the wise;
it refers to those who, thinking "Who else knows? We alone know this," conduct themselves by making themselves out to be the only ones who understand each respective matter.
"Those whose range is speech" means those for whom speech alone is their range or domain; they are "speakers whose range is speech," [concerned] only with the mere basis of words.

They speak because they have not fully understood the meaning. Alternatively, they speak false speech (*musāvāda*), which is outside the range of speech and beyond the domain of the Noble Ones’ discourse;
thus, they are "speakers whose range is speech" (*vācāgocarabhāṇino*). Or else, in the term "gocarabhāṇino," the long vowel *ā* has been shortened to *a*.
They are merely speakers whose range is speech, not those whose range is the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth. How do they speak? As much as they desire.

The meaning is that they speak having extended their mouths as far as they wish to extend them—that is, as far as the opening of the mouth—and they do not contract their mouths out of respect for others and because it is beyond their own capacity.
Alternatively, the meaning is that they speak only within the range of speech;
that is, being ignorant themselves, they are speakers who merely rely on the assertions of others.

For that very reason, the meaning is: they do not consider the extent of the speech by which they ought to be made known, but rather desire only as much as is sufficient for the opening of their own mouths. "They do not know by what they have been led" means:

by what—namely, by forgetfulness and so forth—they have been led into shamelessness and the conceit of thinking themselves wise, saying, "We speak thus," while speaking in such a manner of themselves.
"The wise do not know the cause" means that the ignorant and the cowardly do not understand it.
The commentary on the ninth sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Cūḷapanthaka Sutta.

50. In the tenth [chapter], Cūḷapanthaka is mentioned. Because he was the younger brother of the Elder Mahāpanthaka and because he was born on a path (*pantha*), he received the name "Cūḷapanthaka" during his childhood;
even later in life, this venerable one was known by that very name.

However, due to his special qualities—being a possessor of the six supernormal knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*) and having attained the analytical insights (*pabhinnapaṭisambhida*)—he was declared: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples..."
“Among those monks who manifest mind-made bodies, this one is the foremost, namely Cūḷapanthaka; among those skilled in the turning away of the mind, this one is the foremost, namely Cūḷapanthaka.
Thus was he placed by the Blessed One in these two ranks among the eighty great disciples.
One day, having returned from his alms round after the meal, he sat for his midday rest in his own daytime dwelling place.
Having spent the day in meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), when it was evening and the lay followers had not yet arrived for the sake of hearing the Dhamma,
he entered the midst of the monastery. Finding the Blessed One seated in the Perfumed Chamber (*gandhakuṭī*), he thought,
"It is not yet the time to approach the Blessed One for attendance," and sat down cross-legged at one side near the entrance of the Perfumed Chamber.

Having crossed his legs. Therefore it was said: "Now at that time the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka was sitting not far from the Blessed One, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him.
For he had sat down at that time after determining a time limit and entering into meditative attainment.
"Having understood this matter" means having known this matter consisting in the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka’s state of being rightly directed in both body and mind.

"This inspired utterance" refers to that which pertains to the attainment of distinction— culminating in final Nibbāna through non-clinging— for any other monk as well who, with body calmed, is established in mindfulness and concentrated in all postures.
He uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) concerning the manifestation of what has become manifest.
Therein, "with the body established" means: by abandoning and refraining from unrestrained conduct pertaining to the door of the body, the moving body is properly established;
likewise, it refers to the eyes and other sense-faculties being well-established by bringing them to a state of non-indulgence.

By means of the body of the five doors; and by means of the physical body (karaja-kāya) which remains motionless due to its lack of agitation—because it is characterized by restrained hands and feet and is thus free from fidgeting of the hands and so forth—in brief, by means of the entire body remaining in a state of immobility known as "unperturbedness.
By this, his purity of virtue (sīla-pārisuddhi) is shown. And this instrumental case ending is used here in the sense of a characteristic of the state attained (itthambhūta-lakkhaṇe).
By the phrase "with a steady mind," he demonstrates the perfection of concentration (*samādhi*), for concentration is indeed called the "steadiness" of the mind.

Therefore, when there is one-pointedness by way of serenity (*samatha*) or insight (*vipassanā*), the mind is said to be "steady" through its attainment of a state of singleness toward the object, and not otherwise. And this [refers to] the aforementioned body and mind...
Showing that fixing and concentrating [the mind] must be practiced at all times and in all postures, he said:
"Whether standing, sitting, or lying down. Herein, the word *vā* has the sense of non-restriction;
by it, the meaning "whether standing, or sitting, or lying down, or in any other posture" is illustrated, and thus walking meditation (*caṅkamana*) is also included.
Herein, "support" is to be understood.

Regarding the phrase "a bhikkhu who is intent upon this mindfulness": by means of that mindfulness through which he has already purified his conduct, and having made both body and mind unagitated by calming their coarseness, and having established himself in blameless happiness, he [proceeds] by way of the tranquility of body and mind.
Having made the mind light, pliant, and wieldy, one who correctly establishes and concentrates it develops the meditation subject and brings it to its culmination.
A bhikkhu who resolves upon that very mindfulness— which is of great assistance at the beginning, middle, and end of the practice of the meditation subject—
proceeds from the purification of virtue as the starting point until the attainment of distinction in each respective stage.
The meaning is "he resolves. "He would obtain successive distinction" means that he, by thus increasing, developing, and expanding the meditation subject with a mind protected by mindfulness,

would obtain successive distinction— that is, a distinction consisting of successive stages, occurring in a sequence of earlier and later parts, characterized by degrees such as "excellent" and "more excellent."

In this context, the distinction between what precedes and what follows is twofold: by way of serenity (*samatha*) and by way of insight (*vipassanā*). Among these, first, regarding that by way of serenity:

the specific excellence of development (*bhāvanāvisesa*) proceeding from the arising of the sign (*nimitta*) up until the attainment of mastery over the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) constitutes the distinction between what precedes and what follows.
Regarding that by way of insight, however, for one who enters into [the object] by way of the form-portal (*rūpamukha*):

The distinction between earlier and later stages (*pubbāpariyavisesa*) refers to the specific excellence of development that proceeds from the time of grasping material phenomena—while for the other [type of person], from the time of grasping mental phenomena—up until the attainment of Arahatship. And this alone is intended here.
Having attained the distinction between earlier and later, one reaches Arahatship, which is the pinnacle of excellence and the ultimate limit.

"Having attained": "He goes beyond the sight of the King of Death" means that by way of severing the life-faculty, he would go beyond the sight—that is, beyond the range—of death, which is designated as the King of Death, because he has transcended the three realms of existence (bhava) which constitute its domain.
Whatever has not been stated in this section is according to the method already explained below.
The commentary on the Tenth Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Mahāvagga is also finished.
6. The Chapter on the One Born Blind.
1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Relinquishing of the Life-Faculty (Āyusaṅkhārossajjanasutta). 51.
Regarding the first sutta of the Jaccandhavagga, beginning with "At Vesālī," the meaning has already been explained above. "He entered Vesālī for alms": when did he enter it?
It was at the time when, having departed from Ukkācela, he had gone to Vesālī. For the Blessed One [stayed] in the village of Veḷuva...
Having spent the rains retreat, he departed from there and, traveling by stages, arrived at Sāvatthī and dwelt in the Jeta Grove.
At that time, the Dhammasenāpati, having surveyed his own life-span and knowing that it would last for only seven more days, requested leave from the Blessed One;
he then went to Nāḷakagāma and established his mother in the fruit of stream-entry.
He attained final Nibbāna. The Teacher, having taken the relics brought by Cunda and having had a relic-shrine (dhātucetiya) constructed, went to Rājagaha surrounded by a great community of bhikkhus.
While he was there, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna attained final Nibbāna.
The Blessed One, having taken his relics as well and having had a shrine built, departed from Rājagaha and in due course arrived at Ukkācelā.

There, having sat on the bank of the Ganges surrounded by the community of monks and taught the Dhamma concerning the final passing away (parinibbāna) of his chief disciples, the Blessed One departed from Ukkācela and went to Vesālī. Having gone there, it is said:
“In the morning, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, he entered Vesālī for alms. Therefore it was said: “From Ukkācela...”
“...after departing and having gone to Vesālī.

Regarding the “seating mat”: here, a piece of leather is intended. As for the “Cāpāla Shrine,” it was known as the “Cāpāla Shrine” because it was formerly the dwelling place of a yakkha named Cāpāla. It was there that the Blessed One made his residence.
By that conventional usage, it is called the “Cāpāla Cetiya. The same principle applies to such names as the “Udena Cetiya” and others.

Regarding the “Sattamba”: it is said that seven princesses, daughters of King Kiki of Kāsī, having become spiritually stirred (saṃvega-jātā), departed from the royal palace and practiced meditation at a certain place; that site they call the “Sattamba Cetiya.”
*Bahuputta* refers to a single banyan tree (*nigrodha-rukkha*) with many branches;
because many people prayed for sons to the deity residing therein, that place became known as the *Bahuputta Cetiya*.
*Sārandada* is the dwelling place of a yakkha named Sārandada. Thus, all of these existed prior to the appearance of the Buddha.

Because they were protected by deities, they came to be designated by the term *cetiya* (shrine); even though monasteries (*vihāra*) were later constructed there, they continued to be known in that same way.

Regarding the word "delightful" (*rāmaṇīya*): here, the quality of being delightful should be understood first in Vesālī itself, due to its excellence of terrain, the excellence of its people, and the ease with which requisites are obtained.
As for the monasteries, however, it is because they are not too far from the city...

Its delightful nature is to be seen through its proximity [to a monastery], its suitability for coming and going, its location in an uncluttered dwelling place, its possession of shade and water, and its resemblance to seclusion.
Regarding the "four bases of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*), the meaning of the term *iddhipāda* has already been explained above.
"Developed" (*bhāvitā*) means increased. "Cultivated" (*bahulīkatā*) means practiced repeatedly. "Made a vehicle" (*yānīkatā*)...
“Made into a vehicle” means made like a vehicle by means of a yoke. “Made into a foundation” means made like a foundation in the sense of being a support.
“Established” means resolved upon. “Cultivated” means built up on all sides, well-increased. “Well undertaken” means properly undertaken, excellently accomplished.
Having thus spoken without specific restriction, he said, “Of the Tathāgata indeed,” and so forth, in order to show it again with specific restriction. Herein—
And they endure for the duration of a *kappa*. "He might remain" means that he might remain or persist, having fulfilled whatever measure of human lifespan exists at that particular time.
"Or for the remainder of a *kappa*" means more than a hundred years—whether it be little or more—as it has been stated.
However, the Elder Mahāsīva said: "Thundering in a place where Buddhas do not appear..."

"There is no such thing. For just as he suppressed the death-proximate pains that arose in the village of Veḷu for ten months, so too, by repeatedly entering that attainment and suppressing them, he would have remained for this very auspicious aeon. But why did he not remain?
Because a body subject to clinging is overcome by decrepitude and the like; [this was not the case for] the Buddhas...
Furthermore, without having reached a state of decay and so forth, they attain final nibbāna while still beloved and dear to the multitude during the fifth portion of their lifespan.

When the Buddhas and those awakened by the Buddha—the Chief Disciples and Great Disciples—have attained final nibbāna, one must remain either alone without a retinue, or accompanied only by young novices. Then [one reflects]: "Oh, the assembly of the Buddhas!"
He would incur contempt; therefore, he is not "standing. Even when this was said, that [explanation] was not accepted;
rather, it is precisely this—"for the duration of a lifespan"—that is established in the Aṭṭhakathā.
"In a gross sign" means in a coarse production of perception. For this is the production of a coarse perception: "Let the Blessed One remain..."

"Kappa" means the ability to remain for an entire eon through the request for stability; that is, by means of an indirect statement such as "Ānanda, whoever has developed the four bases of psychic power," he demonstrates his own capacity to remain for an eon through the power of his cultivation of the four bases of psychic power.
"Obhāseti" means in explicit speech. And this speech is explicit because it is not a figurative expression (pariyāya).

Having set aside his own direct manifestation of his personal intention, [he spoke] "for the welfare of many" (bahujanahitāya) for the sake of the benefit of the great multitude; "for the happiness of many" (bahujanasukhāya) for the sake of the well-being of the great multitude;
"out of compassion for the world" (lokānukampāya) out of compassion for the world of sentient beings. For which world of sentient beings? That which belongs to the Blessed One...

Having heard the teaching of the Dhamma, one penetrates it and drinks the drink of the Deathless. Indeed, through the Blessed One’s teaching of the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta*, eighteen koṭis of Brahmās, headed by Aññāta-Koṇḍañña, penetrated the Dhamma.
Thus, from that point until the conversion of the wanderer Subhadda, there is no counting the number of beings who have penetrated the Dhamma;
such as [those reached] through the *Mahāsamaya Sutta*, the *Maṅgala Sutta*, and the *Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta*.
Regarding the *Samacittasutta*: at the time of the teaching of these four discourses, there was no limit to the number of beings who attained realization;
thus, the Blessed One’s opportunity arose out of compassion for this immeasurable world of beings.
He speaks with the intention that it will be so in the future as well. As for the phrase "of gods and humans," it refers not only to gods and humans alone, [but to all beings].
The Blessed One’s presence is for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of the remaining beings as well, such as the *nāgas* and *supaṇṇas*.

However, this was said specifically to show those individuals capable of realizing the paths and fruits who possess the necessary causes for rebirth (*sahetuka-paṭisandhika*). Therefore, the meaning is:
"May the Blessed One remain for the sake of the welfare, benefit, and happiness of others too. In that context, "for the sake of welfare" (*atthāya*) means for the sake of prosperity in this world.
“For his welfare” means for the sake of benefit that serves as the cause for success in the world beyond. “For his happiness” means for the sake of the bliss of the element of Nibbāna.
However, the previous mention of "welfare" and "happiness" should be understood in a sense common to all.
The phrase *yathā taṃ* (as it is) is merely a particle; it is used here just as in the expression *yathā mārena pariyuṭṭhitacitto* (just as one whose mind is obsessed by Māra).
The meaning is that just as no other ordinary person (*puthujjana*) whose mind is overwhelmed would be able to penetrate [the truth], even so he was unable to penetrate it.
For Māra obsesses the mind of anyone who has not abandoned any of the perversions (*vipallāsa*);
however, for one in whom all twelve perversions have been abandoned in every respect, there is simply nothing to be said.
The Elder had not yet abandoned the four perversions (*vipallāsa*); therefore, his mind was obsessed (*pariyuṭṭhita*). What does one who brings about such obsession of the mind do?
He displays a terrifying object of form (*rūpārammaṇa*) or makes a sound as an object of hearing (*saddārammaṇa*) resound.
Then, upon seeing or hearing it, living beings lose their mindfulness and have their mouths wide open. From their mouths—
Having thrust its hand inside, it crushes the heart; then, having lost consciousness, they remain there.
But how could this [demon] thrust its hand into the Elder’s mouth? Rather, it displays a terrifying object.
Having seen that, the Elder did not penetrate the radiance of the sign (*nimittobhāsa*). Knowing [the answer] already, for what purpose did the Blessed One address him up to three times?
When [Sundarika-Bhāradvāja] later requested, "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One stay," [the Buddha replied], "This misdeed is yours alone;
this transgression is yours alone," in order to alleviate his grief by attributing the fault to him. For the Blessed One saw: "This man’s heart is exceedingly tender toward me;
having heard later about the cause of the earthquake and the relinquishing of the life-force, he will request that I remain for a long time."
Then [he thought]: "If I say, 'Why did you not ask earlier?', I shall cast the blame upon his very head;
and since beings do not suffer so much through their own fault, his grief will thereby be diminished.

"Go, Ānanda," he said, because Ānanda had come there for the sake of his midday rest; therefore, Ānanda, go to whatever place you prefer for your midday rest. For this very reason he said: "Now, go as you deem fit."
Regarding the phrase "Māra the Evil One": here, he is called *Māra* because he kills (*māreti*) beings by directing them toward what is harmful. "The Evil One" (*Pāpimā*) is a synonym for him;
indeed, he is called "the Evil One" because he is possessed of evil qualities (*pāpadhamma*). Furthermore, as for the statement "this was spoken":
after the Blessed One had spent seven weeks at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), while staying at the Goatherd’s Banyan tree (*ajapālanigrodha*), [he spoke this] concerning his own daughters.

Having arrived and encountered the frustration of his desire, he departed; then, thinking, "There is this means," he returned and said, "Bhagavā, that purpose for which you fulfilled the perfections has now been reached; omniscient knowledge has been penetrated.
What is the use of your wandering through the world? Having spoken thus, just as he does today, he said, "Venerable Sir, let the Bhagavā now attain final Nibbāna."
He made a request. The Blessed One, having said to him, "Not yet," and so forth, refused it. Referring to that, he now says, "But this has been spoken," and so on.
In that context, "learned" (*viyatta*) means skilled by way of the attainment of the Noble Path; "disciplined" (*vinīta*) means likewise through the disciplining of the defilements.
"Vinītā" means disciplined. "Visāradā" means having attained a state of confidence through the abandonment of those things that cause timidity, such as wrong views and doubt.
"Bahussutā" means those by whom much has been heard, according to the three Piṭakas; thus they are "bahussutā. "Dhammadharā" means those who bear that very Dhamma in mind.
Alternatively, "bahussutā" refers to those who are learned in the scriptures (pariyatti) and those who are learned through realization (paṭivedha). "Dhammadharā" means...
The meaning here should be understood as follows: they are "bearers of the Dhamma" (dhammadhara) because they bear both the Dhamma of the scriptures and the Dhamma of realization.
"Practicing in accordance with the Dhamma" (dhammānudhammapaṭipanna) means practicing the Dhamma of insight (vipassanā), which is the secondary Dhamma (anudhamma) to the Noble Dhamma (ariyadhamma).
"Practicing with propriety" (sāmīcippaṭipanna) means practicing the successive stages of purification that are appropriate for the purification of knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassanavisuddhi).

"Those who have entered upon the practice. "Practitioners of the Dhamma in accordance with it" means those whose habit is to practice the qualities such as fewness of desires that are appropriate to and conducive of that practice.
"Their own teacher’s doctrine" means their own teacher’s teaching. "They will proclaim" means they will speak of it from the beginning;
the meaning is that they will cause others to learn it according to the method they themselves have mastered. "They will teach" means they will cause it to be recited—that is, the Pāḷi.

“Teaching rightly” means they will cause [others] to learn correctly. “They will proclaim” means they will cause [others] to understand; the meaning is that they will make it manifest. “They will establish” means they will establish it in its proper manner.
“They will reveal” means they will make it open. “They will analyze” means they will make it divided into parts.
“They will clarify” means they will make what is not clear—that which is deep—clear and evident. “In accordance with the Dhamma” (sahadhammena) means...

“With reasoned and causal speech. “Possessing demonstration” means having made it leading to liberation (*niyyānika*). “They will teach the Dhamma” means they will awaken to and proclaim the ninefold supramundane Dhamma; this is the meaning.
And here, by the six phrases beginning with “they will prescribe,” six points of meaning are shown; however, from the beginning—
"By two words there are six phrasing-words. To this extent, the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas has been shown by way of the method of commentary.
For it is said in the *Netti*: "The Sutta consists of twelve words;
all of that is both the phrasing and the meaning."
"Brahmacariya" refers to the entire holy life of the Dispensation, comprised within the three trainings.
"Iddha" means successful, by way of the arising of jhāna. "Phīta" means reached full growth, being in full bloom through the attainment of the higher knowledges (abhiññā).
"Vitthārika" means extensive, by way of being established in various directions and regions. "Bāhujañña" means...
"It is known by many" means it has been penetrated by many people through their realization (*abhisamaya*). "It has become widespread" means it has attained a state of broadness in every respect.
How so? "Well-proclaimed as far as gods and humans" means it has been thoroughly proclaimed by all those who are of a discerning nature among both gods and humans.
“Appossukka” means one who is effortless, whose energy has slackened. He says:
“For you, O Evil One, from the time seven weeks had passed, you have been wandering about crying out, ‘Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One now attain final Nibbāna;
let the Sugata now attain final Nibbāna! But from this day forward, be devoid of zeal; do not exert yourself for the sake of my final Nibbāna.”

"Mindful and clearly comprehending, he relinquished the life-formations (*āyusaṅkhāra*)" means that, having established mindfulness well and delimited [the duration] with knowledge, he released and abandoned the life-formations.
In this regard, the Blessed One did not relinquish the life-formations like throwing a clod of earth with his hand;
rather, having entered a meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) for only three months, he resolved: "Beyond this, I shall not enter [further attainments]."
He gave rise to that thought. It is with reference to this that it is said: “He relinquished,” or alternatively, the reading is “he let go.

But why did the Blessed One—though capable of remaining for an eon or the remainder of an eon—not remain for that long and instead relinquish the life-formations (*āyu-saṅkhāra*) at Māra’s request in order to attain final Nibbāna?
It was not because of Māra’s request that the Blessed One [relinquished them].

He relinquished the life-force; he did not relinquish it because of the Elder’s entreaty, but rather relinquished the life-force after three months because there were no longer any beings to be converted by the Buddha.
For the standing of the Blessed Buddhas is solely for the purpose of training those to be trained;
when there are no people to be trained, for what reason indeed would they remain?
And if he were to attain final Nibbāna at Māra’s request, he would have attained it even earlier.
For it has been said that even at the Seat of Enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa), Māra made his request, and the Elder’s manifestation of the signs was for the purpose of alleviating Māra’s grief.
Furthermore, the manifestation of the signs was for the purpose of demonstrating the power of a Buddha. Such is the great majesty of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Even when remaining [in this world], they remain only by their own will; even when attaining final Nibbāna, they attain it only by their own will.
"A great earthquake" means a massive shaking of the earth. At that time, it is said, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled.
"Terrifying" means causing fear. "And the divine drums resounded" means the celestial drums rang out; the gods...
"Empty thunder" was thunders; "untimely lightning flashes" flashed forth; "momentary rain" rained—this is what is meant.
"Having understood this matter" means having understood in every aspect this matter characterized as the distinction between conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) and the unconditioned (*visaṅkhāra*).
"This inspired utterance" refers to that which, having relinquished all conditioned phenomena without exception, illustrates his own attainment of the unconditioned.
He uttered an *udāna*. Why did he utter it? Someone might say:
"The Blessed One, having been pursued from behind by Māra and harassed by him with the words, 'Venerable Sir, enter final Nibbāna,' relinquished the life-faculty out of fear.

To prevent such an opportunity for this [misconception], and to demonstrate that there is no such thing as an *udāna* uttered by one who is afraid, he uttered this *udāna* which issued forth through the force of rapture.
"He uttered an exclamation" (udānesi) is what is stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Furthermore, because the Buddha’s work was accomplished in just those three months, he saw that "this burden of suffering, which has been carried by me for so long, will soon be laid down.
Upon reflecting on the excellence of his Parinibbāna, a sublime joy and gladness arose in him; through the force of that joy, [he uttered the exclamation].

"Udānesi" (he uttered) seems appropriate. For the Teacher, who was entirely inclined toward the cessation of formations (*visaṅkhāra*) and whose aspiration was fixed on Nibbāna, remained in the world for a very long time for the sake of the welfare of beings, as if by the force of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Thus, he daily employed meditative attainments numbering twenty-four hundred thousand crores; now, because his task of great compassion had been accomplished, he turned toward Nibbāna and [uttered] no small amount...

He experienced rapture and joy. For on that very day of the final nirvana of the aggregates (khandha-parinibbāna), just as on the day of the Blessed One’s final nirvana through the extinction of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna), the radiance of his body was especially serene, pure, and luminous.
In the verse, "tulam" refers to sense-sphere karma (kāmāvacara-kamma), which is weighed and delimited because even jackals, dogs, and other such beings were present to witness it.
"Without equal" (*atula*) means that there is no other worldly action equal to it or similar to it; thus it is "without equal," referring to sublime (*mahaggata*) action.
Sensual-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) or fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) action is "with equal" (*tula*); immaterial-sphere (*arūpāvacara*) action is "without equal.

Or, action with little ripening is "with equal," while action with much ripening is "without equal. "Origination" (*sambhava*) means being the cause for origination, that is, producing rebirth. "Formations of existence" (*bhava-saṅkhāra*)—
That which conditions renewed existence. *Avassajī* means he relinquished. *Munī* refers to the Buddha, the Sage. *Ajjhattarato* means one who delights in what is internal to oneself.
*Samāhito* means concentrated by way of access and absorption concentration. *Abhindi kavacamiva* means he shattered it as if it were armor.
*Attasambhavaṃ* means the defilement born within himself. This is what is meant: "In the sense of having a result..."
He relinquished his own origin— known as the "volitional formations of existence" (bhavasaṅkhāra) in the sense of constructing various states of becoming—
and also the mundane karma known as the "weighing and being weighed. Like a great warrior at the head of battle discarding his armor,
he, being inwardly delighted and composed, shattered both his own origin and the defilements.

Alternatively, "weighing" means comparing and examining. He weighed both the incomparable—the arising of both Nibbāna and existence—and the formative forces of existence, which is karma leading to rebirth.

The Sage abandoned them; that is, the Buddha-Sage, by way of such methods as "the five aggregates are impermanent" and "the cessation of the five aggregates is the permanent Nibbāna," weighing the danger in existence and [the excellence] in Nibbāna...

And having seen the benefit, he abandoned that karma—the formative force of existence which is the root of the aggregates—by means of the Noble Path described as "leading to the destruction of karma," which brings about the exhaustion of karma.
How so? "Delighting within, composed, he shattered his own arising like a coat of mail. For he delighted within by way of insight (*vipassanā*), and by way of serenity (*samatha*)...

"Concentrated": thus, having stood from the preliminary stage onwards, having enveloped his person like armor by the power of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), he shattered the entire web of defilements—which, because it arises within him, is named "born of self.
Because of the absence of defilements, karma becomes "rendered useless," as it no longer leads to rebirth; such is the abandonment of defilements.

He abandoned the kamma. Thus, even while at the foot of the Bodhi tree, the Blessed One—having already relinquished the volitional formations for existence—maintained his physical frame by means of alternating meditative attainments, as if with a dilapidated cart.
Yet, by generating the thought, "From now on, after three months, I shall not grant any further alternating attainments," he relinquished the life-formations.
The commentary on the first sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Sattajaṭila Sutta: 52.
Regarding the phrase "outside the gatehouse": this refers to the area outside the gatehouse of the palace, not the gatehouse of the monastery.
It is said that this palace, like the Lohapāsāda, was surrounded on all sides by four gate-towers and enclosed by a rampart wall.
Outside the eastern gate-tower, in the shadow of the palace, he sat upon an excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared, gazing toward the eastern world-system.
"Jaṭilas" means those with matted hair who wear the garb of ascetics; "Nigaṇṭhas" means those who wear the white-robed appearance of the Nigaṇṭhas.

*Ekasāṭaka* means those who, like the Nigaṇṭhas who wear a single cloth (*ekasāṭaka*), wander about having tied a piece of rags to their hands and covering the front part of the body with that as well.
*Parūḷhakacchanakhaloma* means those whose pubic hair is grown long, whose nails are grown long, and whose other body hair is grown long;
the meaning is that they have long hair in the armpits and so forth, and long nails. *Khārivividhamādāya* means... [text continues]
Having taken up various requisites for those gone forth, consisting of many kinds such as salt and so forth;
"passing by not far" means they enter the city by a road not distant from the monastery.
"I am King Pasenadi of Kosala, venerable sir," means: "I, venerable sir, am King Pasenadi of Kosala; this is my name."

"You know this. But why did the king, sitting in the presence of the foremost person in the world, raise his joined palms to such naked and unseemly men? It was for the sake of conciliation. For he thought:
"If I do not show even this much courtesy to them, then we shall have to abandon our wives and children and endure poor food, miserable lodgings, and the like for his sake."
"He does not even show us the slightest sign of respect. For if he were to do so, people would not regard us as 'spies' but would instead perceive us as 'renunciants.
What is the use of telling him the truth? Thinking thus, they would conceal what they had seen and heard and not speak;
but if [the Teacher] were to act in this way, they would speak without hiding anything. Furthermore, regarding the Teacher...
"He did this also for the purpose of knowing their underlying disposition. It is said that even as he approached the Blessed One, the King did not believe in Perfect Enlightenment for some time.

Therefore, it occurred to him: "If the Blessed One knows everything, he would not grant his approval when I have paid them such homage and say, 'These are Arahants'; yet, if he were to comply with me, he would grant his approval."
"How could he possess omniscience? Thus he acted in that manner for the purpose of discerning the Teacher's intention. However, the Blessed One thought:
"If I were to say directly, 'These ascetics are not spies,' even if the king were to believe it, the great multitude, being ignorant of the matter, would not believe it.
[The Blessed One considered: 'The ascetic Gotama thinks, "The king is listening to my words. " What...
Knowing that if he were to say, "He speaks whatever comes to his lips," it would lead to his harm and suffering for a long time,
and furthermore, that the secret agent's work would be exposed and the king himself would reveal their status as spies, he said,
"This is indeed difficult to discern," and so forth.
In this context, by the phrase "those who enjoy sensual pleasures," he shows the state of being overcome by lust;
by both [phrases], he shows the state of a distracted mind. "A bed crowded with children" means a bed crowded with children. Here, by the term "children," the inclusion of wives is implied;
and by the mind being elated with regard to children and wife, he shows the defilement of the mind due to being overcome by sorrow caused by the household life and so forth.
He shows [this]. "Kāsika sandalwood" means fine sandalwood; or alternatively, the meaning is "Kāsika cloth and sandalwood.
"Garlands, scents, and ointments" refers to one who wears garlands for the sake of beauty and fragrance, scents for the sake of a pleasant aroma, and ointments for the purpose of coloring the skin.
"Gold and silver" refers to gold itself and whatever other wealth remains. "By one who accepts" means by one who receives them.
It reveals only the state of being greedy for all sensual pleasures.

"By living together" means by dwelling together. "Virtue is to be known" means that one who lives together with another in the same place must know whether that person is amiable or immoral. And furthermore, "not briefly, but over a long period of time"—that is how it should be understood.
Virtue is to be known over a long period of time, not by a short one;

for while it is possible to display the appearance of restraint and the appearance of guarded sense faculties for a few days, this can only be known by one who attends to it, not by one who does not attend to it.

Even that [virtue] can be known by one who reflects and attends to it with the thought, "I shall examine his virtue," but not by anyone else. As for "possessing wisdom," that too [is to be known] only by one who possesses wisdom.
By a wise person. For a fool, even though he applies his mind, is unable to understand.
"By means of trade" means by way of speech: "Whoever among men lives by trade—know this, Vāseṭṭha, he is a merchant, not a brahmin."
For here, "trade" means business. In the phrase "the four noble modes of speech," it refers to volition (*cetanā*).
In the phrase "convention, designation, description, and usage," it refers to description (*paññatti*). In the phrase "he should speak by way of mere usage," it refers to discourse.
Here too, that same meaning is intended. For the face-to-face discourse of one person does not coincide with the discourse behind one's back.
A conversation behind one's back contradicts a conversation in one's presence; likewise, a previous statement contradicts a subsequent one, and a subsequent statement contradicts a previous one.
Even while he is speaking, it is possible to know: "This person is impure.

But for one of pure virtue, a previous statement does not contradict a subsequent one, nor does a subsequent statement contradict a previous one, and what is spoken in his presence does not contradict what was spoken in his absence.
What is said in the absence of someone accords with what is said in their presence; therefore, showing that it is possible for one who speaks to be known as pure, he said:
"Purity is to be understood through one's dealings. "Steadfastness" (thāma) means the steadfastness of knowledge.
For one who lacks the steadfastness of knowledge, when calamities arise, [is unable] to grasp what should be grasped...
Not seeing what ought to be done, he wanders about like one who has entered a house without a door. Therefore he said:
"In times of calamity, O Great King, one's strength must be known. By "discourse" (sākacchā) is meant conversation.
For the talk of one lacking wisdom floats away like a ball of snot on water, whereas for one possessed of wisdom, inspired eloquence is infinite as he speaks. Just by the movement of the water—
For a fish, whether small or large, is thus perceived.
Thus the Blessed One, without telling the king directly, "These are such-and-such," revealed the means for knowing who were arahants and who were not.
Having heard this, the king was deeply impressed by the Blessed One’s omniscience and his skill in teaching, and exclaimed, "It is wonderful!"
Having expressed his own confidence with the words beginning “Venerable Sir,” he now reported those matters to the Blessed One exactly as they were, saying:
“These, Venerable Sir, are my spies (*cara*),” and so forth.

In that context, *cara* refers to those who, though not yet ordained, consume the alms of the kingdom in the guise of renunciants because their activities are concealed. *Ocaraka* means those who move about below. For the *cara* [move] along the mountain peaks...
Even while wandering, they are merely wanderers of the lower sort because of their base deeds. Alternatively, *ocaraka* means spies.
*Ocaritvā* means having wandered about or investigated; the meaning is, having learned of various occurrences in various places.
*Osārissāmi* means I will proceed, or I will act. *Rajojallaṃ* means dust and dirt. *Pavāhetvā* means having thoroughly washed away.
Having removed [them] by means of washing. "With hair and beard trimmed" means with hair and beard cut by barbers according to the method prescribed in the treatises on ornamentation.
"By the strands of sensual pleasure" means by the components of sensual desire, or by the fetters of sensual desire;

"endowed" (*samappita*) means thoroughly applied or attached. "Possessed" (*samaṅgibhūta*) means being together with them. "Will amuse themselves" means they will cause their faculties to move about everywhere, or they will sport.

"Having understood this matter": having understood this matter of those royal officers—namely, their deception of the world by means of the guise of one who has gone forth for the sake of their own bellies.
"He uttered this exalted utterance" (udāna): he uttered this exalted utterance which elucidates the rejection of dependence on others and the practice of deceiving others.
In that context, "one should not strive in any way" refers to all evil states, such as the work of a messenger, a spy, and so forth.
Like the king’s men, the one who has gone forth should not strive; he should not exert effort or enthusiasm.
The intention is that, instead of making effort anywhere at all, he should strive only for even a small amount of merit.
"He should not be another’s man" means that, in the form of a renunciant, he should not be a servant-man to any other person. Why? Because even for such a person...

Because one must perform evil deeds such as spying and the like. "One should not live dependent on another" means that one should not conduct one's livelihood with the thought, "My pleasure and pain are dependent on him," by relying on another such as a lord or master;
rather, one should be an island unto oneself, a refuge unto oneself, and have no other refuge. Alternatively, it is called "spying" (*ocaraṇa*) because it brings about what is harmful.
Because he has obtained his name [of "Dhamma"], he should not live by depending on any other unwholesome action.
"He should not practice trade with the Dhamma" means that for the sake of wealth and such, he should not preach the Dhamma.

For whoever teaches the Dhamma to others for the sake of wealth and so forth, he is said to be engaging in trade with the Dhamma; thus, he should not practice it in that way. Alternatively, for the sake of wealth and such...
Just as a man in the service of the King of Kosala, performing tasks such as spying while maintaining a state that cannot be suspected by others,
is said to be "engaging in trade according to the Dhamma" by undertaking the outward signs of renunciation and so forth; even so,
one who here leads the pure holy life (*brahmacariya*) while aspiring for some particular heavenly realm is also "engaging in trade according to the Dhamma."
"Name," thus one should not practice trade according to such a method; the meaning is that one should not do so.
The commentary on the second sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Paccavekkhaṇa-sutta*.
53. In the third [turning], he has abandoned within himself many evil and unwholesome states:

greed, hatred, delusion, distorted attention, lack of shame, lack of dread, anger, resentment, contempt, domineering, envy, avarice, guile, deceit, obstinacy, impetuosity, conceit, arrogance, pride, intoxication, negligence, craving, ignorance, the three kinds of unwholesome roots, misconduct, defilements, uneven perceptions, discursive thoughts, conceptual proliferation, the fourfold perversion, the taints, floods, yokes, fetters, the going and coming of the realms of existence, craving, and the fivefold clinging.

Within one's own continuum, there are more than a thousand defilements (*kilesa*) that have been active since beginningless time, including the five mental barrennesses (*cetokhila*), the five bondages of the mind (*cetovinibandha*),
the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), delighting in worldly things, the root of dispute, craving (*taṇhā*), the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) of the group of beings,

the eight wrong views, the ten unwholesome paths of action rooted in craving, the sixty-two types of speculative views (*diṭṭhigata*), and the hundred and eight modes of craving’s wandering (*taṇhāvicarita*), as well as many other evil states associated with them.

When the unwholesome states—which, in the sense of being produced by lack of skill, are harmful—had been abandoned without remainder at the very foot of the Bodhi tree along with their underlying tendencies, and were utterly cut off by the Noble Path, the Blessed One sat reflecting: "This defilement of mine has been abandoned;
this defilement of mine has been abandoned," thus reflecting through successive review.
"And many wholesome states" refers to: virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;

the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the four noble paths, the four fruits, the four analytical insights, the knowledge that delimits the four modes of birth, the four noble lineages, and the four kinds of intrepidity.
The five factors of striving, right concentration with five factors, right concentration with five kinds of knowledge,
the five faculties, the five powers, the five elements leading to escape, the five knowledges of the bases of liberation, the five perceptions that ripen liberation,
the six bases for recollection, the six respects, the six elements leading to escape, and the six constant abidings.
The six unsurpassables, the six kinds of wisdom partaking of penetration, the six direct knowledges, the six unique knowledges, the seven qualities that prevent decline,
the seven noble treasures, the seven factors of enlightenment, the seven qualities of a true person,

the seven bases for the wearing away [of defilements], the seven perceptions, the teaching on the seven persons worthy of offerings, and the teaching on the seven powers of one whose taints are destroyed.
The teaching on the eight causes for the acquisition of wisdom; the eight rightnesses; the eight transcendences over worldly conditions;
the eight bases for exertion; the teaching on the eight inopportune moments; the eight thoughts of a great person;
the teaching on the eight bases of mastery; the eight liberations; the nine states rooted in appropriate attention; and the nine factors of striving for purification.
The nine abodes of beings; the nine ways of removing resentment; the nine perceptions; the nine diversities; the nine successive dwellings; the ten qualities that provide protection;
the ten bases of totality; the ten courses of wholesome action; the ten rightnesses; the ten noble abodes;
the ten qualities of one beyond training; the ten powers of a Tathāgata; and the eleven benefits of loving-kindness.
The twelve aspects of the Wheel of Dhamma, the thirteen qualities of ascetic practice (dhutaṅga), the fourteen knowledges of a Buddha, the fifteen states that ripen liberation,
the sixteenfold mindfulness of breathing, the sixteen states that burn away the future, the eighteen great insights (mahāvipassanā),
the eighteen qualities of a Buddha, the nineteen knowledges of review, and the forty-four bases of knowledge.
Fifty knowledges of arising and passing away, more than fifty wholesome states, seventy-seven bases of knowledge,
the great diamond-like knowledge that traverses twenty-four million meditative attainments, the knowledges of teaching, reviewing, and analyzing the *Paṭṭhāna* according to its infinite methods,
and likewise the knowledges that discern the inclinations and other traits of infinite beings in infinite world-systems— such are the many wholesome and blameless qualities of his own.

When the perfections (*pāramī*) and the cultivation of the path (*magga-bhāvanā*) have reached fulfillment and growth over an infinite period of time, he sits reflecting, having grouped the Buddha-qualities into clusters and aggregates according to his inclination, bringing them to mind with the thought:
"These blameless qualities (*anavajja-dhamma*) are found in me; these blameless qualities are also found in me.
And these [qualities] are considered together with their bases (*sapadesato*).
Thus it is, but not exhaustively. Even by the Blessed One himself, it is not possible to attend to all the Buddha-qualities one by one without remainder, because they are infinite and immeasurable.
For this has been said:
“Even if a Buddha were to speak the praises of another Buddha for an entire aeon,
without speaking of anything else,
that aeon would be exhausted within its long duration.”
“The praise of the Tathāgata would never be exhausted.
Furthermore, it is said:
“The names of the Great Seer, according to his qualities, are incalculable.”
“By virtue of one’s qualities, one’s name should be engraved even upon a seal worth a thousand.
For at that time, having returned from his almsround after the meal, the Blessed One entered the monastery and stood at the entrance of the Perfumed Chamber.
After he had demonstrated the proper conduct to the bhikkhus and they had departed, he entered the Great Perfumed Chamber and sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared.

Seated there, he directed his knowledge toward the sphere of his own past births. Then, those births appeared to him in uninterrupted succession, one after another, in their infinite and immeasurable variety.
Thinking, "These defilements are the very root of such a vast mass of suffering," he directed the course of his knowledge toward the sphere of the defilements;
having examined them step by step from the perspective of their abandonment, he [proceeded].
Thinking, “Indeed, these defilements have been thoroughly abandoned by me without remainder,” he brought to mind his own faultless qualities—
beginning with virtue— which are infinite and immeasurable in their variety, while reviewing the Noble Path that effects their abandonment, together with its aspects,
its equipment, and its specific details. Therefore it was said:

“Now at that time, the Blessed One was sitting reflecting upon his own many evil, unwholesome states that had been abandoned, and his many wholesome states that had reached the perfection of development.
Having reflected thus, he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*), which describes the joy and gladness that had arisen:
“In this regard, ‘there was formerly’ means all this mass of defilements, beginning with lust, prior to the arising of the knowledge of the path to *arahantship*.”
"In my continuum there was [nothing]; not a single defilement from this mass of defilements existed. At that time—at that moment of the Noble Path—that mass of defilements did not exist;
at that moment of the Supreme Path, there is not even a minute particle of defilement that is said to be "unabandoned.
Some also read "tato nāhu" (from that, it did not exist), meaning from that moment of the path of Arahatship.

The meaning is: "but it was not. "It was not before" means that this immeasurable, blameless dhamma of mine which is now found to have reached the perfection of cultivation did not exist, nor was it present, prior to the moment of the Noble Path.
"But then it was" means that when the knowledge of the supreme path arose for me, then all my blameless dhamma was present. Through the attainment of the supreme path...
Indeed, all the qualities of omniscience are already within the hands of the Buddhas.

It has not been, it will not be, nor is it found at present—that faultless Dhamma, the Noble Path, which arose for me at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), by means of which the entire mass of defilements was abandoned without remainder; just as it is for me...
Prior to the moment of the path, it neither exists nor has it been;

thus, because the defilements to be abandoned by itself are absent, this too will not exist in the future—it will not arise—nor does it exist or is it found at present in the current time, because there is no function to be performed by itself. For the noble path does not occur repeatedly.
For this very reason he said: "They do not go to the further shore twice.

Thus the Blessed One, reviewing the unwholesome states that had been abandoned without remainder in his own continuum by means of the Noble Path, and the immeasurable blameless states that had reached the perfection of cultivation, uttered this inspired exclamation (udāna) released from the force of joy directed toward himself.
He uttered this exclamation. In the preceding discourse, only the first two grounds of self-confidence were spoken of;
the latter two are already implied by the manifestation of his Perfect Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi).
Thus ends the commentary on the third sutta.
4. Commentary on the First Discourse on Various Non-Buddhist Teachers (Paṭhamanānātitthiyasuttavaṇṇanā) 54.

Regarding the fourth [discourse], the phrase "various recluses, brahmins, and wanderers of other sects" (*nānātitthiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇaparibbājakā*): here, a "ford" (*tittha*) is that by which one crosses over the flood of saṃsāra;

it is the path to Nibbāna. However, in this context, it refers to the views as they have been grasped by those holding to wrong views, due to the influence of distorted perversion (*viparītavipallāsa*).

“Fording place” (*tittha*) is what is intended. Those who are engaged in that fording place consisting of various forms such as eternalism and so forth are “adherents of various sects” (*nānātitthiya*).
These include ascetics (*samaṇa*) such as the naked Nigaṇṭhas and others, brahmins (*brāhmaṇa*) such as the followers of Kaṭha and Kālāpa, and wanderers (*paribbājaka*) such as Pokkharasāti;

thus they are called “ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers. Furthermore, they are both adherents of various sects and ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers; hence, they are “adherents of various sects, ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers.”
“View” (*diṭṭhi*) refers to that by which one sees [the self and the world as] “eternal,” etc., or that which sees itself, or that which is merely such a seeing;

it is a designation for wrong adherence (*micchābhinivesa*). Those who possess various—that is, manifold—views characterized by eternalism and so forth are called “those of various views” (*nānādiṭṭhika*).
Adherence (*khanti*) is the acceptance through eternalism and so forth; approval (*ruci*) is the same in meaning as “eternal.”
The perversion of consciousness (*cittavipallāsa*) and the perversion of perception (*saññāvipallāsa*) proceed by way of such [views] as "the self and the world.

Likewise, they are called "those of diverse inclinations" (*nānākhantikā*) because they have various acceptances (*khanti*), and "those of diverse tastes" (*nānārucikā*) because they have various preferences (*ruci*).

For those who follow views (*diṭṭhigatika*) first please and accept their minds in various ways during the preliminary stage, and subsequently adhere to them with the conviction: "This alone is the truth; all else is vain."

Alternatively, it should be understood that by all three terms—view (*diṭṭhi*), inclination (*khanti*), and preference (*ruci*)—only view is being expressed; for they are so called respectively through the act of seeing things as "permanent" when they are "impermanent," and so forth, through the act of tolerating them, and through the act of liking them.

"Based on various bases for views" means: based on the various kinds of foundations, grounds, or causes for views, such as the conceptualizations of eternalism (*sassata*) and so forth; [these are] indeed what are designated as views.
"Or dependent on a support" means relying upon, clinging to, or approaching it; the meaning is that they remain without relinquishing it.
For even views are supports for the modes of dogmatic adherence of those who follow such views.
"Exist" means they are present, found, or obtainable. "Some" means certain ones. "Ascetics and brahmins" refers to those who have entered the homeless life.
"Ascetics" refers to those who are Brahmins by birth, or those who are taken to be ascetics and Brahmins by the world.

"Holders of such a doctrine" (*evaṃvādino*) means those who speak in the manner that is now to be stated. "Holders of such a view" (*evaṃdiṭṭhino*) means those in whom there exists a view that functions in the manner that is now to be stated.
Therein, by the second [phrase], the wrong adherence of the proponents of views (*diṭṭhigatika*) is shown.
By the first [type of view], conventional usage occurs through establishing others in that very same adherence as oneself.
Regarding the statement, "The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false," here "the world" refers to the self (*attā*).

For it is called "the world" (*loka*) by those holding such views because merit, demerit, and their results are experienced therein (*lokiyanti*); or else, it is so called because it is experienced (*lokiyati*) by itself when engaged in the state of being an agent and so forth.
"World" is what is intended here. This view of ours—that it is eternal, deathless, permanent, and stable—is alone the truth and non-perverted;
whereas the views of others, such as that it is non-eternal and so forth, are vain and false—this is the meaning.
By this, all four types of eternalist doctrines are shown. "Non-eternal" means not eternal; it is impermanent, unstable, and subject to decay.

The meaning is as follows: by the very negation of eternalism (*sassata-bhāva*) in the phrase "non-eternal" (*asassata*), annihilationism (*uccheda*) is also indicated; thus, all seven types of annihilationist views are shown.
"Finite" (*anta-vā*) means having a boundary, being enclosed, and having a delimited measure; the sense is that it is not all-pervading. By this, views such as:
"the self (*atta*) is the size of the body," "the size of a thumb," "the size of a limb," or "the size of an atom," are demonstrated.
"Endless and boundless" means "all-pervading. By this, the doctrines of Kapila, Kaṇāda, and others are illustrated.

"That which is the soul is that which is the body": whatever is the body, that very thing is the entity designated as the soul; and whatever is the entity designated as the soul, that very thing is the body.
Thus, one regards the soul and the body as non-dual. By this, [the view] of the Ājīvakas is [indicated].

By this, the doctrine that “the self is material” (rūpī attā) is shown. By the statement “the soul is one thing, the body another,” however, the doctrine that “the self is immaterial” (arūpī attā) is shown.

In the phrase “the Tathāgata exists after death,” the term “Tathāgata” refers to a sentient being (satta); for the proponent of such views conceives of it as a so-called agent, experiencer, and so forth.
Or, because he has attained such a state characterized as eternal, stable, and so forth, he is designated as "Tathāgata.
He exists, is found, after death—that is, beyond the breaking up of this body; this is the meaning.

By means of this approach of the eternalist view (*sassataggāha*), the sixteen theories of those who hold to consciousness (*saññīvāda*), the eight theories of those who hold to non-consciousness (*asaññīvāda*), and the eight theories of those who hold to neither-consciousness-nor-non-consciousness (*nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda*) are shown. "He does not exist" (*na hoti*).
"It does not exist, it is not found"—by this, the doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*) is shown. "It both exists and does not exist" means "it both is and is not";

by this, the doctrines of partial eternalism and the seven views concerning those with perception (*saññīvāda*) are shown. Furthermore, by the statement "it neither exists nor does not exist," the doctrine of the endless equivocation (*amarāvikkhepa*) is to be understood as being shown.
It is said that these proponents of various views, having come from different places and settled in Sāvatthī, once gathered at a time for debate;
having each put forward their own doctrine and disparaging the doctrines of others, they fell into dispute.
Therefore it is said: “They had become quarrelsome,” and so forth.

In this context, "quarrel" (*bhaṇḍana*) refers to the preliminary stage of a dispute. "Engaged in quarreling" (*bhaṇḍanajātā*) means having given rise to quarreling. "Dispute" (*kalaha*) is simply a dispute;
or it should be understood as a "dispute" because it strikes down what is wholesome (*kala*). "Fallen into mutual contradictory speech" means having entered into a dispute.

Because it strikes at the vital points, the mouth itself is a "dagger," thus "mouth-dagger" (*mukhasatti*), which is harsh speech. This is expressed through a metaphorical application of the effect to the cause.

For just as the cause is sometimes spoken of as the effect through metaphorical usage—as in the expressions, "The arising of a Buddha is blissful" and "One experiences the evil deed"—so too, by those "missiles of speech," they dwell piercing and stabbing one another.
"Such is the Dhamma" means that the Dhamma, which is the unerring intrinsic nature (aviparīta-sabhāva), is of such a kind and of such a form, as I have stated: "The world is eternal."
“*Nediso dhammo* means ‘the Dhamma is not like this,’ as you have stated, ‘the world is eternal’;
the same should be applied to the remaining phrases. And that dispute among the sectarians became well known throughout the entire city.
Then, when the bhikkhus had entered Sāvatthī for alms and heard of it, they thought: “We have received this portion of a discourse; what if we were to report this matter...”
“Let us inform the Blessed One; perhaps by means of that we might receive from the Teacher a subtle and refined teaching of the Dhamma.
Thus, after the meal at the time for the preaching of the Dhamma, they informed the Blessed One of this matter.
Therefore it is said: “Then a number of bhikkhus,” and so forth.
Having heard that, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with “Bhikkhus, those of other sects,” in order to demonstrate how those of other sects do not understand the Dhamma as it truly is.
In this context, “blind” means blind due to being deprived of the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*). Therefore he said, “without eyes.
For here, “eye” is intended to mean wisdom. Thus it is said: “They do not know the meaning,” and so forth. In that regard:
"They do not know what is beneficial" means they do not know the welfare of this world or the welfare of the next world; they do not understand growth or prosperity in this world or the next.

Furthermore, they are incapable of discourse regarding the ultimate truth, Nibbāna. For how can those who are utterly deluded even regarding mere worldly occurrence (pavatti) ever know the cessation (nivatti)?
"They do not know what is harmful" means that by the same token as they [do not know] the beneficial...
They do not understand; for that very reason, they do not understand what is harmful either. Because they do not understand what is Dhamma, they do not understand what is non-Dhamma either.

Indeed, due to their grasping through perversion, they treat even what is wholesome as unwholesome, and they treat even what is non-Dhamma and unwholesome as wholesome. And this is not only the case regarding Dhamma and non-Dhamma, but also regarding their respective results.
They are utterly deluded. For they describe even karma as its result, and they describe even the result as karma.
Likewise, they do not know what is Dhamma—that is, that which possesses intrinsic nature—and they do not know what is non-Dhamma—that is, that which lacks intrinsic nature.
Being thus, they proclaim by treating intrinsic nature as non-intrinsic nature, and non-intrinsic nature as intrinsic nature.

Thus the Blessed One, having shown the blindness of the sectarians due to their deficiency in the eye of wisdom caused by their acquisition of deluded views, now spoke the passage beginning with "Once upon a time, monks" in order to illustrate that matter through the simile of one born blind.
Therein, "once upon a time" (*bhūtapurva*) means what occurred in the past, arisen in a former time. "There was a certain king" refers to one of ancient times.
There was a certain king who was unknown by name or lineage in the world.

That king addressed a certain man, for it is said that when this king saw his own state elephant—possessed of all its limbs, endowed with great beauty, and having attained the height of fortune—approaching the audience hall, he thought: "Ah, how excellent indeed is this elephant-vehicle; how beautiful to behold! And by him...
At that time, a certain man blind from birth was walking through the royal courtyard. Seeing him, the king thought:
"These blind people are truly great losers, who do not get to see such a beautiful sight as this.
What if I were to have all the men blind from birth in this Sāvatthī assembled, and having had them touch various parts one by one with their hands, [to describe them]?"
“...might hear these words. King Keḷisīla had all the people born blind in Sāvatthī assembled by means of a certain man and gave that man this instruction:
“Act in such a way that each blind person, having touched only one part of the elephant, such as the head and so forth, will form the perception, ‘I have seen the elephant. That man—
He did so accordingly. Then the king questioned each of those born blind individually, asking, "Tell me, what is an elephant like?
Describing the elephant solely according to the specific limb they had touched, they argued with one another, saying, "An elephant is like this; an elephant is not like that.
Quarreling and attacking one another with their hands and other limbs, they created a great clamor in the royal courtyard.
The king, together with his retinue, seeing their misfortune, laughed a great laugh with a heart that was uplifted and joyful because of the ease [of the situation].
Therefore it is said: “Then, monks, that king... [was] delighted. In this context, *ambho* is a form of address.
*Yāvataka* means as many as there are. *Jaccandha* means blind from birth; [blind] from the very moment of birth.
"Those without eyes. "Together" means in one place. "He speaks" means he converses without respect.
"Show the elephant" means, having laid down the elephant as previously described, show it. And because he was well-trained, he lay down without moving.
"We have seen the elephant," they said, having made their seeing by feeling with the hand. Having had that man feel the head...
Because they were made to perceive it as “such is the elephant,” those born blind, perceiving that very same elephant accordingly, said, “Sire, such is the elephant;
it is like a water-pot (*kumbha*). *Kumbha* means a jar (*ghaṭa*). *Khīla* refers to a wooden peg. *Soṇḍa* means the trunk.
*Naṅgalīsā* means the pole of the yoke-head of a plow. *Kāya* means the body. *Koṭṭha* means a granary (*kusūla*).
*Pāda* means the shank. *Thūṇa* means a pillar. *Naṅguṭṭha* is the upper part of the tail. *Vāladhi* is the tip of the tail.
*Muṭṭhīhi saṃsumbhisuṃ* means they struck with their fists; having clenched their fists, they hit him, they dealt blows with their fists. *Attamano ahosi*:
because of his playful nature, that king was delighted by that quarrel of the blind men; he became joyful and glad at heart.
"Even so, indeed" is the application of the simile. Its meaning is this:

"Monks, just as those born blind, being sightless and seeing only a single limb, failed to see the elephant in its entirety and—regarding only the specific parts they themselves had seen—did not acknowledge what was seen by the others, fell into mutual dispute and engaged in quarreling; even so, these [monks]..."
The followers of other sects, through their own views, perceive a portion of *sakkāya*— such as form, feeling, and so forth—
as "self" according to how they see it; having superimposed upon it such states as permanence and so on, and having adhered to the view that "only this is true,
all else is false," they dispute with one another regarding what is truly so and what is not, and what is Dhamma and what is non-Dhamma.
They do not know. Therefore, they are blind, sightless, like those born blind.

"Having understood this matter" means: having understood as it really is that the adherence to false views and the resulting disputes among the sectarians—who, like those born blind, neither know nor see the true nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva) regarding the elephant—are like the perceptions of those born blind concerning an elephant.
Having understood this in every aspect, he uttered this *udāna* which illuminates that meaning.
Regarding the phrase, "In these, it is said, some recluses and brahmins are attached": here, some are "recluses" by virtue of having entered the homeless life, and "brahmins" by birth alone;
they are attached to these very same coreless destinations of views, such as those proceeding in the manner of "the world is eternal," and so forth.

It is said that they cling by way of delighting in views, or else—regarding these very aggregates of clinging, such as form and so forth, which are thus impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—they cling by way of delighting in craving and delighting in views, thinking, "This is mine," and so on. This shows: "Oh, what delusion is theirs!
Here, the word *kira* (it is said) serves to indicate lack of approval; by means of it, [the author] indicates that therein...
This illuminates precisely the absence of any cause for attachment.

Not only do they become attached, but moreover, having quarreled, they dispute, engaging in contention by means of pursuing contentious talk such as, "You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya; I understand this Dhamma and Vinaya," and so forth. Here, *naṃ* is merely a particle. Alternatively, *viggayha*—

Later, because they hold perverted views, they take up the reliance on views or the very view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*)—which are mutually contradictory due to their eternalism and so forth—and they dispute, that is, they speak with particularity.
Or rather, having made their own doctrine distinguished and non-perverted, they adhere to it and express it. Like what? Just as people who see only one part [of the truth] are like those born blind.

Each of those who saw only a single limb of the elephant—having grasped it with the thought, "Whatever I have touched and known by myself, that alone is the elephant"—quarreled and disputed with one another;
such is the meaning of this [simile]. It should be understood that the word *iva* (like) is here indicated by elision (*luttaniddiṭṭha*).
The commentary on the fourth sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Various Non-Buddhist Teachers (Dutiya-nānā-titthiya-sutta) 55.

In the fifth [discourse], regarding the view that "the self and the world are eternal," they grasp either form (*rūpa*) or one of the other aggregates as both "self" and "world," and then assert and proclaim them to be eternal and permanent. As it is said: "They describe the self and the world thus:

'Form is the self and the world, and it is eternal. They describe the self and the world thus: 'Feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness is the self and the world, and it is eternal.'"* *The full passage continues with the same formula for each of the five aggregates.*
Alternatively, "self" (*atta*) refers to the basis for the conceit "I," while "world" (*loka*) refers to the basis for the conceit "mine," which is called "belonging to self.
