Or, "self" is oneself, and "world" is another. Or, "self" is one of the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), and "world" is the other.
Or, "self" is the conscious continuum of the aggregates, and "world" is that which is unconscious. Thus, in each case, [one regards] that as "self."
And having grasped both "the self" and "the world" in two ways according to their respective views, they adhere to both of them as "permanent, stable, and eternal," and thus express themselves.
By this, the four types of eternalist views (sassatavāda) are shown. By "non-eternal," the seven types of annihilationist views (ucchedavāda) are shown.
By "both eternal and non-eternal," it is meant that some [parts] of the self and the world are eternal, while some are non-eternal; thus, the eternalist view is shown.

And the meaning is "both eternal and non-eternal. Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as follows: for those who hold views regarding the self and the world, that very self and world are both eternal and non-eternal;
it may be eternal—thus is the sense to be known in this context. In every respect, by this, the doctrine of partial-eternalism (ekaccasassatavāda) is shown.
By the phrase "neither eternal nor non-eternal," the doctrine of endless equivocation (amarāvikkhepavāda) is shown; for they [hold] to the doctrine of eternalism...
And having seen the fault in the doctrine of non-eternalism, they dispute by resorting to evasion, saying: "The self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal.

"Self-made" means made by oneself. For just as the self of various beings experiences pleasure and pain by performing its own duties according to the Dhamma, so too the self itself [creates] the self and whatever objects serve as its enjoyments.
They hold the view that he creates and emanates the world known as an obstacle;
this is their doctrine, just like their doctrine regarding the self (*attaladdhi*). "Made by another" (*paraṃkata*) means made by another:

the meaning is that both the self and the world were made by another—by a Lord (*issara*), or by a Puruṣa, or by Pajāpati, or by Time (*kāla*), or by Primordial Nature (*pakati*)—and are thus "emanated. [The phrase] "both self-made and made by another" (*sayaṃkato ca paraṃkato ca*)...
Because Īśvara and others, while fashioning both the self and the world, do not fashion them alone by themselves,
but rather only after obtaining the cooperative causes (sahakārīkāraṇa) of the various beings' merit and demerit (dhamma-adhamma),
therefore the view of some is that "the self and the world are both self-made and made by another. [The view] that "there is neither self-made nor made by another" does not exist.
"Self-making" (*sayaṃkāra*) means it has self-making; "other-making" (*parakāra*) means there is no other-making for it.
By adding the nasal augment (*anunāsika*), it is stated as "aparaṃkāro. Having seen the fault in both positions, he rejects both.
Then, how did it arise? He says: "arisen by chance" (*adhiccasamuppanno*), meaning it arose by its own desire, without any cause.
"Arising without [a cause]" demonstrates the doctrine of fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppannavāda*). By that, the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetukavāda*) is also included.

Now, in order to show the doctrine of those proponents of views who, like the self, adhere to pleasure and pain as being either a quality or a possession of that [self] by way of eternalism and so forth, it says: "There are some recluses and brahmins... and so on.
It has been stated. That is exactly according to the method already explained.

Regarding the phrase "having understood this meaning": here, since the simile of those blind from birth has not yet been introduced, one should apply the meaning by omitting that and following the method explained below, as well as the verse.
In that context, the distinction is: "they sink midway, without even reaching the depths of darkness. Its meaning is as follows: thus, among those who have fallen into wrong views...
While adhering to their reliance on views, these proponents of views sink and founder right in the midst— without even reaching or attaining—
that which is reckoned as the "depth" (ogadha), namely Nibbāna, in the sense of being the further shore or a firm foundation for them,
or else the Noble Path, which is the means for its realization; they do so within the four floods, such as the flood of sensual desire, or within the great flood of saṃsāra itself.
By means of this they plunge in and find a footing; it flows into this, thus it is a "ford" (*ogādha*), namely the Noble Path and Nibbāna.
Here, by shortening the vowel *a* in *ogādha*, it is stated as "ogadha. The analysis of the words is: "that ford" (*taṃ ogadhaṃ*) and "into that ford" (*tamo-gadhaṃ*).
The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Third Discourse on Various Non-Buddhist Teachers (Tatiyanānātitthiyasutta) 56.
In the sixth [discourse], everything follows the same method as stated below. Regarding the phrase "this inspired utterance" (*udāna*):

herein, having seen the fault in views, craving, and conceit, and having avoided them from afar, one sees conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) as they truly are; yet, because of not seeing the disadvantage (*ādīnava*) therein—

The meaning should be construed as follows: he uttered this *udāna*, which illustrates the transcendence and non-transcendence of *saṃsāra* respectively for one who is wrongly obsessed and one who does not see things as they truly are.
In that context, "this generation is intent on the conceit of 'I'" refers to what is called "self-agency" (*sayamkāra*), expressed thus: "The self and the world are created by oneself."
This generation, steeped in and devoted to views such as the ego-conceit (*ahaṅkāra*) thus occurring, is a body of beings wrongly obsessed.
"Associated with the agency of another" means being dependent on the view of the agency of another—such as a Supreme Lord (*issara*) or others—who acts as the doer of everything;
because they are associated with that [view], they are said to be "associated with the agency of another. "Some have not understood this" refers to these two types of views held by some.
The ascetics and brahmins, seeing the fault therein, did not approve. How so?

For if there were self-agency (*sayaṃkāra*), beings would have to experience only what is desirable according to their own will, and never what is undesirable. Indeed, no one desires suffering for themselves, yet the undesirable occurs;
therefore, there is no self-agency. As for other-agency (*paraṃkāra*), if it were caused by Īśvara, then this Īśvara—

He would act either for his own sake or for the sake of others. In that regard, if it were for his own sake, he would have unfulfilled duties, because he would still be striving to accomplish what has not yet been accomplished.
Alternatively, if it were for the sake of others, only the welfare and happiness of all would be produced;

harm and suffering are not produced. Therefore, the agency of another—whether conceived as a Supreme Lord (Issara) or otherwise—is not established. And if [it is] that which is designated as the "Supreme Lord"...
If [the world] were to proceed from a single cause that is eternal and independent of anything else, there would be no arising through karma;
rather, everything would arise simultaneously because the cause is ever-present. If another cooperative cause is required for it, then that alone is the reason;
what is the use of postulating an Īśvara whose causal capacity is never fully established? And as for [the claim that the world] has Īśvara as its cause...

The "made by another" (*paraṅkāra*) is not established; likewise, it is not established even through such causes as *pajāpati*, the person (*purisa*), primordial matter (*pakati*), Brahmā, or time (*kāla*), because those [causes] themselves are unestablished and because one does not escape the aforementioned faults. Therefore it was said: “Some have not understood this.
However, those who do not admit the aforementioned "made by oneself" (*sayaṅkāra*) or "made by another," yet [assert] that the self and [the world] are spontaneously arisen (*adhiccasamuppanna*)...
And they describe the world; yet even they did not see it as a "dart," because they did not know things as they truly are— failing to transcend their false adherence—
and because the speculative views of those who maintain that [the world] arose fortuitously produce suffering here and there,
they did not perceive them in the sense of being a piercing dart.
"And he sees this dart as it is being pulled out": one who has initiated insight and contemplates even the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent,
suffering, and non-self— such a person [sees] this threefold distorted view,
all other forms of wrong adherence, and also the five aggregates of clinging which serve as their basis, because they are difficult to strike and difficult to extract.

And one perceives with the wisdom of insight beforehand, even before it has struck, that "this is an arrow. When one sees in this way, at the moment of the Noble Path, the thought "I am doing it" does not occur to him.
Just as the state of being a doer does not appear to him, likewise the thought "another is doing it" does not occur to him;
rather, there is only the mere phenomenon arisen through dependent origination, which is termed "impermanent."
Thus far, the complete absence of views and conceit in one who has practiced rightly has been demonstrated.
By this, the transcendence of saṃsāra through the attainment of arhatship is made manifest.
Now, in order to show that he who clings to a position of views is unable to lift his head out of saṃsāra:
He spoke the verse beginning with “mānupetā. Therein, “this generation possessed of conceit” (mānupetā) refers to this entire generation, the mass of beings known as those who follow various views;
they are possessed of and endowed with conceit (māna), which is characterized by the intensification of one’s own grasp, thinking, “My view is beautiful, my grasping is beautiful.
They are “bound by conceit, fettered by conceit” because of that very [conceit], which arises again and again from that [grasping].
Just as one does not relinquish that view, so too, because one's own continuum is bound and fettered, there are the fetters of conceit and the bonds of conceit.

Regarding the contentious talk about views, it is said that "one does not transcend saṃsāra" because, through one's own adherence to views—by way of self-exaltation and disparagement of others—one thinks, "This alone is the truth; all else is vain."

Discourse involving contentious talk regarding views and talk of opposition does not transcend, nor does it go beyond, cyclic existence (saṃsāra), because of the non-abandonment of ignorance and craving, which are the leaders of saṃsāra; this is the meaning.
The commentary on the sixth sutta is concluded.
7. Commentary on the Subhūti Sutta. 57.
Regarding the seventh [sutta], "Subhūti" is the name of that elder.

For that venerable one, having made his resolution at the feet of the Blessed One Padumuttara and having accumulated a store of merit for a hundred thousand eons, [was born] during this appearance of a Buddha.
Born into a household of great wealth, he heard the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma and was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).

Having gone forth from home into homelessness, because he had performed his duties, he applied himself and strove, and before long became one possessed of the six supernormal knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*).
Furthermore, through reaching the highest perfection in the cultivation of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), [the Blessed One declared]: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples..."

"Among the monks who dwell in the state of non-conflict (*araṇavihārin*), this one, Subhūti, is foremost"—thus was he designated by the Blessed One as the preeminent among those dwelling in non-conflict.
One day, having descended from his daytime meditation seat onto the monastery courtyard in the evening, he saw the Blessed One teaching the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly.
He made a time-limit for himself, thinking, "I shall rise and pay homage at the conclusion of the discourse."
Having done so, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree not far from the Blessed One and entered the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
Therefore it is said: "Now at that time, the Venerable Subhūti... having entered [the attainment].

In this context, all concentration belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) starting from the second jhāna, as well as all concentration of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*), is concentration without applied thought (*avitakkasamādhi*).
Thus it is. Here, however, the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship, which has the fourth jhāna as its basis, is intended by the term “concentration without applied thought” (*avitakkasamādhi*).
Wrong thoughts abandoned through the second jhāna and so forth have not yet been well-abandoned, because there is no absolute abandonment;

but those abandoned by the Noble Path have indeed been abandoned, since there is no further function of abandoning them. Therefore, the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship, which constitutes the conclusion of the supreme path, [is so designated].

Because it arises at the end of the abandoning of all wrong thoughts, it especially deserves to be called "concentration without applied thought" (*avitakkasamādhi*), let alone that which constitutes the fourth jhāna. Therefore it was said:
"But here, the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship that constitutes the basis for the fourth jhāna is intended by the term 'concentration without applied thought'."

"Having understood this matter": having understood in every aspect this matter—which consists in the abandonment of all wrong thoughts and all defilements—belonging to the Venerable Subhūti, he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) that illuminates that very matter.

Therein, "whose thoughts are blown away" refers to whichever noble person, or for whichever noble person, all wrong thoughts such as sensual thoughts have been blown away—that is, scorched and utterly eradicated by the knowledge of the Noble Path. Internally...

"Completely well-eliminated without remainder" (*suvikappitā asesā*): this means that which is to arise within one's own continuum—designated as "one's own internal"—is completely well-eliminated (*suvikappitā*), thoroughly eliminated;

the sense is that it is utterly cut off without leaving even the slightest remainder. In the phrase "having transcended that attachment, one perceives the formless" (*taṃ saṅgamaticca arūpasaññī*), the word *taṃ* is a mere particle.
Alternatively, the word *taṃ* has the sense of a cause (*hetuattho*); because [attachment] is without remainder...

Wrong thoughts have been utterly cut off; therefore, having transcended—having gone beyond—the fivefold attachment beginning with attachment to passion, or indeed all defilement-attachment, [one takes as an object] Nibbāna, which has received the name "formless" (arūpa) because it is devoid of the intrinsic nature of form and because of the absence therein of any transformation known as "being affected" (ruppana), or because it is the cause of being changeless. It is this Nibbāna that is the object.

Having done so, he is one who perceives the formless through the perceptions of the path and its fruit that have arisen. "One who has gone beyond the four bonds" means that he has gone by transcending, as appropriate, the four bonds—the bond of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*), the bond of existence (*bhavayoga*), the bond of views (*diṭṭhiyoga*), and the bond of ignorance (*avijjāyoga*)—by means of all four paths.

"Never again shall I come back" (*na jātu meti*): the *m* is used for euphonic conjunction (*padasaṃdhikara*); "never" (*jātu*) means that he certainly does not go toward renewed existence (*punabbhava*) again in the future.
The meaning is: "There is no further production of renewed existence for him. Some also read, "Birth is not mine," which has the same meaning.

Thus, concerning the Venerable Subhūti’s dwelling in the attainment of the fruit of arahantship and his parinirvāṇa without remainder, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) released by the force of rapture.
The commentary on the seventh sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Gaṇikā-sutta (58):
"Two groups" means two assemblies. "Of a certain courtesan" means of a certain beauty of the city.
“Infatuated” (*sārattā*) means thoroughly impassioned. “With minds bound” (*paṭibaddhacittā*) means having their minds fettered by the defilements.

It is said that on a certain festival day in Rājagaha, many profligate men, wandering about in groups, each brought a courtesan and entered a park to enjoy the festival games. After that, on two or three more festival days...
Bringing that very same courtesan, they played at the festival game.

Then, on another festival day, other rogues, likewise desiring to play at the festival game, while bringing courtesans, brought a certain courtesan who had already been brought by the previous rogues.
Seeing her, the others said, "This one is our property. They too spoke in the same way. "Thus..."
“[This] is our possession, [this] is our possession,” they said, and having increased their quarrel, they struck one another with their hands and so forth.
Therefore it was said: “At that time, in Rājagaha, there were two groups,” and so on. Therein, *upakkamanti* means they strike.
*Maranampi nigacchanti* means they undergo death through violent attacks; the others as well...
They reach suffering that is as great as death, even unto death itself.
"Having understood this matter" means having understood in every way that greed for sensual pleasures is the root of dispute and the root of all harm.
"This inspired utterance" refers to the elucidation of the danger in the two extremes and the benefit of the middle way of practice.
He uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*).

In this context, "that which has been obtained" refers to the collection of the five strands of sensual pleasure, such as forms and so forth, which have been obtained and are currently being experienced now—whether preceded by the view that "there is no fault in sensual pleasures" or not. And "that which is to be obtained" refers to...

And whatever action one performs in the future by not relinquishing the view that the very class of sensual pleasures "should be enjoyed, sensual pleasures should be consumed, sensual pleasures should be cultivated, sensual pleasures should be indulged in; he who indulges in sensual pleasures increases the world;
he who increases the world produces much merit"—relying upon such a view—[that action leads to future existence].

That which is to be attained and that which is to be experienced—both of these are strewn with the dust of passion. This means both what has been attained and what is to be attained are overspread by the dust of lust and other defilements.
For one who experiences the objects of sensual desire already attained becomes besmeared with the dust of lust;
and when the fruit of a mind so defiled reaches him in the future, he is besmeared with the dust of hatred due to the arising of mental distress.
He is besmeared; he is besmeared by the dust of delusion in both respects. To whom does this dust belong?
He says: "Of one who trains while afflicted," meaning one who is afflicted by defilements through the pursuit of sensual desires, and one who is afflicted by suffering as the result thereof;
that is, of one who trains in both defilement and its fruit out of a desire for a remedy in both cases.
Likewise, "that which has been reached" refers to the self-mortification reached by means of practices such as nakedness;
and "that which is to be reached" refers to the fruit to be reached in the states of misery (apāya) due to the undertaking of actions based on wrong view.

Both of these are "strewn with the dust of passion," meaning both are strewn with the dust of suffering. "Of one who is afflicted" means of one afflicted by the suffering of physical exhaustion. "Training after" means...
[This refers to] wrong view and the person who adopts it, following whom [one trains].
And those for whom the training is the essence (*sikkhāsārā*) are those who, having grasped from the outset the training consisting of virtue, vows, and so forth as being the essence, have declared:
"By this, there is purification from saṃsāra. Therefore he said: "Virtue, vows, livelihood, the holy life, and service are the essence."
In this context, that which one refrains from with the thought, "I shall not do it," is *sīla* (virtue); the practice of austerities such as eating unpalatable food is *vata* (vow);
a livelihood such as subsisting on raw vegetables is *jīvita* (livelihood); abstaining from sexual intercourse is *brahmacariya* (the holy life). The observance of these is *upaṭṭhāna* (attendance);
or alternatively, *upaṭṭhāna* is the attendance upon the deities of the aggregates (*khandha-deva*) and so forth by means of offerings of cooked rice balls and the like. Thus, by these...

Since purification from saṃsāra occurs through the virtues (sīla) and so forth as already described, those ascetics and brahmins who stand having grasped these as essential, taking training as their essence,
should be understood as "having service as their essence" regarding their vows, observances, livelihood, and holy life. "This is one extreme"—
this refers to the pursuit of self-mortification, characterized by the adherence to vows and observances, which stands in contrast to the middle way of practice.
By way of being a wretched thing, it is one extreme. "This is the second extreme":
this devotion to the pleasure of sense desires, consisting in the attainment of indulgence in sense desires, is the second extreme according to the method already stated.
Thus, "these two extremes" refers to these two: devotion to the pleasure of sense desires and devotion to self-mortification.

Furthermore, these two are called "extremes" (*anta*) because they are base and have become deviant paths that ought to be avoided by those who are themselves afflicted by the suffering of the defilements (*kilesa-dukkha*), as well as by those who follow their example while clinging to the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*)— which are strewn with the dust of the suffering of the defilements both now attained and to be attained in the future—
and to self-mortification. They are called "increasers of the cemetery" (*kaṭasivaḍḍhana*) in the sense that they are longed for by blind worldlings (*puthujjana*).

They are the increase of craving and ignorance, which are designated as "cremation grounds. As for the statement "the cremation grounds increase views," those cremation grounds increase various kinds of views.

For when one who observes gratification in sense-objects (vatthukāma) is unable to abandon them, craving and ignorance—acting as co-operative causes—give rise to the nihilistic view (*natthikadiṭṭhi*) such as "there is no giving," and so forth.
They cause one to adopt the view of non-action (akiriya-diṭṭhi) and the view of no-cause (ahetuka-diṭṭhi).

Furthermore, for one intent on self-mortification, having obtained the cooperative causes of ignorance and craving, they cause one to adopt the view of clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbata-parāmāsa-diṭṭhi) through the desire for self-purification, such as saying, "Purification comes through virtue, purification comes through vows.
However, their status as conditions for the view of a personal entity (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) is indeed evident. Thus, by way of dependence upon these two extremes—
It should be understood that craving and ignorance increase views. Some, however, say that "the cemetery" (kaṭasī) is a designation for the five aggregates.
Their intention is that, insofar as there is no purification from saṃsāra through those two extremes, to that same extent one increases the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha).
Others, however, [interpret] the phrase "increasing the cemetery" (kaṭasivaḍḍhanā) ...
“They increase the cemetery with repeated aging and death”—this is what they say.

By these [statements] as well, it is only the absence of being a cause for the purification of saṃsāra in both extremes that has been stated; however, the fact that the cremation ground is a cause for increasing views must also be mentioned.
“Not having directly known these two extremes” means: not having understood these two aforementioned extremes, [they think] “these extremes...”
“...and thus grasped, thus established, thus gone, and thus in their future destiny”—this is due to ignorance, this is caused by ignorance.
In such passages as “Having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed,” it should be understood that the word has the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
“Some shrink back” means some fall into contraction by way of devotion to sensual pleasure. “Some run too far” means some [fall into contraction] by way of devotion to self-mortification.
They overstep. For those devoted to sensual pleasure, because they fail to exert energy, fall back due to indolence, and thus shrink away from right practice, they are said to "lag behind.

Those devoted to self-mortification, however, having abandoned indolence but applying energy through improper means, overstep right practice; therefore, they are said to "run too far ahead. Both of these—
But because of the failure to see the danger therein, it was said: “Not having directly known both extremes, some lag behind, while others run too far.
Herein, it should be understood that they lag behind due to delighting in craving, and they run too far due to delighting in views.
Alternatively, some lag behind due to adherence to eternalism, while others run too far due to adherence to annihilationism.
For some who are devoted to self-mortification by means of the cow-observance (*gosīla*) and so forth, adhering to the view of eternalism, think:
"By this virtue, or vow, or austerity, or holy life, I shall become a god or some other deity;
there, permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, I shall remain just so for all eternity. Thus they cling to the view of eternalism.

They are said to "linger" in saṃsāra. However, some who are devoted to sensual pleasure, desiring to satisfy their faculties by doing whatever it takes—like the Lokāyatikas—cling to a view of annihilationism suited to that end;

because they seek the cessation of the round through an improper means, they are said to "overreach. Thus, lingering and overreaching should be understood by way of eternalism and annihilationism as well.
"But those who have direct knowledge" refers to those noble persons (ariyapuggala) who,

having understood through their distinguished knowledge— the wisdom of the path accompanied by insight— those two aforementioned extremes as being "these extremes are grasped thus, established thus, leading to such a destination,
and resulting in such a future state," have correctly entered upon the middle way; it is by means of that correct practice.
And therein they did not exist: in that regard, they did not fall into those two extremes; the meaning is that they abandoned those two extremes.

And by that they were designated: by means of that abandonment of the two extremes, through the conceiving of craving, views, and pride—such as "This is my abandonment of the two extremes," "I have abandoned the two extremes," or "By this abandonment of the two extremes it is better"—[they were so called].
They did not conceive, because all conceiving has been completely abandoned.

And here, this teaching is set forth with reference to noble persons established in the fruit of the highest attainment, using the past tense in the phrases "therein they were not" and "by that they were named.
However, if the moment of the path is intended, it should be stated using the present tense. For them, the round of existence does not exist.

"For the purpose of making known" means: for the purpose of making known that for those supreme persons who have thus abandoned all conceivings, and who have attained final nibbāna through non-clinging, there exists no threefold round of existence—whether by way of kamma, its result, or defilements.
The meaning is that, after the dissolution of the currently existing aggregates, they go to a state of non-designation, like a fire that has ceased to cling to fuel.
The commentary on the eighth sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Upātidhāvanti Sutta: 59.
In the ninth [sutta], "in the thick darkness of the night's gloom" means in the great darkness of the night. For even the night...
It is free from darkness, like a night of the full moon illuminated by the bright light of the moon.
Even "darkness" (*timitā*) cannot be predicated of a sky that is free from such defilements as clouds and mist; for it is great darkness that is called "pitch-black darkness" (*timitā*).
But this is the night of the new moon, and the sky is shrouded by a mass of clouds. Therefore it was said: "In the pitch-black darkness of the night."
“In the darkness of the night, in the great gloom. “In the open air” means in an uncovered space, such as the courtyard of a monastery.
“While oil lamps were burning” means while oil-lights were blazing.
But does not the Blessed One’s natural fathom-wide radiance, by its very nature, pervade an area of one fathom and surpass the light of the moon and sun?
Having overcome it, she remains emitting a dense and thick Buddha-light that dispels the darkness;
her bodily radiance also remains emitting the six-colored, dense Buddha-rays—blue, yellow, and so forth—illuminating an area of eighty cubits all around by its very nature.
Thus, through the Buddha-light alone, everything becomes a single expanse of light.
Is there no need to provide lamps in the place where the Blessed One sits? Truly, there is not;
nevertheless, lay followers seeking merit establish oil lamps daily for the purpose of making offerings to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
For it is said even in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*: "These lamps are burning in this circular hall. [And: "In the thick darkness of the night..."
This too was said for the purpose of describing the nature of that night, and not because the place where the Blessed One was seated was in darkness;
for even then, lamps were caused to be lit by the lay followers (upāsakas) solely for the purpose of making offerings.
On that day, many lay followers residing in Sāvatthī, having performed their bodily grooming early in the morning, [went] to the monastery...
Having gone there, undertaken the precepts of the Uposatha, invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha,
entered the city, and distributed great alms, they followed the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus; then,
having turned back and returned to their respective homes, they themselves partook of the meal, dressed in clean lower garments and clean upper robes.
Carrying perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, they went to the monastery and, having paid homage to the Blessed One,
some spent part of the day attending upon the venerable monks, while others spent it in proper reflection. In the evening,
having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, [they followed the Teacher] from the Dhamma assembly hall to the vicinity of the fragrant chamber.
While the Blessed One was seated upon the excellent Buddha-throne prepared in the open air, and while the Saṅgha of bhikkhus had approached and were attending upon him,
they remained behind, desiring not to go to the city but to stay right there in the monastery for the purpose of purifying the Uposatha and for the sake of cultivating wise attention.
Then, in order to perform an act of worship for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus...

Having lit many oil lamps, they approached the Teacher, paid homage, and with palms joined toward the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, sat down at the edge of the assembly of bhikkhus and initiated this conversation:
"Venerable sir, these sectarians, adhering to various speculative views, speak accordingly; and while speaking thus, they sometimes assert eternalism and sometimes non-eternalism."

"Among those who hold to annihilationism and other such views, they do not remain fixed in any one position; rather, like madmen, they adopt various new speculative views from time to time, asserting, 'This alone is the truth, all else is false.
For those who are thus obsessed, what is their destination? What is their future state? At that time, many flying insects were repeatedly falling upon them.
They fall upon the oil-lamps. Therefore it was said: “At that time, many *adhipātakas*,” and so forth.
In this context, *adhipātakas* are winged insects (*paṭaṅga-pāṇaka*), who are also called “moths” (*salabha*).
For they are intended as *adhipātakas* because of their habit of flying toward the flame of the lamp. *Āpātaparipātam* means falling repeatedly; having flown down again and again, they fall.
"Having fallen down" means having fallen headlong and having whirled around while falling.
Some read "paripātam āpāthe," which means that when the lamp comes into one's own range of vision (āpātha), one falls down again and again.
"Anaya" means misfortune or suffering; "byasana" means ruin. For by the first phrase, death itself is indicated.
"Suffering" refers to death, which is indicated by the final phrase. In that regard, some insects died along with the falling, while others experienced the suffering of near-death.
"Having understood this matter" means having understood that for those insects who did not know their own welfare, [death occurred] through their own self-inflicted action.

Having recognized that those proponents of wrong views had fallen into a ruinous and futile transgression, he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) which illustrates how they have met with misfortune and ruin due to their dogmatic adherence to views.
In this context, "they run beyond and do not come to the essence" means they do not arrive at the essence consisting of the divisions of virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and so forth.
They do not attain [liberation] by means of the realization of the Four Noble Truths.

However, while remaining in that essential core which possesses the proper means, although they act as if approaching it out of a desire for liberation, they run too far ahead and overstep it due to the perversion of views;
that is, they grasp the five aggregates of clinging by adhering to them as "permanent, beautiful, pleasant, and self."

The meaning is as follows: "Increasing ever new fetters" means that those who grasp in such a way increase and expand the ever-new fetters known as craving and views. "They fall like moths into a flame;
some are settled thus upon what is seen and heard"—thus, because they are bound by the fetters of craving and views, certain recluses and brahmins [are settled] upon what is seen...
Those who, through their own visual consciousness or by means of seeing with views, have seen;

or through hearsay and mere acquisition, have heard—having become settled on the thought, "Thus it is, this alone is the truth," they are adhered by a dogmatic adherence to views (*diṭṭhābhinivesa*), being fixed upon [theories] such as "eternalism" and so forth;
or, not knowing the absolute benefit of deliverance, they are set ablaze by the eleven fires of lust and the rest within what is called the threefold existence.
The meaning is that these [beings] fall upon this light like sparks from a charcoal pit; they are not able to lift up their heads from there.
The commentary on the ninth sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Uppajjanti* Sutta.
60. "For as long as" (*yāvakīvaṃ*) means for whatever length of time. "From when" (*yataḥ*) means "at which time," "starting from when," or "in which period"—such is the meaning.
"Thus it is, Ānanda": Ānanda, when the Tathāgata has arisen, gain and honor increase only for the Tathāgata and for the Tathāgata’s disciples;
but the sectarians (*titthiyā*), being humiliated, their splendor destroyed, and their gain and honor abandoned.
As for what you said—that "they are so"—it is indeed thus; there is no other way for this to be.
For with the appearance of the Wheel-Treasure, the world does not direct its offerings, honors, or respect toward anything else apart from the Wheel-Treasure;
rather, the entire world honors, reveres, respects, and worships the Wheel-Treasure alone in every possible way.
Thus, he shows that even the power of a mere outflow of merit following the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is so great;

how much more so, then, for the Triple Gem—the Buddha-gem, the Dhamma-gem, and the Saṅgha-gem—which is the support for the fruit of merit following the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*), and which is the repository of infinite and immeasurable qualities?
For the Blessed One, having attained perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*) and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, gradually [established] sixty-one [groups] in the world...
When the Arahants had arisen, he dispatched sixty Arahants on a journey through the countryside;
having reached Uruvelā and established the thousand matted-hair ascetics, headed by Uruvelakassapa, in the state of Arahantship, he sat in the Laṭṭhivana Grove surrounded by them.
From the time he resided in Rājagaha, after he had brought twelve million inhabitants of Aṅga and Magadha, headed by Bimbisāra, into the Dispensation...
Just as the abundant gains and honor of the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus increased further and further,
so too did the gains and honor of all the various sectarians decline.
Then one day, while the Venerable Ānanda was seated at his daytime resting place, he [reflected upon] the right practice of the Blessed One and the Noble Saṅgha.
Having reflected thus, filled with joy and gladness, he directed his attention to the practice of the sectarians, wondering, "How indeed do they practice?
Then, to him, their practice appeared in every respect to be a wrong practice. He thought:

"While the Blessed One—who possesses such great majesty, who has reached the pinnacle of perfection through the practice of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma based on the support of merit—and while the Noble Saṅgha still exist..."
"How can these followers of other sects, who practice so wrongly, who have performed no merit, and who are wretched, become successful and honored?

Having thus conceived compassion for the loss of gain and honor suffered by the sectarians, he then reported his own reflection to the Blessed One with the words, "As long as, venerable sir," and so forth. And the Blessed One said to him, "Ānanda, you have erred."
Without saying, "I have reflected upon this," he raised his neck, which resembled a golden pillar, and made his great face—beautiful as a fully blossomed hundred-petaled lotus—even more serene.
Then, expressing his approval with the words, "It is so, Ānanda," he consented to those words with the passage beginning, "As long as...
Thus it was said: "Then the Venerable Ānanda... [the rest of the passage] ...the Saṅgha of bhikkhus."

And so it was said. Then, on that occasion, the Blessed One, referring to the past, related the Bāveru Jātaka, showing how even before his own appearance in the world, certain low-born people had received honor, only to find their gains and reputation destroyed from the moment of my arising.
"Having understood this matter" means: as long as the Perfectly Enlightened Ones have not appeared in the world, there has been honor and respect for those who hold wrong views.
From the moment they arise, however, those [beings] lose their gain and honor;

they become lusterless and powerless, and because of their wrong practice, they are not released from suffering. Having understood this matter in all its aspects, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which illuminates that very meaning.
In this context, "first it shines" means that the *khajjūpanaka* worm first shines, glows, and blazes, as long as the sun—
known by the name "Light-Maker" (*pabhaṅkara*) because it creates light simultaneously across the three great continents—
has not yet risen or ascended. For while the sun has not yet risen, the *khajjūpanaka* worms find their opportunity.
Even when it revolves, it shines in the darkness like the fruit of the *kaṇṭaka* plant.

But when the sun named Vairocana has risen—having dispelled the surrounding darkness with its thousand rays due to its nature of radiating light—that *khajjūpanaka* becomes lusterless, devoid of brilliance, and black; for in the thick darkness, it is eclipsed by the light.
It does not speak nor does it shine.
Thus, "only by those who reason" (takkikānaṃ) means that just as that *khajjūpanaka* tree shines forth even before the rising of the sun,
so too they are called "reasoners" (*takkikā*) because they grasp views merely through conjecturing, speculating, and imagining.

This was proclaimed by the heretics who had acquired their names, and it was illuminated and established by the power of their own doctrines for as long as no Fully Enlightened Ones (Sammāsambuddhas) arise in the world.
However, when Fully Enlightened Ones do arise in the world, those who follow wrong views are neither purified nor do they shine; nor indeed...
Their disciples shine; otherwise, their splendor is destroyed, and like arrows shot in the night, they are no longer seen at all.

Or rather, as long as a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) has not arisen in the world, the illumination provided by logicians—the shining forth of their own tenets that merely deceives fools—lasts only until then, and not beyond.
Why? Because logicians do not attain purity, nor...

And so too their disciples. For they, having been taught a poorly expounded Dhamma and Vinaya, being devoid of right practice, are not purified from saṃsāra because their teaching does not lead to liberation.
Therefore he said: "Those of wrong view are not released from suffering. For those who rely on mere reasoning are of wrong view due to their failure to grasp things as they truly are;
they are possessed of false adherence and possess perverted vision. Without relinquishing that view, [they remain] from the suffering of saṃsāra...
"They are never released.
The commentary on the tenth sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Jaccandhavagga is also finished.
7. Cūḷavagga 1.
Commentary on the First Discourse to Lakuṇḍaka-Bhaddiya 61.
Regarding "Lakuṇḍaka-Bhaddiya" in the first [discourse] of the Cūḷavagga: here, "Bhaddiya" is the name of that venerable one.
However, because of his short stature, people knew him as "Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya.
It is said that he was a son of good family living in Sāvatthī, possessing great wealth and vast property; yet, in appearance, he was unpleasing, ill-favored, unsightly, and hunchbacked.
One day, while the Teacher was dwelling at Jetavana, he went to the monastery with the lay followers and listened to the teaching of the Dhamma.

Having heard this, he gained faith and went forth; having received full ordination, he took a meditation subject from the Teacher and, performing the work of insight, attained the fruit of stream-entry.
At that time, the bhikkhus who were still in training mostly approached the Venerable Sāriputta to request a meditation subject for the sake of the higher paths and for instruction in the Dhamma.
They make requests and ask questions. Fulfilling their intentions, he explains a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), teaches the Dhamma, and answers their questions.

Striving and exerting themselves, some among them attain the fruit of once-returning (*sakadāgāmiphala*), some the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), some arhatship (*arahatta*), some the three types of higher knowledge (*tisso vijjā*), and some the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*).
Some attained the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
Seeing them, Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, though still a trainee (*sekha*), knowing the time had come, reflected upon the fitness of his own mind and his ascetic purification (*sallekha*).
He approached the General of the Dhamma, exchanged greetings, and with joyful conversation, requested a teaching on the Dhamma. [The General] understood his underlying intention...

He spoke in a fitting manner. Therefore it was said: “Now at that time, the Venerable Sāriputta instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya with a discourse on the Dhamma in many ways,” and so forth.
Therein, “in many ways” means: “In this way the five aggregates are impermanent; in this way they are suffering; in this way they are non-self.”
Thus, by means of many reasons. "With a discourse on the Dhamma" means with a discourse on the Dhamma that elucidates the arising, passing away, and so forth of the five aggregates of clinging.

"He instructs" means he correctly shows those very characteristics such as impermanence, as well as the arising and passing away, showing them directly as if grasping them with his own hand. "He encourages" means [he encourages] therein [the mind] which has those characteristics as its object.
He causes insight (vipassanā) to be properly undertaken; he causes it to be grasped so that it proceeds having entered the right path.

"He encourages" means that when insight has been commenced and the arising and passing away of formations become manifest, he causes the cultivation [of the practice] to enter the middle path by means of timely exertion, restraint, and equanimity through the non-erroneous application of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), so that the knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa) [proceeds].
Just as a horse, having become well-pleased, carries [its rider], so too, by making the faculties clear,
one properly encourages the mind of insight and clarifies it by means of making them distinct.

"He gladdens" means that he properly gladdens the mind through the power of the balanced development occurring during such insight, as well as by the strength of the development to be attained hereafter.
Or, it thoroughly satisfies [the mind] by way of providing a taste of what has been attained. "The mind was liberated from the taints through non-clinging" means that,
in whatever manner the General of the Dhamma taught the Dhamma, as the Elder— through the power of that teaching and through the perfection of his own natural aptitude—
reached the full maturity of his knowledge, he came to see the specific characteristics of reality (tathalakkhaṇa) in accordance with that teaching.

The meaning is that while knowledge was not yet fully active, having grasped none of the taints—such as the taint of sensual desire—and following the sequence of the path, his mind was liberated without remainder, and he realized the fruit of arahantship.

"Having understood this matter" means: having understood in every aspect this matter of Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya’s attainment of final knowledge (*aññā*), he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) which illuminates that very matter.
In this context, "above" (*uddhaṃ*) refers to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*). "Below" (*adho*) refers to the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*).

"Everywhere" (*sabbadhi*) means throughout the entire range of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāragata*). "Completely liberated" (*vippamutta*) means liberated in every way: through the liberation of suppression (*vikkhambhana-vimutti*) in the preliminary stage, and through the liberations of eradication (*samuccheda*) and tranquillization (*paṭipassaddhi*) in the subsequent stage.
Furthermore, by the phrase "completely liberated from above," the abandoning of the five higher fetters (*pañca-uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) is indicated.
It shows this. By the phrase "freed from below," the abandoning of the five lower fetters (*pañcorambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) is shown.
By the phrase "freed in every respect," the abandoning of all remaining unwholesome states is shown. Alternatively, "above" is a designation for the future time;
"below" is a designation for the past time. By the inclusion of both, that which is connected to both of those—namely, the present—is indicated.
"Certainly it is included. Therein, by the inclusion of the future time, the future aggregates, bases, and elements are included.
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. "In all" means in every existence, beginning with the division of the sensual realm. This is what is meant:
one who is liberated from all existence comprised within the three times—namely, the future, the past, and the present.

"Not contemplating ‘I am this’" means that one who is thus liberated does not contemplate, by way of views, conceit, or the notion of "I," that among form, feeling, and the rest, "this is the phenomenon (dhamma) and I am it.
The intention is that there is no cause for him to see things in such a manner.
Alternatively, "not contemplating ‘I am this’" refers to the aforementioned liberation.

This is the illumination of the means for attainment. Having made no resolve through the conceiving that has the nature of occurring as "this is mine, this I am, this is my self" regarding the formations comprised within the three realms and consisting of the three planes,
the insight that arises in the form "this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self"— which leads to emergence in the prior stage— is [the means] for liberation.
The proximate cause. Thus liberated, he has crossed over the flood, which was never crossed before, for the sake of non-renewal of existence.

Thus the Arahant, completely liberated from the ten fetters and from all unwholesome states, has—by means of the attainment of the Noble Path—even in his dreams, crossed over that fourfold flood consisting of the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance; indeed, the great flood of saṃsāra itself.
Or, he has crossed over for the sake of non-renewal of existence, for *nibbāna* without residue; the meaning is that having crossed over, he stands on the further shore.
The commentary on the first sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the second *Lakuṇḍaka-Bhaddiya Sutta*.

62. "In the second [verse], 'conceiving of one who is still in training' means conceiving, 'This one is a trainee. Here is the word-meaning: he trains, thus he is a trainee (*sekha*). What does he train in?
In higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom. Alternatively, training is *sikkhā*; he has this as his nature, thus he is a trainee.
For because his training is not yet completed and because he is intent upon it, he is by all means one whose nature is to train."

He is not like one who has completed his training, such as an *asekha*, whose zeal for that [training] has subsided; nor is he like the ordinary person who has abandoned training, who is uninterested in it.
Alternatively, he is a *sekha* because he is born into the noble birth through the three trainings, or because he exists therein.
"To a still greater extent" means beyond measure, exceeding the measure, or more abundantly.

The meaning is as follows: For the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, by means of the first instruction according to the method set forth in the first sutta, attained the destruction of the taints while remaining exactly as he was seated.

However, the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), not having perceived his attainment of Arahatship through non-attention and thinking, "He is still merely a trainee," like a noble person who gives much when asked for little, [spoke] more and more.
In many ways, the Blessed One continued to teach the Dhamma for the destruction of the taints. The Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, however, did not think, "I have already accomplished my task;
what is the use of this exhortation? Out of reverence for the true Dhamma, he listened attentively just as before.
Seeing this, even while seated within his fragrant chamber, the Blessed One, through the power of a Buddha, [spoke] just as the General of the Dhamma had done.
He knew of his destruction of the defilements (*kilesakkhaya*), and having done so, he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*). Therefore it was said: "At that time... and so forth.
Regarding that, whatever needs to be said has already been stated in the immediately preceding sutta.
In the verse, however, "he cut off the cycle" (*acchecchi vaṭṭaṃ*) means he completely severed the cycle of defilements; and once it was severed...

When the cycle of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*) is cut, the cycle of kamma (*kammavaṭṭa*) is also necessarily cut. "He has gone beyond hope" (*byagā nirāsaṃ*): "hope" (*āsā*) refers to craving (*taṇhā*);
"without hope" (*nirāsaṃ*) means that there is no hope here—this is Nibbāna. He has specifically "gone to" (*agā*) that state without hope; thus he is "one who has gone beyond" (*byagā*).

The meaning is that because the supreme path (*aggamagga*) has been attained, it has been reached without further cause for attainment. Since craving is the origin of suffering (*dukkhasamudaya*), [it is abandoned].
When that [craving] has been abandoned, there is no defilement left unabandoned; therefore, demonstrating the abandonment of craving in its specific excellence, he said:
"The dried-up river does not flow. Its meaning is as follows:

by the arising of the knowledge of the fourth path, just as by the appearance of a fourth sun, the river of craving is completely dried up and withered away, leaving nothing behind, like the great rivers.
The river does not flow; from this point on, it no longer proceeds. For craving is called "the flowing" (*saritā*). As it is said:
"The flowing and the endearments are the joys that arise for a person," and "the flowing is the clinging.
"The cycle is cut and does not turn" means that by the total cutting off of the cycle of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*), the cycle—once severed—is subject to non-arising.
By bringing about the state of being subject to non-resultant dhammas, the cycle of kamma is severed; it no longer turns, it does not proceed.

"This indeed is the end of suffering": this non-proceeding of the cycle of kamma, due to the total absence of the cycle of defilements, is the absolute non-arising of the cycle of results in the future; it is the end, the limit, the final enclosure of all the suffering of saṃsāra.
The commentary on the second sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the first of the seven suttas: 63.

In the third [sutta], "in sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu*) means in objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*). "Excessively" (*ativelaṃ*) means having transgressed the proper limit (*velaṃ atikkamitvā*). "Beings" (*satta*) refers to those who abound in improper attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*).
Without regarding even the existing danger and recollecting only the gratification, beings become attached—meaning they are stuck or clinging—by way of their innate nature.
"Lusting" means they are colored by desire and lust, being thoroughly impassioned by the transformation of the mind, just as cloth is dyed by a dye.
"Greedily longing" means they have fallen into greed through covetousness, which has the characteristic of yearning.
"Gadhitā" means bound to that [object] because it is difficult to release, as if intoxicated by passion.
"Mucchitā" means having fallen into a swoon or delusion, being as if rendered unconscious by the defilements and having no other duty.

"Ajjhopannā" means remaining there having swallowed and finalized it, as if making it something not shared with others. "Sammattakajātā" means having reached a state of being drunk upon sensual pleasures.

They have become thoroughly intoxicated, completely drunk, on the feeling of sensual pleasure. There is also a reading, “sammodakajātā,” which means they have become full of mutual affection, with joy having arisen.
By all these terms, he speaks precisely of their being overwhelmed by craving (*taṇhādhipanna*).

And here, although it was first stated “in sensual pleasures” (*kāmesu*), the repetition of the word “in sensual pleasures” is for the purpose of illustrating the extent of those beings’ total absorption in them.
This shows that at that time, they all dwelt in every posture as if endowed with the strands of sensual pleasure.
For on that occasion, with the exception of the noble disciples, all the inhabitants of Sāvatthī proclaimed a festival;
having prepared drinking grounds according to their means, they ate and drank, enjoying sensual pleasures both openly and in secret, and [overindulging] their faculties.

While indulging themselves, they fell into a state of intoxication with sensual pleasures. As monks were wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, they saw people in various houses and in pleasure groves and parks proclaiming festivals and behaving accordingly, being intent upon sensual desires.
Thinking, "Having gone to the monastery, we shall obtain the subtle and refined Dhamma," they reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Therefore it was said: “Then a number of bhikkhus... [omitted] ...dwelling among sensual pleasures.

Having understood this matter—having understood in every way their failure to see the danger in sensual pleasures, which are like the delightful drinking grounds of those people, yet are accompanied by manifold evils, possess terrible and bitter fruits, and are full of peril—and having understood both the sensual pleasures themselves...
And he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) concerning the discernment of the danger in the defilements (*kilesa*).

Therein, "clinging to sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu satto*) means that beings—being impassioned, intoxicated, clinging, attached, bound, and fettered by the defilement of desire (*kilesakāma*) toward the objects of desire (*vatthukāma*)—are stuck.

"Clinging through the attachment to sensual pleasure" (*kāmasaṅgasatto*) means that by means of that very power of desire, they are stuck through the attachment of lust (*rāga*) toward the objects of desire, as well as through the attachments of views, conceit, hatred, and ignorance.

And beings are unattached. "Not seeing the fault in the fetter" means that they do not see the fault, the defect, or the danger—namely, its status as the root of the suffering of the round of existence—in the defilements such as sensual lust known as "fetters," because these fetter beings to the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) through the round of kamma and the round of result, or through one state of becoming and so forth with other states of becoming, or by binding and fettering beings to suffering;
this is due to their contemplation of gratification in those phenomena that are subject to fettering.
"Not seeing. For those who are attached to the fetters and attachments will never cross over the vast and great flood.

Thus, by the absence of the vision of danger, beings who are attached to the objects of the fetters—namely, the phenomena of the three planes which are called "fetters" or are "attachments"—are [caught] in that which is vast due to its extensive range and its beginninglessness.
They would never cross the vast and great flood of sensual desire and so forth, or indeed the flood of saṃsāra;
the meaning is that they would by no means reach the further shore of that flood.
The commentary on the third sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Second Sutta on Beings (Dutiyasattasuttavaṇṇanā) 64.
In the fourth [sutta], "blinded" means that what are called sensual pleasures blind even one who is not blind.
As it has been said:
“The greedy man does not know the goal; the greedy man does not see the Dhamma.
It is utter darkness then for the man whom greed overcomes.
Therefore, even those who were not blind are made blind by sensual desire; thus they are called “made blind. The rest is exactly as explained in the immediately preceding sutta.
For in that case, the conduct of the people was seen by the monks and reported to the Blessed One; here, however, it was seen by the Blessed One himself—this is the distinction.

Having departed from Sāvatthī and while proceeding toward Jetavana, the Teacher saw on the way, by the river Aciravatī, a fish-trap set by fishermen into which the fish had entered and were unable to escape.

He saw many fish; later, he saw a single calf sucking milk, which, out of respect for its mother, followed her and, stretching out its neck due to thirst for milk, was placing its mouth between the mother’s legs.
Then the Blessed One, having entered the monastery and washed his feet, sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared, and [spoke] the last...
Having taken two matters as the basis for the simile, he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*).

Therein, "blinded by sensual desire" (*kāmandhā*) means they have been made blind and sightless by the defilement of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*) regarding objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*).

"Enveloped in a net" (*jālasañchannā*) refers to [being bound] within one's own person and the persons of others, among internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*), and among the phenomena (*dhamma*) dependent upon them, by way of the past and so forth.
Because it brings about harm to those included within it through successive arising from below to above amidst many diverse divisions,
and because it is like a lake surrounded by a net, it is "covered, enveloped, and overwhelmed" by craving—
which acts as a net with fine meshes. "Covered by the covering of craving" means covered by the covering known as craving, which is like moss and seaweed.

"Covered like water" means concealed, hidden, or shut off. By these two phrases, he shows that the movement of the wholesome mind has been obstructed by the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*).

"Bound by the kinsman of negligence" means bound by the Māra of defilements (*kilesa-māra*) and the Māra of the son of a god (*devaputta-māra*). For to the extent that one is bound by the Māra of defilements, to that same extent one is said to be bound by the Māra of the son of a god as well. Indeed, it has been said:
"The snare that moves through the sky, which wanders in the mind..."
“By that I shall afflict him; you shall not escape me, O ascetic!”—*Namuci*, *Kaṇha*, and *Pamattabandhu* are three names of Māra.

For even though he is a son of the gods (*devaputta*), like the Māra of defilements (*kilesamāra*), he binds heedless beings to harm; thus he is called *Pamattabandhu*. They also read: “The heedless are bound in bondage.”
In this context, "bondage" means the bondage of the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇabandhana*). "Bound" means restrained.

How so? Just as fish at the mouth of a net—that is, just as fish that have entered the mouth of a net cast by a fisherman become bound by it and meet their death—so too [are beings bound] by the bondage of the strands of sensual pleasure cast by Māra.

Bound by these fetters, these beings follow after aging and death. Just as a young calf, while still nursing, follows and tracks its mother—drinking her milk and following no other—so too, beings wandering through saṃsāra, bound by the fetters of Māra, follow only after death;
the intention is that they do not follow after the ageless, deathless Nibbāna.
The commentary on the fourth sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Aparalakuṇḍakabhaddiya Sutta*. 65.
In the fifth [sutta], "one behind the other behind many bhikkhus" refers to the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya.
On one occasion, having walked for alms among the villages together with a large number of bhikkhus,
and having finished his meal, he rinsed his bowl, placed it in his bag, slung it over his shoulder, folded his robe, and placed that too on his left shoulder; then,
with a pleasing manner in his advancing and retreating, in his looking ahead and looking aside, and in his bending [of the limbs]...

With his eyes cast down and his deportment perfected, as if demonstrating the fullness of his own mindfulness and wisdom, he walks placing one foot after another with a concentrated mind, having established mindfulness and clear comprehension very firmly.
And as he goes, he walks behind the bhikkhus, unmixed with them. Why?
Because of his dwelling in non-association. Furthermore, that venerable one’s physical form was despised and a source of contempt, so ordinary people reviled him.
Knowing this, the Elder walked behind him, thinking, "May these people not produce demerit on account of me.
Thus those monks and the Elder, having reached Sāvatthī and entered the monastery, went to where—
The Blessed One approached him. Therefore it is said: “Now at that time, the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya,” and so forth.

Therein, “ugly” (*dubbaṇṇa*) means misshapen. By this, he shows his lack of perfection in complexion and lack of perfection in physical form. “Unpleasant to behold” (*duddasika*) means having an unpleasing appearance.
By this, [he shows] his lack of perfection in secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*) and lack of perfection in physical bearing (*ākāra*).
And he shows the absence of height. "Okoṭimaka" means short; by this, he shows the absence of perfection in stature.
"Generally treated with contempt by the bhikkhus" means being despised by ordinary bhikkhus.

Ordinary people—some, such as the group of six (chabbaggiya) and others—not knowing the virtues of that venerable one, treat him with contempt, seizing and touching his hands, ears, head, and so forth, and playing with him.
Neither noble ones nor virtuous worldlings.
Why did he address the bhikkhus? To proclaim the Elder’s qualities. For it occurred to the Blessed One:
"These bhikkhus do not know the great power of my son; therefore they treat him with contempt."
"That will lead to their harm and suffering for a long time; come now, I shall reveal this monk's virtues to the bhikkhus and release him from this contempt.
"Do you see? means "Do you see indeed? And that attainment is not easily obtained which had never before been attained by that bhikkhu.

Regarding those various attainments known as the form-sphere attainments (*rūpasamāpatti*), the formless-sphere attainments (*arūpasamāpatti*), the divine abode attainments (*brahmavihārasamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*)—all such distinctions of attainments shared by disciples—not even a single one among them was easily obtained;
they were difficult to attain, and there was not one that had not previously been attained by that monk Lakunḍaka Bhaddiya. By this [it is shown]...

Regarding what was said, “of great psychic power (mahiddhika) and great majesty (mahānubhāva),” having therein demonstrated his great psychic power, [the Buddha] now spoke the passage beginning with “for whose sake” in order to show his great majesty.
That is according to the method already explained below.
And here, the Blessed One said, “This, monks, is a monk,” and so forth, [showing that] “monks, this monk is not just anyone, nor is he merely someone who is ugly or unsightly.”
One should not despise him merely because he comes following behind the monks by the hundreds of thousands;
rather, he is of great psychic power and great majesty. Whatever can be attained by a disciple has all been attained by him.
Therefore, look upon him with respect, as one would a precious stone umbrella; that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
He shows that [the Elder] will become so.

"Having understood this matter" means: having known in every aspect this mass of virtues of the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, consisting of his great psychic power, great majesty, and so forth, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which illuminates that very meaning.
In this context, "nelaṅgo": *ela* is said to mean fault (*dosa*); that which has no *ela* is *nela*. But what is that? It is perfectly pure virtue (*suparisuddhasīla*).
For that which is intended here as "nela" (faultless) is so called in the sense of being free from defect. That which has this faultless quality as its primary constituent part is "nelaṅga.
It is connected with what he will later call the "chariot"; therefore, the meaning is "one whose constituent parts of virtue are perfectly purified.
For it is the virtue of the fruit of Arahantship that is intended here. "Setapacchādo" means "having a white covering. "Pacchāda" means...

The woolen cloth or similar material that is to be spread over the chariot. Moreover, it is either white due to its state of extreme purity, or it may be any other color such as red, blue, and so forth.

However, in this context, because the liberation consisting of the fruit of Arahatship is intended, it is called "white-canopied" by way of its state of extreme purity, just as elsewhere it is said, "the chariot has virtue as its equipment. One [factor] is reckoned as mindfulness.
"Ekāra" means "of this one" (*etassa*). "Vattati" means "proceeds. He says "chariot" (*ratha*) with reference to the elder’s own person.
"Anīgha" means free from suffering; the meaning is that it is like a vehicle free from the agitation of the defilements (*kilesa*).
"Āyantaṃ" means coming along behind the backs of many monks. "Chinnasotaṃ" means with the stream cut off.
For the sake of the smooth operation of an ordinary chariot, there is a flow, a streaming, and a trickling of ghee, oil, and so forth, smeared upon the axle-tips and the nave;
therefore, it is called "one with unbroken flow.
But this [Arahant] is called "one with broken flow" because thirty-six streams have been abandoned without remainder; that is "the one with broken flow. He has none of these...
"Without bonds": he is one who is free from bonds. For a chariot carpet has many bonds in order to make it immovable together with the axle; therefore, that is "with bonds.

But this one is "without bonds" because all fetters and bonds have been completely exhausted without remainder; he is that one without bonds. "Behold him," said the Blessed One, [praising] the Elder's virtues.
Having attained joy, he spoke of himself.

Thus the Teacher described the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya as having a beautiful wheel by way of the fruit of arahantship, a beautiful upper cover by way of the liberation of the fruit of arahantship,
beautiful spokes by way of well-established mindfulness, and being unshakable due to the absence of agitation from the defilements.
By virtue of the absence of the stain of craving, it is "unstained"; by virtue of the absence of fetters and so forth, it is "unbound.
Having thus made it a well-fenced, well-yoked chariot for a thoroughbred horse, he shows it.
The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Taṇhāsaṅkhaya-sutta* (Sutta 6).
Regarding the sixth [discourse], "Aññā Koṇḍañña": here, "Koṇḍañña" is the name of that venerable one derived from his clan (*gotra*).

However, because he was the very first among the disciples to penetrate the Noble Truths, the Blessed One said, "Koṇḍañña has indeed understood (*aññāsi vata*, O friends). Thus he came to be known as "Aññā Koṇḍañña."
By virtue of the name given at his birth, the Elder became known in the Dispensation as "Aññā-Koṇḍañña.

"Deliverance through the destruction of craving": craving is destroyed—that is, abandoned—in this, thus it is the "destruction of craving," which is Nibbāna. Deliverance in that destruction of craving.
Or, that by which craving is destroyed or abandoned is the "destruction of craving," namely the Noble Path. [This refers to] the deliverance which is the fruit thereof.
Or, liberation as the ultimate consummation is the liberation through the destruction of craving (*taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutti*); in the absolute sense, it is the attainment of the fruit of Arhatship.
He sat reflecting upon that. For this venerable one frequently enters the attainment of the fruit;
therefore, he acted in this way here as well.
"Having understood this matter": having understood this review of the highest fruit by the Elder Aññā-Koṇḍañña, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) to illuminate that meaning.

In this context, "for whom there is no root in the ground": for that noble person, the ignorance which constitutes the root of the tree of his personal existence—that very ignorance has its foundation and cause in what is called the "ground," namely, the defilements (āsava), the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), and improper attention (ayonisomanasikāra).

And there is no [tree], because it has been eradicated by the supreme path (*aggamagga*). Regarding the phrase "there is no leaf, how much less a creeper," the connection between the words is: "there is no creeper, how much less a leaf.
There is not even a creeper—reckoned as branches, twigs, and so forth—consisting of the various types of conceit (*māna*), overweening conceit (*atimāna*), and the rest;
how much less the leaves consisting of intoxication (*mada*), negligence (*pamāda*), deceit (*māyā*), and hypocrisy (*sāṭheyya*)? Or alternatively: "there is no leaf, how much less a creeper."
When a tree sprout grows, first the leaves emerge; later, what are called branches and twigs are produced, which is why it is said [in this way].

In that context, for the "tree" of the personal existence (*attabhāva*) that would otherwise arise in the absence of the cultivation of the Noble Path, because the Noble Path has been cultivated, the root known as ignorance (*avijjā*)—which is the basis for the influxes (*āsava*) and so forth—is destroyed.
And there is none. Furthermore, by the mention of the "root" (*mūla*) here, it should be understood that because karma is the fundamental cause, it stands in the place of the seed;

thus, the absence of that [karma] is also implicitly included. And when the seed of karma is absent, the sprout of consciousness caused by it will not arise, nor will the shoots and branches such as name-and-form, the six sense bases, and so forth, which are caused by the sprout of consciousness, ever come to be. Therefore it was said: "For whom the root..."
“There is no ground, there is no wisdom;
whence could there be a creeper?”—that wise one is “released from bondage” because he has conquered Māra through the application of the energy of the fourfold right exertion (*sammappadhāna*);
for that very reason, he is released from the bondage of all defilements (*kilesa*) and volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*). Who is worthy to censure him?

*Ettha* (here) is a mere particle. Who indeed, being wise by nature, would deserve to censure or revile one who is thus liberated from all defilements and endowed with supreme qualities such as virtue (*sīla*)? For there is simply no basis for censure.

"Even the gods praise him": this means that not only the gods—Sakka and others—who know his specific excellences, but also humans, such as Kṣatriyas and scholars, [praise him]. The word *api* (even/also) implies this.
They praise him. Moreover, he is praised not only by others, but even by Brahmā, by Mahābrahmā, and by other beings such as Brahmas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas; he is indeed extolled.
The commentary on the sixth sutta is concluded.
7. Commentary on the *Papañcasūdanī* Sutta 67.

Regarding the seventh [verse], "the abandoning of the conceptual proliferation of perceptions and formations" (*papañcasaññāsaṅkhāpahāna*): they are called "proliferations" (*papañca*) because wherever they themselves arise, they expand that mental continuum and cause it to persist for a long time;
thus, they are the defilements (*kilesa*). Specifically, these are lust, hatred, delusion, craving, views, and conceit. For it has been said: [as follows].
“Lust is proliferation (*papañca*), hatred is proliferation, delusion is proliferation, craving is proliferation, views are proliferation, and conceit is proliferation.

Furthermore, the meaning of defilement is the meaning of proliferation, and the meaning of rubbish is the meaning of proliferation. In this context, the sign of the perception of beauty is the cause of the proliferation of lust;

the grounds for resentment are the cause of the proliferation of hatred; the taints are the cause of the proliferation of delusion; and [the objects of] craving are the cause of the proliferation of craving.
Feeling (*vedanā*) is the proliferation (*papañca*) of views; perception (*saññā*) is the proliferation of conceit; and thought (*vitakka*) is the sign (*nimitta*) of the proliferation of conceit.

Perception accompanied by those proliferations is "perception-proliferation" (*papañcasaññā*). The "reckonings" (*saṅkhā*), "parts" (*bhāgā*), and "sections" (*koṭṭhāsā*) of such perception-proliferations are "reckonings of perception-proliferation" (*papañcasaññāsaṅkhā*).

In terms of meaning, this refers to the group of defilements belonging to their respective proliferations, together with their signs. And here, the inclusion of the term "perception" (*saññā*) is for the purpose of including that [group of defilements].
This is because they function as a common cause for them. For it has been said: "Proliferation (papañca) and conceptualization (saṅkhā) have perception (saññā) as their source.
Their abandonment means the complete eradication of defilements such as lust by means of the respective paths.
For at that time, the Blessed One [reflected] upon his own past births, numbering many hundreds of thousands of millions, which had served as the basis for misfortune.

Having reflected that the defilements (kilesa) in this final existence have been abandoned along with their latent tendencies (savāsana) by means of the Noble Path at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa),
and having seen the continuum of beings (sattasantāna) and its defiled conduct— polluted by defilements such as lust— as difficult to release, like a gourd filled with sour gruel,
like a bowl filled with buttermilk, or like a rag soaked in fat, [he thought]: "How dense indeed is this cycle of defilements!"
"What has been cultivated by me since beginningless time has been abandoned without remainder; oh, it is well-abandoned!

Thus, with joy and gladness arisen, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna). Therefore it was said: "Then the Blessed One, having understood his own abandonment of the conceptual proliferations of perception, on that occasion uttered this inspired utterance."

In this context, regarding the phrase "for whom there are no proliferations (papañca) and no persistence": because the Blessed One describes himself as if he were another, it means that for that Supreme Person (aggapuggala), who possesses the aforementioned characteristics, there are no proliferations, nor is there any persistence in saṃsāra caused by them.
In the *Nettippakaraṇa*, however, it is stated: "Persistence is the underlying tendency (anusaya). For the underlying tendency is [the cause] of the occurrence of existence.
"Roots": they cause beings to proliferate in saṃsāra, thus they are called *papañcas*. There is also the reading "the persistence of proliferation" (*papañcaṭṭhiti*). Its meaning is as follows:
the persistence of proliferations—their continued existence and non-eradication by means of the Path—is the "persistence of proliferation.

Alternatively, the proliferations themselves constitute the "persistence of proliferation," because they serve as the cause for the occurrence of the remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant states within the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
