That [state] does not exist for that Supreme Person. "Having transcended the tether and the crossbar" means he has specifically transcended by abandoning along with their latent tendencies:
those cravings and views which, because they resemble a continuous stream in the sense of being a bond, are given the name "tether" (*sandāna*);
and ignorance, which, because it resembles a crossbar in its obstruction of entry into the city of Nibbāna, is designated as the "crossbar" (*paligha*). He has thus gone beyond them.
Others, however, say that anger is a "fetter" (*saṃdāna*); that should not be accepted, for it is described as "assailing others.

[The phrase] "that sage wandering free from craving" means: one who is entirely free from craving due to the absence of *taṇhā* in every respect; a sage (*muni*) because of having realized both worlds and because of having realized his own welfare and the welfare of others;
and one who, solely for the sake of the welfare of all beings, through the four modes of conduct...
As he moves through various meditative attainments and through a course of knowledge that is not shared by others,
the entire world— including its devas, its Brahmās, and all beings possessed of wisdom— never despises or looks down upon him;
rather, honoring him as the foremost, the best, the highest, and the most excellent in the world, they treat him with reverence and respect.
“He is devoted to honoring and respecting.
The commentary on the seventh sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Kaccāna Sutta.

68. Regarding the eighth [section], the term *ajjhatta* (internal): here, this word *ajjhatta* occurs in the sense of "one's own internal [states]" in such passages as "the six internal bases" (*cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni*).

It occurs in the sense of "one's own personal [states]" in such passages as "internal phenomena" (*ajjhattā dhammā*) or "contemplating the body in the body internally" (*ajjhattaṃ vā kāye kāyānupassī*).

It occurs in the sense of "the internal object" in such passages as "by not attending to any signs, he dwells having entered upon internal emptiness" (*sabbanimittānaṃ amanasikārā ajjhattaṃ suññataṃ upasampajja viharati*).
The meaning is "in the place of mastery. For the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) is indeed called the place of mastery for Buddhas.
In such passages as, "Therefore, Ānanda, that bhikkhu should settle his mind right within himself upon that same original sign of concentration," it refers to the "object-field" (*gocarajjhatta*).
Here too, it should be understood as referring precisely to the object-field. Therefore, "within" (*ajjhatta*) means being within the sphere of the object-field.
"Having the meditation subject as its object" is what is meant. "In front of the face" means facing it.
"Well established" means by means of mindfulness directed to the body that is well established. And here, by the term "mindfulness," the jhāna is intended. This is what is meant:
"having entered upon the sublime jhāna obtained by way of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body internally."
For one day, while the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, this elder, having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from his almsround after the meal, entered the monastery.

Having performed his duties toward the Blessed One, he sat for his midday rest in the daytime quarters. After spending the day’s portion of time engaged in various meditative attainments, he went into the middle of the monastery during the evening hour.

Having descended, while the Blessed One was seated in the Perfumed Chamber, he thought, "It is not yet time to approach the Blessed One," and so, not far from the Perfumed Chamber, at the foot of a certain tree, he set a time limit and sat down after entering the aforementioned meditative attainment.
While seated in the Perfumed Chamber, the Teacher saw him sitting in that manner. By means of that...
It is said: “Now at that time, the Venerable Mahākaccāna... [the passage] ending with ‘well-established.

Having understood this matter—having understood in every aspect the venerable elder Mahākaccāna’s attainment of jhāna by making the development of the foundations of mindfulness the basis—he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) to illuminate its meaning.
In this context, for one who might have mindfulness at all times, constantly established in relation to the body—

meaning for that practitioner of insight (vipassaka) who has divided the body into six parts, mindfulness is "constantly" and "continuously" directed toward the body as its object, having entered into both types of bodies (the two-fold division of name-and-form) throughout all time by way of the comprehension of the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent and so forth.
Through constant application and persistence, mindfulness may become established.
It is said that this venerable one first developed jhāna by means of the meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body;
taking that as his foundation, he established insight through the gateway of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body, and thereby attained arahantship. He...
In the later period as well, for the most part, having attained that same jhāna and emerged from it, and having likewise practiced insight, he enters the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti).
The Teacher, wishing to show the method by which he attained Arahantship, said:
"For whom mindfulness is always present, constantly established in the body," and then [described] the manner of its establishment.
He said, "May there be neither 'I' nor 'mine,' may there not be [anything], nor may there be 'mine' in the future," in order to make this clear.
Its meaning should be understood in two ways: by way of the preliminary stage prior to full comprehension (*sammasana*) and by way of the time of comprehension itself.
Among these, first, by way of the preliminary stage: "May there be neither 'I' nor 'mine'" refers to the past; in the past, my defilements and kamma were not...
If it had not existed, this present personal existence would not be mine, nor would it have arisen for me.
However, because there were past kamma and defilements for me, this present personal existence of mine proceeds as a result of that.
"It will not be, and it shall not be for me" refers to the attainment of the antidote within this very personal existence.
"Defilement and karma will not exist for me; they will not arise. In the future, the round of result will not exist for me, nor will it proceed.

In this way, the vision of name-and-form together with its conditions is revealed: "This fivefold aggregate known as my own individuality has, throughout the three periods of time, karma and defilements as its cause, and not a creator god or other such causes; and as it is for me, so it is for all beings."
Furthermore, by way of the time of correct contemplation (*sammasana*), one reflects: "It is not, nor shall it be mine.

For this pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*) is impermanent in the sense of its non-existence after having come to be, suffering in the sense of constant oppression, and non-self in the sense of lack of mastery;
thus, if there were such a thing as a self, it would be neither distinct from the pentad of aggregates, nor would it exist, nor could it be.
If it were so, venerable sir, there would not be anything belonging to me. One must regard both self and what belongs to self as "it will not be":
just as this name-and-form is currently empty of self and what belongs to self, and was so in the past, so too it will not be, it will not be mine;
and even in the future, there will be no so-called self distinct from the aggregates.

"Nothing whatsoever will come to be for me, nothing will proceed; therefore, nothing that could serve as an obstacle will come to be for me, and even in the future, nothing called 'mine' will exist for me.

By this, he demonstrates the absence of anything to be grasped as "I" and the absence of anything to be grasped as "mine" across the three periods of time. By that, [he shows] the fourfold alternative (catukkoṭika).
Emptiness is made manifest.
"He dwells there in successive stages"— thus, by contemplating the emptiness of self and what belongs to self within those formations at these three times,
as the various insights such as the knowledge of arising and passing away gradually arise, he dwells by way of successive insight.

"Dwelling in successive stages, one should cross over attachment in due time. Thus, the practitioner of yoga, having reached the culmination of insight (vipassanā), stands at the moment when the faculties have reached maturity, at the moment when insight leading to emergence is joined with the Path, and at the moment of the arising of the Noble Path;
at that time, from the cessation of the continuity of the entire threefold existence, he crosses over what is termed "attachment" (visattikā).
The intention is: "One should cross over craving; having crossed over, one should stand on its further shore.
Thus, by means of this indirect statement (*aññāpadesena*), the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) to illuminate the arising of Arahatship in the Venerable Mahākaccāna.
The commentary on the eighth sutta is finished.
9. Udapānasutta Commentary 69. Regarding the ninth [sutta]:
"Among the Mallans" (*malleṣu*). The "Mallans" (*mallā*) are royal princes belonging to a particular province;
their entire territory is, by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*), called "the Mallans. It is among these Mallans that what is known in the world as "a Malla" is found. However, some [say]...
They read it as “mālesu. “Wandering on a journey” means wandering on a journey through the great maṇḍala districts by way of a non-hurried pace.
“With a large community of bhikkhus” means with a great multitude of recluses whose virtues are immeasurable;
for at that time, the Blessed One had a large retinue of bhikkhus. “Thūṇa, a brahmin village of the Mallas,” is to the southeast.
In the region of Malla, which serves as the boundary for the Middle Country (*majjhima-desa*), there was a brahmin village named Thūṇa due to its abundance of brahmins.

*Tadavasari* means he arrived there; the sense is that he reached the road to the village of Thūṇa. *Assosuṃ* means they heard; the sense is that they came to know [it] by following the sound of the speech that had reached their faculty of hearing.
*Kho* is a particle used for filling out the meter (*padapūraṇe*) or for emphasis (*avadhāraṇatthe*). In this context, it is used in the sense of emphasis.
"They heard," it is said, meaning there was no obstacle to their hearing. [The particle] "eva" serves merely to fill out the meter and provide elegance to the phrasing.
"Thūṇeyyakā" means those dwelling in the village of Thūṇa. Regarding the term "brāhmaṇa-gahapatikā": here, they are called *brāhmaṇas* because they "chant the *brahman*" (the Veda);

the meaning is that they recite the mantras. For this indeed is the etymological derivation for *jāti-brāhmaṇas* (brahmins by birth), whereas the Noble Ones (*ariyas*) are so called because they have "banished evil" (*bāhitapāpa*).
They are called "brahmins. "Householders" refers to anyone living in a household, excluding kshatriyas and brahmins;
specifically, it refers to vaiśyas. "Brahmins and householders" means brahmin-householders.
Now, in order to show the matter they heard, the passage beginning with "The ascetic Gotama, sirs... was spoken.
In this context, he should be understood as a "samaṇa" (ascetic) because he has stilled evil. For it has been said:
"His evil, unwholesome states have been stilled," and so forth. And the Blessed One has completely stilled evil by means of the unsurpassed Noble Path.
Therefore, this name "samaṇa" is one acquired according to his actual qualities. The word *khalu* is a particle used in the sense of tradition.
"Bho" is merely a form of address derived from birth among those of the brahmin caste. For it is said: "He is called 'Bhovādi' (one who says 'bho') if he possesses something.
"Gotama" is a designation of the Blessed One by way of his clan (*gotra*). Therefore, "Samaṇo khalu, bho, Gotamo" means:
"O sir, the ascetic is indeed of the Gotama clan"—this is the meaning here. "Sakyaputta" (son of the Sakyas) [is likewise a designation].
This, however, is an illustration of the Blessed One’s noble lineage. “He went forth from the Sakyan clan” is an illustration of his state of having gone forth out of faith.
What is meant is that he went forth out of a faith aimed at renunciation, abandoning that very clan while it was still undiminished and unexhausted, being himself unsubdued by any loss.
“Until they filled the well with grass and chaff up to its brim” refers to the drinking-well.
They increased [the well] by means of grass and chaff according to the size of its mouth; the meaning is that they filled the well with grass and other materials and covered it over.
It is said that outside that village, on the path by which the Blessed One was coming, there was a certain well used for the consumption of brahmins.
With the exception of that one, all the water sources there—such as wells and ponds—were then completely dried up and devoid of water.
They were [thus]. Then the people of Thūṇeyyaka, who had little faith in the Three Jewels and were characterized by stinginess, having heard of the Blessed One’s arrival, thought:

“If the ascetic Gotama, together with his disciples, should enter this village and stay for two or three days, he would establish all these people in his own teaching, and then the Dhamma of the brahmins would find no foothold. Thus they [acted] there.
Seeking to prevent the Blessed One from staying, they deliberated, saying, "There is no water elsewhere in this village;
we shall make that well unusable, so that the ascetic Gotama, together with his disciples, will not enter this village.
Having thus resolved, all the villagers took seven days' worth of water, filled their jars and other vessels, and [covered] the well with grass and chaff.
And they covered it up. Therefore it was said: “They filled the well with grass and chaff right up to the brim, thinking, ‘Lest those shaveling recluses drink the water.
In that context, while it would be permissible to call those with shaved heads “shavelings” (muṇḍaka) and those who are recluses “recluses” (samaṇa), yet those [who were actually]...
Despising them with the intention of mocking, they spoke thus. *Mā* is a particle of prohibition; the meaning is "do not throw away" and "do not drink.
*Okkamitvā maggā* means having stepped off from the path. *Etamhā* refers to that very well which had been treated by them in such a manner, as he points it out.
But why did the Blessed One speak thus without first reflecting upon the misconduct of those brahmins?
—“Bring water from this well,” did he say, or did he know by means of his mental advertence (*āvajjana*)?
The Blessed One spoke thus in order to manifest his own Buddha-power, to subdue them, and to render them free from their harmful activities; it was not because he desired to drink water.
For that very reason, as in the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta*, he did not say, “I am thirsty. Thus spoke the Dhamma-keeper of the storehouse.
However, not knowing the Teacher’s intention, and pointing out the failure committed by the Thūṇeyyakas, he said, “Now, Bhante,” and so forth.
In that passage, *idāni* means “just now,” with the sense of “at the very moment of our arrival.
They read it as, “Bhante, this well. After the Elder had refused twice, on the third occasion [he said], “Tathāgatas do not [speak] three times...”
"An obstacle must be created; a cause will be seen by one who sees far," he thought. Taking the bowl given by the Great King for the Blessed One, he went to the well.
As the Elder was walking, the water in the well became full and, upon his stepping out, it overflowed on all sides;
all the grass and chaff floated away and cleared of its own accord.
As that flowing water increased further and further, all the reservoirs in that village, such as lotus ponds and the like, were filled to overflowing;
likewise, the moats, ditches, and low-lying areas were filled. The entire village area was completely submerged by the great flood, just as it would be during a time of heavy rain.
Water-born flowers such as the kumuda, uppala, paduma, and puṇḍarīka blossomed.
Breaking through here and there and blooming, they covered the water. Upon the reeds, water-birds such as swans, cranes, ruddy geese, ducks, and herons moved about, crying out in various places.
The people of Thūneyya saw that great flood thus surging upward, agitated on all sides by waves and billows, with beautiful masses of foam and bubbles rising up from its edges.
Seeing this, they were struck with a sense of wonder and amazement and deliberated thus:
"We endeavored to cut off the water supply for the ascetic Gotama, yet this great flood has increased ever since his arrival;
there is no doubt that this is due to his supernatural power. For he is indeed one of great psychic power and great majesty. It is possible..."
"But this is possible: that a great flood might arise and even submerge our village.
Come now, let us approach the ascetic Gotama, attend upon him, confess our transgression, and ask for his forgiveness.
With one mind, they all departed from the village in a large group, forming a multitude, and went to where the Blessed One was.
They approached him. Having approached, some paid homage at the Blessed One’s feet with their heads;
some extended their joined palms in salutation; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One;
some sat down in silence; and some announced their names and clans. Having done this, they all sat down to one side and said: “Here we are, sir...”
"Master Gotama, we indeed imposed a prohibition on water for both you, Master Gotama, and your disciples;

we threw grass and chaff into such-and-such a well. Yet that well, though being insentient, as if it were sentient and as if knowing the virtue of the Master, has itself removed all the grass and chaff and become perfectly pure—indeed, everything."
And here, this low-lying area, filled by the great flood of water, has become delightful;
the beings who depend on the water are well-contented. But we, though being human, did not recognize your virtues, and so we acted thus.
It would be well if Master Gotama would act in such a way that this great flood does not overwhelm this village; it is a transgression.
“An offense has indeed come upon us, as is the way of fools; may the venerable Gotama accept our transgression out of compassion.
Thus they confessed their transgression. The Blessed One also said, “Truly, an offense has come upon you, as is the way of fools;
we accept it from you for the sake of future restraint. Having accepted their transgression and knowing their hearts were clear, he—

He taught the Dhamma further in accordance with their inclinations. Having heard the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, they, with hearts full of faith, established themselves in the refuges and other precepts;
having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him, they departed.
However, even before their arrival, the Venerable Ānanda had already witnessed that miracle and was struck with a sense of wonder and amazement.
Having taken water in his bowl and offered it to the Blessed One, he reported that occurrence. Thus it was said:
“‘So be it, venerable sir,’ said the Venerable Ānanda,” and so forth.
In that context, “having spat from his mouth” means having discarded all that grass and so on by means of his mouth. “Supposing it was overflowing” means...

The stream of water that had previously been drawn up by means of a long rope from the well stood in the Blessed One’s bowl—level to the brim and ready for a crow to drink—seeming as if it were overflowing from his mouth at the moment the Elder had departed.
This was said with reference to the flow of water occurring at the time the Elder left; thereafter, however, it proceeded in the manner previously described.
In that village, the entire low-lying area became filled with water. This miracle, however, was not produced by the Buddha’s resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*), nor by the power of the gods;
rather, it was through the power of the Blessed One’s merit (*puññānubhāva*), as in the case of his journey from Rājagaha to Vesālī for the purpose of teaching the *Paritta*.
Some, however, [say it was] "for the sake of generating faith in the Blessed One among the inhabitants of Thūṇeyyaka..."
“[It was] done by deities who desired their welfare,” some say; others say, “The Naga King dwelling beneath the well did so.
All of that is without foundation, because it is demonstrated that the emergence of the water occurred solely through the power of the Blessed One’s merit.

“Having understood this matter”: having understood in every aspect this matter—consisting of the accomplishment of what he himself desired—without the need for a formal resolution (adhiṭṭhāna), he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which illuminates that matter.
In this regard, what would one do with a well if there were water everywhere? The meaning is:
if water were to exist at all times and in all places—if it were available, if its acquisition were dependent merely upon one’s wish—then what would one do with that well?
What would one accomplish? What would be the purpose? Having cut off craving at its root, of what...?
He who wanders seeking—that craving by which beings, being bound and having performed no merit, are tormented by the suffering of not obtaining what they desire—is the root of that craving;
or rather, standing with its root cut, why, for what reason, would one like me, an omniscient Buddha, wander seeking water or seek other requisites? "Having cut from the root," it is also said.
They recite [the verse], meaning "one who cuts the root of craving right at its root. Alternatively, "one who cuts from the root" means one who cuts off craving starting from its very root.

This is what is intended: he who, beginning from the Great Resolve (mahāpaṇidhāna)—which is the root of enlightenment—did not consider his own immeasurable and entire accumulation of merit for himself, but rather dedicated it solely for the welfare of the world.
Fulfilling [his needs] from the very root and having cut off craving, for what reason— since there is no lack of obtaining what is desired due to the absence of craving as a cause—
would he go about searching for water? But these foolish villagers, being blind and ignorant,
acted thus without knowing this reason.
The commentary on the ninth sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Udena Sutta: 70.
In the tenth [sutta], "of King Udena" means of the king named Udena, who is also called "the Vajji King. "Having gone to the park" means...
[This refers to] one who has gone to a park for the purpose of a pleasure excursion.
This genitive case (*sāmivacana*) is used here in the sense of disregard; however, in relation to the word "palace" (*antepura*), this genitive becomes one expressing a connection.
"Perished" (*kālaṅkatāni*) means they died after being consumed by fire. Regarding "headed by Sāmāvatī": who was this Sāmāvatī, and how did she perish? It is said:
In Bhaddavatiya, there was a merchant’s daughter named Sāmāvatī, who was placed by the merchant Ghosaka in the position of his own daughter;
accompanied by a retinue of five hundred women, she became the chief queen of King Udena. Abiding frequently in loving-kindness (*mettāvihāra*), she was a noble female disciple (*ariyasāvikā*).
This is the summary here; however, the detailed account of Sāmāvatī’s origins from the beginning is found in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*.
This should be understood according to the method already stated. There was a daughter of a brahmin named Māgaṇḍiya who said to her own parents:
“Having seen craving, aversion, and lust, there was no desire even for sexual intercourse.”
"What is this thing filled with urine and excrement,
that one would not even wish to touch it with one's feet?
Having heard this verse taught by the Blessed One, Māgaṇḍiyā, who harbored a deep-seated enmity toward the Teacher, was later [confronted] by the king.

Having learned from Uttara, who had been appointed to the position of chief counselor, that the Blessed One had arrived at Kosambī and that the five hundred women headed by Sāmāvatī had become lay disciples, he thought: "The ascetic Gotama has indeed come to this city;
I shall know what must be done for him, and these women are his attendants—these very ones headed by Sāmāvatī."
Thinking, "I shall know what must be done," she strove in many ways to cause harm to the Tathāgata and to them,
yet being unable to do so, she one day, while going with the king for a pleasure excursion to the park,
sent a message to her younger father: "Go to Sāmāvatī’s palace, open the storehouses of cloth and the storehouses of oil, and [place] cloths into oil-filled jars..."
“Having soaked them and wrapped them around the pillars, gather them all together, close the door, place a mechanism outside,
and having set fire to the house with torches, descend and depart. Having heard this,
he ascended the palace, opened the storehouses, and soaked the clothes in oil-filled vessels.
He began to wrap the pillars. Then the women, headed by Sāmāvatī, approached him saying, "What is this, little father?
He replied, "Ladies, the king has these pillars bound with oil-soaked rags for the sake of strengthening them;
in a royal palace, indeed, what is appropriate and what is inappropriate is difficult to discern; do not remain near me. Having said this, he sent those who had come away to their quarters.
Having made them enter, closed the doors, and placed a mechanical bolt outside, he descended while lighting the fire starting from the beginning.

Sāmāvatī gave them this exhortation: "Ladies, for those wandering through the cycle of existence since time immemorial, whose bodies have been thus consumed by fire, even the wisdom of a Buddha cannot easily determine their limit; therefore, be heedful. To the Teacher...

Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the noble female disciple Khujjuttarā— who had realized the fruit [of stream-entry], understood the teaching, attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) of one still in training,
and was teaching the Dhamma according to the very method of certainty taught by the Teacher— [the Elder] attained the fruit of stream-entry in her presence. From time to time,
being devotedly engaged in the mental application of the meditation subject, he practiced the meditation subject of the discernment of feelings while sitting in his house.
Some of them, attending to the mind, attained the second fruit and some the third fruit, and then passed away.
Then, while wandering for alms in Kosambī, the bhikkhus learned of this occurrence; after their meal, they reported it to the Blessed One and asked about their future destiny.
And the Blessed One explained to the bhikkhus the attainment of the noble fruits by those women.
Therefore it was said: "Now at that time, for King Udena... [and so on] ...they passed away not in vain.

In this context, "not in vain" (*anipphalā*) means not fruitless; they passed away having indeed attained the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*). And while they were attaining those fruits, Sāmāvatī addressed them thus:
"Exert yourselves! Strive! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!"
“Shake off the army of Death, as an elephant shakes down a reed-hut.
Whoever shall dwell heedfully in this Dhamma and Discipline will,
having abandoned the cycle of birth, make an end of suffering.”
Being exhorted with verses, they applied their minds to the meditation subject of the discernment of feelings; having practiced insight, they attained the second and third fruits [of the path].

However, because her lifespan was still remaining and because she had not previously performed such karma, Khujjuttarā remained outside that palace. It is said that she went as far as ten yojanas away. Then the bhikkhus...
In the Dhamma Hall, they raised this discussion: "Friends, it is truly unbecoming for noble female disciples to die in such a manner.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "Monks, even though this was improper for them in this present existence..."
"It is only fitting that they received these things as a result of deeds performed in the past," he said; and being requested by them, he related a story of the past.
"In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, eight Paccekabuddhas used to eat regularly in the king's palace.
Five hundred women attended upon them. Of those [eight], seven persons went to the Himālaya."
One [Paccekabuddha] sat in meditative attainment within a thicket of grass near the riverbank.
Then one day, when the Paccekabuddhas had departed, the king went there with those women, desiring to play in the water.
After playing in the water for part of the day, the women—afflicted by the cold and wishing to warm themselves—climbed up into that thicket, which was covered with dried grass on top.
Having surrounded [the grass] with the perception that it was "a heap of grass" and set fire to it, while the grass was burning and falling away, they saw the Paccekabuddha.
Thinking, "A Paccekabuddha is burning for the king; once the king knows this, he will have us executed.
We must ensure he is completely consumed," they brought wood and other materials from here and there, piled them over him, and set them ablaze.
Thinking, "He will now enter jhāna," they departed. Having previously been unintentional, they were now bound by their own karma.

However, while the Paccekabuddha was within his meditative attainment, even if they had brought a thousand cartloads of wood and set him on fire, they would not have been able to produce even a trace of heat;
therefore, he arose on the seventh day and went wherever he pleased.

She arrived. Because of having performed that deed, after being cooked in hell for many thousands of years and many hundreds of thousands of years, through the remaining ripening of that very same karma, they were burned in this very manner in their homes throughout one hundred successive existences. This was their prior karma.
Because they realized the fruits of the noble ones (ariyaphala) in this present existence and rendered service to the Three Jewels,
some among them were reborn as non-returners (anāgāminī) in the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa); others were reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas,
some among the Yāma devas, some among the Tusita devas, some among the Nimmānarati devas, and some among the Paranimmitavasavatti devas.
King Udena, having heard that Sāmāvatī’s house was burning, arrived at that place with great haste;
yet he reached it only after those women had already been consumed by the flames. Having returned and extinguished the fire, he was overcome with intense grief.
Discovering through skillful means that Māgaṇḍiyā had caused this to happen, and being reproached for the offense he had committed against noble female disciples, he—
She caused the king to issue a command together with her kinsmen. Thus, she, along with her retinue, friends, and relatives, met with ruin and disaster.

"Having understood this matter" means: having understood in every aspect the cause for those women, headed by Sāmāvatī, to meet with ruin and disaster in the fire, as well as the cause for Māgaṇḍiyā and her friends and relatives to meet with ruin and disaster through the king’s command.
He uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) to illuminate that meaning.
In this regard, "the world, bound by delusion, appears as if it were capable [of improvement]" means that the world of beings here,
which appears as if it were endowed with the causes for improvement, is likewise bound by delusion and enveloped by delusion regarding its own welfare and non-welfare.
Not knowing, one does not practice for one's welfare; instead, one accumulates much demerit that brings about harm and suffering.

There is also a reading: “bhavarūpova dissati. Its meaning is as follows: this world, bound by delusion and enveloped by delusion, perceives its self as if it were a permanent form—possessing the nature of eternalism—and appears as if it were ageless and immortal, by which...
He performs such things as the taking of life, which ought not to be done.
Bound by acquisitions, the fool is enveloped in darkness; he appears as if eternal.
This means that this world of blind fools is not only bound by delusion, but is also bound by acquisitions and enveloped by the gloom of ignorance. This...

This is what is meant: because of the absence of that knowledge by which one would see sensual pleasures and the aggregates unerringly as "impermanent, suffering, and subject to change," the foolish worldling—being shrouded and enveloped on all sides by the darkness of ignorance—is thus [bound] by way of these acquisitions:
the acquisition of sensual pleasures (*kāmūpadhi*), the acquisition of defilements (*kilesūpadhi*), and the acquisition of the aggregates (*khandhūpadhi*).
Bound by acquisitions (*upadhi*), precisely because of that, to one who views [the self] as possessing acquisitions, it appears as if eternal, permanent, and existing at all times.
There is also a reading: “It appears as if non-eternal. Its meaning is as follows:

the world’s notion that “the self exists and is found at all times” is a partial misapprehension (*micchābhinivesa*) regarding those acquisitions, whereby [the self] is regarded as something other—namely, as non-eternal and impermanent.
It appears as if [something were there]; the meaning is that it manifests. The letter *ra* serves to connect the words.

"For one who sees, there is nothing" means that for one who, having discerned the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), contemplates them through insight (*vipassanā*) by way of impermanence and so forth—specifically for one who thus sees, knows, and penetrates reality as it is with the wisdom of the path (*magga-paññā*) accompanied by the wisdom of insight—there is no "something" (*kiñcana*) such as lust and the like, by which [one would be bound].
He would be bound in *saṃsāra*. For the intention is that one who does not see thus would indeed be bound in *saṃsāra* by the fetters of ignorance, craving, views, and so forth.
The commentary on the tenth sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Cūḷavagga is completed.
8. The Chapter on the Residents of Pāṭaligāma. 1. Commentary on the First Discourse Connected with Nibbāna.

71. In the first [sutta] of the Pāṭaligāmiya-vagga, "connected with Nibbāna" means by way of proclaiming the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu), which is based upon the deathless element (amata-dhātu).
"With a discourse on the Dhamma" means with a teaching of the Dhamma. "He instructs" means he shows Nibbāna according to its essential nature, intrinsic character, and defining mark.
"He exhorts" means he causes those bhikkhus to grasp that very same meaning. "He inspires" means...

It "incites" (tejeti) and "illuminates" (joteti) by generating enthusiasm for the grasping of that goal. It "gladdens" (sampahaṃseti) by thoroughly satisfying [the mind] in every way with the qualities of Nibbāna.
Alternatively, it "shows" (sandasseti) [Nibbāna] as: "That is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving..."
By such methods as "dispassion is cessation," and so forth, he correctly demonstrates it in every way and by various means, in accordance with the respective inclinations of those individuals.

"He encourages" means that, by saying "this noble path must be realized," he causes the monks to incline toward, lean toward, and tend toward that state, and thus he correctly leads them and causes them to take it up. "He inspires" means...

"This is difficult to do, difficult to accomplish"—by saying this, he encourages [the practitioner] toward the attainment of Nibbāna, thinking: "Do not fall into negligence or reach a premature end in the practice of right conduct;
for one who possesses the necessary support and is endowed with energy, this is not difficult.
Therefore, exert yourselves, strive, and endeavor in the path of purification beginning with the purification of virtue. Or else, he directs the mind toward that [Nibbāna].

He causes them to drink. "He gladdens" means that by demonstrating the benefits of Nibbāna through many methods—such as "the crushing of intoxication, the removal of thirst, the uprooting of attachment," and "the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion;
the unconditioned, the deathless, the peaceful," and so forth—he satisfies, makes laugh, gladdens, and consoles the minds of those bhikkhus.
*Tedhā* means "here. *Aṭṭhiṃ katvā* means having observed thus: "There is something to be attained that is our purpose," and so being desirous of that teaching.
*Manasi katvā* means having placed it in the mind; having made that teaching one's own mental concern, not directed elsewhere.
*Sabbaṃ cetaso samannāharitvā* means with the entire performing-consciousness.
The meaning is: having brought to mind the teaching from the beginning until the end, one directs one's attention precisely toward it.
Alternatively, "having fully attended to it with the whole mind" means having properly and sequentially brought the teaching back from every aspect of the consciousness.
This is what is meant: whatever states of consciousness were employed by the Teacher while delivering the discourse, [one attends] to the activity occurring within all such consciousness.

Not allowing the teaching to go outside [of himself], having properly and without error brought it back step by step, and having brought it back into his own mental continuum, he thoroughly reflects upon the teaching exactly as it was taught.
"With ear attentive" (*ohitasota*) means with the ear directed inward; that is, with the ear well-fixed.
Alternatively, "with ear attentive" means with the ear undistracted; for even while perceiving that very [teaching] in the act of hearing, [he remains focused].
Non-distraction, like the restraint of mindfulness, is applicable to the ear-faculty as it is to the eye-faculty and the others.
And here, by means of all four phrases beginning with "making it a bone," he demonstrates attentive listening through the manifestation of reverence in those monks' hearing,
owing to their state of being intent upon that.
"Having understood this matter": having understood in every way that those bhikkhus had shown respect by listening to that discourse on the Dhamma connected with Nibbāna.
"This inspired utterance": he uttered this *udāna* which, by way of teaching the Dhamma that is opposed to it, reveals the existence of Nibbāna in the ultimate sense.

In this context, "exists" (*atthi*) means that it is found; the meaning is that it is apprehended from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*). "O monks" (*bhikkhave*) is an address to those monks.

Now, is it not the case that what is called an *udāna* is an utterance arising from rapture and joy, or arising from a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) regarding the Dhamma, independent of any recipient of the teaching?
And it is indeed so presented in these many suttas. Here, however—
Why did the Blessed One, while uttering an inspired exclamation (*udāna*), address those bhikkhus? It was for the purpose of instructing them.

For after the Blessed One had taught those bhikkhus the Dhamma connected with Nibbāna, he uttered the inspired exclamation because of the joy and gladness arisen through recollecting the qualities of Nibbāna.
Herein, every phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*), with the exception of Nibbāna, is found to exist solely in dependence upon conditions.

It is not independent of conditions. However, knowing the reflection in the minds of those bhikkhus as to what kind of condition this Dhamma of Nibbāna is found upon, and wishing to inform them, he said, "Bhikkhus, there is that base," and so forth;
it should be understood that he did not do so by making them exclusively the recipients [of his teaching]. "That base" (tadāyatana) means that cause. The letter *da*...

It is a junction of bases (*padasaṇḍhikara*). For Nibbāna is called a "base" (*āyatana*) in the sense of being a cause, because—by virtue of its state as an object-condition for the knowledge of the path, the fruits, and so forth—it serves as an object-condition for them, just as visible forms and the like serve as object-conditions for eye-consciousness and the rest.
By this much, the Blessed One made known to those bhikkhus that the unconditioned element exists in the ultimate sense.

In this regard, the logical sequence of the Dhamma (*dhammanvaya*) is as follows: since conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhatadhamma*) exist here, there must also be an unconditioned element (*asaṅkhatā dhātu*), because it is the opposite of those phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
For just as when suffering exists, its opposite, happiness, also exists; and just as when heat exists, cold also exists; so too, when evil states of mind exist...
Those of virtuous nature also certainly exist. And this has been said:
"Just as when suffering exists, that which is called happiness also exists;
so too, while existence (bhava) exists, non-existence (vibhava) is also to be desired."
“Just as when heat exists, something cool also exists;
so too, while the threefold fire exists, Nibbāna is to be sought.
Just as when evil exists, the wholesome also exists;”
"In the same way, while birth exists, non-birth too must be admitted," and so forth.
Furthermore, the investigation into the existence of Nibbāna in the ultimate sense will be revealed later.
Thus, having directly demonstrated the existence of the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) in the ultimate sense, the Blessed One now...
In order to show its intrinsic nature by way of excluding properties incompatible with it, he said, "Where there is neither earth nor water," and so forth.

In that regard, because Nibbāna has an intrinsic nature entirely devoid of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), just as it does not exist anywhere among conditioned things, likewise all conditioned phenomena do not exist there either. For there is no coexistence of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.
It is possible. Herein, this is the exposition of the meaning:

in that Nibbāna, in that unconditioned element, there is neither the earth element characterized by hardness, nor the water element characterized by cohesion, nor the fire element characterized by heat, nor the air element characterized by distension. Thus, by the statement regarding the absence of the four great elements—

Just as the absence of all derived matter (*upādārūpa*) is stated [in that context] because it depends upon that [great primary matter], so too the absence of the existence of sense-sphere and fine-material realms (*kāmarūpabhava*) is stated there in its entirety,

because their mode of existence is dependent upon it. For neither the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*) nor the one-aggregate existence (*ekavokārabhava*) is possible without dependence on the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Now, even though Nibbāna has the nature of the formless (*arūpa-sabhāva*), in order to show the absence therein of those phenomena included within the formless existence (*arūpa-bhava*), it is said:
"Not the base of infinite space... pe... not the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

In this context, "not the base of infinite space" refers to the arising of consciousness belonging to the base of infinite space—of three kinds, distinguished as wholesome, resultant, and functional—along with its object.

The meaning is "there is not. The same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. And to the extent that there is an absence of the sense-sphere world and so forth in Nibbāna, to that same extent there is also an absence of this world and the other world therein; thus he said: "This world does not exist, nor does the other world.

Its meaning is as follows: that world consisting of the aggregates and so forth, which receives the conventional designation "this state" (*itthatta*), "the visible dhamma" (*diṭṭhadhammo*), and "this world" (*idhaloko*).
Furthermore, that world consisting of the aggregates and so forth, which is conventionally designated as "the future life is otherwise than this," does not exist there at all.
"Neither moon nor sun" means that since darkness would exist where there is matter (*rūpa*), the moon and sun must function for the purpose of dispelling that darkness;
however, where there is no matter whatsoever in any respect...
There is no darkness there; how could there be darkness? Or rather, because the moon and sun dispel darkness, it follows that both the moon and the sun are absent there—this is the meaning.
By this, he shows that nibbāna has the very nature of light.
And to this extent, for those bhikkhus who have not yet fully realized [the truth], it is something never before experienced even in a dream throughout the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra.
While elucidating Nibbāna— which is supremely profound, exceedingly difficult to see, subtle and delicate, beyond the sphere of reasoning, absolutely peaceful, to be realized by the wise,
most refined, and deathless— he first [states], "Bhikkhus,
there is that base," thereby removing their ignorance and other defects regarding its existence, and then [continues], "where there is neither earth... nor both the moon and sun."
Then, by way of excluding other phenomena, the King of Dhamma clarifies that [Nibbāna].

By this, it is shown that Nibbāna is the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) whose intrinsic nature is devoid of all conditioned phenomena such as earth and so forth. For this very reason, he said:
"In that regard, monks, I do not speak of coming."
In that context, "there" (*tatra*) means "in that. The word "also" (*api*) is used in the sense of conjunction.

"Monks, I do not say that there is any coming from anywhere for anyone regarding the occurrence of formations (*saṅkhāra-pavatta*), because there, only a mere phenomenon (*dhamma-matta*) arises according to its conditions.
Likewise, I do not say that there is any coming or arrival from anywhere even to that sphere (*āyatana*), namely Nibbāna, because it is a state where nothing can arrive."
"Because of non-existence. I do not say there is "going," that is, movement to anywhere, because of the non-existence of a place to be gone to.
For in that [sphere], apart from making it an object by means of knowledge, neither coming nor going is possible for beings, nor do I say there is staying, death, or rebirth.
There is also a textual reading: "tadāpahaṃ. Its meaning is: that sphere, too, like going from one village to another village...
There is no coming because there is nothing to be come to; no going because there is nothing to be gone to;

no persistence because, like the earth or mountains, there is no fixed location, or rather, because of the absence of conditions, there is no arising; and because of that, due to its nature as the Deathless, there is no passing away.
Since there is neither arising nor cessation, and since there is no persistence delimited by those two, I say there is no persistence, no falling away, and no rebirth.
But because it has no material nature and is without conditions, that [Nibbāna] is not established anywhere; thus it is "unsupported" (*appatiṭṭha*).
Because there is no occurrence therein and because it is the opposite of occurrence, it is "non-occurrence" (*appavatta*).

And even though it has no material nature, because—unlike feeling and the other aggregates—it does not take any object as its support and is independent of a prop, it is simply "without an object" (*anārammaṇa*).

That which is called "the base" (*āyatana*) is Nibbāna. Furthermore, this word *eva* (indeed) should also be construed with the two phrases "without foundation" (*appatiṭṭha*) and "without occurrence" (*appavatta*). "This indeed is the end of suffering":
that Nibbāna, characterized as previously described and praised with such expressions as "without foundation," is precisely the end of the entire suffering of saṃsāra.

The "end" (*anto*) refers to the conclusion; for when that [Nirvana] is attained, there is an absence of all suffering. Therefore, he shows that "the end of suffering" is its very intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
The commentary on the first sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second Discourse Connected with Nibbāna. 72.
Regarding the second [discourse]: "He uttered this udāna"—he uttered this udāna to illustrate how Nibbāna is difficult to see because of its profound nature as the fundamental essence.
Therein, "difficult to see" means that it is so due to the profundity of its intrinsic nature and because its essential character is exceedingly subtle and refined.
It is "difficult to see" because it cannot be seen by those who have not accumulated the equipment of knowledge. For this has been said:
"Māgandiya, you do not possess that noble eye of wisdom by which you might know health or see Nibbāna.
And it has also been said: "This state, namely, the stilling of all formations, is difficult to see," and so forth.

“*Nata*” means craving (*taṇhā*), so called because it bends toward objects such as forms and toward states of existence such as sensual pleasures, proceeding with a tendency toward them, and because sentient beings bend toward those things.
“*Anata*” means that which has no such bending; the meaning is Nibbāna.
Some also read it as “*ananta*,” meaning devoid of limits because its intrinsic nature is eternal, and characterized by non-decay, cessation.
The meaning is "the deathless" (*amata*). Some, however, state that the word "endless" (*ananta*) has the meaning "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*).

And here, by the term "hard to see" (*duddasa*), he shows that Nibbāna is to be attained with difficulty, because for beings who have long cultivated the defilements such as lust—which weaken wisdom—it is not easy to cultivate the conditionless state. For truth is not...
By the word *sudassanaṃ* (“beautiful to see”), he makes this same meaning clear. In this context, *saccaṃ* (truth) refers to Nibbāna.
For it is truth in the sense of being non-erroneous, because it is exclusively peaceful (*santa*) due to the absence of any state of non-existence by any means whatsoever.

Indeed, it is not “not beautiful to see” (*na sudassanaṃ*), nor is it something that cannot be seen with ease; for even those who have been accumulating the requisites of merit and knowledge for a very long time [can see it].
Because it must be attained with great difficulty. For thus it was said by the Blessed One: "It has been attained by me with hardship.

And that Truth of Cessation, by one who penetrates it through the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of actualization—knowing and seeing that for one who knows and sees there is no "anything" (*kiñcana*)—is [realized] by way of the penetration of the object, the function, and the focal point, through both the penetration of the focal point and the penetration of non-delusion.
And when the truth of suffering has been penetrated by way of the clear realization of full understanding,
and the truth of the path has been penetrated without delusion by way of the clear realization of development,

then craving is likewise penetrated without delusion by way of the clear realization of abandonment. And thus, for one who knows the four truths as they really are through the wisdom of the Noble Path—

When he saw that craving had become exhausted regarding existence and so forth, there was no [craving] left; in its absence, there is the non-existence of the entire cycle of defilements (kilesavaṭṭa), and from that very fact, the cycles of karma and its result (kammavipākavaṭṭa) simply cannot occur.

In this way, the Blessed One revealed to those bhikkhus the majesty of the Great Nibbāna—the Deathless—which is the cause for the complete subsiding of the suffering of the cycles. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the second sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the third sutta connected with Nibbāna: 73.
In the third [sutta], "Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter..."—at that time, it is said, the Blessed One had [already] explained it in many ways.

When the Blessed One had revealed the danger of saṃsāra and delivered a teaching on the Dhamma connected with Nibbāna by way of pointing it out and so forth, this thought occurred to those bhikkhus: "This saṃsāra has been explained by the Blessed One as having causes, such as ignorance and the rest;
but regarding Nibbāna, its pacification, no cause whatsoever has been stated—it would thus be without a cause."

"How is it apprehended in the sense of ultimate reality as a directly perceived fact? Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter—namely, that reflection expressed by those bhikkhus—uttered this inspired exclamation (*udāna*) for the purpose of dispelling the doubts of those bhikkhus:
"In this world, among recluses and brahmins, 'Nibbāna, Nibbāna' is a mere verbal designation; for in the ultimate sense, there is no..."

And for the purpose of shattering the false doctrines of those who have gone astray— such as the Lokāyatikas— and of the various external sectarians who hold divergent views by declaring that Nibbāna exists in the ultimate sense,

he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which demonstrates the actual existence of the great, deathless Nibbāna, [stating]: "Nibbāna is so called because its intrinsic nature is not to be apprehended."
In this context, "unborn" (*ajāta*), "unbecome" (*abhūta*), "unmade" (*akata*), and "unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*) are all mutually synonymous terms.
Alternatively, it is "unborn" because, unlike feeling and the other aggregates, it is not born or produced by the assemblage of causes known as the concurrence of causes and conditions;
it is "unbecome" because, being without a cause, it has not itself come into being, has not manifested, and has not arisen.
Thus, because it is unarisen and non-existent, it is "unmade" (*akata*) in that it is not produced by any cause whatsoever.

Furthermore, the nature of being arisen, become, and made belongs to conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*), such as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), but not to the unconditioned nature of Nibbāna; it is for the purpose of showing this that it is called "unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*).
Alternatively, from the reverse perspective, that which is "made" (*saṅkhata*) by conditions coming together and combining is called "conditioned."
Likewise, it is "unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*) because it is not conditioned, being devoid of the characteristics of the conditioned.

Thus, when the state of having been produced by multiple causes has been refuted, the term "unmade" (*akata*) is stated to show that it is not made by even a single cause, thereby removing the suspicion that "could it perhaps be made by one cause alone?
In this way, although it is likewise without conditions, [the text continues: "of its own accord..."
Because of the apprehension, "Is this truly manifest?", the word "unbecome" (*abhūta*) was stated in order to dispel that doubt.
To show that "this unbecome nature of its being unconditioned is due to its being entirely and in every way subject to non-arising," the word "unborn" (*ajāta*) was stated.
Having thus understood the meaningfulness of these four terms, [the Buddha said]: "Monks, this Nibbāna exists."
It should be understood that the actual existence of Nibbāna has been demonstrated in its ultimate sense (*paramatthato*).
Here, the reason why the Blessed One addressed [the monks] with “O monks” while uttering this *udāna* should be understood according to the method already stated below.
Thus, having said, “O monks, there is the unborn, the unbecome, the unmade, the unconditioned,” the Teacher [proceeded to state] the reason for that.
Demonstrating this, he said, "If this were not so, monks," and so forth. This is the summary of its meaning:

Monks, if the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu), whose intrinsic nature is unborn and so on, did not exist, then here in this world, the escape from—the complete pacification of—the conditioned, which is comprised of the five aggregates such as form whose intrinsic nature is born and so on, would not be discerned, would not be found, and would not be possible.
For the noble path factors, such as right view and the rest, when they proceed taking Nibbāna as their object, utterly eradicate all defilements.
Therefore, herein the non-occurrence and departure of the entire suffering of the round is recognized as the escape.
Having thus shown the existence of Nibbāna by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), [the author] now shows it by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) as well:

“But because,” and so forth, has been stated. That has the same meaning as what was said before. And here, because it has been said: “Monks, there are unconditioned phenomena, unconstructed phenomena; there exists, monks, that sphere wherein there is neither earth... This too is a state difficult to see, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. And I say, monks, that this unconditioned is to be realized by the mind. Thus it is said. Therefore, it is established that the unconditioned exists. Because of this, it is said: “But because... and so forth. Here, “but because” means: because of the reason that the Blessed One has taught the existence of the unconditioned, therefore the unconditioned exists. It is not that the unconditioned does not exist simply because it cannot be apprehended by the eye or other sense faculties. Why? Because the Blessed One has taught its existence. How? By means of numerous sūtra passages such as, "I shall teach the Dhamma and the practice leading to the unconditioned," and also by this sūtra,

"There is, bhikkhus, that which is unborn," the existence of the element of Nibbāna from the perspective of ultimate reality was taught by the Fully Enlightened One out of compassion for the entire world;
therefore, even for those wise people who have not yet realized it for themselves therein—

There is indeed no doubt or perplexity. However, for those individuals whose intellects are dependent on others, this investigation through reasoning by way of determining the underlying intention is provided here for the purpose of dispelling their uncertainty:

just as escape (*nissaraṇa*)—which is the opposite of sensual desires and material forms, etc., being of a nature contrary to them—is understood as that which is superior to what is to be fully known (*pariññeyya*), so too...
There must be an escape characterized by a nature opposed to—that is, incompatible with—the nature of all conditioned phenomena.
And that which is this escape is the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*).

Furthermore, even insight-knowledge whose object is conditioned phenomena, such as conformity-knowledge (*anuloma-ñāṇa*), is not able to abandon defilements by way of their total eradication. Likewise...
Knowledge of the first jhāna and so forth, which has conventional truth as its object, abandons defilements only by way of suppression,

not by way of eradication. Thus, because knowledge that has conditioned phenomena as its object and knowledge that has conventional truth as its object are incapable of eradicating defilements through their total destruction,
[it is contrasted with] the noble path-knowledge which effects such eradication.
The object must have a nature that is the opposite of both of those; it is the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*).

Likewise, the statement, "Bhikkhus, there is that which is unborn, unbecome, unmade, and unconditioned," is a word that indicates the ultimate existence of the term *nibbāna* from the perspective of the highest truth (*paramattha*), because it was spoken by the Blessed One with an unerring meaning. For whatever has been spoken by the Blessed One possesses an unerring meaning.
Just as the ultimate truth (paramattha) is expressed as "All conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā) are impermanent, all conditioned phenomena are suffering,

all phenomena (dhammā) are non-self," so too the word *nibbāna* refers in some instances to the object that is the ultimate truth as it actually is, because it exists there as a mere metaphorical designation, just like the word "lion. Alternatively,
the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) does indeed exist in the ultimate sense, because its intrinsic nature (sabhāva) is free from the opposites of those [conditioned] things.
"Just as the earth element is feeling"— through such methods of reasoning,
one should understand that the unconditioned element exists in the ultimate sense.
The commentary on the third sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discourse Connected with the Fourth Nibbāna (Catutthanibbānapaṭisaṃyuttasutta-vaṇṇanā). 74.
Regarding the fourth [discourse], "Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter":
at that time, it is said, when the Blessed One had delivered a teaching connected with Nibbāna by means of many methods such as instruction and so forth, this thought occurred to those bhikkhus.
—“First, the Blessed One has revealed an extraordinary majesty by showing the manifold aspects and benefits of the great element of the Deathless Nibbāna, which is not shared by others;
yet the means for its attainment has not been spoken of. How, then, should we practice so that this may be attained?
Then the Blessed One [perceived] this reflection, known as their aforementioned deliberation, of those bhikkhus.

"Having understood the goal in all its aspects"— he uttered this *udāna* to clarify the attainment of Nibbāna through the complete abandonment of craving by means of the Noble Path, for one who is independent of anything whatsoever due to the subsiding of craving, whose body and mind are tranquil, and whose insight has entered the right course.

In that context, "the wavering of one who is dependent" means that for one who is dependent on formations such as form through craving and views, there is a wavering consisting of the fluctuation of craving and views, thinking:

"This is mine; this is my self. For a person whose craving and views have not been abandoned, when pleasure and so forth arise, being unable to dwell having overcome them, [there arises the thought]: "This is my feeling; I feel," and so on.
The meaning is that there is a wavering or shaking—meaning a faltering—of the mental continuum from its engagement in the wholesome due to the grip of craving and views.
However, for one who is independent, there is no wavering;
that is, for one who has entered the path of purification, having suppressed craving and views through serenity and insight, and is comprehending formations as impermanent and so forth.
He dwells; for him who is thus independent, there is no such wavering, stumbling, or vacillation, because the cause has been thoroughly suppressed.
"When wavering is absent" means that when the aforementioned wavering is absent, craving and the grasping of views do not arise, just as [they do not arise] in one who is independent.
For one who strives by means of insight that has entered the path, there is "tranquility" (passaddhi).
This tranquility is twofold, serving to pacify the defilements that cause agitation in both body and mind which are co-nascent with the mind of insight.
When there is this tranquility, there is no "bias" (nati); for when there is tranquility characterized by successive excellence, there is an establishment in blameless happiness.
Having increased concentration and, by means of bringing it together with wisdom, having yoked serenity and insight in union,
for one who exhausts the defilements through the succession of the paths, craving— which has received the name "bending" (natī) because it bends toward sense-desire existence and so forth—
is no longer present without remainder at the moment of the path of Arahantship; the meaning is that it does not arise again, because it has been brought to a state of non-arising.

"Because of the absence of inclination (*nati*)," means that because craving has been thoroughly abandoned by the path of Arahatship, there is no obsession consisting of attachment to a basis for the sake of existence and so forth.

"There is no coming or going" means that there is no coming here by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), nor is there any going from here to the next world by way of death—the state of having passed away—does not occur or take place.
"Because of the absence of coming and going," according to the method already stated...
When there is no coming and going, there is no passing away and rebirth; that is, the successive process of death and arising does not exist and does not proceed.
For when the cycle of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*) is absent, the cycle of kamma (*kammavaṭṭa*) is indeed cut off;

and when that is cut off, how could there be the occurrence of the cycle of result (*vipākavaṭṭa*)? Therefore he said: "When there is no passing away and rebirth, there is neither here nor beyond," and so forth.
Regarding that, whatever needs to be said has already been explained in detail below in the Bāhiya Sutta. Therefore, the meaning should be understood according to the method stated therein.

Thus, here too, the Blessed One reveals to those bhikkhus the power of the great Nibbāna—the Deathless—which is the cause for the complete subsiding of the suffering of saṃsāra through right practice.
The commentary on the fourth sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Cunda Sutta 75.

Regarding the fifth [sutta], "In the Mallas": this refers to the district (janapada) of that name. "With a great community of bhikkhus" means with one that is great both in terms of the greatness of its qualities and the greatness of its numbers.
For that community of bhikkhus was great there even by virtue of its excellence in qualities such as moral discipline (*sīla*), for it included even the very last member [of the Buddha's lineage].
It is "great" (mahā) both because of its numerical magnitude and because it is beyond counting, owing to the state of being stream-enterers.
Indeed, from the moment the life-force was relinquished, the monks who arrived one after another did not depart. "Cunda's" refers to one of that name.
"The smith’s son" means the son of a goldsmith. It is said that he was a wealthy man with a large household, and upon his very first sight of the Blessed One, he became a stream-enterer.

Having offered [the land] and having constructed in his own mango grove a fragrant cell (gandhakuṭi) suitable for the Teacher’s residence, as well as night-quarters, day-quarters, a hall for attendance, huts, pavilions, walkways, and so forth for the community of monks, he built a monastery surrounded by a wall and provided with gate-towers, and dedicated it to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
With reference to that, it is said: “There, indeed, the Blessed One was dwelling at Pāvā.”
“...in the mango grove of Cunda the smith’s son.
Regarding the word *paṭiyādāpetvā*, it means having prepared or accomplished. In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* (Great Commentary), it is stated:
“*Sūkaramaddava* is the soft, tender, and succulent meat of a boar that has recently died. However, some say: “*Sūkaramaddava* is not boar meat; it is a bamboo shoot crushed by boars.”
Some say this. Others say it is "ahichattaka" grown in a place trampled by pigs. Still others said, "Sūkaramaddava is a certain elixir.

For Cunda the smith, having heard that "Today the Blessed One will attain final Nibbāna," gave it out of a desire for the Teacher's long life, thinking, "Perhaps by consuming it, he might remain for a little longer. Thus they say.
"Serve me with that" means "feed me with that. Why did the Blessed One speak thus? Out of compassion for others (*parānuddayatā*).
And that reason has indeed been stated in the Pāḷi itself. It is shown that it was appropriate to speak in such a way because the alms-food brought by him was not fit to be consumed by others.
Regarding that *sūkaramaddava*, in the [world-system] surrounded by two thousand islands...
The deities of the four great continents infused it with vital essence (*oja*). Therefore, no one else is able to digest it properly;

demonstrating this fact, the Teacher uttered a lion’s roar for the sake of being released from the accusations of others, beginning with the words: “Cunda, I do not see anyone... for those whom others might accuse, saying:
‘He did not give the remains of what he himself had eaten to the monks... [and so forth].
“He did not give it to other people; having had it buried in a pit, he destroyed it.
To prevent others from finding an opening for such criticism and to refute the slander of others, he let out a lion’s roar.
In that context, regarding the phrases beginning with “sadevake”: *sadevako* means together with the devas; *samārako* means together with Māra; *sabrahmuno* means together with Brahmā.
"Together with Brahmā" means together with recluses and brahmins (*sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī*). "The generation" (*pajā*) refers to those who have been born.

"Together with gods and humans" means together with gods and humans (*sadevamanussā*). In that world "together with its gods"... [and so on] ... "together with its gods and humans. Therein, by the term "together with its gods," the inclusion of the five classes of sense-sphere gods is intended;
by the term "together with Māra," the inclusion of the sixth class of sense-sphere gods is intended; and by the term "together with Brahmā,"...

By the inclusion of "Brahmā" starting with the Brahmakāyika deities, there is the inclusion of the Brahmās; by the expression "together with recluses and brahmins," there is the inclusion of those recluses and brahmins who are adversaries and enemies of the Dispensation, as well as those recluses and brahmins who have stilled evil and cast out evil; by the word "generation" (pajā), there is the inclusion of the world of beings;

and by the expression "with its gods and humans," there is the inclusion of conventional gods and the remaining humans. Thus, here, by three terms it is according to the world of space (okāsaloka), and by two, according to the world of generation (pajā).

It should be understood that the world of beings (*sattaloka*) is included. According to another method: by the term "together with devas" (*sadevaka*), the immaterial-sphere world (*arūpāvacaraloka*) is included;

by the term "together with Māras" (*samāraka*), the six celestial worlds of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*); by the term "together with Brahmas" (*sabrahmaka*), the material Brahma-world (*rūpī brahmaloka*);

and by the term "together with recluses and brahmins" (*sassamaṇabrāhmaṇa*), it should be understood that the human world is included along with the conventional deities (*sammutideva*) by way of the four assemblies, or else the remaining world of beings is included.
"Bhuttāvissa" means "of one who has eaten. "Khara" means harsh. "Ābādho" means a disease of a discordant nature. "Pabāḷhā" means powerful.
"Māraṇantikā" means ending in death, capable of bringing about the vicinity of death.
"Sato sampajāno adhivāsesī" means he endured it having established mindfulness and delimited it with knowledge. "Avihaññamāno" means without being disturbed by way of following after the feeling.
As if he were unaware of the phenomenon, he endured it without turning this way or that, as if unoppressed and without suffering.
For those pains had arisen for the Blessed One while he was still at Veḷuva Village;
however, through the power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), they were suppressed and did not arise again until the day of his Parinibbāna, for he entered into attainments day after day.

Because of his intention to transfer [his merit]. On that day, however, desiring to attain final Nibbāna, he entered a meditative attainment for the purpose of inspiring a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) in sentient beings, thinking:

"If even for those who possess the strength of a thousand million elephants, whose bodies are like the impact of a thunderbolt, and who have accumulated a mass of merit over immeasurable time, such sensations as these arise, how much more so for others?"
He did not attain [the meditative absorptions], and because of that, painful sensations arose. "Come, let us go" means: "Come, let us go.
"Having eaten Cunda’s meal," etc., are verses established later by the compilers of the Dhamma.
Therein, "of him who had eaten the *sūkaramaddava*" means it arose for one who had eaten; however, it was not caused by the eating itself. For if...

Had he not eaten, it would have arisen [in him] and would have been exceedingly severe; however, because he had eaten soft food, the pain was slight, and for that very reason he was able to go on foot.
By this, the purposefulness of that lion’s roar uttered by him—“For whomsoever that [food] has been consumed, it would lead to a proper digestion except in the case of a Tathāgata”—is demonstrated.
For there is no such thing as thundering out of place for the Buddhas.

Since that [food] which was consumed did not produce any alteration in the Blessed One, but rather—by suppressing through heedfulness the alteration that would have arisen had it found an opportunity through karma—it produced strength in his body, by means of which he accomplished the threefold purpose that will be explained; therefore...
It had indeed undergone that transformation; however, because the sensations were terminal, it remained unperceived and undisclosed.
"Being purged" means being in a state of frequent discharge of blood. "He spoke" means he said this for the sake of attaining final nibbāna in the place of his own choosing.
But why did the Blessed One go to Kusinārā when such an illness had arisen; was it not possible for him to attain final nibbāna elsewhere?
It was certainly not impossible to attain final nibbāna anywhere; however, he thought thus:

"When I have gone to Kusinārā, there will be the occasion for the teaching of the Mahāsudassana Sutta, and through that, [the merit] similar to what is to be experienced in the world of the devas [will arise]."
I shall teach the prosperity I experienced in the human world, adorning it with two recitations (*bhāṇavāra*);
having heard this, many people will think that wholesome deeds ought to be performed.
And as for Subhadda, where did he approach me, ask his question, and at the conclusion of the answer, establish himself in the refuges, go forth, and receive full ordination?
"While I am still living, having developed this meditation subject, he will attain Arahatship and become known as the 'Last Disciple.
Elsewhere, after my Parinibbāna, there will be a great dispute over the relics; blood will flow like a river.
But when I have attained Parinibbāna at Kusinārā, the Brahmin Doṇa will quell that conflict and [distribute] the relics."
Seeing these three reasons—namely, that [the relics] would be distributed [after his passing]—the Blessed One went to Kusinārā with great effort.
*Iṅgha* is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation (*codana*). "I am weary" means I am exhausted. By this, he demonstrates precisely the intensity of the aforementioned feelings.
For at that time, the Blessed One traveled on foot by his own power, unlike others.
But just as it was impossible even to lift up his foot, so too did the sensations become sharp, harsh, and bitter.
For this reason he said, "I shall sit down.
"Now" means at this moment. "Agitated" (luḷita) means as if crushed or confused. "Turbid" (āvila) means stirred up. "Clear water" (acchodaka) means water that is thin and serene.
“Sātodakā” means having sweet water. “Sītodakā” means having cool water. “Setodakā” means having clear (white) water. For water is white by its very nature;
it becomes otherwise through the turbidity of mud caused by the ground. Even the Kakudha River flows with clear sand strewn about, appearing white in color.
Therefore it is said, “having clear water. “Supatitthā” means having beautiful fords.
“Delightful” means it is a place to be enjoyed because of its charming terrain and its delightful nature due to the aforementioned excellence of water.
“I am weary, Cundaka, I shall lie down”—for to the Tathāgata there were [these four horses]:
Kāḷāvaka, Gaṅgeyya, Paṇḍara, and Tambapiṅgala.
"Gandha, Maṅgala, Hema, Uposatha, Chaddanta, and Meṇḍa.
When these ten elephant lineages have been mentioned, the strength of ten ordinary elephants—those known as the Kālāvaka—is equal to that of one Gaṅgeyya.
Thus, by this tenfold calculation, the strength of ordinary elephants is measured at one thousand million (one billion).
As for his physical strength, on that day from after the meal onwards, it all reached exhaustion, like water poured into a leaking jar.
Pāvā was three *gāvutas* from Kusinārā. Having sat down at twenty-five places along the way and exerted great effort, the Blessed One arrived at Kusinārā at the time of sunset.

He said, "I am weary, Cundaka, I shall lie down," speaking these words that inspire a sense of urgency in the world with its devas, demonstrating this meaning: "Disease indeed comes, crushing all health.

Regarding the "lion's posture" (*sīhaseyyā*): there are four postures—the posture of those who indulge in sensual pleasures, the posture of the hungry ghosts (*petaseyyā*), the posture of the Tathāgatas, and the lion's posture.
In this context, “Monks, for the most part those who enjoy sensual pleasures lie on their left side”—this is the reclining posture of those who enjoy sensual pleasures.
“Monks, for the most part hungry ghosts lie on their backs”—this is the reclining posture of hungry ghosts. The fourth jhāna is the reclining posture of the Tathāgata.
“Monks, Sīha, the king of beasts, lies down on his right side”—this is the lion’s reclining posture. For this—
Because it possesses the most excellent postures characterized by brilliance, it is called the "supreme reclining. Therefore it is said: "He lay down on his right side in the lion’s posture.
"Foot upon foot" means placing the left foot upon the right foot. "Accādhāya" means having placed [it] excessively;
that is, having set it down so as to exceed the ankle. For if the ankle were to touch the ankle, or the knee the knee, there would be constant friction.
When [the body] touches [the ground], painful sensations arise and the bed becomes uncomfortable.
However, when it is placed so as not to touch [the ground], sensations do not arise and the bed is comfortable. Therefore, he lay down in this manner.
The verses beginning with "Having gone, the Buddha... were placed there later by the compilers of the Dhamma. In that context, *nadikaṃ* means...
"Into the river. "Peerless in this world" means peerless here in this world with its devas.
"Having bathed and drunk, he crossed over" means that having bathed for the purpose of cooling his limbs and having drunk water, he emerged from the river.
