At that time, it is said, while the Blessed One was bathing, there were fish and turtles within the river, the water itself, and the groves of forest on both banks.
"And that entire area of ground" means it became entirely the color of gold.

"Honored" means he was honored by the world including the devas through worship and respect, due to his status as the most excellent and venerable being distinguished by his virtues. "In the midst of the company of monks" means in the middle of the Saṅgha of monks.
At that time, the monks, having perceived the extreme intensity of the Blessed One’s physical ailments, drew near and stood on all sides.
They go along surrounded [by them]. "Teacher" (*satthā*): he is a teacher because he instructs beings in the ultimate sense regarding matters pertaining to this life and the life to come.
"The Blessed One is the one who sets forth the Dhamma here": he is "Blessed" (*bhagavā*) due to his fortune and other such qualities;
here, he is the one who sets forth, or causes to proceed, the Dhamma of the teaching consisting of virtue and so on, or the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma.
“Ambavana” means a mango grove on the bank of that very river.

He addressed Cundaka because, it is said, at that moment the Venerable Ānanda was delayed while wringing out his bathing cloth, and the Elder Cundaka was nearby; therefore, the Blessed One addressed him.
“He sat down in front” means he sat before the Teacher in accordance with the requirements of formal conduct, thinking, “What does the Teacher command?”
At this point, the treasurer of the Dhamma arrived. When he had thus arrived, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Upadaheyya” means he would produce; there might be some person who is a producer of remorse.
“Alābhā” refers to those gains which are called the benefits of giving for others when they give gifts—those are the losses. “Dulladdhaṃ” means...
Even human birth, though obtained through a particular excellence of merit, is difficult to obtain. "Yassa te" means "for you. Who knows what it was?
Whether it was rice with too much husk or rice that was overcooked; having eaten whatever kind of last alms-food it may have been, the Tathāgata attained final Nibbāna.
Surely, by that [act], something or other must have been given. "Lābhā" refers to gains pertaining to both the present life and the future life.
"Gains" refers to the benefits reckoned as the fruits of giving. "Well-gotten" means that your human state has been well-attained.

"Face-to-face" (*sammukhā*) means directly before one's eyes; the meaning is not by hearsay or through tradition. "This for me" (*metan me*) means "this is mine" or "by me this. "These two" (*dve me*) means "these two.
"Equal and equal in fruit" (*samasamaphalā*) means equal in fruit in every respect.
But surely, when the Tathāgata attained full enlightenment after consuming the alms-food given by Sujātā, that was a gift given at a time when defilements had not yet been abandoned;
whereas this gift of Cunda was given at a time when the outflows were exhausted. Why, then, are these two gifts equal in their fruit?

It is because of the equality of the final *parinibbāna*, the equality of the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), and the equality of the recollection (*anussaraṇa*). For the Blessed One, [regarding] Sujātā...
Having eaten the alms-food given by Cunda, he attained final Nibbāna through the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining;

having eaten what was given by Cunda, he attained final Nibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without residue. Thus, they are equal in their fruit even by virtue of the equality of their final passing away.
Furthermore, on the day of his full enlightenment, there were two hundred and forty million meditative attainments that served as the causes for the supreme path.
On the day of his final nibbāna, he entered all of them as well. Thus, due to the equality of their attainments, they yield equal fruits.
For this was said by the Blessed One:

"For one who, having consumed this almsfood, dwells having attained the unsurpassed, immeasurable concentration of mind, immeasurable is the outflow of merit, the outflow of the wholesome," and so forth.
And at a later time, Sujātā heard: "It seems that was not a tree deity; it was indeed the Bodhisatta.
Having consumed that alms-food, he has awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. It is said that for seven weeks his sustenance was provided by that [food].
Upon hearing this, as she recollected, "What a gain for me!", a powerful surge of rapture and joy arose within her.
It arose. Later, when Cunda heard that "I have indeed given the final alms-food; I have indeed received the head of the Dhamma;

having consumed my alms-food, the Teacher has attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue, which he had long desired," he recalled, "What a gain for me! and a powerful surge of rapture and joy arose within him.
Thus it arose. In this way, it should be understood that even two gifts of alms-food, through the equality of their recollection, yield equal fruits.

"Conducive to long life" means conducive to a long lifespan. "Accumulated" means heaped up, produced. "Conducive to fame" means conducive to a retinue. "Conducive to sovereignty" means conducive to a state of excellence.
"Having understood this matter" refers to both the great fruitfulness of giving and one's own state of being a supreme recipient of offerings (*dakṣiṇeyya*) due to qualities such as virtue.
Having understood in every aspect these three meanings—namely, parinibbāna through non-clinging—he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which illuminates those meanings.

In that context, "merit increases for one who gives" means that for one giving a gift, merit consisting of giving is accumulated through both the excellence of the mind and the excellence of the recipient; and it becomes more fruitful and brings greater benefit.

Alternatively, regarding the statement "merit increases for one who gives": when one relinquishes the object of giving, through the repeated cultivation of the volition of renunciation, one gradually becomes largely free from offenses in all respects;
having thus guarded perfectly purified virtue, one is able to develop serenity and insight.
Thus, by way of giving and so forth, his threefold merit increases—this is how it should be understood here.

The meaning should be understood as follows: “From restraint” means for one who restrains himself by the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃyama*); the sense is that he stands firm in the protective barrier (*saṃvara*).

“Enmity does not accumulate” means that the fivefold enmity does not increase. Alternatively, because higher virtue (*adhisīla*) is dominated by non-hatred, one who restrains himself through body, speech, and mind and possesses perfectly purified virtue does not create enmity toward anyone due to his abundance of patience; how then could there be its accumulation?
Therefore, for one who is thus restrained, for one who is practicing restraint, or because of that restraint, no enmity accumulates. Furthermore, the skilled person abandons evil:

the "skilled person" here is one endowed with wisdom, established in perfectly purified virtue, who—having taken up a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suitable to himself among the thirty-eight objects—accomplishes jhāna, distinguished by its access and absorption stages, and thereby abandons evil.
He abandons—that is, relinquishes—the base unwholesome states such as sensual desire by way of suppression.
Taking that very jhāna as a basis, he establishes the contemplation of the destruction and fall of formations;
performing the work of insight and bringing insight to its peak, he abandons all evil, base, and unwholesome states without remainder by way of complete eradication through the Noble Path.
"Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he has attained Nibbāna"— having thus abandoned evil, through the destruction of lust and the other defilements,
he has attained Nibbāna by means of the extinction of all remaining *kilesas*, and thereafter, by the extinction of the aggregates (*khandha-nibbāna*). Thus,
based upon Cunda’s excellence as a recipient of offerings and his own excellence as one worthy of offerings, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*), released by the force of joy.
The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Pāṭaligāmiya Sutta: 76.
Regarding the sixth [sutta], "in Magadha" means in the kingdom of Magadha. "Great" (mahatā) here also refers to its greatness in virtue, as well as its being beyond measure in number.
With a great community of monks, vast in number. Pāṭaligāma is the name of a certain village in the kingdom of Magadha.
It is said that on the day that village was being founded, two or three *pāṭala* sprouts emerged from the earth at the site where the village was to be established.
Therefore, they designated it as "Pāṭaligāma. He arrived there—at that Pāṭaligāma.
He arrived [at Pāṭaligāma]. But when did the Blessed One arrive at Pāṭaligāma?

According to the method explained below, after having the shrine of the Dhammasenāpati built at Sāvatthī, departing from there and staying at Rājagaha, after having the shrine of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna built there, departing from there and staying at Ambalaṭṭhikā, he proceeded by way of a journey without haste.
Wandering on a tour through the countryside, staying for a single night here and there while bestowing favor upon the world, he eventually arrived at the village of Pāṭaligāma.
"The residents of Pāṭaligāma" refers to the lay followers (*upāsakas*) dwelling in that village; it is said that some of them had their first sight of the Blessed One.
Some were established in the refuges, some in the precepts, and some in both the refuges and the precepts; therefore, it is said, "lay followers" (*upāsaka*).

"They approached the Blessed One"—it is said that in Pāṭaligāma, people belonging to Ajātasattu and the Licchavi kings would go from time to time, escorting householders out from their homes and staying for a month or even half a month. For that reason...
The people living in Pāṭaligāma were constantly troubled [by the influx of travelers], thinking, "There must be a place for these people to stay when they arrive. Thus,
they prepared a place on one side for the goods of the lords to be stored, a place on another side for their residence, a place on another side for visiting travelers,
a place on another side for poor and destitute people, and a place on another side for the sick to stay.
Thinking, "It shall be so," they had a great mansion built in the center of the city, large enough for all of them to live together without crowding one another; its name was Āvasathāgāra.
On that very day, it reached completion. Having gone there, they found it perfectly finished and well-adorned through handiwork, plastering, painting, and other crafts, resembling a celestial palace.
Having surveyed it starting from the gateway tower, they thought, "This guest house is exceedingly delightful and magnificent;
by whom was it first used so that it might be for our long-term welfare and happiness?
And at that very moment, they heard that "the Blessed One has arrived in that village. Consequently, they were filled with joy and gladness.
“The Blessed One could have been brought by us even after we had gone to fetch him; however, he has arrived at our dwelling place of his own accord.
Today, having had the Blessed One dwell here, we shall first cause him to partake [of food], and likewise the Saṅgha of monks.
When the Saṅgha of monks has arrived, the Buddha-word consisting of the Three Piṭakas will surely have arrived as well. [We shall offer] a blessing to the Teacher.”
“We shall cause [the Dhamma] to be proclaimed; we shall have the Dhamma preached. Thus, after it has been utilized by the Three Jewels, there will be its utilization for both ourselves and others;
in this way, it will lead to our welfare and happiness for a long time.
Having reached this conclusion, they approached the Blessed One for that very purpose. Therefore, they spoke thus: “May he consent...”
"No, Bhante, Blessed One, it is a rest-house.

They approached the rest-house. Although it was well-adorned and well-maintained like a celestial mansion because it had been completed on that very day, it had not yet been prepared after being made worthy for the Buddha.

“Buddhas are by nature inclined toward the forest and delight in the forest; whether they dwell within a village or not, we shall make our arrangements only after ascertaining the Blessed One’s preference.

Having thought this, they approached the Blessed One. Now, desiring to make their arrangements accordingly after ascertaining the Blessed One’s preference, they went to the guest-house. [They prepared it] with a complete carpeting.
"Having spread the dwelling-house" means having spread it so that the entire area is covered.
First of all, thinking "cow dung is appropriate for all auspicious occasions," one should have the ground—even if already prepared with plaster—covered with a layer of fresh cow dung.
Once one knows it has dried, [one should arrange it] so that the footstep in the place where one steps...

It was not known [how much they had spread]. Thus, having smeared it with four kinds of perfumes, having spread various colored rugs on top of that, having made large bolsters and pillows upon them, they had the entire space covered with various colored floor coverings such as elephant-rugs and so forth, which were suitable to be spread there.
Therefore it is said: "Having spread the guest-house with everything spread."
In the center of the seating area, having prepared a magnificent Buddha-seat supported by an auspicious pillar,
and having spread upon it whatever coverings were soft and beautiful, and having placed a pleasing pillow red on both sides,
he then fastened a canopy above, variegated with stars of gold and silver.
Having adorned [the area] with garlands of perfumes, flower wreaths, and the like, and having had a lattice-work of flowers constructed within a space twelve cubits on all sides,
he had the area measuring thirty cubits surrounded by a curtain of cloth; then, leaning against the western wall, he arranged for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus seats,
backrests, couches, stools, and so forth, and had them covered above with white spreads.
They had the eastern side of the hall prepared for his own seating; it is with reference to this that it is said, "having prepared seats.

"A water-jar" (*udakamaṇika*) means a large-mouthed water-vessel. Thus, so that the Blessed One and the community of monks might wash their hands and feet and rinse their mouths as they pleased, [water] the color of a jewel was placed in those various locations.
Having filled [the vessel] for the purpose of perfuming it, they added various flowers and water-perfume powders, covered it with plantain leaves, and set it down.
Thus it is said: "having set down a water-jar.
"Having lit an oil lamp" refers to lamps with handles made of silver, gold, and so forth, which were adorned with figures of warriors and graceful statues.
Having lit oil lamps in small bowls made of gold, silver, and other materials held in their hands, they approached the Blessed One.
Regarding the phrase "they approached where the Blessed One was," it should be understood that those lay followers of Pāṭaligāma did not merely prepare the rest-house;
rather, they had the streets throughout the entire village adorned, banners raised, and full water-jars placed at the doors of the houses.
Having had banana trees planted so that the entire village was strewn with rows of lamps like scattered stars, he gave this command:
"Give milk to the nursing infants; feed the young children quickly and put them to bed; do not make a loud noise.
Today the Teacher will dwell within the village for one night; indeed, Buddhas are those who desire quietude."
Having had the drum beaten, they themselves took up torches and approached the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having dressed himself and taken his bowl and robe, approached the guest-house together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
[They said: "Venerable sir, it is now time for the Blessed One to do as he deems fit. Thus, it is said, they [announced] the time.
When this had been announced, the Blessed One—having fashioned a red double-layered robe with the color of a ripe, red *koviḷāra* flower dyed with lac juice, as if cutting out a lotus with scissors;
having put it on, covering the three circles [of the body]; having girded himself with a golden waistband as if encircling a cluster of lotuses;
and having fastened a belt of lightning-like splendor over a red woolen cloth—[proceeded].
It was as if he were covering the frontal globes of an elephant; as if he were casting a net of coral over a golden pinnacle a hundred ratanas high;
as if he were donning a cloak of red woolen cloth upon a great golden cetiya; as if he were veiling the full moon in its course with a crimson cloud;
or as if he were sprinkling well-ripened lac juice upon the summit of the Golden Mountain.
As if encircling the summit of Mount Cittakūṭa with a network of lightning-garlands, and having caused the entire Cakkavāḷa, Sineru, Yugandhara,
and the great earth to tremble, he donned a fine, deep-red rag-robe (paṃsukūla) the color of a fresh *nigrodha* sprout;
like a maned lion emerging from a dense forest, or like the full moon rising from the peak of the Eastern Mountain, or like the young sun.
And as if by his own will, he emerged from the beautiful pavilion where he was seated.

Then, rays of light issued forth from his body like flashes of lightning from the mouth of a cloud, and they made the trees on all sides appear as if their branches, twigs, flowers, fruits, and leaves had been turned golden-yellow by being sprinkled with streams of liquid gold.
At that very moment, the great community of monks, each taking his own bowl and robe, [emerged].
They surrounded the Blessed One. And those monks who stood surrounding him were such as these:

few in desire, contented, secluded, unattached, energetic, speakers, patient with speech, reprovers, censurers of evil, endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, endowed with wisdom, endowed with liberation, and endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Surrounded by them, the Blessed One shone like a mass of gold encircled by red woolen cloth,
like the full moon surrounded by the constellations, like a golden ship situated in the midst of a thicket of red lotuses,
or like a golden palace encircled by a coral railing. But the great elders, headed by Mahākassapa, wore rag-robes the color of a rain cloud.

Having clothed themselves, like great elephants clad in jeweled armor, those whose passions had vanished, whose defilements were shattered, whose matted locks were untangled, and whose bonds were severed—unattached to family or group—surrounded him.
Thus the Blessed One, himself free from passion, was surrounded by those free from passion; free from hatred, by those free from hatred; free from delusion, by those free from delusion.
Free from craving, he was surrounded by those free from craving; free from defilement, he was surrounded by those free from defilement.

The self-awakened one was surrounded by those who had awakened after him, like the filaments surrounded by the petals, like the pericarp surrounded by the filaments, like the six-tusked king of elephants surrounded by eight thousand elephants, like the swan-king Dhatarattha surrounded by ninety thousand swans, and like a general surrounded by his military divisions.
Like a wheel-turning monarch, like Sakka, king of the gods, surrounded by a host of Maruts,
like Hārita the Great Brahmā surrounded by a host of Brahmas, and like the full moon surrounded by a host of stars,
he set out upon the road toward Pāṭaligāma in the incomparable garb of a Buddha and with the immeasurable grace of a Buddha.
Then, from his front body, thick golden rays of Buddha-light arose and reached a distance of eighty cubits;
likewise, from his back, right side, and left side, thick golden rays of Buddha-light arose and reached a distance of eighty cubits;
and starting from the hair-tufts on top of his head, all the curls of his hair [emitted light].
Cloud-like Buddha-rays, the color of a peacock’s neck or a royal turban, rose up and reached eighty cubits into the sky;
from the soles of his feet, cloud-like Buddha-rays the color of coral rose up and reached eighty cubits into the solid earth;
and from his tusks, the white parts of his eyes, and the fleshless parts of his nails, cloud-like Buddha-rays of pure white arose.
Rising up, they reached a distance of eighty cubits; from the places where the red and yellow colors intermingled, rays of deep crimson rose up and reached a distance of eighty cubits;
and everywhere, radiant rays shone forth. Thus, within a space of eighty cubits all around, the six-colored rays of the Buddha blazed and quivered.

Running about and emerging from golden-handled torches, they leaped into the sky like a great mass of flames or like flashes of lightning issuing from a great cloud over the four continents, scattering in every direction. By them,
all the quarters of space were as if strewn with golden campaka flowers, like streams of liquid gold pouring from golden jars.

They shone as if being sprinkled with liquid, as if draped in outspread cloths of refined gold, as if strewn with the pollen of *kiṃsuka*, *kaṇikāra*, and *koviḷāra* flowers tossed up by the *veramba* wind,
and as if anointed with the powder of Chinese lacquer. The Blessed One, too, was radiant,
encircled by the halo of his fathom-wide aura and adorned with the eighty minor marks and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
The body was free from the defilements of clouds, mist, and the like, shining like the radiance of stars,
like the vault of the sky, like a blooming lotus grove, like a hundred-yojana *pāricchattaka* tree in full flower,
and like thirty-two suns, thirty-two moons, thirty-two universal monarchs (*cakkavattī*), and thirty-two divine kings arranged in succession.
He shone as if surpassing the glory of thirty-two Great Brahmās with his own splendor,
being adorned by the thirty pāramīs— namely, the ten pāramīs, the ten upapāramīs, and the ten paramatthapāramīs— which had been perfectly fulfilled;
and by the giving given, and the guarding maintained, for four incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand aeons.

It is like the time when a thousand ships' cargo, having been produced as if crowded together because it could find no opportunity to give its fruit within a single existence due to the wholesome karma performed through virtue, is loaded onto a single ship;
or like the time when a thousand wagons' cargo is loaded onto a single wagon; or at the confluence of the twenty-five Ganges rivers.
It was as if time itself had been gathered into a single heap.
Even as the Blessed One shone with this splendor of a Buddha, they raised up many thousands of torches before him;
likewise, behind him, on his left side, and on his right side, [they held] flowers such as jasmine, campaka, vanamālī, red lotuses, blue lotuses, bakula, and sinduvāra.
Blue, yellow, and other colored powders, along with fragrant scents, were scattered like showers of rain released from the great clouds that overspread the four continents.

The sounds of the fivefold musical instruments and the cries of praise connected with the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha filled all directions, as if they were voices issuing from the very mouths [of the beings]. [This was witnessed by] the devas, supaṇṇas, nāgas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and humans.
They obtained eyes as if they were a drink of the Deathless. Now, it is appropriate here to provide a description of the journey by means of a thousand verses.
Of these, this is merely the introduction:
“Thus, endowed with every excellence, making the earth tremble;”
Not harming living beings, the Guide of the World proceeds.
Raising his right foot first, that bull among men, endowed with glory, moves along;
the supreme among bipeds shines resplendent.
“As the Best of Buddhas walks, the soles of his feet are soft;
they touch the ground evenly, and he is not defiled by dust.
As the Leader of the World walks, the low ground rises up.”
That which was high became level, and the earth was insentient.
"Stones and pebbles, as well as potsherds, stumps, and thorns—
all paths avoided him as the Leader of the World passed by."
“He draws up his foot neither too far nor too near when setting it down;
he walks without clashing his limbs, with both knees and ankles aligned.
The Sage, whose gait is perfected, does not step forward too quickly.”
Nor does he walk slowly, as he goes with mind composed.
Neither looking up nor down, nor to the side, nor toward the cardinal or intermediate directions,
he walks looking only the distance of a yoke’s length ahead.
“With the majestic stride of a nāga, the Jina shines as he walks;
the Foremost One in the world moves with grace, bringing joy to the world including the devas.
Resplendent like the king of bulls, he moves with the beautiful gait of a lion.”
“Gladdening many beings, the Best One approached the village.

This, it is said, was called the “Time of Praise. On such occasions as these, whether regarding the physical beauty of the Blessed One’s body or the praise of his virtues, the only measure for a preacher of the Dhamma is his own strength;
he should say as much as he is able, using either prose or verse compositions.
One should not say, "He has been poorly prepared," or "He has leaped over the ford.
For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess immeasurable virtues; even the Buddhas themselves are unable to describe their virtues in their entirety.
Even if they were to praise them for an entire eon (*kappa*), they would not be able to reach the end, let alone other beings. Thus, he was adorned and arrayed with this splendor and majesty.
He entered Pāṭaligāma; having entered, the Blessed One, being honored by people with devout hearts with flowers, perfumes, incense, scents, powders, and so forth, entered the rest-house.
Therefore it was said: “Then the Blessed One, having dressed himself and taken his bowl and robe, approached the rest-house together with the community of bhikkhus.”

"Having washed his feet": although dust and dirt did not adhere to the Blessed One’s feet, the Blessed One nevertheless washed his feet out of a desire for the increase of the spiritual merit of those lay followers, and so that others might follow his example.
Furthermore, it is also for the purpose of cooling the physical body, which is subject to grasping, that the Blessed One performs such acts as bathing and washing his feet.
He indeed did so. "Placing the Blessed One at the front" means having placed the Blessed One in front.

There, the Blessed One sat in the midst of the monks and lay followers; [the image] was bathed with scented water, the excess water was wiped away with a *dukūla* cloth pillow, it was polished with vermilion, wrapped in red woolen cloth, and set upon a pedestal.
He shone exceedingly, like a solid statue of red gold.
Here, however, is the manner of the ancient eulogies:
"Having gone to the circular pavilion, he who moves with the gait of a majestic elephant..."
Illuminating the world, the Foremost One sat upon the excellent seat.
Seated there, the Charioteer of men to be tamed,
the God beyond gods, endowed with the marks of a hundred merits;
Seated in the center of the Buddha’s throne,
he shines like a golden coin upon a pale woolen cloth.
Like a coin of Jāmbūnada gold placed upon a pale woolen cloth, he glows with splendor.
He shines, free from stain, like the radiant *verocana* gem.
Like a great *sāla* tree in full bloom, like the king of mountains Meru adorned,
he resembles a golden sacrificial pillar, like a red *paduma* or *kokanada* lotus.
“Blazing like a lamp-tree, like a fire on a mountain peak,
he shines forth, fully blossomed like the Pāricchattaka tree of the devas.
He addressed the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma because among those lay followers, many people were firmly established in the precepts.

Therefore, having first explained the danger of failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*), he addressed the householders with the words, "These five, householders," and so forth, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma in order to show the benefits of perfection in virtue (*sīlasampadā*).

In this context, "immoral" (*dussīla*) means devoid of virtue. "One who has failed in virtue" (*sīlavipanna*) means one whose virtue has degenerated and whose restraint (*saṃvara*) is broken. And here, "immoral" refers to...
By the word *pada*, the absence of virtue in a person is stated. That absence of virtue is twofold: either through non-undertaking, or through the breaking of what has been undertaken.
Of these two, the former is not as blameworthy as the latter, which is more blameworthy.

In order to show, by means of a teaching addressed to a person, that absence of virtue which serves as the cause for the intended disadvantage, it is said, "one who has failed in virtue. By this, [the term] "immoral" (*dussīla*)...
It shows the meaning of the word. "On account of negligence" means by reason of negligence. And this sutta is presented with reference to householders;
however, it certainly applies to those who have gone forth as well.
For when a householder maintains his livelihood by whatever craft—whether by agriculture, trade, or cattle-herding—if he becomes negligent through such acts as the taking of life, then [he falls].
If one is unable to accomplish that at the proper time, then one’s work perishes.
Furthermore, by committing acts such as the taking of life during the festival season, one suffers a great loss of wealth due to punishment.
A monk who is immoral, through negligence, suffers loss of virtue, loss of the Buddha’s word, loss of meditative absorption, and loss of the seven treasures of the noble ones.

“An evil reputation”: for a householder, an evil reputation spreads abroad in the midst of the assembly, saying, “Such-and-such a person, born into such-and-such a family, is immoral and of evil character;
having abandoned both this world and the next, he does not give even a share of food from his ration. For one who has gone forth, [an evil reputation spreads]:
“The elder named so-and-so, having gone forth in the Teacher’s dispensation, was unable to guard his moral precepts, nor did he [master] the Buddha’s word...”
"Because he seeks to be taken hold of, lives by means of medical practice and the like, and is possessed of the six kinds of lack of respect"—thus an evil reputation spreads abroad.

As for "lacking confidence": first of all, a householder, when approaching a place where many people have gathered, necessarily approaches with fear, thinking, "Someone might find out about my business;
then they will criticize me, or perhaps report it to the royal court," and he does so feeling abashed.
With shoulders drooping and face cast down, he sits; having become diffident, he is unable to speak.

Even when ordained, when a great assembly of monks has gathered, he approaches full of fear, thinking, "Surely someone will find out about my deed, and then they will suspend both my Uposatha and Pavāraṇa ceremonies, deprive me of the status of a recluse, and cast me out"—he does not approach with confidence.
Having offered the sacrifice, he is unable to speak. Furthermore, some person, though being immoral, conducts himself as if he were virtuous;
yet even he is indeed dejected in his underlying disposition.
"He dies deluded" means that for the immoral person lying upon the deathbed, the deeds of immorality that he has undertaken—
The places where [the results of his deeds] have been set in motion come into the range of his vision. Opening his eyes, he sees this world;
closing his eyes, he sees the other world. The four states of misery appear before him according to his karma;
it is as if he were being struck by a hundred spears, and as if he were being consumed by the impact of a mass of flames. Crying out, "Save me! Save me! he...
He dies. Therefore it is said: "he passes away bewildered.
"With the breakup of the body" means the relinquishing of the aggregates that have been grasped. "After death" means the taking up of the newly produced aggregates immediately thereafter.
Alternatively, "with the breakup of the body" means the cutting off of the life-faculty. "After death" means subsequent to the moment of death (cuti).
"Apāya," and so forth, are all synonyms for "niraya. Indeed, it is called *niraya* because it is devoid (*apeta*) of "merit" (*aya*), which is reckoned as the cause for heaven and liberation;
or else, because there is no arrival (*āgama*) of "bliss" (*sukha*) or of "gain" (*aya*). It is called *duggati* because it is a destination (*gati*) or refuge for suffering (*dukkha*);
or else, because it is a destination produced by defiled (*duṭṭha*) karma due to an abundance of hatred (*dosa*). They fall down helpless (*vivasā*).
In this context, "the place for those who have done evil" refers to the *vinipāta*. It is called *vinipāta* because those who are perishing fall into it with their limbs and members shattered.
It is called *niraya* because there is no substance (*āya*) here that is perceived as a gratification (*assāda*).

Alternatively, by the mention of the "woeful states" (*apāya*), he indicates the animal realm (*tiracchānayoni*); for the animal realm is a woeful state because it is departed from the happy destinies (*sugati*).

There is no miserable destination (*duggati*) for those of great influence, such as the *nāga* kings and others, because such a state does not occur for them. By the mention of "miserable destination," the sphere of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*) is indicated;
for that is both a state of deprivation (*apāya*) and a miserable destination, because it is departed from the happy destinations (*sugati*) and because it is a realm of suffering.

However, it is not a "fall" (*vinipāta*), because [the *nāgas*] do not fall [into such a state] like the asuras, and because even among the hungry ghosts there exist those with great psychic power (*mahiddhika*). By the mention of "fall,"...

It illuminates the host of asuras. For in the sense already described, it is called an "apāya" (a state of loss), a "duggati" (an unhappy destination), and a "vinipāta" (a fallen state) because one has fallen away from all heights of excellence.
By the mention of "niraya" (hell), it specifically illuminates the many varieties of hell, such as Avīci and others.
"Upapajjati" means to be reborn or produced.
The discourse on the benefits should be understood by reversing what has been said above. However, this is the distinction: "Virtuous" (*sīlavā*) means virtuous by way of undertaking the precepts.
"Endowed with virtue" (*sīlasampanna*) means endowed with virtue by having undertaken the precepts in a manner that is both purified and complete.

"Mass of wealth" (*bhogakkhandha*) means a heap of wealth. Regarding "a happy destination, a heavenly world" (*sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ*): here, by the inclusion of the term "happy destination," the human destination is also included.

It is included; by the inclusion of "heaven" (*sagga*), only the celestial realm (*devagati*) is meant. Therein, a beautiful destination is a "good destination" (*sugati*); it is called "heaven" (*sagga*) because it is an excellent (*su-agga*) state through its objects such as forms and so forth.
All of that is also called "the world" (*loka*) in the sense of crumbling and falling away.
[The phrase] "for much of the night with a discourse on the Dhamma" refers to a discourse on the Dhamma other than those found in the canonical texts (*pāḷimutta*).
And also by means of the discourse on the approval of the guest-house.

For at that time, as Ajātasattu was having the city of Pāṭaliputta built there, he would summon from other villages, market towns, districts, and royal capitals those householders endowed with virtue and good conduct;
having brought them there, he provided them with wealth, grain, houses, sites for dwellings, fields, and so forth, as well as tax exemptions, and settled them there.
Therefore, because the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma were especially devoted to virtue due to their vision of its benefits,
and because virtue is the foundation for all qualities, [the Blessed One] first explained the benefits of virtue to them;
thereafter, as if pouring down the celestial Ganges, as if drawing up the essence of the earth, or as if grasping a great rose-apple tree by its top and shaking it, he spoke.

Just as one who, having crushed a yojana-long root of *madhuka* with a press, drinks its sweet juice, he spoke a miscellaneous discourse bringing welfare and happiness to the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma, saying:
"Householders, this gift of a dwelling place brings great merit; your dwelling has been used by me and has also been used by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. By me...
Furthermore, when it is used by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, it is indeed as if the Jewel of the Dhamma itself has been used.
Thus, when that which is used by the Three Jewels is enjoyed, the result is immeasurable. Moreover, when a dwelling place is given, every kind of gift is effectively given;
this includes a leaf-hut built on the ground or a pavilion made of branches, constructed for the sake of the Saṅgha.
"The benefit cannot be delimited. Indeed, by the power of the gift of a dwelling, even for one being reborn in existence, there is no such thing as a cramped stay in the womb;
rather, his mother’s womb becomes as spacious as a twelve-cubit inner chamber.
Having spoken thus, he delivered a vast discourse on the Dhamma, variegated by many methods.
“It wards off cold and heat, as well as wild beasts,
reptiles, mosquitoes, the chill, and even rains. Then,
when a terrible wind and sun arise, it wards them off.”
“For the sake of shelter, for the sake of comfort, to meditate, and to practice insight—
‘The gift of a dwelling to the Saṅgha is praised as supreme by the Buddha;
therefore, a wise person, seeing their own welfare, [should give it].’”
“One should have delightful monasteries built and dwell there with those who are learned;
one should give them food and drink, as well as clothing and lodgings,
with a mind full of serene confidence to those who have become upright.”
“They teach him that Dhamma which removes all suffering;
having understood that Dhamma here, he attains final Nibbāna, free from taints.
Thus, this too is a benefit of giving a dwelling place. For much of the night—indeed, for more than one and a half watches—he spoke on the benefits of giving a dwelling place.
He spoke. In that regard, these verses have been included in the collection (*saṅgaha*), but the miscellaneous teachings on the Dhamma (*pakiṇṇakadhammadesanā*) do not enter the collection.
"Having shown" (*sandassetvā*) and so forth have already had their meaning explained.
"The night has passed" (*abhikkantā*) means two watches have gone by. "Now, consider it the time for whatever [you intend]" refers to the departure.
"You should consider it time; it is time for you to go—go," this is what was said. But why did the Blessed One dismiss them?

Out of compassion. For if they were to spend the three watches of the night sitting there, illness might arise in their bodies, and it would also be necessary to find space within the Saṅgha of monks for lying down and sitting at dawn.
Thus, out of compassion for both, he urged them on. "An empty place" (*suññāgāra*) means a separate, distinct empty room;

there was no such thing [previously] there. It is said that the householders had a curtain drawn around one side of that very guest hall, prepared a proper couch, spread a proper covering upon it, and decorated it above with gold, silver stars, perfumes, garlands, and so forth.
Having tied up a canopy, they set up an oil lamp, thinking, "Perhaps the Teacher, having risen from the Dhamma-seat and wishing to rest for a short while, might lie down here;
thus this guest-house will have been used by the Blessed One in all four postures, which will lead to our welfare and happiness for a long time. The Teacher, too, at that very moment—
Having spread his outer robe there and arranged it, he lay down in the lion’s posture. It is with reference to this that it is said, “He entered an empty place.
From the place for washing his feet up to the Dhamma-seat, he proceeded; over such a distance his walking was accomplished.
Having reached the Dhamma-seat, he stood for a short while; this was his standing there. The Blessed One—
He sat on the Dhamma-seat for two watches; thus far, the sitting posture was accomplished.

Having dismissed the lay followers, he descended from the Dhamma-seat and, at the place already mentioned, assumed the lion’s posture. In this way, that place was utilized by the Blessed One through all four postures.
"Sunidha and Vassakāra" refers to the two brahmins, Sunidha and Vassakāra.
"Ministers of Magadha" means the great ministers of the King of Magadha; alternatively, they are called "great ministers" because they are endowed with great authority over the kingdom of Magadha.
"Building a city at Pāṭaligāma" means they are building a city on the site of ground designated as Pāṭaligāma. [Of] the Vajjis...
"By way of warding off" means for the purpose of cutting off the sources of income for the Licchavi kings.
"In groups of thousands" means being in groups of one thousand each. "Sites" refers to house-sites.
"Their minds incline toward constructing residences" means that the minds of the site-experts (vatthuvijjāpāṭhakā) incline toward constructing the residences of the king and the royal ministers.
It is said that by the power of their own crafts, they know within a space of thirty cubits beneath the earth: "Here is a place for catching nāgas;
here is a place for catching yakkhas; here is a place for catching bhūtas; here there is a rock or a stump.
Then, having recited their craft-mantras, they construct [the foundations] as if in consultation with the deities.
Alternatively, deities, having become intent upon their bodies, incline their minds to construct dwellings here and there.
As soon as the site is taken, they strike stakes at the four corners and vanish.
Deities of faithful families act in this way; deities of faithless families do likewise. For what reason?
For those with faith think thus: "When people here are building a residence, they will first have the Saṅgha of bhikkhus sit down and have auspicious blessings pronounced;

then we shall be able to see those possessed of virtue, hear the Dhamma talk, the answering of questions, and the expression of thanksgiving, and people, having given gifts, will offer us the merit. Those without faith...
The deities also act in such a way, thinking, "How shall we be able to see their practice and hear what they say according to our own wishes?

Regarding the phrase "by the Tāvatiṃsa [gods]": just as, based on a single wise person in a family or a single learned monk in a monastery, there arises a reputation such as, "The people in such-and-such a family are wise; the monks in such-and-such a monastery are learned."

Just as the fame of Sakka, the king of the gods, and the divine son Vissakamma has spread abroad so that they are known as "the wise Tāvatiṃsa," so too has the report spread. Therefore he said, "by the Tāvatiṃsa.
By the phrase beginning with "just as if" (seyyathāpi), he shows that Sunīdha and Vassakāra were building the city as if after consulting with the Tāvatiṃsa gods.
"To whatever extent there is a noble resort, Ānanda"— that is, to whatever extent there exists a place of refuge for noble persons;
"to whatever extent there is a marketplace"— that is, to whatever extent there exists a place for the buying and selling of goods brought by merchants,
or a dwelling place for merchants— "this is the foremost city" among those noble resorts and marketplaces.
"This city shall be the foremost, the eldest, and the preeminent. 'Puṭabhedana' means a place for opening packages of goods;
it is said to be a place for unloading bundles of merchandise.
For even goods not obtainable anywhere else in the entire Jambudīpa will be obtained here alone, and those that do not go on sale elsewhere will find their market right here."

Therefore, the meaning is that they will burst open right here. For indeed, four hundred thousand [coins] will arise there every day—four at the four gates and one in the assembly hall—and he shows that these are the natural revenues (*sabhāvāni āyāni*).
In the phrase "or from fire," etc., the word *vā* has the sense of conjunction; thus, it means "it will perish through fire, through water, and through the breaking of friendships."
This is the meaning. For one portion of it will be destroyed by fire; they will not be able to extinguish it.

One portion the Ganges will carry away. One portion will be destroyed through the mutual dissension of people who have been split apart by malicious speech—those who speak of what has not been said by this person to that person, and of what has not been said by that person to this person.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One went to the banks of the Ganges at dawn; having washed his face, he sat down, waiting for the time of the alms-round.
Sunīdha and Vassakāra also thought, "Our king is a patron of the ascetic Gotama; when we approach him, he will ask us:
'The Teacher has reportedly gone to Pāṭaligāma. Did you go to visit him, or did you not?'"
When we say, “We went there,” he will ask, “Did you invite us, or did you not invite us?
When we say, “We did not invite you,” he will find fault with us and rebuke us;
moreover, we are building this city in an improper place, for wherever the ascetic Gotama goes, ill-omened beings retreat from that spot.
Thinking, "We shall cause that city to be consecrated with auspicious rites," they approached the Teacher and invited him.
Thus it is said: "Then Sunidha and Vassakāra... and so forth.

"At the time of the forenoon" means at the hour of the morning. "Having dressed" means having put on the lower garment in the manner used for entering a village, and having fastened the waistband. "Taking bowl and robe" means having donned the upper robe and taken the bowl in his hand.
"Virtuous here" means virtuous ones in their own dwelling place. "Self-restrained" means restrained in body, speech, and mind.
"One should dedicate the offering to them" means that when the four requisites have been given to the Saṅgha, one should dedicate the merit to those household deities;
one should give the gift. "Being honored, they honor in turn": "These people are not even our kinsmen; nevertheless..."
"By not giving a share," they provide well-arranged protection; they provide excellent protection.

"Honored and honoring": being honored from time to time by the performance of offerings, [the deities] think, "These people are not even our kinsmen, yet every four, five, or six months they perform offerings for us," and thus they protect against any danger that has arisen.
They carry him away; from there they kill that man who is wise by nature. "Orasanti" means having placed [him] upon their breast and reared him;
the meaning is that they show compassion just as a mother shows compassion for her own breast-born son, striving in such a way as to remove whatever dangers have arisen for him.
"Bhadrāni passatī" means he sees beautiful things.
"Having rejoiced" means that they performed a discourse on the Dhamma by way of expressing appreciation for the merit that had been offered at that time.
Sunidha and Vassakāra, having heard the Blessed One’s words, "Whatever deities were present there, dedicate the gift to them," gave the merit to those deities.
That became known as the Gotama Gate; it was through this gate of the city that the Blessed One [entered].
He departed; that became known as the Gotama Gate. However, because he had not yet crossed over for the purpose of crossing the Ganges, it was not yet called the Gotama Ford (*gotamatittha*).
"Full" (*pūrā*) means filled. "Level with the banks" (*samatittikā*) means the water was brimful and overflowing to the very edge.
"Drinkable by crows" (*kākapeyyā*) means the water could be drunk by crows standing on the bank. By both phrases, the state of being completely full, level with both banks, is expressed.
[The Blessed One] shows [this]. A *uḷumpa* is made by joining pieces of wood together for the purpose of crossing to the other shore and driving in stakes.
A *kulla* is made by binding bamboo poles and such with creepers and the like.
"Having understood this matter" means having understood that the great multitude was entirely incapable of even crossing the water of the Ganges.
Having understood in every aspect that he and his community of monks had crossed over and stood firm upon the vast and exceedingly deep great ocean of *saṃsāra*,
he uttered this *udāna* to illuminate that meaning.
In this context, "ocean" (*aṇṇava*) refers to that which is, at its minimum extent, one *yojana* in depth and breadth.
And this is a designation for a place of water. Here, "river" (nadī) is intended in the sense of that which flows after having flowed.

This is what is meant: those who cross over the ocean of saṃsāra, so deep and vast, as well as the river of craving—having built the bridge known as the Noble Path and having cast it aside—they do not touch the marshy places, those low-lying spots filled with water; but this, however...
Desiring to cross this small amount of water, people indeed bind together a raft; they undergo the exertion of binding a raft.

But "the wise have crossed": because they are endowed with wisdom (*medhā*)—which is to say, the knowledge of the Noble Path—the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha have crossed over and established themselves on the further shore even without a raft.
The commentary on the sixth sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Dvidhāpatha Sutta (Sutta 77):
"On the seventh [sutta], 'set out upon a journey' means one who has set out and is traveling along a long road known as an *addhāna*."
"By Nāgasamāla" means by the Elder of that name. "With a junior monk as attendant" (pacchāsamaṇena): at that time, this person was the Blessed One’s attendant.
Having made him his junior monk, he set out on the road. For during the first twenty years of his enlightenment, the Blessed One’s attendants were not fixed;
thereafter, until his Parinibbāna, they remained so for twenty-five years.
The Venerable Ānanda followed like a shadow; however, this was a time when there was no fixed attendant. Therefore it is said: "with the Venerable Nāgasamāla as his junior companion.
"A forked path" means a road that has split into two. They also read it as "dvedhāpathaṃ";
the Venerable Nāgasamāla, because he had previously practiced familiarity there himself, spoke with reference to its straightness.
He said, "Venerable Blessed One, this is the path.
But the Blessed One, knowing at that time that it was fraught with danger and wishing to go by another way, said, "Nāgasamāla, this is the path.
And when it was said, "It is dangerous," he did not believe it, thinking, "The Blessed One would not [go] there..."
If one were to say, "This path is beset by dangers," that would lead to his harm and suffering for a long time; therefore, he did not say it was "beset by dangers.
After saying three times, "This is the path; let us go by this way," on the fourth occasion [the Blessed One said], "The Blessed One does not wish to go by this road;
this indeed is the direct path. Come now, let me give the Blessed One my bowl and robe, and by this..."
Thinking, "I shall go by way of the path," and being unable to give the Teacher his bowl and robe, he placed them on the ground;
yet, being urged on by the karma that leads to suffering which had arisen against him, he departed without even heeding the Blessed One’s words.
Thus it is said: "Then the Venerable Nāgasamāla [left] the Blessed One’s bowl and robe right there..."
“Having set it down on the ground, he departed. In that context, “the Blessed One’s bowl and robe” refers to the bowl and robe held in his own hands.
“Right there” means that having set them down on the ground—that is, on the earth—along that very same path, he departed.
“This is your bowl and robe; if you wish, take it,” [he said], provided that [they took] only the path they themselves desired.
The intention is that they wished to go. The Blessed One himself took his bowl and robe and set out upon the path as intended.

Regarding the phrase "robbers came out onto the road": it is said that at that time five hundred men—hunters with blood-stained hands who had become criminals against the king—had entered the forest and were making their living by robbery, intending to obstruct the king’s path.
Thinking, "We shall cut him off," they remained in the forest near the path.
Seeing the Elder traveling along that road, they thought, "This ascetic is coming by this path; he is using a path that should not be used, and he does not know of our presence.
Come now, let us make him aware. Thus, becoming angry, they emerged swiftly from their place of concealment.

Having suddenly thrown the elder to the ground, they beat him with their hands and feet, broke his clay alms-bowl, and tore his robe into pieces; yet, because he was a monk, they released him, saying, "We will not kill you;
from now on, know that this path is full of dangers. Thus it is said: "Then, venerable... [the text continues] ...they were torn asunder."
The Blessed One, knowing, "This man has gone by that path, was harassed by bandits,
and will come back this very moment after searching for me," went a short distance, left the road, and sat down at the foot of a certain tree.
When the Venerable Nāgasamāla returned and proceeded along the very path taken by the Teacher, he [saw] the Blessed One at the foot of that tree.
Having seen him, he approached, paid homage, and reported the entire situation. Therefore it is said:
“Then the Venerable Nāgasamāla... [and so on] ...opened his outer robe.

Having understood this matter—that the Venerable Nāgasamāla had disregarded his own words and set out on a path that was not secure, while he himself had set out on a secure path—he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) to illuminate that point.
In this context, "they move together" means moving in company. "Dwelling together" is a synonym for that same thing; the meaning is "dwelling together.

He should be understood as a "knower of the Vedas" (*vedagu*) in the sense of one who has gone to, or attained, the knowledge of the Noble Path of the Four Truths—which is designated as "Veda"—along with other people.
Alternatively, he is a "knower of the Vedas" because he has gone to the further shore of the entire "Veda," which is to say, all that is to be known. [He knows] his own welfare and non-welfare...
"One who does not know" means another; the meaning is "an ignorant fool. "Mixed with that other person" means mixed merely by association with that other person.
"The wise one abandons evil": by virtue of being a *vedagū* (one who has attained knowledge), the wise one—knowing—abandons what is evil, what is inauspicious, and what brings suffering upon oneself;
or else, he abandons an evil, unwholesome person. How so? Like a crane.
"Like a milk-drinker, he avoids low ground": just as a crane, when presented with milk mixed with water,
drinks only the milk without the water because it is accustomed to drinking milk alone, and thus by going to low-lying places abandons and shuns what is called "low ground"—
namely, water— so too, it is said, a wise person, even when staying together with those of poor wisdom in standing, sitting, and so forth, abandons them through his conduct.
It is never mixed at all.
The commentary on the seventh sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Visākhā Sutta.
78. Regarding the eighth [case]: "The granddaughter of Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, has passed away.
This means that the daughter—the young girl—of the son of the Great Laywoman Visākhā had died. It is said that she was perfect in her conduct and possessed deep faith in the Teaching;
she used to perform the services that ought to be done for the monks and nuns who entered the house of the Great Laywoman.
Before and after the meal, they were diligent and acted in accordance with what was pleasing to her grandmother’s mind.
Consequently, whenever Visākhā went outside the house, she would go leaving everything under her grandmother’s care;
moreover, she was beautiful and lovely to behold. Thus, she became especially dear and agreeable to her. When she was overcome by illness, she passed away.
Therefore it was said: “Now at that time, Visākhā Migāramātā’s granddaughter had died, one who was dear and pleasing to her.
Then the Great Laywoman (Mahā-upāsikā), unable to sustain the grief caused by her death, being pained and dejected, had the body disposed of, thinking:
“Perhaps when I have gone into the presence of the Teacher, I might find solace for my heart.”
She approached the Blessed One. Thus it is said: “Then Visākhā, Migāra’s mother,” and so forth.
Therein, *divā divassa* means “during the day of the day,” that is, at midday.
Knowing Visākhā’s delight in worldly existence (*vaṭṭābhirati*), the Blessed One, for the purpose of diminishing her grief by means of a skillful method, said: “Would you wish...”
He spoke the passage beginning with “Visākhā. Therein, “yāvatikā” means as many as there are. At that time, it is said, seven million people were residing in Sāvatthī.
With reference to them, the Blessed One asked: “But how many people, Visākhā, die every day in Sāvatthī?
Visākhā replied: “Ten, Bhante,” and so forth. Therein, “tīṇi” means three. This very [is the meaning].
Or this is the reading: *avivittā* means "not empty.
Then the Blessed One, making manifest his own intention, said: "Could you ever, at any time, be without washed clothes or without washed hair?
Is it not the case that, such being so, you are at all times overcome by sorrow?
[The Teacher] shows that, according to the custom of treating the death of children and others as an inauspicious occasion, one must descend into water and remain with wet clothes and wet hair.
Having heard this, the laywoman was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*);
she rejected it, saying, "Certainly not, Bhante," and reported to the Teacher the state of her mind turning away from the objects of affection due to remorse, saying: "Enough for me!"
"Venerable sir, [I have been widowed] by so many sons and grandsons," she said.
Then the Blessed One said to her: "This thing called suffering has its cause in what is dear; as many as are the things that are dear, so many are the sufferings.
Therefore, one who desires happiness and is averse to suffering should completely detach the mind from whatever is dear."
While teaching the Dhamma, he said: “For those, Visākhā, who have a hundred dear things, for them there are a hundred sorrows,” and so forth.
In this context, *sataṃ piyāni* means “a hundred objects of affection. Some read it as *sataṃ piyaṃ*.
Furthermore, since the number from one up to ten is primarily concerned with the thing being numbered, therefore: “for those... [the text continues].
The Pāḷi is handed down as: “ten dear things, ten sufferings for them,” and so forth.
However, some read it as: “for those who have ten dear things, ten are their sufferings,” and so forth; that is not good.
Since, from twenty up to one hundred, the number is always subordinate to the thing numbered, therefore even in that case, the state of being subordinate to the thing numbered [is maintained].
Having taken this up, the Pāḷi has come down as: “Visākhā, for those who have a hundred dear things, there are a hundred sufferings,” and so forth.
For all [versions], however, the reading is “for those who have even one dear thing, there is one suffering,” and not “of suffering.
For in that alternative, the Blessed One’s teaching would be of a single flavor and a single intention. Therefore, the Pāḷi should be understood according to the manner already stated.
Having understood this matter— that mental and physical suffering, such as sorrow and lamentation,
arises when there is an object of affection and does not arise when that object is absent— and having known this matter in all its aspects,
he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) which elucidates that very point.

The meaning of this is as follows: for a fool who is afflicted by calamities such as those concerning relatives, wealth, disease, conduct, or views, and who broods inwardly, there are various kinds of sorrows—whether mild, moderate, or otherwise—characterized by a burning distress of the mind;
or, for one similarly afflicted, there are lamentations characterized by verbal outpourings provoked by the burden of grief; or, for one whose body is struck by undesirable tactile objects...
Suffering, characterized by bodily affliction, or— by means of the word "or" (*vā*) in the sense of an alternative for a meaning not explicitly stated—
mental distress (*domanassa*), despair (*upāyāsa*), and so forth, are seen and found in this world of beings in many forms and various ways according to their different bases;
all of these arise depending upon, relying on, and coming into existence through a beloved being or a beloved conditioned phenomenon (*saṅkhāra*).

Taking that as a condition, they arise and are produced. However, when that aforementioned object of affection is absent, and when the desire and lust that create the state of affection have been abandoned, these [sufferings] never occur at all. For it has been said:
"From the beloved arises sorrow... from endearment arises sorrow," and so forth. Likewise: "Quarrels and disputes are born of the beloved..."
“...lamentation and sorrow along with envy,” and so forth. Here, the expression “lamentation or suffering” is stated using a shift in grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*);
it should be understood that although one ought to say “lamentations or sufferings,” the case ending has been elided.
Therefore, “they are happy, free from sorrow” means that because they lack the sorrows and so on arising from what is dear, they are [happy].
Thus they are called "happy and free from sorrow. But who are they? They are those noble ones for whom there is nothing dear anywhere in the world;

because they are entirely free from passion, in both the world of sentient beings and the world of conditioned phenomena, there exists in them no "dear thing," no state of dearness—no endearment such as "son," "brother," "sister," or "wife"—nor any state of being dear or anything that is cherished, even in the world of conditioned phenomena.
"There is no sense of 'this is mine,' nor the feeling of 'I obtain this pleasure by means of this' or 'I shall obtain it.
Therefore, one who aspires to the sorrowless and the stainless should not hold anything dear anywhere in the world.
And because those called "happy" are free from sorrow, and precisely because they are free from sorrow, there is no sense of endearment toward any object whatsoever.
Therefore, desiring Nibbāna— which is called "sorrowless" (*asoka*) because of his own absence of the aforementioned sorrow,
and "dustless" (*viraja*) because of the departure of the dust of passion and so forth, or because it is the cause for the non-existence of sorrow, passion, and the like—
[he] becomes possessed of desire through the power of wholesome desire characterized by the wish-to-act. Somewhere...
In the world, one should not form—nor should one produce—an attachment or a state of fondness even toward phenomena such as visible forms, and even toward phenomena such as serenity and insight.
For it has been said: “Bhikkhus, even phenomena are to be abandoned, let alone unwholesome things.
The commentary on the eighth sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the First Dabbasutta 79.
In the ninth [sutta], "Venerable" (*āyasmā*) is a term of affection. "Dabba" is the name of that elder. "Son of the Malla" (*Mallaputta*) means the son of the Malla king.
For that venerable one had made his aspiration at the feet of the Blessed One Padumuttara for a hundred thousand aeons.
Having accumulated a store of merit during the time of our Blessed One, he was reborn in the womb of Queen Devikā of the Malla king.
Because of his past deeds, at the age of only seven years, he approached his parents and requested ordination.
They replied, "Even if you go forth, first train in proper conduct; if you do not find delight there, you will surely return here."
They granted him permission. He approached the Teacher and requested the going forth. The Teacher, having observed his excellence in spiritual potential (*upanissaya*), granted him the going forth.
At the moment of his going forth, through the instruction given to him, the three realms of existence appeared to him as if ablaze.
Having established insight (*vipassanā*), he attained *arahantship* on the very razor’s edge. Whatever...

Having attained everything that is to be attained by a disciple—namely, the three types of higher knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*), the four analytical insights (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidah*), the six direct knowledges (*ṣaḍ abhijñāḥ*), and the nine supramundane states (*nava lokottara-dharmāḥ*)—he became one of the eighty great disciples. Indeed, it was said by that venerable one:
"When I was seven years old, I realized Arhatship; whatever is to be attained by a disciple, all that has been attained by me," and so forth.
"He approached the Blessed One" means that on a certain day, after walking for alms in Rājagaha and returning from his almsround after the meal,
that venerable one performed his duty toward the Blessed One, went to his daytime dwelling, took water from a water-jar,
washed his feet, cooled his limbs, spread out his leather mat, and sat down, setting a time limit.
Having performed [the preliminary work], he entered into meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).

Then, the Venerable One, having emerged from attainment at the predetermined time, surveyed his own life-formations (*āyusaṅkhāra*). He saw that they had been exhausted and would last for only a few moments.
He thought: "It is not fitting for me to depart without informing the Teacher and without being known by my fellow celibates."
"Right here, seated as I am, I shall attain final Nibbāna.

What if I were now to approach the Teacher, obtain his permission for my final Nibbāna, perform the duties toward the Teacher, and—demonstrating my supernormal power to show the world-protecting nature of the Dispensation—sit in the air, enter the fire-element, and attain final Nibbāna? For if this were so, those who..."
“Those who have no faith and no confidence in me—may confidence arise in them as well; that will be for their long-term welfare and happiness.
Having thought thus, that venerable one approached the Blessed One and did everything exactly in that manner.
Therefore it is said: “Then the venerable Dabba Mallaputta approached the Blessed One,” and so forth.
In this context, "The time for my final Nibbāna has arrived" shows: "The Blessed One’s time for final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue has presented itself to me;
having informed the Blessed One of that, I wish to attain final Nibbāna. However, some say:
"The Elder was neither yet old nor ill, and he asks the Teacher for permission to attain final Nibbāna—what is the reason for that?"
What is the reason? "In the past, the monks of Mettiya and Bhūmajja groundlessly accused me of an offense entailing expulsion;
even though that legal dispute had been settled, they continued to revile me. Believing them, other worldlings as well have shown me disrespect and contempt.
What purpose is there in carrying this useless burden of suffering?"
"Therefore, I shall attain final Nibbāna right now," having made this resolve, he requested permission from the Teacher.

That is not the reason. For those whose taints are destroyed do not, while their life-formations are not yet exhausted, intend, strive, or exert themselves for the sake of final Nibbāna out of fear of the reproach of others;
nor do they remain for a long time for the sake of praise and the like from others. Rather, [they remain]...
They wait for the exhaustion of their own life-formations as if with a sickle. As it is said:
"I do not long for death, nor do I long for life;
I await my time, just as a hired laborer awaits his wages."
The Blessed One, having observed his life-force (*āyusaṅkhāra*) and knowing that it was exhausted, said: "Dabba, you may now do as you think fit.
"Having ascended into the air" (*vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā*) means having gone up into the sky; "having gone into the air" is the sense.
For this is an accusative case due to its connection with the prefix *abhi*, but its meaning should be understood as a locative. Having ascended into the air, what [did he do]?

He said, "He did so," [explaining] "having sat cross-legged in the sky, in the firmament," and so forth. Therein, "having attained the fire-element" means having attained the fourth jhāna of the fire-kasiṇa.

For at that time, after the Elder had paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him three times, he stood to one side and said: "Blessed One, for a hundred thousand aeons together with you..."
"Living here and there and performing meritorious deeds, I did this with reference to this very matter;
today that purpose has reached its culmination—this is my final sight," he said.

Among those monks present there—both worldlings (*puthujjana*) and stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*)—some felt great compassion, while others were moved to tears. Then, to him...
The Blessed One, knowing the movement of Dabba’s mind, said: “In that case, Dabba, show a miracle of psychic power to me and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

Immediately, the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus assembled. Then the Venerable Dabba, having displayed all the miracles common to disciples as they are described in the sequence beginning with “being one, he becomes many,” and so forth, [concluded].
Again, having paid homage to the Blessed One, he rose up into the air; having created earth in the sky, he sat cross-legged upon it.
Having performed the preliminary work for the attainment of the fire-kasiṇa (tejokasiṇa), he entered that attainment, and emerging, he directed his attention to his own body.
Entering the attainment once more, he resolved upon the element of fire (tejodhātu) for the purpose of incinerating his body.
He attained final Nibbāna. Simultaneously with his resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*), his entire body was consumed by fire.

In an instant, that fire—like the fire at the end of an eon—extinguished itself through the power of his resolve, having incinerated everything belonging to the conditioned (*saṅkhāra*) without remainder, not even a speck of ash remaining.
Thus it is said: "Then the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta," and so forth.

"Having emerged from that, he attains final Nibbāna" means: having emerged from the consciousness of psychic power (*iddhicitta*), he attains final Nibbāna by means of the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅgacitta*).
"While burning" means while being set ablaze. "While being consumed" is a synonym for the same.

Alternatively, "while burning" is said with reference to the moment when the flames are active, whereas "while being consumed" refers to the moment when the embers have been extinguished. "Ashes" means...
"Bhasman" means ashes; "masī" means soot (kajjala). "Na paññāyittha" means it was not seen; the meaning is that by the power of his resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*), everything vanished in an instant.

But why did the Elder display this superhuman state, this miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*), when the Blessed One has indeed prohibited the performance of miracles of psychic power? This is not to be questioned.
Because performing miracles in the presence of householders had been forbidden. And that was by way of transformation (*vikubbana*), not by way of such a resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
However, this venerable one displayed the miracle only after being commanded by the Lord of Dhamma.
"Having understood this matter" means: having understood in every aspect this parinirvāṇa without clinging of the venerable Dabba Mallaputta, he uttered this *udāna* which elucidates that very point.
Therein, "the body broke up" means that the entire physical body, consisting of the fourfold continuity of the primary elements and derived matter, was broken;
it was completely consumed by fire, vanished, and entered the state of non-arising.

"Perception ceased" means that all perceptions—such as the perception of form and so forth, categorized by their respective objects like the sense-base of form—ceased through a cessation that leaves no rebirth-linking. "Feelings became cool."

"All" refers to all feelings—both resultant feelings and functional feelings—which, because they have ceased through non-relinking (appaṭisandhika-nirodha), have become cooled due to the absence of even the slightest craving for feeling.
However, wholesome and unwholesome feelings have reached cessation at the very moment of the fruit of Arahatship.
Some also read "sītirahimsu," meaning they became tranquil or ceased. They were stilled (vūpasamiṃsu).

"Formations" (*saṅkhārā*) refers to all phenomena belonging to the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), including contact and the rest, which are divided into the categories of resultant and functional;
these have especially subsided because they have ceased through non-relinking (*appaṭisandhika-nirodha*). "Consciousness has reached its end":
consciousness as well—comprising all divisions of resultant and functional—has reached, gone to, and undergone its end, destruction, and cutting off through non-relinking.

Thus the Blessed One, relying on the state of cessation through non-relinking— like a fire that has gone out due to the complete cessation of the prior defilements, volitional formations, and clinging regarding the five aggregates of the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta—
uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) released by the force of rapture.
The commentary on the ninth sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the second Dabbasutta: 80.
Regarding the tenth [sutta], "There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus": the Blessed One, having dwelt at Rājagaha for as long as he desired, [departed].
While wandering on a tour of the countryside, having arrived in due course at Sāvatthī and staying in Jeta’s Grove, he—
wishing to make manifest and show to those monks who had not personally witnessed the final passing away (parinibbāna) of the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta,
and also to those who, because of the false accusation made by Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, had lost their reverence for the Elder— [acted accordingly].
He addressed them for the purpose of generating great respect toward those elders. In this context, *tattha* (there) is a mere particle used to indicate the location of the speech.
*Khu* (indeed) is used for emphasis. By the word *tatra* (there), he illuminates the fact that the phrases "the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus" are precisely what is being spoken.
However, by the word *kho*, it is emphasized that he indeed addressed them; there was no hesitation in his addressing them.
This shows the meaning: "Was there some obstacle? Alternatively, *tatra* means "in that monastery. *Kho* is a particle used as an ornament of speech.
*Āmantesi* means "he addressed" or "he spoke. But why did the Blessed One address the bhikkhus alone?
Because they are the eldest, the most excellent, those who are near, those who are always present, and especially because they are the fit vessels for the teaching of the Dhamma.
"Bhikkhave" is a demonstration of the manner of addressing them. "Bhadante" is the response given by the addressed bhikkhus out of reverence for the Teacher.
In this context, when the Blessed One says "Bhikkhave," he addresses those bhikkhus;

when they say "Bhadante," they respond to him. Furthermore, by the word "Bhikkhave," [the Buddha] speaks with a preamble consisting of a heart made gentle and serene through the expansion of compassion.
By that word, the Blessed One causes those bhikkhus to turn away from their attention to meditation subjects, reflection on the Dhamma, and so forth, and to direct themselves toward his own face.

By the words "Venerable Sir," these bhikkhus announce their desire to listen and their state of reverence for receiving instruction, using a phrase that demonstrates respect, esteem, and veneration for the Teacher. Of the Blessed One...
"They replied" means those bhikkhus responded to the Blessed One’s words, generating a desire to hear them.

"He said this" means the Blessed One spoke this entire discourse which is now about to be recited. "Of Dabba Mallaputta, bhikkhus," and so forth, has the same meaning as what was stated in the immediately preceding sutta.
Regarding "This matter," and so on, there is nothing new; it should be understood according to the method already explained in the immediately preceding sutta.
In the verses, however, *ayoghanahatassa* means: "iron is struck by this, thus it is an iron hammer (*ayoghana*)"—namely, the iron sledgehammer and the iron mallet of smiths.
[The phrase refers to] that which is struck, beaten, by that iron hammer. Some, however, explain the meaning as:
"*Ayoghanahatassa* means struck by a mass of solid iron (*ghana-ayopiṇḍa*). Here, the word *eva* is merely a particle (*nipātamatta*). *Jalato jātavedaso* means "of the burning fire."
“Of fire”: this is a term of respect (*sāmivacana*) used here in a sense of disregard. “Of that which has gradually subsided” means of that which has been calmed, extinguished, and ceased by degrees.
“So that its destination is not known” means that its destination is not understood. This is what is meant:
[of fire] struck and crushed by a great iron hammer such as an iron fist or a spike, or [fire] contained within a bronze vessel or the like.
Just as in the case of a fire being extinguished by water, or likewise a sound that has arisen which gradually subsides and becomes completely stilled—
no destination for it is discerned anywhere in the ten directions because, through the cessation of its conditions, it has ceased without reconnection—

so too is it with those who are rightly liberated (*sammāvimutta*); that is, those who are rightly liberated by means of the cause, the method, preceded by liberation through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-vimutti*) and suppression (*vikkhambhana-vimutti*).
Because they are liberated from both the four kinds of clinging and the taints by means of the Noble Path, they are "rightly liberated.

For that very reason, having crossed over the flood of sensual desire—comprising the bonds of sense-pleasure—as well as the remaining floods such as the flood of existence, they are "crossers of the flood of the bonds of sensual desire.
Because all the agitation of the defilements has been thoroughly stilled, they are [unshaken] by the winds of the formative forces of the defilements.

And because there is no state to be designated as "this is such-and-such" among the various destinies—such as those of gods or humans—for those who have reached and attained the bliss known as *nirvāṇa* without remainder, which is characterized by the subsiding of all conditioned phenomena and is immovable due to its unshakability, it cannot be designated and is not found;
for its destination is a state of non-designation, just like the aforementioned fire. This is the meaning.
The commentary on the Tenth Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Pāṭaligāmiya Vagga is also finished.
The words of conclusion.
And to this extent:
One who has well relinquished the grasping for existence, honored by gods and dānavas,
whose stream of craving is severed, and who illuminates joy and spiritual urgency.
Delighting in the gift of the True Dhamma and bringing about the destruction of clinging,
the Guide uttered those inspired utterances (udāna) here and there.
Having brought them all together, let us compile them into a collection.
The *Udāna* was thus compiled by the Dhamma-recorders.
To elucidate its meaning, I have undertaken this commentary on the sense,
relying upon the method of the ancient commentaries.
Therein, the elucidation of the ultimate meanings as they appropriately appear in the discourses is,
by name, called the *Paramatthadīpanī*.
It has reached its completion through unconfused analysis.
From the recitation sections of the thirty-four-fold Pāḷi—
thus compiling it, whatever merit has been attained by me,
by the power of that merit, [may there be success for] the teaching of the Lord of the World.
May all embodied beings, having entered upon the practice of virtue and the other perfections and being purified thereby, partake of the essence of liberation.
May the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One endure for a long time in the world.
May all living beings always be full of reverence toward him.
May the Lord of the World, the deity, also rain down in due season;
and may he, devoted to the True Dhamma, govern the world through the Dhamma alone.
The commentary on the Udāna composed by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla,
a resident of the Badaratittha Monastery, is completed.
